summary: Research vendor-neutral system and infrastructure design for a HIPAA multi-tenant database-per-tenant .NET/Angular scheduling platform, verify every citation, and resolve five blocking design questions
logs: Researching 14 design areas blind to the current implementation, then verifying every citation
Resolving the five blocking design questions
Completeness and neutrality critique across the whole body of research

research.area: Tenancy and data architecture: multi-tenant data models, SQL Server hard limits and edition constraints on database-per-tenant, connection pooling under N databases, and the operational-attention cost of a database fleet
research.design_space: In 2026 the viable relational multi-tenant data models remain a small, well-documented set, and the published guidance from Microsoft and AWS has converged on the same axes: scale (tenant count, storage per tenant, aggregate storage, workload), tenant isolation (data and performance), per-tenant cost, development complexity, operational complexity (monitoring, schema management, restoring one tenant, disaster recovery), and customisability. At one extreme is the fully siloed stack  -  a complete application and database deployment per tenant, which AWS calls the silo model and Microsoft calls a standalone single-tenant app or a single-tenant deployment stamp; it gives the strongest isolation and the simplest security story and is explicitly rated by Microsoft as suiting "medium" scale, 1 to 100s of tenants. Next is database-per-tenant behind one shared application tier, rated by Microsoft as "high" scale, 1 to 100,000s of tenants; it keeps strong data isolation and per-tenant restore granularity while sharing the compute tier, and is the model on which platform vendors have built the most fleet-management machinery. Schema-per-tenant sits between database-per-tenant and shared schema; it is largely absent from first-party Microsoft and AWS guidance and the 2026 practitioner consensus is that it inherits the migration fan-out cost of database-per-tenant while giving up the backup, restore and relocation granularity that justifies it. Shared schema with a tenant discriminator column is the density and cost winner and, with row-level security, is the default recommendation for most B2B SaaS; Microsoft is explicit that it "necessarily sacrifices tenant isolation" and carries increased noisy-neighbour risk because the engine has no built-in way to monitor or manage per-tenant resource use inside one database. Sharded pools of shared databases extend that model to effectively unlimited scale (Microsoft: 1 to 1,000,000s) at the cost of a shard-map catalog, split/merge tooling, a mandatory tenant-identifier leading key, and materially harder single-tenant management. Hybrid or tiered models  -  most tenants pooled, some promoted to dedicated databases  -  are the mature scale-up shape and are what both Microsoft's hybrid sharded model and AWS's bridge model describe. Cutting across all of these, AWS draws a distinction that the models themselves obscure: data partitioning describes how tenant data is stored, and partitioning does not by itself achieve isolation; isolation is a separate enforcement concern, distinct from authentication and authorisation, and a user can be fully authenticated and authorised and still reach another tenant's data. Finally, the model choice is only half the decision  -  the other half is whether the platform supplies the fleet control plane (per-tenant provisioning, schema fan-out, per-tenant restore, per-tenant metrics), because every published account of database-per-tenant working at scale describes purpose-built automation as the thing that made it work.

options.name: Database-per-tenant on a single shared SQL Server instance (the current design)
options.how_it_works: One application tier resolves the tenant per request and selects a connection string; each office gets its own SQL Server database on one instance. Here the connection string is derived, not stored: the host Default connection string has its database name swapped to CaseEvaluation_{slug}, so relocating every office database to a different instance is one configuration key. Tenant schema is applied by a provisioner that calls EF Core Database.MigrateAsync(), creating the database if absent.
options.operational_cost: Setup is already paid. Ongoing: one migration fan-out per release across N+1 databases; N+1 backup chains; N+1 sets of statistics, indexes and query plans. Assumes the team can read a per-tenant schema-version report and act on drift. Realistically 3-5 hours/month at 11 offices and 6-9 at 33, dominated by release-time fan-out verification and backup checking, provided the fan-out reports per-tenant outcome. Assumes no DBA expertise beyond reading a table of tenant vs migration id.
options.why: At 11 offices growing to 33 this sits comfortably inside every published envelope: Microsoft rates database-per-tenant at 1-100,000s of tenants, the engine allows 32,767 databases per instance, and 34 databases is roughly a third of what a managed SQL Server platform such as Azure SQL Managed Instance will even permit on one instance. The decisive property for this team is the failure mode. A missing migration in one office produces an invalid-object-name exception on the next request into that office - loud, attributable, and impossible to ignore. The equivalent defect in a shared-schema model is a query that quietly returns another practice's patient. Given a two-SDE1 team with no QA and no on-call rotation, a model that fails loudly is worth more than a model that is denser. The derived connection string is also a genuine and unusual strength: it makes 'move all office data to a different SQL instance' a configuration change, which is exactly the degree of freedom the platform-selection exercise that follows this one will want.

options.name: Database-per-tenant spread across multiple SQL Server instances (a pool of single-tenant databases)
options.how_it_works: Same as above, but the tenant-to-instance mapping is data rather than a single template, so offices can be distributed across two or more instances and moved between them. Requires a catalog of tenant to connection string instead of a derived name.
options.operational_cost: Adds a catalog to maintain and back up, a move procedure, and N instances to patch, monitor and back up instead of one. Roughly doubles the surface the team must watch per additional instance. Setup 30-60 hours; ongoing at least +2-4 hours/month per extra instance.
options.why: This is the correct next step, but not yet. It becomes right when one instance can no longer hold the fleet - by storage, by buffer pool, or because one office's workload is measurably harming others. None of those is true at 33 offices of IME scheduling data, where measured business volume is 16 appointments producing ~1,450 audit rows. Adopting it now converts the system's best current property (relocate everything by changing one key) into a mapping table that must itself be correct, backed up, and consistent with reality, and it multiplies the number of things to patch at exactly the moment the team has no monitoring. Note the design is already latent: the override key App:TenantDbTemplate means moving to a per-tenant catalog later is a contained change, not a rewrite.

options.name: Shared schema with a tenant discriminator column, enforced by ORM global query filters
options.how_it_works: All offices in one database, every tenant-owned table carries a TenantId column, and the ORM appends a tenant predicate to every query. This is ABP's own default multi-tenancy mode and is what the framework does when no per-tenant connection string is configured.
options.operational_cost: Lowest steady-state operational cost of any option: one database to migrate, back up, monitor, patch and restore. Setup to migrate to it would be substantial - remapping 37 aggregate roots, re-keying data, rewriting the provisioner - call it 120-200 hours plus a data migration. Ongoing perhaps 1-2 hours/month.
options.why: The honest case is strong and I want to state it before rejecting it: it collapses the migration fan-out problem to nothing, it makes cross-office reporting a single query, it removes the entire split-schema-version hazard, it removes N backup chains, and ABP supports it natively so the framework does most of the work. It is rejected on exactly one ground, and the ground is the team constraint rather than the technology. Microsoft states plainly that a multitenant database 'necessarily sacrifices tenant isolation' and that the platform has 'no built-in way to monitor or manage the use of these resources by an individual tenant'. More important: the isolation of every row of PHI in eleven separate medical practices would then depend on a query filter being present and correct on every query path, forever, maintained by two SDE1s with no QA function. One entity mapped without the filter, one raw projection, one report that joins across the filter boundary, and a workers' compensation IME for one practice appears in another practice's list. That defect is silent, it is a HIPAA breach, and this team will not detect it. The failure mode is the disqualifier, not the density.

options.name: Shared schema with a discriminator plus SQL Server row-level security
options.how_it_works: As above, but the tenant predicate is enforced in the database by a security policy over an inline table-valued function, with the application setting tenant context via SESSION_CONTEXT after opening a pooled connection - the middle-tier pattern Microsoft documents for exactly this case.
options.operational_cost: Everything from the shared-schema option, plus a security policy and predicate function per table to author, test and keep in step with the schema; plus a strict discipline that SESSION_CONTEXT is set on every connection acquisition including background jobs. Setup adds 60-100 hours over shared schema; ongoing +1-2 hours/month and a permanent review burden on every new table.
options.why: This is the strongest version of the shared-schema case and it is a real, first-party-documented multi-tenancy mechanism - Microsoft lists 'a multitenant application can create a policy to enforce a logical separation of each tenant's data rows' as a primary use case. Two things sink it here. First, Microsoft's own multitenancy guidance says row-level security 'can be complex to design, implement, test, and maintain' and that 'many multitenant solutions don't use row-level security because of those complexities'. Second, and decisively for this system: the application connects to SQL Server as sa. RLS offers no protection against a sysadmin connection, because ALTER ANY SECURITY POLICY lets that principal disable the policy outright, and a table without a policy has no filter at all. Adopting RLS would therefore require first fixing the credential model - and once the credential model is fixed, database-per-tenant already gives a stronger boundary for less work. The new-table failure mode is also silent: forget the policy on one table and it is simply unfiltered.

options.name: Schema-per-tenant (one database, one SQL schema per office)
options.how_it_works: A single database holds N schemas, each a full copy of the tenant table set; the application sets the default schema or qualifies names per tenant.
options.operational_cost: Migration fan-out is as bad as database-per-tenant (N schemas to alter) but restore granularity is worse (restoring one office means restoring the whole database elsewhere and extracting one schema). One backup chain, one set of instance-level metrics. Setup to convert: 100-160 hours.
options.why: The honest case is that it halves the connection-pool count problem - one connection string, so one pool - while keeping tenant tables physically separate, and it makes cross-office reporting possible without cross-database queries. But it is the worst trade on the board for this system: it keeps the N-way migration fan-out that is the main operational cost of database-per-tenant while surrendering the two properties that pay for that cost - per-tenant backup and restore, and per-tenant relocation. Notably, neither Microsoft's SaaS database tenancy patterns article nor the Azure Architecture Center storage-and-data approaches article lists schema-per-tenant as a recommended pattern at all; the closest thing they discuss is table-based isolation, which is named explicitly as an antipattern. The 2026 practitioner consensus is the same: rarely the right pick. It also does nothing for the actual isolation gap, since every schema is reachable from the same connection.

options.name: Sharded multi-tenant databases with a shard-map catalog
options.how_it_works: Tenants are grouped into a small number of shared databases; a catalog maps tenant to shard; split/merge tooling moves tenants between shards; every tenant-owned table carries the tenant identifier as the leading element of its primary key.
options.operational_cost: Highest development complexity of the relational options. Requires a catalog database, a move/split/merge procedure that takes tenants offline and back online, and a re-keying of the entire data model. Setup 200+ hours. Ongoing cost is low once built, but individual-tenant management is complex - Microsoft rates operational complexity for this model as 'Low-High. Individual tenant management is complex.'
options.why: Sharding solves a problem this system does not have. Microsoft positions it for 1 to 1,000,000s of tenants; the ceiling here is 33. Building a shard map and split/merge machinery to manage 33 practices would be pure ceremony, and it would reintroduce the discriminator-column isolation model inside each shard - the same silent failure mode as shared schema - while adding a catalog that can itself become inconsistent with reality. It is the right answer at a scale this business is not pursuing and, given one doctor's practice per tenant, arguably cannot reach.

options.name: Hybrid/tiered: pooled databases for most, dedicated for some
options.how_it_works: All databases carry the tenant identifier in the schema so any database can hold one or many tenants; low-demand tenants share, high-demand or high-requirement tenants are promoted to their own database. Microsoft's hybrid sharded model; AWS's bridge model.
options.operational_cost: The union of two models' operational costs plus the promotion/demotion machinery. Setup 150-250 hours. Ongoing higher than either pure model because two shapes must both be operated and tested.
options.why: This is the mature end-state for a SaaS with heterogeneous tenants - free-trial tenants pooled, premium tenants isolated. It is wrong here because the tenant population is homogeneous by construction: one tenant is one doctor's practice, all of them paying, all of them holding PHI under the same regulatory regime, none of them a free tier. There is no axis along which to tier. Adopting a hybrid model means paying for two data models and testing both, to serve a population that has one requirement. It also weakens rather than strengthens the compliance story, because 'some offices are isolated and some are not' is a harder thing to explain to a practice than 'every office is its own database'.

options.name: Full silo: one complete stack (app, auth, database) per office
options.how_it_works: The Deployment Stamps pattern with single-tenant stamps. Each office gets its own application instance, its own auth server, its own database. No multi-tenancy logic in the application at all.
options.operational_cost: Onboarding becomes an infrastructure deployment rather than a UI action. Eleven stacks to patch, certificate-manage, deploy to and monitor, rising to 33. Even fully automated this is a substantial control plane. Setup 200+ hours to build the automation; ongoing scales linearly with offices, plausibly 1-2 hours/month per office without excellent automation.
options.why: The honest case is real: it is the strongest isolation available, it eliminates cross-tenant defects by construction, it removes the noisy-neighbour question entirely, and Microsoft notes single-tenant stamps 'don't require multitenancy logic or capabilities in the application layer'. It is rejected because it destroys the single most valuable business property this system currently has: adding an office is a host-UI action, not a deployment. AWS's own silo guidance names the cons precisely - onboarding automation becomes 'a much more heavyweight process', and decentralised management and monitoring means aggregating a fleet you now have to build a view over. For a team with one developer-week per month and no CD pipeline at all, converting office onboarding from a button into a deployment is the single most damaging change that could be made. The application is already multi-tenant; the isolation gap it has is not one that stamping would be a proportionate fix for.

research.recommendation:
Keep database-per-tenant. Do not change the tenancy model. But the reasons the team probably believes it is right are not the load-bearing ones, and the things that actually need fixing are not in the model - they are in the boundary that enforces it, the fan-out that maintains it, and the edition that will host it.

Why the model is right, stated properly. At 11 offices growing to 33, database-per-tenant sits inside every published envelope by two or three orders of magnitude: Microsoft rates the pattern at 1-100,000s of tenants, the engine permits 32,767 databases per instance, and even the most restrictive managed SQL Server platform permits 100 user databases per instance. Tenant count is not, and will not become, the binding constraint. The binding constraint is the two-SDE1 team, and against that constraint the model wins on failure mode: a missing tenant migration surfaces as an invalid-object-name exception on the next request into that office, which this team will notice within minutes. The same defect under a shared-schema discriminator model surfaces as one practice's injured worker appearing in another practice's appointment list, which this team will not notice at all. Microsoft states that a multitenant database "necessarily sacrifices tenant isolation" and that there is "no built-in way to monitor or manage the use of these resources by an individual tenant"; AWS states that partitioning data "does not ensure isolation". Database-per-tenant is the only option on the board whose isolation property survives an ordinary coding mistake, and that is worth more than density to a team with no QA function.

Now the part that matters more than the model choice. AWS's framing is the correct lens: data partitioning and tenant isolation are different things. This system has excellent partitioning and thin isolation. Every office's database is reachable from the same process, over the same sa login, and the only thing standing between an authenticated user of office A and office B's PHI is which string a C# tenant resolver returns. That resolver is one item in an ordered list that ABP populates by default with a query-string resolver at index 0. I verified in ABP's own source that the resolver chain iterates in order and breaks at the first contributor that resolves, that the ASP.NET Core module registers QueryString, Route, Header and Cookie in that order, and that ABP's own helper for domain resolution is documented as a shortcut for Insert(0, ...) rather than Add(...). If the custom HostAwareDomainTenantResolveContributor was appended rather than inserted at index 0, then a single query-string parameter selects a different office's database, and because the connection string is derived from the tenant id, the request reads that office's data. The brief records "Host header only" as intended but never tested. That test is a single curl command and it is the highest-value thing in this entire area. Do it before anything else in this document.

The four things to build, in order, all of which preserve the model:

1. Prove the resolution boundary, then pin it. Test that __tenant as query string, route value, header and cookie cannot change the resolved tenant on any of the three hostnames, and that a token minted at one office's auth server is rejected at another office's API. Then make it a permanent test, because the failure is silent and one framework upgrade can reintroduce it.

2. Break the causal chain that produces sa. The reason everything connects as sa is not laziness - it is that adding an office is a runtime action that must CREATE DATABASE, and EF Core's own guidance says database creation "typically requires a different connection, elevated permissions". Split provisioning from runtime: a provisioning identity with dbcreator that the provisioner alone holds, and a runtime identity with data rights only. This is the change that converts database-per-tenant from partitioning into isolation, and it is a prerequisite for almost every other hardening idea anyone will propose later.

3. Make the fan-out honest. The migration runner loops offices with no per-tenant error handling and no report, so one office failing mid-loop leaves the fleet on split schema versions with nobody knowing which. Three cheap, documented fixes apply directly: run `dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes` in CI for both DbContexts, which catches the "mapped an entity in the shared model configuration but only wrote a migration for one context" hazard before it ships; use idempotent scripts or a migration bundle, which EF Core documents as being for exactly the case of "deploying to multiple databases that may each be at a different migration"; and make the runner catch per office, continue, and emit a tenant-vs-applied-migration table at the end. The output of that table is the entire fleet-management practice this system needs at 33 offices - the Dynamics case study ran a million databases with two engineers, but only because they built a control plane; the proportionate version of that control plane here is one report.

4. Add Application Name={slug} to the derived per-tenant connection string. It costs one line. It makes every office's sessions attributable in sys.dm_exec_sessions without a DBA, it makes connection-pool behaviour visible, and it supplies the classification key that Resource Governor would need if per-office resource limits ever become necessary - which cannot be done from a single undifferentiated sa login.

One decision to take deliberately rather than by default: the recovery model. BACKUP and RESTORE are per database, which is the granularity this model exists to provide, but point-in-time restore requires the full recovery model plus a log-backup regime for every office database. Under simple recovery you can only restore to the end of a backup. Pick one per-office RPO consciously, and be aware of the consequence Microsoft flags explicitly: when related databases must be logically consistent, restoring one to a point in time while others stay current requires special procedures. Restoring one office to Tuesday while the host database - which holds the tenant registry and the Hangfire schema - stays at Friday is a real inconsistency, not a theoretical one.

What I am explicitly not recommending: any change to the model, any move to multiple instances, any shard map, any tiering, and any adoption of row-level security. All of them are defensible engineering and all of them would spend the team's one developer-week per month on a problem that does not exist yet, while the problem that does exist - a tenant boundary that has never been tested and a fleet nobody can see the state of - stays open.
research.operational_cost_of_recommendation:
Setup, one-off, as discrete pieces so they can be scheduled independently: proving and pinning the tenant-resolution boundary, 6-10 hours (the manual test is under an hour; making it a durable automated test across three hostnames and four resolver channels is the rest). Splitting the provisioning identity from the runtime identity, 12-20 hours - this is the largest item because it touches the provisioner, the migrator, the two DbContexts' connection configuration, and the secrets file, and because it needs a rollback plan given the provisioner currently relies on being able to CREATE DATABASE at runtime. Making the migration fan-out report per-tenant outcome and adding has-pending-model-changes to CI, 8-12 hours. Adding Application Name to the derived connection string and a per-tenant schema-version query, 2-4 hours. Choosing a recovery model per database and performing one documented, timed restore of one office database to a scratch instance, 8-12 hours - most of which is the restore rehearsal, which has never been done and should be assumed to fail the first time. Total 36-58 hours, which is one to one and a half developer-months at the stated one-developer-week-per-month allocation, and should be sequenced across two or three months rather than attempted in one.

Ongoing, at 11 offices: 3-5 hours per month. That decomposes as roughly 1-2 hours per release verifying the fan-out report shows all tenants at the same migration id, 1 hour per month reading backup outcomes and database sizes, and 1-2 hours of slack for the one office that will drift. At 33 offices: 6-9 hours per month. The growth is not linear in database count for most of the work - reading one report of 34 rows is barely harder than reading one of 12 - but it is linear for anything that requires acting per office, which is why the report must be a report and not a manual sweep.

The threshold, stated as the brief asks. This recommendation is operable at 8 or more hours per month of genuine infrastructure attention. Between roughly 4 and 8 hours per month it still works but the restore rehearsal stops happening and the recovery-model decision silently becomes whatever the default is. Below about 4 hours per month sustained, it decays in a specific and predictable way: the per-tenant schema-version report stops being read, drift accumulates unobserved across releases, and the model degrades into N databases nobody is watching - at which point database-per-tenant has all of its costs and none of its benefits, because the per-tenant restore that justifies the fan-out cost has never been tested and will not work when it is first needed. If the allocation cannot be held above 4 hours per month, the honest response is not to change the tenancy model - it is to reduce the number of things that need per-tenant attention, which means automating the fan-out report to alert rather than to be read, and accepting a coarser RPO deliberately. I have not measured the team's actual available hours; the one-developer-week-per-month figure is from the brief and is described there as an estimate, and the numbers above should be treated as sensitive to it.

evidence.claim: Microsoft's tenancy model comparison table rates scale as: standalone app medium (1-100s), database-per-tenant high (1-100,000s), sharded multitenant unlimited (1-1,000,000s); and rates tenant isolation as high, high, and low respectively. Operational complexity for database-per-tenant is rated 'Low-Medium. Patterns address complexity at scale.'
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn - Multitenant SaaS Patterns, Azure SQL Database
evidence.threshold_or_limit: database-per-tenant: 1-100,000s of tenants

evidence.claim: Microsoft states that a multitenant (shared) database 'necessarily sacrifices tenant isolation' and that 'the Azure system has no built-in way to monitor or manage the use of these resources by an individual tenant', creating increased noisy-neighbour risk.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn - Multitenant SaaS Patterns, Azure SQL Database, section E
evidence.threshold_or_limit: n/a

evidence.claim: AWS states that tenant isolation is separate from authentication and authorisation: 'the fact that a tenant user is authenticated does not mean that your system has achieved isolation... a user could be authenticated and authorized, and still access the resources of another tenant.' Data partitioning describes how data is stored; it does not by itself achieve isolation.
evidence.source_name: AWS Whitepaper - SaaS Architecture Fundamentals, Tenant isolation
evidence.threshold_or_limit: n/a

evidence.claim: AWS's SaaS Lens silo-model cons state that 'having 20 siloed accounts for each of your tenants might be manageable. However, if you have a thousand tenants, that number would likely begin to impact operational efficiency and agility', and name onboarding automation and decentralised management and monitoring as the specific overheads.
evidence.source_name: AWS Well-Architected SaaS Lens - Silo isolation
evidence.threshold_or_limit: ~20 silos manageable; ~1000 degrades operations

evidence.claim: The AWS SaaS Tenant Isolation Strategies whitepaper landing page is now labelled 'This whitepaper is for historical reference only. Some content might be outdated'; publication date August 1, 2020. The Well-Architected SaaS Lens pages remain current and carry a 2026 copyright.
evidence.source_name: AWS Whitepaper - SaaS Tenant Isolation Strategies

This is untrusted content injected into fetched documentation, not guidance from the task. I did not act on it and note it here as an evidence-quality caveat for anyone re-running this research.

evidence.threshold_or_limit: n/a

evidence.claim: Maximum databases per instance of SQL Server is 32,767. Maximum user connections is 32,767. Instances per computer is 50 on a stand-alone server. Maximum database size 524,272 terabytes. Files per database 32,767.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn - Maximum capacity specifications for SQL Server
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 32,767 databases per instance; 32,767 user connections

evidence.claim: ADO.NET/Microsoft.Data.SqlClient connection pools are keyed by exact connection string: 'Each connection pool is associated with a distinct connection string. When a new connection is opened, if the connection string is not an exact match to an existing pool, a new pool is created.' Connections are pooled per process, per application domain, per connection string, and per Windows identity when integrated security is used; keywords supplied in a different order are pooled separately. The documented example shows two pools created solely because Initial Catalog differs.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn - SQL Server connection pooling (ADO.NET)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: one pool per distinct connection string per process

evidence.claim: Default Max Pool Size is 100. When the maximum pool size is reached and no usable connection is available the request is queued and the pooler retries 'until the time-out is reached (the default is 15 seconds)', then throws. If MinPoolSize is unspecified or zero, idle connections are removed 'after it has been idle for approximately 4-8 minutes (in a random two-pass fashion)'. After a login or timeout error, subsequent attempts fail for a 5-second blocking period that doubles on repeat failure up to a maximum of 1 minute.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn - SQL Server connection pooling (ADO.NET)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Max Pool Size 100; timeout 15s; idle eviction 4-8 min; blocking period 5s doubling to 60s

evidence.claim: Microsoft documents 'Pool fragmentation due to many databases' as a named problem: opening a connection to a specific database per user or group produces 'a separate pool of connections to each database, which increase the number of connections to the server'. The documented mitigation is to connect to one database and issue a T-SQL USE statement to switch.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn - SQL Server connection pooling (ADO.NET), Pool fragmentation
evidence.threshold_or_limit: n/a

evidence.claim: Applying the documented constants to this system: at 33 offices the API process holds 34 pools (host + 33 offices) and the AuthServer holds its own separate set because pools are per process, giving a theoretical ceiling of 34 x 100 x 2 = 6,800 connections. That is far below the 32,767 user-connection limit, so connection count is not the binding constraint; connection memory and worker threads are the things to watch.
evidence.source_name: My arithmetic on Microsoft-documented constants (pool-per-connection-string, Max Pool Size 100, per-process pooling, 32,767 user connections)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 34 pools/process; 6,800 theoretical max connections; 32,767 limit

evidence.claim: SQL Server memory per user connection is approximately (3 * network_packet_size + 94 KB); default network packet size is 4 KB, giving roughly 106 KB per connection.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn - Memory Management Architecture Guide, 'Memory used by SQL Server objects specifications'
evidence.threshold_or_limit: (3 * network_packet_size + 94 KB); ~106 KB at 4 KB packets

evidence.claim: Applying that formula: 6,800 fully-populated pooled connections would consume roughly 720 MB of connection memory, about 10 percent of the configured 7,168 MB MSSQL_MEMORY_LIMIT_MB, competing with the buffer pool. This is a bound worth measuring, not a present problem.
evidence.source_name: My arithmetic on the documented per-connection memory formula and the system's stated memory cap

evidence.claim: Default max worker threads on a 64-bit machine with 4 or fewer logical CPUs is 512. A worker thread 'is assigned only to active requests and is released once the request is serviced... even if the user session/connection on which the request was made remains open.' When all worker threads are busy with long-running queries, SQL Server 'might appear unresponsive'.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn - Server configuration: max worker threads
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 512 worker threads at <=4 logical CPUs (the VM has 4 vCPU)

evidence.claim: Because idle pooled connections are evicted after 4-8 minutes and the three highest-frequency recurring jobs run every 15 minutes, each sweep will in practice find empty pools and pay a full connect, TLS handshake and login for every office database, every cycle. Connection pooling therefore provides little benefit to the fan-out jobs specifically, though it still benefits interactive traffic.
evidence.source_name: My reasoning combining the documented 4-8 minute idle eviction with the system's stated 15-minute job schedule
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 4-8 min eviction vs 15 min job interval

evidence.claim: SQL Server 2022 edition scale limits: Standard is limited to the lesser of 4 sockets or 24 cores, 128 GB buffer pool per instance, 524 PB maximum database size. Express is limited to the lesser of 1 socket or 4 cores, 1,410 MB buffer pool per instance, and 10 GB maximum relational database size. Resource Governor is Enterprise-only in 2022; Always On availability groups are Enterprise-only; Standard gets basic availability groups.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn - Editions and supported features of SQL Server 2022
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Standard: 24 cores / 128 GB buffer pool. Express: 4 cores / 1,410 MB buffer pool / 10 GB per database

evidence.claim: SQL Server Developer edition 'includes all the functionality of Enterprise edition, but is licensed for use as a development and test system, not as a production server.' Evaluation edition is 180 days.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn - Editions and supported features of SQL Server 2022
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Developer: dev/test only, not production

evidence.claim: SQL Server 2025 changes the relevant edition limits materially: Standard rises to the lesser of 4 sockets or 32 cores and a 256 GB buffer pool, Express maximum database size rises to 50 GB, Web edition is removed, and Resource Governor becomes available in Standard edition (previously Enterprise and Developer only). SQL Server 2025 reached general availability on 18 November 2025.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn - Editions and supported features of SQL Server 2025; Microsoft Learn - Resource Governor
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Standard 2025: 32 cores / 256 GB buffer pool / Resource Governor Yes. Express 2025: 50 GB per database

evidence.claim: Resource Governor - the only in-engine mechanism for limiting CPU, memory and physical I/O per workload, and thus the only in-engine noisy-neighbour control for co-located tenant databases - was available only in Enterprise and Developer editions before SQL Server 2025. It classifies sessions by attributes such as login name or program name via a classifier function.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn - Resource Governor
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Enterprise/Developer only before SQL Server 2025; Standard from 2025

evidence.claim: Basic availability groups, the only availability-group form available on SQL Server Standard edition, are limited to two replicas, no read access on the secondary, no backups on the secondary, and 'Support for one availability database'. Multiple basic availability groups may be connected to a single instance.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn - Basic availability groups for a single database
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 2 replicas, 1 database per basic AG, Standard edition only

evidence.claim: It follows that HA for 34 databases on Standard edition means 34 independent basic availability groups failing over independently - which is incompatible with a design that derives every office connection string from one server name. Instance-level failover (a failover cluster instance, two nodes on Standard) is the only shape that preserves the derived-connection-string design. This is my inference from the documented basic-AG limits and the system's stated connection-string derivation.
evidence.source_name: My reasoning from Microsoft's basic availability group limitations and the system's TenantConnectionStringProvider design
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 34 databases would require 34 basic AGs

evidence.claim: Always On availability groups impose per-database thread costs: one Log Capture thread per primary database and one Log Send thread per secondary database, with total AG threads capped at max worker threads minus 40. Microsoft has tested up to 10 availability groups and 100 databases per physical machine, stating this 'isn't a binding limit'. AG databases must use the full recovery model.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn - Availability group: prerequisites, restrictions, and recommendations
evidence.threshold_or_limit: tested to 10 AGs / 100 DBs per machine; AG threads = max worker threads - 40

evidence.claim: Azure SQL Managed Instance caps user databases at 100 per instance in General Purpose and Business Critical ('a hard limit that can't be changed'), and 500 in Next-gen General Purpose. General Purpose also caps database files at 280 per instance. This is evidence that a managed SQL Server platform can bind two to three orders of magnitude below the engine's 32,767 limit.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn - Resource limits, Azure SQL Managed Instance
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 100 user databases per instance (GP/BC); 500 (Next-gen GP); 280 database files per instance (GP)

evidence.claim: ABP's ASP.NET Core multi-tenancy module registers tenant resolvers in this order: QueryStringTenantResolveContributor (index 0), RouteTenantResolveContributor, HeaderTenantResolveContributor, CookieTenantResolveContributor - all via TenantResolvers.Add(), i.e. appended in that sequence.
evidence.source_name: ABP Framework source - AbpAspNetCoreMultiTenancyModule.cs (dev branch)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: QueryString at index 0

evidence.claim: ABP's TenantResolver iterates the configured resolvers in order and breaks at the first one that resolves: 'foreach (var tenantResolver in Options.TenantResolvers) { await tenantResolver.ResolveAsync(context); ... if (context.HasResolvedTenantOrHost()) { ... break; } }'. Later resolvers do not run and cannot override an earlier result.
evidence.source_name: ABP Framework source - TenantResolver.cs (dev branch)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: first-resolver-wins, with break

evidence.claim: HasResolvedTenantOrHost() returns 'Handled || TenantIdOrName != null', so a contributor that sets context.Handled = true stops the chain even when it resolved no tenant. ABP's stock DomainTenantResolveContributor sets Handled = true unconditionally, which is what makes a domain resolver at index 0 a hard boundary rather than a preference.
evidence.source_name: ABP Framework source and ABP issue #7968 'DomainTenantResolveContributor will affect other TenantResolveContributor'
evidence.threshold_or_limit: HasResolvedTenantOrHost() = Handled || TenantIdOrName != null

evidence.claim: ABP's AddDomainTenantResolver helper is documented as a shortcut for 'options.TenantResolvers.Insert(0, new DomainTenantResolver("{0}.mydomain.com"))' - Insert at index 0, not Add. A custom domain resolver added with .Add() would therefore run after the query-string, route, header and cookie resolvers.
evidence.source_name: ABP.IO documentation - Multi-Tenancy
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Insert(0, ...) vs Add(...)

evidence.claim: I could not verify how this system's custom HostAwareDomainTenantResolveContributor is registered (Insert(0) versus Add) or whether it sets Handled on the no-match path, because the source was not available to me. This is precisely the gap the brief records as untested, and it determines whether __tenant can override the Host header.
evidence.source_name: Attempted verification against ABP source; system source not available in this session
evidence.threshold_or_limit: n/a

evidence.claim: EF Core documents idempotent scripts as being for the case where 'you are deploying to multiple databases that may each be at a different migration' - the exact split-schema-version hazard created by a fan-out loop with no per-tenant error handling.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn - Applying migrations (EF Core)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: n/a

evidence.claim: Starting with EF Core 9, Migrate() and MigrateAsync() acquire a database-wide lock before applying migrations, and throw when the model has pending changes relative to the last migration (RelationalEventId.PendingModelChangesWarning). Microsoft recommends detecting this before deployment with 'dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes' in CI/CD.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn - Applying migrations (EF Core), Migration locking
evidence.threshold_or_limit: EF Core 9+

evidence.claim: EF Core guidance states: 'Use a separate identity for deployment that has permission to change the schema. The identity used by the application at run time should normally have only the permissions the application needs to read and write data.' It also states that migration scripts update an existing database and that 'Database creation typically requires a different connection, elevated permissions'. Separately it endorses the one-shot migration job pattern: 'run it as a one-shot deployment job after the database is healthy... don't make every application replica run migrations from its entrypoint.'
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn - Applying migrations (EF Core)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: n/a

evidence.claim: SQL Server recovery models determine restore granularity: the simple recovery model does not support transaction log backups and 'Can recover only to the end of a backup'; point-in-time restore requires the full recovery model plus complete log backups. Microsoft warns that 'If you have two or more related databases in the full recovery model that must be logically consistent, you might have to implement special procedures to ensure the recoverability of these databases.'
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn - Recovery models (SQL Server)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: simple = no PITR; full = PITR with log backups

evidence.claim: Microsoft's row-level security documentation lists multi-tenancy as a primary use case and documents the SESSION_CONTEXT middle-tier pattern for applications where tenants share one SQL login. It also warns that security policy managers with sufficient permissions can exfiltrate data via side channels, and that changing security policies should be monitored. The Azure multitenancy guidance adds that RLS 'can be complex to design, implement, test, and maintain. Many multitenant solutions don't use row-level security because of those complexities.'
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn - Row-level security; Azure Architecture Center - Storage and data approaches for multitenancy
evidence.threshold_or_limit: n/a

evidence.claim: The Azure Architecture Center names four relational multitenancy antipatterns: table-based isolation (one table set per tenant in a shared database), column-level tenant customization, manual schema changes, and version dependencies - and instructs teams to 'build tooling or an automated pipeline to deploy your schema changes' and to 'Track the schema version that you use for each tenant in a dedicated database or lookup table.'
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn - Architectural approaches for storage and data in multitenant solutions (updated 2026-08-21)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: n/a

evidence.claim: On dedicated databases per tenant, Microsoft notes: 'It's important to use automated deployment approaches when you provision databases for each tenant. Otherwise, the complexity of manually deploying and managing the databases becomes overwhelming.' On schema upgrades across a fleet: 'In a small estate of databases, you might consider using a deployment pipeline to deploy schema changes. As the number of databases increases, it might be better for your application tier to detect the schema version for a specific database and to initiate the upgrade process.'
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn - Architectural approaches for storage and data in multitenant solutions
evidence.threshold_or_limit: n/a

evidence.claim: Microsoft's own million-database case study (Dynamics 365 / Power Platform) reports that the fleet is operated by roughly two dedicated engineers - but only because the team built a custom resource-management control plane ('Spartan', an ARM resource provider automating database CRUD, pool rebalancing, backup retention and point-in-time restore) plus a separate Data Administration and Management Service for scheduled index and plan maintenance. Published 8 October 2020.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Azure SQL Dev Blog - Running 1M databases on Azure SQL for a large SaaS provider
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 1,000,000 databases, ~2 dedicated engineers, custom control plane required

evidence.claim: 45 CFR 164.316(b)(2)(i) requires: 'Retain the documentation required by paragraph (b)(1) of this section for 6 years from the date of its creation or the date when it last was in effect, whichever is later.' Paragraph (b)(1) covers policies and procedures implemented to comply with the Security Rule and written records of actions, activities or assessments the subpart requires to be documented. It does not itself set a retention period for patient medical records, which are governed by separate (largely state) requirements.
evidence.source_name: 45 CFR 164.316 (via Cornell Legal Information Institute)

As your number of tenants grows, managing a fleet of single-tenant stamps becomes more difficult.' Microsoft recommends modelling a solution as a stamp even when using a multitenant or sharded database inside it.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn - Architectural approaches for a multitenant solution
