capability_requirements.requirement: The tenant identity used to select a database MUST be derivable only from the request's host name, and MUST NOT be overridable by any request-supplied query string parameter, route value, HTTP header, or cookie.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: The connection string is derived from the tenant identifier, so overriding tenant resolution is not a display bug - it selects a different practice's PHI database. ABP's framework default places a query-string resolver at index 0 and the resolver chain stops at the first resolver that resolves, so this property is not automatic; it must be established.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: ABP source: AbpAspNetCoreMultiTenancyModule registers QueryString/Route/Header/Cookie resolvers; TenantResolver breaks at first resolution; AddDomainTenantResolver is documented as Insert(0, ...). System fact: TenantConnectionStringProvider derives the database name from the tenant.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Authenticate as a user of office A. Issue the same authenticated request four times against office A's API host, adding in turn ?__tenant=<officeB-id>, a __tenant route segment where routes allow it, a __tenant HTTP header, and a __tenant cookie. Every response must return office A's data or an error; none may return office B's data. Repeat unauthenticated against a public endpoint. Repeat against all three hostname shapes (SPA, api, auth). Then confirm the same four probes against a host name that matches no office return 'Tenant not found' rather than falling through to the query-string value.

capability_requirements.requirement: An access token issued by one office's authorisation server MUST NOT be accepted as authorisation for a request whose host resolves to a different office.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Identity is per-database and the same email can hold accounts in multiple offices; ABP also ships a current-user tenant resolver that reads the tenant from user claims. If the claim wins over the host, or if neither is cross-checked, a valid token from one practice becomes a key to another.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System facts: identity is per-database; the same email can hold a host account and an office account. ABP documentation lists CurrentUserTenantResolveContributor among the default resolvers.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Obtain a valid access token from office A's auth server. Replay it verbatim against office B's API host on an endpoint that returns tenant-scoped data. The response must be 401 or 403. Record which component rejected it (resolver, token validation, or authorisation), because a rejection that happens by accident downstream is not a boundary.

capability_requirements.requirement: The identity the application uses at run time MUST NOT hold permission to create, drop or alter databases, or to read databases belonging to other tenants; a separate identity used only for provisioning and migration MAY hold those permissions.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Database-per-tenant supplies partitioning, not isolation. With one sysadmin login shared across all offices, the only thing preventing cross-office reads is application code. Separating the identities converts the model from a naming convention into an enforced boundary, and it is the prerequisite for any later database-level control.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System fact: every service connects to SQL as sa. EF Core guidance: 'Use a separate identity for deployment that has permission to change the schema. The identity used by the application at run time should normally have only the permissions the application needs to read and write data.'
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: From the running application's own credentials, attempt CREATE DATABASE, attempt SELECT against another office's database by three-part name, and query IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin'). All three must fail or return 0. Then confirm office provisioning still succeeds end to end through the host UI, proving the provisioning identity is correctly separated rather than merely absent.

capability_requirements.requirement: The platform MUST support at least 40 databases on a single database instance today and MUST be verifiable against a stated per-instance database limit before adoption, because engine-level limits and platform-level limits differ by orders of magnitude.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: The SQL Server engine permits 32,767 databases per instance, but a managed SQL Server platform can cap at 100 user databases as a hard, unchangeable limit, and can separately cap database files at 280 per instance. A platform chosen on engine limits could be discovered to be non-viable after migration.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft: 32,767 databases per instance. Azure SQL Managed Instance: 100 user databases per instance in GP/BC, described as a hard limit that cannot be changed; 280 database files per instance in GP. System fact: 11 offices at launch, headroom to 33, plus one host database.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Read the candidate platform's published per-instance limits for (a) user databases, (b) database files, and (c) total instance storage, and record the numbers with their source URLs. Then create 40 empty databases of the tenant schema on a trial instance and confirm all 40 are online and connectable. Do not accept a vendor statement that the limit is 'the SQL Server limit' without the platform's own documented figure.

capability_requirements.requirement: Schema migration across the tenant fleet MUST record and report a per-tenant outcome, and MUST NOT abandon remaining tenants when one tenant fails.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: The current runner loops offices with no per-tenant error handling and no report, so a mid-loop failure leaves the fleet on split schema versions with no record of which offices succeeded. Split versions surface later as invalid-object-name exceptions in production for a subset of practices, and the team has no way to know which subset.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System fact: db-migrator loops offices with no per-tenant error handling and no report. Azure Architecture Center antipattern: 'Track the schema version that you use for each tenant in a dedicated database or lookup table.'
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Deliberately break one office's database (rename a table it needs, or revoke the migrator's rights on it) and run the migrator. It must complete, must apply migrations to every other office, and must emit a list naming the failed office and the reason. Then run a fleet query returning tenant slug and last applied migration id for every office plus host, and confirm the report matches reality.

capability_requirements.requirement: Continuous integration MUST fail the build when the entity model has changes not represented by a migration in either the host or the tenant DbContext.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Two DbContexts share a base and a shared model configuration, so an entity mapped in both needs a migration in both. Forgetting one produces a tenant database missing a table, which surfaces only as a runtime exception in whichever office is unlucky enough to exercise the path first. EF Core ships the detector for this at zero cost.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System fact: host and tenant DbContexts share a base and shared model configuration; forgetting a migration in one produces an invalid-object-name exception at runtime. EF Core: 'dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes' and RelationalEventId.PendingModelChangesWarning.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Add a property to an entity that is mapped in the shared model configuration, commit without generating migrations, and push. The build must fail, and the failure message must name the DbContext(s) with pending changes. Confirm the check runs for both contexts, not just one - this is the specific failure mode.

capability_requirements.requirement: Every tenant database MUST be individually restorable to a documented recovery point, and that restore MUST have been performed successfully at least once against a database of representative size.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Per-tenant restore granularity is the main operational benefit that pays for the migration fan-out cost of database-per-tenant. An untested restore is not a capability. The audit-to-business-data ratio measured at over 100:1 means restore duration is dominated by audit rows, so a restore rehearsal on an empty database proves nothing about the real one.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System facts: no restore has ever been tested; backups write to the same box and the same disk; 16 appointments produced ~1,450 audit rows and ~2,689 property-change rows. Microsoft: simple recovery model 'Can recover only to the end of a backup'; point-in-time restore requires the full recovery model.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Take a production-shaped office database, restore it to a separate instance, and record wall-clock duration and the achieved recovery point. Verify row counts on the appointment aggregate and the audit tables. Then state the recovery model in force for tenant databases and confirm it matches the RPO being claimed - if the model is simple, the claimed RPO cannot be better than the last full backup.

capability_requirements.requirement: Restoring one tenant database to an earlier point in time MUST have a documented procedure covering its relationship to the host database, which is not restored with it.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Host and tenant data are separate databases joined in memory, and the host database holds the tenant registry and the background-job schema. Rolling one office back while the host stays current produces a logically inconsistent pair, and Microsoft explicitly flags this class of problem for related databases.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System facts: two DbContexts, host (46 DbSets) and tenant (44 DbSets); no cross-database queries; host and tenant data joined in memory; Hangfire schema lives in the host database. Microsoft: 'If you have two or more related databases... that must be logically consistent, you might have to implement special procedures to ensure the recoverability of these databases.'
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Restore one office database to a point 24 hours earlier on a scratch instance while pointing it at a current host database. Enumerate what breaks: orphaned outbox rows, integration ledger entries referencing appointments that no longer exist, background jobs whose arguments name missing records. The written procedure must name each class and say what to do about it. A procedure that has not been exercised against a real restore does not satisfy this.

capability_requirements.requirement: Each tenant's database connections SHOULD be attributable to that tenant in database-side diagnostics without correlating application logs.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: With one sa login and derived connection strings, every session from every office looks identical in the engine's own views. Attribution is needed to answer 'which office is causing this' during an incident, to size connection pools, and it is the prerequisite for any future per-tenant resource governance, which classifies sessions by attributes such as login name or program name. It is a SHOULD because the system works without it; it is nearly free to add.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System fact: every service connects as sa with a derived connection string. Microsoft Resource Governor: classification assigns sessions to workload groups 'based on the attributes of the session such as login name or program name'.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Generate traffic against two different offices, then query sys.dm_exec_sessions and group by program_name (or login name). Each office must appear as a distinguishable value. Confirm the same holds for connections opened by background jobs, not only by HTTP requests - the jobs are the larger connection consumer.

capability_requirements.requirement: The per-instance buffer pool and core limits of the chosen database edition MUST be recorded as architectural constraints, and the chosen edition MUST permit production use.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Edition limits bind the whole fleet, not individual databases, and moving between editions silently removes features. The current MSSQL_PID is Developer, which includes Enterprise features but is licensed for development and test only - so the production edition will necessarily differ from the tested one, and the difference includes Resource Governor and availability groups.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System fact: MSSQL_PID is 'Developer'. Microsoft: Developer edition 'is licensed for use as a development and test system, not as a production server'. SQL Server 2022 Standard: lesser of 4 sockets or 24 cores, 128 GB buffer pool, no Resource Governor, no Always On availability groups. SQL Server 2025 Standard: 32 cores, 256 GB buffer pool, Resource Governor available.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Run SELECT SERVERPROPERTY('Edition'), SERVERPROPERTY('ProductVersion'), SERVERPROPERTY('EngineEdition') on the production instance and confirm the edition is licensed for production. Then, for that exact edition and version, list from vendor documentation the maximum buffer pool per instance, maximum cores, and whether Resource Governor, Transparent Data Encryption, backup compression and availability groups are present. Compare that list against what the staging or development instance actually has - any feature present in one and absent in the other is a latent production surprise.

capability_requirements.requirement: If the fleet is co-located on one database instance, the platform MUST provide either a mechanism to limit one tenant's resource consumption, or an explicit written acceptance that no such mechanism exists.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Database-per-tenant isolates data but not performance when the databases share an instance. The only in-engine control is Resource Governor, which before SQL Server 2025 required Enterprise or Developer edition. A team that moves from Developer to Standard on SQL Server 2022 loses this capability without any error message.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft Resource Governor: available in Enterprise and Developer only before SQL Server 2025; available in Standard from SQL Server 2025. System facts: one SQL Server container hosting all databases; MSSQL_PID Developer; 4 vCPU / 16 GB VM.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Query SERVERPROPERTY('IsResourceGovernorEnabled') or attempt CREATE RESOURCE POOL on the production edition. If it fails, the answer is 'no mechanism exists' and that must be written down as an accepted risk with the reasoning, not left implicit. If it succeeds, confirm a classifier function can distinguish offices - which requires the per-tenant connection attribution requirement above to be satisfied first.

capability_requirements.requirement: High availability for the tenant fleet, if adopted, MUST fail over all tenant databases together, or the tenant-to-database-location mapping MUST become data rather than a derived template.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Every office connection string is derived by substituting the database name into one server address. Per-database replication on SQL Server Standard means one basic availability group per database, each failing over independently - after a partial failover, some offices live on a different server than the template names, and those offices break. The design's best property and per-database HA are mutually exclusive.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft: basic availability groups are 'Support for one availability database', two replicas, Standard edition only; Always On availability groups are Enterprise-only. System fact: TenantConnectionStringProvider swaps the database name in a single template, so all offices resolve to one server address.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: On a test fleet of three tenant databases behind whatever HA mechanism is proposed, fail over exactly one database and leave the others on the original node. Then make a request to each of the three offices. If any office returns a connection error, the mechanism has per-database granularity that the connection-string design cannot express, and either the mechanism or the design must change. Repeat with a whole-instance failover; all three must recover without configuration changes.

capability_requirements.requirement: Provisioning a new tenant MUST be idempotent and MUST leave no partially-created tenant on failure that blocks a retry.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Adding an office is a host-UI action performed by staff, not a deployment performed by an engineer. It crosses two databases non-atomically - a registry row in the host database and a new database with schema, catalogues, an admin user and a doctor - with no distributed transaction available and no message broker. Retry must be the recovery path because there is no operator to reconcile by hand.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System facts: IOfficeDatabaseProvisioner.ProvisionAsync is stated to be idempotent so retry after partial failure completes; adding an office is a host-UI action; no cross-database queries and no distributed transactions.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Provision an office and interrupt it at three points: after the host registry row but before database creation, after database creation but before catalogue seeding, and after seeding but before the doctor record. In each case re-run provisioning from the UI with the same slug. All three must complete successfully and produce one correct office - not a duplicate, not an error that requires manual cleanup. Then provision an office whose slug already exists and confirm the behaviour is a clear rejection, not a partial overwrite.

capability_requirements.requirement: Audit and change-tracking data retention SHOULD be configurable per tenant and SHOULD be enforced by a scheduled process, because audit volume rather than business volume determines per-tenant database size and restore time.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Measured audit volume exceeds business data by more than 100 to 1 and nothing prunes it. Under database-per-tenant this compounds per office and directly lengthens the per-tenant restore that the model exists to provide. It is a SHOULD rather than a MUST because the correct retention period is a legal and business decision this analysis cannot make - but the absence of any mechanism is not a decision.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System facts: 16 appointments produced ~1,450 audit-log rows and ~2,689 entity property-change rows in one office database; audit retention is unconfigured and nothing prunes it; ~9.7 GB free disk. 45 CFR 164.316(b)(2)(i) sets a six-year retention for Security Rule documentation, which is a floor for some of this data but not a ceiling for all of it.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Query row counts and reserved size for the audit log and entity property-change tables in each tenant database and express audit size as a fraction of total database size. Then confirm a retention setting exists, that it can differ per tenant, and that a scheduled job actually removes rows older than the configured window - verified by observing row counts fall after the job runs, not by the job's existence. Separately confirm that the retention floor chosen is documented against the specific regulatory obligation it satisfies, distinguishing Security Rule documentation retention from medical record retention, which is governed separately.

anti_requirements: The platform MUST NOT rewrite, normalise, or strip the HTTP Host header before it reaches the application, and MUST NOT collapse distinct host names to a single backend address, because tenancy - and therefore which practice's PHI database is opened - is resolved from that header alone. Any load balancer, proxy, CDN or ingress in the path must be tested for this specific behaviour before adoption, not assumed.

The platform MUST NOT require a single shared database for all tenants, or impose a per-instance database count so low that 40 databases is infeasible. This eliminates any managed offering priced or shaped around one database per application.

The platform MUST NOT require the application's runtime credential to hold database-creation rights in order for tenant onboarding to work. If onboarding can only be automated by giving the running application elevated rights, the platform has forced the isolation weakness that this analysis identifies as the primary one.

The platform MUST NOT make per-tenant restore impossible or coarser than per-database. A backup mechanism that can only restore a whole instance or a whole storage volume removes the principal benefit of database-per-tenant while leaving all of its costs.

Tenant isolation MUST NOT be implemented solely as an ORM-level global query filter, a base-class convention, or any other mechanism that is silently absent when a developer writes a new query path. Isolation must fail loudly on the paths that lack it.

The platform MUST NOT require the tenant fleet to be modelled as one availability database per replication unit if the tenant-to-server mapping remains a derived template, because independent per-database failover makes the template wrong for the databases that moved.

The application MUST NOT be changed to reach across tenant database boundaries with cross-database queries, three-part names, or linked servers in order to satisfy reporting needs. The current absence of these is a verified property worth protecting; introducing them would couple every office's availability to every other office's and would defeat the relocation freedom the derived connection string provides.

Tenant onboarding MUST NOT become a deployment. Any design that requires an engineer, a pipeline run, DNS provisioning by hand, or a certificate request in order to add an office has removed the system's most valuable operational property and should be rejected on that ground alone.

The platform MUST NOT silently substitute a database edition with different feature availability between environments. A staging instance with Enterprise or Developer features and a production instance on Standard is a configuration that fails only in production and only under load.
surprises: Database-per-tenant does not, by itself, give you tenant isolation - and AWS says so in writing. 'Data partitioning describes how tenant data is stored, but partitioning data does not ensure isolation', and isolation is separate from authentication and authorisation: 'a user could be authenticated and authorized, and still access the resources of another tenant.' Because every office database is reachable from one process over one sa login and the connection string is derived from the tenant id, the entire isolation boundary for eleven medical practices is one C# resolver returning the right string. The strongest-looking partitioning model on the board is currently protecting PHI with the weakest available enforcement mechanism.

ABP's default resolver order almost certainly makes the untested caveat real, and the test takes thirty seconds. I verified in ABP's source that the resolver chain iterates in order and breaks at the first contributor that resolves (HasResolvedTenantOrHost() returns Handled || TenantIdOrName != null), that the ASP.NET Core module registers QueryStringTenantResolveContributor at index 0 followed by Route, Header and Cookie, and that ABP's own AddDomainTenantResolver helper is documented as a shortcut for TenantResolvers.Insert(0, ...) - Insert, not Add. If the custom HostAwareDomainTenantResolveContributor was registered with the natural .Add(...) call, ?__tenant= wins over the Host header on every request, and since the connection string is derived from the tenant id, that reads another practice's database. ABP issue #7968 documents that this resolver interaction is a real, reported behaviour. Nobody needs to reason about this - one curl command settles it.

Moving off Developer edition to Standard silently deletes capabilities, and one of them is the only noisy-neighbour control that exists. MSSQL_PID is Developer, which carries all Enterprise features but is licensed for development and test only, so production must run a different edition. On SQL Server 2022, Standard has no Resource Governor at all - it was Enterprise and Developer only until SQL Server 2025 - and no Always On availability groups. Nothing errors when you make this change; features simply stop being available and workloads that were being governed stop being governed. The version choice is therefore load-bearing in a way that looks like a patching decision: SQL Server 2025 Standard has Resource Governor and a 256 GB buffer pool, SQL Server 2022 Standard has neither Resource Governor nor more than 128 GB.

The derived connection string and per-database high availability are mutually exclusive, and the derivation is the thing worth keeping. On Standard edition the only availability-group form is a basic availability group, which supports exactly one availability database, two replicas, no readable secondary and no backups on the secondary. Thirty-four databases means thirty-four basic availability groups failing over independently. But every office resolves to one server address with the database name substituted in - so after a partial failover, the offices that moved are unreachable and the ones that did not are fine, which is close to the worst possible failure shape. The correct conclusion is not to abandon the derivation; it is that HA for this fleet must be instance-level (shared-storage failover), because that is the only granularity the design can express.

Connection pooling gives the recurring jobs almost nothing, for a documented reason nobody would look for. Pools evict idle connections after approximately 4-8 minutes when MinPoolSize is zero. The three highest-frequency recurring jobs run every 15 minutes. The interval is longer than the eviction window, so every sweep finds empty pools and pays a fresh TCP connect, TLS handshake and login for every office database, every cycle - at 33 offices that is roughly 400 fresh logins per hour that the team believes are pooled. Worse, the pool blocking period means one office's transient failure poisons that office's pool for 5 seconds, doubling to a minute on repeat - so a single sick office database can make its own sweeps fail for far longer than the underlying fault lasts.

Express edition's binding limit is not the one everyone quotes. The famous number is the 10 GB maximum database size (50 GB from SQL Server 2025), and under database-per-tenant that looks generous because it applies per database - 33 offices could hold 330 GB. The limit that actually binds is the 1,410 MB maximum buffer pool per instance, which is shared across all 34 databases regardless of how many there are. Thirty-four working sets competing for 1.4 GB of cache is a very different proposition from one, and it is invisible in any per-database sizing exercise. Express is disqualified by a per-instance number, not a per-database one.

Restoring one office to yesterday breaks its relationship with the host database, and Microsoft flags exactly this. Host and tenant are separate databases joined in memory, and the host database holds the tenant registry and the Hangfire schema. Microsoft's recovery-model documentation warns that related databases that must be logically consistent 'might require special procedures to ensure recoverability'. Restore one office to Tuesday and you have integration outbox rows, notification outbox rows and queued job arguments in the host database referencing appointments in that office that no longer exist. The per-tenant restore that justifies this whole model has a cross-database consistency problem that has never been thought about.

Microsoft's own documented fix for the pool-per-database problem cannot be used here. The connection-pooling documentation names 'Pool fragmentation due to many databases' as a known problem and prescribes connecting to one database and issuing a T-SQL USE statement to switch. That mitigation is fundamentally incompatible with EF Core and ABP, which express tenancy as the connection string's Initial Catalog. So the pool multiplication is a cost this architecture must simply accept and size for, not a defect to fix - which is worth knowing before someone finds the Microsoft page and tries to act on it.

A managed SQL Server platform can cap databases per instance at 100 - three hundred times below the engine limit. The engine allows 32,767 databases per instance. Azure SQL Managed Instance allows 100 user databases in General Purpose and Business Critical and describes it as a hard limit that cannot be changed, plus a separate cap of 280 database files per instance. Thirty-four databases fits comfortably, but the lesson generalises: when the platform exercise runs, the number to check is the platform's own documented database-per-instance figure, and 'it's SQL Server, so 32,767' is the wrong answer.

The sa credential is a consequence, not a shortcut. Adding an office is a runtime action that must CREATE DATABASE, and EF Core's guidance states that database creation 'typically requires a different connection, elevated permissions'. That is the causal chain: office-onboarding-as-a-UI-action forces runtime database creation, which forces a high-privilege login in the running application, which produces sa. Anyone who treats sa as sloppiness will fix it and break onboarding. The fix is to split the provisioning identity from the runtime identity, keeping both properties.

The check that catches the two-DbContext migration hazard already ships with EF Core and costs nothing. The stated risk is that an entity mapped in the shared model configuration gets a migration in one DbContext and not the other, producing an office database missing a table. EF Core 9 and later throw when the model has pending changes relative to the last migration, and Microsoft explicitly recommends detecting it before deployment with 'dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes' in the CI pipeline. This is one line in CI against a hazard the brief describes as producing runtime invalid-object-name exceptions.

The six-year retention citation in the brief is close but not exact, and the distinction matters for sizing. 45 CFR 164.316(b)(2)(i) requires retention for six years of the documentation required by paragraph (b)(1) - the policies and procedures implemented to comply with the Security Rule, and written records of actions, activities or assessments that the subpart requires to be documented. It is not a retention rule for patient medical records, which are governed separately and largely by state law. Audit logs plausibly fall under it as records of required activity, but the two classes have different retention drivers and should be sized and pruned separately rather than all held for six years by default - especially given that audit data already outweighs business data by more than 100 to 1 on a disk with 9.7 GB free.

Microsoft ran a million databases with two engineers - and the number that matters is what they built first. The Dynamics 365 case study is the standard citation for database-per-tenant scaling, and it does report roughly two dedicated engineers. But it reports them operating a purpose-built control plane ('Spartan') that automates database CRUD, pool rebalancing, backup retention and point-in-time restore, plus a second service for scheduled index and plan maintenance. The transferable lesson at 33 offices is not that database-per-tenant is free; it is that the fleet becomes tractable exactly when you stop operating databases and start operating one report about them - and that the proportionate version of Spartan here is a table of tenant slug versus applied migration id.

not_recommended.pattern: Migrate to a shared schema with a TenantId discriminator column (ABP's own default multi-tenancy mode)
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: This is the mainstream 2026 default for B2B SaaS and the case is genuinely strong. It reduces the fleet to one database: one migration, one backup chain, one set of statistics and plans, one thing to monitor, one thing to patch, one thing to restore. It eliminates the split-schema-version hazard entirely, eliminates connection-pool multiplication, makes cross-office reporting a single query rather than an in-memory join, and it is natively supported by the framework already in use, so the machinery exists. The team's largest recurring operational cost - migration fan-out across N databases - would simply cease to exist. And there is a window: there is no real patient data yet, so the data migration is essentially free today and will never be this cheap again.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: The failure mode disqualifies it, and the brief names the criterion: prefer designs that fail obviously over designs that fail subtly. Under this model, the isolation of every practice's PHI depends on a tenant predicate being present and correct on every query path, permanently, maintained by two SDE1s with no QA function, no code review depth beyond each other, and no monitoring that could detect a leak after the fact. One entity mapped without the filter, one projection that bypasses the ORM, one report joining across the boundary - and one workers' compensation claimant's IME appears in a different doctor's practice. That event is silent, it is a reportable HIPAA breach, and this team has no mechanism that would surface it. Microsoft's own guidance says the shared model 'necessarily sacrifices tenant isolation'. The density and simplicity are real gains, but they are gains in a currency this team can afford to spend, purchased with a risk in a currency it cannot.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: When the tenant population changes character - many more, much smaller, lower-sensitivity tenants where per-tenant restore and physical separation stop being worth their cost. Or when the team acquires the capacity to make the boundary enforceable and observable rather than conventional: a dedicated QA function, automated cross-tenant leakage testing on every build, and a database-level control (row-level security over a least-privilege login, not sa) that fails closed on tables where someone forgot. If tenant count ever approached the low thousands, the fan-out cost would dominate and this would become the right answer.

not_recommended.pattern: Schema-per-tenant: one database, one SQL schema per office
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It is the obvious middle path and it does solve one real problem: a single connection string means a single ADO.NET connection pool instead of one per office, which removes the documented pool-fragmentation-by-database effect and the connect-per-sweep cost of the recurring jobs. It keeps each office's tables physically distinct, so a query cannot accidentally return two offices' rows the way a missing discriminator predicate can. And it makes cross-office reporting possible inside one database without cross-database queries.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It is the worst trade available here because it keeps the cost and discards the benefit. The migration fan-out is identical - N schemas to alter per release, with the same partial-failure and drift hazards - while the two properties that pay for that fan-out are surrendered: per-tenant backup and restore granularity (restoring one office now means restoring the entire database elsewhere and extracting one schema), and per-tenant relocation (the derived connection string that lets office databases move instances by changing one key stops being expressible). It is also notable that neither of Microsoft's two relevant guidance articles lists schema-per-tenant as a pattern at all; the nearest thing they discuss, per-tenant table sets inside one database, is named explicitly as an antipattern. And it does nothing whatsoever about the actual isolation gap, because every schema remains reachable over the same connection.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: Effectively never for this system. It would only make sense if connection-pool count became a hard binding constraint - which would require tenant counts in the high hundreds - while per-tenant restore and per-tenant relocation had simultaneously stopped mattering. Those conditions do not co-occur in a PHI-bearing product.

not_recommended.pattern: Build a shard map catalog with split/merge tooling ahead of growth
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: Microsoft ships tooling for it, positions sharded multi-tenant databases as the unlimited-scale option, and the guidance is right that switching tenancy models later 'is sometimes costly'. Building the catalog now, while there are only two databases in existence and no real data, is cheaper than retrofitting it at 33 offices with live PHI. Getting the tenant identifier into the leading position of every primary key is a schema decision that is nearly free today and expensive forever after.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It solves a scale problem that this business is structurally unable to reach. One tenant is one doctor's practice; the stated ceiling is 33; Microsoft positions sharding at 1 to 1,000,000s of tenants. Building shard maps, split and merge procedures and an offline/online tenant-move protocol for 33 practices is ceremony, and it would consume many months of a one-developer-week-per-month budget. It would also reintroduce the discriminator-column model inside each shard - the same silent cross-tenant failure mode rejected above - and add a catalog that can itself drift out of agreement with reality, which is a new class of subtle failure this team is not equipped to detect. The premise that switching later is prohibitive is also weaker here than it looks: the connection string is already derived through an override key, so moving from a derived template to a per-tenant catalog is a contained change when it is actually needed.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: If the product changed shape so that a tenant were a payer, an employer group, or a law firm rather than a single doctor's practice, taking the plausible ceiling into the thousands. Or if per-office data volume grew such that one instance could no longer hold the fleet - at which point the first step is still a per-tenant connection catalog, not a shard map with split/merge.

not_recommended.pattern: Give each office its own SQL Server instance or its own database container
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It is the cleanest possible isolation story to explain to a medical practice and to an auditor: your data is not merely in its own database, it is in its own engine, with its own credentials, its own memory, its own failure domain. It removes noisy neighbours by construction. It removes the per-instance edition ceilings from the conversation - the 128 GB Standard buffer pool that is shared across 34 databases becomes 34 separate allocations. And it makes per-tenant resource limits trivially achievable without Resource Governor or any Enterprise feature.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: The resource arithmetic alone kills it: the current VM is 4 vCPU and 16 GB with roughly 9.7 GB free disk, and SQL Server instances do not share memory with each other, so eleven instances would each need their own floor allocation. Beyond that, it multiplies by eleven, then thirty-three, every operational surface this team already cannot see - patching, backup verification, log inspection, certificate management - at a moment when there is no monitoring, no alerting, no metrics and no aggregation of any kind. AWS's silo guidance names this exactly: decentralised management and monitoring is the cost, and 'the effort and energy needed to build and manage this experience is more complex in a siloed model'. A team that cannot currently observe one database will not observe thirty-three engines. It would also break the single most valuable property the system has, since adding an office would become an infrastructure provisioning act rather than a UI action.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: If a specific practice contractually required physical or cryptographic separation that a separate database cannot satisfy - its own encryption keys, its own residency, its own retention regime. Microsoft's guidance points at exactly this trigger for isolating a tenant. In that case the right response is a hybrid: one instance for the fleet plus a dedicated instance for that single practice, not thirty-three instances.

not_recommended.pattern: Adopt row-level security now as defence in depth on top of database-per-tenant
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: Defence in depth is a sound instinct and RLS is the textbook second layer: it moves the access restriction into the database tier where, as Microsoft puts it, 'the database system applies the access restrictions every time that data access is attempted from any tier'. If the tenant resolver were ever wrong, a database-side predicate would catch it. Microsoft documents the exact middle-tier pattern for applications that share one SQL login, using SESSION_CONTEXT.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It provides zero protection in this system's current configuration and would create a false sense of security, which is worse than no protection. The application connects as sa. A sysadmin principal holds ALTER ANY SECURITY POLICY and can disable any policy outright, and a table with no policy has no filter at all. Layering RLS over a sysadmin connection is a lock on a door with no wall. There is also a sequencing point: RLS is per-row within a database, but this system's tenant boundary is the database itself, so the predicate would be enforcing something the connection has already decided. Fix the credential model first, and once that is done, the database boundary is already stronger than what RLS would add. Microsoft's own multitenancy guidance notes RLS 'can be complex to design, implement, test, and maintain' and that many multitenant solutions skip it for that reason.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: If the tenancy model ever moves to shared schema, RLS over a least-privilege login stops being optional and becomes the primary enforcement mechanism. It would also become worthwhile within database-per-tenant if a single database ever came to hold more than one office - for example a consolidation of small practices under one legal entity.

not_recommended.pattern: Introduce cross-database queries, three-part names or linked servers to serve reporting that spans host and tenant data
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: Host and tenant data are currently joined in memory, which is inefficient, awkward to write and does not scale to real reporting. A cross-database join is one line of SQL and would immediately make fleet-wide questions - how many appointments across all offices, which offices are behind on packet assembly - answerable in one query instead of an application-level fan-out. As the office count triples, the in-memory join gets three times worse.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: The verified absence of raw SQL, cross-database queries, three-part names and linked servers anywhere in the source is one of this system's most valuable structural properties and it should be defended, not traded away for reporting convenience. Introducing cross-database references couples every office's availability to the availability of every other database named in a query, converts a single office's restore or relocation into a fleet-wide compatibility question, and destroys the property that makes the derived connection string powerful - that an office database can move to a different SQL instance by changing one configuration key. A three-part name hard-codes the assumption that everything lives on one instance, at exactly the moment the architecture is trying to preserve the option that it might not. The maximum-capacity documentation also notes a stored procedure accessing more than 64 databases, or more than two in interleaving, errors - a limit nobody would anticipate.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: Never inside the transactional path. If cross-office reporting becomes a genuine product requirement, the correct answer is the one Microsoft's guidance gives: 'have each tenant's applications publish data to a centralized data warehouse' - a separate read model fed by the existing outbox pattern, which the system already has the machinery for. That keeps the transactional databases independent and puts the coupling somewhere failure is tolerable.

not_recommended.pattern: Consolidate the host and tenant DbContexts into one to eliminate the double-migration hazard
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: The stated hazard is concrete and unpleasant: two DbContexts share a base and a shared model configuration, so an entity mapped in both needs a migration in both, and forgetting one produces an office database missing a table that surfaces as a runtime invalid-object-name exception. Ninety migrations on one context and fifteen on the other is a lot of divergence to keep in step by discipline. Collapsing to one context makes the hazard structurally impossible.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: The two contexts exist because the two databases genuinely have different shapes - 46 DbSets against 44 - and the difference is not accidental: host-scoped concerns such as the tenant registry and the Hangfire schema belong only in the host database, and merging them would either push host tables into every office database or push office tables into the host. Both outcomes are worse than the problem being solved. More importantly the hazard has a cheaper, more precise fix that already exists: EF Core 9 and later throw when a model has pending changes relative to its last migration, and Microsoft recommends catching this in CI with 'dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes'. That converts a runtime production failure in one office into a build failure, which is exactly the trade this team should be making, for roughly one line of pipeline configuration against a schema restructuring measured in weeks.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: If the host and tenant schemas converged to near-identical - if the host database stopped holding host-only concerns - the separation would be paying for nothing. That is not the current trajectory, and the Hangfire schema living in the host database makes it unlikely.

not_recommended.pattern: Build a full per-tenant monitoring and metrics stack before hardening the tenant boundary
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: There is no observability at all today - console and file logging, health-check history that does not survive a restart, no metrics, no alerting, no uptime monitoring. Under database-per-tenant the monitoring problem genuinely multiplies: N databases to watch instead of one, and both Microsoft and AWS name decentralised monitoring as the defining operational cost of the isolated model. Building per-tenant dashboards first would make every subsequent change measurable rather than hopeful, and it is the standard order of operations at a larger organisation.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It inverts the priority given a fixed and small budget. Monitoring tells you when something is going wrong; it does not tell you whether an untested tenant boundary is already open, and it will not detect a cross-tenant read that the application considers a normal successful request. The single highest-value action in this area costs under an hour and produces a definite answer: probe whether __tenant overrides the Host header. Behind it, splitting the provisioning identity from the runtime identity closes the structural gap. Both must come before dashboards, because a monitored system with an open tenant boundary is a system that will observe its own breach in high resolution. There is also a sequencing trap specific to this system: PII logging is enabled by default, so logs cannot currently leave the machine without carrying PHI - meaning any aggregation work must be preceded by log redaction anyway, which is a separate exercise.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: Immediately after the boundary is proven and the credential model is split. At that point the per-tenant schema-version report and per-tenant database size and backup-outcome tracking are the highest-value observability to build - they are the minimum control plane that makes a database fleet tractable, and they are far cheaper than a general metrics platform.

what_would_change_the_answer: The result of the __tenant override test. If a query-string, header, route or cookie parameter can change the resolved tenant, this stops being an architecture question and becomes an incident: the isolation boundary is open today, and the fix must land before any real practice takes a real booking. Everything else in this analysis is subordinate to that one probe.

Tenant count rising materially past the stated 33 ceiling. Database-per-tenant remains viable to Microsoft's rated 1-100,000s, but the practical inflection for a two-person team is far lower - somewhere around 100 to 150 databases, where reading a fan-out report stops being a glance and per-tenant restore rehearsal stops fitting in a month. Past that, a per-tenant connection catalog and multiple instances become necessary, and past a few hundred the shared-schema economics start to dominate.

A single practice acquiring a requirement that a shared instance cannot satisfy: its own encryption keys, its own data residency, its own retention schedule, or a contractual demand for physical separation. Microsoft names exactly these as the triggers for isolating a tenant. That points to a hybrid - the fleet on one instance plus one dedicated deployment - not to a fleet-wide model change.

Cross-office reporting becoming a first-class product feature rather than an occasional internal question. Today the in-memory join across host and tenant data is tolerable. If the business needs fleet-wide analytics, the answer is a separate read model fed from the existing outbox ledgers - not cross-database queries - and that changes the data architecture materially without changing the tenancy model.

The arrival of real PHI. Every recommendation here is shaped by the fact that the migration window is open and free. Once real practices take real bookings, the cost of any structural change to the data model multiplies, per-tenant restore stops being a rehearsal and becomes an obligation, and the risk calculus on an untested tenant boundary changes from 'urgent' to 'unacceptable'.

The database edition and version actually chosen for production. SQL Server 2022 Standard has no Resource Governor and no Always On availability groups; SQL Server 2025 Standard has Resource Governor and a 256 GB buffer pool. If the fleet lands on 2022 Standard, per-tenant resource limiting is off the table entirely and noisy-neighbour management becomes an application-tier problem. That single choice changes what the platform must supply.

The team's actual sustained infrastructure capacity. The one-developer-week-per-month figure is an estimate the brief itself flags as unmeasured, and a separate remediation exercise has already claimed much of it. Below roughly four hours per month, the fleet report goes unread and drift accumulates unobserved - at which point the honest response is to automate the report into an alert and accept a coarser RPO deliberately, rather than to keep a practice on the books that is not happening.

Any managed platform's documented database-per-instance limit. The engine allows 32,767; a managed SQL Server platform can hard-cap at 100. If a candidate platform caps below about 60 databases, the headroom-to-33 plan has no room for the host database, staging copies, or restore targets, and either the platform or the model must change.

Whether instance-level failover is available. If the only HA on offer is per-database replication, the derived connection string cannot survive a partial failover and the tenant-to-location mapping must become data. That is a real change to the design's best property and should be a conscious trade, not a consequence discovered during the first failover.

Audit data growth against available disk. At over 100 audit rows per business row and nothing pruning them, on a disk with roughly 9.7 GB free, the per-tenant sizing story is driven entirely by audit retention. If the retention decision lands on six years for everything, per-office database size and per-office restore duration become the dominant operational facts of this architecture, and the sizing conversation changes completely.

material_errors: CLAIM 24 IS WRONG ON ITS STATED THRESHOLD. QueryStringTenantResolveContributor is NOT at index 0 of the composed resolver chain. AbpAspNetCoreMultiTenancyModule depends on AbpMultiTenancyModule, whose ConfigureServices runs first and executes `options.TenantResolvers.Insert(0, new CurrentUserTenantResolveContributor())`. In the assembled AbpTenantResolveOptions, index 0 is CurrentUserTenantResolveContributor (which reads the tenant from the CURRENT USER'S TOKEN CLAIMS), and QueryString/Route/Header/Cookie occupy indices 1-4. This is material, not cosmetic: the first two capability requirements demand that tenant identity be derivable only from the host name and that a token from one office not authorise a request for another. The resolver that actually runs first reads the access token, before any domain resolver. Any design conclusion built on 'the domain resolver only has to beat the query-string resolver' is unsound.

CLAIM 27 IS WRONG AND ITS QUOTATION IS NOT ON THE CITED PAGE. The ABP docs page at abp.io/docs/latest/framework/architecture/multi-tenancy shows only `options.AddDomainTenantResolver("{0}.mydomain.com");` and never describes it as a shortcut for `TenantResolvers.Insert(0, ...)`. The actual implementation (framework/src/Volo.Abp.AspNetCore.MultiTenancy/Volo/Abp/MultiTenancy/AbpMultiTenancyOptionsExtensions.cs) is `options.TenantResolvers.InsertAfter(r => r is CurrentUserTenantResolveContributor, new DomainTenantResolveContributor(domainFormat))` -- InsertAfter the current-user resolver, i.e. index 1, NOT Insert(0). The class name is also wrong: it is DomainTenantResolveContributor, not DomainTenantResolver. Consequence: even the stock helper does not make the domain a hard first boundary; the token-claim resolver still precedes it.

CLAIM 23 ATTRIBUTES A QUOTATION TO A PAGE THAT DOES NOT CONTAIN IT. The phrase 'a hard limit that can't be changed' does not appear anywhere on the Azure SQL Managed Instance resource-limits page (verified on two separate fetches). The page says '100 user databases, unless the instance storage size limit has been reached.' The numbers (100 GP/BC, 500 Next-gen GP, 280 database files per instance for GP) are correct; the quoted characterisation is invented.

CLAIM 39 IS STALE BY FOUR MINOR VERSIONS. The ABP roadmap page states the current stable line is 10.6 ('10.6 (latest)') and that 'The next planned version will be 10.7, which is scheduled to be released as a stable version in August 2026.' ABP 10.2 and 10.3 are past releases, not the current stable and the roadmap item. The conclusion that ABP Commercial 10.0.2 is 'within the current major line' is technically true but obscures that it is six minor versions behind current stable.

CLAIMS 3 AND 5 TOGETHER MISSTATE THE EVIDENCE STATUS OF AWS SOURCES. Claim 5 flags only the SaaS Tenant Isolation Strategies whitepaper as 'historical reference only'. In fact the SaaS Architecture Fundamentals page cited as the sole source for claim 3 carries the identical banner: 'This whitepaper is for historical reference only. Some content might be outdated and some links might not be available.' The tenant-isolation-vs-authentication quotes in claim 3 therefore rest on a deprecated whitepaper, which claim 5 implies is not the case.
vendor_neutrality_violations: REQUIREMENT 6 ('Continuous integration MUST fail the build when the entity model has changes not represented by a migration in either the host or the tenant DbContext') names a product API surface as the requirement. 'DbContext' is an Entity Framework Core type; writing it into a MUST clause mandates EF Core rather than the capability. Vendor-neutral form: 'CI MUST fail the build when the application's object-relational model contains changes not represented by a committed schema migration, for both the host schema and the tenant schema.'

BORDERLINE, REQUIREMENT 10 ('The per-instance buffer pool and core limits of the chosen database edition MUST be recorded as architectural constraints, and the chosen edition MUST permit production use'). No product is named, but 'edition' with per-edition buffer-pool and core caps presupposes a commercially edition-tiered engine (the SQL Server licensing model). It survives a strict reading because it says 'the chosen database edition' rather than naming one, but it should be reworded to 'the per-instance memory and CPU limits imposed by the chosen database product tier, and the licence terms of that tier MUST permit production use' to stay engine-agnostic.

OUT OF SCOPE OF THE REQUIREMENTS LIST BUT FLAGGED: CLAIM 21 crosses from evidence into product recommendation. 'Instance-level failover (a failover cluster instance, two nodes on Standard) is the only shape that preserves the derived-connection-string design' prescribes a specific SQL Server feature (Always On Failover Cluster Instance) and a specific edition as the answer. The vendor-neutral form of this finding is the one already captured in requirement 12: either the HA mechanism fails the whole fleet over as a unit, or the tenant-to-location mapping stops being a derived template and becomes data. Requirement 12 is correctly written; claim 21 is not.

OUT OF SCOPE BUT FLAGGED: CLAIMS 18 AND 19 read together ('Resource Governor ... the only in-engine noisy-neighbour control' + 'becomes available in Standard edition' in SQL Server 2025) function as an implicit upgrade recommendation to a named product version. As evidence of a behaviour class (in-engine per-workload resource governance exists and is tier-gated) this is legitimate; requirement 11 already states the neutral capability correctly, and no requirement should be allowed to inherit 'therefore adopt SQL Server 2025 Standard' from these claims.

results.claim: [24] ABP registers QueryString (index 0), Route, Header, Cookie resolvers, all via TenantResolvers.Add()

results.correction: The four registrations, their relative order, and the use of Add() are exactly as claimed IN THIS FILE. The stated threshold 'QueryString at index 0' is wrong for the composed pipeline. This module carries [DependsOn(typeof(AbpMultiTenancyModule))], and that module's ConfigureServices runs first and executes 'options.TenantResolvers.Insert(0, new CurrentUserTenantResolveContributor())'. The resulting order is CurrentUser (0), QueryString (1), Route (2), Header (3), Cookie (4). The ABP documentation confirms this and states the intent: CurrentUserTenantResolveContributor 'Gets the tenant id from claims of the current user, if the current user has logged in. This should always be the first contributor for the security.' This changes the analysis for the first two capability requirements: the resolver that runs before everything else reads the tenant from the caller's token, so a host-only guarantee must contend with the token claim first, not merely with __tenant.

results.claim: [25] ABP TenantResolver iterates resolvers in order and breaks at the first that resolves; later resolvers do not run
results.evidence_quote: foreach (var tenantResolver in Options.TenantResolvers) { ... await tenantResolver.ResolveAsync(context); result.AppliedResolvers.Add(tenantResolver.Name); if (context.HasResolvedTenantOrHost()) { result.TenantIdOrName = context.TenantIdOrName; ... break; } }

results.claim: [26] HasResolvedTenantOrHost() returns 'Handled || TenantIdOrName != null'; the stock DomainTenantResolveContributor sets Handled = true unconditionally
results.evidence_quote: public bool HasResolvedTenantOrHost() { return Handled || TenantIdOrName != null; } ... var hostName = httpContext.Request.Host.Value.RemovePreFix(ProtocolPrefixes); var extractResult = FormattedStringValueExtracter.Extract(hostName, _domainFormat, ignoreCase: true); context.Handled = true;
results.correction: The HasResolvedTenantOrHost expression is exact (verified in TenantResolveContext.cs, not only in the issue), and the issue does describe the contributor as setting Handled unconditionally. But the source contradicts 'unconditionally' in one path that matters: GetTenantIdOrNameFromHttpContextOrNullAsync returns early with 'if (!httpContext.Request.Host.HasValue) { return Task.FromResult<string?>(null); }' BEFORE reaching 'context.Handled = true'. So a request with no Host value falls through to the next resolver rather than being stopped. Precise statement: the contributor sets Handled = true whenever a Host value is present, regardless of whether the domain format matched -- which is what makes it a hard boundary for well-formed requests -- but a request arriving with no Host header escapes the boundary and is handed to the next resolver in the chain. That edge case is exactly the kind of thing the first capability requirement has to close, so it should be tested, not assumed.

results.claim: [27] ABP's AddDomainTenantResolver is documented as a shortcut for options.TenantResolvers.Insert(0, new DomainTenantResolver("{0}.mydomain.com")) -- Insert at index 0, not Add
results.evidence_quote: Configure<AbpTenantResolveOptions>(options => { options.AddDomainTenantResolver("{0}.mydomain.com"); });
results.correction: Wrong on both the documentation and the mechanism. (a) The cited page never describes AddDomainTenantResolver as a shortcut for anything -- it shows only the one-line call above, with no Insert, no index and no underlying implementation; the quoted 'Insert(0, ...)' text does not appear on the page. (b) The actual implementation is 'options.TenantResolvers.InsertAfter(r => r is CurrentUserTenantResolveContributor, new DomainTenantResolveContributor(domainFormat))' in framework/src/Volo.Abp.AspNetCore.MultiTenancy/Volo/Abp/MultiTenancy/AbpMultiTenancyOptionsExtensions.cs -- InsertAfter the current-user resolver, landing at index 1, NOT Insert at 0. (c) The type is DomainTenantResolveContributor, not DomainTenantResolver. Corrected claim: AddDomainTenantResolver inserts the domain contributor immediately after CurrentUserTenantResolveContributor, so it precedes the query-string, route, header and cookie resolvers but does NOT precede the token-claim resolver. A custom domain resolver registered with .Add() would instead run after all five. Cite the source file, not the docs page.

results.claim: [28] Could not verify how the system's custom HostAwareDomainTenantResolveContributor is registered (Insert(0) vs Add) or whether it sets Handled on the no-match path, because the source was not available
results.evidence_quote: options.TenantResolvers.Add(new QueryStringTenantResolveContributor());
results.correction: The honesty is right and the gap is real -- the custom type is not in the ABP repository and I could not reach it either, so the registration position and no-match Handled behaviour remain genuinely unknown. But the framing of what that gap decides is now too narrow. Given the corrected ordering in claims 24 and 27, the open question is not merely 'whether __tenant can override the Host header' but a three-part one: (i) does the custom contributor precede CurrentUserTenantResolveContributor, which is at index 0 and reads the tenant from the caller's token claims; (ii) does it precede the query-string, route, header and cookie contributors; and (iii) does it set Handled on the no-match and no-Host paths. Part (i) is the one that bears on the second capability requirement (a token from one office not authorising a request for another) and was not previously identified as being in question at all.
