evidence.claim: SetApplicationName sets DataProtectionOptions.ApplicationDiscriminator. To share protected payloads across apps, BOTH conditions are required: configure SetApplicationName with the same value in each app, AND 'Use the same version of the Data Protection API stack across the apps'  -  either the same shared framework version or the same Data Protection package version. By default apps are isolated by content root path even when sharing a physical key repository.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn  -  Configure ASP.NET Core Data Protection
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Two conditions, both mandatory

evidence.claim: The Data Protection key ring is cached in memory and the backing store is re-checked 'approximately every 24 hours or when the current default key expires, whichever comes first'. New keys are created with an activation date of now + 2 days and expiry of now + 90 days; the 2-day delay exists specifically 'to allow other applications pointing at the backing store to observe the key at their next auto-refresh period'. Default key lifetime is 90 days and cannot be set shorter than 7 days. Deleting a key is described as 'truly destructive behavior'  -  all data protected by it becomes permanently undecipherable.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn  -  Key management in ASP.NET Core
evidence.threshold_or_limit: ~24 h refresh; activation now+2 days; expiry now+90 days; minimum lifetime 7 days

evidence.claim: Microsoft's Data Protection configuration guidance states that 'Only Redis versions supporting Redis Data Persistence should be used to store keys.'
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn  -  Configure ASP.NET Core Data Protection, 'Persisting keys with Redis'
evidence.threshold_or_limit: n/a

evidence.claim: Redis eviction: the default maxmemory-policy is noeviction and maxmemory is unset by default (no limit on 64-bit). allkeys-lru / allkeys-lfu / allkeys-lrm / allkeys-random evict ANY key, including keys with no TTL. volatile-* policies evict only keys with an associated expiration and 'behave like noeviction if no keys have an associated expiration'. Under noeviction, Redis returns errors on commands that would use more memory but continues to serve read-only commands.
evidence.source_name: Redis Documentation  -  Key eviction; redis.conf 7.4
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Default maxmemory-policy = noeviction; default appendonly = no

evidence.claim: DistributedLock.Redis (Medallion.Threading.Redis) is currently maintained: version 1.1.1 published 2025-10-26, following 1.1.0 on 2025-08-10. It implements the RedLock algorithm; robustness increases only by constructing the lock with multiple independent databases, where 'the lock is only considered acquired if it is successfully acquired on more than half of the databases'. Held leases are extended automatically in the background until the handle is disposed.
evidence.source_name: NuGet  -  DistributedLock.Redis; madelson/DistributedLock Redis documentation
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 1.1.1 on 2025-10-26; majority quorum = more than half of N databases; depends on StackExchange.Redis >= 2.7.33

evidence.claim: The correctness of Redis-based distributed locking is contested. Redlock is designed for N independent Redis masters with majority acquisition; a single instance loses the lock entirely if the node fails, and a primary/replica failover can allow two clients to hold the same lock. Kleppmann argues Redlock's safety rests on timing assumptions and is unsuitable for correctness-critical locks; antirez's Redlock write-up defends it. Sources disagree.
evidence.source_name: Redis  -  Distributed Locks with Redis; Martin Kleppmann  -  How to do distributed locking; antirez  -  The Redlock Algorithm
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Quorum = N/2+1 independent masters

evidence.claim: Starting with EF Core 9, Migrate() and MigrateAsync() automatically acquire a database-wide lock before applying migrations. 'This protects against database corruption that could result from multiple application instances running migrations concurrently, which is a common scenario when applying migrations at runtime.' The lock is held for the migration and any seeding code. On SQL Server it is implemented as a session-scoped sp_getapplock on resource '__EFMigrationsLock' in Exclusive mode.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn  -  Applying Migrations (EF Core); dotnet/efcore issue #34439
evidence.threshold_or_limit: EF Core 9 and later; sp_getapplock @Resource='__EFMigrationsLock', @LockOwner='Session', @LockMode='Exclusive'

evidence.claim: Microsoft's current EF Core deployment guidance for containers directly endorses the one-shot migrator pattern this system already uses: 'Generate the bundle during the build and run it as a one-shot deployment job after the database is healthy. Don't install the SDK or run dotnet ef in the application image, and don't make every application replica run migrations from its entrypoint. Configure the deployment platform not to restart the migration container after it exits successfully.'
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn  -  Applying Migrations (EF Core), 'Containers and deployment jobs'
evidence.threshold_or_limit: n/a

evidence.claim: Starting with EF Core 9, Migrate()/MigrateAsync() throws when the model has pending changes compared to the last migration (RelationalEventId.PendingModelChangesWarning). Microsoft recommends detecting this before deployment with `dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes` in CI, and states that suppressing the warning 'is generally not recommended in production scenarios'.

evidence.threshold_or_limit: EF Core 9 and later; command: dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes

evidence.claim: ADO.NET connection pools are keyed per process, per application domain, per connection string (exact string match, keyword order significant), and per Windows identity where integrated security is used. 'A connection pool is created for each unique connection string.' Default Max Pool Size is 100. On exhaustion the request is queued and an exception is thrown after the connection timeout, default 15 seconds. Idle connections are removed after approximately 4-8 minutes when MinPoolSize is 0 or unset.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn  -  SQL Server connection pooling (ADO.NET)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Max Pool Size default 100; connection timeout default 15 s; idle reaping 4-8 minutes; login-failure blocking period 5 s doubling to max 1 minute

evidence.claim: Microsoft names this system's exact architecture as a connection-pooling anti-pattern: under 'Pool fragmentation due to many databases' it states that opening a connection to a specific database per user or group means 'there is a separate pool of connections to each database, which increase the number of connections to the server.'

Standard edition is limited to the lesser of 4 sockets or 24 cores and a 128 GB buffer pool per instance; Express is limited to the lesser of 1 socket or 4 cores, 1,410 MB buffer pool, and a 10 GB maximum relational database size.

evidence.claim: The MinIO open-source object storage server repository is archived and unmaintained. GitHub displays 'This repository was archived by the owner on Apr 25, 2026. It is now read-only.' and the README states 'THIS REPOSITORY IS NO LONGER MAINTAINED.' The most recent release is RELEASE.2025-10-15T17-29-55Z, which was itself a security fix for 'Privilege Escalation via Session Policy Bypass in Service Accounts and STS'.
evidence.source_name: GitHub  -  minio/minio repository and releases
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Archived 2026-04-25; last release 2025-10-15

evidence.claim: Microsoft.Data.SqlClient 4.0 changed the default of the Encrypt connection setting from false to true, which is why TrustServerCertificate=True is required to connect to a server without a client-trusted certificate. Every pooled connection establishment therefore performs a TLS handshake.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn  -  Encryption and certificate validation (ADO.NET)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Encrypt default changed to true in Microsoft.Data.SqlClient 4.0

evidence.claim: 45 CFR 164.316(b)(2)(i) requires retention for 6 years, but its scope is the DOCUMENTATION required by 164.316(b)(1)  -  'the policies and procedures implemented to comply with this subpart' and 'a written (which may be electronic) record of the action, activity, or assessment'. It reads: 'Retain the documentation required by paragraph (b)(1) of this section for 6 years from the date of its creation or the date when it last was in effect, whichever is later.' The rule does not by its own terms set a retention period for an application's entity-level audit trail; treating the AuditLogs and property-change tables as in scope is a defensible organisational policy decision, not a literal statutory mandate on those tables.
evidence.source_name: 45 CFR 164.316 (via GovInfo, CFR Title 45)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 6 years from creation or last effective date, whichever is later

evidence.claim: ABP's distributed cache automatically adds the current tenant id to the cache key for IDistributedCache<T>, and supports AbpDistributedCacheOptions.KeyPrefix for sharing a cache server across applications. The HideErrors option defaults to true, meaning cache failures are logged rather than thrown outside Development. ABP's documentation does not describe cross-instance invalidation or pub/sub for the plain distributed cache; a separate HybridCache feature keeps a local in-process cache backed by the distributed cache.
evidence.source_name: ABP.IO Documentation  -  Distributed Caching
evidence.threshold_or_limit: HideErrors default true (disabled in Development)

evidence.claim: ABP's dynamic permission/feature/setting definition stores keep an in-process memory cache validated against a 'cache stamp' held in the distributed cache, with a periodic re-check rather than immediate invalidation. Convergence across application instances is therefore eventual and bounded by that check interval, not immediate.
evidence.source_name: ABP support/community discussion of DynamicPermissionDefinitionStore and DynamicPermissionDefinitionStoreInMemoryCache (CacheStamp, LastCheckTime)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Exact default check interval not confirmed; direct source read of DynamicPermissionDefinitionStore.cs returned 404 on the dev branch path tried

evidence.claim: The ABP stack in use is materially behind current: Volo.Abp.BackgroundJobs.HangFire latest stable is 10.6.0 (2026-07-27) against the deployed ABP 10.0.2.
evidence.source_name: NuGet Gallery  -  Volo.Abp.BackgroundJobs.HangFire

evidence.claim: MY REASONING, not a sourced fact: at 33 offices, one API process holding a distinct connection string per office database can open up to 33 x 100 = 3,300 pooled connections by default, and two processes up to 6,600, against a SQL Server instance whose auto-configured worker thread limit at 4 logical CPUs is 512. Pool exhaustion and worker starvation are different limits reached by different paths, but both are plausible well before the tenant ceiling is reached, and neither is visible without instrumentation.
evidence.source_name: Derived from Microsoft connection pooling and max worker threads documentation
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 33 x 100 = 3,300 per process; 512 worker threads at 4 CPUs

evidence.claim: MY REASONING, not a sourced fact: because pooled connections are reaped after 4-8 minutes of idleness when MinPoolSize is 0, and the three 15-minute recurring sweeps touch every office database once per cycle, each sweep almost always pays a full login and TLS handshake per office rather than reusing a warm connection. This cost scales linearly with office count and would double with a second processing server. It is invisible in application logs.
evidence.source_name: Derived from Microsoft connection pooling documentation and the stated 15-minute job schedule
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Idle reaping 4-8 min vs 15-min sweep interval

evidence.claim: MY REASONING, not a sourced fact: the recurring-job scheduler's lock-timeout path logs at Debug level, so under a typical Information-level Serilog configuration a server that never wins the lock emits nothing. If the lock holder stalls, all twelve recurring jobs stop fleet-wide with no log line above Debug. This is the archetypal silent-degradation failure the team has stated it cannot detect.
evidence.source_name: Derived from Hangfire RecurringJobScheduler source (log level Debug on DistributedLockTimeoutException)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Log level Debug; lock timeout 1 minute

capability_requirements.requirement: Whether a process runs background processing (the Hangfire processing server and ABP background workers) MUST be controlled by explicit configuration, not implied by which application role the process happens to be, and the platform MUST allow running the same image with that setting differing per instance.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: This is the only true blocker to a second API instance. Without it, adding a replica silently adds a second processing server, and Hangfire's own documentation states duplicate execution cannot be reliably prevented. Everything else in horizontal scale is negotiable; this is not.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System fact: only HttpApi.Host runs the Hangfire processing server, and it does so by virtue of being HttpApi.Host. Hangfire throttling docs: 'there's no reliable way to prevent multiple executions of the same background job other than by using transactions in background job method itself.' ABP background workers docs: 'Stop the background workers ... in all application instances except one of them.'
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Start two instances of the API image with the flag off and on respectively. Query the Hangfire storage Server table (or the dashboard's Servers view) and assert exactly one server row is present with a recent heartbeat. Then start two instances both with the flag on and assert two rows appear  -  proving the flag actually controls registration rather than being ignored.

capability_requirements.requirement: Every one of the twelve recurring jobs MUST be idempotent under repeated execution with the same arguments, and this MUST be true independent of instance count.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Hangfire documents at-least-once semantics as an inherent property, not a multi-instance artefact. A single-instance deployment already re-runs jobs after a crash mid-execution. Jobs that send email or write to the Case Tracker integration outbox can therefore already double-send today.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Hangfire throttling documentation, and the durable per-recipient email outbox and per-office integration outbox described in the system facts.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: For each recurring job, invoke it twice in immediate succession against a database in a fixed state (the Hangfire dashboard's requeue button does this, or a direct method call in a test). Assert the second run produces no additional rows in AppNotificationOutboxItems or AppIntegrationOutboxItems, no additional outbound email, and no state transition beyond the first run's result.

capability_requirements.requirement: The platform MUST allow the number of pooled database connections per tenant database per process to be bounded explicitly, and the effective bound MUST be observable at runtime.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Database-per-tenant creates one connection pool per office per process, each defaulting to 100. Microsoft names this exact pattern as pool fragmentation. Unbounded, the arithmetic exceeds the database's auto-configured worker thread count long before the 33-office ceiling, and the failure appears as an unexplained 15-second timeout in an unrelated feature.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft ADO.NET connection pooling documentation (pools per process per connection string, Max Pool Size default 100, 'Pool fragmentation due to many databases'); Microsoft max worker threads documentation (512 at <=4 logical CPUs); system fact that TenantConnectionStringProvider derives one connection string per office.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Set Max Pool Size explicitly on the tenant connection template. Then run `SELECT DB_NAME(dbid) AS db, COUNT(*) FROM sys.sysprocesses WHERE dbid > 0 GROUP BY dbid ORDER BY 2 DESC` (or the sys.dm_exec_sessions equivalent) while all recurring sweeps are running, and assert no single office database exceeds the configured bound times the number of running processes.

capability_requirements.requirement: Both application processes MUST agree on the Data Protection application discriminator AND on the Data Protection stack version, and both values MUST be emitted at startup so a mismatch is detectable without a debugger.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Microsoft states two conditions for sharing protected payloads, not one. Matching SetApplicationName alone is insufficient. A mismatch does not fail at startup  -  it fails later as unexplained logouts and dead email-confirmation links, which is precisely the subtle failure mode this team cannot diagnose.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft Learn Data Protection configuration: 'Configure SetApplicationName in each app with the same value' AND 'Use the same version of the Data Protection API stack across the apps.'
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Add a startup log line resolving IOptions<DataProtectionOptions>.Value.ApplicationDiscriminator plus the assembly version of Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection, in both AuthServer and API. Start both, grep both logs, assert both strings are byte-identical. As a behavioural check, complete a login on one process and assert the session is honoured by the other.

capability_requirements.requirement: The store holding the Data Protection key ring MUST NOT be able to evict or expire those keys, and the configured eviction behaviour MUST be assertable by a single command.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Data Protection keys are stored without a TTL. An allkeys-* eviction policy on the cache would make them eligible for eviction under memory pressure, and Microsoft describes losing a key as making protected data 'permanently undecipherable' with no emergency override. The blast radius is every session and every in-flight confirmation link, and the cause would be invisible.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Redis eviction documentation (allkeys-* evict any key; volatile-* evict only keys with a TTL and behave like noeviction when none have one; default policy is noeviction); Microsoft key management documentation ('Deleting a key is truly destructive behavior'); Microsoft's requirement that only Redis with data persistence be used for key storage.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Run `CONFIG GET maxmemory-policy` and `CONFIG GET maxmemory` against the cache and assert either that maxmemory is 0, or that the policy is noeviction or a volatile-* variant. Stronger: write a canary key with no TTL, drive the instance to its memory limit, and assert the canary survives. Strongest: move the key ring to a store with no eviction concept at all and assert the key material is not present in the cache.

capability_requirements.requirement: Every network hop in front of the application MUST forward the client's original Host header byte-for-byte to the application, and any health probe MUST be configurable to send a Host header that resolves to a valid office.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Tenancy resolves from the Host header and a request matching no office returns 'Tenant not found'. nginx's own documented default is to REWRITE the Host header, so preserving it is an opt-in on every new hop. A health probe defaulting to IP:port will mark every instance unhealthy simultaneously and take the entire system down at the exact moment a load balancer is introduced.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: nginx documentation: 'By default, the header fields "Host" and "Connection" from the original request are not passed to the proxied server' with default 'proxy_set_header Host $proxy_host'. System fact: tenancy resolves from the Host header and nothing else; a bare IP cannot reach the application.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: From outside the edge, `curl -H 'Host: <office>.api.<base>' https://<edge>/...` and assert the response is that office's data, not 'Tenant not found'. Separately, capture what the application receives (log the inbound Host on one endpoint) and assert it equals what the client sent. For the probe: point a health check at the raw instance address with no Host override and confirm it fails  -  if it passes, something is resolving tenancy by another route and requirement 7 applies.

capability_requirements.requirement: It MUST be demonstrated, not assumed, that a request cannot select a tenant by any means other than the Host header  -  specifically that the __tenant query string, route value, header and cookie resolvers cannot override or substitute for the subdomain.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: ABP registers CurrentUser, QueryString, Route, Header and Cookie tenant resolvers by default, and the domain resolver is added separately. Whether the defaults are removed here has never been tested. Every topology conclusion  -  that a cell can own a DNS suffix, that an edge can route by Host, that Host preservation is the whole contract  -  rests on this being true. If it is false, the routing model is not what anyone believes and the security posture changes too.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: ABP multi-tenancy documentation listing the five default resolvers and their order; the system's own recorded caveat that this has never been tested.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Authenticate as a user of office A. Then issue a request with `Host: officeA.api.<base>` and `?__tenant=<office B tenant id>`, and repeat with the `__tenant` header and cookie. Assert every variant returns office A's data or an error, never office B's. Repeat unauthenticated against a public endpoint. Any response containing office B data proves the Host-only property is false.

capability_requirements.requirement: Schema migration MUST run as a one-shot job that both application processes gate on, and that job MUST report per-office success or failure by name and MUST exit non-zero if any office failed.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: The current design's shape is correct and matches Microsoft's explicit guidance; the defect is the missing per-tenant result. A partial fleet migration with no report produces offices on divergent schema versions, surfacing later as an invalid-object-name exception in an unrelated feature  -  a subtle failure this team will not connect to the deploy that caused it. A non-zero exit converts it into a refused startup, which is loud.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft EF Core deployment guidance: 'run it as a one-shot deployment job ... don't make every application replica run migrations from its entrypoint'; system fact that db-migrator loops offices with no per-tenant error handling and no report; system fact that both app services gate on service_completed_successfully.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Deliberately break one office database (revoke permissions, or rename a table the next migration touches). Run the migrator. Assert (a) stdout names that office as failed and names the others as succeeded, (b) the process exit code is non-zero, and (c) neither the API nor the AuthServer starts. Then repeat with two application instances starting simultaneously and assert no corruption and no duplicate application of the same migration.

capability_requirements.requirement: Continuous integration MUST fail the build if any DbContext's model has pending changes relative to its last migration.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: The host and tenant DbContexts share a base and a shared model configuration, so an entity mapped in both requires a migration in both. EF Core 9+ already throws on pending model changes at migrate time; a CI gate moves that discovery from deploy time to commit time at near-zero cost, and permanently converts a subtle runtime failure into an obvious build failure  -  exactly the trade this team has said it wants.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft EF Core documentation: Migrate() throws on RelationalEventId.PendingModelChangesWarning from EF Core 9, and 'To detect this condition before deployment, use the dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes command in your CI/CD pipeline.' System fact: two DbContexts sharing a base and a shared model configuration.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Add `dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes` for each DbContext to CI. Prove it works by mapping a new property on an entity shared by both contexts, adding a migration to only one context, and asserting CI fails naming the other context.

capability_requirements.requirement: Any state cached in process memory MUST either be provably identical across instances or MUST converge within a stated, tested bound; the codebase MUST have no in-process cache of tenant-scoped or permission-scoped data whose staleness window is unbounded.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: The shared Redis distributed cache is coherent by construction, but ABP's dynamic definition stores keep an in-process layer validated by a cache stamp, and application code may hold its own IMemoryCache or statics. These diverge silently across instances and produce the worst class of bug: correct behaviour on one replica and incorrect on another, with no error anywhere.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: ABP dynamic definition store cache-stamp mechanism; ABP caching documentation describing HybridCache as a separate local-plus-distributed feature; system fact of 56 application services whose in-process caching has not been surveyed.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Grep src for IMemoryCache, MemoryCache, `static readonly ConcurrentDictionary`, `static readonly Dictionary`, `Lazy<`, and untyped IDistributedCache usage; every hit is a finding requiring a written justification. Behaviourally: run two instances, change a permission and a setting via instance A, poll instance B, and record the observed convergence time. Assert it is under a stated bound (and that a bound exists at all).

capability_requirements.requirement: If a second application instance is introduced, the platform MUST make it possible to attribute any given request, log line, and background job execution to a specific instance.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: With no aggregation, no metrics and no APM, a two-instance deployment where one instance is misbehaving is indistinguishable from a healthy one. ABP's tenant-ambient fallback hazard for jobs (a null ambient tenant resolves to the host database) is already hard to diagnose; with two instances it becomes impossible without instance attribution. This requirement is what makes the difference between horizontal scale being an improvement and being a regression.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System facts: no aggregation, no metrics, no APM, no OpenTelemetry, no alerting; container logs capped at 10 MB x 5 and rotating away; ABP ambient-tenant fallback to the host database in workers.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Issue 20 requests through the edge and assert that for each one, a person with only log access can name which instance served it. Trigger a background job and assert the same for its execution. Kill one instance mid-test and assert the logs show which one died and when.

capability_requirements.requirement: The recovery story MUST be a restore that has actually been performed against a copy of production data, with a recorded elapsed time and a recorded data-loss window, and it MUST be re-performed on a stated schedule.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Replica count does not address the failure the business cares about. Microsoft states plainly that availability features do not replace a tested backup and restore strategy. The tenancy model has already eliminated the low-effort clustering options, so restore is not a fallback here  -  it is the primary control.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft SQL Server business continuity documentation: 'A backup and restore strategy is the most fundamental building block of any availability solution.' System facts: backups written to the same box and same disk, no confirmed cron, no restore ever tested.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Take the current backup set, restore the host database and at least two office databases onto a clean machine, bring the stack up against them, and log in as an office user. Record wall-clock elapsed time (the RTO) and the timestamp of the newest recoverable transaction (the RPO). Assert backups exist on storage that would survive loss of the application host. Repeat quarterly and assert the numbers have not regressed.

capability_requirements.requirement: The data tier's high-availability design MUST be evaluated against the actual number of databases in the fleet, not against a single-database assumption, and the chosen option MUST fail over all tenant databases as one unit or explicitly accept per-database failover.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: This is the constraint most likely to be discovered too late. Database-per-tenant plus a Standard-edition database engine yields 12-34 independent Basic Availability Groups, each covering one database, with no readable secondary and no secondary backups  -  a fleet-management problem disguised as an HA solution. The alternatives (instance-level failover with shared storage, or accepting restore-based recovery) have very different platform implications.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft Basic Availability Groups documentation: 'Support for one availability database', 'Limit of two replicas', 'No read access on secondary replica', 'No backups on secondary replica', 'only supported for Standard edition servers'. Microsoft editions table: Always On availability groups Enterprise-only; Standard FCI limited to two nodes. Microsoft Linux business continuity: 'All FCIs require some shared storage' which 'is a single point of failure'.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Count the databases the fleet will hold at target office count (host plus one per office). For any proposed HA design, state how many failover units it creates and demonstrate a failover of the whole fleet, timing it. If the answer is one failover unit per database, assert that someone has written down who performs 34 failovers and in what order.

capability_requirements.requirement: Every third-party component in the runtime path SHOULD have a release within roughly the last twelve months, and any component without one MUST have a written replacement or mitigation plan with a date.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: SHOULD as a general hygiene rule, but it escalates to MUST for the storage layer specifically: MinIO's open-source server repository is archived and unmaintained, its last release was a privilege-escalation security fix, and it holds PHI. That is a topology constraint as well as a security one, because it bounds what the storage tier can become and it interacts with an external partner's credential schedule that the team does not control.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: GitHub minio/minio: archived 2026-04-25, 'THIS REPOSITORY IS NO LONGER MAINTAINED', last release 2025-10-15 addressing 'Privilege Escalation via Session Policy Bypass in Service Accounts and STS'. System fact: an external partner holds scoped credentials against the partner bucket and must be re-credentialed on their schedule.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: For each of MinIO, Redis, SQL Server, Hangfire, ABP and the packet renderer's Python dependencies, record the deployed version, the current released version, and the date of the current release. Assert every gap is either under twelve months or has a named owner and a target date. For the storage layer specifically, assert a written plan exists that accounts for the partner's re-credentialing lead time.

anti_requirements: The platform MUST NOT terminate, rewrite, or normalise the Host header at any hop in front of the application. This forbids the default behaviour of most L7 proxies, including nginx's own documented default of proxy_set_header Host $proxy_host, and it forbids any managed edge product that presents its own hostname to the origin. Tenancy resolves from this header and nothing else.

The platform MUST NOT require reaching the application by IP address for any purpose  -  health probing, monitoring, internal service-to-service calls, or debugging. A bare IP cannot reach this application at all, and any platform feature that assumes it can will report the application as down while it is serving traffic normally.

The platform MUST NOT silently evict or expire arbitrary keys from whatever store holds the Data Protection key ring. A cache tier whose eviction policy is not assertable, or which the platform may reconfigure, is disqualified for that role regardless of how convenient it is for the application cache.

The platform MUST NOT automatically scale the process that runs background processing. Horizontal replication of the processing role produces duplicate work against a two-worker packet renderer and one SMTP relay that are already the throughput ceiling; Hangfire's own documentation states duplicate execution cannot be reliably prevented at the framework level.

The platform MUST NOT run schema migration from the application's own entrypoint on every replica. Microsoft's current guidance is explicit: do not make every application replica run migrations from its entrypoint, and do not restart the migration job after it exits successfully.

The platform MUST NOT require session affinity or sticky routing for correctness. There is no SignalR, no WebSocket, and no in-process session; requiring affinity would mask a Data Protection key-sharing defect rather than expose it, converting a fixable startup-detectable bug into an intermittent one that only appears when an instance dies.
The platform MUST NOT place the only copy of a database backup on the same storage device, host, or failure domain as the database it protects.

The platform MUST NOT require a database edition licensed only for development and test. The current MSSQL_PID of 'Developer' is licensed for development and test, not production, and this is a hard constraint on any target platform rather than a preference.

The platform MUST NOT require the application to be reachable over plain HTTP internally in a way that would let the tenancy-bearing Host header be observed or altered by anything between the edge and the application, given that the header is the sole tenancy discriminator for a PHI-bearing system.

The platform MUST NOT collapse the host database and the office databases into a single logical database or require cross-database queries to make them work. There is no raw SQL, no three-part naming and no linked server anywhere in the source; host and tenant data are joined in memory. Any platform requiring a shared schema would be a rewrite, not a migration.
surprises: The database-per-tenant decision has already eliminated the standard SQL Server high-availability answer, and nobody discovers this until they try to build HA. Always On availability groups are Enterprise-only. Standard edition offers Basic Availability Groups, which support exactly ONE database each, with no readable secondary and no backups on the secondary. Twelve to thirty-four databases therefore means twelve to thirty-four independent availability groups, each with its own listener and its own failover. Failover Cluster Instances cover the whole instance in one unit but require shared storage, which Microsoft explicitly calls a single point of failure, and SQL Server on Linux permits only one installation per host. Microsoft further states that a containerised SQL Server recovered by an orchestrator 'isn't truly highly available'. The failover story is constrained by a tenancy decision made for entirely unrelated reasons.

QueuePollInterval = TimeSpan.Zero is not aggressive polling. Hangfire's source clamps it to a 200 ms long-polling delay bounded between 100 ms and 1000 ms, and Hangfire's own documentation calls TimeSpan.Zero with SlidingInvisibilityTimeout 'the recommended value'. The characterisation of it as a continuous query floor is wrong in the team's favour. What genuinely scales badly is that the poll floor multiplies by the number of processing servers  -  so the correct lever is 'exactly one processing server', not 'raise the interval'.

The Hangfire server that loses the recurring-jobs lock logs at Debug level. Under a normal Information-level Serilog configuration it emits nothing at all. If the lock holder stalls, all twelve recurring jobs  -  including the three fifteen-minute reconciliation and failure-alert sweeps  -  stop across the whole fleet, and the only trace is a log line the configuration is discarding. This is the exact silent degradation the team has said it cannot detect, and it is one line of logging configuration away from being visible.

Hangfire is at-least-once by its own documentation, today, at one instance. Its throttling page states there is 'no reliable way to prevent multiple executions of the same background job other than by using transactions in background job method itself', and that DisableConcurrentExecution's lock can be released by a broken connection 'without any notification'. Mutexes and semaphores are commercial add-ons, not in the open-source package. Job idempotency is therefore a present-tense requirement for the email outbox drain and the Case Tracker integration drain, not a future multi-instance concern.

Sharing a Data Protection key ring requires TWO matching conditions, not one. Microsoft requires the same application name AND 'the same version of the Data Protection API stack across the apps'. Two container images built weeks apart can both call SetApplicationName("CaseEvaluation") and still be unable to read each other's payloads. The symptom is unexplained logouts and dead email-confirmation links  -  which the system facts already record as having produced real support incidents.

Data Protection is already designed for the multi-instance case, and this is good news the team does not know it has. New keys activate at now-plus-two-days specifically so peer instances observe them at their next roughly-24-hour refresh. Adding an API instance is safe for session continuity. The danger is entirely on the other side: losing or clearing the key ring, which Microsoft describes as making protected data 'permanently undecipherable' with no emergency override.

The key ring lives in a cache, and caches evict. Redis's default policy is noeviction and maxmemory is unset, so the current setup is safe  -  but by accident, not by decision. If anyone ever sets maxmemory with an allkeys-* policy (a completely natural thing to do to a 512 MB Redis labelled 'cache'), the key ring becomes an eviction candidate because Data Protection keys carry no TTL. Note also that the 512 MB figure in the compose file is a container memory limit, which OOM-kills and reloads from AOF  -  a safer failure than eviction. That accident is worth converting into a deliberate, asserted configuration.

EF Core already solved the concurrent-migration problem the team is probably worried about. From EF Core 9 onward, Migrate() and MigrateAsync() acquire a database-wide lock automatically  -  on SQL Server, a session-scoped sp_getapplock on '__EFMigrationsLock'  -  held for the migration and any seeding. N migrators starting simultaneously serialise per database. The real migrator risk is not concurrency; it is that a partial fleet run produces no report of which offices succeeded.

EF Core 9+ also throws when a model has pending changes versus its last migration. The 'entity mapped in both DbContexts, migration added to only one' trap should therefore already be a hard startup exception rather than a runtime invalid-object-name. If it is currently surfacing at runtime instead, the warning is being suppressed somewhere and that is worth finding. Either way, `dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes` per DbContext in CI closes the trap permanently for about two hours of work  -  the single best cost-to-benefit item in this entire analysis.

Microsoft has a name for what this architecture does to connection pooling, and the name is a warning: 'Pool fragmentation due to many databases'. Pools are per process, per application domain, per connection string, with a default Max Pool Size of 100. Thirty-three offices means up to 3,300 pooled connections from one process and 6,600 from two, against a database whose auto-configured worker thread limit at four logical CPUs is 512. Nothing in the application will tell them this is happening until a request times out after fifteen seconds in a feature that has nothing to do with the cause.

The fifteen-minute sweeps guarantee cold connections forever. Idle pooled connections are reaped after roughly four to eight minutes when MinPoolSize is zero. A sweep every fifteen minutes therefore almost never finds a warm connection, so every office pays a full login and TLS handshake on every cycle  -  and TLS is unavoidable because Microsoft.Data.SqlClient 4.0 changed Encrypt to default true, which is precisely why TrustServerCertificate=True appears in the connection strings. This cost is linear in office count and invisible in application logs.

nginx's own default rewrites the Host header. The documented default is proxy_set_header Host $proxy_host, and the docs state plainly that the original Host is not passed through. For a system where tenancy resolves from Host and nothing else, this means every future hop  -  load balancer, WAF, CDN, mesh sidecar  -  must be explicitly configured to preserve it. The consolation is that it fails loudly: 'Tenant not found', not wrong data.

A load balancer health probe will take the entire system down on the day it is introduced, unless it is configured with an office hostname. It probes the instance address, no office matches, the application returns 'Tenant not found', every instance is marked unhealthy simultaneously, and the load balancer removes all of them. This is obvious in hindsight and catastrophic in the moment, and it is a direct consequence of Host-only tenancy.

The MinIO open-source server is archived and unmaintained as of 25 April 2026  -  the README says 'THIS REPOSITORY IS NO LONGER MAINTAINED'  -  and the final release, from 15 October 2025, was itself a privilege-escalation security fix. A PHI-bearing storage layer with no patch stream is a topology constraint, not only a security finding, because the long pole in replacing it is an external partner who holds scoped credentials against the partner bucket and must be re-credentialed on their own schedule. That lead time should be started before it becomes urgent.

ABP's own clustered-environment deployment checklist does not mention Data Protection at all. It covers distributed cache, BLOB storage, background jobs, distributed locking, background workers and SignalR. A team following the framework's guidance faithfully would leave the single most session-breaking multi-instance issue unaddressed. This system happens to have it right already.

ABP's distributed event bus is in-process by default. With no broker configured, the implementation is LocalDistributedEventBus, which behaves exactly like the local event bus. Any framework or application feature that publishes a distributed event expecting other instances to receive it silently does nothing the moment there are two instances. This fails partially and silently, which makes it the most dangerous single property in the stack for a horizontal move.

The distributed lock is currently decorative. It is registered in both processes with no application acquisition sites, and the ABP feature that would use it  -  the distributed event outbox  -  is moot because the event bus is in-process. Its correctness properties therefore do not matter yet, and treating them as urgent is a distraction. What matters is that its mere presence invites someone to make it load-bearing later, at which point single-instance RedLock offers best-effort mutual exclusion, not guaranteed mutual exclusion, and the literature genuinely disagrees about how much weight it will bear (Kleppmann against, antirez for).

The tenant key prefix question is a red herring for scaling. The t:{tenantId} prefix on typed IDistributedCache<T> is a tenancy-isolation control, and untyped usage bypassing it is a cross-tenant leak that is exactly as broken at one instance as at two. Adding instances changes nothing about it. It should be audited  -  but as an isolation defect, not as a scaling blocker, and conflating the two would misdirect scarce hours.

The team already owns the expensive half of a cell architecture without knowing it. Because office connection strings are derived from a single template key, the entire fleet can be relocated to a different SQL instance with one configuration change and no code change; and because tenancy resolves from the Host header, a cell can own a DNS suffix. The only missing piece is per-office placement rather than one global template  -  and ABP supports per-tenant connection strings natively. This is the highest-leverage thing to preserve through any platform change, and it is easy to accidentally destroy by moving to a platform that manages connection strings for you.

not_recommended.pattern: Run multiple Hangfire processing servers to scale background work with office count
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: This is what Hangfire is built for. Coordination across servers is documented and real: the recurring scheduler takes a single global lock, servers register with distinct identifiers, and the queue fetch is designed for concurrent consumers. Background work genuinely does scale with office count  -  three fifteen-minute sweeps each opening a connection per office is 33 sequential connections per sweep at full scale, and parallelising that across servers is the textbook answer. It would also remove background processing as a reason not to restart the API.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: The bottleneck is not the Hangfire server. It is a two-worker packet renderer and a single SMTP relay, and the system facts record that the worker pool is already pinned specifically because bursts oversubscribe both into timeouts. A second processing server increases concurrent pressure on those two fixed resources while adding nothing to their capacity  -  it makes throughput worse, not better. It also doubles the queue-poll floor against the host database and doubles the per-office connection pools. And it moves the twelve recurring jobs from 'coordinated by one lock, one holder' to 'coordinated by one lock, with a documented open race about timestamp truncation'  -  accepting a correctness risk for a throughput loss.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: After the packet renderer is horizontally scaled beyond two workers and the SMTP relay's actual rate limit is measured, so there is real downstream capacity to feed. At that point measure whether job latency, not job throughput, is the complaint.

not_recommended.pattern: Introduce a message broker so the distributed event bus works across instances
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It is the correct fix for the real defect. ABP's default LocalDistributedEventBus silently does not cross processes, which is a genuine landmine for any multi-instance future, and ABP supports RabbitMQ, Kafka and Azure Service Bus as drop-in providers. A broker would also give the two outboxes a proper transport, decouple the packet renderer from synchronous pressure, and provide natural backpressure for exactly the burst problem that forced the worker pool to be pinned.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: There is no cross-process event requirement today because there is one instance. The durability a broker would provide already exists in two durable database outboxes that fail closed by configuration  -  the hard part is already built and it is built in the database, which this team can inspect with a SELECT. A broker adds a new stateful single point of failure with its own persistence, its own memory behaviour, its own failure modes, and its own operational vocabulary, to a system that has no observability to watch it and no one on call. It would be the sixth single point of failure on a box that already has five.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: When there are genuinely two or more instances AND a feature exists that requires cross-instance eventing that an outbox drain cannot satisfy. Introducing it before both conditions hold buys a liability, not a capability.

not_recommended.pattern: Add read replicas or a separate read model to cope with audit data volume
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: The measured ratio is over 100:1 against business data  -  roughly 1,450 audit rows and 2,689 property-change rows for 16 appointments. That volume will dominate index maintenance, backup duration, restore duration and query plans, and separating reads from writes is the textbook response. If a six-year retention policy is adopted, the audit tables become the largest thing in every office database by a wide margin.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: Readable secondary replicas are Enterprise-only, and Standard-edition Basic Availability Groups explicitly forbid read access on the secondary  -  so the mechanism is not available at the current edition anyway. More importantly, the problem is retention, not read contention. There is no reporting workload competing with OLTP; there is simply data nobody deletes. Deleting old audit rows on a schedule is a background job this team can write in a day. A read replica is an architecture with replication lag, a second failover unit per database, and a whole new class of 'why is this stale' bug. Solving a retention problem with a replication topology is how a small team acquires an operational burden it never needed.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: If a genuine reporting or analytics workload appears that must query historical audit data at a volume that measurably degrades transactional latency, and retention pruning has already been implemented and is insufficient.

not_recommended.pattern: Enable sticky sessions / session affinity when adding a second instance
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It is the standard reflex, it is one checkbox on essentially every load balancer, and it genuinely would make a second instance appear to work immediately even if the Data Protection key ring were not correctly shared. For a team with limited time it looks like exactly the kind of pragmatic shortcut that lets them ship.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It converts a startup-detectable configuration bug into an intermittent production one. If the Data Protection stack versions differ between images, affinity hides it  -  everything works until an instance restarts or fails, at which point every user pinned to it is logged out with no error anywhere explaining why. That is precisely the subtle failure this team cannot diagnose, purchased deliberately. And it buys nothing real: there is no SignalR, no WebSocket, and no in-process session state, so affinity has no correctness role to play. It also forfeits even load distribution and makes rolling deploys worse, which is the one thing a second instance was supposed to enable.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: Only if in-process, non-replicable per-user state is deliberately introduced  -  which would itself be a decision to reject. For this system as designed, never.

not_recommended.pattern: Shard offices across multiple SQL Server instances now, since the connection-string template almost supports it
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It is the natural evolution of database-per-tenant and the prerequisite is nearly in place: one configuration key relocates the office databases. Doing it while there is no real patient data is enormously cheaper than doing it later, and the system facts explicitly flag that this migration window is time-limited. Connection-pool arithmetic at 33 offices genuinely does look uncomfortable against a single four-vCPU instance.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: Eleven offices, sixteen appointments in one of them, and a database instance nowhere near saturation. Sharding solves a capacity problem that does not exist while creating a placement problem that would need a registry, per-shard deploys, per-shard migration reporting, and cross-shard reporting  -  all of which fail subtly rather than obviously. The connection-pool concern is real but has a far cheaper fix: bound Max Pool Size explicitly. Note also that the current template is global, so today sharding is all-or-nothing; making it per-office is a genuinely useful change, but making it per-office is not the same as using it.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: When measured connection pressure or buffer-pool contention on a single instance is documented, or when one office's regulatory posture or data volume demands isolation from the others. Build the per-office connection-string capability now; exercise it then.

not_recommended.pattern: Move to Kubernetes to get rolling deploys, health-gated rollout and declarative topology
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: This is the strongest of the rejected options and it deserves to be taken seriously. It would solve real, present pain: deployment is entirely manual over SSH with no CD, the --env-file trap silently blanks every secret, and the nginx stale-upstream trap silently breaks routing after every backend rebuild  -  both of which are exactly the class of problem a declarative orchestrator eliminates. Microsoft's current EF Core guidance describes the one-shot migration job pattern in orchestrator terms, so the migrator design would translate directly. It would also give restart-on-failure and health-gated rollout, which this system has none of.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It substitutes one system this team does not understand for a much larger one they understand less, and the substitution changes the failure character in the wrong direction. The compose traps fail loudly  -  a blank database password stops the stack, a stale upstream IP returns errors. Orchestrator failures are subtle: a pod evicted under memory pressure, a volume that binds to the wrong node, an ingress controller that normalises the Host header and silently breaks tenancy, a readiness probe that passes while the application is degraded. With no aggregation, no metrics and no alerting, none of those are visible. And it does not solve the data tier: Microsoft states that a containerised SQL Server recovered by an orchestrator 'isn't truly highly available'. The two loud traps are each a one-line fix in a deploy script; the orchestrator is a permanent second system to operate.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: When there is a third engineer who owns infrastructure as their actual job, or when the accumulated cost of manual deploys demonstrably exceeds the cost of operating the platform. Fix the two named traps with a scripted deploy first  -  that captures most of the benefit for a tiny fraction of the cost, and it makes the eventual migration easier rather than harder.

not_recommended.pattern: Remove the DbMigrator and migrate on application startup, now that EF Core locks migrations
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It is a genuinely defensible simplification and Microsoft's own guidance has softened toward it: since EF Core 9 the database-wide lock makes concurrent runtime migration safe, and the documentation now says runtime migration 'can be acceptable for applications that prefer simple deployment'. It would delete a container, a compose dependency, and a class of 'the migrator did not finish' confusion.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: The gate on service_completed_successfully is currently the only mechanism preventing an application process from serving traffic against a half-migrated fleet, and Microsoft's guidance in the same document is explicit in the other direction: 'don't make every application replica run migrations from its entrypoint.' The lock protects one database at a time; it does nothing about fleet consistency across 12 to 34 databases. Removing the one-shot job would trade a loud, gating failure for a quiet, partial one  -  the exact wrong direction for this team's stated preference.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: Not for this system. The one-shot job is the recommended pattern and it is already implemented; the work belongs in its error reporting, not its existence.

not_recommended.pattern: Autoscale the API tier
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It is default practice, it costs nothing to configure on most platforms, and it would absorb any future burst without anyone having to think about it. Given that the team cannot watch the system, letting it react automatically has real appeal.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: There is nothing to react to. The load driver here is a fixed schedule  -  twelve recurring jobs, three of them every fifteen minutes  -  not a user-traffic curve, and the tiers behind the API (a two-worker renderer, one SMTP relay, one database) are all fixed capacity. An autoscaler would add instances that cannot help and that each multiply the per-office connection pools against a fixed database. Worse, it makes the number of running instances nondeterministic, which in an environment with no instance-level observability means nobody can answer 'how many are running and are they all healthy'. It adds variance to a system whose main deficit is the ability to observe variance.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: If user-driven load ever becomes genuinely bursty AND the packet renderer and database can absorb the resulting concurrency AND per-instance health is observable. All three, not any one.

what_would_change_the_answer: The __tenant resolver test. If the query-string, header, route or cookie resolvers are live alongside the Host resolver, then tenancy is not Host-only, and the entire topology story  -  that a cell can own a DNS suffix, that Host preservation is the whole edge contract, that a bare IP cannot reach the application  -  is false. This is a fifteen-minute curl test and it should be run before any other work in this area. It also changes the security posture, not just the topology.

What the migrator actually does on a per-office failure. If it exits zero and reports success while some offices are unmigrated, that single fact makes every other recommendation here unsafe, because no conclusion about fleet consistency can be trusted. Determine this first; it is a one-line experiment (break one office, run the migrator, echo $?).

Whether real patient data has landed. Every argument for doing structural work now rests on the stated fact that all records are synthetic. The moment a practice takes a real booking, the cost of relocating databases, changing connection-string derivation, or replacing the storage layer multiplies, and the recommendation shifts from 'build the option cheaply now' to 'change as little as possible'.

Whether the one-developer-week-per-month figure is real. It is described as an estimate, not a measurement, and a separate code-standard remediation has already claimed part of it. If sustained availability is below four hours a month, the recommendation should shrink to just two items  -  the CI pending-model-changes gate and one tested restore  -  because everything else will silently not happen and a half-implemented plan is worse than a small complete one.

Whether the packet renderer stays at two workers. It is the actual throughput ceiling and the stated reason the Hangfire worker pool is pinned. Widening it changes which tier is the bottleneck, which is the single fact that would make a second processing server worth reconsidering.

Whether deploy outages become commercially unacceptable. Today every deploy is an outage and that appears to be tolerated. If practices start booking during business hours and a mid-day deploy becomes impossible, rolling deploys become a hard requirement, which forces a two-instance web tier and forces expand/contract (backward-compatible) migrations as a standing discipline  -  a much larger change than the role split.

Office count growth beyond roughly 33, or one office growing disproportionately. Either pushes connection-pool arithmetic and buffer-pool contention from theoretical to measured, and makes per-office connection-string placement a hard requirement rather than a nice-to-have.

Team size. A third engineer, particularly one who owns infrastructure, flips the calculus on orchestration and on horizontal scale, because both are gated on operability rather than on technical merit.

The MinIO replacement timeline. The archived, unmaintained storage layer will force a change, and the external partner's re-credentialing schedule is the long pole and is outside the team's control. If that migration has to happen anyway, it should be sequenced into the same window as any other topology change rather than done separately  -  which could justify doing more structural work at once than this recommendation otherwise supports.

Confirmation of whether Hangfire issue #1208's recurring-job double-fire race still affects 1.8.x. If it does, job idempotency moves from 'should be verified' to 'must be audited job by job before anything else changes', because the three fifteen-minute reconciliation jobs are the ones most likely to be affected and the most consequential if they double-run.

Whether ABP's dynamic definition-store in-memory cache interval is bounded and acceptable. I could not read the source directly to confirm the default check interval. If it turns out to be long or unbounded, cross-instance permission convergence becomes a real obstacle to a second instance rather than a manageable one, and the horizontal option moves from 'conditional' to 'no'.

results.claim: [38] REASONING: 33 offices x 100 default Max Pool Size = 3,300 pooled connections per process, 6,600 across two processes, against a 512 worker-thread limit at 4 logical CPUs; pool exhaustion and worker starvation are different limits reached by different paths.
results.evidence_quote: A connection pool is created for each unique connection string. ... up to the maximum pool size specified (100 is the default)
results.correction: The premises are sound and the arithmetic is right, but the juxtaposition of 3,300 against 512 invites a false comparison and should be rewritten. Per the max-worker-threads page, 'A worker thread is assigned only to active requests and is released once the request is serviced. This happens even if the user session/connection on which the request was made remains open'  -  so 3,300 open connections do not consume 3,300 worker threads, and SQL Server routinely holds far more connections than workers. The defensible statement is that concurrent *active* requests, not open connections, are what meet the 512 ceiling. Also, 3,300 is a per-process ceiling only if all 33 connection strings differ in more than the database name in ways the app actually opens concurrently; add the host/Hangfire storage pools to the count. Correct as reasoning, mislabelled if presented as two comparable numbers.

results.evidence_quote: If LoadBalanceTimeout (or Connection Lifetime) isn't set (default value = 0), the connection pooler removes a connection from the pool after it has been idle for approximately 4-8 minutes ... If MinPoolSize is either not specified in the connection string or is specified as zero, the connections in the pool will be closed after a period of inactivity.
results.correction: The mechanism is correctly sourced and the 15-minute > 8-minute inference is valid for a database touched only by the sweep. Two qualifications: the reaping window is conditioned on LoadBalanceTimeout/Connection Lifetime being unset (default 0), which should be stated; and 'almost always' overreaches for any office database that also receives interactive request traffic inside the window, which will keep its pool warm. The TLS-handshake component depends on Encrypt being effectively true (see claim 33) and applies to new *physical* connections  -  which is exactly the case here, so the conclusion holds, but say 'new physical connection' rather than 'pooled connection establishment'.

results.claim: [40] REASONING: the lock-timeout path logs at Debug, so under Information-level Serilog a server that never wins the lock emits nothing; if the lock holder stalls, all twelve recurring jobs stop fleet-wide with no log above Debug  -  archetypal silent degradation.

results.correction: The first half is correct and important: the timeout path is Debug-only, so at Information level a losing server is silent. The second half overstates. The source's own comment says the timeout normally means another server did the work, so silence is the expected healthy steady state, not evidence of stoppage  -  which is precisely why it is a poor signal, but it is not the same as 'all twelve jobs stop'. A stalled holder is a real but separate failure mode whose duration is bounded by the storage's lock expiry, not by the 1-minute acquisition timeout, and it is not established by this file. Rewrite as: the Debug-only log means neither the healthy nor the stalled case is distinguishable above Debug, so the absence of recurring-job execution is undetectable from logs  -  which is the actual gap, and is a stronger argument than the overstated one.
