vendor_neutrality_violations: No cloud-vendor recommendation found. I checked all fourteen requirements for a 'therefore use <product>' construction and none is present: no hyperscaler, managed service, or commercial SKU is recommended anywhere. Requirements 3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 and 14 are cleanly capability-phrased (e.g. 'the store holding the Data Protection key ring MUST NOT be able to evict or expire those keys' names a property, not a store). The items below are borderline and reported for strictness, not because any names a vendor as a choice.

BORDERLINE - Requirement 1 ('Whether a process runs background processing (the Hangfire processing server and ABP background workers) MUST be controlled by explicit configuration'): two product names, Hangfire and ABP, appear inside a normative MUST. They are the incumbent components and read as scope rather than endorsement, but as written the requirement can only be satisfied by those specific products - a replacement scheduler would not literally comply. Neutral rewording: 'Whether a process runs background processing - the job-processing server and the recurring-worker host - MUST be controlled by explicit configuration', with the current components named parenthetically as the present implementation.

BORDERLINE - Requirement 4 ('Both application processes MUST agree on the Data Protection application discriminator AND on the Data Protection stack version'): 'Data Protection' is a named framework component (ASP.NET Core Data Protection), and 'application discriminator' is its specific API surface. This is the mechanism actually in use rather than a selection among alternatives, so it is not a vendor recommendation. Neutral rewording if strictness is wanted: 'Both processes MUST derive the same key-isolation identity for the shared key ring, and MUST run compatible versions of the payload-protection stack; both values MUST be emitted at startup.'

BORDERLINE - Requirement 9 ('Continuous integration MUST fail the build if any DbContext's model has pending changes relative to its last migration'): 'DbContext' is EF Core-specific vocabulary. Descriptive of the codebase rather than a recommendation; the capability-neutral form is 'if any mapped data model has changes not represented in its latest migration'.

BORDERLINE - Requirement 7 (the __tenant query string, route value, header and cookie resolvers): '__tenant' is an ABP-specific default parameter name. It is cited as the concrete artifact that must be proven unreachable, which is evidence-of-behaviour usage and correct here; only note that the requirement should also cover any renamed equivalent if AbpTenantResolveOptions changes the parameter name, otherwise the test proves less than it appears to.

research.area: State and session architecture: where the distributed cache, the ASP.NET Core Data Protection key ring, and the distributed lock should live  -  and whether they belong in the same store
research.design_space: The viable 2026 design space is not "which Redis topology" but "how many distinct classes of shared mutable state exist, and what does each actually require". An ASP.NET Core/ABP system of this shape has at most five: (a) derived, reconstructible cache (permission grants, settings, features, application configuration, dynamic claims) whose source of truth is a database  -  loss costs latency and database load, nothing else; (b) cryptographic key material (the Data Protection key ring) which is derivable from nothing, is written roughly four times a year, is read once per process start and once per ~24 hours, and whose loss is unrecoverable; (c) coordination primitives (leases/locks) which are ephemeral by definition and need a single authoritative arbiter and fail-closed semantics, not durability; (d) server-side session state, which this system deliberately does not have (cookie-based auth, no SignalR, no AddSession); and (e) durable work queues, which live in SQL Server here via Hangfire. The placement options for each are: in-process memory; a co-located sidecar container; a dedicated instance on a separate host; a replicated pair with automated failover; a sharded cluster; a managed cache service (a capability where an operator other than you runs it, and where persistence is typically an opt-in tier feature rather than a default); the relational database already in the system; or a plain filesystem/object store. The industry default  -  one Redis holding all of it  -  is a *collapse* of classes (a), (b) and (c) into one durability contract, and it is defensible only when that contract is the strictest of the three. It is not: Redis documents AOF `everysec` as "you may lose 1 second of data if there is a disaster", while class (b) tolerates zero loss. In 2026 the genuinely modern answer for small systems has moved toward *unbundling* rather than toward more Redis: put reconstructible cache in a cache, put key material in whatever store is already backed up, and either eliminate the lock or back it with the transactional store. Redis's own eviction documentation reaches the same conclusion from the other direction, advising that mixing caching and persistent keys in one instance is a reason to "consider running two separate Redis instances".

options.name: Status quo  -  one co-located Redis holding cache + Data Protection key ring + lock provider, AOF on a named volume
options.how_it_works: A single redis container on the same VM, 512 MB container cap, AOF persistence to a named docker volume. ABP's AbpCachingStackExchangeRedisModule uses it as IDistributedCache; Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection.StackExchangeRedis stores the key ring in it as a single Redis LIST key under CaseEvaluation-Protection-Keys with no TTL; Medallion.Threading registers a Redis lock provider against it in both API and AuthServer.
options.operational_cost: Setup: zero, already built. Ongoing: appears to be zero, which is the trap  -  the real ongoing cost is a standing, unbudgeted obligation to never run FLUSHALL/FLUSHDB, never set an allkeys-* eviction policy, never prune the volume, and never let the container OOM. That obligation is currently undocumented and held only in whoever remembers it. Assumes knowledge (Redis persistence semantics, DataProtection key-ring storage internals) that neither SDE 1 has been given.
options.why: The cache part of this is correct and should be left alone. The key ring part is the problem: an unreconstructible secret is stored in a component whose administrative vocabulary includes a bulk-delete command that is the standard remedy for a poisoned cache, whose documented durability is one second of possible loss, and whose default memory behaviour under a container cap is to be OOM-killed rather than to evict. Microsoft's own key-storage page carries an explicit warning that Redis does not persist by default and that this 'can cause Data Protection to issue new keys, invalidating previously protected data'. The team has enabled AOF, which addresses the specific default Microsoft warns about, but not the eviction, flush, volume-loss or OOM paths.

options.name: Split by durability class  -  cache stays in the co-located Redis; key ring moves to the host SQL Server database; lock moves to SQL Server or is removed
options.how_it_works: Redis keeps only reconstructible cache and becomes genuinely disposable (AOF can be turned off, maxmemory set, allkeys-lru policy). The Data Protection key ring moves to a dedicated DbContext implementing IDataProtectionKeyContext, pinned to the HOST connection string and explicitly non-tenant-aware, encrypted at rest with ProtectKeysWithCertificate using a mounted read-only PFX (the pattern already operated for the OpenIddict signing certificate, with a different certificate), and UnprotectKeysWithAnyCertificate configured for rotation. SetApplicationName stays identical in both processes. If a distributed lock is ever actually needed, DistributedLock.SqlServer (sp_getapplock) from the same Medallion library replaces the Redis provider behind the same IDistributedLockProvider interface.
options.operational_cost: Setup: ~12-16 hours total  -  4-6 h for the key DbContext plus one migration in the host migration set only, 2-3 h for certificate generation/mount/rotation wiring, 1-2 h for a pre-cutover copy of the existing keys (or zero, if done now while all data is synthetic and a mass logout is free), 1 h for Redis maxmemory/policy/AOF changes, 2 h for a cache-reachability health check, 2 h for one rehearsed restore test. Ongoing: ~0.5 h/month, essentially certificate-expiry watch. Assumes only skills the team already exercises: EF Core migrations, docker volume mounts, appsettings wiring.
options.why: It removes the only piece of state in the entire system that cannot be reconstructed from the databases out of the only component whose contract permits losing it, and puts it where the team's single real backup mechanism (native BACKUP DATABASE of the host database) already covers it with no new artefact to remember. Every failure mode it introduces is loud: SQL unreachable at startup means the app cannot start (which is already true); an expired or missing certificate means a hard startup failure; a missing migration means an invalid-object-name exception. None of them is a silent data-loss path. It also shrinks the AuthServer's Redis dependency to optional-cache only, which materially reduces the blast radius on the login path.

options.name: Two co-located Redis instances  -  one 'cache' (no persistence, allkeys-lru) and one 'persistent' (AOF, noeviction) for the key ring
options.how_it_works: A second redis container in the same compose file with its own volume, its own memory cap, and its own connection string; DataProtection points at the persistent one, ABP caching at the ephemeral one.
options.operational_cost: Setup: ~4-6 hours. Ongoing: ~1-2 h/month  -  but the ongoing cost is deceptive, because it adds a second container to the backup story, a second thing to remember not to prune, a second thing to health-check, and a second set of Redis config to keep straight. It also multiplies the compose --env-file trap surface the team has already been bitten by.
options.why: This is precisely what Redis's own eviction documentation suggests when mixing cache and persistent keys, and it is a legitimate answer. It is rejected here because it solves the eviction and FLUSH problems while leaving the harder ones  -  the one-second AOF loss window, the unclean-shutdown/OOM path, and above all the fact that a Redis volume is not part of any backup this team actually runs  -  completely untouched. It buys separation at the cost of a second stateful component, when a table in a database that is already backed up buys the same separation plus durability plus backup coverage for less.

options.name: Dedicated Redis on a separate host
options.how_it_works: Redis moves off the application VM onto its own machine, reachable over the private network.
options.operational_cost: Setup: ~8-12 hours (host provisioning, network, TLS or network isolation, auth, firewalling). Ongoing: ~2-4 h/month (patching a second OS, monitoring a second host). Assumes basic Linux host operations the team does not currently do for anything but the one VM.
options.why: It correctly decouples cache capacity and cache restarts from application restarts, and it is the right shape once there is more than one application instance. But it does nothing about durability class  -  a dedicated Redis is still a Redis  -  and today, with one application instance, it converts a local socket into a network hop and adds a second machine to operate in exchange for no reduction in blast radius. This becomes right at the same moment a second application host appears, not before.

options.name: Replicated pair with Redis Sentinel
options.how_it_works: One primary, one or more replicas, and at least three Sentinel processes monitoring; Sentinel promotes a replica on primary failure and clients discover the current primary through Sentinel.
options.operational_cost: Setup: ~24-40 hours including a genuine failover drill. Ongoing: ~4-8 h/month, and a standing obligation to rehearse failover, because an HA cluster nobody has ever failed over is not an HA cluster. Assumes distributed-systems operational literacy the team explicitly does not have.
options.why: Rejected on three separate documented grounds, any one of which is sufficient. First, Redis's Sentinel documentation states that Docker port remapping 'break[s] Sentinel auto discovery of other Sentinel processes and the list of replicas for a master'  -  this entire deployment is docker-compose. Second, it requires 'at least three Sentinel instances' on machines 'believed to fail in an independent way', and there is one VM. Third, and decisively, Redis states that 'Sentinel + Redis distributed system does not guarantee that acknowledged writes are retained during failures, since Redis uses asynchronous replication'  -  so it does not actually make the key ring safe, and the key ring is the only thing here worth making safe. It buys availability for a cache whose unavailability is already survivable.

options.name: Redis Cluster
options.how_it_works: Sharded keyspace across multiple primaries with replicas, cluster-aware client, hash-slot routing.
options.operational_cost: Setup: 40+ hours. Ongoing: 8+ h/month. Assumes cluster operations expertise.
options.why: There is no capacity problem. The cached working set is permission grants, settings and application configuration for at most 33 small tenants, measured in tens of megabytes. Clustering introduces CROSSSLOT constraints on multi-key commands (which ABP's SetManyAsync/GetManyAsync uses) and a cluster-aware client requirement, for zero benefit. Included only to be explicit that capacity is not the axis this decision turns on.

options.name: Managed cache service (as a capability, not a product)
options.how_it_works: Someone other than this team operates the cache process, patches it, monitors it, and offers optional persistence and backup as configurable features.
options.operational_cost: Setup: ~4-8 hours of integration. Ongoing: near zero for the process itself, but non-zero for the connection/credential/network path. Assumes almost nothing operationally, which is its real value here.
options.why: Genuinely attractive for the CACHE. Removing a stateful container from a stack operated by two SDE 1s with no on-call is a real win, and the capability requirement is worth recording for the platform exercise. But it is not an answer to the key-ring problem, and treating it as one is the specific mistake to avoid: Microsoft's own Data Protection page documents that persistence on a managed Redis is a tier/feature you must remember to enable ('Azure Cache for Redis needs a premium or higher tier to enable data persistence'). Moving a cache under someone else's management does not change its contract from 'cache' to 'system of record'. Vendor selection is deliberately downstream of this exercise; the requirement is stated as a capability below.

options.name: No shared cache at all  -  in-process memory cache per process, key ring in the database
options.how_it_works: Redis is removed entirely (ABP supports Redis:IsEnabled=false, falling back to the in-memory IDistributedCache); each of API and AuthServer holds its own cache; the key ring lives in SQL Server.
options.operational_cost: Setup: ~6-8 hours (mostly the key-ring move, which is shared with the recommended option). Ongoing: zero  -  one fewer container, one fewer volume, one fewer secret. Assumes nothing.
options.why: Worth taking seriously because it is nearly right, and because evaluating it reveals what Redis is actually for in this system. At current volumes Redis is not carrying a cache workload that justifies its existence  -  its two real jobs are holding the key ring (misplaced) and acting as a cross-process coherence bus so that API and AuthServer agree on permissions and settings. That second job is genuine: with two independent in-memory caches, a permission or setting change made through the API would not invalidate the AuthServer's copy, and stale authorisation state that heals only on process restart is exactly the class of subtle failure this team will not notice. Rejected for that reason, and because it forecloses a second application instance. But it establishes that the cache tier is small, cheap and replaceable  -  which is why the cache is the wrong thing to spend the HA budget on.

research.recommendation:
Split the state by durability class, and do it now while every record is synthetic.

The key question  -  is it correct to keep cache, key ring and lock in one Redis?  -  has a clean answer: no for the key ring, yes for the cache, and the lock should not be in Redis either but for a different reason. This is my judgement, argued from sourced facts below; the facts are cited, the conclusion is mine.

The three have contradictory loss functions. Cache loss is self-healing: ABP hides cache errors by default (HideErrors defaults to true) and falls back to querying the original source, so the correct behaviour on cache loss is degrade-and-repopulate, and the application already does that. Lock loss is a bounded correctness window that Redis itself says a delayed restart covers, and there are no application acquisition sites today anyway. Key-ring loss is unrecoverable and total: Microsoft states that a deleted key makes protected data 'permanently undecipherable' with 'no emergency override', and that losing the ring 'leads to users being logged out of an app that uses the standard ASP.NET Core cookie authentication'. One of these three is not like the others, and it is the one currently stored as a single un-TTL'd Redis LIST key sharing a keyspace with cache entries.

Concretely:

(1) Move the Data Protection key ring to the HOST SQL Server database via PersistKeysToDbContext on a dedicated DbContext that implements IDataProtectionKeyContext, is explicitly non-tenant-aware, and is pinned to the host connection string. This is the decisive move and it is small. The reason to prefer SQL over a backed-up bind-mount is not elegance  -  it is that the host database is the only thing this team actually backs up, so the ring rides along automatically with no new artefact anyone has to remember. Three traps must be handled deliberately: the DbContext must not resolve its connection string through ICurrentTenant (the key ring is loaded lazily, possibly inside a tenant-scoped request, and would otherwise land in an office database); the DataProtectionKeys table belongs in the host migration set only, which interacts with the documented two-DbContext hazard; and the db-migrator loop that has no per-tenant error handling is not involved here, which is a small mercy.

(2) Encrypt the ring at rest with ProtectKeysWithCertificate against a mounted read-only PFX  -  the pattern the team already operates for the OpenIddict signing certificate, with a *different* certificate  -  and configure UnprotectKeysWithAnyCertificate so rotation is possible. This is not optional polish: Microsoft warns that specifying an explicit persistence location 'deregisters the default key encryption at rest mechanism' so keys are stored unencrypted, and recommends an explicit mechanism for production. On Linux with no vault, X.509 is the only in-box cross-platform option, and choosing a vault is deliberately the next exercise's job.

(3) Having removed the ring, make the Redis genuinely disposable: set an explicit maxmemory below the 512 MB container cap (Redis defaults to unlimited on 64-bit, so the container cap currently guarantees an OOM kill rather than an eviction), set maxmemory-policy to allkeys-lru, and turn AOF off. A pure cache does not need persistence, and turning it off deletes the disk-full-during-AOF-rewrite failure mode and, more importantly, the illusion that there is a backup of Redis. Turning AOF off is only safe *after* the ring is out, and doing it in that order is itself a useful forcing function.

(4) Do not use the Redis lock provider for anything that must be correct. Redis documents the single-instance lock as viable only 'in applications where a race condition from time to time is acceptable', and documents failover-based locking as an outright safety violation. Leave the registration in place if ABP framework code wants it, but if the team ever needs a lock for correctness  -  the obvious candidate is preventing two API instances from double-running the per-office recurring sweeps  -  use DistributedLock.SqlServer (sp_getapplock) behind the same interface. One fewer failure domain, and it fails closed: no SQL means the job does not run, which is correct for a job whose only effect is writing to SQL.

(5) Make cache failure loud. Keep HideErrors true  -  fail-open is right for a cache  -  but add a cache-reachability health check and surface the ABP cache-error log event. Today, Redis dying produces a silent, permanent 100% cache-miss regime with elevated SQL load and no alarm. That is precisely the slow degradation this team will not notice, and it is the one place the current design fails subtly.

Timing matters more than usual. Cutting over the key store logs every user out. Right now that costs nothing because every record is synthetic and there are no real bookings. The moment a real practice takes a real appointment, this becomes a change that needs a maintenance window, a pre-cutover key copy, and a communication plan. Do it while it is free.
research.operational_cost_of_recommendation:
Setup: roughly 12-16 developer-hours, i.e. under half of one developer-week. Broken down: 4-6 h for the dedicated key DbContext, IDataProtectionKeyContext implementation, non-tenant-aware connection wiring in both API and AuthServer, and one migration in the host migration set only; 2-3 h to generate and mount a key-encryption certificate and wire ProtectKeysWithCertificate plus UnprotectKeysWithAnyCertificate; 0 h for key migration if done now (a mass logout is free while all data is synthetic) or 1-2 h later to copy existing key XML into the new store before cutover; 1 h to set Redis maxmemory/maxmemory-policy and disable AOF; 2 h for a cache-reachability health check and a log-based alert on ABP's hidden cache errors; 2 h for one rehearsed restore test that ends in a successful login.

Ongoing: approximately 0.5 hours per month. The key ring self-rotates every 90 days with no human involvement (Microsoft: 'When a key expires, the app automatically generates a new key and sets the new key as the active key'). The only recurring obligation is watching the key-encryption certificate's expiry, and the only recurring observation is a glance at the cache-error counter.

Threshold: this remains operable at 2 hours per month of infrastructure time. Below that, the single thing that decays is certificate-expiry watch  -  and that was chosen deliberately because it fails obviously (a hard startup failure, not silent data loss). Total neglect of this design produces a visible outage, never a quiet corruption. That is the whole point of the choice.

Treat the stated one-developer-week-per-month as unverified. If the real figure turns out to be closer to 8 hours a month, this recommendation still holds  -  it is roughly two months of that budget to set up and then near-free. What does NOT hold below about 16 hours per month is any of the rejected HA options: Sentinel and cluster each need 24-40 h of setup and 4-8 h/month plus a quarterly failover drill, and below that threshold they decay into decorative high availability  -  extra failure modes with no rehearsed recovery, which is strictly worse than a single instance.

Cost of the alternative recommended fallback (bind-mounted key directory instead of SQL): about 4 h setup instead of 6-9, but +0.5 h/month forever and one more artefact that must be remembered in every backup and restore conversation. That ongoing memory tax is why it is the fallback and not the recommendation.

evidence.claim: The key ring is cached in memory and the backing store is only checked approximately every 24 hours or when the current default key expires, whichever comes first  -  so the key store is not on the request hot path.

evidence.claim: When the key store is briefly unreachable and a cached key ring already exists, ASP.NET Core extends the cached ring's lifetime by 2 minutes and rethrows the exception to the immediate caller only  -  so the symptom is roughly one failed request per 2-minute window, not an outage. On a cold start with no cached ring, all callers block and each retries until one succeeds.

evidence.threshold_or_limit: 2 minutes. Verbatim code comments: 'we'll create a new keyring object whose expiration is now + some short period of time (currently 2 min)'; 'The immediate caller should fail so that they can report the error up the chain.'; 'if there is no usable existing cached keyring, all callers must block until the keyring exists'; 'If we don't have an existing keyring (perhaps because this is the first call), then there's nothing to extend, so each subsequent caller will keep going down this code path until one succeeds.'
