evidence.claim: Redis is not, at this system's data volumes, carrying a cache workload that would justify it on performance grounds; its two real jobs are holding the key ring and acting as a cross-process coherence bus between exactly two processes (API and AuthServer). Removing the shared cache would leave permission and setting changes made in one process invisible to the other until restart.
evidence.source_name: My reasoning from the measured system facts (16 appointments, 11 offices, two processes, ABP cache-aside semantics)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: n/a  -  architectural judgement, not a sourced fact. The underlying ABP mechanism (removal of a distributed cache entry on permission/setting change, visible to all processes sharing the cache) is documented cache-aside behaviour; the conclusion about this system's scale is mine and should be argued with.

capability_requirements.requirement: The platform must provide a durable store for cryptographic key material that is independent of the cache tier and is covered by the same backup and restore procedure as business data.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: The Data Protection key ring is the only state in the system that cannot be reconstructed from the databases. Microsoft documents that a deleted key makes protected data permanently undecipherable with no emergency override. Everything else in the state tier is derivable.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft Learn key-management: 'all data protected by the key is permanently undecipherable, and there's no emergency override'; system fact that the ring currently lives in a Redis volume with no confirmed backup.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: On a running system with an established logged-in session, stop the cache service, delete its data volume entirely, and start it again. Then refresh the authenticated page. The session must remain valid and no user must be logged out. Separately, restore the system from its most recent backup onto a clean host and confirm that the same key IDs are present in the restored key store (list them via IKeyManager.GetAllKeys or by reading the store directly).

capability_requirements.requirement: Total loss of the cache tier must not prevent any user-facing request from succeeding.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Cache contents are derived from the databases; the correct behaviour is degrade-and-repopulate. ABP already implements this via HideErrors defaulting to true. Making it a stated requirement prevents a future platform choice from quietly converting the cache into a hard dependency.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: ABP documentation: cache errors are hidden, logged, and the framework will 'query from the original source'; system fact that the cache holds permission grants, settings and application configuration whose source of truth is SQL Server.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Stop the cache service entirely. Then, without restarting the application: perform a login, load an authenticated page that requires a permission check, and perform an authenticated write. All three must return 2xx. Response times may increase. Any 5xx fails the test.

capability_requirements.requirement: Loss or unreachability of the cache tier must produce an externally observable unhealthy signal within five minutes.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Because the previous requirement makes cache loss survivable, it is by construction silent. A permanent 100% cache-miss regime with elevated database load and no alarm is exactly the slow degradation a two-person team without on-call will not notice. This is the one place the current design fails subtly rather than obviously.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: ABP HideErrors default true (errors hidden and logged only); system fact that there is no metrics aggregation, no APM and no alerting, and container logs rotate at 10 MB x 5.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Stop the cache service. Within five minutes, an HTTP health endpoint must report a degraded or unhealthy status naming the cache, and a notification must reach a human by a channel that does not require someone to be looking at a dashboard. Restart the cache and confirm the signal clears.

capability_requirements.requirement: Key material at rest must be encrypted by a mechanism whose decryption key is not stored in the same medium as the encrypted key ring.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Specifying an explicit key persistence location deregisters the default at-rest encryption, so the ring is stored as plaintext XML unless a mechanism is configured explicitly. Microsoft recommends configuring one for production. This is also the specification most likely to move from Addressable to Required if the 2025 HIPAA Security Rule NPRM is finalised.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft Learn: 'the data protection system deregisters the default key encryption at rest mechanism, so keys are no longer encrypted at rest. It's recommended that you additionally specify an explicit key encryption mechanism for production deployments.' 45 CFR 164.312(a)(2)(iv) (currently Addressable).
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Read the raw stored key ring  -  the SQL row, the file, or the Redis value, whichever applies. Every key element must appear as an encryptedKey/EncryptedXml payload. If any base64 masterKey material is directly readable in the stored representation, the test fails.

capability_requirements.requirement: No routine cache-maintenance action available to an operator may destroy key material.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: The standard remedy for a poisoned or stale cache is a bulk flush. If the key ring shares a keyspace with the cache, that single command is an irreversible, fleet-wide, unrecoverable logout with no confirmation prompt. This is the highest-severity finding in this area and it is a design property, not a discipline problem.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System fact that the key ring is a Redis key in the same instance and keyspace as the ABP cache; Microsoft's statement that deleted keys are permanently undecipherable; Redis's own advice to run separate instances when mixing caching and persistent keys.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Follow the team's written 'clear the cache' runbook step exactly as an operator would (for a Redis cache, that is FLUSHALL or FLUSHDB). Then restart both application processes and present a session cookie issued before the flush. It must still validate. If any user is logged out, the test fails.

capability_requirements.requirement: All processes sharing a key ring must be deployed as a unit, with an identical application name and the same Data Protection stack version.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Microsoft lists the matching stack version alongside the matching application name as a joint requirement for sharing protected payloads. A partial deploy that rebuilds one process and not the other is a documented incompatibility that would present as 'login works but the API rejects the cookie'  -  a symptom nobody would attribute to a version skew.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft Learn, Configure Data Protection: 'Configure SetApplicationName in each app with the same value. Use the same version of the Data Protection API stack across the apps.' System fact that SetApplicationName is set identically in both AuthServer and API today.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Log the resolved ApplicationDiscriminator on startup in both processes and assert the two values are byte-identical. Then assert that both images resolve the same Microsoft.AspNetCore.App shared-framework version (or the same explicit Data Protection package version). A deployment pipeline that can ship one process without the other fails this requirement regardless of the current version state.

capability_requirements.requirement: Tenant isolation in the shared cache must be verified by test, not assumed from the framework.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Every office has its own database, and there is no cross-database query anywhere in the system. The cache is therefore the single component where tenant boundaries are enforced by a string prefix rather than by a physical boundary  -  and that prefix is added by ABP's typed cache but not by the untyped ASP.NET Core IDistributedCache. In a per-tenant-database architecture, a cache key collision is the one place a tenancy bug becomes a disclosure rather than a 'tenant not found'.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: ABP documentation: tenant-id prefixing is a behaviour of the generic IDistributedCache<TCacheItem>, disableable via IgnoreMultiTenancy; Microsoft multitenancy guidance: 'your application is solely responsible for keeping tenant data separate'; system fact that untyped usage does not prefix.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: With at least two tenants populated, grant a distinctive permission to a user in tenant A only. Exercise the application as both tenants. Then enumerate every key in the cache (SCAN, not KEYS) and assert that every key produced by a tenant-scoped code path contains a tenant discriminator. Separately, grep the codebase for injections of the non-generic IDistributedCache and assert each one is either tenant-agnostic by design or explicitly namespaced.

capability_requirements.requirement: Any distributed lock relied on for correctness must be arbitrated by a single authoritative node, must fail closed when that node is unreachable, and must not depend on asynchronous replication for its safety property.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Redis documents that a primary/replica Redis lock is an outright safety violation because replication is asynchronous, and that a single-instance Redis lock is acceptable only 'in applications where a race condition from time to time is acceptable'  -  which nobody on this team has chosen. The provider is currently registered in both processes with no application acquisition sites, so its semantics are inherited rather than decided.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Redis Distributed Locks doc: the A/B failover race labelled 'SAFETY VIOLATION!'; the single-instance caveat; the recommendation to implement fencing tokens. System fact: RedisDistributedSynchronizationProvider registered in API and AuthServer with no acquisition sites in src.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Identify every code path that acquires a lock (today: none  -  assert that, and the requirement is trivially met). For any lock added later: make the lock store unreachable and attempt the guarded operation. It must decline to run and log the refusal. It must never proceed on the assumption that an unreachable lock store means the lock is free.

capability_requirements.requirement: The cache process must have an explicit memory ceiling below its container or host ceiling, together with an eviction policy, so that memory pressure causes eviction rather than process termination.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Redis defaults maxmemory to 0 (unlimited) on 64-bit, while Docker enforces its limit by having the kernel kill the process. A container cap without a Redis cap therefore guarantees an unclean shutdown rather than a graceful degradation  -  and unclean shutdown is precisely the condition under which AOF everysec loses writes. SHOULD rather than MUST because once the key ring is moved out, the consequence is a cache restart, which the application survives.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Redis eviction doc: maxmemory 0 is 'the default behavior for 64-bit systems'; Docker: 'By default, if an out-of-memory (OOM) error occurs, the kernel kills processes in a container'; system fact: redis container capped at 512 MB.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: CONFIG GET maxmemory must return a non-zero value strictly below the container limit, and CONFIG GET maxmemory-policy must return an allkeys-* policy. Then write data until the ceiling is crossed: the process must survive, INFO stats evicted_keys must increase, and the container must not restart. Note that an allkeys-* policy is only safe once no unreconstructible data is in the instance.

capability_requirements.requirement: Reading the key store must not be on the request hot path; a key-store outage that begins after startup must not take the application down.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: ASP.NET Core caches the key ring in memory and only rechecks the backing store roughly every 24 hours, extending the cached ring by 2 minutes on a refresh failure and surfacing the error to one caller. This is desirable behaviour and should be preserved by any store choice  -  but it also means the observable symptom of a degraded key store is a trickle of unexplained errors rather than an outage, which is worth knowing before diagnosing it.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: KeyRingProvider source: 2-minute temporary extension, 'The immediate caller should fail so that they can report the error up the chain'; KeyManagementOptions.KeyRingRefreshPeriod 'currently fixed at 24 hours'.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Start the application successfully. Then make the key store unreachable (stop the database or block the port). Drive steady traffic for 20 minutes. Overall availability must stay above 99%, with failures clustered at roughly one per two-minute window rather than continuous. Restore the store and confirm errors stop without a restart.

capability_requirements.requirement: A key-ring restore must be a written, rehearsed procedure with a recorded time-to-first-successful-login.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: HIPAA's Required emergency access procedure and emergency mode operation plan bear on whether authorised staff can reach the system during a failure, and total key-ring loss denies access to everyone at once. The system currently has a backup script whose restore has never been tested. An untested restore is not a restore.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: 45 CFR 164.312(a)(2)(ii) Emergency access procedure (Required); 45 CFR 164.308(a)(7)(ii)(B) Disaster recovery plan (Required) and (C) Emergency mode operation plan (Required); system fact that no restore has ever been tested.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Take a backup. On a separate host, destroy the key store, restore from that backup following only the written runbook (no improvisation, no reading source code), and time from start to a successful login. Record the number. Any step that required knowledge not in the runbook is a defect in the runbook.

capability_requirements.requirement: The platform must not require session affinity (sticky sessions) for the application to function correctly across multiple instances.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: This system has no server-side session store, no SignalR and no WebSockets  -  its only cross-instance shared state is the key ring. That is a valuable property that a platform choice could silently destroy (for example by making the key ring instance-local again). Stating it as a requirement prevents reintroducing an assumption the codebase does not currently carry.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System fact: no @angular/ssr, no hub, no client, no AddSession; the reverse proxy carries dead WebSocket upgrade config referencing a hub that does not exist.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Run two application instances behind a load balancer configured for round-robin with affinity explicitly disabled. Complete a login, then perform twenty subsequent authenticated requests. Confirm from access logs that the requests landed on both instances, and that all twenty succeeded.

capability_requirements.requirement: The cache tier must not contain electronic protected health information.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Cache contents are not encrypted in memory and the AOF file, where persistence is enabled, is plaintext on disk. The cache is also the one shared-state component that spans tenants. Keeping ePHI out of it means a cache compromise or a cross-tenant key collision is an identity-data incident rather than a PHI breach. SHOULD rather than MUST because the current contents (permission grants, settings, application configuration, dynamic claims) are identity data, not clinical data  -  but this must be re-verified whenever a new cache item type is introduced.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Azure Architecture Center multitenancy guidance: 'The service doesn't encrypt data stored in memory... consider implementing application-level encryption before writing sensitive data to the cache.' System facts: six-year retention obligation under 45 CFR 164.316(b)(2)(i); one shared Redis across all tenants.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: On a system loaded with realistic (or realistically-shaped synthetic) data, dump every cache key and value. Search the dump for patient names, dates of birth, claim numbers, diagnosis text and appointment clinical detail. Zero hits required. Repeat as a checklist item whenever a new class implementing a cache item is added.

capability_requirements.requirement: The state tier must be unreachable from outside the application's private network.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: The cache holds identity material and, today, key material; neither authenticates callers strongly. The current deployment already satisfies this (only the reverse proxy publishes host ports), and the requirement exists to make sure a platform migration preserves it rather than exposing a state endpoint on a public address by default.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System fact: the reverse proxy is the only service publishing host ports (80, 443); Redis, SQL Server and MinIO publish none.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: From a host outside the application's network boundary, attempt a TCP connection to the cache port and to the database port. Both must be refused or time out. Repeat from a second network position (for example, another tenant's network if the platform is shared).

anti_requirements: MUST NOT store the Data Protection key ring in any component whose routine administrative vocabulary includes a bulk-delete or flush used as a maintenance action, or whose documented durability contract permits losing recent writes. A cache is such a component by definition, however it is hosted or however durable its persistence is configured to be.
MUST NOT make cache reachability a hard dependency of serving a request. If a future change causes a cache miss or a cache error to produce a 5xx, that is a regression, not a hardening.

MUST NOT rely on Redis replication or automated failover for the safety property of any lock. Redis documents the primary/replica lock race as a safety violation; adding replicas makes locks look safer while making them no safer.

MUST NOT introduce a second stateful component purely to obtain durability that the system's existing transactional store already provides. SQL Server here is fully durable by default; a second Redis is not.

MUST NOT rotate or replace the key-ring encryption certificate without first configuring UnprotectKeysWithAnyCertificate with the outgoing certificate. Doing so in the wrong order is indistinguishable from deleting the key ring.

MUST NOT enable an allkeys-* eviction policy on any Redis instance that still contains the key ring, and MUST NOT enable one before verifying the ring has moved. Under allkeys-lru the ring is the most likely eviction victim precisely because it is read about once a day.
MUST NOT reintroduce sticky sessions or server-side session state as a side effect of a platform choice. The absence of both is a load-bearing simplification.
MUST NOT store ePHI in the cache tier, and MUST NOT assume that a managed or encrypted-at-rest cache changes that answer  -  cache contents are not encrypted in memory.
MUST NOT treat HideErrors=true as sufficient handling of cache failure. Suppressing an error is not the same as detecting it; the suppression must be paired with a signal.

MUST NOT deploy the API and the AuthServer independently while they share a key ring. Sharing a ring requires a matching application name and a matching Data Protection stack version, which makes them a single deployment unit whether or not the team thinks of them that way.

MUST NOT move durable work (the two outboxes, Hangfire jobs) into the cache tier to relieve database load. Their delivery guarantee is the only thing standing between a patient-facing email and silence.
surprises: FLUSHALL is a one-command, irreversible, fleet-wide logout  -  and it is the standard remedy for a poisoned cache. The key ring is a plain Redis key sharing a keyspace with cache entries. `redis-cli FLUSHALL` or FLUSHDB deletes it, with no confirmation and no undo, and Microsoft states that deleting a key makes protected data 'permanently undecipherable' with 'no emergency override'. A junior engineer clearing a stale cache at 2am would do exactly the right thing for the cache and destroy the only unreconstructible secret in the system. This is the single most important finding in this area.

The key ring is one single Redis LIST key with no TTL. RedisXmlRepository uses ListRange/ListRightPush against one key. It is therefore exactly one eviction, one expiry mistake, or one DEL away from gone  -  and under an allkeys-lru policy it would be the FIRST candidate for eviction, because it is read roughly once per day per process while cache keys are read constantly. The property that makes it low-cost to store is the same property that makes it the least-recently-used key in the instance.

Redis capped at 512 MB by Docker is not 'capped at 512 MB'  -  it is 'OOM-killed at 512 MB'. Redis's own maxmemory defaults to 0 (unlimited) on 64-bit; Docker enforces its limit through the kernel OOM killer. So the container cap guarantees an unclean shutdown rather than graceful eviction, and unclean shutdown is precisely the condition under which AOF everysec loses up to a second of writes. The memory cap and the persistence choice are interacting in a way neither was configured to account for.

A brief key-store outage does not log everyone out  -  it fails exactly one request every two minutes. Verified directly in KeyRingProvider source: on a refresh failure with a cached ring present, the ring's lifetime is extended by two minutes and the exception is rethrown to the immediate caller only ('The immediate caller should fail so that they can report the error up the chain'). The observable symptom of a degrading key store is therefore a thin trickle of unexplained 500s, easy to misattribute for weeks  -  not an outage anyone would connect to Redis.

A cold start with the key store unreachable is a hard total failure, and that is the good case. The source says 'all callers must block until the keyring exists' and each retries until one succeeds. This is the fail-obviously behaviour the team should deliberately preserve  -  and it is an argument for putting the ring behind SQL Server, which the application cannot start without anyway. Note also that docker-compose currently gates api and authserver on db-migrator completing, but has no equivalent gate on the key store being ready.

Sharing a key ring requires matching Data Protection stack VERSIONS, not just matching application names. Microsoft lists both as joint requirements. A deploy that rebuilds the API on a newer base image and leaves the AuthServer on an older one is a documented incompatibility whose symptom would be 'login succeeds but the API rejects the cookie'  -  a failure nobody would trace to a shared-framework version. Two processes sharing a ring are a single deployment unit whether or not anyone has decided that.

Redis is the ONLY piece of shared state that spans tenants. Every office has its own database. There is no cross-database query, no linked server, no three-part name anywhere in src. But every office's cached permission grants, settings and dynamic claims share one keyspace, separated only by a string prefix that ABP's typed IDistributedCache<T> adds and the untyped ASP.NET Core IDistributedCache does not. In a per-tenant-database architecture, the cache is the one place a tenancy bug stops being 'tenant not found' and starts being a disclosure.

Redis is not carrying a cache workload that justifies its existence at this scale  -  it is a coherence bus. With 16 appointments and 11 offices, the cached working set is tens of megabytes. Its two actual jobs are holding the key ring (misplaced) and letting the API and AuthServer agree on permissions and settings (genuine, and the only real reason to keep it). Recognising this reframes the whole decision: the thing worth protecting is not cache availability, it is key durability and cross-process coherence, and only one of those needs Redis.

Redis's own documentation tells you to do the split. From the key-eviction page: 'The volatile-lru, volatile-lrm, and volatile-random policies are mainly useful when you want to use a single Redis instance for both caching and for a set of persistent keys. However, you should consider running two separate Redis instances in a case like this, if possible.' The vendor's guidance and Microsoft's warning converge independently on the same conclusion.

Redis Sentinel is documented to break under Docker. 'Docker performs port remapping, breaking Sentinel auto discovery of other Sentinel processes and the list of replicas for a master.' The obvious HA upgrade path for a compose-based Redis is one the vendor specifically warns against in exactly this deployment shape  -  and it would not have made the key ring safe anyway, because Sentinel 'does not guarantee that acknowledged writes are retained during failures'.

The Redis lock provider is registered in both processes and has no application acquisition sites  -  so today its only possible contribution is a failure. If ABP framework code ever begins using IDistributedLockProvider, the system silently acquires Redis single-instance lock semantics, which Redis documents as safe only 'in applications where a race condition from time to time is acceptable'. Nobody chose that trade-off; it arrived with the registration. There is also a shape here worth noticing: the correct future use of a lock in this system is almost certainly to stop two API instances from double-running the same per-office recurring sweep  -  and the sweep writes to SQL Server, so a SQL-backed lock would fail closed in exactly the right way.

Moving the key ring out shrinks the AuthServer's Redis dependency to nothing that matters. The AuthServer has IsJobExecutionEnabled=false and no Hangfire; its Redis dependency is the key ring plus optional cache reads. Once the ring lives in SQL, the login path  -  the most sensitive path in a HIPAA system  -  no longer depends on Redis being alive at all. That is a free, non-obvious reduction in blast radius that falls out of the split.

The 'Redis 7' in the compose file may not be open-source software. Redis 7.2 and earlier are BSD-3; 7.4.x through 7.8.x are RSALv2/SSPLv1 (source-available, not OSI open source); 8.0+ added AGPLv3 as a tri-licence option. Valkey, the Linux Foundation fork from Redis 7.2.4, remains BSD. Which of these a healthcare business is actually running is a real constraint on hosting and redistribution arrangements, and it is completely invisible from a `redis:7-alpine` tag.

The window to do this for free closes the day a real practice takes a real booking. Cutting over the key store logs every user out. Today that costs nothing  -  every record is synthetic. After go-live it needs a maintenance window, a pre-cutover key copy from the old store to the new one, and a comms plan. The cheapest version of this change is available now and only now.

Identity is per-database, so the same email can hold a host account and an office account with separate password hashes  -  but the key ring is emphatically NOT per-tenant. It is one ring shared by all offices and both processes. If anyone ever reasons 'tenant isolation means per-tenant keys' and wires PersistKeysToDbContext to a tenant-resolved DbContext, the ring will be written into whichever office database happened to be the ambient tenant when the ring was first loaded lazily  -  and the result will be intermittent, tenant-dependent cookie failures. The DbContext used for the key ring must be explicitly non-tenant-aware and pinned to the host connection string.

not_recommended.pattern: Redis Sentinel with a replicated pair, to make the state tier highly available
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: This is the standard open-source answer and it is not a bad one in the right setting. Three Sentinels plus a replica give genuine automatic failover; StackExchange.Redis supports Sentinel endpoints natively so the client change is small; there is no licence cost; and it appears to address the exact fear stated in the brief  -  'losing Redis contents invalidates every session'. A reasonable engineer reading that sentence would reach for replication first.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: Three independent reasons, any one sufficient. (1) Redis's Sentinel documentation states that Docker port remapping 'break[s] Sentinel auto discovery of other Sentinel processes and the list of replicas for a master'  -  this entire deployment is docker-compose, and debugging Sentinel-under-NAT is not a skill this team has or should acquire. (2) It requires 'at least three Sentinel instances' on machines 'believed to fail in an independent way', and there is one VM; three Sentinels on one host is theatre. (3) Decisively: Redis states that 'Sentinel + Redis distributed system does not guarantee that acknowledged writes are retained during failures, since Redis uses asynchronous replication'. So it does not make the key ring safe. And the failure modes that actually destroy the key ring  -  FLUSHALL, an eviction policy, a volume prune  -  replicate faithfully to the replica. Replication protects against the one failure (hardware) that is not the likely one.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: When there are at least two application hosts, an orchestrator giving stable network identities without port remapping, at least three failure-independent placements, and a named person whose job includes rehearsing a failover quarterly. Roughly: a team of five with someone doing infrastructure more than half-time.

not_recommended.pattern: Redlock across five independent Redis masters, to make the distributed lock actually correct
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: If you are going to use a Redis lock, this is the documented-correct way to do it, and the argument 'do it properly or not at all' is a good instinct. Redlock is what the vendor recommends over the single-instance approach, and the library already in the stack (Medallion.Threading) supports multi-server Redlock directly with no new dependency.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: There are zero application-level lock acquisition sites in src. Standing up five independent Redis masters  -  the algorithm's own worked example  -  to correctly serialise nothing is not proportionate by any measure. Worse, Redis's own consistency disclaimer says that if you care about correctness you 'should implement fencing tokens' and warns that 'Redis is not using monotonic clock for TTL expiration mechanism', so a wall-clock shift can hand the lock to two processes. Fencing tokens are application work nobody has scoped. When a lock is genuinely needed here, the right answer is a different technology, not more Redis.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: If the system ever needed a lock guarding a resource NOT in SQL Server  -  for instance serialising writes to the MinIO partner bucket across instances  -  and could not use a database-backed lease. Even then, five Redis masters would be a strange first choice ahead of an object-store conditional-write primitive.

not_recommended.pattern: Moving the whole state tier to a managed cache service to remove operational burden
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: This is genuinely attractive and I want to be clear it is half-right. Removing a stateful container from a stack operated by two SDE 1s with no on-call rotation is a real, large win: no patching, no memory tuning, no volume management, no OOM. For the CACHE this is probably the correct long-term destination, and the capability requirement is worth carrying into the platform exercise. The instinct is sound.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: Rejected specifically as a solution to the key-ring problem, which is the problem this area is actually about. Microsoft's own Data Protection page documents that persistence on a managed Redis is an opt-in tier feature you must remember to enable  -  'Azure Cache for Redis needs a premium or higher tier to enable data persistence'. Handing a cache to someone else to operate does not change its contract from 'cache' to 'system of record'; it changes who forgets to enable persistence. And the durability that matters here is not the store's uptime, it is the ability to restore the ring after an operator error or a deletion, which no cache tier is designed around. Separately, and importantly: vendor selection is deliberately downstream of this exercise, so the output must be a capability statement, not a product.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: For the cache specifically, as soon as the platform decision is made  -  record it as a capability now. For the key ring, only if the platform offers a durable, versioned, backed-up key or secret store as a distinct service from its cache, which is a different capability with a different name.

not_recommended.pattern: Running two Redis instances on the same host  -  one ephemeral cache, one persistent key store
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: This is exactly what Redis's own eviction documentation suggests when mixing caching and persistent keys, and it is the smallest possible change that separates the durability classes. It solves the FLUSHALL problem, solves the eviction problem, keeps the code identical apart from a connection string, and needs no new technology. If the team refuses to touch a DbContext, this is the honest fallback and it is genuinely better than the status quo.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It separates the classes without fixing the durability of the important one. The persistent Redis still carries a one-second loss window under appendfsync everysec, still gets OOM-killed under a container cap, and  -  decisively  -  still lives in a docker volume that no backup this team runs will ever capture. It swaps one unbacked-up store for two, and adds a second container, a second volume, a second secret, and a second entry in the --env-file trap that has already broken this stack once. The point of the split is to land the key ring somewhere already covered by the one backup mechanism that actually exists, and a second Redis does not achieve that.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: If the platform provides an object store or block volume with real, verified, restore-tested snapshots covering that Redis volume, and if for some reason the key ring cannot live in a relational store. Then two instances is a clean design.

not_recommended.pattern: Introducing server-side session state (AddSession or a distributed session store) so the application can scale out
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: This is the textbook web-farm answer, and it would be right in a system that had server-side session state to distribute. It also feels like it addresses the 'losing Redis invalidates every session' fear head-on by making sessions an explicit, managed thing rather than an implicit consequence of cookie encryption.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It misdiagnoses the fear. Sessions are not stored in Redis today; cookies are self-contained and encrypted with a key that is stored in Redis. The system is already stateless across instances except for that one key ring. Adding a session store would create precisely the hard Redis dependency this analysis is trying to remove, convert a survivable cache outage into a total outage, and reintroduce a scale-out constraint the codebase does not currently have. The absence of server-side session and of SignalR is one of the most valuable simplifications in this system and should be defended, not traded away.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: If the application ever genuinely needs server-side state per user that cannot fit in a cookie  -  a multi-step wizard holding large draft state, or true server-push. Neither exists today, and the packet-assembly workflow has not asked for either.

not_recommended.pattern: Adopting a vault or KMS for the key ring as the first move, rather than an X.509 certificate
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: This is the correct end state and I do not want to argue otherwise. Encryption of key material at rest with an independently-managed key, with rotation and access audit, is what Microsoft recommends and is what the 2025 HIPAA Security Rule NPRM would move toward mandating. It also fixes the adjacent, genuinely bad problem that 35 secrets live in a single mode-600 file with no rotation and several values already pasted into chat transcripts.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: Not on merit  -  on sequencing. There is no vault in this environment, choosing one is explicitly the next exercise, and anchoring this design to a specific secret-management product would invert the intended order. Meanwhile the in-box, cross-platform, zero-new-infrastructure option is an X.509 certificate, and the team already operates a mounted read-only PFX for OpenIddict signing, so the pattern, the mount, and the passphrase-from-environment discipline all exist. Do the certificate now; record 'the platform must provide a managed key/secret store with rotation and access audit' as a requirement for the exercise that follows.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: Immediately after platform selection. At that point the certificate becomes the migration source, not the destination, and UnprotectKeysWithAnyCertificate makes the transition non-destructive.

not_recommended.pattern: Moving durable work (the two outboxes, or Hangfire) into Redis to relieve pressure on SQL Server
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: There is a real problem underneath this. QueuePollInterval is set to TimeSpan.Zero, which puts a continuous query floor on the host database even at idle, and the three 15-minute recurring jobs each open one connection per office  -  11 today, 33 at target. Redis Streams are a legitimate durable queue and would remove that floor entirely. Someone will propose this, and their diagnosis of the load will be correct.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It moves the system's only delivery guarantee from a store that is fully durable by default  -  'log records are persisted to disk before the transaction commit succeeds and returns control to the client'  -  into one whose default guarantee is 'you may lose 1 second of data if there is a disaster'. The AppNotificationOutboxItems and AppIntegrationOutboxItems ledgers are what stand between a patient-facing email and silence, and they are currently written in the same transaction as the business data that justifies them. Redis cannot participate in that transaction. The fix for the polling floor is to raise QueuePollInterval, not to change the durability class of the queue.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: Effectively never for the outboxes, because their value is transactional co-location with the business write. For Hangfire's job storage specifically, a different backing store would be defensible once there is a second API instance and the polling load is measured rather than assumed  -  but the candidate should be evaluated on durability, not on latency.

what_would_change_the_answer: If the DataProtection registration in this solution turns out to already use an EF Core or filesystem store and Redis holds only the cache, the entire recommendation collapses to 'set maxmemory, add a health check, done'  -  about 3 hours of work. Verify by grepping for PersistKeysTo* in both the API and AuthServer host projects before doing anything else.

If OpenIddict is configured with UseDataProtection(), the blast radius of key-ring loss grows to include refresh tokens and authorization codes, not just cookies and Identity email tokens  -  which raises the priority of the move but does not change its direction. Verify by grepping for UseDataProtection in the AuthServer.

If ABP's four default __tenant resolvers (query string, header, cookie, route) are in fact still enabled  -  which the source document honestly records as never tested  -  then a cookie- or query-supplied tenant id could steer a tenant-scoped cache write, which changes the cache's tenant-isolation test from a formality into an urgent one. Test by sending ?__tenant=<other-office-guid> and a __tenant cookie against an authenticated endpoint and observing which database is hit.

If a second application instance is planned within six months, the case for a dedicated (not necessarily replicated) cache host strengthens considerably, and the key-ring-in-SQL decision becomes load-bearing for scale-out rather than merely for durability.

If the team will not accept a new DbContext and migration, the recommendation degrades gracefully to PersistKeysToFileSystem on a bind-mounted host directory with the same certificate encryption, plus an explicit line in the backup script. Same durability, ~2 hours less setup, +0.5 h/month of forever-memory-tax and one more thing to lose during a host migration.

If the ~one-developer-week-per-month figure turns out to be closer to two days per month, this recommendation still holds  -  it is roughly two months of budget then near-free. It is the rejected HA options that become impossible, not this one. Below about 16 hours/month, treat any proposal involving Sentinel, clustering, or a second stateful component as automatically out of scope.

If real PHI enters the system before this change lands, the cutover cost rises from zero to a maintenance window plus a pre-cutover key copy plus a communication plan. That is the single strongest argument for sequencing this work early rather than by severity.

If an audit-retention policy is implemented (currently unconfigured, with a measured 100:1 audit-to-business-data ratio and a six-year expectation), SQL Server storage growth becomes the dominant capacity concern and 'add one tiny table for keys' remains trivially safe. If instead the host database is ever moved to a size-constrained edition, re-check that the DataProtectionKeys table (a handful of rows of a few kilobytes each) is still negligible  -  it will be.

If the deployed Redis image turns out to be 7.4+ rather than 7.2, the licence is RSALv2/SSPLv1 rather than BSD-3, which may matter to the business independently of any technical argument. Check the exact tag; if it matters, Valkey is wire-compatible, BSD-licensed and Linux Foundation governed, and the client library does not change.

If ABP framework code is found to be acquiring the distributed lock (for example for distributed-event outbox processing), the lock stops being a dormant registration and becomes a live correctness dependency on Redis single-instance semantics  -  which would move the lock from 'leave it alone' to 'move it to SQL now'. Verify by enabling debug logging on Medallion.Threading and watching for acquisition events under normal load.

verification.area: state-session (Data Protection key ring, Redis cache/lock tier, HIPAA contingency hooks)

results.claim: [1] Microsoft explicitly warns Redis does not persist by default, causing Data Protection to issue new keys and invalidate previously protected data
results.evidence_quote: When using Redis to persist data protection keys, be aware that Redis doesn't persist data by default when restarting. This can cause Data Protection to issue new keys, invalidating previously protected data. [page metadata: ms.date 2025-11-07, updated_at 2026-02-11]

results.claim: [2] Explicit key persistence location deregisters default key-encryption-at-rest; MS recommends an explicit encryption mechanism for production
results.evidence_quote: If you specify an explicit key persistence location, the data protection system deregisters the default key encryption at rest mechanism. Consequently, keys are no longer encrypted at rest. We recommend that you specify an explicit key encryption mechanism for production deployments.
results.correction: Substance is correct, but the text quoted as 'verbatim' is NOT the wording on the cited page. The quoted sentence ('...so keys are no longer encrypted at rest. It's recommended that you additionally specify...') appears on key-storage-providers, not key-encryption-at-rest. The key-encryption-at-rest page words it as two sentences with 'Consequently' and 'We recommend'. Attribute the quote to the correct page or use the correct wording.

results.claim: [3] Deleting a key permanently destroys protected data; no emergency override unlike revocation
results.evidence_quote: At that point, all data protected by the key is permanently undecipherable, and there's no emergency override like there's with revoked keys. Deleting a key is truly destructive behavior. [and, on default-settings: 'We recommend not deleting data protection keys.']

results.claim: [4] Losing the key ring logs every user out of an app using standard ASP.NET Core cookie authentication
results.evidence_quote: any app using Data Protection won't be able to decrypt stored data using the key ring inside the previous slot. This leads to users being logged out of an app that uses the standard ASP.NET Core cookie authentication, as it uses Data Protection to protect its cookies.

results.claim: [5] 90-day default lifetime; activation now+2d, expiry now+90d; auto-persist when default key expires within 2 days; 7-day minimum; plus source constants KeyPropagationWindow 48h, KeyRingRefreshPeriod 24h, AutoGenerateKeys=true, NewKeyLifetime 90d with 7-day floor throwing ArgumentOutOfRangeException
results.evidence_quote: When a key is created, it's automatically given an activation date of { now + 2 days } and an expiration date of { now + 90 days }... If the default key will expire within 2 days and if the key ring doesn't already have a key that will be active upon expiration of the default key, then the data protection system will automatically persist a new key... The default key lifetime is 90 days... The default key lifetime cannot be shorter than 7 days.
results.correction: The four documented facts are fully supported. The four SOURCE CONSTANTS are not on this page at all  -  the cited Learn URL contains no mention of KeyPropagationWindow, KeyRingRefreshPeriod, AutoGenerateKeys or ArgumentOutOfRangeException. I verified them independently in src/DataProtection/DataProtection/src/KeyManagement/KeyManagementOptions.cs: _keyPropagationWindow = TimeSpan.FromDays(2) with remark 'This value is currently fixed at 48 hours'; _keyRingRefreshPeriod = TimeSpan.FromHours(24) with remark 'currently fixed at 24 hours'; AutoGenerateKeys default true; _newKeyLifetime = TimeSpan.FromDays(90) with a `if (value < TimeSpan.FromDays(7)) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException` guard. All four are ACCURATE but must be cited to KeyManagementOptions.cs, not to the docs page. (Bonus fact the researcher missed: _maxServerClockSkew = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5).)

results.claim: [6] Key ring is cached in memory; backing store checked ~every 24h or when the default key expires, whichever comes first  -  so the key store is not on the request hot path
results.evidence_quote: When the data protection system initializes, it reads the key ring from the underlying repository and caches it in memory. This cache allows Protect and Unprotect operations to proceed without hitting the backing store. The system will automatically check the backing store for changes approximately every 24 hours or when the current default key expires, whichever comes first.

results.claim: [7] On a brief key-store outage with a cached ring, the ring's lifetime is extended by 2 minutes and the exception is rethrown to the immediate caller only; on cold start all callers block and retry until one succeeds
results.evidence_quote: create a new keyring object whose expiration is now + some short period of time (currently 2 min) ... The immediate caller should fail so that they can report the error up the chain. ... if there is no usable existing cached keyring, all callers must block until the keyring exists ... If we don't have an existing keyring (perhaps because this is the first call), then there's nothing to extend, so each subsequent caller will keep going down this code path until one succeeds.

results.claim: [8] The Redis DP provider stores the whole key ring as one Redis LIST key with no TTL, using ListRange/ListRightPush, with no connection-failure handling
results.evidence_quote: Repository stores all key ring elements in a single Redis LIST accessed via the _key constructor parameter; operations are ListRange(_key) and ListRightPush(_key, ...); no calls set TTL or expiry; no try/catch or retry logic  -  'inability to read any value is considered a fatal error', handled by exception propagation.

results.claim: [9] AOF appendfsync everysec can lose up to 1s of writes; snapshotting alone is 'not very durable'; shipped redis.conf defaults are appendonly no, appendfsync everysec, # maxmemory-policy noeviction, aof-load-truncated yes, save 3600 1 / 300 100 / 60 10000
results.evidence_quote: appendfsync everysec: fsync every second. Fast enough... and you may lose 1 second of data if there is a disaster. ... so you can only lose one second worth of writes. ... Snapshotting is not very durable. ... The suggested (and default) policy is to fsync every second.
results.correction: The three durability quotes are exact. The redis.conf DEFAULT LINES are not on this page and cannot be cited to it. The page never prints 'appendonly no', never prints the save 3600 1 / 300 100 / 60 10000 tuple (its only save example is the illustrative 'save 60 1000'), and never prints 'aof-load-truncated yes' as a config line  -  it only shows that string inside a sample log message ('AOF loaded anyway because aof-load-truncated is enabled'). Cite the shipped redis.conf itself (github.com/redis/redis/blob/<version>/redis.conf) for any default-value claim, and pin the version  -  redis.conf defaults are version-specific.

results.claim: [10] Redis says use both AOF and RDB for PostgreSQL-comparable data safety; unclean shutdown can truncate the AOF tail, loaded anyway by default with the last malformed command discarded
results.evidence_quote: The general indication you should use both persistence methods is if you want a degree of data safety comparable to what PostgreSQL can provide you. ... the last command in the AOF could be truncated. The latest major versions of Redis will be able to load the AOF anyway, just discarding the last non well formed command in the file... # AOF loaded anyway because aof-load-truncated is enabled ... the default configuration is to continue regardless of the fact the last command in the file is not well-formed, in order to guarantee availability after a restart.

results.claim: [11] Redis's own docs advise running two separate instances rather than mixing caching and persistent keys in one
results.evidence_quote: The volatile-lru, volatile-lrm, and volatile-random policies are mainly useful when you want to use a single Redis instance for both caching and for a set of persistent keys. However, you should consider running two separate Redis instances in a case like this, if possible.

results.claim: [12] maxmemory defaults to 0 (unlimited) on 64-bit; default eviction policy is noeviction, under which writes error and reads keep working; redis.conf ships '# maxmemory-policy noeviction'
results.evidence_quote: Set maxmemory to zero to specify that you don't want to limit the memory for the dataset. This is the default behavior for 64-bit systems, while 32-bit systems use an implicit memory limit of 3GB. ... noeviction: Keys are not evicted but the server will return an error when you try to execute commands that cache new data. If your database uses replication then this condition only applies to the primary database. Note that commands that only read existing data still work as normal.
results.correction: Two of three parts hold. The page NEVER states that noeviction is the default maxmemory-policy  -  it lists ten policies (noeviction, allkeys-lru, allkeys-lrm, allkeys-lfu, allkeys-random, volatile-lru, volatile-lrm, volatile-lfu, volatile-random, volatile-ttl) without designating a default, and the redis.conf line '# maxmemory-policy noeviction' does not appear. This matters: the 'memory pressure causes eviction not termination' requirement rests on noeviction being the shipped default, so cite the versioned redis.conf for it. Also note the page has been updated since the researcher's memory of it  -  allkeys-lrm/volatile-lrm (Least Recently Modified, new in Redis 8.6) are now listed, and the noeviction error condition is qualified with 'If your database uses replication then this condition only applies to the primary database.'

results.claim: [13] A container exceeding its Docker memory limit is killed by the kernel OOM killer by default
results.evidence_quote: By default, if an out-of-memory (OOM) error occurs, the kernel kills processes in a container. [and: 'To change this behavior, use the --oom-kill-disable option. Only disable the OOM killer on containers where you have also set the -m/--memory option.']

results.claim: [14] Redis replication is asynchronous; acknowledged writes can be lost during failover; min-replicas-to-write is best-effort only
results.evidence_quote: acknowledged writes can still be lost during a failover, depending on the exact configuration of the Redis persistence ... because Redis uses asynchronous replication it is not possible to ensure the replica actually received a given write, so there is always a window for data loss ... You may think of it as a best effort data safety mechanism, where consistency is not ensured for a given write, but at least the time window for data loss is restricted to a given number of seconds.

results.claim: [15] Sentinel needs >=3 instances on independently-failing machines, does not guarantee retention of acknowledged writes, and is documented as breaking under Docker port remapping
results.evidence_quote: 1. You need at least three Sentinel instances for a robust deployment. 2. The three Sentinel instances should be placed into computers or virtual machines that are believed to fail in an independent way... 3. Sentinel + Redis distributed system does not guarantee that acknowledged writes are retained during failures, since Redis uses asynchronous replication. ... 6. Sentinel, Docker, or other forms of Network Address Translation or Port Mapping should be mixed with care: Docker performs port remapping, breaking Sentinel auto discovery of other Sentinel processes and the list of replicas for a master. ... So please deploy at least three Sentinels in three different boxes always.

results.claim: [16] Single-instance Redis lock acceptable only where an occasional race is tolerable; failover-based locking is an explicit safety violation; safety across restarts needs fsync=always or a delayed restart longer than max lock TTL
results.evidence_quote: 4. Client B acquires the lock to the same resource A already holds a lock for. SAFETY VIOLATION! ... this is actually a viable solution in applications where a race condition from time to time is acceptable ... In theory, if we want to guarantee the lock safety in the face of any kind of instance restart, we need to enable fsync=always in the persistence settings. ... To guarantee this we just need to make an instance, after a crash, unavailable for at least a bit more than the max TTL we use. Using delayed restarts it is basically possible to achieve safety even without any kind of Redis persistence available ... You should implement fencing tokens. ... Redis is not using monotonic clock for TTL expiration mechanism.
results.correction: Verified in full. One nuance worth carrying into the design doc: immediately after the SAFETY VIOLATION passage the page adds 'Sometimes it is perfectly fine that, under special circumstances, for example during a failure, multiple clients can hold the lock at the same time. If this is the case, you can use your replication based solution.' So Redis frames failover-based locking as unsafe-for-correctness rather than categorically forbidden  -  which is exactly the distinction the capability requirement already draws.

results.claim: [17] ABP AbpDistributedCacheOptions.HideErrors defaults true (disabled in Development); errors hidden+logged and the original source is queried; 20-min sliding default; tenant-id prefixing on IDistributedCache<TCacheItem>, disableable with IgnoreMultiTenancy
results.evidence_quote: HideErrors (bool, default: true): Enables or disables hiding errors when reading from or writing to the cache server. In the development environment, this option is disabled to help developers detect and fix any cache server issues. ... silently hide (and log) the error and query from the original source. This is what the ABP does by default. ... GlobalCacheEntryOptions ... The default value uses the SlidingExpiration as 20 minutes. ... It automatically adds the current tenant id to the cache key to distinguish cache items for different tenants... Define IgnoreMultiTenancy attribute on the cache item class to disable this.

Perform either of the following in the apps' project files: Reference the same shared framework version via the Microsoft.AspNetCore.App metapackage. results.claim: [19] On Linux with no cloud KMS the only in-box cross-platform key-encryption-at-rest mechanism is X.509 (ProtectKeysWithCertificate) with UnprotectKeysWithAnyCertificate for rotation; DPAPI and DPAPI-NG are Windows-only; the CAPI caveat is scoped to .NET Framework
results.evidence_quote: ## Windows DPAPI  -  Only applies to Windows deployments. ... ## Windows DPAPI-NG  -  This mechanism is available only on Windows 8/Windows Server 2012 or later. ... ## X.509 certificate ... ProtectKeysWithCertificate ... Due to .NET Framework limitations, only certificates with CAPI private keys are supported. See the content below for possible workarounds to these limitations.
results.correction: Two defects. (a) UnprotectKeysWithAnyCertificate does NOT appear anywhere on this page. It is documented on configuration/overview ('## Unprotect keys with any certificate (UnprotectKeysWithAnyCertificate)'  -  'You can rotate certificates and decrypt keys at rest using an array of X509Certificate2 certificates'). Re-cite that half. (b) The claim that the CAPI-private-key caveat is 'scoped to .NET Framework, not .NET 10 on Linux' is the researcher's inference, not the page's statement. The sentence sits unqualified inside the X.509 section whose moniker range explicitly includes aspnetcore-10.0, and the page offers no Linux carve-out. This is load-bearing  -  the whole recommended Linux at-rest mechanism depends on it  -  so it must be settled by test (load a PFX and call ProtectKeysWithCertificate on .NET 10/Linux) rather than asserted. Also note the page title is 'Key encryption at rest in Windows and Azure', which is a signal it was never written to answer the Linux question.

results.evidence_quote: SQL Server transaction commits can be either fully durable, the SQL Server default, or delayed durable (also known as lazy commit). ... Durability is guaranteed on commit. Corresponding log records are persisted to disk before the transaction commit succeeds and returns control to the client. ... DISABLED [default] With this setting, all transactions that commit on the database are fully durable, regardless of the commit level setting.

results.evidence_quote: While OpenIddict uses the JSON Web Token format for all its tokens, it can be optionally configured to use ASP.NET Core Data Protection to create opaque binary tokens instead of JWT tokens. For more information on how to use ASP.NET Core Data Protection, read ASP.NET Core Data Protection integration.
results.correction: The two load-bearing facts (JWT is the default; Data Protection is optional) are confirmed verbatim. Two details are not settled by this page: (a) the method name UseDataProtection() never appears  -  the page only links out to a separate 'ASP.NET Core Data Protection integration' page, so cite that page for the API; (b) 'identity tokens are always JWT' is not stated. The only relevant sentence is about the typ header  -  'access tokens produced by OpenIddict 3.0+ are always issued with a "typ": "at+jwt" header while identity tokens still use "typ": "JWT" for backward compatibility'  -  which is about header values under the JWT format, not about whether identity tokens are exempt from the Data Protection format. The researcher's own caveat stands and is the right one: read the deployment's AddOpenIddict() configuration before relying on the blast-radius scoping.

results.claim: [24] 164.312(a)(2)(ii) emergency access Required; 164.312(a)(2)(iv) encryption Addressable; 164.316(b)(2)(i) six-year documentation retention Required
results.evidence_quote: (ii) Emergency access procedure (Required). Establish (and implement as needed) procedures for obtaining necessary electronic protected health information during an emergency. ... (iv) Encryption and decryption (Addressable). Implement a mechanism to encrypt and decrypt electronic protected health information. [Confirmed absent: any text of 164.316.]
results.correction: CITATION ERROR. The two 164.312 items are exactly right, but 164.316(b)(2)(i)  -  the six-year retention requirement  -  is not on this page and cannot be. 45 CFR 164.312 is 'Technical safeguards'; 164.316 is 'Policies and procedures and documentation requirements', a separate section at a separate URL (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/45/164.316). Split the citation. Also worth adding for completeness: (a)(2)(i) Unique user identification is Required and (a)(2)(iii) Automatic logoff is Addressable.

results.claim: [25] The DP key ring is not ePHI, so the Required data-backup spec does not directly mandate backing it up; the specs actually engaged are 164.312(a)(2)(ii) emergency access and 164.308(a)(7)(ii)(C) emergency mode operation
results.evidence_quote: (C) Emergency mode operation plan (Required). Establish (and implement as needed) procedures to enable continuation of critical business processes for protection of the security of electronic protected health information while operating in emergency mode.
results.correction: Correctly self-labelled as a scoping judgement, and it is a defensible one  -  the regulation nowhere defines key material as ePHI, and 164.308(a)(7)(ii)(A) speaks only of 'retrievable exact copies of electronic protected health information'. Two notes. (a) The 164.312(a)(2)(ii) half of the claim is not on the cited 164.308 URL; it needs the 164.312 citation. (b) The judgement is arguable in the opposite direction and should be presented as contested, not settled: a key ring whose loss renders all stored ePHI permanently undecipherable is plausibly within the reach of (a)(7)(ii)(A)'s 'retrievable' and (B)'s 'procedures to restore any loss of data', since an unreadable copy is not a retrievable one. The researcher's own framing  -  that the operational conclusion does not depend on which hook you pick  -  is the safe way to write this.

results.claim: [26] The 2025 HIPAA Security Rule NPRM is still not final as of Aug 2026, with final action pushed to July 2027; published 6 Jan 2025; ~4,745 comments; OCR agenda had listed May 2026

OCR received almost 5,000 comments in response to the proposed rule ... the final rule has been pushed back a year, with the final action due in July 2027 ... results.evidence_quote: [The page documents IDistributedCache<TCacheItem>, cache-name and tenant-id key normalization, HideErrors, GlobalCacheEntryOptions and batch operations. But the one sentence presented as sourced  -  'the underlying ABP mechanism (removal of a distributed cache entry on permission/setting change, visible to all processes sharing the cache) is documented cache-aside behaviour'  -  is NOT documented on the cited page. I read the full page: it covers the cache abstraction and its options, and says nothing about permission or setting invalidation or cross-process coherence. Cite the Permission Management / Setting Management module docs, or better, verify against PermissionStore/SettingStore cache-invalidation code in the ABP source, since the whole 'keep the shared cache' argument turns on this mechanism actually existing and firing across process boundaries. material_errors: [24] CFR citation error: 164.316(b)(2)(i) (six-year documentation retention, Required) is cited to https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/45/164.312, which is 'Technical safeguards' and does not contain any part of 164.316. Confirmed absent on the page. The correct URL is .../45/164.316. The substance of the retention requirement is not in dispute; the citation is simply wrong and will not survive review.

More seriously, the assertion that the 'only certificates with CAPI private keys are supported' caveat is 'scoped to .NET Framework, not .NET 10 on Linux' is the researcher's inference, not the page's text  -  the sentence sits unqualified inside an X.509 section whose moniker range includes aspnetcore-10.0, on a page titled 'Key encryption at rest in Windows and Azure'. This is load-bearing: it is the sole recommended at-rest mechanism for the Linux/no-cloud-KMS case, so it must be settled by an actual ProtectKeysWithCertificate test on .NET 10/Linux before the design depends on it.

[12] 'The default eviction policy is noeviction' is not stated anywhere on the cited eviction page, and the redis.conf line '# maxmemory-policy noeviction' does not appear on it. The page lists ten policies without naming a default. This is load-bearing for the capability requirement that memory pressure must cause eviction rather than process termination, so it needs a citation to a version-pinned redis.conf.

[9] The shipped redis.conf defaults (appendonly no; save 3600 1 / 300 100 / 60 10000; aof-load-truncated yes) are quoted as if from the Redis persistence page. None of them appear there  -  the page's only save example is the illustrative 'save 60 1000', and 'aof-load-truncated' appears solely inside a sample log message.
