The entire 'keep the shared cache' argument rests on this mechanism, so it needs a real citation or a source-code verification.

[5] Four source constants (KeyPropagationWindow 48h, KeyRingRefreshPeriod 24h, AutoGenerateKeys=true, NewKeyLifetime 90d with a 7-day ArgumentOutOfRangeException floor) are cited to a Microsoft Learn docs page that contains none of them. All four are factually ACCURATE  -  I confirmed them in KeyManagementOptions.cs  -  but the citation must point at the source file.

[2] The text presented as verbatim from the key-encryption-at-rest page is actually the wording used on the key-storage-providers page; the cited page words the same warning differently ('Consequently...' / 'We recommend...'). The substance is correct; the quote is misattributed.
vendor_neutrality_violations: Requirement 6 ('All processes sharing a key ring must be deployed as a unit, with an identical application name and the same Data Protection stack version') states a mandate in one vendor's product vocabulary. 'Data Protection stack' is the name of a specific ASP.NET Core subsystem, and 'application name' is its SetApplicationName knob. Because the exercise's incumbent stack is ASP.NET Core this reads as constraining what already exists rather than recommending adoption, so it is the mildest kind of violation  -  but it is still the one requirement whose text a non-.NET platform could not satisfy or even parse. Vendor-neutral rendering: 'All processes that share cryptographic key material must be deployed and versioned as a unit, presenting an identical key-derivation identity and running the same version of the key-management library.'

Borderline, flagged under the strictness instruction rather than asserted: 'key ring' in requirements 1, 5, 10 and 11 is ASP.NET Core Data Protection vocabulary. It has become near-generic and the requirements are otherwise capability-phrased, so this is a house-style note, not a substantive breach  -  'key material' or 'key store' would read as platform-independent if the document wants to be strict.

Borderline, in the claim set rather than the requirements: claim [30] appends 'Valkey (Linux Foundation fork from Redis 7.2.4) remains BSD' with no citation. As a licensing fact it is evidence; but naming an unsourced alternative product alongside a licence-restriction finding edges toward implying a migration target. Either cite it properly and keep it strictly as licence evidence, or drop it.

research.area: Availability and disaster recovery for a database-per-tenant, single-VM workers' compensation IME scheduling platform (11 offices now, headroom to 33; two SDE-1 developers; no on-call rotation; SQL Server 2022 + Redis + MinIO in Docker Compose)
research.design_space: Before looking at this system at all, the 2026 range of defensible availability designs runs across six rungs, and NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 already names most of them: (1) single instance with restore from backup  -  NIST's "cold site" tier, where the recovery asset is a set of artefacts plus a procedure, and RTO is dominated by human and rebuild time rather than restore time; (2) single instance with an engineered, verified, off-box restore path  -  the same rung, but with the restore proven rather than assumed; (3) warm standby, where data is continuously shipped to a second machine but promotion is a deliberate human act (log shipping, storage replication, or a periodically-restored standby); (4) active-passive with automated failover (Always On availability groups, failover cluster instances, orchestrator-driven promotion), which converts an availability problem into a distributed-consensus problem; (5) active-active, where more than one application instance serves traffic against shared or replicated state; and (6) geographic distribution  -  separate power/network/facility failure domains (an "AZ"-shaped requirement) and separate regions. NIST maps these to FIPS 199 availability impact: low -> cold site with tape/relocate, moderate -> cold or warm site, high -> hot site with mirrored systems, and it explicitly ties exercise rigour to the same axis (tabletop for low, functional exercise *including recovery from backup media* for moderate, full-scale failover for high). Two things moved the boundaries between rungs since roughly 2020, and both matter here: SQL Server 2022 can write and read backups directly to any S3-compatible object endpoint over the REST API, which removes the "backups land on the same disk then a script copies them somewhere" failure mode entirely; and SQL Server 2022's T-SQL snapshot backup can freeze write I/O across *all* user databases at once (`BACKUP SERVER`) so a single storage-level snapshot yields one write-consistent recovery point across every database on the instance, on Linux and in containers, without any vendor agent. Together those push the crossover point at which rung (3) starts to pay for itself substantially further out than it used to sit: a well-built rung (2) now gets you an off-box, immutable, instance-consistent, machine-verified recovery point with no second machine to keep alive. The countervailing force is that every rung above (2) adds a component whose *failure mode is silence*  -  a lagging log-shipping secondary, a cluster that failed over and back, a replica that stopped applying  -  and silence is precisely what a two-person team with no on-call rotation cannot detect. Finally, database-per-tenant deforms this ladder in a way that single-database SaaS does not: replication and availability features in SQL Server are configured *per database* (a Standard-edition basic availability group carries exactly one database), so every rung above (2) multiplies by N offices, while backup and restore of a single user database is version-portable and independent of every other database  -  meaning the granular thing (restore one office) is easy and the coarse thing (make the fleet highly available) is what explodes.

options.name: Rung 1  -  Single instance, backup script only (the current design, unimproved)
options.how_it_works: A shell script issues native BACKUP DATABASE to a bind-mounted host directory (default ./backups, same box and same disk). No confirmed cron. No log backups, no differential backups, no checksums, no verification, no off-box copy, no restore procedure, no restore ever attempted. Recovery = someone SSHes in, finds a .bak, and improvises.
options.operational_cost: Setup: already done (0 h). Ongoing: ~0 h/month  -  which is the problem: the maintenance cost and the assurance are both zero. Assumes no expertise, and delivers no evidence that recovery is possible.
options.why: This is not a cheap version of DR; it is the absence of DR wearing DR's clothes. Three independent facts make it non-viable rather than merely weak. (a) It fails 45 CFR 164.308(a)(7)(ii)(A) and (B), both marked (Required), not addressable  -  'create and maintain retrievable exact copies' and 'procedures to restore any loss of data'; a backup nobody has ever restored is not demonstrably retrievable. (b) The backups share a disk with the thing they protect, on a volume with ~9.7 GB free, so the single most likely loss event (host or disk loss) takes the backups with it. (c) Most sharply: the office databases are created by EF Core `Database.MigrateAsync()` and therefore inherit the `model` database's recovery model, which on Developer edition (all Enterprise functionality) is FULL. Microsoft documents that a newly created full-recovery database reuses its log 'similar to a database using the simple recovery model ... up until the time you create a full database backup'. The first successful BACKUP DATABASE against each office therefore *ends* that grace period, and because no log backups are ever taken the log can never truncate again (log_reuse_wait_desc = LOG_BACKUP) and grows until the disk fills. Switching this script on is what fills the disk. It has probably not bitten yet only because the script's cron is unconfirmed.

options.name: Rung 2  -  Single instance with an engineered, verified, off-box restore path ("cold compute, warm data")
options.how_it_works: Every database (host + every office) runs in FULL recovery with an explicit schedule: periodic full backups, log backups at the cadence that defines the RPO, all written WITH CHECKSUM and COMPRESSION straight to an off-box S3-compatible endpoint using SQL Server 2022's `BACKUP DATABASE ... TO URL = 's3://...'`, under a credential that can write but cannot delete, into a versioned bucket with a retention lock. Optionally, once per day, `ALTER SERVER CONFIGURATION SET SUSPEND_FOR_SNAPSHOT_BACKUP = ON` + a storage-level snapshot + `BACKUP SERVER ... WITH METADATA_ONLY` produces one write-consistent recovery point across host and every office database simultaneously. Redis (DataProtection keyring), the MinIO object data, the OpenIddict signing PFX and the secrets file are captured into the same off-box store by explicit, separate procedures. A scheduled job restores one rotating database to a scratch instance and runs DBCC CHECKDB. Recovery is: provision a host, restore, re-point DNS.
options.operational_cost: Setup: ~50-90 hours total, staged  -  recovery-model and schedule work using a maintained script set ~8-12 h; the S3 target including getting the CA into /var/opt/mssql/security/ca-certificates before SQL Server starts and pre-creating buckets (SQL Server cannot create them) ~8-16 h; snapshot-coordinated instance-consistent point ~8-16 h and only if the platform offers a scriptable snapshot; per-office restore runbook and script ~8-16 h; automated weekly verification restore ~8-16 h; the written contingency-plan artefacts required by 164.308(a)(7) ~8-16 h. Ongoing: ~3-6 h/month (review verification results, quarterly timed rehearsal, retention housekeeping including sp_delete_backuphistory). Expertise assumed: T-SQL RESTORE sequences and a scheduler. No clustering, no replication, no quorum, no distributed systems knowledge.
options.why: It is the only rung whose failure modes can be made to shout. A checksum failure fails the backup outright. A verification restore that does not go green is a red line on a dashboard. The subtle residual is RTO drift  -  the restore gets slower as audit data accumulates and nobody notices  -  and the fix is cheap: the quarterly rehearsal is *timed*, and the measured elapsed time is the published RTO. It also matches what NIST prescribes for a FIPS 199 moderate-availability system: cold-or-warm strategy, and a functional exercise that 'include[s] an element of system recovery from backup media'. It buys: survival of host loss, disk loss, accidental deletion, ransomware (given immutability), and a bad migration. It does not buy: continuity during the outage.

options.name: Rung 3  -  Warm standby: a second host kept data-current, promoted by hand
options.how_it_works: Two variants. (a) SQL Server log shipping: a backup job on the primary, and copy + restore jobs on the secondary, per database, all driven by SQL Server Agent (which is disabled by default in the Linux container and must be enabled with MSSQL_AGENT_ENABLED). Failover is explicitly manual  -  Microsoft states 'A log shipping configuration doesn't automatically fail over'. (b) Periodic restore: the secondary simply replays the same off-box backup chain from rung 2 on a schedule, so it is a standby that costs nothing extra to produce. Either way the application containers exist on the second host, stopped, and promotion is a documented human procedure ending in a DNS change.
options.operational_cost: Variant (a) setup: ~40-80 h, and it scales with offices  -  log shipping is configured per database, so 11 offices plus the host is 12 configurations and roughly 36-48 Agent jobs; at 33 offices it is 34 configurations and ~100+ jobs. Ongoing: ~4-8 h/month plus lag monitoring, and every new office provisioned through the host UI silently arrives *outside* log shipping until someone adds it. Variant (b) setup: ~16-24 h on top of rung 2. Ongoing: ~1-2 h/month. Expertise: variant (a) assumes someone comfortable with Agent jobs, log chains and lag alerting; variant (b) assumes nothing rung 2 did not already assume.
options.why: Variant (b) is a genuinely good fit and is mostly free once rung 2 exists  -  it converts RTO from 'provision a host, then restore' to 'start containers, then replay the last few log backups'. Variant (a) is where I would say no: it is per-database, it depends on a SQL Agent this deployment deliberately does not run, its lag is silent unless the alert job and an operator are configured, and  -  the killer for this system  -  adding an office is a *host-UI action* performed by non-engineers, so the fleet's DR coverage would silently diverge from the fleet's membership. Log shipping does have one property nothing else offers: a user-specified delay between backup and restore on the secondary, which Microsoft documents as a defence against an accidental change on the primary. If the dominant feared event were 'someone deleted a practice's data', a delayed secondary would be the right tool. It is not the dominant feared event here.

options.name: Rung 4  -  Active-passive with automated failover (availability groups or failover cluster instance)
options.how_it_works: Two SQL Server nodes with either an Always On availability group per database or a failover cluster instance over shared storage, plus a cluster manager (WSFC on Windows, Pacemaker/Corosync on Linux) to arbitrate, plus a listener or floating address, plus application-side reconnection, plus an equivalent story for Redis, MinIO and the reverse proxy so that failing over the database does not just relocate the outage.
options.operational_cost: Setup: 200-400+ hours realistically, and that is the build, not the competence. Ongoing: 8-20 h/month plus an on-call expectation, because a cluster that loses quorum at 03:00 does not wait. Assumes cluster administration, fencing/STONITH, quorum design, and rehearsed failover  -  a discipline, not a weekend.
options.why: There is an honest case: it is the only rung that materially reduces *downtime* rather than data loss, and healthcare buyers ask about it. But two hard, documented facts kill it here specifically. First, Always On availability groups (multi-database) are Enterprise-edition only; Standard edition offers *basic* availability groups, and Microsoft's limitations list says flatly 'Support for one availability database', two replicas, 'No read access on secondary replica' and 'No backups on secondary replica'. Database-per-tenant therefore means one basic AG per office  -  12 today, 34 at the planned ceiling  -  each independently seeded, monitored and failed over, and each new office needing a new AG created by hand at provisioning time. Second, a failover cluster instance is instance-level and does cover all databases at once, but Standard edition supports only two nodes and it needs shared storage plus a cluster manager. Either way the team acquires a distributed system whose characteristic failure is a silent half-failover, and the brief's own constraint  -  prefer designs that fail obviously  -  rules it out. This is the rung to revisit when there is a person whose job is operations.

options.name: Rung 5  -  Active-active application tier
options.how_it_works: Two or more HttpApi.Host and AuthServer instances behind the proxy, sharing one SQL Server, one Redis and one MinIO. Requests distribute; any single application process can die without an outage.
options.operational_cost: Setup: ~40-80 h, most of it in making the Hangfire processing server singleton-safe and in getting the proxy to health-check and to preserve the Host header per upstream. Ongoing: ~2-4 h/month. Assumes understanding of at-least-once job semantics.
options.why: The honest case here is stronger than usual and deserves saying out loud: this application is unusually ready for it. There is no SignalR and no sticky-session requirement, the SPA is static files, identity is OIDC bearer tokens, and the ASP.NET DataProtection keyring is *already* shared in Redis with a common SetApplicationName across both processes  -  which is exactly the work most teams have to do to get a second instance running. So the marginal cost is low. But it buys the wrong thing. It protects against application-process failure while every genuinely fatal component  -  one SQL Server, one Redis, one MinIO, one nginx, one VM  -  remains a single point of failure, so the availability number barely moves. And it introduces one specific, subtle hazard: only HttpApi.Host runs the Hangfire processing server today; a second instance started identically would register a second processing server against the same Hangfire schema, and Hangfire's documented model is retry-based re-entrancy, not exactly-once  -  meaning twelve recurring jobs, three of which run every fifteen minutes and iterate every office, would run twice. Duplicate outbox drains send duplicate emails to real external parties. Do this later, deliberately, with processing explicitly disabled on all but one instance  -  not as an availability strategy.

options.name: Rung 6  -  Geographic distribution (independent failure domains / multi-region)
options.how_it_works: The stack is present in two or more facilities with independent power, cooling and network, with data replicated between them either synchronously (bounded by round-trip latency, cost paid on every write) or asynchronously (accepting a non-zero RPO), plus a traffic-steering layer and a data-residency story.
options.operational_cost: Setup: 400+ hours and a permanent operational commitment. Ongoing: 20+ h/month. Assumes replication topology design, split-brain policy, failback procedure and regular full-scale exercise.
options.why: NIST reserves mirrored/hot-site strategies for FIPS 199 *high* availability impact, and reserves full-scale functional exercises including failover to the alternate site for the same tier. The honest case is that a facility-level event is the one thing rung 2 cannot recover from quickly  -  but it can recover from it *at all*, because the backup artefacts are off-box by construction, which is precisely the 'geographic area: distance from the organization and the probability of the storage site being affected by the same disaster' criterion NIST applies to offsite storage. The correct expression of geography for this system is therefore a requirement on where the *backups* live, not a second live stack. There is also a specific trap: the tenancy design resolves offices purely from the HTTP Host header, so any traffic-steering layer that terminates and re-proxies will return 'Tenant not found' for every office unless it explicitly preserves Host  -  and nginx's own default is `proxy_set_header Host $proxy_host`, not `$host`.

research.recommendation: Build rung 2, add rung 3 variant (b) opportunistically, and explicitly do not build rungs 4-6. Concretely: put every database (host and every office) on an explicit full + log backup schedule written WITH CHECKSUM and COMPRESSION directly to an off-box S3-compatible endpoint via SQL Server 2022's native `BACKUP ... TO URL = 's3://...'`, under a write-only credential into a versioned bucket with a retention lock; add a once-daily instance-consistent recovery point using `ALTER SERVER CONFIGURATION SET SUSPEND_FOR_SNAPSHOT_BACKUP = ON` + a platform storage snapshot + `BACKUP SERVER ... WITH METADATA_ONLY`; script per-office point-in-time restore as a first-class operation; and put a weekly automated restore-and-CHECKDB of one rotating database behind an alert that fires on *absence* of a green result. HOW TO DERIVE THE NUMBERS, RATHER THAN ME ASSERTING THEM. NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 gives the chain and I am recommending you follow it literally: Maximum Tolerable Downtime is a business decision  -  'the total amount of time the system owner/authorizing official is willing to accept for a ... process outage'  -  so it is elicited from whoever owns the scheduling business, not derived by engineers. RTO 'must normally be shorter than the MTD' and is the engineering target. RPO is separate and, in NIST's words, 'Unlike RTO, RPO is not considered as part of MTD. Rather, it is a factor of how much data loss the ... process can tolerate.' For this business the MTD question has a specific and answerable form: can the front desk run today's booked appointments from a printed schedule and a phone? You need that answer anyway, because 164.308(a)(7)(ii)(C) Emergency mode operation plan is (Required) and it is exactly this. If the answer is yes, MTD is measured in a working day or more and rung 2 is proportionate. If the answer is no  -  because ex-parte notice deadlines or same-day packet assembly bind  -  MTD collapses to hours and rung 3(b) becomes mandatory rather than optional. The RPO question has a second, non-obvious input: the *business* records lost in a gap are re-keyable (the measured data density is 16 appointments per office), but the audit records are not, and 164.312(b) Audit controls is a standard, not an addressable specification. So the RPO should be set by audit reconstructability, not by booking volume. On what a business of this size lands on, I will not invent a figure. The two anchors that actually exist are: NIST's FIPS 199 mapping  -  categorise availability, and if it comes out MODERATE ('serious adverse effect ... significant degradation in mission capability to an extent and duration that the organization is able to perform its primary functions, but the effectiveness ... is significantly reduced') then the prescribed strategy is 'Cold or Warm site', which is rung 2/3; and the only regulatory number in circulation, the 72-hour restoration procedure in the January 2025 HIPAA Security Rule NPRM, which is *proposed and not in force* (HHS has moved it to Long-Term Actions with July 2027 targeted for final action). Treat 72 hours as a ceiling to design under, not a requirement to meet today. Then replace both with a measured number: the quarterly rehearsal is timed, and the elapsed wall-clock of a per-office point-in-time restore performed by one developer against the written runbook *is* your RTO. WHY PER-OFFICE RESTORE IS THE PRIMARY OPERATION, NOT INSTANCE RESTORE. Restoring one user database is portable: the target instance need only be the same SQL Server version or higher ('No SQL Server backup can be restored to an earlier version'), the database upgrades automatically, MOVE handles file paths, and because every service connects as `sa` there is no orphaned-login work  -  an accidental benefit of a bad security decision. Restoring the *instance* is not portable: master must be restored with the server started in single-user mode, the instance shuts down afterwards, Microsoft warns the recovery instance must match 'version, edition, and patch level ... the same selection of features and the same external configuration (hostname, cluster membership...)', and 'Backups of master, model and msdb that were created by using an earlier version of SQL Server cannot be restored'. The architectural conclusion is clean: treat the SQL Server *instance* as disposable and rebuildable from configuration, and treat the *database* as the portable unit of recovery. Do not back up master/msdb as a recovery strategy; back up the configuration that recreates them. HOW BACKUP WINDOWS SCALE WITH N DATABASES. Native BACKUP is per-database  -  there is no instance-wide streaming backup  -  so a sweep is N sequential operations unless you fan them out across sessions. They do parallelise, and what binds is memory before I/O: each concurrent operation reserves BUFFERCOUNT x MAXTRANSFERSIZE from SQL Server's own memory, and the S3 connector's MAXTRANSFERSIZE runs 5-20 MB against a 7,168 MB instance limit. At this data volume the full backup is not the constraint; the *log* backup cadence is, because it is what sets RPO and it is the thing that multiplies: 34 databases at a 15-minute cadence is 3,264 log backup operations per day, each producing an object and rows in msdb's backup history  -  which is why `sp_delete_backuphistory` must be scheduled from day one, since Microsoft notes 'More rows are added to the backup and restore history tables after each backup or restore operation'. T-SQL snapshot backup collapses the full-backup sweep from N operations to one freeze plus one snapshot regardless of N  -  until 64 databases, where it hard-stops. WHAT PER-OFFICE POINT-IN-TIME RESTORE REQUIRES THAT FULL RESTORE DOES NOT, AND WHAT BREAKS. The mechanics are documented and unremarkable: a full backup whose endpoint precedes the target time, every subsequent log backup, the *identical* STOPAT clause on every RESTORE LOG, and a tail-log backup first. The hard part is the cross-references, and here the honest answer is that SQL Server cannot give you what you want. Point-in-time restore is per-database and carries no cross-database consistency guarantee; Microsoft's own note says related databases that must be logically consistent 'might have to implement special procedures', and the documented mechanism is marked transactions  -  `BEGIN TRANSACTION ... WITH MARK` recorded in the logs of *all* affected databases, then STOPATMARK. This system cannot use it: it has no raw SQL anywhere, no cross-database transactions, and joins host and tenant data in memory. So restoring one office to T-1 while the host stays at T produces four specific, foreseeable divergences: Hangfire jobs in the host database carry appointment identifiers that no longer exist and will retry-and-fail into a dashboard; the office's AppNotificationOutboxItems and AppIntegrationOutboxItems roll back to 'unsent', so the drain jobs re-send  -  duplicate ex-parte-addressed emails to real attorneys and duplicate messages to Case Tracker, whose reconcile loop runs every fifteen minutes; MinIO objects written between T-1 and T are *not* rolled back and become orphaned PHI with no row referencing them; and the audit rows for the lost window are destroyed and cannot be reconstructed. The design consequence is the useful part: this system's recovery must be *reconcilable*, not consistent. Make the outbox drains idempotent against a partner-visible dedupe key, give blob writes a reconciliation sweep that can find orphans, and require that any restore into a non-production context be provably unable to send mail or reach the partner. Separately, the only mechanism available to you that gives a genuinely instance-wide write-consistent point across host and every office without touching application code is `BACKUP SERVER` + storage snapshot  -  which is why I am recommending it despite the 64-database ceiling. BACKUP VERIFICATION AND REHEARSAL, MINIMUM VIABLE FOR TWO PEOPLE. Four layers, in increasing cost: (1) every backup WITH CHECKSUM  -  Microsoft is explicit that without a backup checksum, 'restore cannot reliably verify page checksums', so this is the gate that makes everything downstream meaningful, and it fails the backup outright rather than warning; (2) RESTORE VERIFYONLY immediately after each backup, recorded  -  cheap, and supported over S3; but understand what it is not: it validates the media and checksums, it does not prove the database is logically restorable; (3) weekly, automated: restore one rotating database to a scratch instance under a different name, run DBCC CHECKDB, drop it, write a dated pass/fail  -  `Test-DbaLastBackup` in dbatools (2.8.4, published 2026-07-31) does exactly this end-to-end and is actively maintained; with 12 databases a weekly rotation proves every office each quarter; (4) quarterly, human: one timed per-office point-in-time restore executed by one developer against the written runbook, and annually one full rebuild onto a clean host using *only* off-box artefacts, with the original machine treated as unreachable  -  this is the exercise that finds the secrets and certificate gaps, and it is NIST's 'functional exercise ... include an element of system recovery from backup media' for a moderate-impact system. Layer 3 is the one that must alert on *absence*: if no green verification result has appeared in 21 days, page someone and treat the system as having no backups. DO THIS NOW, NOT LATER. There is no real PHI in the system yet. Today a restore rehearsal is a developer exercise. The moment real practices take real bookings, every rehearsal environment becomes an in-scope system holding ePHI and inherits the full control set  -  access control, audit, encryption, disposal, and a business associate analysis for wherever you restore it. The engineering is identical; only the compliance surface changes. Build and rehearse the restore path while it is free.
research.operational_cost_of_recommendation: Setup: roughly 50-90 developer-hours, stageable across a quarter and best sequenced so each stage is independently valuable  -  (1) recovery models + full/log schedules + retention + sp_delete_backuphistory, 8-12 h; (2) off-box S3 backup target, 8-16 h, of which the fiddly parts are placing the CA into /var/opt/mssql/security/ca-certificates *before* the SQL Server process starts (Linux reads it only at startup, max 50 certificates) and pre-creating buckets, since SQL Server 2022 cannot create them; (3) per-office point-in-time restore script + written runbook, 8-16 h; (4) automated weekly restore-and-CHECKDB with an absence alert, 8-16 h; (5) instance-consistent snapshot point via SUSPEND_FOR_SNAPSHOT_BACKUP + BACKUP SERVER, 8-16 h, and only worth starting once the platform is known to offer a scriptable storage snapshot; (6) the written contingency-plan artefacts that 164.308(a)(7) requires, 8-16 h. At the stated ~1 developer-week per month that is roughly two to three months of the infrastructure allowance  -  and the brief itself flags that allowance as an estimate already partly consumed by code-standard remediation, so plan it as a quarter with stage 1 and stage 2 non-negotiable and stages 5 deferrable. Ongoing: 3-6 h/month  -  about 1 h reviewing weekly verification results and retention, 2 h/quarter for the timed rehearsal amortised, 1 day/year for the clean-host rebuild. THRESHOLD, stated as the brief asks: this design is operable at 4 or more hours per month of sustained attention. Between 2 and 4 h/month it still works but the rehearsal cadence slips from quarterly to opportunistic and the measured RTO becomes stale  -  you will still recover, but you will not know how long it takes. Below roughly 2 h/month it decays to rung 1 with extra steps: backups keep being produced, verification results go stale unnoticed, and the first real restore is an experiment. That decay is silent, which is why the single most important line item in the whole recommendation is the *absence* alert on the weekly verification job  -  it is the one mechanism that converts a silent decay into a hard error, and it costs about two hours to build. If you implement only two things from this entire recommendation, implement off-box backup with a write-only credential, and the absence alert.

evidence.claim: 45 CFR 164.308(a)(7) Contingency plan makes three implementation specifications (Required): (A) Data backup plan  -  'Establish and implement procedures to create and maintain retrievable exact copies of electronic protected health information.'; (B) Disaster recovery plan  -  'Establish (and implement as needed) procedures to restore any loss of data.'; (C) Emergency mode operation plan. Two are (Addressable): (D) Testing and revision procedures  -  'Implement procedures for periodic testing and revision of contingency plans.'; (E) Applications and data criticality analysis.
evidence.source_name: eCFR, 45 CFR 164.308 (retrieved via eCFR versioner API, XML, as in force 2026-08-01)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: (A),(B),(C) Required; (D),(E) Addressable

evidence.claim: 'Addressable' is not optional. 45 CFR 164.306(d)(3) requires the entity to assess whether the specification is reasonable and appropriate and either implement it, or 'Document why it would not be reasonable and appropriate to implement' it and 'Implement an equivalent alternative measure if reasonable and appropriate.' 164.306(b)(2) lists size, complexity and capabilities of the entity, and cost, as factors that may properly be weighed  -  which is the clause a two-person team relies on to justify a proportionate design.
evidence.source_name: eCFR, 45 CFR 164.306 Security standards: General rules

evidence.claim: The brief's premise that '[a] six-year retention expectation applies (HIPAA 45 CFR 164.316(b)(2)(i))' is a misreading and should be corrected before it drives backup sizing. That paragraph reads: 'Retain the documentation required by paragraph (b)(1) of this section for 6 years from the date of its creation or the date when it last was in effect, whichever is later.' Paragraph (b)(1) is policies and procedures, and written records of actions/activities/assessments the Security Rule requires to be documented. It is a documentation-retention rule. It is not a retention period for ePHI, audit logs, or database backups. HIPAA sets no ePHI retention period at all.
evidence.source_name: eCFR, 45 CFR 164.316 Policies and procedures and documentation requirements
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 6 years, applies to documentation under 164.316(b)(1) only

evidence.claim: The actual retention driver for a California workers' compensation IME platform is state regulation, not HIPAA. 8 CCR  39.5: 'All QMEs shall retain a copy of all comprehensive medical-legal reports completed by the QME for a period of five years from the date of each evaluation report,' and an electronic copy satisfies this 'as long as the electronic copy retained is a true and correct copy of the original, showing the QME signature.' The same section also requires that, on written request, original radiological films, imaging studies and original medical records be returned to whoever supplied them or to the injured worker.
evidence.source_name: California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 CCR  39.5, Records, Retention by QMEs
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 5 years from date of each evaluation report

evidence.claim: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 definitions, verbatim: MTD  -  'The MTD represents the total amount of time the system owner/authorizing official is willing to accept for a mission/business process outage or disruption and includes all impact considerations.' RTO  -  'RTO defines the maximum amount of time that a system resource can remain unavailable before there is an unacceptable impact on other system resources, supported mission/business processes, and the MTD.' RPO  -  'The RPO represents the point in time, prior to a disruption or system outage, to which mission/business process data can be recovered ... Unlike RTO, RPO is not considered as part of MTD.' The publication also states 'the RTO must normally be shorter than the MTD.'
evidence.source_name: NIST Special Publication 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems (Ch. 3, BIA)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: n/a  -  definitions, not thresholds

evidence.claim: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Table 3-2 maps FIPS 199 availability impact to strategy: Low -> 'Backup: Tape backup / Strategy: Relocate or Cold site'; Moderate -> 'Backup: Optical backup, WAN/VLAN replication / Strategy: Cold or Warm site'; High -> 'Backup: Mirrored systems and disc replication / Strategy: Hot site'. Section 3.5.4 ties exercise rigour to the same axis: 'For low-impact systems, a tabletop exercise ... is sufficient'; 'For moderate-impact systems, a functional exercise ... Exercise procedures should be developed to include an element of system recovery from backup media'; 'For high-impact systems, a full-scale functional exercise ... should include a system failover to the alternate location.'
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Moderate availability -> cold or warm site; functional exercise including recovery from backup media

evidence.claim: FIPS 199 defines AVAILABILITY as 'Ensuring timely and reliable access to and use of information...' and sets MODERATE impact as a 'serious adverse effect', amplified as effects that 'cause a significant degradation in mission capability to an extent and duration that the organization is able to perform its primary functions, but the effectiveness of the functions is significantly reduced ... or (iv) result in significant harm to individuals that does not involve loss of life or serious life threatening injuries.' HIGH is reserved for 'severe or catastrophic adverse effect'.
evidence.source_name: FIPS PUB 199, Standards for Security Categorization of Federal Information and Information Systems
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Moderate = serious adverse effect, explicitly excluding loss of life / life-threatening injury

evidence.claim: A scheduling platform for IME appointments plausibly categorises as FIPS 199 MODERATE for availability and HIGH for confidentiality. Unavailability delays legally-scheduled evaluations and degrades the practices' effectiveness but does not involve loss of life; the FIPS 199 MODERATE amplification language ('significant harm to individuals that does not involve loss of life or serious life threatening injuries') fits. This categorisation is the single load-bearing judgement behind rejecting rungs 4-6, so it should be made explicitly and by the business owner, not assumed by engineers.
evidence.source_name: My architectural judgement applying FIPS 199 to this system
evidence.threshold_or_limit: n/a

evidence.claim: SQL Server recovery models: only FULL supports point-in-time restore. Microsoft's table gives Simple: 'Can recover only to the end of a backup'; Full: work loss 'Normally none' and 'Can recover to a specific point in time'; Bulk-logged: 'Point-in-time recovery isn't supported.' The Simple model explicitly cannot be used with log shipping, availability groups/mirroring, or point-in-time restores. Note: 'SQL Server Enterprise and Standard editions use the full recovery model by default, while SQL Server Express edition uses the simple recovery model by default.'
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn  -  Recovery Models (SQL Server)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: PITR requires FULL recovery model + unbroken log chain

evidence.claim: THE LOG TRAP. Microsoft: 'If a transaction log is never truncated, it eventually fills all the disk space allocated to physical log files.' Under full recovery, 'truncation occurs after a log backup'. Critically: 'When you first create a database that uses the full recovery model, the transaction log is reused as needed (similar to a database using the simple recovery model), up until the time you create a full database backup.' The stall is diagnosable as sys.databases.log_reuse_wait_desc = 'LOG_BACKUP'  -  'A log backup is required before the transaction log can be truncated.'
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn  -  The Transaction Log (SQL Server), Transaction log truncation / Factors that can delay log truncation
evidence.threshold_or_limit: log_reuse_wait value 2 = LOG_BACKUP

evidence.claim: Applying that to this system: office databases are created by EF Core Database.MigrateAsync() and inherit the model database's recovery model, which on Developer edition (all Enterprise functionality) is FULL. They are therefore in the 'pseudo-simple' grace state today. The first successful BACKUP DATABASE ends that grace state permanently, and with no log backups scheduled the log grows until the volume  -  which has roughly 9.7 GB free  -  fills, producing error 9002 and read-only databases. Turning the existing backup script on reliably is the action that breaks the box.
evidence.source_name: My inference chaining the Microsoft transaction-log and recovery-model documentation onto the stated system facts
evidence.threshold_or_limit: ~9.7 GB free disk stated in brief; recovery model not directly observed by me

evidence.claim: Documented single-database point-in-time restore sequence: 'As a prerequisite to a point-in-time restore, you must first restore a full database backup whose endpoint is earlier than your target restore time'; 'In every RESTORE LOG statement of the restore sequence, you must specify your target time or transaction in an identical STOPAT clause'; recommendations are 'Use STANDBY to find unknown point in time' and 'Specify the point in time early in a restore sequence'. A tail-log backup is taken first where required. If the log backup does not contain the requested time 'a warning is generated and the database remains unrecovered.'
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn  -  Restore a SQL Server Database to a Point in Time (Full Recovery Model)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: identical STOPAT on every RESTORE LOG

evidence.claim: SQL Server offers NO automatic cross-database point-in-time consistency. The recovery-models page notes: 'If you have two or more related databases in the full recovery model that must be logically consistent, you might have to implement special procedures.' The documented mechanism is marked transactions: 'If a marked transaction spans multiple databases on the same database server or on different servers, the marks must be recorded in the logs of all the affected databases', restored with WITH STOPATMARK / STOPBEFOREMARK. This requires the application to issue BEGIN TRANSACTION ... WITH MARK spanning the databases.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn  -  Recover related databases with marked transaction
evidence.threshold_or_limit: marks must exist in the logs of all affected databases

evidence.claim: Marked transactions are unavailable to this system as built. The brief states there is no raw SQL anywhere in src, no cross-database queries, and host/tenant data are joined in memory. Marked transactions require raw T-SQL spanning the host and tenant databases in one transaction. Therefore the only route to a cross-database consistent recovery point without a code change is instance-wide snapshot coordination.
evidence.source_name: My inference from the stated system facts against the Microsoft marked-transaction documentation
evidence.threshold_or_limit: n/a

evidence.claim: SQL Server 2022 T-SQL snapshot backup can freeze write I/O across all user databases at once and record one consistent recovery point: 'ALTER SERVER CONFIGURATION SET SUSPEND_FOR_SNAPSHOT_BACKUP = ON;' then 'BACKUP SERVER TO DISK = ... WITH METADATA_ONLY, FORMAT;'. Microsoft: 'write operations are paused on SQL Server (read requests are still allowed), and control is handed over to the backup application to complete the snapshot.' It supports point-in-time recovery 'using log backups taken with the normal streaming approach after the snapshot FULL backup'. HARD LIMIT: 'The maximum number of databases you can back up with this feature is 64.' System databases (master, model, msdb) cannot be suspended. Available in every edition per the 2022 editions table ('Snapshot backup: Yes' across Enterprise/Standard/Web/Express).
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn  -  Create a Transact-SQL snapshot backup
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 64 databases maximum; error Msg 925 above that; system databases excluded

evidence.claim: SQL Server 2022 can back up and restore directly to any S3-compatible object store over the REST API using s3:// URLs, and it is edition-gated: 'Backup and restore to S3-compatible object storage over REST API' is Yes for Enterprise, Standard and Web, No for Express. TLS is mandatory: 'URLs beginning with s3:// always assume that the underlying protocol is https' and 'Back up to S3-compatible object storage with a nonsecure http URL isn't supported.' On Linux 'the CA must be placed on a predefined location to be created at /var/opt/mssql/security/ca-certificates, only the first 50 certificates can be stored ... The CA must be in place before SQL Server process is started.' Buckets 'can't be created or configured from SQL Server 2022'. Limits: 10,000 parts per file, MAXTRANSFERSIZE 5-20 MB (default 10 MB), 'A single backup file can be up to 200,000 MiB per URL (with MAXTRANSFERSIZE set to 20 MB)', striping across a maximum of 64 URLs, path or virtual-host style, total URL length 259 characters. RESTORE VERIFYONLY and STOPAT/STOPATMARK are supported over S3; NOINIT/INIT (appending) is not  -  use WITH FORMAT.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn  -  SQL Server back up to URL for S3-compatible object storage
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 10,000 parts x MAXTRANSFERSIZE 5-20 MB; 64 URLs; 200,000 MiB/URL; 50 CA certs on Linux; URL <=259 chars

evidence.claim: SQL Server 2022 edition limits that bind an availability design for database-per-tenant. Always On availability groups: Enterprise only. Basic availability groups: Standard only, and the documented limitations are 'Limit of two replicas', 'No read access on secondary replica', 'No backups on secondary replica', 'No integrity checks on secondary replicas', 'Support for one availability database', and 'Basic availability groups can't be part of a distributed availability group'  -  though 'You might have multiple Basic availability groups connected to a single instance'. Always On failover cluster instances: Standard supports two nodes. Log shipping: Enterprise/Standard/Web yes, Express no. Backup compression and Encrypted backup: Enterprise/Standard only. Express: 10 GB maximum relational database size, 1,410 MB buffer pool, no SQL Server Agent.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn  -  Editions and Supported Features of SQL Server 2022
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Basic AG = 2 replicas, 1 database; Standard FCI = 2 nodes; Standard buffer pool 128 GB / 24 cores; Express 10 GB per database

evidence.claim: SQL Server Developer edition 'includes all the functionality of Enterprise edition, but is licensed for use as a development and test system, not as a production server.' The Linux/container environment-variable documentation likewise describes MSSQL_PID='Developer' as 'the freely licensed Developer Edition of SQL Server for non-production use'. The current deployment sets MSSQL_PID=Developer.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn  -  Editions and Supported Features of SQL Server 2022; Configure Environment Variables for SQL Server on Linux
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Developer = non-production licensing

evidence.claim: SQL Server Agent is disabled by default in the Linux container: MSSQL_AGENT_ENABLED 'Enables SQL Server Agent. For example, true enables, and false disables the agent. By default, the agent is disabled.' Log shipping is built entirely from SQL Server Agent jobs  -  a backup job on the primary, a copy job and a restore job on each secondary, and an alert job on the monitor  -  and is configured per database. 'A log shipping configuration doesn't automatically fail over from the primary server to the secondary server. If the primary database becomes unavailable, any of the secondary databases can be brought online manually.' It uniquely offers a 'user-specified delay between when the primary server backs up the log ... and when the secondary servers must restore', documented as useful 'if data is accidentally changed on the primary database'.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn  -  About Log Shipping (SQL Server); Configure Environment Variables for SQL Server on Linux
evidence.threshold_or_limit: per database; ~3-4 Agent jobs per configuration; manual failover only

evidence.claim: Restoring one database is version-portable; restoring an instance is not. 'No SQL Server backup can be restored to an earlier version of SQL Server than the version on which the backup was created,' and 'Backups of master, model and msdb that were created by using an earlier version of SQL Server cannot be restored by SQL Server.' Restoring master requires starting the instance in single-user mode (-m/-f); 'After master is restored, the instance of SQL Server shuts down and terminates the sqlcmd process'; and Microsoft warns the recovery instance 'should be the same version, edition, and patch level, and it should have the same selection of features and the same external configuration (hostname, cluster membership, and so on) as the original instance. Doing otherwise can result in undefined SQL Server instance behavior.'
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn  -  RESTORE (Transact-SQL), Compatibility support; Restore the master Database (Transact-SQL)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Backups restore forward-only; master/model/msdb not restorable across versions

evidence.claim: Backup verification semantics. 'If a backup contains a backup checksum, RESTORE and RESTORE VERIFYONLY statements can check for errors.' Conversely, 'If there is no backup checksum, either restore operation proceeds without any verification; this is because without a backup checksum, restore cannot reliably verify page checksums.' If a page error is found during backup, 'the backup fails' by default; RESTORE VERIFYONLY by default 'continues'. A damaged backup set is flagged in msdb..backupset.is_damaged.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn  -  Media errors: Backup and Restore (SQL Server)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: WITH CHECKSUM is the precondition for meaningful verification

evidence.claim: Backup encryption creates a second, absolute single point of failure. 'It's very important to back up the certificate or asymmetric key, and preferably to a different location than the backup file it was used to encrypt. Without the certificate or asymmetric key, you can't restore the backup, rendering the backup file unusable.' And: 'the certificate shouldn't be renewed on expiry or changed in any way. Renewal can result in updating the certificate triggering the change of the thumbprint, therefore making the certificate invalid for the backup file.' Express and Web editions cannot encrypt during backup (they can restore encrypted backups).
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn  -  Backup encryption (SQL Server)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: certificate must never be renewed for the life of the backups it encrypts

evidence.claim: msdb backup history grows per operation and must be pruned. 'More rows are added to the backup and restore history tables after each backup or restore operation is performed; therefore, we recommend that you periodically execute sp_delete_backuphistory.' It affects backupfile, backupfilegroup, backupmediafamily, backupmediaset, backupset, restorefile, restorefilegroup, restorehistory. 'The physical backup files are preserved, even if all the history is deleted.'
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn  -  sp_delete_backuphistory (Transact-SQL)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: n/a

evidence.claim: Concurrent backups are memory-bounded, not only I/O-bounded. 'Your BACKUP operation will consume BUFFERCOUNT * MAXTRANSFERSIZE in RAM', and Books Online warns that 'large numbers of buffers might cause "out of memory" errors'; the archived Microsoft support post documents a real failure with 'Msg 701 ... There is insufficient system memory to run this query' at 200 MB of total buffer space. Default BUFFERCOUNT for a database backup is (NumberOfBackupDevices x (1+GetSuggestedIoDepth)) + NumberOfBackupDevices + (2 x DatabaseDeviceCount).
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn (archived MSDN support blog)  -  Incorrect BufferCount data transfer option can lead to OOM condition
evidence.threshold_or_limit: memory per backup = BUFFERCOUNT x MAXTRANSFERSIZE; S3 MAXTRANSFERSIZE up to 20 MB; instance limit here is MSSQL_MEMORY_LIMIT_MB 7168

evidence.claim: SQL Server capacity ceilings that are NOT the binding constraint here: 32,767 databases per instance, 32,767 user connections, 524,272 TB database size. Nothing about 33 tenant databases stresses the engine; the constraints that bind are per-feature (basic AG = 1 database; snapshot backup = 64 databases), not per-instance.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn  -  Maximum Capacity Specifications for SQL Server
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 32,767 databases/instance; 32,767 user connections

evidence.claim: Redis AOF with the default policy loses up to one second: 'appendfsync everysec: fsync every second. Fast enough ... and you may lose 1 second of data if there is a disaster.' More importantly for backup design, naively copying the Redis volume is unsafe: since 7.0 the AOF is multi-part in a directory, and 'if this is done during a rewrite, you might end up with an invalid backup'  -  you must set auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 0, confirm INFO persistence shows aof_rewrite_in_progress = 0, copy, then restore the setting. Redis also advises 'At least one time every day make sure to transfer an RDB snapshot outside your data center or at least outside the physical machine' and 'You also need some kind of independent alert system if the transfer of fresh backups is not working.' (The BACKUP command family that makes this clean requires Redis 8.10.0; this deployment is on Redis 7.)
evidence.source_name: Redis documentation  -  Redis persistence
evidence.threshold_or_limit: appendfsync everysec  <=1 s loss; BACKUP command family requires Redis >= 8.10.0

evidence.claim: nginx does not preserve the client Host header to upstreams by default. The proxy_set_header documentation gives the default block verbatim as 'proxy_set_header Host $proxy_host; proxy_set_header Connection close;' and explains 'By default, the header fields "Host" and "Connection" from the original request are not passed to the proxied server.' Because tenancy in this system resolves from the Host header and nothing else, any recovery or failover path that introduces or reconfigures a proxy without an explicit Host directive returns 'Tenant not found' for every office.
evidence.source_name: nginx documentation  -  ngx_http_proxy_module, proxy_set_header
evidence.threshold_or_limit: default is $proxy_host, not $host

evidence.claim: Both recommended tooling options are current and actively maintained. Ola Hallengren's SQL Server Maintenance Solution most recent release 16 August 2026 (prior releases 9 August 2026 and 8 August 2026); supports SQL Server 2017+ including 2022 and 2025, SQL Server on Linux, and backup destinations including AWS S3 (S3 support was added in collaboration with AWS and is SQL Server 2022+ only). dbatools, which provides Test-DbaLastBackup (restore under a different name + DBCC CHECKDB + drop), latest published version 2.8.4 on 2026-07-31.
evidence.source_name: ola.hallengren.com version history; PowerShell Gallery package feed for dbatools
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Ola: 2026-08-16; dbatools: 2.8.4, published 2026-07-31

evidence.claim: The 72-hour restoration figure is PROPOSED, not in force. HHS's own NPRM fact sheet describes a requirement to 'Establish written procedures to restore the loss of certain relevant electronic information systems and data within 72 hours,' plus a criticality analysis to prioritise restoration and a 24-hour business-associate notification on contingency-plan activation, and it proposes removing the required/addressable distinction. The NPRM was published in the Federal Register on 6 January 2025 and the comment period closed 7 March 2025. As of 2026 no final rule has issued; secondary reporting states HHS moved RIN 0945-AA22 to the Unified Agenda's Long-Term Actions with July 2027 as the anticipated final action date (slipped from a prior May 2026 target). I could not fetch reginfo.gov directly to confirm the agenda entry first-hand.
evidence.source_name: HHS.gov  -  HIPAA Security Rule NPRM fact sheet (primary, for the proposal's content); law-firm and trade reporting (secondary, for the delay)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 72 hours (proposed); 24 hours BA notification (proposed); final action targeted July 2027 (unverified against reginfo.gov)

evidence.claim: CISA's #StopRansomware Guide recommends maintaining offline, encrypted backups that are regularly tested, and recommends immutable backups. I could not fetch the guide PDF directly (cisa.gov returned HTTP 403 to my fetch; a state-government mirror of StopRansomware-Guide-508C-v3_1.pdf exists), so I have NOT verified the widely-repeated vendor claim that CISA 'explicitly endorses 3-2-1-1-0'. Treat 3-2-1 as the well-established baseline (three copies, two media types, one offsite) and 3-2-1-1-0 (adding one immutable/air-gapped copy and zero verified recovery errors) as a widely-used industry extension repeated mainly in vendor material, not as a cited government standard. The defensible primary anchors for the same behaviour are NIST SP 800-34 3.4.2 offsite-storage criteria and 45 CFR 164.308(a)(7)(ii)(A).
evidence.source_name: CISA #StopRansomware Guide (October 2023, v3.1)  -  attempted primary fetch; NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 3.4.2 used as the substitute primary anchor
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 3-2-1 baseline verified as industry convention; '3-2-1-1-0 endorsed by CISA' NOT verified

evidence.claim: Hangfire's model is retry-based re-entrancy, not exactly-once. Its Best Practices documentation states 'Reentrancy means that a method can be interrupted in the middle of its execution and then safely called again' and that 'The interruption can be caused by many different things (i.e. exceptions, server shut-down), and Hangfire will attempt to retry processing many times.' The consequence for DR: restoring the host database (which holds the Hangfire schema) to an earlier point re-arms jobs that already ran, and running a second processing server during a failover double-executes them.
evidence.source_name: Hangfire documentation  -  Best Practices
evidence.threshold_or_limit: n/a  -  Hangfire documents retry/re-entrancy; it does not use the phrase 'at least once' on this page

evidence.claim: Restoring one office backward while the host stays current produces externally visible side effects, not merely internal inconsistency: the office's AppNotificationOutboxItems and AppIntegrationOutboxItems roll back to unsent, so the drain jobs re-send  -  duplicate ex-parte-addressed emails to real external parties and duplicate messages to the Case Tracker partner, whose reconciliation runs every 15 minutes. MinIO objects written in the lost window are not rolled back and become orphaned PHI with no referencing row. Audit rows for the window are destroyed and cannot be reconstructed, which touches 45 CFR 164.312(b) Audit controls. Therefore the recovery design requirement is reconcilability (idempotent drains keyed on a partner-visible identifier, plus an orphan-object sweep), not consistency.
evidence.source_name: My architectural analysis of the stated outbox/blob/audit design against the restore semantics documented by Microsoft
evidence.threshold_or_limit: n/a

evidence.claim: Recovery has a fleet-wide single point of failure that only manifests during recovery. Per the stated facts, db-migrator loops offices with no per-tenant error handling, and both authserver and api gate on its service_completed_successfully. During a rebuild, one office database whose schema application fails mid-loop therefore prevents the entire stack  -  all offices  -  from starting, with no report of which succeeded. This inverts the usual tenant-isolation benefit exactly when isolation matters most.
evidence.source_name: My analysis of the stated docker-compose gating and migration-runner behaviour
evidence.threshold_or_limit: n/a

capability_requirements.requirement: The platform must provide block or filesystem storage with a point-in-time snapshot facility that can be initiated and completed from a script, so that a snapshot can be taken inside a SQL Server write-freeze window.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: This is the only mechanism that yields a write-consistent recovery point across the host database and every office database without changing application code, because the alternative (marked transactions) requires cross-database T-SQL this system does not and structurally cannot issue.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft Learn, Create a Transact-SQL snapshot backup (SUSPEND_FOR_SNAPSHOT_BACKUP / BACKUP SERVER); Microsoft Learn, Recover related databases with marked transaction; the stated system fact that there is no raw SQL in src.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: On the candidate platform: run `ALTER SERVER CONFIGURATION SET SUSPEND_FOR_SNAPSHOT_BACKUP = ON;`, immediately invoke the platform's snapshot API for the volume holding the data and log files, then `BACKUP SERVER TO DISK='...' WITH METADATA_ONLY, FORMAT;`. Record the wall-clock duration writes were frozen. Then, on a different host, mount the snapshot and `RESTORE DATABASE ... FROM DISK='...' WITH METADATA_ONLY, MOVE ...`. Pass = every database recovers and the freeze window is under the application's request timeout. Fail = no scriptable snapshot exists, or the freeze exceeds the timeout.

capability_requirements.requirement: The platform must expose an S3-compatible object endpoint reachable from the database host over HTTPS, presenting a certificate that chains to a CA installable on the database host, and supporting S3 multipart upload.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: It removes the entire class of failure where backups land on the same disk as the data and a separate script is responsible for moving them. SQL Server 2022 writes the backup stream directly to the object store; there is no intermediate file and no copy step to fail silently.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft Learn, SQL Server back up to URL for S3-compatible object storage: 'URLs beginning with s3:// always assume that the underlying protocol is https'; 'Back up to S3-compatible object storage with a nonsecure http URL isn't supported'; on Linux the CA must be at /var/opt/mssql/security/ca-certificates before the SQL Server process starts, first 50 certificates only.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Place the CA in /var/opt/mssql/security/ca-certificates and restart SQL Server. Then: `CREATE CREDENTIAL [s3://<endpoint>/<bucket>] WITH IDENTITY='S3 Access Key', SECRET='<key>:<secret>';` followed by `BACKUP DATABASE <db> TO URL='s3://<endpoint>/<bucket>/test.bak' WITH FORMAT, COMPRESSION, CHECKSUM, STATS=10;` and then `RESTORE VERIFYONLY FROM URL='s3://<endpoint>/<bucket>/test.bak';`. Pass = both succeed. Fail = TLS validation error, or the backup succeeds only over http.

capability_requirements.requirement: The backup destination must reside in a failure domain that shares no host, no disk, no power feed and no hypervisor with the primary compute.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: The single most probable total-loss event for a one-VM deployment is loss of that VM or its disk. A backup on the same disk does not survive it, so it does not satisfy 'retrievable exact copies'.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: 45 CFR 164.308(a)(7)(ii)(A) (Required); NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 3.4.2 offsite-storage criteria  -  'Geographic area: distance from the organization and the probability of the storage site being affected by the same disaster as the organization's primary site'.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Power off (or, in a test tenancy, destroy) the primary host. From a completely different machine with only the backup credentials, list the backup objects and run `RESTORE VERIFYONLY` against the most recent full and the most recent log backup for at least two databases. Pass = both verify. Fail = the objects are unreachable or were stored on a volume attached to the destroyed host.

capability_requirements.requirement: Backup storage must support object versioning together with a retention or object-lock mechanism that the credential used by the backup writer cannot bypass, override or shorten.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Without it, any compromise of the application host  -  which authenticates to its object store as root today  -  also destroys the backups. Immutability is the difference between a backup and a ransomware target.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: MinIO AIStor object locking (GOVERNANCE vs COMPLIANCE modes; versioning required); 45 CFR 164.308(a)(7)(ii)(A); CISA #StopRansomware guidance on offline/immutable, regularly tested backups.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Authenticate with exactly the credential the backup job uses. Attempt: (a) DELETE of a backup object written one hour ago; (b) overwrite of the same key with different content; (c) a call to shorten or remove the retention rule. All three must fail. Then repeat with the application's own object-store credential; it must not be able to read the backup bucket at all.

capability_requirements.requirement: The backup writer must use a credential that is distinct from any credential the running application holds, and that grants write and list but not delete on the backup location.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: The application currently authenticates to its object store as root. If the same identity can write and delete backups, the blast radius of an application compromise includes the recovery path.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft Learn, S3 backup permissions: backup requires ListBucket + WriteOnly; restore requires ListBucket + ReadOnly  -  the two are separable by design.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Enumerate every credential present on the host. Assert that (a) the credential in the SQL Server CREDENTIAL object is not present in the application's environment file, (b) it cannot delete from the backup bucket, and (c) the application's credential returns AccessDenied when listing the backup bucket.

capability_requirements.requirement: The platform must allow provisioning a replacement database host running the same SQL Server major version or higher, within the declared RTO, with no dependency on any artefact that exists only on the original host.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Because the portable unit of recovery here is the user database, not the instance, the recovery design should treat the instance as disposable. That is only true if a replacement instance can actually be produced, and if nothing needed for recovery lives solely on the machine being replaced.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft Learn, RESTORE Compatibility support: 'No SQL Server backup can be restored to an earlier version of SQL Server than the version on which the backup was created'; Restore the master Database: the recovery instance must match version, edition and patch level, so master restore is not a portable strategy.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Time-box a drill: with the original host declared unreachable, provision a new host, install the same or higher SQL Server version, restore the host database and every office database from the off-box artefacts, and bring the stack up. Record elapsed wall-clock. Pass = the stack serves a request for at least two offices and no step required SSH to the original machine. Fail = any artefact had to be fetched from the original host.

capability_requirements.requirement: All key material and secrets required to operate the system  -  database credentials, the OpenIddict token-signing certificate and its passphrase, any backup-encryption certificate, and either the ASP.NET DataProtection keyring or a documented, tested procedure for operating without it  -  must be recoverable independently of the primary host.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Restoring all 34 databases onto a clean host produces a stack that cannot mint a token or decrypt a protected payload. The DR critical path runs through a mode-600 file and a PFX, not through the database, and today both exist in exactly one place.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft Learn, Backup encryption: 'Without the certificate or asymmetric key, you can't restore the backup, rendering the backup file unusable'; the stated facts that the OpenIddict PFX is mounted from the host and that the DataProtection keyring lives in Redis under CaseEvaluation-Protection-Keys with a shared SetApplicationName across both processes.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: With the primary host powered off, hand a second engineer only the off-box artefacts and the documented runbook. They must obtain every value in the environment file and the signing certificate, start the stack, complete an interactive login, and receive a working access token. Pass = login succeeds. Fail = any secret is unobtainable, or login fails because tokens cannot be signed.

capability_requirements.requirement: Every network element in the request path  -  in steady state and in any recovery or failover path  -  must deliver the client's original Host header unmodified to the application.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Tenancy resolves from the Host header and nothing else; a bare IP cannot reach the application at all. A recovery path that terminates and re-proxies without explicit Host preservation returns 'Tenant not found' for every office simultaneously  -  a total, fleet-wide outage introduced by the failover itself.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: nginx ngx_http_proxy_module documentation: the default is `proxy_set_header Host $proxy_host;`  -  the original Host is explicitly not passed; and the stated HostAwareDomainTenantResolveContributor design.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Through every candidate path (direct, and via each proxy/load-balancer/CDN layer), issue `curl -sS https://{office}.api.{base}/api/abp/application-configuration` and assert the response carries that office's tenant identity rather than a 'Tenant not found' error. Independently, log the Host header as received by the application and assert it equals the requested hostname. Repeat for the auth and SPA hostnames.

capability_requirements.requirement: It must be possible to restore any single office database to an arbitrary point in time, under a different database name and/or on a different instance, without stopping, locking or otherwise disturbing any other office.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Database-per-tenant exists precisely so that one practice's problem is not every practice's problem. If per-office restore requires an instance-wide outage, the tenancy model has been paid for and not used.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft Learn, Restore a SQL Server Database to a Point in Time (Full Recovery Model)  -  RESTORE DATABASE ... NORECOVERY followed by RESTORE LOG ... WITH STOPAT, per database; the stated TenantConnectionStringProvider which derives each connection string by database-name substitution.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: While synthetic load runs against three other offices, restore one office to a timestamp 30 minutes in the past as `CaseEvaluation_{slug}_rehearsal` and recover it. Assert: the restore completes; the three loaded offices show zero failed requests for the duration; and a query against the restored copy returns the pre-change state.

capability_requirements.requirement: Every backup must be produced WITH CHECKSUM, and a scheduled, unattended process must both verify backups and perform a genuine restore plus integrity check of at least one database on a rotation that covers every database within a declared period.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: RESTORE VERIFYONLY without a backup checksum verifies almost nothing  -  Microsoft states restore 'cannot reliably verify page checksums' in that case  -  and verification is not restoration. The only evidence that a backup is restorable is a restore.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft Learn, Media errors: Backup and Restore; 45 CFR 164.308(a)(7)(ii)(D) Testing and revision procedures (Addressable, therefore requiring documented assessment under 164.306(d)(3)); NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Table 3-6 System Backup (CP-9) 'Test backup information to verify media reliability and information integrity'.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Inspect the backup command text and assert CHECKSUM is present. Query `SELECT database_name, has_backup_checksums FROM msdb.dbo.backupset` and assert has_backup_checksums = 1 for all recent sets. Then inspect the verification job's output store and assert that within the declared rotation period every database has a dated record of a successful restore plus DBCC CHECKDB with zero errors.

capability_requirements.requirement: The absence of a recent successful verification result must itself raise an alert, within a declared window, through a channel that reaches a human.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: This is the single control that converts the team's characteristic failure mode  -  silent decay of an unattended process  -  into a hard error. Every other backup control in this design fails loudly only if this one exists.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: The stated team constraint 'prefer designs that fail obviously over designs that fail subtly'; Redis documentation's own equivalent advice: 'You also need some kind of independent alert system if the transfer of fresh backups is not working for some reason.'
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Disable the verification job (or block its write to the result store). Assert that within the declared window (e.g. 21 days, or a shortened test window) an alert is delivered to a named recipient. Then re-enable and assert the alert clears. Fail = nothing happens, or the alert goes only to a log file.

capability_requirements.requirement: For every database in the FULL recovery model, log backups must exist within the declared RPO, and this must be observable from outside the database.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Full recovery without log backups is a slow-motion disk-full outage, and it is caused by the act of starting to take backups. It is invisible until the volume fills.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft Learn, The Transaction Log: 'If a transaction log is never truncated, it eventually fills all the disk space allocated to physical log files'; log_reuse_wait_desc = LOG_BACKUP means 'A log backup is required before the transaction log can be truncated.'
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Run: `SELECT name, recovery_model_desc, log_reuse_wait_desc FROM sys.databases;` and assert no database shows recovery_model_desc = 'FULL' with log_reuse_wait_desc = 'LOG_BACKUP' persisting across two consecutive checks. Separately, from a monitoring path outside SQL Server, assert the newest log-backup object for every database is younger than the declared RPO.

capability_requirements.requirement: The database platform must run an edition licensed for production use that supports transaction log backups, backup compression and backup encryption.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Three edition-gated capabilities sit directly on the recovery path. Express cannot do log shipping, backup compression, backup encryption, S3 backup or SQL Server Agent, and caps databases at 10 GB. Developer has every feature but is not licensed for production.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft Learn, Editions and Supported Features of SQL Server 2022 (High availability and Security tables; Developer edition definition); Configure Environment Variables for SQL Server on Linux (MSSQL_PID='Developer' = 'non-production use').
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: `SELECT SERVERPROPERTY('Edition'), SERVERPROPERTY('ProductVersion');`  -  assert the edition is not 'Developer Edition', 'Evaluation Edition' or an Express variant. Then confirm `BACKUP DATABASE ... WITH COMPRESSION, ENCRYPTION (ALGORITHM = AES_256, SERVER CERTIFICATE = ...)` succeeds.

capability_requirements.requirement: Any recovery or rehearsal environment must be provably incapable of emitting outbound email or reaching the partner integration endpoint.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Restoring an office backward resets its durable outboxes to unsent; the drain jobs will then re-deliver. Because addressing is ex-parte-safe (one primary party, others CC'd), a duplicate send is a compliance-visible event involving real attorneys and claims administrators, not merely noise.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: The stated design of AppNotificationOutboxItems and AppIntegrationOutboxItems as durable ledgers drained by jobs; Hangfire's documented retry/re-entrancy model.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Restore an office into the rehearsal environment with its outbox rows deliberately reset. Run the drain jobs. Assert, from the SMTP relay's own logs and from the partner endpoint's access logs, that zero messages were received. Additionally assert the rehearsal host's egress to ports 587 and to the partner host is blocked at the network layer, not only by configuration.

capability_requirements.requirement: Exactly one background-processing server must be active against the Hangfire schema at any time, including during and after any failover, restore or scale-out.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Hangfire's model is retry-based re-entrancy, not exactly-once. Twelve recurring jobs, three of which run every fifteen minutes and iterate every office, would double-execute  -  including the outbox drains, which have external side effects.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Hangfire Best Practices documentation on reentrancy and retries; the stated fact that only HttpApi.Host runs the processing server and AuthServer sets IsJobExecutionEnabled=false.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: During a simulated failover in which old and new instances briefly overlap, query Hangfire's registered servers list (or `SELECT * FROM HangFire.Server`) and assert the count of servers with processing enabled never exceeds one. Independently, enqueue a job that appends to an audit table and assert exactly one row appears.

capability_requirements.requirement: Recovery of one office must not be able to block the availability of any other office, including during the migration/seed step that runs on every bring-up.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Today db-migrator loops offices with no per-tenant error handling, and both the API and AuthServer gate on its successful completion. That converts one office's schema failure into a fleet-wide startup failure  -  precisely during a recovery, when the fleet is most likely to be in mixed states.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: The stated migration-runner behaviour and the docker-compose service_completed_successfully gating.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: In a rehearsal environment, deliberately corrupt or lock one office database so its migration fails, then bring the stack up. Pass = the API and AuthServer start, the healthy offices serve requests, and a machine-readable report names the failed office. Fail = the stack does not start, or it starts with no indication which office failed.

capability_requirements.requirement: Retention should be configurable independently per artefact class, so that clinical records, Security Rule documentation, audit data and operational backups can carry different periods.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: The real retention drivers differ and none of them is a blanket six years. Applying one long period to everything, in particular to backups of audit data already running at a measured 100:1 against business rows, sizes the storage and the restore time for a requirement that does not exist.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: 8 CCR 39.5 (five years for QME comprehensive medical-legal reports); 45 CFR 164.316(b)(2)(i) (six years, for Security Rule documentation only); the measured 1,450 audit-log rows and 2,689 property-change rows against 16 appointments.
