capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Inspect the retention configuration and assert at least three independently settable periods exist, and that changing one does not change the others. Then verify by observation: set a short test period for one class and confirm objects in that class age out while objects in the others do not.

capability_requirements.requirement: The platform should permit relocating office databases to a different database instance by configuration alone, without a code change or redeployment.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: This property already exists  -  connection strings are derived from a single template key  -  and it is the cheapest available recovery lever: it converts 'restore into the damaged instance' into 'restore into a healthy instance and re-point'. A platform choice that removes it would remove a working DR mechanism nobody has written down.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: The stated TenantConnectionStringProvider behaviour (App:TenantDbTemplate; database name substituted to CaseEvaluation_{slug}).
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Restore all office databases onto a second SQL Server instance. Change only the App:TenantDbTemplate configuration value to point at that instance and restart the API. Assert every office resolves and serves data from the second instance, with no rebuild and no code change.

anti_requirements: The platform must NOT rewrite, normalise, canonicalise or drop the HTTP Host header at any layer  -  proxy, load balancer, WAF, CDN or ingress. Tenancy resolves from Host and nothing else, so a Host-rewriting element does not degrade one office; it takes every office down at once with a 'Tenant not found' that looks like an application bug rather than a routing bug.

The platform must NOT require that the running application hold credentials capable of deleting or overwriting backups. Today the application authenticates to its object store as root; if the backup store accepts that identity, a single compromise removes both the data and the recovery path.

The platform must NOT require synchronous cross-site replication of the database. There is no workload justification at this scale, and it converts a remote-facility risk into a latency tax paid on every write, in a system whose steady-state connection pattern is already dominated by three fifteen-minute jobs iterating every office.

The platform must NOT permit more than one background-processing server to attach to a single Hangfire schema. Hangfire retries rather than guaranteeing exactly-once, and duplicate execution of the outbox drains sends real duplicate correspondence to external parties.

The platform must NOT make any part of the documented recovery procedure depend on an artefact that exists only on the primary host  -  not the secrets file, not the signing certificate, not a backup-encryption certificate, not a script, not a note. Recovery must be executable with the primary host declared destroyed.

The platform must NOT couple the availability of one office to the health of another. A failed migration, a locked database or an in-progress restore for one office must not prevent the others from starting or serving.

The platform must NOT depend on a feature whose documented ceiling is exceeded by the 33-office plan. Two ceilings bind concretely: a Standard-edition basic availability group carries exactly one database, and T-SQL snapshot backup stops at 64 databases.

The platform must NOT auto-renew or rotate on a schedule any key used to encrypt backups. Microsoft is explicit that renewing the certificate changes its thumbprint and makes it invalid for existing backup files  -  an automated rotation policy applied uniformly would silently render the entire backup history unrestorable.

The platform must NOT require an instance-wide maintenance window, outage or single-user mode in order to back up or restore one office. If per-office restore costs a fleet outage, the database-per-tenant design has been paid for without being used.

The platform must NOT store backups on media or in a location that is only reachable through the primary host's credentials, network path, or DNS name. A recovery path that requires the failed system to still be answering is not a recovery path.

not_recommended.pattern: Always On availability groups (or a failover cluster instance) for the SQL Server tier
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It is the correct, mainstream, vendor-endorsed answer for keeping a SQL Server workload available, and it is what a healthcare customer's security questionnaire will ask about by name. It is the only approach that reduces downtime rather than only bounding data loss. Synchronous-commit replicas give an RPO of zero for committed transactions. And a failover cluster instance is genuinely instance-wide, so it would cover host and all offices in one configuration  -  which is exactly the coverage this system's database-per-tenant shape otherwise makes expensive.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: Two documented edition limits and one team limit. On Standard edition, multi-database availability groups do not exist; basic availability groups are limited to two replicas and, verbatim, 'Support for one availability database'  -  so database-per-tenant means one basic AG per office, 12 today and 34 at the planned ceiling, each seeded, monitored and failed over independently, and each new office (provisioned by non-engineers through a host UI, not a deployment) silently arriving outside HA coverage until someone remembers. Basic AGs also forbid backups on the secondary, so the standby cannot even offload the backup work that is the actual bottleneck. A failover cluster instance avoids the per-database explosion but needs shared storage plus a cluster manager (WSFC or Pacemaker) and is capped at two nodes on Standard. Either way the team acquires a consensus system whose signature failure is a half-failover nobody notices, and they have no on-call rotation to notice it. The expected outcome is that the cluster becomes the top cause of outages, which is the classic result when HA infrastructure is added without an operations owner.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: When there is a person whose job is operations  -  not a developer with an operations sideline  -  and the business has stated an MTD measured in hours with no workable paper fallback. Enterprise edition (removing the one-database-per-AG limit) or a move to a platform-managed database that hides the cluster entirely would also change the calculus, but that is a platform-selection question for the next exercise, not an architecture question for this one.

not_recommended.pattern: Multi-region or multi-facility active-active
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It is the only design that survives the loss of a whole facility with continuity rather than with a rebuild, and PHI-handling businesses do get asked about geographic resilience. If the platform makes it a checkbox, the temptation to take it is real.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: NIST reserves mirrored and hot-site strategies for FIPS 199 HIGH availability impact, and reserves full-scale functional exercises including failover to the alternate location for the same tier. An appointment-scheduling platform whose unavailability delays evaluations but does not endanger anyone sits at MODERATE, where NIST's prescribed strategy is 'Cold or Warm site'. Beyond the tiering argument, this system is not built for it: tenancy resolves from the Host header alone, so a traffic-steering layer becomes a fleet-wide correctness dependency; the DataProtection keyring, the distributed cache and the distributed lock all live in one Redis; and the Case Tracker partner integration has one endpoint and one token. The correct expression of geography here is a requirement on where the backup artefacts live, not a second live stack  -  which is exactly NIST's offsite-storage criterion.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: If a customer contract imposes an availability SLA that a rebuild cannot meet, or if the availability categorisation moves to HIGH because the platform starts carrying something time-critical to patient care rather than to scheduling.

not_recommended.pattern: Automated failover of any component, driven by health checks
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: Automation removes the human from the critical path, which is attractive precisely because this team has no on-call rotation  -  nobody is awake at 03:00 to promote a standby, so a machine that does it seems strictly better. It is also standard practice essentially everywhere above a certain size.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: Automated failover trades a loud failure for a quiet one. A manual promotion fails obviously: the system is down, someone follows a runbook, and either it works or it visibly does not. An automated promotion can fail partially  -  promoted but not repointed, repointed but not promoted, flapped and returned, split-brain  -  and in this system a partial promotion has teeth: two Hangfire processing servers against one schema would double-execute twelve recurring jobs including the outbox drains, sending duplicate ex-parte correspondence to real attorneys. The brief's own stated constraint is to prefer designs that fail obviously. An automated failover is the archetype of the opposite, and it is worse for a team that cannot investigate ambiguity at 03:00 than a clean outage is.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: When there is an on-call rotation to catch the partial failures automation creates, and when duplicate execution of the outbox drains has been made harmless by idempotency keyed on a partner-visible identifier. Automate the failover after making double-execution safe, never before.

not_recommended.pattern: Container orchestration (Kubernetes or equivalent) adopted as the availability mechanism
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It gives declarative desired-state, self-healing restarts, rolling deploys, readiness gating and a genuinely better story than manual SSH plus docker compose  -  and the brief itself documents two operational traps that orchestration would eliminate: the mandatory --env-file that silently blanks every secret when forgotten, and the nginx worker that resolves upstreams once at start so routing breaks on stale container IPs after a rebuild. Those are real, recurring, self-inflicted outages that a scheduler would not have.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It solves the wrong layer. Every component whose loss is actually fatal here is stateful and singleton: one SQL Server, one Redis holding the DataProtection keyring, one MinIO holding every PHI document, one nginx terminating the only TLS. Orchestrating the stateless tier improves restart behaviour for the part that was not the problem, while adding a control plane, a storage abstraction, an ingress with its own Host-header semantics, and a body of operational knowledge two SDE-1 developers do not have and have roughly one week a month to acquire. The honest fix for the two named traps is far cheaper than a scheduler: make the compose invocation a single checked-in script that cannot be run without the env file, and give the proxy the resolver-plus-variable-proxy_pass treatment the MinIO block already has. Buy the outcome without buying the platform.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: If the team grows past roughly four engineers with one owning deployment, or if the platform decision in the next exercise brings a managed control plane where the operational burden is genuinely someone else's. Adopting it as a DR strategy for a single-VM stateful system is the wrong reason at any size.

not_recommended.pattern: Continuous replication or change-data-capture into a second data store as the DR mechanism
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It appears to give a near-zero RPO without the licensing and clustering weight of availability groups, and it is a familiar pattern from larger systems. It also decouples the DR copy from the SQL Server version and edition.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It replaces a well-understood, vendor-documented restore sequence with a bespoke pipeline that this team would own, debug and be woken by. It has no documented restore semantics  -  the moment you need to answer 'restore this one office to 14:20 yesterday' you are writing that logic yourself, whereas RESTORE ... WITH STOPAT already exists and is documented. Replication lag is invisible by default, so it fails subtly in exactly the way the team cannot detect. And at 33 offices it becomes 33 pipelines with 33 lag states. The measured data volume  -  16 appointments producing roughly 1,450 audit rows in one office  -  does not remotely justify a streaming architecture.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: If the RPO derived from the BIA lands below the shortest practical log-backup interval, which would be surprising for a business whose records are re-keyable, or if a genuine analytics/reporting requirement needs a second store anyway and DR can ride along on infrastructure that exists for another reason.

not_recommended.pattern: Log shipping every office database to a standby (rather than restoring the standby from the ordinary backup chain)
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It is native, free in Standard edition, well documented, and gives a continuously-current warm standby with a much shorter RTO than a cold restore. It also has one property nothing else in the SQL Server toolbox offers: a user-specified delay between the primary's log backup and the secondary's restore, which Microsoft documents as a defence against an accidental change on the primary  -  a real protection against the 'someone deleted a practice' scenario.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It is configured per database and built entirely from SQL Server Agent jobs  -  a backup job on the primary, copy and restore jobs on each secondary, an alert job on the monitor. This deployment does not run SQL Server Agent (it is disabled by default in the Linux container), so adopting log shipping means adopting Agent as well. At 11 offices that is 12 configurations and roughly 36-48 jobs; at 33 it is 34 configurations and over a hundred. Worst of all, adding an office is a host-UI action performed as a business operation, not a deployment, so the DR configuration would drift out of step with the fleet silently and by design. A standby restored from the same off-box backup chain you are already producing gets most of the RTO benefit for a fraction of the moving parts, and cannot drift because it enumerates the offices from the backup store.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: If the dominant feared event turns out to be logical corruption or malicious deletion rather than host loss  -  the delayed-restore secondary is genuinely the best available tool for that  -  and if office provisioning can be made to register the new database with the DR configuration automatically.

not_recommended.pattern: A commercial backup product or backup appliance with agents, a catalogue and a console
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It centralises scheduling, retention, verification and reporting; it produces the audit artefacts a HIPAA assessor likes to see; and it removes the need for the team to write and maintain backup tooling at all. For a team with one developer-week a month, buying rather than building is usually the right instinct, and this is the one place where 'buy' is the conventional answer.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: The build cost it displaces is already near zero: SQL Server 2022 writes backups directly to object storage with a single T-SQL statement, and a maintained script set (Ola Hallengren's solution, last released 16 August 2026, supporting SQL Server on Linux and S3 destinations) supplies scheduling, retention and per-database iteration for free. What an appliance adds instead is another product to license, patch, credential and recover  -  and it must itself be recovered before anything else can be, so it inserts a new dependency at the front of the critical path. It also tends to want an agent, a catalogue database and a console, none of which fit a two-person, container-based deployment. Note this rejection is about operational shape, not price; cost is out of scope here.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: If the estate grows beyond SQL Server  -  several distinct data technologies each needing their own backup logic  -  so that a single catalogue genuinely reduces total moving parts rather than adding one.

not_recommended.pattern: Tiered, per-tenant RTO/RPO commitments (a 'gold/silver/bronze' DR offering)
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: Database-per-tenant makes it technically natural: each office already has its own database, its own backup chain and its own restore path, so differentiated recovery is nearly free to implement and could be sold. Larger multi-tenant SaaS businesses do exactly this.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It multiplies the thing that is scarce  -  attention  -  rather than the thing that is abundant. Each tier is a separate schedule, a separate retention policy, a separate rehearsal cadence and a separate promise that must be kept and evidenced, all landing on two developers. It also creates an obligation to detect and report per-tenant RPO breaches, which requires the observability this system does not have (Serilog to console and file, HealthChecks UI with in-memory storage, no aggregation, no alerting). Give every office the same recovery guarantee, set it at what the weakest realistic case supports, and let the uniformity be the operational feature.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: When there is a contractual reason  -  a large practice demanding and paying for a stronger commitment  -  and when there is monitoring capable of proving per-tenant RPO continuously, so the promise is evidenced rather than asserted.

not_recommended.pattern: Quarterly full-scale DR failover exercises with the whole team, formal scenarios and an after-action report
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It is the gold-standard practice, it directly evidences 45 CFR 164.308(a)(7)(ii)(D), and any auditor will recognise and reward it. Exercising DR is the single highest-leverage assurance activity in existence  -  untested recovery is the default cause of failed recovery.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: NIST explicitly scales exercise rigour to impact level, and a full-scale functional exercise 'includ[ing] a system failover to the alternate location' is what it prescribes for HIGH-impact systems. For a MODERATE-impact system it prescribes a functional exercise whose procedures 'include an element of system recovery from backup media'  -  which is a timed restore, not a theatrical failover. There is also no alternate location to fail over to under the recommended design, so a full-scale exercise would be rehearsing a capability that deliberately does not exist. And with roughly one developer-week a month, a quarterly full-scale exercise would consume the entire infrastructure budget in ceremony rather than in the automated weekly verification restore that actually catches bad backups. Do the smaller thing more often.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: If the availability categorisation moves to HIGH, or if the design ever acquires a standby that is claimed to be promotable  -  the moment you claim a failover capability, you owe an exercise that proves it.

surprises: Turning the backup script on is what will fill the disk. The office databases are created by EF Core and inherit the model database's recovery model, which on Developer edition is FULL. Microsoft documents that a newly created full-recovery database reuses its log 'similar to a database using the simple recovery model ... up until the time you create a full database backup'  -  so these databases are in a pseudo-simple grace state today. The first successful BACKUP DATABASE ends that grace state permanently, and with no log backups scheduled the log can never truncate again (log_reuse_wait_desc = LOG_BACKUP) and grows until the ~9.7 GB of free space is gone. The reason this has not bitten yet is almost certainly that the backup script's cron is unconfirmed. The fix is one line per database  -  either add log backups, or set the databases to SIMPLE and accept losing point-in-time recovery  -  but the trap is that doing the responsible thing (making backups run reliably) is what triggers the outage.

HIPAA does not require six years of backup retention, and the brief's own premise on this is a misread that will oversize the design. 45 CFR 164.316(b)(2)(i)'s six years applies to 'the documentation required by paragraph (b)(1)'  -  policies, procedures and written records of required actions  -  not to ePHI, audit logs or backups. HIPAA sets no ePHI retention period at all. The retention driver that actually applies to a California workers' compensation IME platform is 8 CCR  39.5: 'All QMEs shall retain a copy of all comprehensive medical-legal reports ... for a period of five years from the date of each evaluation report,' with electronic copies explicitly acceptable. That same regulation also requires returning original records on written request  -  a deletion obligation that interacts awkwardly with immutable backups and should be thought about before immutability is switched on, not after.

There is no way to restore host and office databases to a mutually consistent point using the tools the codebase permits. Point-in-time restore is per-database and carries no cross-database guarantee; Microsoft's documented mechanism for related databases is marked transactions (BEGIN TRANSACTION ... WITH MARK recorded in the logs of all affected databases, restored with STOPATMARK)  -  which requires raw cross-database T-SQL that this system deliberately does not contain anywhere. The one mechanism that closes the gap without touching application code is SQL Server 2022's T-SQL snapshot backup: ALTER SERVER CONFIGURATION SET SUSPEND_FOR_SNAPSHOT_BACKUP = ON followed by BACKUP SERVER freezes writes across every user database at once, so a single storage snapshot yields one consistent recovery point across the whole fleet. It works on Linux and in containers, and it is available in every edition.

The mechanism that solves the consistency problem has a ceiling of 64 databases  -  roughly twice the planned tenant count. 'The maximum number of databases you can back up with this feature is 64', failing with Msg 925 above that, and it cannot suspend master, model or msdb. With 11 offices plus host that is 12 databases; at the stated headroom of 33 offices it is 34. There is comfortable room, but the tenant-growth ceiling and the backup-consistency ceiling are now coupled, and nobody has written that down. Crossing 64 offices would require re-architecting the recovery point, not just adding a database.

'Add a standby SQL Server' is not one thing; on Standard edition it is 34 things. Always On availability groups with multiple databases are Enterprise-only. Standard offers basic availability groups whose documented limitations include, verbatim, 'Limit of two replicas', 'No read access on secondary replica', 'No backups on secondary replica' and 'Support for one availability database'. Database-per-tenant therefore turns a single HA decision into one availability group per office, each created by hand  -  and since adding an office is a host-UI action performed by non-engineers rather than a deployment, every new practice would arrive outside HA coverage silently. This is the specific point at which the tenancy decision, which is otherwise excellent, becomes expensive.

The object store holding every PHI document is now unmaintained software. The minio/minio repository was archived by its owner on 25 April 2026 and carries the notice 'THIS REPOSITORY IS NO LONGER MAINTAINED'; the README states 'The MinIO community edition is now distributed as source code only. We will no longer provide pre-compiled binary releases for the community version.' This is a DR problem, not only a security one: the recovery runbook now depends on a binary the team must build themselves from an archived tree, and the object-locking/WORM capability needed for immutable backups is documented under the commercial AIStor product. It also collides with a constraint the brief already flags  -  an external partner holds scoped credentials against minio.<domain> and would have to be re-credentialed on their schedule if the store is replaced. That partner's calendar is now on the critical path of a component-lifecycle decision.

The disaster-recovery critical path is a mode-600 file and a PFX, not a database. Restore all 34 databases perfectly onto a clean host and you get a stack that cannot mint a token (the OpenIddict signing certificate is mounted from the host and its passphrase comes from the environment) and cannot read any protected payload (the DataProtection keyring lives in Redis under CaseEvaluation-Protection-Keys). The 35-variable secrets file exists in exactly one place, on the machine most likely to be lost, and several of its values were pasted into chat transcripts and are already flagged for rotation. The single most valuable half-day of DR work in this whole area is not database-related: it is getting the secrets and the signing certificate into a second location and proving, with the primary host powered off, that a second person can start the system.

If you encrypt backups  -  which you should  -  you create a second absolute single point of failure with a counter-intuitive rule. Microsoft: 'Without the certificate or asymmetric key, you can't restore the backup, rendering the backup file unusable,' and 'the certificate shouldn't be renewed on expiry or changed in any way. Renewal can result in updating the certificate triggering the change of the thumbprint, therefore making the certificate invalid for the backup file.' Any sensible-looking automated certificate-rotation policy, applied uniformly across the estate, would silently render the entire backup history unrestorable. The backup encryption certificate must be exempted from rotation by explicit, documented policy, and stored separately from the backups it protects.

Recovery has a fleet-wide single point of failure that exists only during recovery. db-migrator loops offices with no per-tenant error handling, and both the API and AuthServer gate on its service_completed_successfully. During a rebuild  -  the exact moment when databases are most likely to be in mixed states  -  one office's failed migration prevents the entire fleet from starting, with no report of which offices succeeded. The tenancy design's whole promise is that one office's problem is not everyone's problem, and this one line of compose configuration inverts that promise precisely when it matters most.

A failover or recovery path that introduces a proxy will break tenancy, not just routing  -  and nginx's own default is the trap. The documented default is `proxy_set_header Host $proxy_host;`, and the docs state plainly that 'the header fields "Host" and "Connection" from the original request are not passed to the proxied server'. Because tenancy resolves from the Host header and nothing else, and a bare IP cannot reach the application at all, any new proxy layer introduced during recovery returns 'Tenant not found' for every office at once. That failure is loud, which is good, but it will read as an application bug at 03:00 rather than as a one-line proxy configuration miss.

Backing up Redis by tarring the volume can silently produce an invalid backup  -  and that volume holds the DataProtection keyring, which is not cache. Redis documents that since 7.0 the AOF is a multi-file set, and 'if this is done during a rewrite, you might end up with an invalid backup'; the supported procedure is to set auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 0, confirm INFO persistence shows aof_rewrite_in_progress = 0, copy, then restore the setting. The BACKUP command family that makes this clean requires Redis 8.10.0 and is unavailable on Redis 7. Meanwhile the default appendfsync everysec means 'you may lose 1 second of data if there is a disaster'  -  fine for a cache, and worth a deliberate decision for a keyring whose loss invalidates every session and breaks in-flight email-confirmation links.

Restoring one office is an externally visible act, not an internal one. Rolling an office back to T-1 resets its AppNotificationOutboxItems and AppIntegrationOutboxItems to unsent, so the drain jobs re-deliver: duplicate ex-parte-addressed emails to real attorneys and claims administrators, and duplicate messages to the Case Tracker partner whose reconciliation runs every fifteen minutes and will now be reconciling against a state it has already moved past. Simultaneously, MinIO objects written in the lost window are not rolled back and become orphaned PHI with no referencing row  -  a disposal and accounting problem, not merely a storage leak. The design conclusion is worth stating plainly: this system's recovery can never be externally consistent, so the requirement is that it be reconcilable  -  idempotent drains keyed on a partner-visible identifier, plus an orphan-object sweep. That is a code change, and it is cheaper now than after the first real restore.

Restore duration and backup size are governed by audit data, not by business data. The measured ratio is roughly 1,450 audit-log rows and 2,689 property-change rows for 16 appointments  -  over 100:1  -  with retention unconfigured and nothing pruning it. The practical consequences are that per-office restore time is an audit-table problem, that the RTO you measure today will drift upward continuously until audit retention is configured, and that configuring audit retention is therefore a disaster-recovery task masquerading as a housekeeping one. Fixing it changes restore arithmetic by roughly two orders of magnitude.

The rehearsal window is closing and it is worth more than anything else in this list. There is no real PHI in the system yet, so today a restore rehearsal is a developer exercise with no compliance surface. The moment real practices take real bookings, every rehearsal environment becomes an in-scope system holding ePHI, inheriting access control, audit, encryption, disposal and a business-associate analysis for wherever it is restored. The engineering is identical either way; only the cost changes, and it changes sharply and permanently. Build and prove the restore path now.
what_would_change_the_answer: The MTD, once actually elicited from the business owner. If the front desk can run a booked day from a printed schedule and a phone, MTD is a working day or more and rung 2 is proportionate. If ex-parte notice deadlines or same-day packet assembly mean a lost morning is a lost claim event, MTD collapses to hours, and rung 3 (a standby host kept current from the same backup chain) becomes mandatory rather than opportunistic. This single answer moves the recommendation more than any technical fact in this document.

The FIPS 199 availability categorisation, made explicitly rather than assumed. I have argued MODERATE, which is what licenses the cold/warm answer under NIST SP 800-34 Table 3-2. If the business categorises availability as HIGH, NIST's own guidance points to mirrored systems and a hot site, and rungs 4-6 stop being over-engineering.

Whether the HIPAA Security Rule NPRM is finalised with the 72-hour restoration requirement intact. Today it is proposed only, with HHS targeting July 2027 for final action and a compliance window typically 180-240 days after. If it lands as drafted, the 'Testing and revision procedures' specification stops being addressable, the 72-hour figure becomes a hard design target, and the criticality analysis and the 24-hour contingency-activation notification to covered entities become deliverables rather than good practice.

Office count crossing roughly 64 databases on one instance. That is the documented ceiling of T-SQL snapshot backup, and it is the mechanism the recommendation leans on for a cross-database consistent recovery point. Past it, the consistency strategy must change entirely  -  most likely by splitting offices across instances, which is already possible by configuration alone thanks to the derived connection strings.

Whether audit retention gets configured and pruning lands. At the measured 100:1 ratio, audit data dominates backup size and restore time. If retention is capped, restore arithmetic improves by roughly two orders of magnitude, and options that looked slow become fast. If it stays unconfigured, RTO drifts upward forever and the quarterly timed rehearsal will show it.

The team composition. The moment there is a person who owns operations rather than a developer with an operations sideline, automated failover stops being a liability and becomes an option  -  and the roughly 4 hours/month threshold that this design depends on stops being the binding constraint.

Whether MinIO is replaced. Given the community edition was archived on 25 April 2026, a replacement is likely on some horizon. When it happens, the external partner holding scoped credentials against minio.<domain> must be re-credentialed on their schedule, which places a third party on the critical path of a component decision. If the replacement is chosen with backup immutability in mind, one requirement in this document gets satisfied for free; if it is chosen only to replace the object store, immutability becomes a separate project.

Whether any customer contract introduces an availability SLA. The whole proportionality argument rests on there being no external commitment tighter than what a rebuild can deliver. One signed SLA invalidates it.

Whether the outbox drains are made idempotent against a partner-visible key. Until they are, every restore is an externally visible event and rehearsals must be network-isolated. Once they are, both restore and eventual multi-instance operation become materially safer, and several other options open up.

material_errors: Claim [24]: the sentence presented as a quotation - 'Your BACKUP operation will consume BUFFERCOUNT * MAXTRANSFERSIZE in RAM' - does NOT appear anywhere on the cited archived Microsoft page. The page instead demonstrates the arithmetic via trace flag 3213 output ('Buffer count: 10 / Max transfer size: 4096 KB / Total buffer space: 40 MB'). A verbatim quotation that is not in the cited source is the single most serious provenance defect in this set.

Claim [24], second and more consequential defect: the documented Msg 701 failure at 200 MB of total buffer space is explicitly a 32-BIT failure mode. The post states 'When I switch this over to a 32-bit instance' and attributes the OOM to 'My largest contiguous block available in the non-BPool (MemToLeave) region of my 32-bit instance was only 157MB.' The deployment under analysis is 64-bit SQL Server on Linux with MSSQL_MEMORY_LIMIT_MB=7168, where MemToLeave/virtual-address-space exhaustion does not apply. Citing 200 MB as a relevant threshold here is a category error; the real 64-bit constraint is ordinary memory pressure against the 7 GB limit, which is a different and much looser bound. Do not size concurrent backups off this figure.

Claim [16] omits a precondition that gates its own headline number. The cited page states: 'The use of COMPRESSION is required in order to change MAXTRANSFERSIZE values.' The claimed maximum of '200,000 MiB per URL (with MAXTRANSFERSIZE set to 20 MB)' is therefore only reachable on a COMPRESSED backup. Since backup compression is Enterprise/Standard-only per the editions table (No for Web, Express), the 200,000 MiB/URL ceiling is not available on Web edition even though Web edition does support S3 backup. This interaction is load-bearing for any sizing exercise and is not stated.

Quote-provenance failures across four claims: verbatim quotations are attributed to pages that do not contain them. [17] the entire Basic AG limitation list ('Limit of two replicas', 'No read access on secondary replica', 'No backups on secondary replica', 'No integrity checks on secondary replicas', 'Support for one availability database', "can't be part of a distributed availability group", 'You might have multiple Basic availability groups connected to a single instance') is cited to the editions page but lives on /database-engine/availability-groups/windows/basic-availability-groups-always-on-availability-groups. [20] the master-restore quotes ('single-user mode', 'the instance of SQL Server shuts down and terminates the sqlcmd process', 'same version, edition, and patch level ... undefined SQL Server instance behavior') are cited to RESTORE (Transact-SQL) but live on /backup-restore/restore-the-master-database-transact-sql. [19] the MSSQL_AGENT_ENABLED quote is cited to the log shipping page but lives on /linux/configure/environment-variables. [30] the Federal Register dates are cited to the HHS fact sheet, which gives neither. In every case I confirmed the quoted text is accurate at its true home - the defect is citation, not fact - but a reader following the given URL will not find the quote.

Claim [8]: the categorisation is sound but the reasoning should state the rule that makes it sound. FIPS 199 applies the high-water mark PER SECURITY OBJECTIVE ('the potential impact values assigned to the respective security objectives (confidentiality, integrity, availability) shall be the highest values (i.e. high water mark)'), so an availability rating of MODERATE survives intact alongside confidentiality HIGH. This matters because NIST SP 800-34 keys its recovery-strategy and exercise-rigour guidance specifically to the availability objective - 'The depth and rigor of ISCP TT&E activities increases with the FIPS 199 availability security objective' - and without stating the per-objective rule, a reader could wrongly conclude the system is a 'HIGH-impact system' and that rungs 4-6 are back in scope.

Claim [11] rests on an inference the cited pages do not license. The recovery-models page names defaults only for 'SQL Server Enterprise and Standard editions' (full) and 'SQL Server Express edition' (simple); it says nothing about Developer edition's default recovery model, and nothing about new databases inheriting from model. The Developer=FULL step is an inference from 'Developer includes all the functionality of Enterprise edition', which is a FEATURE statement, not a DEFAULTS statement. Separately, the 'read-only databases' consequence is real but is documented on the error 9002 page, not the cited transaction-log page: 'If the log fills while the database is online, the database remains online but can only be read, not updated.' The chain is plausible and the conclusion is probably right, but it must be settled by observing recovery_model_desc on the running instance before it is used to justify a change freeze.
vendor_neutrality_violations: Requirement 2 ('must expose an S3-compatible object endpoint ... supporting S3 multipart upload') is the one requirement that states a vendor-originated API name as the requirement itself. I judge this ACCEPTABLE rather than a true violation - 'S3-compatible' is a behaviour class with no vendor-neutral synonym, Microsoft's own documentation uses exactly that phrase as a class, and claim [16] establishes that SQL Server 2022 BACKUP TO URL speaks only the S3 REST API or Azure Blob, so the constraint is genuine and not a preference. Flagging it because it is the sole place a reader could mistake an interface constraint for a vendor selection; a neutral rewording would be 'an object endpoint implementing the S3 REST API (the only object protocol the database engine's native BACKUP TO URL supports besides Azure Blob Storage)'. No specific S3 provider is named or recommended anywhere.

Requirement 10 ('Every backup must be produced WITH CHECKSUM') prescribes a product's T-SQL syntax rather than the capability. This is a wording issue, not a vendor recommendation - it names no product to buy. The capability-level statement would be: 'every backup must carry an end-to-end integrity checksum that the restore path verifies by default', with WITH CHECKSUM named as the incumbent engine's mechanism. Worth fixing because as written it cannot be evaluated against a non-SQL-Server platform, and because the underlying evidence (claim [21]) is precisely about the CAPABILITY: without a backup checksum 'either restore operation proceeds without any verification'.

Requirements 6 and 13 fix the database platform to SQL Server ('the same SQL Server major version or higher'; an edition 'licensed for production use'). I do NOT count these as violations: SQL Server is the incumbent engine of the system under analysis, not a product being selected, and the forward-only restore constraint in requirement 6 is a factual property of the existing backup artefacts verified in claim [20] ('No SQL Server backup can be restored to an earlier version of SQL Server than the version on which the backup was created'). Requirement 13 is notably well-drafted for neutrality - it specifies the capability set (log backups, backup compression, backup encryption) rather than naming Standard or Enterprise, even though the editions table shows only those two editions satisfy it. Similarly, OpenIddict, ASP.NET DataProtection and Hangfire (requirements 7 and 15) appear only as existing artefacts that must be recoverable, never as recommendations to adopt. NO CLOUD VENDOR IS RECOMMENDED ANYWHERE IN THE 18 REQUIREMENTS, and no requirement concludes 'therefore use <product>'.

results.claim: [1] 45 CFR 164.308(a)(7) Contingency plan: (A) Data backup plan, (B) Disaster recovery plan, (C) Emergency mode operation plan are Required; (D) Testing and revision procedures, (E) Applications and data criticality analysis are Addressable
results.evidence_quote: (A) Data backup plan (Required). Establish and implement procedures to create and maintain retrievable exact copies of electronic protected health information. ... (D) Testing and revision procedures (Addressable). Implement procedures for periodic testing and revision of contingency plans. (E) Applications and data criticality analysis (Addressable).
results.correction: None. All five implementation specifications and their Required/Addressable designations are exact. Note on access: the ecfr.gov HTML URL 302-redirects bot traffic to unblock.federalregister.gov; I confirmed the text via the official eCFR renderer API for the identical section and independently via Cornell LII. The URL is correct and works in a browser.

results.claim: [2] 'Addressable' is not optional; 164.306(d)(3) requires assess-then-implement-or-document-plus-equivalent-alternative, and 164.306(b)(2) lists size/complexity/capabilities and cost as weighable factors
results.evidence_quote: (B) If implementing the implementation specification is not reasonable and appropriate -  (1) Document why it would not be reasonable and appropriate to implement the implementation specification; and (2) Implement an equivalent alternative measure if reasonable and appropriate. ... (b)(2)(i) The size, complexity, and capabilities of the covered entity or business associate. ... (iii) The costs of security measures.
results.correction: None. Subparagraph numbering 164.306(d)(3)(ii)(B)(1)-(2) and factors at (b)(2)(i)-(iv) are both exact. Worth adding for completeness: the four factors also include (ii) technical infrastructure, hardware and software security capabilities and (iv) the probability and criticality of potential risks - (iv) cuts against a proportionality argument as often as (i) and (iii) cut for it, so a two-person team's cost defence is not unconditional.

results.claim: [3] The six-year period in 164.316(b)(2)(i) is a documentation-retention rule tied to 164.316(b)(1), not a retention period for ePHI, audit logs or database backups; HIPAA sets no ePHI retention period
results.evidence_quote: (2) Implementation specifications: (i) Time limit (Required). Retain the documentation required by paragraph (b)(1) of this section for 6 years from the date of its creation or the date when it last was in effect, whichever is later. ... (b)(1) Standard: Documentation. (i) Maintain the policies and procedures implemented to comply with this subpart in written (which may be electronic) form; and (ii) If an action, activity or assessment is required by this subpart to be documented, maintain a written (which may be electronic) record of the action, activity, or assessment.
results.correction: None - this is a correct catch and the strongest single finding in the set. The 6 years attaches only to (b)(1) documentation. The section also carries two further Required specs the brief should not overlook: (ii) Availability (make documentation available to those responsible for implementing the procedures) and (iii) Updates (review periodically and update in response to environmental or operational changes) - the latter is what turns a DR plan into a maintained artefact rather than a one-off.

results.claim: [4] 8 CCR 39.5 requires QMEs to retain comprehensive medical-legal reports for five years from the date of each evaluation report; electronic copies suffice if a true and correct copy showing the QME signature; originals returned on written request
results.evidence_quote: All QMEs shall retain a copy of all comprehensive medical-legal reports completed by the QME for a period of five years from the date of each evaluation report. ... A QME may satisfy this requirement by retaining only an electronic copy of the report, as long as the electronic copy retained is a true and correct copy of the original, showing the QME signature, that was served on the parties.
results.correction: None; five years and the electronic-copy and originals-return provisions all check out. Two refinements for backup sizing: (a) the electronic-copy allowance is conditioned on the copy being the one 'that was served on the parties', which is a stronger fidelity requirement than merely retaining a PDF - the served artefact and its signature must be preserved, not regenerated; (b) the same section imposes a duty to submit reports to the Medical Director on request, which is a retrieval-latency requirement on the archive, not just a retention-period one.

results.claim: [5] NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 verbatim definitions of MTD, RTO and RPO, plus 'the RTO must normally be shorter than the MTD'
results.evidence_quote: The MTD represents the total amount of time the system owner/authorizing official is willing to accept for a mission/business process outage or disruption and includes all impact considerations. ... RTO defines the maximum amount of time that a system resource can remain unavailable before there is an unacceptable impact on other system resources, supported mission/business processes, and the MTD. ... Unlike RTO, RPO is not considered as part of MTD. ... Because the RTO must ensure that the MTD is not exceeded, the RTO must normally be shorter than the MTD.
results.correction: None. All four quotations are verbatim from Section 3.2 (p. 15 of the PDF). One caution if these definitions are reused: the Appendix ISCP template on a later page states RPO slightly differently - 'to which mission/business process data must be recovered' rather than 'can be recovered' - so quote the Section 3.2 wording, which is the one reproduced here.

results.claim: [6] Table 3-2 maps FIPS 199 availability impact to backup/strategy (Low: tape / relocate or cold site; Moderate: optical, WAN/VLAN replication / cold or warm site; High: mirrored systems and disc replication / hot site), and Section 3.5.4 ties exercise rigour to the same axis
results.evidence_quote: Moderate ... Backup: Optical backup, WAN/VLAN replication / Strategy: Cold or Warm site ... [3.5.4] For moderate-impact systems, a functional exercise at an organization-defined frequency should be conducted. ... Exercise procedures should be developed to include an element of system recovery from backup media.
results.correction: None; Table 3-2 rows and the 3.5.4 bullets are exact, and the section number 3.5.4 ('TT&E Program Summary') is correctly assigned - the low/moderate/high bullets fall under 3.5.4, not under 3.5.3 ('Exercises') where the exercise types are defined. The framing sentence immediately above the bullets is worth quoting too because it is the one that authorises keying all of this to availability specifically: 'The depth and rigor of ISCP TT&E activities increases with the FIPS 199 availability security objective.' Also note Table 3-2's own caption calls these 'Examples', so it is illustrative guidance, not a mandate.

results.claim: [7] FIPS 199 defines AVAILABILITY as 'Ensuring timely and reliable access to and use of information'; MODERATE = serious adverse effect with the quoted amplification; HIGH = severe or catastrophic adverse effect
results.evidence_quote: AMPLIFICATION: A serious adverse effect means that, for example, the loss of confidentiality, integrity, or availability might: (i) cause a significant degradation in mission capability to an extent and duration that the organization is able to perform its primary functions, but the effectiveness of the functions is significantly reduced; ... or (iv) result in significant harm to individuals that does not involve loss of life or serious life threatening injuries.
results.correction: None of substance. Trivial fidelity point: the glossary rendering of the availability definition ends with a period, not an ellipsis - 'AVAILABILITY: Ensuring timely and reliable access to and use of information. [44 U.S.C., SEC. 3542]' - so the trailing '...' in the claim is the researcher's, not the document's. HIGH as 'severe or catastrophic adverse effect' is confirmed in the categorisation table.

results.claim: [8] An IME scheduling platform plausibly categorises as FIPS 199 MODERATE for availability and HIGH for confidentiality, and this is the load-bearing judgement behind rejecting rungs 4-6
results.evidence_quote: the potential impact values assigned to the respective security objectives (confidentiality, integrity, availability) shall be the highest values (i.e., high water mark) from among those security categories that have been determined for each type of information resident on the information system.
results.correction: The DOCUMENT supports the quoted amplification language but cannot support the categorisation itself, which is a judgement no standard can settle - the claim is right to say so and right to push it to the business owner. Two additions make it defensible rather than merely plausible. First, state the per-objective high-water-mark rule quoted above: it is what lets availability=MODERATE coexist with confidentiality=HIGH without the system becoming a 'HIGH-impact system' for contingency-planning purposes, and it is the precise reason SP 800-34's moderate-tier guidance applies. Second, FIPS 199 requires INTEGRITY to be rated too - 'the value of not applicable cannot be assigned to any security objective' - and the claim omits it. For a platform whose outbox tables can re-send to external parties on restore (claim [33]), integrity is not obviously MODERATE and should be rated explicitly rather than left blank.

results.claim: [9] Only the FULL recovery model supports point-in-time restore; Simple recovers only to the end of a backup, Bulk-logged does not support PITR; Simple cannot be used with log shipping, AGs/mirroring or PITR; Enterprise/Standard default to full, Express to simple
results.evidence_quote: SQL Server Enterprise and Standard editions use the full recovery model by default, while SQL Server Express edition uses the simple recovery model by default. ... You can't use the following features with the simple recovery model: Log shipping; Always On availability groups and database mirroring; Media recovery without data loss; Point-in-time restores ... [Bulk-logged] Can recover to the end of any backup. Point-in-time recovery isn't supported.
results.correction: None; every quoted cell and the edition-defaults note are verbatim. Two small completions: the Simple-model exclusion list has a fourth entry the claim drops, 'Media recovery without data loss', which is directly relevant to a DR argument; and the Full row's work-loss cell is conditional in full - 'Normally none. If the tail of the log is damaged, changes since the most recent log backup must be redone' - which is the clause that makes tail-log backup capability a requirement rather than a nicety.

results.claim: [10] The log trap: an untruncated log fills the disk; under full recovery truncation occurs after a log backup; a new full-recovery database behaves like simple until the first full backup; diagnosable as log_reuse_wait_desc = LOG_BACKUP (value 2)
results.evidence_quote: If a transaction log is never truncated, it eventually fills all the disk space allocated to physical log files. ... When you first create a database that uses the full recovery model, the transaction log is reused as needed (similar to a database using the simple recovery model), up until the time you create a full database backup. ... | 2 | LOG_BACKUP | A log backup is required before the transaction log can be truncated.
results.correction: None; all three quotations and the numeric code 2 are exact. One precision worth carrying into the runbook: the page's full statement of full-recovery truncation is conditional - 'if a checkpoint has occurred since the previous backup, truncation occurs after a log backup (unless it's a copy-only log backup)'. The copy-only exclusion matters operationally, because a monitoring script that takes copy-only log backups will not relieve the condition it is monitoring.

results.claim: [11] Office databases created by EF Core MigrateAsync inherit model's recovery model, FULL on Developer edition, so they are in the pseudo-simple grace state; the first BACKUP DATABASE ends it permanently and the log then grows until the ~9.7 GB free volume fills, producing error 9002 and read-only databases
results.evidence_quote: When you first create a database that uses the full recovery model, the transaction log is reused as needed (similar to a database using the simple recovery model), up until the time you create a full database backup.
results.correction: The grace-state mechanism is exactly right and correctly cited; three links in the chain are not established by the cited page. (1) Developer edition's default recovery model is nowhere stated - the recovery-models page names only Enterprise/Standard (full) and Express (simple), and 'Developer includes all the functionality of Enterprise edition' is a feature statement, not a defaults statement. Inheritance from model is likewise not stated on either page. Settle this by observing SELECT name, recovery_model_desc FROM sys.databases before relying on it. (2) The read-only outcome is real but documented elsewhere - the error 9002 page states 'If the log fills while the database is online, the database remains online but can only be read, not updated' (and marks the database RESOURCE PENDING if the log fills during recovery instead). (3) 'Grows until the volume fills' presumes unlimited autogrow; the same page lists 'Log size is set to a fixed maximum value or autogrow is disabled' as an independent 9002 cause, so the failure may arrive at a configured MAXSIZE well before 9.7 GB. The ~9.7 GB free figure is from the brief and I could not verify it.

results.claim: [12] Documented single-database PITR sequence: full backup with endpoint earlier than target; identical STOPAT in every RESTORE LOG; use STANDBY to find unknown point in time; specify the point in time early; tail-log backup first where required; a warning is generated and the database remains unrecovered if the log backup lacks the requested time
results.evidence_quote: In every RESTORE LOG statement of the restore sequence, you must specify your target time or transaction in an identical STOPAT clause. As a prerequisite to a point-in-time restore, you must first restore a full database backup whose endpoint is earlier than your target restore time. ... If the transaction log backup does not contain the requested time ... a warning is generated and the database remains unrecovered.
results.correction: None; all five elements verify verbatim, including both Recommendations headings and the tail-log step ('Take tail-log backup before restore will be selected if it is necessary for the point in time that you have selected'). Add one caveat the page flags in an Important box and the claim omits: 'Under the bulk-logged recovery model, if a log backup contains bulk-logged changes, point-in-time recovery is not possible to a point within that backup' - relevant because index rebuilds under bulk-logged silently forfeit PITR for that window.

results.claim: [13] SQL Server offers no automatic cross-database point-in-time consistency; the documented mechanism is marked transactions, requiring marks in the logs of all affected databases, restored with STOPATMARK/STOPBEFOREMARK, and requiring BEGIN TRANSACTION ... WITH MARK
results.evidence_quote: If a marked transaction spans multiple databases on the same database server or on different servers, the marks must be recorded in the logs of all the affected databases. ... Use the WITH STOPATMARK = '<mark_name>' clause to specify that the marked transaction is the recovery point. ... Use the WITH STOPBEFOREMARK = '<mark_name>' clause ...
results.correction: None. The companion quote from the recovery-models page ('If you have two or more related databases in the full recovery model that must be logically consistent, you might have to implement special procedures') is also verbatim. Two operational details the claim could add: marks are recorded in msdb..logmarkhistory on EACH server, so cross-server recovery requires reading that table on every instance; and the page notes 'recovering to a mark is disallowed when the database is undergoing operations that are bulk-logged', the same restriction that limits ordinary PITR.

results.claim: [14] Marked transactions are unavailable to this system as built (no raw SQL, no cross-database queries), so the only route to a cross-database consistent recovery point without a code change is instance-wide snapshot coordination
results.evidence_quote: To insert marks into the transaction logs, use the BEGIN TRANSACTION statement and the WITH MARK [description] clause.
results.correction: The documentary half holds: marks are created only by BEGIN TRANSACTION ... WITH MARK, so they cannot arise from EF Core's generated SQL without deliberate T-SQL. The codebase premises (no raw SQL in src, no cross-database queries, in-memory joins) are the brief's, not the document's, and I cannot verify them. The word 'only' in the conclusion is too strong on the evidence given: T-SQL snapshot backup is one route, but so are (a) quiescing writes at the application layer for the duration of a coordinated backup round, and (b) storage-level crash-consistent snapshots of all volumes, which give a consistent point without SQL Server's cooperation at the cost of crash-recovery on restore. Recommend rewording to 'the only route that does not require an application change or a write freeze imposed outside the database'.

results.claim: [15] SQL Server 2022 T-SQL snapshot backup freezes write I/O across all user databases and records one consistent recovery point; supports PITR via subsequent streaming log backups; hard limit of 64 databases (Msg 925); system databases cannot be suspended; available in every edition
results.evidence_quote: write operations are paused on SQL Server (read requests are still allowed), and control is handed over to the backup application to complete the snapshot. ... The maximum number of databases you can back up with this feature is 64. ... Msg 925, Level 19, State 1 ... None of these commands support suspending system databases (master, model, and msdb) for snapshot backup.
results.correction: None; syntax, the pause statement, the 64-database limit with Msg 925, system-database exclusion and PITR support ('Perform point-in-time recovery using log backups taken with the normal streaming approach after the snapshot FULL backup') all verify. The edition claim, which the claim transparently attributes to the 2022 editions table rather than this page, is also correct: Snapshot backup is Yes across Enterprise, Standard, Web, Express with Advanced Services and Express. Two design-relevant details omitted: SUSPEND_FOR_SNAPSHOT_BACKUP clears the differential bitmap by default (use MODE = COPY_ONLY to avoid invalidating subsequent differentials), and a restore requires copying the database files from the snapshot URI to the mount point BEFORE issuing RESTORE - the .bkm file is metadata only, so the restore runbook has a manual storage step that the backup runbook does not.

results.claim: [16] SQL Server 2022 S3 backup: edition-gated Yes for Enterprise/Standard/Web and No for Express; https mandatory; Linux CA at /var/opt/mssql/security/ca-certificates with first 50 certificates, in place before start; buckets not creatable from SQL Server; 10,000 parts, MAXTRANSFERSIZE 5-20 MB default 10 MB, 200,000 MiB per URL, 64 URLs, 259-character URL limit; VERIFYONLY and STOPAT supported, NOINIT/INIT not
results.evidence_quote: Each file can be split up to 10,000 parts, each part size ranges from 5 MB to 20 MB ... The default value of MAXTRANSFERSIZE is 10 MB ... A single backup file can be up to 200,000 MiB per URL (with MAXTRANSFERSIZE set to 20 MB). ... Backups can be striped across a maximum of 64 URLs. ... the CA must be placed on a predefined location to be created at /var/opt/mssql/security/ca-certificates, only the first 50 certificates can be stored and supported in this folder. The CA must be in place before SQL Server process is started. ... The total URL length is limited to 259 characters.
results.correction: Every stated limit is exact, and the edition gating is confirmed by the editions table (Yes/Yes/Yes for Enterprise/Standard/Web, No for both Express variants). Three omissions worth adding, one of them consequential. (1) CONSEQUENTIAL: 'The use of COMPRESSION is required in order to change MAXTRANSFERSIZE values' - so the 200,000 MiB/URL ceiling presupposes a compressed backup, and compression is Enterprise/Standard-only, making that ceiling unreachable on Web edition. (2) The page recommends staying under 200 characters of URL, not 259: 'the usable limit is 254 characters. However, we recommend sticking to a limit of 200 characters.' (3) Failed or cancelled backups leave uncommitted multipart data in the bucket that SQL Server does not clean up - 'aren't removed if there are backup failures' - which interacts badly with an object-lock retention policy and with storage-cost monitoring.

results.claim: [17] SQL Server 2022 edition limits: AGs Enterprise-only; Basic AGs Standard-only with the quoted limitation list; Standard FCI two nodes; log shipping Enterprise/Standard/Web yes, Express no; backup compression and encrypted backup Enterprise/Standard only; Express 10 GB, 1,410 MB buffer pool, no Agent
results.evidence_quote: Always On availability groups | Yes | No | No | No | No ... Basic availability groups | No | Yes | No | No | No ... Backup compression | Yes | Yes | No | No | No ... Encrypted backup | Yes | Yes | No | No | No ... SQL Server Agent | Yes | Yes | Yes | No | No ... Maximum relational database size | 524 PB | 524 PB | 524 PB | 10 GB | 10 GB ... [footnote 4] On Standard edition, there's support for two nodes. [footnote 6] A basic availability group supports two replicas, with one database.
results.correction: Every FACT is correct, but the verbatim Basic AG limitation list is attributed to the wrong page. The cited editions page carries only footnote 6's one-sentence summary; the seven quoted bullets ('Limit of two replicas', 'No read access on secondary replica', 'No backups on secondary replica', 'No integrity checks on secondary replicas', 'Support for one availability database', "Basic availability groups can't be part of a distributed availability group", 'You might have multiple Basic availability groups connected to a single instance') appear on https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/database-engine/availability-groups/windows/basic-availability-groups-always-on-availability-groups, where I confirmed all seven verbatim. Re-cite them there. Two additions from that page that strengthen the design argument: Basic AGs 'can't be upgraded to advanced availability groups' without dropping and recreating, and on Linux they support an extra configuration-only replica. Also confirmed: Standard buffer pool 128 GB and 'lesser of 4 sockets or 24 cores'.

results.claim: [18] Developer edition includes all Enterprise functionality but is licensed for development and test, not production; MSSQL_PID='Developer' is described as the freely licensed Developer Edition for non-production use
results.evidence_quote: SQL Server Developer edition lets developers build any kind of application on top of SQL Server. It includes all the functionality of Enterprise edition, but is licensed for use as a development and test system, not as a production server.
results.correction: None; both quotes are verbatim and the claim transparently attributes the second to the Linux environment-variable documentation, where I confirmed it ('MSSQL_PID specifies the freely licensed Developer Edition of SQL Server for non-production use'). One forward-looking note if the platform requirement in this exercise permits 'the same SQL Server major version or higher': in SQL Server 2025 (17.x) the MSSQL_PID value 'Developer' no longer exists - it is replaced by 'EnterpriseDeveloper' and 'StandardDeveloper' - so a container definition carrying MSSQL_PID=Developer is not portable to a 2025 image unchanged. The deployment's actual MSSQL_PID setting is a repo fact I could not verify.

results.claim: [19] SQL Server Agent is disabled by default in the Linux container; log shipping is built from Agent jobs (backup on primary, copy and restore on each secondary, alert on monitor), configured per database, with manual-only failover and a user-specified restore delay useful against accidental data change
results.evidence_quote: A log shipping configuration doesn't automatically fail over from the primary server to the secondary server. If the primary database becomes unavailable, any of the secondary databases can be brought online manually. ... Allows a user-specified delay between when the primary server backs up the log of the primary database and when the secondary servers must restore (apply) the log backup. A longer delay can be useful, for example, if data is accidentally changed on the primary database.
results.correction: The log shipping substance is fully verified: all four job types and their locations (backup job on primary, copy and restore jobs on each secondary, alert job on the monitor), per-database configuration ('When log shipping is enabled on a database, the job category ... is created'), manual failover, and the delay benefit. The MSSQL_AGENT_ENABLED quote is misattributed - it is not on this page. It is verbatim at https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/linux/configure/environment-variables: 'Enables SQL Server Agent. For example, true enables, and false disables the agent. By default, the agent is disabled.' Re-cite it there. Also note the monitor server is optional ('An optional third server instance'), so the minimum is three job types, not four - the claim's '~3-4 Agent jobs per configuration' is right but the reason should be stated. One hard constraint the claim omits: 'Once the monitor server has been configured, it can't be changed without removing log shipping first.'

results.claim: [20] Backups restore forward-only; master/model/msdb from an earlier version cannot be restored; restoring master requires single-user mode, after which the instance shuts down and terminates sqlcmd; the recovery instance should match version, edition, patch level, features and external configuration
results.evidence_quote: Backups of master, model and msdb that were created by using an earlier version of SQL Server cannot be restored by SQL Server. ... No SQL Server backup can be restored to an earlier version of SQL Server than the version on which the backup was created.
results.correction: The first two quotes are verbatim on the cited page and the claim's headline finding is sound. The master-restore material is misattributed: I searched the full RESTORE (Transact-SQL) page and it contains no mention of single-user mode, of the instance shutting down, of terminating sqlcmd, or of matching version/edition/patch level. All of it is verbatim on https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/backup-restore/restore-the-master-database-transact-sql, including 'Doing otherwise can result in undefined SQL Server instance behavior, with inconsistent feature support, and isn't guaranteed to be viable.' Re-cite. Two additions from the cited page that reinforce the same conclusion: restoring an earlier-version database created in an old default path requires the MOVE option, and a database attached or restored to a NEW instance needs OPEN MASTER KEY / ALTER MASTER KEY REGENERATE before its database master key works - a silent failure mode in a rebuild-onto-fresh-host runbook.

results.claim: [21] Backup verification requires a backup checksum; without one, restore proceeds with no verification; BACKUP fails by default on a page error while RESTORE VERIFYONLY continues; damaged backup sets are flagged in msdb..backupset.is_damaged
results.evidence_quote: If there is no backup checksum, either restore operation proceeds without any verification; this is because without a backup checksum, restore cannot reliably verify page checksums. ... By default, after encountering a page checksum error, a BACKUP or RESTORE operation fails and a RESTORE VERIFYONLY operation continues. ... Marks the backup set as containing this type of error (in the is_damaged column of msdb..backupset).
results.correction: None; all elements verify verbatim, and the conclusion that WITH CHECKSUM is the precondition for meaningful verification is exactly what the page supports. Two additions that sharpen the requirement it underwrites: backup checksums also set has_backup_checksums in msdb..backupset, which is the column an external monitor should assert on to prove the checksum policy is actually in force; and the page notes checksums carry real CPU cost ('carefully monitor the CPU overhead incurred'), which is worth acknowledging rather than treating WITH CHECKSUM as free.

results.claim: [22] Backup encryption creates a second absolute single point of failure: without the certificate the backup is unusable; the certificate must not be renewed or changed because the thumbprint changes; Express and Web cannot encrypt during backup but can restore encrypted backups
results.evidence_quote: It's very important to back up the certificate or asymmetric key, and preferably to a different location than the backup file it was used to encrypt. Without the certificate or asymmetric key, you can't restore the backup, rendering the backup file unusable. ... the certificate shouldn't be renewed on expiry or changed in any way. Renewal can result in updating the certificate triggering the change of the thumbprint, therefore making the certificate invalid for the backup file. ... SQL Server Express and SQL Server Web don't support encryption during backup. However restoring from an encrypted backup to an instance of SQL Server Express or SQL Server Web is supported.
results.correction: None; all three quotations are verbatim and the 'never renew for the life of the backups it encrypts' framing is correct. Three additions for the key-material requirement: a database master key in master is a prerequisite for backup encryption at all; the restoring account needs VIEW DEFINITION on the certificate, so key custody is an authorisation problem as well as a possession problem; and 'Appending to an existing backup set option isn't supported for encrypted backups', which independently reinforces the WITH FORMAT discipline that claim [16] derives from the S3 path.

results.claim: [23] msdb backup history grows per operation and should be pruned with sp_delete_backuphistory, which affects eight named tables; physical backup files are preserved even if all history is deleted
results.evidence_quote: More rows are added to the backup and restore history tables after each backup or restore operation is performed; therefore, we recommend that you periodically execute sp_delete_backuphistory. ... The physical backup files are preserved, even if all the history is deleted.
results.correction: None; the recommendation, all eight tables (backupfile, backupfilegroup, backupmediafamily, backupmediaset, backupset, restorefile, restorefilegroup, restorehistory) and the file-preservation sentence are exact. One operational consequence the claim should draw out, because it cuts against a naive pruning schedule: SSMS's restore dialog populates its database list 'only [with] databases that have been backed up according to the msdb backup history', and the error-9002 diagnostic script in Microsoft's own troubleshooting article queries msdb.dbo.backupset. Pruning history therefore degrades both the recovery UI and the RPO-observability requirement, so the retention window for history should be set deliberately against those needs rather than minimised.

results.claim: [24] Concurrent backups are memory-bounded: BACKUP consumes BUFFERCOUNT * MAXTRANSFERSIZE in RAM, large buffer counts can cause out-of-memory errors, with a documented Msg 701 failure at 200 MB of buffer space, and a stated default BUFFERCOUNT formula
results.evidence_quote: You can specify any positive integer; however, large numbers of buffers might cause "out of memory" errors because of inadequate virtual address space in the Sqlservr.exe process. ... Msg 701, Level 17, State 17, Line 1 There is insufficient system memory to run this query. ... Total buffer space: 200 MB ... My largest contiguous block available in the non-BPool (MemToLeave) region of my 32-bit instance was only 157MB.
results.correction: Two corrections, one of them decision-affecting. FIRST: the sentence quoted as 'Your BACKUP operation will consume BUFFERCOUNT * MAXTRANSFERSIZE in RAM' does not appear on this page in any form. The page establishes the relationship by demonstration (buffercount 10 x 4 MB = 'Total buffer space: 40 MB'), not by that sentence. Either drop the quotation marks and state it as the arithmetic the page demonstrates, or find its true source. SECOND and more important: the Msg 701 failure is explicitly a 32-BIT phenomenon caused by contiguous virtual-address-space exhaustion in the MemToLeave region, as the quoted line shows. On 64-bit SQL Server on Linux with MSSQL_MEMORY_LIMIT_MB=7168 that mechanism does not exist, so 200 MB is not a threshold that binds here and should not be used to cap backup concurrency. The default BUFFERCOUNT formula IS correct as quoted - (NumberOfBackupDevices x (1+GetSuggestedIoDepth)) + NumberOfBackupDevices + (2 x DatabaseDeviceCount) - but note it comes from the summary table at the foot of the post, which differs from the formula given in the body text earlier, and the author concedes in the comments that the post's GetSuggestedIoDepth treatment needed correction. Finally, the page is a 2010 archived blog marked NOINDEX,NOFOLLOW - acceptable as colour, not as a limit to design against.

results.claim: [25] Instance ceilings that are not binding here: 32,767 databases per instance, 32,767 user connections, 524,272 TB database size; the binding constraints are per-feature (basic AG one database, snapshot backup 64 databases)
results.evidence_quote: Database size | 524,272 terabytes ... Databases per instance of SQL Server | 32,767 ... User connections | 32,767
results.correction: None; all three figures are exact, and the reasoning that per-feature limits bind before per-instance ones is correct and well supported by claims [15] and [17]. Worth adding a fourth ceiling from the same table that is closer to binding than any of the three cited, given a 33-database estate that will grow: 'Nested stored procedure levels | 32', whose note reads 'If a stored procedure accesses more than 64 databases, or more than two databases in interleaving, you'll receive an error.' That 64-database figure is a genuine cross-database access limit sitting at the same magnitude as the snapshot-backup limit, and it deserves a place in the same list.

results.claim: [26] Redis AOF everysec loses up to one second; naive volume copying is unsafe since 7.0 multi-part AOF and may yield an invalid backup during a rewrite; disable auto-aof-rewrite-percentage, confirm aof_rewrite_in_progress = 0, copy, restore; transfer an RDB offsite daily; use an independent alert if transfers fail; the BACKUP command family requires Redis 8.10.0
results.evidence_quote: appendfsync everysec: fsync every second. Fast enough (since version 2.4 likely to be as fast as snapshotting), and you may lose 1 second of data if there is a disaster. ... However, if this is done during a rewrite, you might end up with an invalid backup. ... At least one time every day make sure to transfer an RDB snapshot outside your data center or at least outside the physical machine running your Redis instance. ... You also need some kind of independent alert system if the transfer of fresh backups is not working for some reason. ... Since Redis 8.10.0, the BACKUP command family produces a self-contained, restorable backup without stopping writes or manually managing AOF rewrites.
results.correction: None; every quotation and the 8.10.0 version gate verify exactly, and the four-step safe-copy procedure matches the page. Two additions that reduce the operational cost of the workaround: the page documents a hard-link optimisation that shortens the window during which rewrites are disabled ('you may create hard links to the files in appenddirname ... and then re-enable rewrites'), and it warns that if the server restarts mid-backup the disabled-rewrite setting is lost unless persisted with CONFIG REWRITE - a failure mode that silently re-arms the very risk being mitigated. The deployment being on Redis 7 is a repo fact I could not verify.

results.claim: [27] The MinIO open-source repository is archived and unmaintained, community edition is source-only with no pre-compiled binaries, users directed to AIStor; object locking documentation is now under AIStor with GOVERNANCE and COMPLIANCE modes, requiring versioning, settable on existing buckets via mc retention set --default since RELEASE.2025-05-20T20-30-00Z
