results.claim: [28] nginx does not preserve the client Host header to upstreams by default; the documented default is proxy_set_header Host $proxy_host and Connection close, and the original Host and Connection fields are not passed to the proxied server
results.evidence_quote: Default: proxy_set_header Host $proxy_host; proxy_set_header Connection close; ... By default, the header fields "Host" and "Connection" from the original request are not passed to the proxied server.
results.correction: None; the default block and the explanatory sentence are verbatim, and $proxy_host (not $host) is confirmed as the default value. One addition that matters for any recovery path terminating HTTP/2: 'For HTTP/2, the ":authority" pseudo-header field with the $proxy_host value is sent by default, unless it is replaced with an explicit "Host" header field' - so the same tenant-resolution failure reaches an HTTP/2 upstream through a different header, and a fix that only sets Host on the HTTP/1.1 path is incomplete. The claim's downstream assertion that tenancy in this system resolves from the Host header alone is a repo fact I could not verify.

results.claim: [29] Ola Hallengren's SQL Server Maintenance Solution most recent release 16 August 2026 (prior 9 and 8 August 2026), supporting SQL Server 2017+ including 2022 and 2025, Linux, and AWS S3 destinations; dbatools latest published version 2.8.4 on 2026-07-31, providing Test-DbaLastBackup

January 13, 2025: Replaced variable self-concatenation with STRING_AGG. The minimum required version is now SQL Server 2017.

Two sub-details I could not confirm from the cited page and which should be dropped or re-sourced: that S3 support was added 'in collaboration with AWS', and that it is 'SQL Server 2022+ only' (plausible, since claim [16] establishes the engine feature is 2022+, but the version history does not say it). The description of Test-DbaLastBackup's behaviour (restore under a different name, DBCC CHECKDB, drop) is also not evidenced by either cited page - cite the dbatools command documentation for it. results.claim: [30] The 72-hour restoration figure is proposed, not in force: the NPRM proposes 72-hour restoration procedures, 24-hour business associate notification on contingency plan activation, and removal of the required/addressable distinction; published in the Federal Register 6 January 2025, comments closed 7 March 2025, no final rule as of 2026, with a reported July 2027 target

Require business associates to notify covered entities (and subcontractors to notify business associates) upon activation of their contingency plans without unreasonable delay, but no later than 24 hours after activation. ... Remove the distinction between 'required' and 'addressable' implementation specifications and make all implementation specifications required with specific, limited exceptions.
results.correction: The three substantive quotations verify verbatim and the central finding - that 72 hours is proposed and not in force - is correct and important. The dates are misattributed but independently correct: the HHS fact sheet states only that the NPRM was issued 27 December 2024 with comments due 60 days after Federal Register publication. I verified the rest against the Federal Register API: publication_date 2025-01-06, comments_close_on 2025-03-07, citation 90 FR 898, RIN 0945-AA22. I also confirmed something the claim asserts but did not evidence - querying the Federal Register for RIN 0945-AA22 returns exactly one document, of type Proposed Rule, so NO FINAL RULE HAS ISSUED as of this check. Cite federalregister.gov for the dates and for the no-final-rule finding rather than the fact sheet. The July 2027 Unified Agenda target remains unverified, as the claim honestly states; keep that caveat.

results.claim: [31] CISA's #StopRansomware Guide recommends offline, encrypted, regularly tested and immutable backups, but the widely-repeated claim that CISA explicitly endorses 3-2-1-1-0 is NOT verified; treat 3-2-1 as industry convention and anchor the behaviour to NIST SP 800-34 3.4.2 and 45 CFR 164.308(a)(7)(ii)(A) instead
results.evidence_quote: [cisa.gov returned HTTP 403 Forbidden to both the resource page and the direct PDF, including with a browser user-agent; the guide's content could not be retrieved to check for '3-2-1' or '3-2-1-1-0']
results.correction: I reproduce the researcher's failure exactly: both https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/resources/stopransomware-guide and the direct PDF return 403 to automated fetches, so the CISA text remains unchecked. The claim's handling of this is the correct behaviour and should be preserved - it declines to assert the 3-2-1-1-0 attribution rather than repeating it, which is precisely the failure mode this review exists to catch. Both fallback anchors it proposes DO verify: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 section 3.4.2 is indeed titled 'Backup Methods and Offsite Storage' and contains the offsite-storage criteria, and 45 CFR 164.308(a)(7)(ii)(A) is the Required Data backup plan specification confirmed in claim [1]. Recommendation: build the requirement on those two primary anchors alone and drop the CISA citation entirely rather than carrying an unverifiable URL in an evidence base - nothing in the design depends on it.

results.claim: [32] Hangfire's model is retry-based re-entrancy, not exactly-once; restoring the host database re-arms jobs that already ran, and a second processing server during failover double-executes them
results.evidence_quote: Reentrancy means that a method can be interrupted in the middle of its execution and then safely called again ... The interruption can be caused by many different things (i.e. exceptions, server shut-down), and Hangfire will attempt to retry processing many times.
results.correction: None. Both quotations are verbatim, and the claim's own caveat is accurate and unusually scrupulous: the page does not use the phrase 'at least once', and I confirmed it does not appear anywhere on the page. The DR consequence (restore re-arms completed jobs; a second processing server double-executes) is inference rather than documentation, but it follows directly from retry semantics plus the fact that job state lives in the restored database, and the claim presents it as a consequence rather than as a quotation. The requirement it underwrites - exactly one active processing server against the Hangfire schema, plus idempotent handlers - is the right shape given that the documentation promises re-entrancy safety only if the developer provides it.

results.claim: [33] Restoring one office backward while the host stays current produces externally visible side effects: outbox rows roll back to unsent so drains re-send duplicate emails and partner messages, MinIO objects become orphaned PHI, audit rows are destroyed touching 45 CFR 164.312(b); the requirement is reconcilability, not consistency
results.evidence_quote: (b) Standard: Audit controls. Implement hardware, software, and/or procedural mechanisms that record and examine activity in information systems that contain or use electronic protected health information. [45 CFR 164.312(b), verified via eCFR]
results.correction: The regulatory citation is correct - I verified 45 CFR 164.312(b) is indeed the Audit controls standard and quoted it above - but the cited SQL Server URL supports none of this claim. The PITR page documents restore mechanics and says nothing about outbox tables, object stores, audit rows or duplicate external sends; those are all application-level consequences drawn from the brief's description of the system, which I cannot verify. Re-cite: use 164.312(b) from eCFR for the audit point, and either drop the Microsoft URL or replace it with a statement it actually supports (that a point-in-time restore rolls the database back to a chosen time, from which the application-level consequences follow). The reasoning itself is sound and the reconcilability-over-consistency conclusion is the most useful design judgement in the set; it just needs its citations attached to the right propositions. Note also that 164.312(b) requires mechanisms that 'record and examine' activity - destroying audit rows in a restore window is a gap in the recording arm specifically, which is worth saying precisely.

results.claim: [34] Recovery has a fleet-wide single point of failure: db-migrator loops offices with no per-tenant error handling and both authserver and api gate on service_completed_successfully, so one failing office database prevents the entire stack from starting with no report of which succeeded
results.evidence_quote: [The cited page is reachable (HTTP 200) and is Microsoft's restore-and-recovery overview; it contains nothing about container orchestration, migration loops, service dependency gating, or per-tenant error handling.]
results.correction: The cited URL is reachable but irrelevant to the claim - it is a SQL Server restore-and-recovery overview and cannot speak to db-migrator, service_completed_successfully gating, or per-tenant error handling, all of which are Compose/application facts from the brief that I could not verify. This claim needs a code citation (the migrator source and the Compose dependency declarations), not a Microsoft documentation link; carrying an unrelated URL here weakens an otherwise strong argument. The underlying observation - that a fail-fast, all-or-nothing migration step inverts tenant isolation precisely during recovery - is a genuine architectural finding and pairs directly with the requirement that recovery of one office must not block any other, including during the migration/seed step on every bring-up. Recommend restating it as an observed property of the codebase with file references, and adding that the fix has two parts: per-tenant error isolation in the loop, and a machine-readable report of which offices succeeded, since without the latter an operator cannot resume a partial recovery.

research.area: Environment Strategy: how many environments, with what parity, provisioned how  -  for a Host-header-resolved, database-per-tenant IME platform run by two SDE 1s
research.design_space: In 2026 the viable answers span a wider range than the classic dev/staging/prod ladder, because containerisation moved most of what used to be "an environment" into the build artifact, and test harnesses can now start real backing services per test run. The honest range is: (1) one environment plus strong reversibility  -  production only, safety from rehearsed restores, feature flags, progressive exposure and observability; (2) one environment plus an ephemeral test harness  -  production plus disposable real infrastructure created and destroyed inside CI, which is not an environment you maintain and therefore cannot drift; (3) dev/prod, a second long-lived deployment; (4) dev/staging/prod with staging deliberately production-shaped; (5) ephemeral per-PR environments, the strongest parity and the highest standing cost; (6) production-as-the-last-environment, where progressive exposure inside production (deployment rings, a canary tenant) replaces a pre-production mirror; and (7) hybrids  -  most commonly production plus a canary tenant plus ephemeral CI plus a staging environment that is rebuilt from the release artifact for a change window and then destroyed. Crucially, "parity" is not one axis but nine that drift independently: topology, component versions/builds, configuration, data shape, data volume, identity and secret material, network/DNS/TLS naming, the deployment procedure itself, and scale/fan-out. Each has its own cost to hold and its own failure signature, and most teams hold three of them and believe they hold all nine. The 2026 literature is genuinely split: the twelve-factor dev/prod parity factor remains the canonical statement, while a live counter-tradition argues that a mirror of a distributed system is unachievable and that the engineering spent on staging is better spent on production safety  -  a position whose validity depends entirely on whether continuous deployment, feature flags and production observability are already in place. A design that picks a point on this range without first naming which parity axes it is buying, and which it is knowingly abandoning, is not a design.

options.name: A. One environment, plus a rehearsed restore and an ephemeral CI harness (no staging at all)
options.how_it_works: Production remains the only long-lived deployment. Correctness confidence comes from an ephemeral test harness in CI that starts real SQL Server 2022 and Redis containers per test run (Testcontainers-style), runs the real DbMigrator, provisions three test offices plus the host, and asserts tenant isolation, migration completeness and job behaviour. Recoverability confidence comes from a scheduled, timed restore rehearsal into a throwaway instance. Nothing long-lived exists to drift.
options.operational_cost: Setup ~32-52 h (8-12 h to make the deploy artifact reproducible and fail-fast; 24-40 h to build the harness). Ongoing ~4-8 h/month. Assumes only skills the team already has: C#, xUnit, docker-compose. No DNS, no certificates, no second host, no second secrets file.
options.why: The harness is created from the release artifact on every run, so the single most common failure of a non-production environment  -  silent divergence  -  is structurally impossible. It catches exactly the bug class that matters here (tenant isolation, dual-DbContext migration gaps, host-vs-tenant confusion) because those are code-level, not topology-level. What it does not catch is anything that lives in the edge: DNS, wildcard certificates, nginx upstream resolution, Host-header resolution end to end. Those are precisely the things this system's tenancy depends on, which is why A alone is incomplete.

options.name: B. A second full stack on the existing VM (compose profile / second project name)
options.how_it_works: Run a second, differently-named docker-compose project on the same host with its own volumes and a second set of hostnames, sharing the box with production.
options.operational_cost: Setup ~16-24 h. Ongoing ~4 h/month. But the resource arithmetic settles it: the eight long-running services' memory caps already total 17,336 MB (~16.9 GB) on a 16 GB machine, with MSSQL_MEMORY_LIMIT_MB at 7,168 MB, and only ~9.7 GB of 48 GB disk free. Caps are limits rather than reservations, so production is currently over-committed by construction; a second SQL data volume plus its backups does not fit in the free disk at all.
options.why: Rejected on measured facts, not preference. Worse, it fails in the most damaging possible way: the second stack does not refuse to start, it competes for RAM and disk with production, so the first symptom is production degradation attributed to something else. A non-production environment that can take production down is not a safety mechanism. (Memory and disk arithmetic is mine, from the figures given.)

options.name: C. A permanently-running staging environment on a separate host
options.how_it_works: A second VM running the identical compose stack, on its own DNS names with its own wildcard certificates, its own secrets file, its own SQL/Redis/MinIO, deployed by the same procedure, holding a small set of test offices.
options.operational_cost: Setup ~60-90 h  -  and the bulk of that is not the application. It is a second DNS zone, three wildcard certificates issued via DNS-01 (HTTP-01 and TLS-ALPN-01 cannot issue wildcards), certificate renewal automation, a second secrets file with no vault, a second backup story, and a second host to patch. Ongoing ~8-16 h/month, rising as it ages. Assumes DNS and PKI competence the team does not currently have.
options.why: This is the textbook answer and it is defensible  -  NIST CM-4(1) wants changes analysed in a separate test environment, and it is the only option that exercises DNS, TLS and Host-header resolution end to end. But a standing staging environment is a standing asset that rots, and this team has no mechanism to detect rot: no observability, no config diffing, no CD. Fowler's snowflake problem applies directly. Conditional on: the deploy being artifact-based and automated FIRST, and on ~24 h/month of infrastructure time. Built before those preconditions, it manufactures false confidence  -  the most expensive possible outcome.

options.name: D. A staging environment that is rebuilt on demand from the release artifact and destroyed after the change window
options.how_it_works: Same as C, but not permanent. The host is created (or unpaused), the digest-pinned resolved compose artifact is deployed by the same script as production, three test offices are provisioned by the same idempotent provisioner, the change is exercised, and the environment is torn down. Triggered for three change classes only: migrations touching both DbContexts, anything touching tenant resolution or connection-string derivation, and major SQL Server/ABP upgrades.
options.operational_cost: Setup ~24-32 h on top of an artifact-based deploy (mostly the DNS zone and cert automation, which must be permanent even when the environment is not). Ongoing ~4-6 h per activation, perhaps 4-8 activations per year, so ~2-4 h/month amortised.
options.why: This is C with the drift removed. Because it is created from the artifact every time, its configuration cannot silently diverge  -  there is no long-lived state to diverge. It fails obviously: either the rebuild succeeds or it does not, and a failed rebuild is itself the most valuable signal in the system (it means production is no longer reproducible). Conditional on the deploy already being scripted and artifact-pinned; without that, the rebuild reproduces nothing.

options.name: E. Ephemeral per-PR environments
options.how_it_works: A full stack per pull request, created on open and destroyed on merge or close, each with its own hostnames, database set and tenants.
options.operational_cost: Setup measured in months, not hours, and ongoing maintenance is continuous. The naming alone is disqualifying here: each PR needs labels at three DNS depths, and wildcard certificates require DNS-01 with an automatable DNS API. Let's Encrypt allows up to 50 certificates per registered domain every 7 days and up to 5 per exact same set of identifiers every 7 days  -  a per-PR wildcard scheme collides with these quickly. Then a SQL Server per PR, and per-PR tenant provisioning.
options.why: Genuinely the strongest parity available and the most significant evolution in this space since the original twelve-factor text  -  the honest case is real. But it is an order of magnitude more platform engineering than this team has, and the cost is dominated by exactly the part of this system that is hardest (DNS and TLS per environment), not the part that is easy (containers). It also fails subtly in one specific way: idle per-PR environments accumulate cost and drift while nobody looks at them.

options.name: F. Production plus a canary office (deployment ring 0)
options.how_it_works: A real tenant on a real slug, in production, owned by the team, holding only synthetic data, exercised by a scripted smoke test after every deploy and always the first office through any tenant-loop change. Microsoft's multitenant guidance states directly that a canary ring 'includes your own test tenants'.
options.operational_cost: Setup ~6-8 h (provision one office, write a smoke script covering login, packet assembly, a document upload and one outbox drain). Ongoing ~1-2 h/month. One extra database. Because adding an office is a host-UI action and the provisioner is idempotent, this costs no deployment.
options.why: This is the only option that tests the real DNS, the real wildcard certificates, the real nginx, the real Host-header resolution, the real fan-out and the real Hangfire scheduling  -  because it IS them. It is cheap precisely because this system's tenancy model makes tenant creation a UI action rather than a deployment. Its limit is honest: it validates after the change reaches production, not before, so it is a detection mechanism, not a prevention one. It pairs with, and does not replace, A.

options.name: G. Mono-environment: production only, with feature flags, continuous deployment and observability as the safety mechanism
options.how_it_works: Abandon non-production entirely. All changes go to production behind flags, exposed progressively, with production monitoring as the feedback loop. Argued seriously in 2026 on the grounds that users only get value from production and that staging diverges on load and data anyway.
options.operational_cost: Setup is deceptive: near-zero infrastructure, but it requires continuous deployment, a feature-flag system, and production observability with alerting. Building those three here is 150+ h and none exists today.
options.why: The argument is sound and I do not dismiss it  -  its diagnosis of staging (unrepresentative load, unrepresentative data, misaligned incentives) is exactly right for this system. But its prescription has three named preconditions and this system satisfies none: deployment is entirely manual over SSH with no CD, there are no feature flags, and observability is Serilog to console and file with HealthChecks UI storing history in memory. Adopting the conclusion without the preconditions is not the mono-environment pattern; it is the status quo with a justification attached.

research.recommendation:
Do not build a standing staging environment yet. Build, strictly in this order, because each step is a precondition for the next being worth anything.

STEP 1  -  Make the one environment you have reproducible and fail-fast (~8-12 h, once). Docker Compose's documented behaviour is that "if an environment variable is not set, Compose substitutes with an empty string"  -  that is the entire mechanism behind the operational trap where a missing `--env-file` recreates the stack with a blank DB password. The fix is one character per variable: `${SA_PASSWORD:?SA_PASSWORD is required}`, which "exit[s] with error" when unset or empty. Add `docker compose config --quiet` as a pre-deploy gate, capture `docker compose config --resolve-image-digests` output as the release artifact so image tags cannot drift underneath you, and wrap the whole deploy  -  env file, digest-pinned artifact, and the mandatory nginx force-recreate  -  in one script that is the only supported way to deploy. This is parity work with zero monthly cost, and it converts the system's two known-fatal operational traps from silent to loud. It is the highest value-per-hour change in this entire area.

STEP 2  -  Ephemeral test harness in CI with three offices plus the host (~24-40 h; ~2-4 h/month). Real SQL Server 2022 and Redis started per test run via Testcontainers for .NET (4.14.0, published 2026-08-14  -  actively maintained, with releases roughly every six weeks through 2026), running the real DbMigrator and the real IOfficeDatabaseProvisioner. This has no drift because it is created from the artifact every time.

STEP 3  -  Spend the no-PHI window on drills, in production (~32-40 h, one-off, and it expires). Right now production is a legitimate destructive-test target because every record is synthetic. Run: a full restore rehearsal with a measured elapsed time; a 33-office provisioning drill followed by one sweep cycle, then teardown; a deliberate mid-loop migrator failure against a broken office; an OpenIddict PFX rotation; a Redis flush to observe session invalidation. Record every timing. This produces the CP-4 and 45 CFR 164.308(a)(7)(ii)(D) evidence you will need regardless, at zero PHI risk, and it is the only time you will ever be allowed to do it in the real environment.

STEP 4  -  A canary office in production (~6-8 h; ~1-2 h/month). Microsoft's guidance is explicit that a canary ring "includes your own test tenants." One office, real slug, synthetic data, smoke-tested after every deploy, always first through any tenant-loop change. It is the only mechanism that exercises the real DNS, the real wildcard certificates and the real Host-header path.

STEP 5  -  Only then, a rebuild-on-demand staging environment (option D), on a separate host and  -  this matters  -  on a **separate registrable domain**, not a subdomain of production. Rebuilt from the artifact for a change window and destroyed after. Triggered for three change classes only: migrations touching both DbContexts, anything touching tenant resolution or connection-string derivation, and major SQL Server or ABP upgrades.

The reasoning, which is mine: this system's failure modes divide cleanly into two families. Code-level tenancy bugs (isolation leaks, the ambient-null-tenant hazard, the dual-DbContext migration gap, the un-error-handled migrator loop) are caught by step 2, cheaply and without drift. Topology-level bugs (DNS, three wildcard certificates, nginx upstream resolution, Host-header preservation) are caught only by something that actually has DNS and certificates  -  and the cheapest such thing is production itself, via step 4, because this system makes tenant creation a UI action rather than a deployment. A standing staging environment sits between the two, costs more than either, and is the only one of the three that can silently stop being true. Build the two ends first and add the middle when you can afford to keep it honest.

Test-tenant count, which is the question this system actually poses: **host plus three offices  -  four databases  -  is the minimum that proves the tenancy model, and eleven is waste.** NIST's Interaction Rule holds that "most failures are induced by single factor faults or by the joint combinatorial effect (interaction) of two factors," so what you need is coverage of tenant-distinguishing *attribute pairs*, not a headcount matching production. Eleven homogeneous offices exercise identical code paths eleven times and add no new attribute combination. Concretely: office 1 seeded at genesis, loaded with synthetic data, plain alphabetic slug; office 2 provisioned fresh *after* the change under test, empty, with a hyphenated slug; office 3 the isolation probe, loaded with distinctly-tagged data that office 1 must never see. Plus the host, which is a fourth database with a different schema (46 DbSets and 90 migrations versus 44 and 15), which owns the Hangfire schema, and which is where the documented ambient-null-tenant hazard resolves  -  any plan counting only offices has a hole exactly where the known correctness bug lives. Two offices is not enough for a reason that is easy to miss: with two, "iterate all offices", "process only the first" and "process all but the last" are indistinguishable; with three they separate. A fourth, deliberately-broken office should be created and destroyed on demand for the migrator failure drill, so it is not a standing cost. What genuinely scales with N  -  the three 15-minute jobs opening a connection per office  -  is a load property, not an isolation property, and belongs in a temporary 33-office drill you tear down, not in a standing environment.
research.operational_cost_of_recommendation:
One-off setup: step 1, 8-12 h; step 2, 24-40 h; step 3, 32-40 h (window-limited, cannot be deferred past first real PHI); step 4, 6-8 h. Total ~70-100 h, roughly 2.5-3.5 developer-weeks, spread across 3-4 months at the stated one-developer-week-per-month. Step 5 adds ~24-32 h of setup  -  most of it DNS zone and DNS-01 certificate automation, which must be maintained permanently even though the environment is not  -  plus ~4-6 h per activation at perhaps 4-8 activations a year.

Ongoing steady state without step 5: ~4-8 h/month (CI harness upkeep 2-4 h; canary smoke maintenance and quarterly restore rehearsal 2-4 h). With step 5: ~8-12 h/month.

THRESHOLDS, stated explicitly because the one-week-per-month figure is an estimate and a separate code-standard exercise has already claimed much of it. The full recommendation is operable at ~10-14 h/month. Below ~8 h/month, drop step 5 and the fan-out drill entirely and keep 1+2+4  -  that subset degrades gracefully because none of it is a standing asset that can rot: the harness is rebuilt every run, the canary is one database, and the deploy script either works or refuses. Below ~4 h/month it decays to "one environment with a rehearsed restore and a fail-fast deploy," which is still a defensible design and strictly better than a drifting staging environment. Above ~24 h/month, or on hiring a third engineer, promote step 5 from rebuild-on-demand to a standing environment on a separate host.

The specific decay mode to watch: if step 5 is ever built while step 1 is incomplete, the arrangement inverts  -  a staging environment deployed by a different procedure from an unpinned artifact costs 8-16 h/month and produces confidence that is actively wrong. That is worse than having no staging environment, so the ordering above is not a preference, it is a constraint.

evidence.claim: A serious 2026 counter-position exists: 'any effort that goes into delivering software to staging is inherently wasteful', staging 'presents a misalignment of incentives between developers and users', it 'reduces the throughput of changes to production', and 'the data in staging is often unrepresentative of data in production'. The alternative proposed requires five practices: TDD, ephemeral local environments, feature flagging, continuous deployment and production monitoring.
evidence.source_name: Tom Phillips  -  Staging is a wasteful lie: the case for the mono-environment
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Published 2026-01-08. Three of its five named preconditions (feature flags, continuous deployment, production monitoring) are absent from this system.

evidence.claim: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CM-4(1) requires analysing changes 'in a separate test environment before implementation in an operational environment' but explicitly permits logical separation: 'Separate environments can be achieved by physical or logical means.' CM-2(6) adds that test configurations 'mirror configurations in the operational environment to the extent practicable' and that 'Separate baseline configurations do not necessarily require separate physical environments.'
evidence.source_name: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 control catalog (OSCAL JSON, first-party)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Controls CM-4(1), CM-2(6), SA-3(1), CP-4, CP-9(1), PM-25

evidence.claim: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 PM-25 requires policies limiting PII in testing and states: 'When possible, organizations use placeholder data to avoid exposure of personally identifiable information when conducting testing, training, and research.' CP-9(1) requires testing backup information 'to verify media reliability and information integrity'.
evidence.source_name: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 control catalog (OSCAL JSON, first-party)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: PM-25 'Minimization of Personally Identifiable Information Used in Testing, Training, and Research'; CP-9(1) 'Testing for Reliability and Integrity'

evidence.claim: HIPAA 45 CFR 164.308(a)(7)(ii)(D) 'Testing and revision procedures (Addressable): Implement procedures for periodic testing and revision of contingency plans.' (a)(7)(ii)(A) Data backup plan and (B) Disaster recovery plan are Required. 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A) requires a risk analysis covering ePHI 'held by the covered entity or business associate'  -  which is the hook that pulls any PHI-holding non-production environment into scope.

evidence.threshold_or_limit: (a)(7)(ii)(D) is Addressable, not Required; (a)(7)(ii)(A)-(C) are Required

evidence.claim: NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 names 'System recovery on an alternate platform from backup media' as an element that 'should be addressed in a contingency plan test', and defines the graduated ladder of tabletop (discussion only), functional (simulated operational environment) and full-scale functional exercises. This gives a defensible cheap-to-expensive sequence for restore rehearsal.
evidence.source_name: NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, 3.5
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Published May 2010, updated 2010-11-11. It is old  -  I flag that honestly; NIST SP 800-53r5 CP-4 is the current normative control and points at the same practice.

evidence.claim: NIST's Interaction Rule: 'Most failures are induced by single factor faults or by the joint combinatorial effect (interaction) of two factors, with progressively fewer failures induced by interactions between three or more factors.' Empirical data suggest failures are triggered by six or fewer interacting variables, and 'pairwise testing may miss 10% to 40% or more of system bugs'.
evidence.source_name: NIST SP 800-142, Practical Combinatorial Testing
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Published October 2010; interaction strengths 1-6; pairwise miss rate 10-40%

evidence.claim: RFC 9525 6.3 constrains TLS wildcards: 'There is only one wildcard character' and 'The wildcard character appears only as the complete content of the left-most label', and 'A wildcard in a presented identifier can only match one label in a reference identifier.' Therefore {office}.<base>, {office}.api.<base> and {office}.auth.<base> require three separate wildcard certificates per environment.
evidence.source_name: RFC 9525, Service Identity in TLS
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 6.3; published November 2023; obsoletes RFC 6125

evidence.claim: DNS wildcards match differently from TLS wildcards  -  they DO synthesise across multiple labels. RFC 4592 2.2.1: for 'QNAME=foo.bar.example. QTYPE=TXT' with only *.example. in the zone, 'the answer will be "foo.bar.example. IN TXT ..." because bar.example. does not exist, but the wildcard does.' One DNS wildcard resolves every tier; one TLS wildcard covers exactly one.
evidence.source_name: RFC 4592, The Role of Wildcards in the Domain Name System
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 2.2.1 worked example; published July 2006

evidence.claim: Wildcard certificates can only be issued via DNS-01. Let's Encrypt: HTTP-01 'cannot be used to issue wildcard certificates'; TLS-ALPN-01 'cannot be used to validate wildcard domains'; DNS-01 'allows you to issue wildcard certificates' and 'it only makes sense to use DNS-01 challenges if your DNS provider has an API you can use to automate updates.' This makes an automatable DNS API a hard platform requirement generated by the tenancy model.
evidence.source_name: Let's Encrypt  -  Challenge Types
evidence.threshold_or_limit: n/a

evidence.claim: Let's Encrypt production rate limits: 'Up to 50 certificates can be issued per registered domain... every 7 days' and 'Up to 5 certificates can be issued per exact same set of identifiers every 7 days', with 'Up to 5 authorization failures per identifier... every hour'. A staging environment for rehearsing cert automation exists at acme-staging-v02.api.letsencrypt.org with far higher limits, but its roots are 'not present in browser/client trust stores'.
evidence.source_name: Let's Encrypt  -  Rate Limits and Staging Environment
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 50/registered domain/7d; 5/exact identifier set/7d; 5 auth failures/identifier/hour. Rate-limits page last updated 2026-08-05; staging page 2026-04-10.

evidence.claim: Every publicly-trusted TLS certificate is published to public, append-only Certificate Transparency logs and is searchable via aggregators such as crt.sh; CT logging is enforced by the Chrome Root Program. Issuing a certificate for a non-production hostname therefore publicly announces that environment's existence.
evidence.source_name: Chrome Certificate Transparency Policy; MDN Certificate Transparency
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Chrome Root Program Policy v1.8 (2026-06-15) strengthened CT requirements; Chrome 148 (2026-05-05) removed SCT delivery via stapled OCSP. I verified the policy exists and mandates logging; I did not independently confirm the v1.8 date beyond secondary reporting.

evidence.claim: HSTS preload submission requires max-age of at least 31536000, the includeSubDomains directive and the preload directive, and the form warns it 'will prevent all subdomains and nested subdomains from being accessed without a valid HTTPS certificate'. evidence.claim: SQL Server Developer edition 'includes all the functionality of Enterprise edition, but is licensed for use as a development and test system, not as a production server.' Standard edition caps the buffer pool at 128 GB and compute at the lesser of 4 sockets or 24 cores; Express caps database size at 10 GB. Always On availability groups are Enterprise-only; Standard offers only basic availability groups, which support 'two replicas, with one database'.
