capability_requirements.requirement: Non-production environments MUST be servable from a registrable domain distinct from the production domain, not merely a subdomain of it.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Three independent mechanisms bind subdomains to their parent in ways that cannot be cheaply undone: Certificate Transparency publishes the parent-child relationship permanently; HSTS preload with includeSubDomains binds every current and future subdomain with removal latency measured in months; and cookie scoping at the apex can bleed across environments. Choosing the naming scheme is a one-way door taken before anyone realises it is one.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: hstspreload.org submission requirements and removal warning; Chrome CT policy; the system's own wildcard-per-tier naming ({office}.<base>, {office}.api.<base>, {office}.auth.<base>).
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Search a CT aggregator (crt.sh) for '%.<production-apex>' and confirm no non-production hostname appears. Then query the production apex's HSTS header and, if the preload directive is present, confirm the apex is not on the preload list with includeSubDomains while any non-production hostname exists beneath it.

capability_requirements.requirement: The platform MUST support issuing and renewing at least three distinct wildcard certificates per environment, at three different DNS depths, plus at least one exact-match hostname.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: RFC 9525 6.3 makes this arithmetic non-negotiable: a wildcard 'can only match one label', so *.<base> cannot cover {office}.api.<base>. The tenancy model, which resolves from the leftmost DNS label at three tiers, therefore generates a hard multiplier of three wildcards plus one exact name for every environment that exists. A platform selection that assumes 'one wildcard per environment' will be short by two.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: RFC 9525 6.3; the system's Host-header tenant resolution across SPA, api and auth subdomains, plus the exact-match minio.<base>.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: For any candidate environment, run `openssl s_client -connect <host>:443 -servername {slug}.api.<base>` for each of the three tiers and confirm the returned certificate's subjectAltName contains the correct single-label wildcard for that exact depth. A single certificate satisfying all three tiers is proof the test was set up wrong, not proof of success.

capability_requirements.requirement: The DNS provider for every environment MUST expose an API that a script can use to create and delete TXT records unattended.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Wildcards can only be issued via DNS-01  -  HTTP-01 'cannot be used to issue wildcard certificates' and TLS-ALPN-01 'cannot be used to validate wildcard domains'. Since the previous requirement makes wildcards mandatory, an automatable DNS API becomes mandatory transitively. This is the clearest case in this area of the architecture generating a platform requirement rather than the reverse, and it is easy to discover too late.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Let's Encrypt challenge-types documentation; RFC 9525 wildcard constraint; the Host-header tenancy model.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Using only an API credential and no console access, run a script that creates a TXT record at _acme-challenge.<test-label>, polls an authoritative resolver until it appears, then deletes it. Record elapsed time; it must be well inside the ACME authorisation window.

capability_requirements.requirement: A single build artifact MUST be deployable to any environment without rebuilding, with all environment-varying values supplied at run time.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Twelve-factor's build/release/run separation makes this general good practice, but here it is forced: the Angular SPA served at {office}.<base> must reach {office}.api.<base>, so the API base URL varies per tenant, not merely per environment. Any build-time baking of API or issuer URLs makes one artifact per tenant, which is unmaintainable at 11 offices and impossible at 33.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Twelve-factor factors III (Config) and V (Build, release, run); ABP Angular's documented remoteEnv runtime-configuration mechanism; the per-tenant hostname scheme.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Take the exact artifact (container image digests and SPA bundle hash) running in non-production, deploy it to production without any rebuild step, and show `docker inspect` reports identical image digests in both. Separately, load the SPA at two different office hostnames and confirm each issues API calls to its own {office}.api.<base> without a per-tenant build.

capability_requirements.requirement: A missing or empty required configuration value MUST abort deployment before any container starts, naming the missing variable.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Compose's documented default is to substitute an empty string for an unset variable, which is precisely how the stack has previously recreated itself with no database password. This is a design defect with a documented one-character fix (${VAR:?error}), not an operational discipline problem, and it converts the single most damaging failure mode in the current deployment from silent to fatal. Every additional environment multiplies the exposure, so it must be fixed before a second environment exists.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Docker Compose variable interpolation documentation; the recorded operational trap where omitting --env-file blanks every secret.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: On a scratch host, remove exactly one required variable from the environment file and run the standard deploy command. The deploy must exit non-zero, name the missing variable in its output, and `docker ps` must show zero new containers. Repeat with the variable present but set to an empty string; the result must be identical.

capability_requirements.requirement: Tenant provisioning and teardown MUST be invocable from a script without a browser.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Every cheap option in this area  -  the CI harness with three offices, the 33-office fan-out drill, the rebuild-on-demand staging environment  -  depends on creating and destroying tenants unattended. Provisioning is already idempotent and already creates the database, catalogues, admin user and doctor, so the capability substantially exists; what must be guaranteed is a non-interactive entry point to it. Microsoft's multitenant antipatterns list names 'relying on manual deployments' explicitly.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: IOfficeDatabaseProvisioner.ProvisionAsync being idempotent and UI-invoked today; Azure Architecture Center multitenant checklist ('Use automation to manage the tenant life cycle').
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: From a shell with no browser, provision three offices with distinct slugs, assert all three respond at their three hostnames, then tear all three down and assert each hostname returns 'Tenant not found' and each CaseEvaluation_{slug} database no longer exists.

capability_requirements.requirement: A migration run across multiple tenant databases MUST report per-tenant outcomes and MUST exit non-zero if any tenant failed.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: The migrator currently loops offices with no per-tenant error handling, so one failure mid-loop leaves the fleet on split schema versions with no report of which succeeded. That is the archetype of a design that fails subtly, and this team cannot absorb subtle failures. Requiring an explicit per-tenant result converts a silent fleet-splitting event into a loud one, and it is a precondition for any environment strategy in which a migration is validated somewhere before production.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: The recorded migration-runner hazard; NIST SP 800-53 CM-3(2), 'Test, validate, and document changes to the system before finalizing the implementation of the changes'.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Provision three offices, deliberately break one (for example take its database offline or drop a table the next migration depends on), run the migrator, and require: a non-zero exit code, a printed list naming each office as succeeded or failed, and the broken office named as failed. Re-run after repair and require a clean exit.

capability_requirements.requirement: A production backup MUST be restorable into an isolated environment and verified by a scripted content check, with the elapsed time recorded.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: No restore has ever been tested. 45 CFR 164.308(a)(7)(ii)(A) and (B) make backup and disaster recovery Required specifications, and NIST CP-9(1) requires testing backup reliability. NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 names 'System recovery on an alternate platform from backup media' as a contingency-plan test element. Recording elapsed time now, on synthetic data, also produces the evidence the pending Security Rule NPRM would require if finalised.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Take the most recent production backup set, restore it onto a host that has never seen this system, start the application against it, and run a scripted assertion that a known appointment, its documents and its audit trail are all present. Record wall-clock time from 'backup file in hand' to 'assertion passed'. The test fails if any manual step was undocumented.

capability_requirements.requirement: Backups MUST be readable after total loss of the production host.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Backups currently default to a bind-mounted directory on the same box and the same disk as the database they protect, which means a single disk or host failure destroys both. This is not an environment-strategy nicety; it is the precondition that makes the one-environment option defensible at all. Without off-host backups, 'one environment plus good backups' collapses to 'one environment'.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: 45 CFR 164.308(a)(7)(ii)(A) 'retrievable exact copies'; NIST SP 800-53r5 CP-9 requiring protection of backup confidentiality, integrity and availability.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Destroy or fully disconnect the production host (or simulate by denying all access to it), then, from a different machine, obtain and read the most recent backup and complete the restore test above. If any step requires reaching the production host, the test fails.

capability_requirements.requirement: Any environment holding no PHI MUST be provably distinguishable from one that does, by a repeatable scan rather than by assertion.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: The whole value of the current window depends on 'this environment contains no real patient data' being a checkable fact rather than a belief. Once it becomes a belief, destructive testing stops being safe and the environment silently enters HIPAA Security Rule scope, since the required risk analysis covers ePHI 'held by the covered entity or business associate' wherever held. NIST PM-25 directs the use of placeholder data precisely to keep this boundary crisp.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: 45 CFR 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A); 45 CFR 164.514(b)(2) safe-harbor identifier classes; NIST SP 800-53r5 PM-25.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Run a scripted scan across every table in a non-production office database for the 18 safe-harbor identifier classes, and require that every match falls inside a known synthetic-fixture allowlist (for example, all surnames drawn from a published fixture list, all dates within a generated range, all emails at a reserved domain). Any match outside the allowlist fails the environment.

capability_requirements.requirement: Token signing and encryption material MUST be loaded by the same mechanism in every environment, with different key material per environment.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: OpenIddict's documentation deliberately separates a development-certificate path from a production-certificate path. If any non-production environment takes the development path, the mounted-PFX path  -  file mount, read-only permissions, passphrase from environment, expiry handling  -  executes only in production. That is the single code path whose failure invalidates every issued token in the system, and it would then have no rehearsal anywhere.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: OpenIddict encryption-and-signing-credentials documentation; the system's OPENIDDICT_PFX_PATH mount with passphrase from environment.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Grep every deployed configuration for AddDevelopmentSigningCertificate and AddDevelopmentEncryptionCertificate and require zero occurrences in any deployed environment. Then fetch /.well-known/jwks from each environment's AuthServer and require the `kid` values to be disjoint across environments.

capability_requirements.requirement: Every environment SHOULD report an identical, ideally empty, set of edition-restricted database features.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: SHOULD rather than MUST because it constrains a future decision rather than a current one. Production runs Developer edition, which includes all Enterprise functionality but is not licensed for production use. Any move to a licensed edition creates a parity trap in the opposite direction from the usual one: the non-production environment becomes MORE capable than production, so it silently permits what production will forbid. The detector is one query and costs nothing to run continuously.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft SQL Server 2022 editions documentation (Developer 'includes all the functionality of Enterprise edition... not as a production server'); sys.dm_db_persisted_sku_features ('A database that contains these features can't be moved to an edition of SQL Server that doesn't support them').
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Run `SELECT feature_name FROM sys.dm_db_persisted_sku_features` against the host database and every CaseEvaluation_{slug} database in every environment. Require identical result sets across environments and, ideally, zero rows everywhere.

capability_requirements.requirement: Component versions MUST be pinned by immutable identifier, not by moving tag, and the pinned set MUST be identical across environments that exchange backups.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: 'No SQL Server backup can be restored to an earlier version of SQL Server than the version on which the backup was created.' With a moving image tag, two environments drift apart on their own at the next pull, and the drift is invisible until a restore is attempted  -  which is exactly the moment it must not fail. This is the sharpest example in this area of an environment failing subtly.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft RESTORE (Transact-SQL) documentation; Docker Compose `config --resolve-image-digests`.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Run `docker compose config --resolve-image-digests` in each environment and diff the outputs; the image digests must match exactly. Then take a backup in the non-production environment and restore it into production (or a production-build clone) and require success.

capability_requirements.requirement: An integration whose failure mode is silent MUST be assertable positively in non-production against a designated non-production counterpart.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Both directions of the Case Tracker integration fail closed by configuration. That means 'no errors' is simultaneously the expected output of a healthy integration under no load and of a completely unconfigured one. A non-production environment without a counterpart will therefore look green while testing nothing  -  the definition of false confidence. Because Case Tracker is operated by the same business, a non-production counterpart is negotiable rather than impossible, which makes this a MUST rather than a SHOULD.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: The AppIntegrationOutboxItems ledger and reconcile endpoint both failing closed by configuration; Azure multitenant checklist requirement to 'Configure and test alerts to notify you when specific tenants experience problems'.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: In non-production, enqueue one integration outbox item, run the drain job, and require positive evidence of receipt at a designated non-production endpoint  -  a recorded request with a matching correlation identifier. Separately require, by inspecting the production endpoint's logs, that it received nothing during the test.

capability_requirements.requirement: The platform SHOULD allow provisioning and destroying a temporary fleet of at least 33 tenant databases to measure recurring-job fan-out.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: SHOULD because it is a measurement capability rather than a correctness one, but it is the only way to answer a question this design provably poses: three jobs every fifteen minutes, each opening one connection per office, means the steady-state connection pattern is driven by tenant count rather than user traffic. At 11 offices that is 33 sequential connections per quarter-hour; at 33 it is 99. Nobody has measured what that costs, and the drill is nearly free today because provisioning is idempotent and script-invocable.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: The twelve recurring jobs iterating offices inside ICurrentTenant.Change scopes; AWS SaaS Lens REL 3 'Validate the scale and repeatability of tenant onboarding'.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Provision 33 empty offices in a non-production environment, let one full sweep cycle of the three 15-minute jobs complete, and record peak concurrent SQL connections, sweep wall-clock duration and host CPU. Then destroy all 33 and confirm the databases and blob prefixes are gone. Compare the sweep duration against the 15-minute schedule interval  -  if it approaches it, the schedule is the constraint, not the hardware.

capability_requirements.requirement: Non-production environments SHOULD be able to generate tenant data at production-realistic volume, including the measured audit-to-business ratio, without copying production data.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Measured ratio is roughly 1,450 audit rows and 2,689 property-change rows per 16 appointments  -  over 100:1  -  with no retention configured against a six-year expectation. A non-production office seeded with a handful of appointments therefore differs from a two-year-old production office by three orders of magnitude on the table that dominates storage and query cost. DORA's guidance points the same way: acquire test data on demand rather than copying production. SHOULD rather than MUST because the correctness tests do not need it; only the performance and backup-window questions do.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Measured 16 appointments to ~1,450 audit rows and 2,689 property-change rows; 45 CFR 164.316(b)(2)(i) six-year retention; DORA test data management.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Generate one office containing two years of synthetic activity at the measured ratio, then time a full backup, a restore, and the three heaviest list screens. Each must complete inside a stated budget. If no budget has been stated, the test's output is the budget.

anti_requirements: The platform MUST NOT require non-production hostnames to be subdomains of the production domain. Certificate Transparency publishes the relationship permanently, HSTS preload with includeSubDomains binds it with months-long removal latency, and apex-scoped cookies can bleed between environments.

The platform MUST NOT require copying production data into any non-production environment in order to make that environment representative. Representativeness must be achievable by generating shape and volume, because the moment real PHI exists a copy pulls the non-production environment into HIPAA Security Rule scope and imposes recurring de-identification work on every refresh.

The platform MUST NOT require a permanently-running second full stack in order to validate a change. A standing mirror is a standing asset that drifts, and this team has no mechanism  -  no observability, no configuration diffing, no CD  -  capable of detecting that drift before it produces a wrong answer.

The platform MUST NOT require per-tenant TLS certificates. Beyond the operational cost at 11 to 33 offices, per-office certificates would publish every customer medical practice's slug into permanent, public, append-only Certificate Transparency logs, which is a customer-confidentiality disclosure with no mechanism for retraction.

Any environment's ingress MUST NOT alter, normalise or replace the Host header between the edge and the application. Tenancy resolves from the leftmost DNS label of the Host header and nothing else, so a rewriting ingress does not produce an error  -  it produces the wrong tenant, or the host tenant, silently. Any candidate ingress must be verified on this specific behaviour before adoption, not assumed.

The platform MUST NOT require the two developers to maintain two divergent deployment procedures. A non-production environment deployed differently from production tests the artifact but not the deployment, and in this system both known-fatal traps  -  the mandatory env file and the nginx force-recreate  -  live in the deployment rather than the artifact.

Non-production environments MUST NOT be publicly reachable without authentication. They will be discovered via Certificate Transparency within minutes of certificate issuance regardless of whether they are linked or indexed, and they will predictably carry weaker controls than production.

The platform MUST NOT make anything that has to be available depend on a free third-party wildcard-DNS-for-IP service. Those services are unsigned, share certificate-issuance rate limits with every other user, and offer no service-level agreement; they are acceptable for a developer laptop and unacceptable for anything a second person relies on.

Production MUST NOT run SQL Server Developer edition, which is licensed for use as a development and test system and not as a production server. The corollary is a permission, not a prohibition: non-production environments may run Developer edition freely and get full Enterprise functionality, provided the edition-portability check above is run to prevent that capability from masking a future production limit.
surprises: A staging environment for this application cannot be reached by IP address  -  it needs working DNS before it serves a single byte. The two-person team's natural first move, 'spin up a box and hit its IP, sort out names later', is structurally impossible here because a bare IP cannot reach the application at all. The usual fallback is worse: /etc/hosts has no wildcard mechanism, so every office slug needs its own line, which means the environment silently tests only the slugs somebody remembered to type. This single fact is why a staging environment costs several times more here than the team will estimate.

DNS wildcards and TLS wildcards obey different matching rules, and the gap between them produces a diagnostic dead end. RFC 4592 2.2.1 shows a DNS wildcard synthesising an answer for foo.bar.example. from *.example. 'because bar.example. does not exist, but the wildcard does'  -  so one DNS wildcard resolves every tier. RFC 9525 6.3 forbids the TLS equivalent: a wildcard matches exactly one label. The result in a new environment is that names resolve, connections reach nginx, and TLS fails opaquely  -  and the engineer debugging it goes straight to the tenant resolver, which is entirely innocent. Provision explicit DNS records per tier rather than one broad wildcard, so a missing name fails as NXDOMAIN rather than as a certificate mismatch.

The wildcard certificate is protecting customer confidentiality, and nobody chose it for that reason. Every publicly trusted certificate is published to public, permanent, append-only Certificate Transparency logs. A wildcard publishes only '*.<base>'; per-office certificates would publish the name of every medical practice using the product. For a workers'-compensation IME platform where the tenant is a named doctor's practice, that is a disclosure with no takeback. The operational convenience and the confidentiality property happen to point the same way  -  which means an innocent-looking future optimisation ('let's just issue per-office certs, it's simpler') would quietly cause a customer-relations problem.

The edge-security work the team is already planning will, if taken one step further, permanently constrain their environment naming. Adding HSTS is correct. Submitting the apex to the preload list with includeSubDomains is the tempting next click, and it makes every future subdomain  -  stage., dev., anything  -  unreachable in Chrome without a publicly trusted certificate, with removal that 'takes months to reach users with a Chrome update'. The environment naming decision must therefore be made before, not after, the security hardening. Almost nobody sequences it that way.

Developer edition makes non-production more capable than production, for free  -  and that is a hazard, not a bonus. It 'includes all the functionality of Enterprise edition'. If production is ever licensed onto Standard, staging will silently permit what production forbids. The specific landmine for a database-per-tenant system: Always On availability groups are Enterprise-only, and Standard's basic availability groups support 'two replicas, with one database'  -  structurally incompatible with 12 to 34 databases. A team that builds and validates an HA design on a Developer-edition staging box will discover this only when they try to license production.

Backups are one-directional across builds, so environment version drift silently destroys the restore path. 'No SQL Server backup can be restored to an earlier version of SQL Server than the version on which the backup was created.' A moving container image tag means two environments diverge on their own at the next pull, with no signal  -  and the divergence surfaces at exactly the moment it must not, during a restore. It also inverts the usual upgrade habit: to keep restore rehearsal working, the non-production SQL Server must be at the same build or newer than production, never older.

The mandatory-env-file trap is a documented Compose behaviour with a one-character fix, and the team has been treating it as a discipline problem. 'If an environment variable is not set, Compose substitutes with an empty string.' Writing ${SA_PASSWORD:?SA_PASSWORD is required} makes Compose 'exit with error' instead. This is the highest value-per-hour change available anywhere in this area: roughly an hour of work converts the operational failure most likely to destroy the stack from silent to fatal, in every environment, permanently.

The host database is a fourth environment that nobody counts. It has a different schema from the tenant databases  -  46 DbSets and 90 migrations versus 44 and 15  -  it owns the Hangfire schema, and it is where the documented worker hazard lands, because ABP falls back to the ambient tenant and the ambient tenant in a worker is null, which resolves to host. Any test-tenant plan that counts only offices therefore has a hole positioned precisely over the known correctness bug. The right count is host plus three offices, and the host is not optional.

An office slug is simultaneously a DNS label and a fragment of a SQL Server database name, and the two grammars disagree. DNS labels permit hyphens (RFC 1035 letter-digit-hyphen syntax); SQL Server regular identifiers permit only letters, digits and _ @ # $, and anything else 'must be delimited'. So CaseEvaluation_north-bay is a perfectly reasonable slug and a database name that requires bracket delimiting wherever DDL is emitted. Whether the provisioner actually handles it is unverified  -  which is exactly the argument for making a hyphenated slug one of the three standing test offices. It is the cheapest adversarial tenant in existence and nobody would think to create it.

A staging environment will make the Case Tracker integration look perfectly healthy while testing nothing at all, because both directions fail closed by configuration. 'No errors' is the expected output of a working integration under no load and of a completely unconfigured one; the two are indistinguishable from the outside. Any environment claiming integration parity must assert positively  -  a correlation identifier observed at a designated non-production endpoint  -  and must also assert that production received nothing.

The twelve-factor text everyone will cite in the design review is dated 2017, and its official community successor has stalled: the rewrite's next branch's newest commit is 2025-07-10 and main's is 2024-11-21. Meanwhile the strongest 2026 counter-argument  -  that staging is inherently wasteful  -  is genuinely well-reasoned, but its author names five preconditions and this system lacks three of them (continuous deployment, feature flags, production observability). Both positions are honest; neither applies unmodified. Cite twelve-factor as a durable principle, not as living guidance, and do not let anyone win the argument by quoting either side.

The cheapest scale test this system will ever get is available today and expires with the no-PHI window. Because adding an office is a host-UI action rather than a deployment, and the provisioner is idempotent, provisioning 33 offices, running one sweep cycle of the three 15-minute jobs, measuring the connection fan-out, and destroying them again is an afternoon's work  -  in production, with real DNS and real certificates. Nobody thinks of this because 'load testing' sounds like a project. Here it is a chore, and only until the first real booking.

The one untested caveat in the tenancy design has an environment-strategy payoff that nobody would predict. ABP registers four __tenant resolvers by default (query string, header, cookie, route) and whether they are disabled here has never been tested. If they turn out to be enabled that is a security problem  -  but it also means dev and CI environments could select tenants without any DNS at all, which would materially cheapen every non-production environment this analysis costs out. Testing it early therefore pays twice, and the second payoff is invisible if you frame the question as purely a security one.

not_recommended.pattern: Ephemeral per-PR environments
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: This is the strongest parity mechanism available and the single biggest evolution in this space since the original twelve-factor text. It removes the 'who broke staging' contention problem entirely, gives every change an isolated place to be exercised, and destroys the environment on merge so drift is impossible by construction. For a database-per-tenant system it is especially attractive, because each PR could get its own tenant fleet and isolation bugs would surface per-change rather than per-release. Teams that have it rarely give it up.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: The cost here is dominated by the part of this system that is hardest, not the part that is easy. Containers per PR are straightforward; DNS labels at three tiers per PR, each requiring wildcard certificates issuable only via DNS-01 against an automatable provider API, are not. Let's Encrypt permits 50 certificates per registered domain every 7 days and 5 per exact identifier set every 7 days  -  a per-PR wildcard scheme collides with the duplicate-set limit quickly and needs a naming scheme designed around it. Add a SQL Server instance per PR (against 9.7 GB of free disk on the only host that exists), per-PR tenant provisioning, and per-PR secrets, and it is months of platform engineering plus continuous maintenance for two SDE 1s who have roughly a week a month between them. It would consume the entire infrastructure budget and deliver nothing until it was finished.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: When the DNS and certificate automation already exists and is proven for production, when the deployment target makes a whole stack a single declarative object, and when there is a third engineer or a genuine platform owner. In that order  -  the DNS automation is the gate, not the containers.

not_recommended.pattern: A permanently-running staging environment that mirrors production one-to-one
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It is the textbook answer and it has real force. NIST SP 800-53 CM-4(1) directs analysing changes 'in a separate test environment before implementation in an operational environment'. Auditors and prospective healthcare customers expect it, and asking 'do you have a separate test environment?' is a standard due-diligence question. It is the only option that exercises DNS, three wildcard certificates, nginx upstream resolution and Host-header tenancy end to end before a change reaches a user  -  and those are exactly the mechanisms this system's tenancy depends on. It also gives the team somewhere to click around, which is not a trivial benefit for two people with no QA.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: Three reasons, in descending order of force. First, the compliance driver does not actually require a mirror: CM-4(1) itself says 'Separate environments can be achieved by physical or logical means', and CM-2(6) says test configurations mirror production 'to the extent practicable' and that 'Separate baseline configurations do not necessarily require separate physical environments'. Second, it cannot run on the existing host  -  the eight services' memory caps already total ~16.93 GB against 16 GB of RAM, with ~9.7 GB of 48 GB disk free  -  so it means a second host, a second DNS zone, three more wildcard certificates with their own renewal automation, a second secrets file with no vault, and a second backup story. Third and decisively: a standing staging environment is a standing asset that rots, and this team has no mechanism capable of detecting rot. No observability, no configuration diffing, no CD, nothing comparing the two. Fowler's diagnosis applies precisely  -  'You can't easily mirror your production environment for testing' once it has become a snowflake. The rebuild-on-demand variant (option D) keeps the benefit and removes the rot, which is why it is in the recommendation and this is not.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: When a third engineer joins, when infrastructure time reliably exceeds about 24 hours a month, or when the first real PHI makes destructive testing in production legally unavailable  -  whichever comes first. The last of these is a date, not a maybe, so this should be planned for rather than merely deferred.

not_recommended.pattern: Refreshing a non-production environment from a production data copy
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It is the only way to get genuinely real data shape, real volume and real edge cases, and unrepresentative data is a recognised parity failure in its own right  -  DORA notes that a change 'might have the desired behaviour in staging but fail in production' because of it. Here the argument is unusually strong: the measured audit-to-business ratio is over 100:1, retention is unconfigured against a six-year expectation, and no synthetic fixture anyone writes by hand will reproduce that. A production copy would.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: Right now it is pointless, because production data is already synthetic  -  there is nothing to copy that a generator could not produce. And by the time it would be valuable, it is expensive and risky: NIST PM-25 directs that 'When possible, organizations use placeholder data', DORA specifically cautions against 'Using a full copy of the production database', and the moment real PHI exists the copy pulls the non-production environment into the scope of the required risk analysis, which covers ePHI 'held by the covered entity or business associate'. De-identification under 164.514(b) is either an expert determination or removal of 18 identifier classes plus an actual-knowledge test  -  recurring work on every single refresh, forever, done by two developers with no privacy specialist. The correct substitute is available now and only now: build the synthetic generator during the window, while you can still validate its output against 'real' production and while getting it wrong costs nothing.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: Effectively never for this team at this size. The nearest legitimate case is a one-off forensic investigation of a specific production defect that cannot be reproduced synthetically  -  and even then the right shape is a minimal extract under a documented authorisation, not a refresh pipeline.

not_recommended.pattern: A shared long-lived 'dev' environment that both developers deploy to
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It is the cheapest thing that looks like a second environment. It gives both developers somewhere to see their work running as a real deployment rather than on localhost, it catches container-level and configuration problems that unit tests miss, and with two people the contention that plagues larger teams barely exists. For a system where local development is genuinely awkward  -  because Host-header tenancy needs wildcard DNS that /etc/hosts cannot provide  -  a shared dev box is a real convenience, not just laziness.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It is the purest form of the snowflake. Two people deploying by hand, with no CD and nothing comparing it to production, produces a machine that diverges within weeks and whose divergence is undetectable  -  so it does not just stop being useful, it starts giving wrong answers, confidently. That is the exact failure class this team cannot absorb: it degrades slowly rather than breaking loudly. It also competes for the same infrastructure hours as the CI harness while catching a strict subset of what the harness catches, minus reproducibility. The convenience it offers is real, but it is better bought with a wildcard-capable local resolver and a private CA for laptops than with a shared server.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: If it were rebuilt from the release artifact on a schedule  -  nightly, from the same digest-pinned compose file as production  -  it stops being a snowflake and becomes a useful thing. That is a different pattern with the same name, and it is only worth building after the artifact is reproducible.

not_recommended.pattern: Blue/green or a full second production stack serving as the test environment
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It is elegant: one investment buys zero-downtime deployment, instant rollback and a production-parity test target, and the guidance the team will read pushes hard in this direction ('Deployments should require zero downtime'). Here it looks especially tempting because two of the usual obstacles are absent  -  there is no SignalR or WebSocket usage, so no sticky-session requirement, and the SPA is static files with no Node runtime to coordinate.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: The stateless half is easy and the stateful half is the whole problem. One SQL Server holds 12 to 34 databases; one Redis holds the DataProtection keyring shared between AuthServer and API under a common application name, and losing its contents invalidates every session and breaks in-flight email-confirmation links; one MinIO holds six logical containers across two buckets, one of them partner-facing with externally held credentials. A blue/green cutover would swap the application tier while both colours shared exactly the components most likely to fail  -  producing the appearance of a second environment with none of the isolation. Worse, it fails subtly: green looks healthy because it is reading blue's data. Attempting it before the data tier has a replication story would consume the infrastructure budget and increase risk.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: After the data tier has a real story  -  database replication or a managed equivalent, a Redis arrangement that survives failover without invalidating sessions, and object storage that is not a single container. At that point blue/green becomes the natural next step and this analysis should be revisited.

not_recommended.pattern: Putting non-production on a subdomain of the production domain (stage.<base>)
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It is free, it reuses the existing DNS zone and registrar relationship, it needs no new domain purchase or delegation, and it is what nearly every team does. It also keeps the naming legible: everyone immediately understands what stage.example.com is. For a two-person team counting hours, avoiding a second domain and a second zone is a genuine saving.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It creates three bindings that are individually cheap and collectively very hard to unwind. Certificate Transparency permanently and publicly associates the non-production environment with the production domain, so the environment is discoverable from the moment its certificate is issued  -  and it will predictably carry weaker controls. HSTS preload with includeSubDomains, which the planned edge-security work makes likely, binds every subdomain including future ones, with removal that 'takes months to reach users with a Chrome update'. And apex-scoped cookies can bleed between environments. Against that, a second registrable domain costs a trivial annual fee and an hour of delegation. The asymmetry is stark: hours saved now against a constraint that is measured in months to reverse.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: If the non-production environment were never publicly resolvable at all  -  split-horizon DNS with an internal certificate authority, reachable only over a VPN. That is a defensible alternative design, and it removes the CT and preload problems entirely, but it substitutes DNS and PKI infrastructure this team does not yet have, so it is a later option rather than a cheaper one.

not_recommended.pattern: Provisioning one test office per production office (eleven test tenants in a non-production environment)
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It has surface plausibility that is hard to argue with in a meeting: it matches production, so nobody can accuse you of testing something different. And there is a real mechanism behind the instinct  -  twelve recurring jobs iterate offices, opening a connection per office database inside a tenant scope, so tenant count genuinely drives the steady-state connection pattern more than user traffic does. Eleven test tenants would reproduce that.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It conflates two properties that need different treatments. Isolation and correctness are attribute-driven: NIST's Interaction Rule holds that 'Most failures are induced by single factor faults or by the joint combinatorial effect (interaction) of two factors', so eleven homogeneous offices exercise identical code paths eleven times and add no new attribute pair. Coverage comes from making the tenants different  -  one seeded at genesis and loaded, one provisioned fresh after the change with a hyphenated slug, one as an isolation probe, plus the host  -  not from making them numerous. Meanwhile the property that genuinely scales with N is fan-out, and that is a load measurement, better served by temporarily provisioning 33 offices, running one sweep and destroying them, than by carrying eleven forever. Eleven standing tenants means eleven databases to migrate on every change, eleven to seed, eleven to back up, and eleven chances for the migrator to fail mid-loop in the environment that is supposed to be reassuring you.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: The moment offices stop being homogeneous. Per-office schema variation, per-office feature flags, or offices relocated onto different SQL instances would each add a real attribute dimension, and at that point the test-tenant count should track the number of distinct office configurations  -  which is still not the same as the number of offices, but it stops being three.

not_recommended.pattern: Mono-environment: production only, with feature flags, continuous deployment and observability as the safety mechanism
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: The diagnosis is correct and deserves to be taken seriously rather than waved away. 'Your users can only use and get value from production, therefore any effort that goes into delivering software to staging is inherently wasteful.' Staging typically runs under lower load, on unrepresentative data, and 'configuring smaller resources for staging adds complexity and further diverges staging from production'. Every one of those criticisms lands on this system specifically  -  a staging office with 16 appointments and 1,450 audit rows is not a model of a two-year-old production office by any measure. And the incentive point is real: a staging environment can become the thing developers deploy to, subtly displacing responsibility for production.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: Not because the argument is wrong, but because its author names five practices that replace the environment  -  test-driven development, ephemeral local environments, feature flagging, continuous deployment and production monitoring  -  and this system has none of the last three. Deployment is entirely manual over SSH with no CD; there are no feature flags; observability is Serilog to console and file with HealthChecks UI storing history in memory so it does not survive a restart, no metrics, no alerting, no uptime monitoring. Adopting the conclusion without the preconditions is not the mono-environment pattern; it is the current situation with a citation attached, and it would be the most dangerous possible outcome of this analysis  -  a well-argued reason to change nothing. Notably, the recommended path builds toward this position rather than away from it: an ephemeral CI harness is 'ephemeral local environments', and the canary office is progressive exposure.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: When continuous deployment, feature flags and production observability with alerting all exist. At that point the mono-environment argument becomes the correct one and the rebuild-on-demand staging environment can be retired. That is the right long-term destination for this system; it is simply not reachable from here in one step.

what_would_change_the_answer: The first real patient booking. This is a date, not a possibility, and it closes the window in which production is a legitimate destructive-test target. Every drill in step 3  -  restore rehearsal, 33-office provisioning trial, deliberate migrator failure, PFX rotation, Redis flush  -  becomes either impossible or a reportable-risk event afterwards. If that date is known, work backwards from it; if it is not known, find out, because it is the most important scheduling input in this entire area.

A third engineer, or any dedicated ops or platform capacity. The recommendation is shaped almost entirely by two SDE 1s having roughly a week a month between them. At meaningfully more capacity, the rebuild-on-demand staging environment should become a standing one on a separate host, and per-PR environments move from unreasonable to merely expensive.

Offices ceasing to be homogeneous. Per-office schema variation, per-office feature flags, or offices relocated onto different SQL instances via the App:TenantDbTemplate key would each add a genuine attribute dimension, and the minimum test-tenant count would rise from three toward the number of distinct office configurations.

The January 2025 HIPAA Security Rule NPRM being finalised. It is not final as of August 2026 and final action is currently signalled for July 2027, but if it lands with mandatory contingency testing and a documented 72-hour restoration capability, restore rehearsal moves from addressable good practice to a compliance obligation with a stated frequency  -  which changes the cost calculus for an isolated restore target from optional to required.

Production moving off SQL Server Developer edition. Developer edition carries all Enterprise functionality, so today non-production and production are feature-identical for free. A move to Standard introduces a real parity gap in the unexpected direction  -  non-production more capable than production  -  and makes the sys.dm_db_persisted_sku_features check load-bearing rather than merely prudent. Standard's basic availability groups supporting two replicas and one database would also force a rethink of any HA design validated on Developer.

Adoption of feature flags, continuous deployment and production observability. These are the three named preconditions of the mono-environment argument. Once all three exist, the correct answer shifts toward retiring pre-production environments rather than adding them, and this analysis should be re-run rather than extended.

A customer, prospective customer or BAA counterparty contractually requiring a separate non-production environment. Due-diligence questionnaires in healthcare ask this routinely, and a contractual requirement overrides the engineering argument regardless of whether CM-4(1)'s logical-separation allowance would technically satisfy an auditor.

The Case Tracker operator providing  -  or refusing to provide  -  a non-production endpoint. Because both directions of the integration fail closed, a non-production environment without a counterpart cannot positively test the integration at all. Since the same business operates both systems this is negotiable, but the answer materially changes what a staging environment is worth.

ABP's four default __tenant resolvers turning out to be enabled. This is the one caveat the source document records as never having been tested. If they are enabled it is a security finding, but it also means non-production environments could select tenants without DNS at all  -  which would cut the dominant cost of every non-production environment in this analysis. Test it early: it is cheap, and it changes the economics in a direction nobody is expecting.

Adoption of any deployment substrate where a complete stack is a single declarative object with automated DNS and certificate issuance already solved. That is the specific condition under which per-PR environments stop being unreasonable  -  and it is a platform capability question, which is deliberately the next exercise rather than this one.

verification.area: Environments (dev/staging/prod parity, tenancy, TLS/DNS, HIPAA/NIST, SQL Server edition parity, build/config separation)
