material_errors: [12] Citation misattribution across three Microsoft pages. The antipatterns list and both checklist requirements are NOT on the cited .../considerations/updates URL  -  only the canary-ring sentence is. The checklist items are on .../multitenant/checklist and the named antipatterns on .../multitenant/approaches/deployment-configuration. Anyone opening the cited URL to check will find two of three quotes missing.

[15] Wrong operational conclusion drawn from a correctly-quoted RFC. RFC 9525 6.3 constrains each wildcard NAME, not the number of certificates. Three wildcard identifiers at three DNS depths plus an exact-match host can be carried as SANs in a SINGLE multi-SAN certificate; ACME issues these routinely. 'Three separate wildcard certificates per environment' is not what the RFC implies. This error propagates into capability requirement 2 and into any cost/rate-limit sizing derived from it (a single cert consumes one of Let's Encrypt's 50-per-registered-domain slots, not three).

[2] Licence and quotations attributed to the wrong document. CC-BY-4.0 and 'will ultimately replace the one hosted at 12factor.net' are in the GitHub repo, not the Heroku blog. The quote 'the core concepts are still remarkably relevant' could not be located in either source and should be removed unless a primary source is produced. The 2024-08-28/2024-09-10 call-for-participation dates are unsupported by the cited URL.

[33] Over-committed-RAM conclusion does not follow from the evidence. Summing Docker memory CEILINGS to 17,336 MB against 16 GB RAM shows the caps cannot all be honoured at once; it does not show the single stack is 'already over-committed by ~0.93 GB'. The brief's own MSSQL_MEMORY_LIMIT_MB of 7168 inside a 10240 MB cap contradicts the assumption that caps approximate usage. The load-bearing infrastructure conclusion ('a second full application stack cannot run on the existing VM') currently rests on a category error and needs measured resident memory to stand.

[9] The '72-hour restoration expectation' attributed to the January 2025 HIPAA Security Rule NPRM is not supported by the cited article, which does not mention it. The comment-period close date of 2025-03-07 is likewise absent from the cited page. Both need the Federal Register notice as a primary source, and the 72-hour element must be stated precisely (restoration of certain relevant electronic information systems and data) rather than as a blanket restore SLA.
vendor_neutrality_violations: NONE FOUND  -  no named product appears as a recommendation. All sixteen capability requirements are written as capabilities ('the platform MUST support...', 'the DNS provider MUST expose an API...', 'a single build artifact MUST be deployable...') with no vendor, cloud, or product named anywhere in the requirement text. Every vendor appearance in the research (Microsoft Learn, AWS Well-Architected, Let's Encrypt, Docker, OpenIddict, ABP, nip.io, NuGet) is confined to the CLAIMS as evidence of a behaviour class or as a documented constraint of software already in use, which the brief permits.

NEAR-MISS, flagged for the author's judgement, NOT scored as a violation: requirement 12 ('Every environment SHOULD report an identical, ideally empty, set of edition-restricted database features') is vendor-shaped rather than vendor-named. 'Edition-restricted database features' is SQL Server vocabulary drawn directly from sys.dm_db_persisted_sku_features and presupposes an edition-tiered commercial RDBMS; a Postgres or MySQL deployment has no such concept and could not satisfy or fail this requirement as written. It names no product and describes a real behaviour class (a stored database that is pinned to a licensing tier and cannot be moved down), so it stays inside the rule  -  but if the exercise must survive an RDBMS substitution, restate it as 'no environment may enable storage-level features that make its databases non-portable to the edition or tier used by any other environment', and cite the SQL Server DMV as the concrete instrument rather than the requirement itself.

NEAR-MISS, flagged: requirement 3 ('The DNS provider for every environment MUST expose an API that a script can use to create and delete TXT records unattended') is correctly vendor-neutral in wording, but it is derived solely from Let's Encrypt's DNS-01 guidance (claim 17). That derivation is legitimate  -  DNS-01 is the only ACME challenge type that validates wildcards, and that is a protocol property, not a vendor property  -  so this is not a violation. Worth confirming in the write-up that the requirement is stated as 'an ACME DNS-01-capable provider' rather than implying any specific CA or DNS host.

research.area: Network and exposure architecture  -  Host-header-bound multi-tenant edge, health checking, TLS/naming, administrative surface containment, internal segmentation, and Host-header attack surface
research.design_space: In 2026 the viable ways to expose a multi-tenant HTTP application fall into five structural classes, and they differ mainly in how many components parse and potentially rewrite HTTP before the application sees it. (1) A single terminating L7 reverse proxy at the edge  -  one TLS terminator, one HTTP parser, one hop  -  which is the minimum-component design and still the dominant pattern for single-region business applications. (2) A managed L7 HTTP load balancer as the terminator, which trades operational ownership for a vendor-defined default set of header transformations you do not control and cannot patch. (3) An L4 or TLS-passthrough front door with the L7 proxy behind it, which makes the front door structurally incapable of touching HTTP at all, at the cost of losing edge WAF, edge rate limiting, HTTP-aware health checks and edge-injected response headers. (4) A globally distributed edge (CDN class) which adds a cache  -  a stateful, keyed, shared store in the request path  -  and a second identity for the origin. (5) An orchestrator ingress plus optional service mesh, which adds two or three more HTTP-aware hops (cloud LB, ingress controller, sidecar) each with its own Host and SNI semantics. Cutting across all five is an independent decision about the administrative plane: whether management surfaces share the public request path, sit on a separate hostname or port, are restricted by network, gated by mTLS or an identity-aware proxy, or are simply not published at all and reached out-of-band. Naming and TLS are a third independent axis: single-label subdomains under one wildcard, multi-level subdomains needing one wildcard per depth, or customer-supplied custom domains needing per-domain validation and certificates. The binding constraint that selects among all of these is not throughput or latency  -  at eleven to thirty-three small practices neither is a real constraint  -  but how much of the HTTP request the application depends on surviving the trip, and how many independent parsers get a vote on what that request means.

options.name: A. Single Host-preserving L7 terminating proxy as the sole edge (hardened version of what exists)
options.how_it_works: One self-managed reverse proxy terminates TLS for four routing rules  -  *.<base> to the SPA static files, *.api.<base> to HttpApi.Host, *.auth.<base> to AuthServer, minio.<base> exact to MinIO  -  and forwards the client's Host verbatim. Wildcard DNS and one wildcard certificate per label depth mean office count never appears in edge configuration. A default_server on 443 terminates everything unmatched. limit_req zones keyed on client address and $host apply to both the API and AuthServer because both traverse the same proxy. Backends sit on internal Docker networks with no published ports; the administrative path is not routed at the edge at all.
options.operational_cost: Setup 12-20 hours (config rewrite, default_server, security headers, TLS pinning, limit_req zones, network segmentation, resolver fix, ACME DNS-01 automation). Ongoing 1-3 hours/month, mostly certificate-automation checks and reading proxy logs. Assumes ability to read nginx/HAProxy documentation and run curl with an explicit Host  -  no new expertise.
options.why: It is the only option where the number of components that can break tenant resolution stays at one, and that one is a component the team already operates and can read the source configuration of. Every failure mode is a hard error: wrong Host means 'Tenant not found', a missing certificate means a browser interstitial, a dead upstream means 502. Nothing degrades quietly. It also preserves the property that adding an office is a host-UI action rather than a deployment, because no per-office edge configuration exists.

options.name: B. Managed L7 HTTP load balancer as the TLS terminator in front of the application
options.how_it_works: A vendor-operated application load balancer terminates TLS, evaluates listener rules on Host, and forwards to the application. Host preservation depends entirely on the product's default: the class splits, with some preserving the client Host and others substituting the backend/origin hostname unless explicitly told not to. Health checks are configured on the balancer, not the application.
options.operational_cost: Setup 8-16 hours if the product preserves Host by default and permits a Host header on health probes; 25-40 hours plus an application change if it does not. Ongoing 1-2 hours/month. Assumes familiarity with the specific product's header-transformation table, which is the expertise most often missing.
options.why: Viable only if two capabilities are confirmed by test before commitment: verbatim Host forwarding, and an operator-settable Host on the health probe. Both exist somewhere in the class and are absent somewhere in the class  -  the documented defaults across major products include substituting the origin hostname, and health probes that send the target's private IP, the load balancer node's IP, or literally 127.0.0.1 as Host. Where the probe Host is not settable, the design problem is real and the fix has to move into the application (a liveness path exempt from tenant resolution), which is a code change this team must schedule.

options.name: C. L4 / TLS-passthrough front door with the L7 proxy behind it
options.how_it_works: A layer-4 device forwards TCP or terminates nothing, passing the TLS session through to the existing L7 proxy which remains the sole TLS terminator and sole HTTP parser. The front door provides address stability, DDoS absorption and cross-host failover without ever reading the Host header.
options.operational_cost: Setup 6-12 hours. Ongoing under 1 hour/month. Requires understanding PROXY protocol if client IP must survive, which adds 4-6 hours and a matching setting on the proxy.
options.why: It structurally eliminates the Host problem: a component that never parses HTTP cannot rewrite HTTP. What you lose is real and should be stated plainly  -  no edge WAF, no edge HTTP rate limiting at the front door, no HTTP-aware health checks (TCP-only liveness, which for this application is arguably more honest anyway), no edge-injected response headers, and no path-based blocking of administrative routes at the front door. Every one of those capabilities remains available at the L7 proxy behind it, so nothing is actually lost  -  it just does not move outward. Client IP requires PROXY protocol or it is lost, and losing it silently degrades both audit logging and rate limiting, which is the one subtle failure in this option.

options.name: D. SNI-routed L4 edge fronting multiple L7 proxies
options.how_it_works: An L4 edge reads the TLS ClientHello's SNI extension without decrypting, and routes to one of several backend L7 proxies based on server name. This is how you split traffic across independent stacks without terminating TLS centrally.
options.operational_cost: Setup 15-25 hours including a proxy build with the preread module compiled in. Ongoing 2-4 hours/month. Requires understanding that SNI and Host are two independent, separately attacker-controlled values.
options.why: There is no second stack to route to  -  every office hostname resolves to one application reading one Host header. The routing capability solves a problem this system does not have, and it introduces one it does not currently have: routing decided by SNI while tenancy is decided by Host means the two can be made to disagree by any client that sends SNI=office-a and Host=office-b. That is textbook virtual host confusion, and it is exactly the divergence the current single-terminator design avoids by construction. Reconsider only if offices are ever split across physically separate deployments.

options.name: E. CDN / global edge network in front of the application
options.how_it_works: A distributed edge terminates TLS close to the user, caches responses under a cache key, and forwards to the origin. Host treatment varies by product: some send the original client hostname to the origin by default, others require an explicit origin host header and substitute it otherwise. The cache key composition is the second, independent decision.
options.operational_cost: Setup 20-35 hours, dominated by proving what is and is not cacheable. Ongoing 3-6 hours/month, and materially more the first time a cache-related incident occurs. Assumes someone can reason confidently about cache keys, Vary, and Cache-Control interaction  -  expertise this team does not have.
options.why: The user population is staff at Californian practices; there is no latency problem a CDN solves. Against that near-zero benefit sits the single most dangerous failure mode available to this system: a cache in front of a Host-keyed multi-tenant application, where a cache key that omits or normalises the host serves office A's authenticated response to office B. Google's own documentation warns that force-caching 'might not be appropriate if the backend serves private, per-user (user identifiable) content', and the standard mitigation  -  Cache-Control: private/no-store on everything user-specific  -  depends on the application getting it right on every endpoint, which nobody has audited across 52 controllers. This failure produces a 200 OK with the wrong patient's data and no error anywhere. It is the archetypal design that fails silently, in a team that will not notice silent degradation.

options.name: F. API gateway in front of the application
options.how_it_works: A gateway matches routes on host and path, applies policies (rate limiting, quotas, auth offload, request transformation) and forwards to an upstream service definition. Host treatment is governed by an explicit preserve/override setting.
options.operational_cost: Setup 25-45 hours including a datastore for gateway configuration in most products. Ongoing 4-8 hours/month. Assumes willingness to operate another stateful component.
options.why: The honest attraction is real: centralised rate limiting is precisely the capability this system lacks, and it would cover both the API and the AuthServer in one place, which is the structural shape of the problem. But the product class defaults the wrong way  -  the documented default for at least one major gateway is to replace the upstream Host with the service's configured host, and another overrides Host with the API's service-URL host unless a policy is added. The default configuration of the product category breaks tenancy. And the rate-limiting need is met by the L7 proxy already in the path, keyed on the client address and $host, at a fraction of the operational surface.

options.name: G. Orchestrator ingress plus service mesh / sidecar proxies
options.how_it_works: A cloud load balancer fronts an ingress controller which fronts per-pod sidecar proxies. mTLS is established between sidecars; the sidecar derives upstream SNI from the request's Host/authority when SNI is not explicitly configured, and certificate validation follows from that.
options.operational_cost: Setup 120-250 hours to reach a defensible production state, including cluster, ingress, certificate plumbing, probes and a deployment pipeline. Ongoing 15-30 hours/month for upgrades alone. Assumes a platform engineer.
options.why: It takes the number of independent HTTP parsers between client and application from one to three or four, each with its own Host and SNI semantics, and makes the health-probe Host problem mandatory rather than optional because kubelet probes default to the Pod IP as Host. The mesh's automatic derivation of SNI from the Host header is a genuinely elegant property in a service-to-service mesh and a genuinely hazardous one when Host is the tenant selector, because it couples the certificate validated on the wire to an attacker-supplied header. With no second application instance, no scaling pressure and no on-call rotation, none of the benefits are being bought. Revisit only when a second instance is genuinely required and a person exists who has operated this before.

options.name: H. Administrative plane: not published at all, reached out-of-band
options.how_it_works: No administrative surface is present in the edge routing table. Management interfaces (the job dashboard, the object-store console, health-check UIs, database ports) bind only to internal container networks. An operator reaches them by an authenticated SSH session to the host with a local port forward to the internal service, so the SSH daemon and its key-based authentication are the policy enforcement point and it is a separate component from the interface being protected.
options.operational_cost: Setup 2-4 hours (delete the edge route, confirm ports are unpublished, document the forward command). Ongoing effectively zero. Requires no new component, no new credential type, no certificate lifecycle.
options.why: It satisfies the strongest published guidance in this space  -  CISA's directive on internet-exposed management interfaces requires either removing them from the internet or protecting them with a policy enforcement point separate from the interface itself  -  using infrastructure that already exists and that the team already uses for every deployment. It fails obviously: if the forward is not set up, nothing answers. And it is independent of the application code fix, so the dashboard's authorisation filter and the edge exposure are two controls that fail independently rather than one control with two names.

options.name: I. Administrative plane: public admin hostname gated by mutual TLS at the edge
options.how_it_works: A dedicated hostname (or a location block) requires a client certificate; the edge verifies it against a private CA and refuses the TLS handshake or the request otherwise. Certificates are issued to the two developers' machines.
options.operational_cost: Setup 10-16 hours (private CA, issuance, distribution, edge configuration, revocation procedure). Ongoing 1-2 hours/month, spiking at renewal and on any device change.
options.why: Technically strong  -  client-certificate verification is a first-class, well-documented capability of the proxy already in the path, and it authenticates the operator rather than their network location, so it survives a change of ISP or a coffee-shop connection. The reason it is second rather than first is that it creates a private certificate lifecycle for a two-person team with no automation and no secret store, and a private CA whose key lives in the same single mode-600 secrets file that is already flagged for rotation. It becomes the right answer the moment a third person needs administrative access, or the moment administrative access must come from a device that cannot hold an SSH key to the host.

research.recommendation:
Recommendation: Option A as the edge (a single Host-preserving L7 terminating proxy, hardened), Option H as the administrative plane (nothing administrative published; reached out-of-band), with Option C available later as a pure addition if address stability or a second host is ever needed. Reject D, E, F and G outright at this size, and treat B as conditional on two tests you must run before committing.

The reasoning starts from a fact about this system that I think has not been named yet: the number of edge routing rules is four, and it does not grow with office count. Every office hostname resolves to the same three application processes; the office is selected inside the application by reading Host and swapping a database name. The edge does not need Host-based tenant routing at all  -  it needs Host-based *product* routing (SPA / API / AuthServer / object store), which is four rules whether there are two offices or thirty-three. This is why "adding an office is a host-UI action, not a deployment" is currently true, and it is the single most valuable property in the whole design. Every option above either preserves that property (because it can be configured with wildcards) or destroys it (because it requires a configuration entry, a certificate, or a DNS record per hostname). Protecting that property should be the first filter applied to any platform candidate, ahead of throughput, ahead of availability, ahead of everything.

The second observation is that "tenancy resolves from the Host header" is not one property but two, and the team is conflating them. Property one is *routing*: the request must arrive at the application with Host intact. Property two is *trust*: the application uses a client-controlled string to select which database it talks to. Property one is an infrastructure requirement and is satisfied by preserving Host. Property two is a security posture, and it is unusual. Microsoft's own architecture guidance states flatly, in the article that otherwise argues *for* host name preservation, "Never use the value of the host in a security mechanism. The browser or another user agent provides the value, and a user can change it." That does not make this design wrong  -  selecting a tenant by hostname is how most multi-tenant SaaS works, and the guidance's own multitenancy section endorses passing the incoming host name unmodified precisely because a multitenant deployment cannot statically define a single domain. What it means is that the *allowlist* is load-bearing: the safety of the design rests entirely on the fact that an unrecognised Host produces "Tenant not found" rather than a fallback. That property must be tested, enforced at two independent layers (edge and application), and defended against every documented way of making two HTTP parsers disagree about what the Host is.

Concretely, for the edge. Preserve Host explicitly and never rely on a default: nginx's documented default is `proxy_set_header Host $proxy_host`, i.e. it *rewrites* Host to the upstream's name, and the current configuration works only because somebody wrote an explicit `proxy_set_header Host`. Worse, that directive's inheritance is all-or-nothing per configuration level  -  adding any `proxy_set_header` inside a location block silently discards every inherited one, including the Host line. So the Host directive should be repeated in every location that proxies, with a comment saying why, and there should be a test that asserts it. Add a `default_server` on 443 that terminates unmatched names, because without one nginx routes unmatched Host values to the first server block for the port, which is documented behaviour and is the same mechanism the virtual-host-confusion literature identifies as the precondition for origin confusion; the observed symptom (the bare apex reaching the AuthServer) is not cosmetic. Fix the stale-upstream-IP problem generally, not just for the object store, by using a resolver with variables in `proxy_pass` on every upstream, since nginx resolves a literal upstream name once at worker start and a variable form goes through the resolver. Add `limit_req` zones keyed on the client address and on `$host`, applied at the proxy: this is the structural answer to the two-process rate-limiting problem, because sign-in is served by the AuthServer whose Razor pages never touch API middleware, and the proxy is the only component both processes traverse. Add the response-header set and TLS version pinning that is entirely absent.

For naming and TLS, three layers use three different wildcard rules and this needs to be written down where the team will see it. A TLS wildcard matches exactly one label and only as the complete leftmost label (RFC 9525 6.3), so `*.<base>` does not cover `office.api.<base>` and separate wildcards are needed per depth. An nginx `server_name` wildcard matches *several* label parts, so `*.<base>` will match `office.api.<base>` unless a longer wildcard exists  -  which is exactly why `api.<base>` with no office label falls through to the SPA. And a DNS wildcard matches multiple labels too, but only while no node exists at an intermediate label (RFC 4592 2.2.1: `foo.bar.example` is synthesised by `*.example` "because bar.example. does not exist"). Wildcards require DNS-01 validation, so the DNS provider must expose an API  -  that is now a hard platform requirement, not a preference. And certificate lifetimes are collapsing on a published schedule (200 days from 15 March 2026, 100 days from 2027, 47 days from 2029 under CA/B ballot SC-081v3; Let's Encrypt moving toward 45-day certificates), which means manual certificate handling has an expiry date and automation is not optional.

For health checks, the concrete answer the brief asks for. Because a bare IP cannot reach this application, the platform must satisfy one of two conditions, and you should require the first and implement the second as insurance. Condition one: the probe must permit an operator-specified Host header. This is available in the Kubernetes probe (`httpGet.httpHeaders` with Host, which the documentation explicitly recommends over the `host` field when the pod relies on virtual hosts), in HAProxy (`http-check send ... hdr Host <name>`), in Traefik (`healthCheck.hostname`), in Azure Application Gateway custom probes (the `host` field, which on v2 also sets SNI), and in Google Cloud health checks (a `--host` flag). It is *not* available on AWS Application Load Balancer target-group health checks, where the Host is the target's private IP and optional port and the settings list contains no Host option, nor on Network Load Balancer HTTP health checks, where the Host is the load balancer node's IP and listener port. Azure's default probe sends `Host: 127.0.0.1`. Every industry default is exactly the case this application refuses. Condition two, the insurance: expose a liveness path in each process that returns 200 without tenant resolution, so that a probe carrying an IP as Host still succeeds. This is a small application change and it removes an entire class of platform lock-out. Separately  -  and this is a design point rather than a configuration one  -  with a database per office, "healthy" is per-office, and a load balancer probe that succeeds proves only that the process is alive and the host database is reachable. Keep those two signals apart: liveness for the load balancer (cheap, tenant-free), and a host-scope readiness view for operators that reports per-office database reachability. Do not put the per-office sweep behind the load balancer's probe, or you will have an eleven-connection database fan-out running at the probe interval, on top of three fifteen-minute recurring jobs that already iterate offices.

For the administrative surface, take the strongest available option because it is also the cheapest. Do not route `/hangfire` at the edge at all. The code fix (a real authorisation filter) and the edge removal are two independent controls, and the guidance that matters here  -  CISA's directive on internet-exposed management interfaces  -  asks for the interface to be removed from the internet or placed behind a policy enforcement point *separate from the interface itself*, which an in-process authorisation filter by definition is not. An SSH session with a local port forward to the internal service is that separate enforcement point, costs nothing to build, requires no new credential, and fails obviously. The same treatment applies to the object store console, the health-checks UI and anything else that exists to administer rather than to serve.

For internal segmentation, the current single Docker bridge means the static-file container can open a socket to SQL Server and the packet renderer can reach Redis. Split into purpose-scoped networks with `internal: true` where possible: an edge network (proxy plus the three application front doors), a data network (API, AuthServer, DbMigrator, SQL Server, Redis), a storage network (API, proxy, MinIO) and a render network (API, packet renderer). The renderer should reach nothing but the API; the static-file container should reach nothing at all. This is a compose-file change measured in hours, every violation surfaces as a connection refused, and it is the concrete form of the network-segmentation control that the pending HIPAA Security Rule proposal would make mandatory if finalised  -  noting honestly that as of mid-2026 no final rule has been published and no compliance clock is running.

Finally, on Host-header attacks, because this system's exposure is genuinely unusual. In a normal application, Host injection yields poisoned links and password-reset emails. Here it additionally selects a database. The specific surface is: alternative host headers (X-Forwarded-Host, X-Host, X-Forwarded-Server, X-HTTP-Host-Override, Forwarded); absolute-URI request lines; duplicate Host headers; line-wrapped or space-padded Host headers; and request smuggling, where a front-end and back-end disagreement lets a smuggled request prefix ride on a connection the front end believes belongs to a different office. Two research results bound the risk: "Host of Troubles" found 21 of 33 HTTP implementations did not normalise Host sufficiently when forwarding, and the virtual-host-confusion work established that fallback-to-default-vhost is the exploitable end state. The mitigations are cheap and belong at the edge: allowlist Host at the proxy and reject anything else with a terminal response; strip all the alternative host headers inbound so the application can never see a client-supplied one; keep a default_server; and never enable `X-Forwarded-Host` processing in the application. On that last point the application is safe today only by accident  -  ASP.NET Core's forwarded-headers middleware defaults to `ForwardedHeaders.None` and must be explicitly enabled  -  but the standard recipe for putting an app behind a proxy enables it, and `X-Forwarded-Host` sets `HttpContext.Request.Host`, which is what the tenant resolver reads. Enabling it with `KnownProxies.Clear()`, which is the most-copied fix on the internet for forwarded headers not working in Docker, would hand every client a tenant selector. Microsoft's own advisory for CVE-2018-0787 describes exactly this shape of failure: an elevation-of-privilege condition when an ASP.NET Core app sits behind a proxy that "does not validate or restrict host headers to known good values". Enable `XForwardedFor | XForwardedProto` only, and enable Host filtering middleware with a real allowlist rather than the template's `"*"`.

One caveat I want to state rather than bury. The brief records honestly that whether ABP's four `__tenant` resolvers are disabled has never been tested. The framework registers query-string, route, header and cookie resolvers, plus a current-user resolver from the core module. What actually neutralises them in the stock domain-resolver path is not an explicit removal but the fact that ABP's `DomainTenantResolveContributor` sets `context.Handled = true` unconditionally  -  the subject of an open issue in the ABP repository  -  which short-circuits the loop. If the custom `HostAwareDomainTenantResolveContributor` sets `Handled` only on a match, all four remain live and `?__tenant=<id>` is a tenant selector on every endpoint. This is a fifteen-minute test with curl and it should be run before any of the infrastructure work, because the answer changes what the edge has to defend against: if the resolvers are live, the edge must also strip `__tenant` from query strings, cookies and headers, which is a materially uglier configuration.
research.operational_cost_of_recommendation:
Setup: 30-45 developer-hours total, decomposable into independently shippable pieces. Edge hardening (explicit Host preservation in every proxying location, default_server on 443, resolver-with-variables for all upstreams, security response headers, TLS version and cipher pinning, server_tokens off) 10-14 hours. Host allowlisting plus stripping of alternative host headers plus Host-filtering middleware configuration 4-6 hours. limit_req zones covering both the API and AuthServer paths 3-5 hours. ACME DNS-01 automation for the per-depth wildcards, with an expiry alert 6-10 hours. Administrative de-routing and documenting the SSH-forward procedure 2-4 hours. Docker network segmentation 4-6 hours. Tenant-free liveness path in both processes 2-4 hours (application change; may need to be scheduled against the code-standard remediation).

Ongoing: 1-3 hours/month steady state  -  certificate-renewal verification, reading rejected-Host and rate-limit counters, and re-running the Host-preservation test after any proxy edit. Add roughly 2 hours in each of March 2026, March 2027 and March 2029 when maximum certificate lifetimes step down (200 / 100 / 47 days), since each step halves the renewal margin and is the moment weak automation shows itself.

Threshold, stated because the one-developer-week-per-month figure is an estimate rather than a measurement: this recommendation is operable at roughly 4 hours per month of infrastructure attention. Below about 2 hours per month it decays in a specific and predictable order. First, certificate automation stops being verified and a renewal fails silently until a browser interstitial appears  -  which under a 47-day regime happens roughly three times as often as under 90-day certificates. Second, the Host-preservation assertion stops being re-run after proxy edits, and the all-or-nothing `proxy_set_header` inheritance rule turns a one-line change into a per-location tenancy outage. Third, the rate-limit and rejected-Host counters stop being read, so a credential-stuffing run against the AuthServer is throttled but never noticed. Note that none of these decay paths is silent in the *user-visible* sense  -  each produces a hard error for somebody  -  which is the property that makes this recommendation appropriate for an unattended team, and it is precisely the property that options E (CDN caching) and G (mesh) do not have. If sustained attention falls below 2 hours per month, drop the ACME automation for an externally managed certificate before dropping anything else, because it is the only component here whose failure is time-triggered rather than change-triggered.

evidence.claim: nginx does NOT preserve the client Host header by default when proxying. The documented default is 'proxy_set_header Host $proxy_host', i.e. the upstream's name from the proxy_pass directive. For HTTP/2 the ':authority' pseudo-header is sent with the $proxy_host value by default.
evidence.source_name: nginx documentation  -  Module ngx_http_proxy_module
evidence.threshold_or_limit: proxy_set_header Host $proxy_host; proxy_set_header Connection close;

evidence.claim: nginx proxy_set_header directives are inherited from the previous configuration level ONLY IF no proxy_set_header directive is defined at the current level  -  so adding any single proxy_set_header inside a location silently discards the inherited Host line.
evidence.source_name: nginx documentation  -  Module ngx_http_proxy_module
evidence.threshold_or_limit: All-or-nothing inheritance per configuration level

evidence.claim: When a proxy_pass value contains variables and the address is a domain name, the name is resolved using a resolver rather than being fixed at worker start  -  which is the documented mechanism behind the 'stale container IP' trap the team has already hit for the object-store block.
evidence.source_name: nginx documentation  -  Module ngx_http_proxy_module
evidence.threshold_or_limit: n/a

evidence.claim: An nginx server_name wildcard matches SEVERAL name parts: '*.example.org' matches not only www.example.org but www.sub.example.org as well. Matching precedence is exact name, then longest wildcard starting with an asterisk, then longest wildcard ending with an asterisk, then first matching regular expression.
evidence.source_name: nginx documentation  -  Server names
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Multi-label wildcard match; 4-step precedence order

evidence.claim: If the Host value matches no server name, or the request contains no Host field, nginx routes the request to the default server for that port; without an explicit default_server parameter the default server is the FIRST server block for that port. default_server is a property of the listen directive, not of server_name.
evidence.source_name: nginx documentation  -  How nginx processes a request
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Fallback = first server block for the port

evidence.claim: nginx returns 421 Misdirected Request when a client requests a server name different from the one negotiated in TLS, which occurs when HTTP/2 clients coalesce connections across hostnames covered by one wildcard certificate on one IP. The nginx maintainer states this is correct specification behaviour and that browsers should open a new connection on receiving 421.
evidence.source_name: nginx Trac ticket #1252  -  Multiplexing different hosts into one HTTP/2 connection leads to 421
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Log line: 'client attempted to request the server name different from that one was negotiated'

evidence.claim: nginx limit_req_zone accepts a key composed of variables including $host and $server_name, and limit_req_status defaults to 503 (settable to 429). This makes per-office and per-client rate limiting expressible at the single point both the API process and the AuthServer process traverse.
evidence.source_name: nginx documentation  -  Module ngx_http_limit_req_module
evidence.threshold_or_limit: limit_req_status default 503

evidence.claim: nginx client-certificate verification (ssl_verify_client) defaults to off and accepts on | optional | optional_no_ca, with the trust anchor set by ssl_client_certificate or ssl_trusted_certificate. It is available per server block, so mTLS can be applied to an administrative hostname without affecting tenant traffic.
evidence.source_name: nginx documentation  -  Module ngx_http_ssl_module
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Default: ssl_verify_client off;

evidence.claim: Apache mod_proxy also rewrites Host by default: ProxyPreserveHost defaults to Off, meaning the proxy uses the hostname from the ProxyPass line rather than the incoming Host header. The documentation notes it is 'mostly useful in special configurations like proxied mass name-based virtual hosting'.
evidence.source_name: Apache HTTP Server documentation  -  mod_proxy
evidence.threshold_or_limit: ProxyPreserveHost Off (default)

evidence.claim: Traefik preserves the client Host header by default: passHostHeader is true. Traefik service health checks additionally support a 'hostname' field used as the Host header value on checks, plus arbitrary custom headers.
evidence.source_name: Traefik documentation  -  HTTP Services / load balancing
evidence.threshold_or_limit: passHostHeader default true

evidence.claim: HAProxy forwards the client request including its Host header by default, and HTTP health checks can carry an explicit Host via 'http-check send ... hdr Host <name>'. Without http-check send, checks issue an OPTIONS request to '/'.
evidence.source_name: HAProxy configuration tutorials  -  Health checks
evidence.threshold_or_limit: http-check send meth HEAD uri /healthz ver HTTP/1.1 hdr Host test.local

evidence.claim: Envoy modifies the :authority header only when a host-rewrite specifier is configured (host_rewrite_literal, auto_host_rewrite, host_rewrite_header, host_rewrite_path_regex); the original value is placed in x-envoy-original-host and appended to x-forwarded-host only when the authority is modified. The documentation does not state the no-rewrite default explicitly, but preservation is the necessary implication.
evidence.source_name: Envoy documentation  -  HTTP route components / HTTP header manipulation
evidence.threshold_or_limit: n/a  -  default preservation is implied, not stated

evidence.claim: Kong Gateway defaults to REWRITING the upstream Host: preserve_host defaults to false, in which case the upstream Host header is the Gateway Service's configured host rather than the client's.

evidence.claim: A TLS wildcard certificate matches exactly ONE label, and the wildcard character must appear only as the complete content of the leftmost label. Therefore *.example.com does NOT cover office.api.example.com. RFC 9525 (published 2023) obsoletes RFC 6125.
evidence.source_name: RFC 9525  -  Service Identity in TLS, 6.3
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 6.3: 'A wildcard in a presented identifier can only match one label in a reference identifier'; wildcard must be the complete left-most label

evidence.claim: A DNS wildcard, unlike a TLS wildcard, CAN synthesise answers for names with more than one extra label  -  but only while no node exists at the intermediate label. RFC 4592 2.2.1's own example: a query for foo.bar.example. is answered from *.example. 'because bar.example. does not exist, but the wildcard does'. Conversely, a query for _telnet._tcp.host1.example. gets no wildcard synthesis because '_tcp.host1.example. exists (without data)'  -  i.e. an EMPTY NON-TERMINAL blocks wildcard synthesis.
evidence.source_name: RFC 4592  -  The Role of Wildcards in the Domain Name System, 2.2.1 (ICANN annotated edition)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 2.2.1 worked example; empty non-terminals block synthesis

evidence.claim: Creating the DNS-01 challenge record needed to obtain a *.api.<base> certificate places a TXT record at _acme-challenge.api.<base>, which creates the empty non-terminal api.<base>. By RFC 4592 2.2.1 that empty non-terminal becomes the closest encloser for office.api.<base> and blocks synthesis from *.<base>  -  so unless a wildcard exists at *.api.<base>, the act of setting up the certificate can stop every office API hostname from resolving.
evidence.source_name: Derived from RFC 4592 2.2.1 (empty non-terminal case) applied to ACME DNS-01 record placement
evidence.threshold_or_limit: n/a  -  inference from a verified RFC rule; not observed in this system

evidence.claim: Wildcard certificates can only be validated via the DNS-01 challenge; HTTP-01 cannot issue wildcards. This makes a DNS provider with an automatable API a hard requirement for any multi-level-wildcard naming scheme.
evidence.source_name: Let's Encrypt  -  Challenge Types
evidence.threshold_or_limit: DNS-01 required for wildcards; TXT record at _acme-challenge.<DOMAIN>

evidence.claim: Maximum public TLS certificate validity is stepping down on a published schedule under CA/Browser Forum ballot SC-081v3 (passed April 2025): 200 days from 15 March 2026, 100 days from 15 March 2027, 47 days from 15 March 2029. Let's Encrypt is separately moving default lifetimes from 90 days toward 45 days, roughly doubling renewal frequency; renewals remain exempt from issuance rate limits, and a single certificate may carry up to 100 identifiers.
evidence.source_name: CA/Browser Forum Ballot SC-081v3 and Let's Encrypt  -  Shorter Certificate Lifetimes and Rate Limits
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 200 days from 2026-03-15; 100 days from 2027-03-15; 47 days from 2029-03-15; LE 90->64->45 days; 100 identifiers per certificate

evidence.claim: ASP.NET Core's Forwarded Headers Middleware sets HttpContext.Request.Host from the X-Forwarded-Host header (persisting the old value in X-Original-Host). It is NOT enabled by default and its default ForwardedHeaders value is ForwardedHeaders.None. KnownProxies defaults to a single entry for IPv6 loopback and KnownNetworks to loopback/8; ForwardedHeadersOptions.AllowedHosts defaults to an EMPTY list, which allows ALL hosts.

evidence.claim: Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2018-0787 describes an elevation-of-privilege vulnerability arising when an ASP.NET Core application is 'hosted behind a proxy which does not validate or restrict host headers to known good values', and notes that Kestrel itself cannot validate host headers. Mitigation is a validating proxy or Host Filtering Middleware.

evidence.claim: ABP's ASP.NET Core multi-tenancy module registers four tenant resolve contributors in order  -  QueryString, Route, Header, Cookie  -  with the parameter name __tenant by default; the core module additionally contributes CurrentUserTenantResolveContributor. Adding a domain resolver supplements rather than replaces these.

This, rather than any explicit removal, is what neutralises the __tenant resolvers in a domain-resolver deployment.

evidence.claim: Host header attack techniques for bypassing validation include: absolute URLs in the request line, duplicate Host headers (implementations differ on which wins), line-wrapped/indented headers, and the override headers X-Forwarded-Host, X-Host, X-Forwarded-Server, X-HTTP-Host-Override and Forwarded. Routing-based SSRF exploits intermediary components that can be manipulated into misrouting requests.

evidence.claim: OWASP's Web Security Testing Guide instructs validating the Host header on every incoming request and rejecting unexpected hostnames, and lists impacts including dispatching requests to the first virtual host on the list, redirect to an attacker-controlled domain, cache poisoning, password-reset manipulation, and access to virtual hosts not intended to be externally accessible.

evidence.threshold_or_limit: n/a

evidence.claim: Academic measurement found deployed HTTP implementations parse and interpret the Host header inconsistently: 21 of 33 implementations tested did not normalise requests sufficiently when forwarding them upstream, using multiple Host headers, space-surrounded Host headers and absolute-URI request targets; around 97% of users served by transparent caches were subject to cache-poisoning attacks.
evidence.source_name: Host of Troubles: Multiple Host Ambiguities in HTTP Implementations (ACM CCS 2016)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 21 of 33 implementations; ~97% of transparent-cache users

evidence.claim: Virtual host confusion arises because routing decisions rely on unauthenticated data (IP, port, SNI, Host); when the Host header matches no configured virtual host, systems fall back to the default vhost or the first one, and TLS sessions/tickets opened for one virtual host can be resumed against another unless the server name is bound into the ticket. Mitigations include strict Host/SNI consistency checking and an explicit block-by-default routing action.
evidence.source_name: Vhost Confusion (Tempesta Technologies knowledge base), building on Delignat-Lavaud & Bhargavan, Black Hat 2014 / WWW'15
evidence.threshold_or_limit: n/a

evidence.claim: HTTP request smuggling exploits front-end/back-end disagreement about request boundaries; because the front end 'commonly reuses the same connection for multiple requests', part of an attacker's request can be interpreted by the back end as the start of the NEXT request and prepended to it, interfering with how that request is processed.
evidence.source_name: PortSwigger Web Security Academy  -  HTTP request smuggling
evidence.threshold_or_limit: n/a

Public-facing TLS endpoints therefore continue to expose the requested hostname in cleartext.
