evidence.claim: Docker Compose healthchecks run a command inside the container (test as a list beginning with CMD or CMD-SHELL), so a container-level HTTP check can set an arbitrary Host header (e.g. curl -H 'Host: ...'). This makes container-level checks unconditionally compatible with Host-bound applications, unlike most external load balancer probes.
evidence.source_name: Docker documentation  -  Define services in Docker Compose (healthcheck)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", ...]

evidence.claim: The number of edge routing rules required by this system is four (SPA wildcard, API wildcard, Auth wildcard, object-store exact) and does not grow with the number of offices, because every office hostname is served by the same three processes and the office is selected inside the application. Therefore the edge never needs per-tenant configuration and 'add an office without a deployment' is preserved by any wildcard-capable edge and destroyed by any per-hostname-configuration edge.
evidence.source_name: My architectural reasoning applied to the supplied system facts (one application instance; tenancy resolved in-process from Host; wildcard DNS and certificates)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 4 routing rules regardless of office count (11 today, 33 headroom)

capability_requirements.requirement: Every component in the request path between the client and the application processes must forward the client-supplied Host header byte-for-byte unmodified, and this must be true for every route, not merely the ones currently tested.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Tenancy  -  and therefore which patient database is opened  -  is resolved from Host. Any rewrite does not degrade the system, it selects the wrong database or returns 'Tenant not found'. There is no partial-credit version of this.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System fact: HostAwareDomainTenantResolveContributor reads the office slug from the leftmost DNS label of the Host header. Cross-referenced against nginx's documented default of proxy_set_header Host $proxy_host and Microsoft's host-name-preservation guidance.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Deploy a trivial echo endpoint (or enable an access-log field capturing $http_host) behind every candidate component. From an external client send GET with 'Host: probe-slug.api.<base>' and assert the backend received exactly 'probe-slug.api.<base>'  -  same case, same absence/presence of port. Repeat once per routed location (SPA, API, Auth, object store) and once per HTTP version (1.1 and 2). Any difference at all is a failure.

capability_requirements.requirement: The platform's health-check or probe mechanism must permit an operator-specified HTTP Host header on the probe request.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: A bare IP cannot reach this application. Every widely deployed default sends an IP (target IP, load balancer node IP, forwarding rule IP) or 127.0.0.1 as Host, all of which this application refuses. Without a settable Host the platform cannot ever mark the application healthy.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: AWS ALB sends the target's private IP as Host with no configurable override; AWS NLB sends the load balancer node's IP; Azure Application Gateway's default probe sends 127.0.0.1; Kubernetes probes default to the Pod IP; Google Cloud defaults to the forwarding rule IP unless --host is given.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: In the candidate platform's health-check configuration UI or API, look for a host/hostname/httpHeaders field. Then prove it end to end: configure the probe with 'Host: <reserved-admin-host>' and confirm the target reaches a healthy state, then remove the Host setting and confirm the target goes unhealthy. If the target stays healthy with no Host set, the application is not enforcing tenant resolution on that path and requirement 3 below must be re-checked.

capability_requirements.requirement: Each application process must expose a liveness path that returns 200 without performing tenant resolution, reachable when the Host header is an IP address or is absent.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: This is the insurance that decouples platform selection from a single vendor capability. With it, a platform whose probe cannot set Host is still usable; without it, that platform is permanently excluded. Given that platform selection is a later exercise, this requirement preserves optionality at a cost of a few hours.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System fact: a request whose Host matches no office returns 'Tenant not found'. AWS ALB/NLB probes cannot set Host.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: curl -H 'Host: 10.0.0.5' http://<container-ip>:<port>/health/live and assert HTTP 200 with a body that does not vary by tenant. Then curl --http1.0 with no Host header at all and assert 200. Then assert that a business endpoint under the same IP Host still returns the tenant-not-found response, proving the exemption is scoped to the liveness path only.

capability_requirements.requirement: No component may pass a client-supplied X-Forwarded-Host, X-Host, X-Forwarded-Server, X-HTTP-Host-Override or Forwarded header through to the application, and the application must not be configured to process X-Forwarded-Host.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: In this application X-Forwarded-Host is not a convenience header, it is a tenant selector: ASP.NET Core's forwarded-headers middleware sets HttpContext.Request.Host from it, and that is what the tenant resolver reads. Microsoft's own advisory for CVE-2018-0787 is precisely about proxies that do not restrict Host to known-good values.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft Learn documents that X-Forwarded-Host sets HttpContext.Request.Host; CVE-2018-0787; PortSwigger's list of Host override headers.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Send a request with a valid 'Host: office-a.api.<base>' plus 'X-Forwarded-Host: office-b.api.<base>' (repeat for each of the five header names). Assert (a) the response data is office A's, (b) the backend echo shows the header absent, and (c) grep the application configuration for UseForwardedHeaders and confirm ForwardedHeaders does not include XForwardedHost. Repeat the test with the header duplicated and with a leading space.

capability_requirements.requirement: The edge must reject any request whose Host is not on an explicit allowlist of provisioned office hostnames plus reserved labels, returning a terminal response before the request reaches any application process.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Defence in depth for a design that trusts a client-supplied string to select a database. OWASP's testing guide instructs validating Host on every request and rejecting unexpected hostnames, and the virtual-host-confusion literature identifies fallback-to-default-vhost as the exploitable end state. Two independent layers is the point; the application check alone is one bug away from failing open.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: OWASP WSTG Testing for Host Header Injection; virtual host confusion research; system fact that the nginx template has no default_server on 443.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: From an external client, send requests with: Host absent (HTTP/1.0); Host set to the server's IP; Host: nonexistent-office.<base>; Host: <base> (bare apex); Host: api.<base>; two Host headers with different values; a Host header preceded by a space; and an absolute-URI request line whose authority differs from the Host header. Every one must produce the same terminal response from the edge, and the application access log must show zero corresponding entries.

capability_requirements.requirement: Every listening port on the edge must have an explicit catch-all/default server that returns a terminal response, and the TLS layer must refuse handshakes for unrecognised SNI rather than serving a certificate.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: nginx documents that unmatched Host values go to the default server for the port, and that without an explicit default_server the default is the first server block  -  which is how the bare apex currently reaches the AuthServer. That is the documented precondition for origin confusion, not a cosmetic routing quirk.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: nginx 'How nginx processes a request'; nginx 'Server names'; system fact that no default_server exists on 443 and the apex falls to the AuthServer.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: openssl s_client -connect <ip>:443 with no -servername, and with -servername bogus.example. Assert the handshake is refused or the response is the terminal one, never an application page. Then curl -k -H 'Host: <base>' https://<ip>/ and assert the same. Confirm from the AuthServer's own access log that it received nothing.

capability_requirements.requirement: The TLS certificate set must cover every label depth actually served, with one wildcard per depth; a single *.<base> certificate is not sufficient.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: RFC 9525 6.3 states a wildcard matches exactly one label and must be the complete leftmost label. *.<base> therefore does not cover office.api.<base>. This is a hard protocol rule, not a vendor behaviour.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: RFC 9525 6.3 (obsoletes RFC 6125); CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements; system fact that path-style MinIO addressing was chosen because 'the wildcard TLS certificate covers a single label only'.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: For each of a sample office slug at each depth, run: openssl s_client -connect <edge>:443 -servername <slug>.api.<base> </dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -text | grep -A1 'Subject Alternative Name'. Assert the SAN list contains a wildcard at the matching depth (*.api.<base>). Then run curl without -k and assert no certificate error. Repeat for .auth. and the SPA depth.

capability_requirements.requirement: Certificate issuance and renewal must be fully automated using DNS-01 validation and must complete unattended at no later than one third of the certificate's remaining lifetime, with an alert if any certificate is within one third of expiry.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Wildcards can only be validated by DNS-01, so an automatable DNS API becomes a platform requirement. Maximum lifetimes are dropping on a published schedule (200 days from March 2026, 100 from 2027, 47 from 2029) and Let's Encrypt is moving toward 45 days, so renewal frequency roughly doubles and then doubles again. Manual handling has a known expiry date.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Let's Encrypt challenge types (DNS-01 required for wildcards); CA/Browser Forum ballot SC-081v3 schedule; Let's Encrypt shorter-lifetime announcement.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: In a staging zone, force a renewal (e.g. delete the stored certificate) and confirm a valid certificate is installed and served without any human step, measuring wall-clock time. Separately, set a certificate's expiry monitor threshold and confirm an alert is delivered to a channel a human actually reads. Confirm the DNS provider exposes an API token scoped to TXT records under _acme-challenge only.

capability_requirements.requirement: Provisioning a new office must require no change to DNS records, TLS certificates, edge/proxy configuration, or firewall rules.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: This is the system's most valuable existing property and it is what makes the business model work  -  adding an office is a host-UI action. Every candidate edge component either preserves it (wildcard-capable) or silently converts office onboarding back into a deployment.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System fact: IOfficeDatabaseProvisioner.ProvisionAsync makes adding an office a host-UI action; my analysis that edge routing rules number four and do not grow with office count.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Take a clean snapshot of the DNS zone, the certificate SAN list and the edge configuration file. Provision a new office through the host UI. Without touching any of those three artefacts, from a machine with a cold DNS cache reach https://<newslug>.<base>, https://<newslug>.api.<base>/health and https://<newslug>.auth.<base>, all with a valid certificate. Then diff the three artefacts and assert zero changes.

capability_requirements.requirement: The DNS zone must not contain any node (including empty non-terminals created by descendant records) at an intermediate label used for depth, unless a wildcard exists at that depth.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: RFC 4592 2.2.1 shows that an empty non-terminal blocks wildcard synthesis. Creating any record beneath api.<base>  -  including the _acme-challenge TXT needed to obtain the *.api.<base> certificate  -  creates that node and can stop every office API hostname from resolving. The failure is total and simultaneous across all offices.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: RFC 4592 2.2.1 verbatim examples: 'foo.bar.example ... because bar.example. does not exist' and '_tcp.host1.example. exists (without data)'.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: dig +short randomstring-$(date +%s).api.<base> and assert it resolves. Then enumerate the zone (AXFR against your own nameserver, or the provider's record export) and assert that for each depth label in use there is either no node at that label or a wildcard record one level below it. Re-run this check as a post-condition of every ACME renewal and every DNS change, since the hazard is created by an otherwise-routine operation.

capability_requirements.requirement: Rate limiting must be enforced at a component traversed by both the API process and the AuthServer process, and must be expressible per client and per office hostname.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Sign-in is served by the AuthServer, a separate process that registers no rate limiter, and its Razor pages call application services in-process so API middleware never runs. This is structurally a two-process problem; an in-application fix requires changing two codebases and will drift. The edge is the only shared point.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System fact: one AddRateLimiter exists, in the API process only; the AuthServer registers none. nginx limit_req_zone accepts $host and $binary_remote_addr as key components.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Script N+1 POSTs to <office>.auth.<base>/Account/Login within the configured window from one source address and assert the surplus receives the throttle status (429 if configured). Repeat against a rate-limited API path and against an arbitrary business API path. Then repeat from a second source address against a different office hostname and assert the two are counted independently. Confirm the application code was not modified to achieve this.

capability_requirements.requirement: Administrative and management surfaces (background-job dashboard, object-store console, health-check UI, database and cache ports) must not be routable from the public internet on any published hostname or port.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: CISA's directive on internet-exposed management interfaces requires removal from the internet or protection by a policy enforcement point separate from the interface itself. An in-process authorisation filter is by definition not separate from the interface. NIST SC-7 similarly requires separating management functionality and routing privileged access through a dedicated managed interface.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: CISA BOD 23-02; NIST SP 800-53 SC-7; system fact that an unauthenticated job dashboard with IgnoreAntiforgeryToken is mounted at /hangfire in the production request path.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: From a network outside the deployment, request every known administrative path (/hangfire, /health-ui, the object-store console path, and the same paths under every published hostname including the apex and the api-with-no-office-label case) over both HTTP and HTTPS. Every one must return the same terminal response as an unknown path. Then port-scan the public address and assert only 80 and 443 answer. Then verify the interface is still reachable via the documented out-of-band procedure, so the control is proven to be containment rather than breakage.

capability_requirements.requirement: Internal network reachability must be deny-by-default and documented as an explicit allowed-flow matrix; components must not be able to open connections they have no reason to make.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: All ten compose services currently share one bridge network, so the static-file container can reach SQL Server and the packet renderer can reach Redis. Segmentation of ePHI-bearing networks is an existing NIST boundary-protection control and is one of the specific changes the pending HIPAA Security Rule proposal would make mandatory. The compose-level implementation is hours of work and every violation surfaces as a connection refused.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System fact: ten compose services, one network, only the proxy publishes ports. NIST SP 800-53 SC-7. HIPAA Security Rule NPRM (proposed, not final) network segmentation provision.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Write the allowed-flow matrix first. Then, from a shell in each container, attempt a TCP connection to every other service's port (nc -zv <service> <port> across the full cross product). Assert the observed successes are exactly the matrix and nothing more. Specifically assert the static-file container reaches nothing, and the packet renderer reaches nothing but the API.

capability_requirements.requirement: The application must receive the true client address for audit logging and rate limiting without trusting an arbitrary client-supplied header.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Audit logging is a HIPAA technical safeguard standard (45 CFR 164.312(b)) and this system generates over 100 audit rows per business record; an audit trail attributing actions to the proxy's address is materially less useful. ASP.NET Core's forwarded-headers middleware trusts only known proxies by default (loopback), and the common workaround of clearing KnownProxies removes the protection entirely.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: 45 CFR 164.312(b) Audit controls; Microsoft Learn ForwardedHeadersOptions KnownProxies/KnownNetworks defaults and the warning to trust forwarded headers only from known proxies.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: From an external client send a request with a spoofed 'X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.4'. Assert the address recorded in the application's audit log is the real client address, not 1.2.3.4 and not the proxy's container address. Then confirm the configuration names the proxy explicitly in KnownProxies or KnownNetworks rather than calling Clear() on either.

capability_requirements.requirement: The health signal exposed to a load balancer must be process liveness only, and per-office database readiness must be a separate, operator-facing signal that is not evaluated on the load balancer's probe interval.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: With one database per office, 'healthy' is per-office. A probe that sweeps eleven (later thirty-three) databases at the probe interval adds a connection fan-out on top of three fifteen-minute recurring jobs that already iterate offices, and one slow office would take the whole node out of service. SHOULD rather than MUST because a correct design can also be achieved by keeping the readiness sweep cached.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System facts: 11 offices with headroom to 33, one database each; three 15-minute recurring jobs that open a connection per office; QueuePollInterval = TimeSpan.Zero already places a continuous query floor on the host database.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Stop one office's database. Assert the load balancer keeps the node in service and other offices continue to serve. Assert the operator readiness view reports that specific office as degraded within a defined interval. Then measure database connection counts with the probe running and confirm the probe contributes no per-office connections.

capability_requirements.requirement: The edge must emit HSTS, Content-Security-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options and Referrer-Policy on all responses, must restrict TLS to versions and cipher suites currently considered acceptable, and must suppress server version disclosure.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: 45 CFR 164.312(e)(1) Transmission Security is a required standard, and while its encryption specification is technically Addressable, an unencrypted or downgradeable path for ePHI is not defensible. The current template has zero add_header directives and no protocol pinning at all. These are single-line changes with no ongoing cost.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: 45 CFR 164.312(e)(1) and (e)(2)(ii); system fact that the nginx template has zero add_header directives, no ssl_protocols/ssl_ciphers pinning and no server_tokens off.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: curl -sI https://<office>.<base>/ and assert each header is present with a sane value. Run a TLS scanner (e.g. testssl.sh) against each published hostname and assert no protocol below TLS 1.2 negotiates and no known-weak cipher suite is offered. Assert the Server response header carries no version. If HSTS preloading is adopted, verify every subdomain serves valid HTTPS first, because preloading is deliberately slow to undo.

capability_requirements.requirement: The object-store hostname must expose only the S3 API surface; its administrative console must not be routable, and the application must authenticate with a scoped credential rather than the root credential.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: The object store holds appointment documents and packets, is reachable from the public internet at a dedicated hostname, and the application authenticates as root. A root credential in an internet-adjacent application is a single-credential compromise of every object across every office. An external partner already holds correctly scoped credentials, which proves scoping is available and in use.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System facts: MinIO reachable at minio.<base>, path-style addressing, application authenticates as root, an external partner holds scoped credentials against a separate bucket with listing deliberately withheld.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: From an external network, request the console path and any admin API path on the object-store hostname and assert a terminal response. Then, using the application's own credential, attempt an administrative operation (create a user, list all buckets) and assert denial, while a normal object get/put on the application bucket succeeds. Confirm the root credential appears in no running container's environment.

capability_requirements.requirement: Office slugs must be validated against a reserved-label list at provisioning time, covering at minimum the labels used for depth routing, the reserved host scope, and protocol-well-known labels.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Because tenancy is the leftmost DNS label and the edge distinguishes products by intermediate labels, an office slug colliding with a routing label creates ambiguity between a tenant and a product route. 'admin' is already reserved for host scope; the same reasoning applies to api, auth, minio, www, mail, static and _acme-challenge, and the check is cheap to add at the point of provisioning.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System facts: {office}.<base>, {office}.api.<base>, {office}.auth.<base>, minio.<base> exact, admin reserved for host scope. Microsoft's multitenant domain-name guidance on namespace management and first-come naming.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Attempt to provision offices named api, auth, minio, admin, www, mail, static, localhost and _acme-challenge. Each must be rejected with a clear message at the point of entry, not after partial provisioning. Then attempt a slug with an uppercase letter, a trailing hyphen, a Unicode character and a 64-character length, and assert each is rejected or normalised deterministically.

capability_requirements.requirement: Upstream addresses must not be resolved once at proxy start; the edge must re-resolve backend names so that a rebuilt backend container is reached without recreating the proxy.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: nginx resolves a literal upstream name at worker start and a variable form via the resolver. Only the object-store block currently has the resolver-plus-variable fix, so every other backend rebuild silently routes to a stale container IP. This is a documented operational trap that has already broken the stack, and it fails as a 502 rather than a wrong answer, which is the good kind of failure but still an outage.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: nginx ngx_http_proxy_module documentation on variables in proxy_pass and resolver; system fact that only the minio block has the resolver + variable proxy_pass fix.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: With traffic flowing, docker compose up -d --force-recreate a backend so it obtains a new container IP, and without touching the proxy assert that requests succeed within the resolver's TTL. Repeat for each backend. Then inspect the proxy configuration and assert every proxy_pass uses a variable and a resolver directive is present with an explicit valid= TTL.

capability_requirements.requirement: The tenant-resolution surface must be reduced to Host alone, verified empirically, or the edge must strip every alternative tenant selector.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: The brief records honestly that whether ABP's four __tenant resolvers are disabled has never been tested. ABP registers query-string, route, header and cookie resolvers plus a current-user resolver; what neutralises them in the stock domain path is that the framework's domain contributor sets Handled unconditionally, which is the subject of an open framework issue. If the custom contributor sets Handled only on a match, __tenant is a live tenant selector on every endpoint.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: ABP AbpAspNetCoreMultiTenancyModule source (four resolvers, __tenant key); ABP issue #7968 (Handled set unconditionally); system fact that this has never been tested.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Authenticate as a user of office A. Then issue the same request four ways against office A's hostname: with ?__tenant=<office B id>; with an X-Tenant/__tenant header; with a __tenant cookie; and against the reserved admin hostname with ?__tenant=<office B id>. In every case assert the data returned belongs to office A (or the request is refused). If any returns office B's data, the edge must strip that carrier and the application must remove the resolver. Total time: about fifteen minutes.

anti_requirements: The platform MUST NOT rewrite, normalise, lowercase-collapse, canonicalise, strip the port from, or synthesise the HTTP Host header on its way to the application. This excludes any component whose Host handling is not configurable, and it means the default configuration of several major product classes (nginx as shipped, Apache mod_proxy as shipped, Kong, API-gateway products that substitute the service URL host, CDN origin definitions that require an origin host) is disqualifying until explicitly changed and tested.

The platform MUST NOT require any per-tenant configuration entry  -  no per-office DNS record, no per-office certificate or SAN, no per-office listener rule, no per-office backend, no per-office firewall rule. Anything that does converts office onboarding from a host-UI action back into a deployment and destroys the property the business growth model depends on.
The platform MUST NOT terminate TLS in a component that cannot be proven to preserve Host, because a TLS terminator is by definition also an HTTP parser and re-emitter.

No caching layer may store any response to an authenticated request, and no caching layer may be introduced whose cache key can be configured to omit the full host. A cache that keys on path alone across office hostnames produces a cross-tenant PHI disclosure that returns HTTP 200 and logs nothing anywhere.

The application MUST NOT be configured to process X-Forwarded-Host, and MUST NOT clear KnownProxies/KnownNetworks to make forwarded headers work. In this application X-Forwarded-Host is a tenant selector, not a hint.

No administrative, management or diagnostic interface may be published on a hostname or port reachable from the public internet  -  including the job dashboard, the object-store console, the health-check UI, database ports and the cache port. Authorisation inside the interface does not satisfy this; the enforcement point must be a separate component.

The platform MUST NOT require sticky sessions or session affinity. This system has no SignalR, no WebSockets and no server-side session affinity requirement; accepting affinity because a platform offers it introduces a constraint the application does not have and a cookie the application does not control. The reverse proxy's dead WebSocket upgrade config referencing a non-existent hub should be deleted rather than carried forward as evidence of a requirement.

The platform MUST NOT be adopted on the strength of a health check that succeeds only because tenant resolution is not enforced on the health path. A probe that passes today because /health happens to sit before the multi-tenancy middleware will start failing the moment that middleware ordering changes, and nothing will connect the two events.

No component may be introduced that routes on SNI while the application resolves tenancy from Host, unless it also enforces that the two agree. Divergent SNI and Host is the definition of virtual host confusion and it is currently impossible by construction because there is one terminator; do not give that away.

The certificate strategy MUST NOT enumerate office names in the SAN list of publicly trusted certificates. Every publicly trusted certificate is logged to Certificate Transparency, so per-office SANs publish the client list of a healthcare business to anyone who queries a CT log. Wildcards publish only the wildcard name.

The platform MUST NOT require the application to be reachable by bare IP address as a condition of operation (for probes, for internal service discovery, or for a management agent), because a bare IP request is precisely the request this application is designed to refuse.

No component may be placed in the path that maintains long-lived pooled connections to the backend shared across different office hostnames without re-sending the correct Host per request, because a front-end/back-end disagreement about request boundaries on such a connection lets a smuggled request prefix be attributed to a different office.

not_recommended.pattern: Putting a CDN or global edge network in front of the application
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It is close to universal at scale and for good reasons: TLS termination near the user, absorption of volumetric attacks, an integrated WAF and bot management, free static-asset offload for an SPA that is nothing but static files, and a single place to add security response headers. It would also give the team a managed edge they do not have to patch, which matters when there are two developers and no on-call rotation. For a pure-static Angular SPA it is genuinely the textbook answer.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: The user population is staff at Californian practices; there is no latency or volume problem to solve, so the benefit is close to zero. Against that sits the only failure mode in this entire analysis that is simultaneously catastrophic, silent, and a HIPAA breach: a cache in the path of a Host-keyed multi-tenant application. Cache keys vary by product and by backend type  -  the same vendor uses the full request URI for one backend class and the URI without host for another  -  and the mitigation (Cache-Control: private/no-store on everything user-specific) depends on 52 controllers getting it right, which nobody has audited. A wrong cache key returns office B's authenticated response to office A with HTTP 200 and no error in any log. This team will not notice slow degradation, and this is worse than slow degradation: it is correct-looking output. Separately, several CDN origin definitions require an origin host header and substitute it by default, which breaks tenancy outright.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: When the SPA is served from a hostname that is provably distinct from every hostname that carries authenticated API or auth traffic, so the cache can never see a credentialed response; and when someone on the team can state, unprompted, what the cache key is and what Vary does to it. At that point putting a CDN in front of the static origin only  -  and never in front of the API or AuthServer  -  is reasonable.

not_recommended.pattern: An API gateway in front of the application for centralised rate limiting and policy
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: This is the most tempting rejection on the list, because it addresses the real structural problem correctly. Rate limiting is currently a two-process problem: the AuthServer registers no limiter at all and its Razor pages call application services in-process, so no API middleware ever runs for sign-in. A gateway sits in front of both processes and applies one policy to both. It would also give quotas for the partner integration path, a place to terminate the partner's token, and a coherent story for future public APIs. 'Put a gateway in front of it' is the correct instinct about the shape of the problem.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: The instinct is right and the component is wrong. The product class defaults to rewriting Host  -  one major gateway's preserve_host defaults to false, substituting the configured service host, and another overrides Host with the API's service-URL host unless an inbound policy is added  -  so the out-of-the-box configuration of the category breaks tenancy, and the failure would appear as 'Tenant not found' on every request, which at least fails obviously, but only after the gateway is already adopted. More decisively, gateways are stateful components with their own datastore, their own upgrade cadence and their own configuration model, which is a third system for two people to operate. The identical capability  -  one enforcement point traversed by both processes, keyed per client and per office hostname  -  already exists in the reverse proxy they run, as limit_req zones keyed on $binary_remote_addr and $host, at a few hours of work and no new component.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: When there are genuinely external API consumers requiring quotas, key management and per-consumer analytics  -  more than the one partner integration that already has a durable outbox and a token this application issues  -  or when the number of backing services grows past what a hand-maintained proxy configuration can express.

not_recommended.pattern: Kubernetes with an ingress controller, and/or a service mesh with sidecar mTLS
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It is the default answer for containerised multi-service systems and delivers things this system genuinely lacks: rolling deploys instead of manual SSH, health-check-driven replacement instead of a human noticing, declarative configuration instead of a compose file edited in place, secrets management instead of one mode-600 file, and  -  for the mesh  -  encrypted, authenticated, policy-controlled service-to-service traffic, which is the cleanest available answer to the network-segmentation control that the pending HIPAA Security Rule proposal would make mandatory. The current single-VM, single-instance, manually-deployed arrangement is genuinely fragile and this class of platform is the standard cure.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It takes the number of independent HTTP parsers between client and application from one to three or four (cloud load balancer, ingress controller, sidecar, application), each with its own Host and SNI semantics, in a system where a single Host rewrite is a total outage. It makes the health-probe Host problem mandatory rather than optional, because kubelet probes default to the Pod IP as Host and the documentation explicitly tells you to set the Host header in httpHeaders when the pod relies on virtual hosts  -  a step that will be forgotten once and diagnosed for a day. The mesh's automatic derivation of upstream SNI from the downstream Host/authority header is an elegant property in a service mesh and a hazardous one when Host is the tenant selector, because it couples wire-level certificate validation to a client-supplied header. And the arithmetic is decisive: 120-250 hours to a defensible state plus 15-30 hours a month of upgrade work, against roughly one developer-week a month already partly committed to code-standard remediation. There is one application instance and no scaling pressure; none of the benefits are actually being bought.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: When a second application instance is genuinely required  -  which for this workload means the three 15-minute office-iterating jobs or the packet renderer, not user traffic  -  AND a person exists who has operated a cluster in production before. Not one without the other.

not_recommended.pattern: Per-office DNS records and per-office TLS certificates instead of wildcards
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It gives a smaller blast radius per certificate, per-office revocation without touching anyone else, no single wildcard private key whose compromise covers every practice, and it is what security guidance often prefers on principle  -  wildcards are frequently discouraged precisely because one key covers everything. It also makes each office's exposure explicit and auditable rather than implicit in a wildcard.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It converts 'add an office' from a host-UI action into a deployment, destroying the property that makes the business model work  -  and it does so quietly, because the first few offices will be added by hand without anyone noticing that a threshold has been crossed. It multiplies renewal failure modes by 33 under a regime where maximum lifetimes drop to 200 days in March 2026, 100 days in 2027 and 47 days in 2029; thirty-three certificates renewing every 47 days is roughly 250 renewal events a year for a two-person team with no certificate automation today. And every publicly trusted certificate is logged to Certificate Transparency, so per-office SANs publish the practice names of a healthcare vendor's entire client list to anyone who queries a CT log  -  an information disclosure a customer might reasonably object to, and one that wildcards avoid entirely.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: When offices bring their own domains, which forces per-domain validation and certificates anyway and brings the dangling-DNS/subdomain-takeover problem with it. At that point the per-domain machinery must exist regardless, and the argument reverses.

not_recommended.pattern: A third-party WAF operating in hosted reverse-proxy mode
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: OWASP Core Rule Set coverage, virtual patching for a framework the team cannot patch quickly, bot and credential-stuffing protection at the exact endpoint that currently has no rate limiter, and a compliance checkbox that healthcare customers and their auditors ask about directly. The current edge has no WAF, no bot protection and no request inspection of any kind, and that is a real gap.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: In hosted reverse-proxy mode it is another TLS terminator and another HTTP parser holding PHI in flight, run by a third party who becomes a business associate, and it is another component with its own Host semantics in a path where Host is load-bearing. The capability is worth having; the topology is not. Running the rule set as a module inside the existing proxy keeps the hop count and the terminator count at one and keeps PHI inside the deployment. Even then, deploying a rule set in blocking mode against a document-upload workflow with no staging environment  -  this system has exactly one environment  -  is a self-inflicted outage waiting to happen, so it belongs in detection-only mode first, with a period of log review before anything blocks.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: When a second environment exists to tune rules against, or when a customer contract makes an attested managed WAF a condition of sale  -  at which point the business-associate agreement and the extra terminator are a cost of doing business rather than an engineering choice.

not_recommended.pattern: Enabling ASP.NET Core forwarded-headers processing with the full header set, including X-Forwarded-Host
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It is the documented, officially recommended step when hosting behind a reverse proxy, and it is genuinely needed: without X-Forwarded-Proto the application treats the backend connection as plain HTTP, which is the most common cause of infinite HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect loops and of cookies issued without the secure flag. Every tutorial, every sample and Microsoft's own documentation walk you into this. Adding all three headers 'because we're behind a proxy' is the obvious, well-intentioned move.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: X-Forwarded-Host sets HttpContext.Request.Host, which is exactly what the tenant resolver reads. Enabling it hands every client a tenant selector in a header. The application is safe today only by accident, because the default ForwardedHeaders value is None and the middleware must be explicitly enabled; the danger is the standard recipe, compounded by the standard workaround for forwarded headers not working in Docker, which is to call KnownProxies.Clear() and KnownNetworks.Clear()  -  the middleware's default trusted set is loopback only, so it appears not to work behind a container proxy, and clearing it removes the only guard. Microsoft's own advisory for CVE-2018-0787 describes precisely this failure shape as an elevation of privilege. Enable XForwardedFor and XForwardedProto; never XForwardedHost; and name the proxy explicitly in KnownProxies rather than clearing the list.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: Never for this application while Host determines the database. If tenancy ever moves to a signed token claim as the sole authority, X-Forwarded-Host becomes an ordinary informational header again.

not_recommended.pattern: Consolidating the AuthServer onto a single office-agnostic hostname to fix subdomain-scoped identity
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: This is a real and recurring pain, not a hypothetical: identity is per-database, the same email can hold a host account and an office account with separate password hashes, and password reset and login are subdomain-scoped, which the brief records as having generated actual support incidents. A single sign-in hostname would give one cookie domain, one password-reset flow, one place to reason about session state, and would remove a whole category of support ticket.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: Within this area it must be rejected because it moves tenancy off Host for the one process where the tenant determines which identity database is opened. If sign-in happens at a single hostname, the AuthServer must learn the office from somewhere else  -  a __tenant parameter, a selector page, an email-domain lookup  -  and every one of those re-opens the resolver surface the current design closes by construction, at the most security-sensitive endpoint in the system. Doing it would also invalidate the edge allowlist as a tenancy control, since one hostname would legitimately serve all offices.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: It is a genuine cross-area decision, not a settled no, and it should be escalated to the identity workstream rather than decided here. It becomes viable if identity is unified into a single directory with tenant membership as an attribute rather than a database boundary  -  but that is a change to the tenancy model itself, and the tenancy model is the thing this system is built on.

surprises: nginx does not preserve the Host header by default  -  the documented default is literally `proxy_set_header Host $proxy_host`, i.e. it substitutes the upstream's name. The current stack works only because someone wrote an explicit Host directive. And the inheritance rule makes this a live hazard rather than a historical one: proxy_set_header directives are inherited from the parent level ONLY IF no proxy_set_header exists at the current level, so adding a single unrelated header inside one location block silently drops the Host line for that location alone. One innocuous edit, one route's tenancy broken, and the other routes keep working  -  the worst possible diagnostic signature.

The reverse-proxy product classes split, and the split does not follow reputation. HAProxy, Traefik and Envoy preserve the client Host by default. nginx, Apache mod_proxy (ProxyPreserveHost Off), Kong (preserve_host false) and Azure API Management (overrides with the service-URL host) rewrite by default. Two of the three most likely 'obvious' choices are on the wrong side, and in every case the fix is one setting  -  which means the risk is not that it cannot be done but that nobody knows to check.

Every mainstream health-probe default sends exactly the request this application refuses. AWS ALB sends the target's private IP as Host, with no configurable override anywhere in the health-check settings. AWS NLB sends the load balancer node's IP and listener port. Azure Application Gateway's default probe sends Host: 127.0.0.1. Google Cloud uses the forwarding rule's IP unless --host is given. Kubernetes defaults to the Pod IP. This is not an edge case to design around later; it is a platform-selection filter that must be applied on day one, and on at least one major platform the answer is that it cannot be configured at all and the application must change.

Three layers use three different wildcard rules and they disagree with each other. A TLS wildcard matches exactly one label and only as the complete leftmost label (RFC 9525 6.3), so *.<base> does not cover office.api.<base>. An nginx server_name wildcard matches several labels  -  the documentation's own example is that *.example.org matches www.sub.example.org  -  which is precisely why api.<base> with no office label falls through to the SPA today. A DNS wildcard also matches multiple labels, but conditionally. Three layers, three rules, one mental model in the team's head.

The certificate you need can break the hostnames it is for. RFC 4592 2.2.1 shows that an empty non-terminal blocks wildcard synthesis: a query for _telnet._tcp.host1.example gets no wildcard answer 'because _tcp.host1.example. exists (without data)'. The DNS-01 challenge required to obtain a *.api.<base> certificate places a TXT record at _acme-challenge.api.<base>, which creates the empty non-terminal api.<base>. If the zone relies on *.<base> to synthesise office.api.<base> and no *.api.<base> wildcard exists, setting up the certificate makes every office's API hostname stop resolving  -  all of them, at once, at renewal time. This is my inference from a verified RFC rule rather than an observed incident, and it is exactly the kind of thing that is invisible until the night it happens.

HTTP/2 connection coalescing means browsers will deliberately send office B's requests down office A's connection. Because one wildcard certificate covers many office hostnames resolving to one IP, a browser is entitled to reuse the connection, and nginx correctly answers 421 Misdirected Request with the log line 'client attempted to request the server name different from that one was negotiated'. Browsers are supposed to retry on a fresh connection; historically some have not. The population most likely to trigger this is staff who cover several practices and keep several office tabs open  -  i.e. the exact usage pattern this product is for.

What actually disables ABP's four __tenant resolvers is not a configuration choice but a framework quirk: DomainTenantResolveContributor sets context.Handled = true unconditionally, whether or not the domain matched, which short-circuits the resolver loop  -  the subject of an open ABP issue. If the custom HostAware contributor sets Handled only on a successful match, all four resolvers (query string, route, header, cookie) are live, and ?__tenant= is a tenant selector on every endpoint in the system. This is a fifteen-minute curl test that has never been run, and its answer changes what the edge configuration has to do.

ABP's core module also contributes CurrentUserTenantResolveContributor, so for an authenticated request the tenant claim in the token participates in resolution alongside the Host. 'Host header only' is most defensible as a statement about anonymous requests; for authenticated traffic the relationship between the hostname a request arrived on and the database it reaches is worth establishing empirically rather than assuming  -  particularly given 15-minute access tokens and a DataProtection keyring shared between two processes.

X-Forwarded-Host is a tenant selector in this application, and the team is one well-intentioned commit away from enabling it. ASP.NET Core's forwarded-headers middleware sets HttpContext.Request.Host from X-Forwarded-Host, which is what the tenant resolver reads. It is safe today only because the middleware defaults to ForwardedHeaders.None and must be explicitly turned on  -  but turning it on is the documented step for hosting behind a proxy, and the most-copied fix for it not working in containers is to clear KnownProxies, which removes the loopback-only trust that would otherwise contain it. Microsoft's own advisory CVE-2018-0787 describes this exact shape as an elevation-of-privilege condition.

The number of edge routing rules is four and does not grow with office count  -  SPA wildcard, API wildcard, Auth wildcard, object-store exact. Every office hostname reaches the same three processes; the office is chosen inside the application. This means the edge never needs per-tenant configuration, which is why adding an office is currently a host-UI action, and it means the correct first filter on any platform candidate is 'does this preserve wildcard-only configuration' rather than anything about throughput or availability. Several platform choices would quietly convert office onboarding back into a deployment, and nobody would notice until the fifth office.

The practice's identity is broadcast in cleartext on every connection. The office slug is the leftmost DNS label, so it appears in DNS queries and in the TLS SNI extension, both unencrypted. Encrypted Client Hello would fix this but is not reliably deployable on self-hosted edges in 2026. Anyone on the network path learns which medical practice a browser is talking to. This is not PHI and probably not a HIPAA violation, but it is a disclosure a covered-entity customer may ask about, and it is a direct argument for wildcard certificates over per-office ones, since per-office SANs additionally publish the entire client list to Certificate Transparency logs.

The absence of default_server on 443 is not a routing quirk, it is the textbook precondition for origin confusion. nginx documents that unmatched Host values go to the default server for the port, and that without an explicit default_server the default is the first server block. The virtual-host-confusion literature identifies exactly this  -  'fallback to the host marked as default, or the first one otherwise'  -  as the exploitable end state. The observed symptom (the bare apex reaching the AuthServer) is the mechanism working as designed, pointed at the wrong target.

Host header parsing is measurably unreliable across implementations, which matters more here than almost anywhere. The CCS 2016 'Host of Troubles' work found 21 of 33 HTTP implementations did not normalise requests sufficiently when forwarding them, using duplicate Host headers, space-surrounded Host headers and absolute-URI request targets  -  and that around 97% of users behind transparent caches were exposed to cache poisoning as a result. In a normal application, a Host parsing disagreement yields a poisoned link. Here it selects a database.

A next-generation firewall between the proxy and the backend can break this design in a way no amount of proxy configuration will fix: Microsoft documents that such firewalls may verify that the HTTP Host header resolves to the target IP address, which for a preserved public hostname it will not, requiring split-horizon DNS so the hostname resolves differently from the firewall's vantage point. If a future platform includes an inspecting firewall on the internal path, this becomes a DNS architecture problem rather than a proxy problem, and it is not discoverable from any proxy documentation.

Fixing the job dashboard in code does not satisfy the strongest published guidance on the problem. CISA's directive on internet-exposed management interfaces asks for the interface to be removed from the internet or protected by a policy enforcement point separate from the interface itself  -  and an in-process authorisation filter is, definitionally, not separate from the interface. The cheapest compliant answer here is also the simplest: do not route the path at the edge at all, and reach it by an SSH local port forward, where the SSH daemon is the separate enforcement point. Zero new components, zero new credentials, and it fails obviously.
what_would_change_the_answer: The result of the fifteen-minute __tenant resolver test. If query-string, header, route or cookie resolvers turn out to be live, the edge must additionally strip those carriers on every request and the application must remove the resolvers  -  a materially uglier configuration, and one that changes the Host allowlist from a defence-in-depth measure into the primary control.

Whether the AuthServer's identity model is consolidated onto a single office-agnostic hostname to fix the subdomain-scoped login incidents. That decision belongs to the identity workstream, but if it lands, sign-in stops being Host-scoped, the edge allowlist stops being a tenancy control for that process, and this entire area needs re-deriving for the auth path.

Whether any office is ever permitted to bring its own domain. Custom domains force per-domain validation, per-domain certificates, and the dangling-DNS/subdomain-takeover problem, which reverses the argument against per-office certificate machinery and makes automated domain-ownership verification a hard requirement.

Whether a second application instance becomes necessary. Today everything is single-instance with no sticky-session requirement (no SignalR, no WebSockets), which keeps the edge trivial. A second instance introduces real health-check-driven routing, which is where the Host-on-probe problem stops being avoidable, and it strengthens the case for options that were rejected on complexity grounds.

Whether the HIPAA Security Rule NPRM is finalised. As of mid-2026 there is no final rule and no compliance clock. If mandatory network segmentation, mandatory encryption and the removal of the 'addressable' category are finalised, the internal segmentation requirement moves from prudent to compelled and the timeline stops being the team's to choose.

Whether real PHI is loaded before the network changes land. Every record is synthetic today, which means the Host-allowlist tests, the cross-tenant probes, the smuggling checks and the cache-key experiments can be run destructively against production. That freedom ends the moment the first practice takes a real booking, and several of the tests in this analysis are much harder to justify afterwards.

Whether the office count actually approaches 33 or stops near 11. It changes nothing about the edge, which is four rules either way  -  but it changes the per-office fan-out arithmetic for anything that iterates offices, including any readiness endpoint tempted to sweep all databases on a probe interval.

Whether the DNS provider exposes an automatable API scoped to TXT records. If it does not, DNS-01 automation for the per-depth wildcards is not possible, wildcard certificates become a manual quarterly (soon monthly) chore, and the certificate-lifetime schedule turns that into the single most likely cause of a future outage  -  which would force reconsidering per-office certificates or an externally managed certificate service despite the arguments against both.

QTYPE=TXT ... the answer will be "foo.bar.example. results.claim: [28] The DNS-01 TXT at _acme-challenge.api.<base> creates the empty non-terminal api.<base>, which becomes the closest encloser for office.api.<base> and blocks synthesis from *.<base>
results.evidence_quote: Cited URL 503. The underlying rule is confirmed at rfc-editor.org RFC 4592 s2.2.1 ('_tcp.host1.example. exists (without data)' blocks synthesis). The specific ACME scenario is nowhere in RFC 4592.
results.correction: Reachability aside, this is an inference the RFC does not make and it is stated more absolutely than it holds. The rule is right (an empty non-terminal at api.<base> blocks *.<base> from synthesising office.api.<base>), but two qualifiers are missing: (a) the ENT is created by ANY descendant record under api.<base>, so in practice a deployment already serving office.api.<base> will normally already have such records  -  the ACME TXT is one cause among many, not the cause; (b) the effect is scoped to the zone that is authoritative for <base>, and disappears the moment a wildcard or explicit record exists at api.<base>. Present it as a modelled failure mode to test in the zone, not an observed behaviour. Cite the canonical rfc-editor.org URL.

Two sub-claims are not: this file contains no '__tenant' literal (the default key lives in MultiTenancyConsts / TenantResolverConsts), and it does not register CurrentUserTenantResolveContributor (that comes from AbpMultiTenancyModule, a separate file). Also note this is the 'dev' branch  -  a moving target; pin to a tag or commit SHA so the citation stays valid, since the whole design decision rests on this registration list.

results.claim: [35] ABP DomainTenantResolveContributor sets context.Handled = true unconditionally, exiting the resolver loop early and preventing subsequent contributors from running
results.evidence_quote: Title: 'DomainTenantResolveContributor will affect other TenantResolveContributor'. Body: the contributor sets 'context.Handled = true' even when extractResult.IsMatch is false, causing the resolver loop to exit prematurely. Issue status: Closed.
results.correction: The issue says exactly what the claim says it says  -  but it is a CLOSED issue, and the page shows no fix or PR link. The claim asserts this as ABP's current runtime behaviour, which the issue cannot establish: a closed bug report is evidence the behaviour was reported, not that it persists. Before relying on 'the domain resolver neutralises the __tenant resolvers', read the current DomainTenantResolveContributor source at a pinned commit and confirm whether Handled is still set unconditionally, or verify empirically by sending ?__tenant= against a domain-resolver deployment. Note also that if the behaviour was fixed, the design premise inverts: the __tenant query/route/header/cookie selectors would still be live and would need explicit removal or edge stripping.

results.claim: [36] Host header bypass techniques: absolute URLs in the request line, duplicate Host headers, line-wrapped/indented headers, and override headers X-Forwarded-Host, X-Host, X-Forwarded-Server, X-HTTP-Host-Override, Forwarded; routing-based SSRF misroutes via intermediaries
results.evidence_quote: All five override headers listed verbatim (X-Forwarded-Host, X-Host, X-Forwarded-Server, X-HTTP-Host-Override, Forwarded). Duplicate Host: 'it is common for one of the two headers to be given precedence over the other one.' Line wrapping: 'Some servers will interpret the indented header as a wrapped line'. Routing-based SSRF: intermediaries can be made to 'misroute requests to an arbitrary system of the attacker's choice'.

results.claim: [37] OWASP WSTG instructs validating the Host header on every incoming request and rejecting unexpected hostnames, and lists the impacts (first virtual host, redirect to attacker domain, cache poisoning, password reset, internal virtual hosts)
results.evidence_quote: Impacts confirmed: 'Dispatch requests to the first virtual host on the list', 'Perform a redirect to an attacker-controlled domain', 'Perform web cache poisoning', 'Manipulate password reset functionality', 'Allow access to virtual hosts that were not intended to be externally accessible'.
results.correction: The impacts list is confirmed verbatim. The remediation half is not: WSTG-INPV-17 is a testing procedure and contains no instruction to 'validate the Host header on every incoming request and reject unexpected hostnames'. Attributing that prescription to OWASP from this page overstates it  -  either drop the attribution and state the control in your own voice, or cite a source that actually prescribes it (e.g. the OWASP Cheat Sheet Series, or CVE-2018-0787's mitigation text already cited at claim 32).

results.claim: [38] Academic measurement: 21 of 33 HTTP implementations did not normalise requests sufficiently when forwarding upstream; ~97% of users served by transparent caches were subject to cache-poisoning
results.evidence_quote: dl.acm.org returned HTTP 403 Forbidden to automated retrieval; no abstract or body could be read. No verbatim text was obtained for either the 21-of-33 figure or the ~97% figure.
results.correction: Neither number is verified. dl.acm.org is paywalled/bot-blocked, so this DOI cannot serve as a checkable citation in the deliverable. Either cite an openly retrievable copy of the paper (the CCS 2016 'Host of Troubles' author PDF) and re-verify both figures against its abstract and evaluation section, or drop the two statistics and keep only the qualitative point  -  that deployed HTTP implementations disagree on Host header parsing  -  which is independently supported by claim 36's PortSwigger material. results.claim: [39] Virtual host confusion arises from unauthenticated routing data (IP, port, SNI, Host); unmatched Host falls back to default/first vhost; TLS sessions/tickets can be resumed across vhosts unless the server name is bound into the ticket; mitigations are strict Host/SNI consistency and block-by-default routing
results.evidence_quote: 'Since target IP address and port are not authenticated by TLS, if an attacker can redirect the victim's traffic, it can steal its request with cookies and other important information.' 'a previously opened TLS session with one virtual host can be resumed with the other virtual host'. Mitigations listed are Tempesta FW features: http_chain (no implicit fallback), http_strict_host_checking, block-by-default, and server name + client IP embedded into TLS tickets.
results.correction: The mechanism and the TLS-ticket resumption point are supported, but this is a vendor knowledge-base page and the 'mitigations' it lists are that vendor's own product features (http_chain, http_strict_host_checking, ticket binding), not neutral guidance. Use it as evidence of the behaviour class only; state the mitigations as capability requirements in your own voice (strict Host/SNI consistency check, explicit terminal default route, server-name-bound session tickets) rather than as a cited recommendation, and prefer a neutral source for the routing guidance if one is available.

results.claim: [40] Request smuggling exploits front-end/back-end disagreement about request boundaries; the front end commonly reuses the same connection, so part of an attacker's request is treated as the start of the next request and prepended to it
results.evidence_quote: 'When the front-end server forwards HTTP requests to a back-end server, it typically sends several requests over the same back-end network connection' ... 'The attacker causes part of their front-end request to be interpreted by the back-end server as the start of the next request. It is effectively prepended to the next request, and so can interfere with the way the application processes that request.'

results.claim: [41] Istio sidecars enable auto_sni and auto_san_validation by default, deriving upstream SNI from the downstream Host/authority when no explicit SNI is set in a DestinationRule
results.evidence_quote: The page was retrieved successfully and contains NO mention of auto_sni, auto_san_validation, default-enablement, or SNI derivation from the downstream host/authority header. It covers sidecar and gateway TLS configuration concepts only.
results.correction: This is asserted entirely from memory against a page that does not discuss it. In Istio these behaviours are controlled by istiod feature flags (ENABLE_AUTO_SNI and ENABLE_AUTO_SAN_VALIDATION), whose defaults have changed across releases  -  so 'enabled by default' is version-dependent and cannot be stated flatly for 2026. If the design depends on upstream SNI tracking the client Host, cite the istiod configuration/feature-flag reference for the specific Istio version in use and verify empirically; otherwise remove the claim. Treating SNI-follows-Host as a given is a live failure mode for the mTLS and certificate-matching requirements.

results.claim: [42] nginx stream ssl_preread extracts SNI without terminating TLS, exposing $ssl_preread_server_name; not built by default (--with-stream_ssl_preread_module); cannot be used on a listener with the ssl parameter
results.evidence_quote: 'allows extracting information from the ClientHello message without terminating SSL/TLS, for example, the server name requested through SNI'; 'This module is not built by default, it should be enabled with the --with-stream_ssl_preread_module configuration parameter.'; '$ssl_preread_server_name  -  server name requested through SNI'. Full page text checked: no statement about the listen ssl parameter.
results.correction: The first three parts are confirmed verbatim. The incompatibility clause is not documented on this page  -  nginx nowhere states that ssl_preread 'cannot be used on a listener with the ssl parameter'. It is a true consequence of the design (preread inspects the raw ClientHello at the preread phase, before any TLS termination the ssl parameter would perform) but it is an inference, not a documented limit. State it as a mechanism consequence, or verify it against a configuration test, rather than presenting it as a documented constraint.

results.claim: [43] CISA BOD 23-02 requires FCEB agencies to remove internet-exposed networked management interfaces or protect them with Zero Trust capabilities implementing a policy enforcement point separate from the interface itself, within 14 days of discovery
results.evidence_quote: cisa.gov returned HTTP 403 Forbidden to every automated retrieval attempted (WebFetch and curl with a browser User-Agent, on the directive page, the implementation-guidance page, and the 508c PDF). No text could be read.

results.claim: [44] NIST SP 800-53 SC-7 Boundary Protection requires monitoring/control at external and key internal boundaries, physical or logical separation of publicly accessible components, and external connection only through managed interfaces
results.evidence_quote: The URL returned HTTP 202 with a bot-challenge interstitial ('/.well-known/sgcaptcha/'), serving no control text; the r5 path was likewise unreadable. No SC-7 text was retrieved.

Control-enhancement numbering under SC-7 differs between the revisions, so an r4 citation cannot support statements about Rev 5 enhancements (and the claim's own caveat concedes the enhancement numbers were never checked). Cite the authoritative NIST source for Rev 5 (csrc.nist.gov SP 800-53 Rev. 5 / the OSCAL catalog) and quote SC-7 and the specific enhancements (e.g. SC-7(a)-(c) and the management-interface-related enhancements) directly.

results.evidence_quote: The HTML URL 302-redirects automated fetchers to unblock.federalregister.gov and serves no document. results.claim: [47] Microsoft multitenant domain-name guidance: wildcard DNS per subdomain; all web components must handle each tenant's Host header; rewriting Host 'can cause other problems'; validate domain ownership before onboarding; dangling DNS/subdomain takeover; CAA records
results.evidence_quote: 'Use wildcard Domain Name System (DNS) entries to simplify the management of subdomains ... create a wildcard entry for *.contoso.com'. 'All web components within Contoso's European deployment must know how to handle requests that include Fabrikam's domain name in their Host request header.' 'However, rewriting a Host header can cause other problems.' 'You must validate the ownership of custom domains before you onboard them.' Section 'Dangling DNS and subdomain takeover attacks'.
