results.claim: [48] HSTS preload eligibility requires max-age >= 31536000, includeSubDomains, preload, HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect on the apex, and every subdomain serving valid HTTPS; removal is slow (request, review, queue, stable browser release  -  months)
results.evidence_quote: 'The max-age must be at least 31536000 seconds (1 year).' 'The includeSubDomains directive must be specified.' 'The preload directive must be specified.' 'Redirect from HTTP to HTTPS on the same host, if you are listening on port 80.' 'Serve all subdomains over HTTPS...' Removal: 'Domains can be removed, but it takes months for a change to reach users with a Chrome update and we cannot make guarantees about other browsers.'
results.correction: Every threshold is confirmed; two details are embellished. The redirect requirement is worded 'from HTTP to HTTPS on the same host, if you are listening on port 80'  -  it is conditional on listening on port 80 and is not specifically about the apex. And the removal process is not described as a 'request, review, queue, and a stable browser release'; the site says only that removal is possible but 'takes months' to reach users via a Chrome update, with no guarantees for other browsers. The operational conclusion (preload is effectively one-way on a months timescale) stands; trim the invented procedural detail.

results.claim: [49] ECH is not reliably deployable on self-hosted edges as of 2026: browser support broadly default-on, self-hosted server support for ECH key generation and DNS publication limited; public TLS endpoints still expose the hostname in cleartext
results.evidence_quote: URL resolves: -12 is the current version, an Active Internet-Draft (individual submission) dated 6 July 2026, expiring 6 January 2027, carrying 'no formal IETF endorsement'. The document contains no browser-adoption data, no deployment statistics, and no server-side ECH key-generation or DNS-publication implementation status. Nearest text: 'Some client software (such as web browsers) may offer configuration options to disable ECH'.
results.correction: The URL is live and the draft is current, but it supports none of the three assertions. It is an individual-submission draft about enterprise operational impacts of ECH, not a deployment-status survey; it states no browser support level and nothing about self-hosted server support. Also note the status caveat the draft itself carries  -  an expired-in-January-2027 individual I-D with no IETF endorsement is weak evidence for a 2026 capability statement. If the SNI-exposure point matters, support it from RFC 8446/RFC 9525-adjacent material (SNI is sent in the cleartext ClientHello) and verify ECH server-side availability against the specific edge software's release notes. As written, 'browser support is broadly default-on' is unsourced.

results.claim: [50] Every publicly trusted certificate is logged to Certificate Transparency and searchable, so certificates enumerating hostnames publish them; a wildcard certificate publishes only the wildcard name
results.evidence_quote: Homepage reachable; it is a 'Certificate Search' interface accepting 'an Identity (Domain Name, Organization Name, etc), a Certificate Fingerprint (SHA-1 or SHA-256), or a crt.sh ID'. The page contains no statement about Certificate Transparency logging requirements and none about wildcard certificates.
results.correction: crt.sh demonstrates that logged certificates are searchable  -  which is one third of the claim  -  but it asserts nothing about the other two. The premise that EVERY publicly trusted certificate is logged is a browser root-program policy (Chrome and Apple CT policies require SCTs for public trust), not something crt.sh states, and it is a policy that has exceptions and changes over time. The wildcard point (a *.example.com certificate discloses only the wildcard label, not the names served beneath it) is a property of the certificate's SAN list, not of crt.sh. Cite the Chrome/Apple CT policies for the logging requirement and state the wildcard point as a straightforward consequence of SAN contents; keep crt.sh only as evidence that the logs are publicly queryable.

results.claim: [51] Docker Compose healthchecks run a command inside the container (test list beginning CMD or CMD-SHELL), so a container-level HTTP check can set an arbitrary Host header, making container checks unconditionally compatible with Host-bound applications
results.evidence_quote: 'If it's a list, the first item must be either NONE, CMD or CMD-SHELL. If it's a string, it's equivalent to specifying CMD-SHELL followed by that string.' 'Using CMD-SHELL runs the command configured as a string using the container's default shell.' Example: 'test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "http://localhost"]'. Works 'in the same way ... as the HEALTHCHECK Dockerfile instruction'.
results.correction: The mechanism is confirmed: the check is a command executed inside the container, so an arbitrary Host header is expressible. The word 'unconditionally' is not earned and the page does not support it. The check depends on a suitable HTTP client actually being present in the image (curl or wget is not guaranteed  -  many distroless and slim images ship neither), on the shell existing for CMD-SHELL form, and the docs give no -H 'Host: ...' example. Restate as: container-level checks CAN carry an operator-specified Host header provided the image contains an HTTP client capable of setting it  -  which then becomes an image requirement to verify per service, not a free property.

results.claim: [52] Exactly four edge routing rules are required and the count does not grow with office count, so 'add an office without a deployment' is preserved by any wildcard-capable edge and destroyed by any per-hostname-configuration edge
results.evidence_quote: The page supports wildcard DNS generally but says nothing about edge routing-rule counts. On the contrary, for the single-stem pattern it states: 'Each new onboarded customer requires a new subdomain. The number of subdomains increases with each customer.' The wildcard benefit it describes is DNS-record-level ('Contoso doesn't need to create subdomain records for every customer'), not routing-rule-level, and it warns that with custom domains 'each tenant's domain name might require further configuration, which adds extra operational overhead to tenant onboarding.'
results.correction: The specific '4 routing rules, invariant in office count' figure is this system's own design conclusion, not something the cited page establishes  -  and the page's nearest statement points the other way for the non-wildcard pattern. Two substantive qualifications are also missing. First, invariance holds only WITHIN an already-provisioned label depth: by claim 26, a TLS wildcard matches exactly one label, so any new depth (office.api.<base> under an existing *.<base>) requires a new certificate and a new edge rule  -  the count is invariant in offices, not in naming shape. Second, by claim 27/28 it also requires that no node or empty non-terminal exist at the intermediate label without a wildcard at that depth. Restate as a conditional: the rule count is invariant in office count provided every served label depth already has its own DNS wildcard and its own wildcard certificate. Cite this page only for the wildcard-DNS mechanism and the Host-header-handling warning.

material_errors: [41] Istio auto_sni/auto_san_validation 'enabled by default' is asserted entirely from memory  -  the cited Istio TLS-configuration page contains no mention of either. These are istiod feature flags (ENABLE_AUTO_SNI / ENABLE_AUTO_SAN_VALIDATION) whose defaults have changed across releases, so 'default-on' is version-dependent and cannot be stated flatly for 2026. Any design assuming upstream SNI automatically follows the client Host header rests on nothing here.

[30] The Let's Encrypt lifetime progression '90 -> 64 -> 45 days' is unsupported by any cited source and does not match Let's Encrypt's published direction (a 90-day default plus an opt-in short-lived profile of roughly 6 days). The renewal rate-limit exemption is also overstated: only ARI-driven renewals are exempt from all limits; non-ARI renewals are exempt from just two of them. The renewal-cadence requirement (complete unattended at one third of remaining lifetime) is being sized against a lifetime number that was invented.

[30] The CA/Browser Forum step dates (200 days from 2026-03-15, 100 days from 2027-03-15, 47 days from 2029-03-15) are stated as verified but the cited ballot page gives only the March 2026 -> March 2029 envelope and the 398 -> 47 endpoint, deferring the schedule to a linked redline. A certificate-automation requirement keyed to a 200-day window in March 2026 is resting on a memory-supplied threshold.

[44] NIST SP 800-53 Revision 4 is cited (/r4/ path). Rev 4 was withdrawn on 23 September 2021 and is superseded by Rev 5; SC-7 control-enhancement numbering differs between the revisions, so this citation cannot support statements about Rev 5 enhancements. The URL is additionally behind a bot challenge and returns no control text at all.

[52] The load-bearing architectural conclusion  -  four edge routing rules, invariant in office count  -  is attributed to a page that never discusses routing-rule counts and that states the opposite for single-stem subdomains ('The number of subdomains increases with each customer'). The conclusion is also unconditionally stated when it holds only within an already-provisioned label depth: per claim 26 a TLS wildcard matches exactly one label, so adding a depth forces a new certificate and rule.

[12] Envoy's x-forwarded-host is appended only when append_x_forwarded_host is explicitly true, and x-envoy-original-host is suppressed when suppress_envoy_headers is true. The claim presents both as automatic consequences of a host rewrite. A design that expects to recover the original authority from those headers without setting the flag will not receive it.

[35] The ABP unconditional 'context.Handled = true' behaviour is sourced from a CLOSED GitHub issue with no fix or PR shown. A closed bug report establishes that the behaviour was reported, not that it persists. If it was fixed, the design premise inverts and the __tenant query/route/header/cookie selectors remain live  -  directly contradicting the requirement that the tenant-resolution surface be reduced to Host alone.

[24] The CloudFront mechanism is inverted: the managed policy that strips the viewer Host (and causes CloudFront to substitute the origin domain) is AllViewerExceptHostHeader, not 'Managed-AllViewer'. The claim's premise that the viewer Host is forwarded only when a policy includes it is also not established by the cited page.

[43] CISA BOD 23-02 is cited for a 14-day remediation deadline and a 'policy enforcement point separate from the interface' requirement, but cisa.gov returns HTTP 403 to every automated retrieval (directive page, implementation guidance, and the 508c PDF). Nothing in that claim is verified, and BOD 23-02 binds federal civilian executive branch agencies only  -  it is an analogy, not an applicable obligation for this system.

[38] Both statistics (21 of 33 implementations; ~97% of transparent-cache users) are unverifiable: dl.acm.org returns HTTP 403 to automated retrieval. Precise-sounding figures behind a paywalled DOI should not be carried into a deliverable a reader cannot check.

[27][28] The cited RFC 4592 mirror (rfc-annotations.research.icann.org) returned HTTP 503 on repeated attempts. The substance is correct and confirmed at rfc-editor.org, but the empty-non-terminal DNS requirement  -  one of the more consequential and least intuitive requirements in the set  -  currently points at an unreachable host.

[17][21][33][34][37] A recurring pattern: each of these claims bundles a correct, verbatim-confirmed fact with a second threshold or prescription that the cited page does not contain (ALB's 'no Host setting in the settings list'; GCP's '--host defaults to the forwarding rule IP'; the ASP.NET template '"AllowedHosts": "*"' and subdomain-wildcard semantics; ABP's '__tenant' default key and CurrentUserTenantResolveContributor; OWASP's 'validate on every request and reject unexpected hostnames'). Each needs its own citation or must be dropped.
vendor_neutrality_violations: Requirement 17 ('The object-store hostname must expose only the S3 API surface; its administrative console must not be routable...') names a vendor product API as the mandated interface. 'S3' is Amazon S3  -  a named product  -  and here it appears as a requirement, not as evidence or as an example of a behaviour class. Restate capability-first: 'the object-store hostname must expose only the object-store data-plane API; its administrative console must not be routable on any published hostname or port.' If S3 API compatibility is a genuine constraint inherited from the existing implementation, say so explicitly as a stated constraint of this system rather than as an architectural requirement.

Borderline, flagged for the record rather than as a breach: requirement 8 mandates 'DNS-01 validation', which fixes a specific ACME challenge type. DNS-01 is an open standard (RFC 8555), not a vendor product, so this is not a product recommendation  -  but it does hard-code one mechanism where the underlying capability is 'issuance must be automatable for wildcard names without inbound HTTP reachability'. Claim 29 establishes that wildcards force DNS-01, so the constraint is justified; state that justification inline so the requirement reads as a derived consequence rather than a preselected tool.

No other requirement names a product. Claims 9-14, 17-25, 41 and 47 all cite vendor documentation (nginx, Apache, Traefik, HAProxy, Envoy, Kong, Azure, AWS, Google Cloud, Cloudflare, Istio, Kubernetes, Docker) purely as evidence of a behaviour class  -  which is permitted  -  and none of the twenty capability requirements concludes 'therefore use <product>'. Two notes on presentation rather than substance: claim 39's mitigations are one vendor's product features (Tempesta FW's http_chain, http_strict_host_checking, ticket binding) and are generalised in the claim as neutral guidance, so if any requirement is derived from it the wording must be the capability, not the feature; and the requirement set leans heavily on Azure-sourced evidence (four of the fifty-two claims cite a single Microsoft article)  -  this is legitimate evidence but the deliverable should draw its Host-preservation requirement from the vendor-independent behaviour demonstrated across nginx, Apache, Kong, Envoy and Traefik so the requirement does not read as one vendor's house style.

research.area: Area 8  -  Secrets and configuration architecture (runtime secrets, build-time secrets, unrecoverable key material, the DataProtection keyring, rotation practice, and fail-fast configuration validation)
research.design_space: In 2026 the viable designs for secret handling in a small self-hosted regulated system fall on two independent axes, and most teams conflate them. Axis one is STORAGE AT REST: a plaintext file with filesystem permissions; an orchestrator-managed secret object (Docker Swarm and Kubernetes encrypt these at rest, plain Compose does not); an encrypted-in-repo file (SOPS with age or PGP recipients, or a sealed-secrets style asymmetric controller) where ciphertext is version-controlled and one bootstrap private key is the only thing that must live outside; a network secret store exposing per-secret ACLs, versioning, access audit and often dynamic short-lived credentials (Vault/OpenBao class, or a platform-managed equivalent); and a hardware root of trust (TPM 2.0, PKCS#11 HSM, or a PIV/FIDO token) that wraps one of the above rather than replacing it. Axis two is DELIVERY SHAPE: environment variables, files mounted into the container (the /run/secrets convention, consumed in .NET by the Key-per-file configuration provider), a configuration provider that fetches from a store during host build, or a sidecar/agent that renders templates and signals reload. The two axes are genuinely independent  -  encrypted-in-repo storage can deliver as files, and a managed store can deliver as environment variables  -  and delivery shape, not storage, is what determines whether a secret shows up in `docker inspect`, `/proc/<pid>/environ`, a crash dump or a debug log. A third, separate problem sits underneath both: non-secret configuration needs a schema, typed binding, defaults, and a startup gate, and treating it as "the same thing as secrets, just less sensitive" is what produces the silent-empty-string failure. Build-time secrets are a fourth, distinct class with only one correct 2026 answer  -  BuildKit secret mounts  -  because build arguments provably persist into image history and into `mode=max` provenance attestations. Finally, key material splits into subclasses that standards treat OPPOSITELY: NIST SP 800-57 says private signature keys generally should not be backed up (provision a standby key pair instead) while symmetric data-encryption keys are appropriate to back up, so "escrow everything unrecoverable" is not a defensible default. Any design must also decide whether it is buying change audit (who edited the secret) or access audit (who read it)  -  these are different capabilities and only the second requires a store.

options.name: A. Status quo  -  single mode-600 env file on the box, injected as environment variables via compose --env-file
options.how_it_works: 35 KEY=VALUE lines in secrets/env.prod, chmod 600, read by `docker compose --env-file`. Compose interpolates ${VAR} into the compose file; values reach containers as environment variables and are visible in `docker inspect`, `/proc/1/environ`, `docker compose config`, and any crash dump or verbose startup log. No versioning, no audit, no rotation mechanism, no validation. Omitting --env-file causes Compose to warn and substitute the empty string for every variable, then recreate the stack misconfigured.
options.operational_cost: Setup 0h (exists). Ongoing ~0h/month nominal, but each incident it causes costs 2-6h of two people's time; it has already caused two. Assumes no expertise. Recovery from loss of the VM disk is total loss of every secret with no copy anywhere.
options.why: It fails obviously for the DB password (login refused) and subtly for everything else: a blank SMTP password degrades to an outbox that retries forever; a blank PFX passphrase fails at AuthServer start but only when a token is first requested; a blank BASE_DOMAIN breaks Host-header tenant resolution into a generic 'Tenant not found' that looks like a DNS problem. Docker's own Compose documentation states the unset-variable behaviour is a warning plus empty-string substitution, so this failure mode is designed-in, not a bug. It is also the only option with no copy of the secrets off the machine, which means the one VM is simultaneously the only place PHI-adjacent credentials exist and the only place they are recoverable from.

options.name: B. Compose file-based secrets (/run/secrets) consumed by the .NET Key-per-file provider, plus a hard startup gate
options.how_it_works: Top-level `secrets:` entries with `file:` sources; each service declares only the secrets it needs; Docker mounts them at /run/secrets/<name>. The three .NET processes call AddKeyPerFile("/run/secrets", optional:false), where the file name becomes the configuration key (double underscore = section delimiter) and the file contents the value. Every ${VAR} in the compose file becomes ${VAR:?message}, which Docker documents as 'value of VAR if set and non-empty, otherwise exit with error'. Each process binds options classes with [Required] and calls .ValidateOnStart().
options.operational_cost: Setup 10-14h (rewrite compose, one options class per config group in three processes, rewrite the deploy script, write the runbook). Ongoing ~0.5h/month. Assumes only C# and compose file editing  -  no new tool, no new daemon, no new expertise. Does not change storage at rest: the source files are still plaintext on the box.
options.why: This is the single highest ratio of failure-mode elimination to operational cost available. It converts the exact incident that has occurred twice from 'stack comes up misconfigured' into 'compose refuses to run' and 'process exits non-zero naming the key'. It also removes the secrets from environment-variable exposure surfaces for the processes that matter. Its honest limitation: plain Compose secrets are NOT the Swarm secrets people think they are  -  Docker explicitly documents that swarm's Raft-encrypted, in-memory-filesystem guarantees apply to swarm services, not standalone containers  -  so this is a delivery-shape improvement, not encryption at rest. Sold as the latter to an assessor it is a misrepresentation.

options.name: C. Encrypted-in-repo (SOPS + age), decrypted at deploy time into the Compose secrets directory
options.how_it_works: Secrets live as ciphertext in the repository in a SOPS-encrypted file, with the keys visible in cleartext and only the values encrypted, so diffs are reviewable. Recipients are multiple age public keys: developer A, developer B, a deploy identity, and an offline escrow identity. `sops -d` at deploy time writes the per-secret files that option B consumes, then deletes them. Git history gives who-changed-what-when. SOPS is a CNCF Sandbox project, current release v3.13.3 (23 July 2026); age is current at v1.3.2 (29 August 2026).
options.operational_cost: Setup 8-12h on top of B (key generation and distribution, .sops.yaml, deploy-script integration, escrow procedure, runbook). Ongoing ~0.5-1h/month. Assumes willingness to run one CLI and to treat an age private key as an object with a custody procedure. Shifts, but does not remove, the bootstrap problem: the age identity becomes the highest-value secret in the organisation.
options.why: It fails obviously in the two ways that matter: a missing or wrong age key makes decryption fail loudly at deploy, and a corrupted file fails the MAC check rather than silently producing partial values. It gives an off-machine, multi-copy, reviewable store without adding a running component or a bootstrap network dependency, which matters enormously on a single VM where every new daemon is a new single point of failure. The honest limitation is that git history is a CHANGE log, not an ACCESS log  -  it can answer 'who last edited the SMTP password' but never 'who read it', and OWASP's audit expectations are framed around the latter. Encrypting to a single recipient recreates the single-point-of-failure it was adopted to remove; multi-recipient is not optional here.

options.name: D. Self-hosted network secret store (Vault / OpenBao class)
options.how_it_works: A daemon holding an encrypted storage backend, unsealed at start with Shamir key shares (default 5 shares, threshold 3), exposing per-secret paths with policy-based ACLs, versioned KV, an audit device that logs every request and response, and dynamic secrets engines that can mint short-lived database credentials. Applications authenticate with a token or role and fetch at start or continuously. OpenBao is current at v2.6.2 (18 August 2026); it can configure the audit device in the config file so requests are audited from the very first one.
options.operational_cost: Setup 30-60h (install, storage backend, seal strategy, policies, auth method, app integration in three processes, backup of the storage backend, unseal runbook). Ongoing 4-8h/month (version upgrades, policy changes, token/lease hygiene, backup verification), plus an unbounded tail on the first unplanned reseal. Assumes at least one person who has operated one before.
options.why: Everything about it is correct in the abstract and wrong in this deployment. It becomes a new stateful single point of failure on the same VM, in front of the application's ability to boot at all  -  and the stack already gates authserver and api on db-migrator completing, so the boot dependency chain lengthens. Its characteristic failures are quiet: a sealed vault after a host reboot, an expired token, a revoked lease, a policy that silently returns 403 for one path. That is precisely the class of failure the brief says this team will not notice. Unsealing after an unplanned reboot is a manual multi-share ceremony performed by two people with no on-call rotation, at whatever hour the VM restarted. The audit device is a genuine capability nothing else on this list provides, and that is the reason to keep it on the roadmap, not to adopt it now.

options.name: E. Platform-provided managed secret store, consumed through a configuration provider at host build
options.how_it_works: As a CAPABILITY, not a product: a store external to the VM offering per-secret identity-based access control, immutable versioning with rollback, retrievable version history, an access log recording principal and time, and a client library that plugs into the .NET configuration pipeline so values arrive as ordinary IConfiguration keys. The application authenticates with a workload identity or a single bootstrap credential.
options.operational_cost: Setup 8-16h. Ongoing 1-2h/month. Assumes the platform exists and provides an identity the app can present without a long-lived bootstrap secret; if it does not, a bootstrap credential must still be stored by option A, B or C, and the chain is only as strong as that link.
options.why: Conditional on two things this exercise cannot yet answer: whether the eventual platform provides a workload identity (which removes the bootstrap secret) or only an API key (which does not), and whether the store's outage becomes an application outage. If values are fetched once at host build and cached in-process, a store outage blocks restarts but not running traffic  -  acceptable. If fetched per-request or refreshed aggressively, the store joins the availability critical path of a system that today has none of its dependencies outside the box. This is the option that most cleanly satisfies the access-audit requirement, and it is the correct thing to write into the platform requirements document without naming a provider.

options.name: F. Hardware-backed key storage (TPM 2.0, PKCS#11 HSM, or PIV/FIDO token) wrapping the bootstrap key
options.how_it_works: Rather than storing secrets, the hardware holds one non-exportable private key that unwraps the rest  -  e.g. an age identity held on a PIV token via a hardware plugin, or a TPM-sealed key bound to platform state. Decryption requires physical presence (a touch) or the specific machine.
options.operational_cost: Setup 4-8h for a token-based identity on top of option C; near-zero ongoing. Assumes each developer carries and does not lose a token, and that a spare enrolled token exists.
options.why: Genuinely attractive today because deployment is manual over SSH  -  a human is always present, so a touch-to-decrypt requirement costs nothing. It becomes actively harmful the moment CD lands, because an unattended pipeline cannot touch a token, and the usual workaround is to add a second, softer, non-hardware-backed recipient  -  at which point the hardware protects nothing. There is also a hard constraint specific to this system: the ABP string-encryption passphrase must be handed to the framework as a plaintext string, so it cannot live as a non-exportable hardware key; hardware can only protect the key that decrypts the file the passphrase lives in. Worth adopting only if the team accepts that it constrains the CD design that has not been made yet.

research.recommendation:
Recommend a four-tier package that treats the 35 variables as four different problems, not one, and that spends its budget on eliminating silent failure before it spends anything on cryptography. This is my architectural judgement; the mechanisms it relies on are sourced.

TIER 0  -  THE GATE (do this first, alone, and ship it). Replace every ${VAR} in the compose file with ${VAR:?message}, which Docker documents as exiting with an error rather than substituting empty. Add one options class per configuration group in EACH of the three processes, with [Required] on every mandatory string, bound with .ValidateOnStart(). RequiredAttribute.AllowEmptyStrings defaults to false, so [Required] rejects the present-but-empty case as well as the absent case  -  which is exactly the failure this system has hit twice. This must be done in AuthServer and DbMigrator as well as the API: AuthServer is a separate process serving sign-in, and a gate on the API alone leaves the login path able to boot misconfigured. Cost ~10-14h, and it converts the single most-repeated operational incident into a refused deploy.

TIER 1  -  DELIVERY SHAPE. Move the three .NET processes off environment variables onto file-mounted secrets: top-level Compose `secrets:` with `file:` sources, mounted at /run/secrets, consumed with AddKeyPerFile  -  a first-party .NET provider Microsoft documents as being for Docker hosting scenarios, where the file name is the key and its contents the value. Keep environment variables only where the component forces it (SQL Server and MinIO), and record that exception explicitly rather than leaving it implicit. Say plainly in the runbook that plain-Compose secrets are a delivery-shape improvement, NOT encryption at rest  -  Docker documents the Raft-encrypted, in-memory guarantees as swarm-only.

TIER 2  -  STORAGE AT REST. Adopt SOPS with age, ciphertext committed to the repository, encrypted to four recipients: both developers, a deploy identity, and an offline escrow identity. Decrypt at deploy into the Tier-1 secrets directory and remove the plaintext afterwards. Both tools are current and maintained (SOPS v3.13.3, 23 Jul 2026; age v1.3.2, 29 Aug 2026). This buys off-machine copies, multi-person recoverability, reviewable diffs of non-secret keys, and change audit. Be explicit with any assessor that it buys CHANGE audit and not ACCESS audit.

TIER 3  -  THE THREE PIECES OF KEY MATERIAL, HANDLED SEPARATELY BECAUSE THE STANDARD TREATS THEM SEPARATELY.
(i) The OpenIddict token-signing certificate is a PRIVATE SIGNATURE KEY. NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev 5 Table 7 says these generally should not be backed up, and B.3.1.1 gives the alternative directly: "Instead of backing up the private signature key, a second private signature key and corresponding public key could be generated and the public key distributed ... for use if the primary private signature key becomes unavailable." OpenIddict supports exactly this natively  -  register multiple certificates; it prefers the furthest NotAfter and ignores not-yet-valid ones. So generate a standby certificate now with a later validity window, register both, and let loss of the primary be a restart rather than a catastrophe. This is cheaper AND more standards-aligned than escrow.
(ii) The ABP string-encryption passphrase is a SYMMETRIC DATA-ENCRYPTION KEY, which NIST Table 7 marks "OK" to back up. This is the one that genuinely wants escrow: two sealed offline copies in two physically separate locations, with a written recovery procedure that a second person has executed end-to-end from the document alone. Before doing any of that, run the cheap test in "what would change the answer": if nothing in this system is actually encrypted with it, it is not unrecoverable and can simply be set to a strong value and forgotten.
(iii) The DataProtection keyring is STATE, not a secret to rotate. It auto-rotates on a 90-day lifetime with a two-day activation delay, retired keys must be retained to unprotect old payloads, and Microsoft warns that deleting a key is "truly destructive behavior". Treat it as backed-up application state on the same schedule as the databases, and fix the real defect: because the system persists it to an explicit location (Redis), Microsoft documents that "the data protection system deregisters the default key encryption at rest mechanism. Consequently, keys are no longer encrypted at rest." Add ProtectKeysWithCertificate plus UnprotectKeysWithAnyCertificate, which exists precisely so the wrapping certificate can be rotated without losing the ability to read old keys.

BUILD-TIME. Convert the Dockerfile to BuildKit secret mounts for both the ABP licence and the NuGet feed configuration. Docker states without qualification that "Build arguments and environment variables are inappropriate for passing secrets to your build, because they persist in the final image", that "mode=max exposes the values of build arguments" in provenance, and that "Secret mounts don't leak outside of the build and are never included in provenance attestations." Treat NuGet.Config as a credential file, not a config file, because the ABP Commercial feed URL embeds a per-customer identifier in the path  -  the URL IS the secret. Cost ~3h.

ROTATION. Do not adopt a calendar. Adopt a per-secret classification table stating, for each of the 35, the blast radius, the restart set, and whether it rotates without downtime  -  then rotate on trigger (exposure, departure, incident) plus a documented cryptoperiod per class. NIST 8.2.2.2 frames the recovery/rotation decision as per key type and per application, and OWASP notes manual rotation "can lead to mistakes". Rotate NOW, while there is no PHI, every value that was pasted into a chat transcript; the same operation costs a maintenance window with real practices after go-live.

WHAT I AM NOT RECOMMENDING AND WHY IT MATTERS: no secret-store daemon, no dynamic database credentials, no per-office credential sets, no Kubernetes-shaped tooling. Each is defensible at a larger organisation and each adds a subtle failure mode to a system whose operators will only catch loud ones.
research.operational_cost_of_recommendation:
SETUP, sequenced so each tier ships independently and each is useful alone:
- Tier 0 (compose ${VAR:?} + options validation with [Required]/.ValidateOnStart in all three processes): 10-14h. Highest value; do it first even if nothing else happens.
- Tier 1 (compose `secrets:` + AddKeyPerFile in three processes, document the SQL Server / MinIO exceptions): 6-8h.
- Tier 2 (SOPS+age, four recipients, deploy-script integration, runbook): 8-12h.
- Tier 3 (standby signing certificate; passphrase escrow with a witnessed recovery drill; ProtectKeysWithCertificate + UnprotectKeysWithAnyCertificate + keyring backup): 8-10h, of which ~2h is the drill.
- Build-time (BuildKit secret mounts for licence + NuGet.Config, history/provenance verification): 3-4h.
- Per-secret rotation classification table for all 35: 4-6h once, largely research not code.
TOTAL 39-54h, i.e. roughly 1.5 to 2 developer-weeks spread over two to three months at the stated ~1 developer-week per month, competing with a code-standard remediation exercise that already claims a large share of it.

ONGOING: ~1-1.5h/month steady state (secret edits through SOPS, occasional key-recipient changes, reading the rotation table when something changes). Plus two fixed annual events that must be diarised, not left to memory: the standby-signing-certificate refresh and the escrow recovery drill, ~4h each.

THRESHOLD  -  WHERE THIS STOPS BEING VIABLE (stated because the brief instructs that the one-week-per-month figure is an estimate, not a measurement):
- The recommendation is operable at 6+ hours per month of genuine infrastructure attention. Below that it still holds, because Tiers 0 and 1 are code that keeps working with no maintenance  -  they are the durable part.
- Below roughly 3 hours per month, Tier 2 decays in a specific and predictable way: the encrypted file in the repository drifts from what is actually on the server, because under pressure someone edits the plaintext on the box "just this once" and never re-encrypts. The observable symptom is a redeploy that reverts a setting nobody remembers changing. Mitigation if the team knows it will be below this line: make the deploy script refuse to start if a plaintext secrets file exists on the host outside the decrypt window, so the shortcut fails loudly.
- Below roughly 1 hour per month, Tier 3 decays first and worst  -  the escrow copies stop being refreshed after passphrase changes, and the standby certificate expires unnoticed. At that budget, do Tiers 0 and 1 only, put the passphrase and PFX in a documented offline location, and do not pretend to a rotation practice.
- The threshold in the OTHER direction: a second environment doubles the number of secret sets and is the point where manual file management stops scaling and a store starts paying for itself. So does the arrival of hosted CI, because the build-time credentials must then live somewhere the developers do not control.

evidence.claim: Docker states that build arguments and environment variables are inappropriate for passing secrets to a build because they persist in the final image; the supported mechanism is RUN --mount=type=secret, which mounts the secret at /run/secrets/<id> for the duration of one instruction and does not write it to any layer.
evidence.source_name: Docker Docs  -  Build secrets
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Quote: "Build arguments and environment variables are inappropriate for passing secrets to your build, because they persist in the final image." Default mount path /run/secrets/<id>; options target= and env=.

evidence.claim: BuildKit provenance attestations in mode=max expose the values of build arguments, and Docker explicitly directs users passing credentials via build args to refactor to secret mounts. Secret mounts are never included in provenance attestations. Provenance is not generated by default.
evidence.source_name: Docker Docs  -  SLSA provenance attestations
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Quotes: "Note that mode=max exposes the values of build arguments." / "If you're misusing build arguments to pass credentials, authentication tokens, or other secrets, you should refactor your build to pass the secrets using secret mounts instead." / "Secret mounts don't leak outside of the build and are never included in provenance attestations."

evidence.claim: The contents of build secrets are NOT part of the Docker build cache key, so changing a secret's value does not invalidate the cache; only the secret's id and mount path participate in the cache checksum.
evidence.source_name: Docker Docs  -  Build cache invalidation
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Quote: "The contents of build secrets are not part of the build cache. Changing the value of a secret doesn't result in cache invalidation." Docker's suggested workaround is to pass a build argument alongside the secret and change its value to force invalidation.

evidence.claim: Docker Compose, when it cannot resolve a substituted variable and no default is defined, displays a WARNING and substitutes an empty string. The ${VAR:?error} form exits with an error if the variable is unset or empty; ${VAR?error} exits if it is unset.
evidence.source_name: Docker Docs  -  Compose interpolation
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Quote: "If Compose can't resolve a substituted variable and no default value is defined, it displays a warning and substitutes the variable with an empty string." / "${VAR:?error} -> value of VAR if set and non-empty, otherwise exit with error"

evidence.claim: Docker documents that injecting passwords and API keys as environment variables risks unintentional information exposure, that environment variables are often available to all processes and hard to track access to, and that they can be printed in logs during debugging. Compose secrets are mounted at /run/secrets/<secret_name> and support file: and environment: sources.
evidence.source_name: Docker Docs  -  Use secrets in Compose
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Quotes: "If you're injecting passwords and API keys as environment variables, you risk unintentional information exposure." / "Environment variables are often available to all processes, and it can be difficult to track access. They can also be printed in logs when debugging errors without your knowledge."

evidence.claim: Docker's swarm-secret guarantees (encrypted Raft log, mutual-TLS distribution, in-memory filesystem mount, never exposed as environment variables) apply to SWARM SERVICES ONLY, not to standalone containers. Plain Compose secrets therefore give the delivery shape without the at-rest encryption.
evidence.source_name: Docker Docs  -  Manage sensitive data with Docker secrets (swarm)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Quotes: "The secret is stored in the Raft log, which is encrypted." / "Docker secrets are only available to swarm services, not to standalone containers."

evidence.claim: .NET ships a first-party Key-per-file configuration provider (AddKeyPerFile) explicitly intended for Docker hosting: the file name is the configuration key, the file contents the value, and double-underscore in the file name is the section delimiter. This is the supported path from /run/secrets into IConfiguration with no custom code.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn  -  Configuration providers in .NET
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Quote: "The Key-per-file configuration provider is used in Docker hosting scenarios." directoryPath must be absolute; Logging__LogLevel__System produces Logging:LogLevel:System.

evidence.claim: Options validation in .NET is lazy by default (it runs when the options instance is created); ValidateOnStart / AddOptionsWithValidateOnStart forces it at application start and throws OptionsValidationException, and ValidateDataAnnotations enables [Required]-style checks.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn  -  Options pattern in ASP.NET Core
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Pattern: services.AddOptions<T>().BindConfiguration(path).ValidateDataAnnotations().ValidateOnStart(). AddOptionsWithValidateOnStart calls ValidateOnStart internally. ValidateOnStart introduced in .NET 6.

evidence.claim: RequiredAttribute.AllowEmptyStrings defaults to FALSE, meaning an empty string FAILS [Required] validation by default. This makes [Required] + ValidateOnStart sufficient to catch the present-but-blank failure mode, not just the absent one.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn  -  RequiredAttribute.AllowEmptyStrings Property
evidence.threshold_or_limit: "true if an empty string is allowed; otherwise, false. The default value is false."

evidence.claim: Pointing ASP.NET Core Data Protection at an explicit key repository DEREGISTERS the default key-encryption-at-rest mechanism, so keys are stored unencrypted unless an explicit mechanism is configured. Microsoft recommends specifying one for production.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn  -  Key encryption at rest in ASP.NET Core
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Quote: "If you specify an explicit key persistence location, the data protection system deregisters the default key encryption at rest mechanism. Consequently, keys are no longer encrypted at rest. We recommend that you specify an explicit key encryption mechanism for production deployments." ProtectKeysWithCertificate is available cross-platform; DPAPI/DPAPI-NG are Windows-only.

evidence.claim: The Data Protection key ring auto-rotates: keys get an activation date of now+2 days and expiry of now+90 days; created, active and expired keys can all unprotect payloads; deleting a key permanently destroys the data it protected with no override. UnprotectKeysWithAnyCertificate exists so the wrapping certificate can be rotated while old keys stay readable. SetApplicationName sets the ApplicationDiscriminator and is what allows two apps sharing one key repository to read each other's payloads.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn  -  Key management in ASP.NET Core / Configure Data Protection
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 90-day default lifetime, minimum configurable lifetime 7 days, 2-day activation delay, ~24h key-ring refresh. Quote: "all data protected by the key is permanently undecipherable, and there's no emergency override... Deleting a key is truly destructive behavior." / "By default, the Data Protection system isolates apps from one another based on their content root paths, even if they share the same physical key repository."

evidence.claim: NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev 5 Table 7 marks private signature keys as generally NOT to be backed up, and Appendix B.3.1.1 recommends generating a second signature key pair and distributing its public key as the alternative to backing up the private key. The same Table 7 marks symmetric data-encryption keys as OK to back up.
evidence.source_name: NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5, Recommendation for Key Management
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Table 7 (8.2.2.1): "Private signature key  -  No (in general); support for non-repudiation would be in question... Symmetric data encryption key  -  OK". B.3.1.1: "Instead of backing up the private signature key, a second private signature key and corresponding public key could be generated and the public key distributed in accordance with Section 8.1.5.1 for use if the primary private signature key becomes unavailable." 8.3.1: archive "shall continue to provide the appropriate protections" and "will require a strong access-control mechanism". 8.2.2.2: the key-recovery decision "should be made on a case-by-case basis" based on key type and application.

evidence.claim: NIST defines split knowledge as splitting a key into n shares such that knowledge of any k-1 shares reveals nothing about the key, and requires that each share be distributed separately to its intended recipient when used for manual key distribution.
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Glossary: "A process by which a cryptographic key is split into n key shares, each of which provides no knowledge of the key... knowledge of any k - 1 key shares provides no information about the key other than, possibly, its length." 8.1.5.2.2.1: "each key share shall be distributed separately to its intended recipient."

evidence.claim: OpenIddict supports registering multiple signing/encryption credentials for key rotation and selects deterministically: X.509 certificates are ordered by NotBefore/NotAfter, not-yet-valid certificates are skipped, and the furthest expiration date is preferred. It recommends two RSA certificates in production, distinct from the HTTPS certificate  -  one for signing, one for encryption.
evidence.source_name: OpenIddict documentation  -  Encryption and signing credentials
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Quote: "certificates with the furthest expiration date are always preferred"; "it is recommended to use two RSA certificates, distinct from the certificate(s) used for HTTPS: one for encryption, one for signing." The docs do NOT state whether previously issued tokens survive a signing-key change  -  unverified there.

evidence.claim: ABP's AbpStringEncryptionOptions has a published, well-known DEFAULT passphrase ("gsKnGZ041HLL4IM8"), default salt and default IV; ABP recommends changing it. In the ABP framework repository IStringEncryptionService is referenced by only a handful of components  -  notably SettingEncryptionService (encrypted settings) and the AWS/Aliyun blob-storing client factories for cached temporary credentials.

ABP COMMERCIAL modules are closed-source and were not searchable  -  additional uses there are UNVERIFIED.

evidence.claim: ABP does NOT encrypt tenant connection strings by default; the SaaS/tenant-management module validates and stores them as plain text, and encrypting them requires overriding the connection-string resolver. evidence.claim: The ABP Commercial NuGet feed URL embeds a per-customer identifier in the path (https://nuget.abp.io/<GUID>/v3/index.json), so the NuGet.config file itself functions as a credential. The general shape  -  root credentials are env-only and are entangled with backend encryption  -  is corroborated across two independent issue threads.

evidence.claim: Microsoft warns that environment variables are commonly stored as plain, unencrypted text and are accessible to untrusted parties if the machine or process is compromised; that the Secret Manager tool does not encrypt secrets and is development-only; and that secrets should never be stored in source code or configuration files.

It's for development purposes only."

Addressable does not mean optional.

evidence.threshold_or_limit: 164.306(d)(3): assess "whether each implementation specification is a reasonable and appropriate safeguard in its environment"; then implement, or document why not and "Implement an equivalent alternative measure if reasonable and appropriate."

evidence.claim: SOPS and age are both actively maintained as of August 2026: SOPS v3.13.3 (23 July 2026), a CNCF Sandbox project since 2023 under getsops maintainers; age v1.3.2 (29 August 2026). Sealed-secrets is also current (v0.39.1, 20 August 2026) but is Kubernetes-only. OpenBao is current (v2.6.2, 18 August 2026). Gitleaks is current (v8.30.1, 21 March 2026).

OpenBao can configure the audit device in its config file so that requests are audited from the very first one, whereas in Vault requests made before the audit device is configured are not logged.
