The Vault-vs-OpenBao audit-bootstrapping difference comes from a secondary comparison and is UNVERIFIED against OpenBao's own reference.

evidence.claim: MY REASONING, NOT A SOURCED FACT: because this system persists the Data Protection key ring to Redis via an explicit provider, and Microsoft documents that an explicit persistence location deregisters at-rest encryption, the master keys protecting login state and email-confirmation tokens for BOTH the AuthServer and the API are stored unencrypted in Redis, in its AOF file on the redisdata volume, and in any backup of that volume. Read access to Redis is therefore equivalent to the ability to forge authentication payloads across every office.
evidence.source_name: Derived from Microsoft Data Protection documentation applied to the stated system facts
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Verifiable in ten minutes: read the Redis key CaseEvaluation-Protection-Keys and inspect whether each <key> element carries a plaintext <masterKey> or an <encryptedKey>/EncryptedXmlDecryptor descriptor. Whether Redis additionally requires AUTH in this deployment is UNVERIFIED and materially changes the urgency.

evidence.claim: MY REASONING, NOT A SOURCED FACT: the two secrets the brief calls unrecoverable belong to different NIST key classes with opposing guidance, so a single 'escrow both' policy is wrong on one of them. The signing certificate should get a pre-provisioned standby credential (which OpenIddict natively supports) rather than a backup; the string-encryption passphrase is the one that warrants escrow.
evidence.source_name: Derived from NIST SP 800-57 Pt1 Rev5 Table 7 / B.3.1.1 applied to OpenIddict's documented multi-credential behaviour
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Both underlying facts are individually verified; the synthesis is mine and is arguable  -  a reasonable engineer could say the non-repudiation concern NIST cites does not apply to an OIDC access-token signing key used purely for integrity, and therefore escrow is acceptable. If you take that view, escrow it AND provision the standby; the standby costs almost nothing either way.

capability_requirements.requirement: The deployment mechanism MUST refuse to bring up or recreate the stack when any required secret or configuration variable is absent OR set to the empty string, rather than substituting a blank value and continuing.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: This exact failure has occurred twice in production practice, and Docker documents the default behaviour that causes it (warning plus empty-string substitution). It is the single highest-frequency defect in the area and the fix is a documented one-character change per variable.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Recorded system fact: '--env-file secrets/env.prod is mandatory on every compose invocation; without it every secret resolves to a blank string and the stack recreates with no DB password.' Docker Compose interpolation documentation.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: On a scratch copy, run the deploy command with the environment file omitted; then again with one variable present but set to an empty value. In BOTH cases the command must exit non-zero and `docker ps -a` must show no container created, recreated or restarted. If any container starts, the requirement fails.

capability_requirements.requirement: Each of the three runtime processes MUST validate its own configuration at startup and terminate with a non-zero exit code and a log line naming the offending key(s) before accepting any work.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: The AuthServer is a separate process serving sign-in whose Razor pages call application services in-process, so a validation gate placed only in the API leaves the authentication path unguarded; DbMigrator runs on every bring-up and writes to every office database. A gate that covers one of three processes is not a gate.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System fact: three runtime processes with independent configuration; Microsoft options-validation documentation (ValidateOnStart / AddOptionsWithValidateOnStart, ValidateDataAnnotations).
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: For each of HttpApi.Host, AuthServer and DbMigrator in turn, blank one required key and start the process. Each must exit non-zero, and its last log lines must name the failing key. For the API specifically, confirm with `curl` that no HTTP port ever accepted a connection. Repeat with the key entirely absent.

capability_requirements.requirement: Build-time credentials MUST be injectable into the container build without appearing in any image layer, image history, image configuration, or build provenance output.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Docker states categorically that build arguments and environment variables persist in the final image and are inappropriate for secrets, and that mode=max provenance exposes build-argument values. There is a supported mechanism (secret mounts) with no meaningful cost, so anything weaker is a choice to leak.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System fact: the ABP Commercial licence code and a private NuGet feed key are needed at image build time. Docker build-secrets and SLSA-provenance documentation.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Build the image supplying the credential. Then run `docker history --no-trunc <image>` and `docker image inspect <image>` and grep the output for the credential value and for the per-customer feed identifier  -  neither may appear. Then rebuild with `--provenance=mode=max`, export the attestation, and grep it likewise. Finally `docker run --rm <image> env` and `docker run --rm <image> find / -name 'NuGet.Config'` must not surface it.

capability_requirements.requirement: The NuGet feed configuration containing the per-customer identifier MUST be treated and stored as a credential, not as a checked-in configuration file.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: The ABP Commercial feed URL embeds a per-customer GUID in its path, so possession of the URL is possession of package-feed access. Teams routinely commit NuGet.Config because it looks like configuration; the file's name is what makes this requirement necessary to state explicitly.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: ABP Commercial feed URL format (https://nuget.abp.io/<GUID>/v3/index.json), evidenced across ABP support threads on Docker and CI package restore.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Run `git log -p --all -- '**/NuGet.Config' '**/nuget.config'` and confirm no commit in history contains a per-customer feed URL. Then clone the repository fresh into an empty directory and run `dotnet restore`; it must FAIL without a separately supplied secret. If restore succeeds from a clean clone with no extra input, the credential is in the repository.

capability_requirements.requirement: Secret values consumed by the three .NET processes MUST be delivered as mounted files rather than environment variables.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Docker and Microsoft both document that environment variables are plaintext, broadly readable by processes, and prone to appearing in logs and dumps. .NET has a first-party provider (Key-per-file) designed for exactly this, so the cost is near zero for the processes the team controls. Scoped to the .NET processes because SQL Server's file-based password support is undocumented and MinIO's root credentials are environment-only  -  those exceptions must be documented rather than silently accepted.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Docker Compose secrets documentation; Microsoft app-secrets documentation; Microsoft Key-per-file configuration provider documentation.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: For each of the three .NET containers run `docker inspect <container> --format '{{json .Config.Env}}'` and, inside the container, `tr '\0' '\n' < /proc/1/environ`. Neither may contain the SMTP password, the MinIO secret, the token-signing PFX passphrase, the string-encryption passphrase or the partner integration token. Then run `docker compose config` and confirm those values do not appear in its output either.

capability_requirements.requirement: The Data Protection key ring MUST be encrypted at rest, and the certificate or key that encrypts it MUST be rotatable without invalidating sessions protected under previous wrapping keys.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Microsoft documents that choosing an explicit persistence location deregisters the default at-rest encryption, so the current configuration almost certainly stores master keys in cleartext in Redis; those keys protect login state and email-confirmation tokens for both processes. UnprotectKeysWithAnyCertificate exists precisely so this can be fixed without a one-way door.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft Data Protection key-encryption-at-rest and configuration documentation; system fact that the keyring lives in Redis under CaseEvaluation-Protection-Keys with SetApplicationName("CaseEvaluation") in both processes.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Read the raw key-ring value from its store and inspect the XML: every <key> must carry an encrypted descriptor (an <encryptedKey> / EncryptedXmlDecryptor form), not a plaintext base64 <masterKey>. Then add a second certificate to the unprotect set, restart both processes, and confirm a browser session established before the restart still authenticates without re-login.

capability_requirements.requirement: The Data Protection key ring MUST be backed up as application state to a location that survives destruction of the Redis volume, and that restore MUST have been exercised at least once with a recorded date.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: The key ring is not a secret to be regenerated  -  it is auto-rotating state whose retired keys are required to unprotect old payloads, and Microsoft warns that deleting a key is 'truly destructive behavior'. Losing it logs out every user and breaks in-flight email-confirmation links across every office, which is a customer-visible incident rather than an internal one.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft key-management documentation (90-day lifetime, retired keys retained for unprotect, deletion irreversible); system fact that Redis persistence is AOF on a named volume on the same disk.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: In a scratch copy, issue a session cookie, then destroy the Redis volume entirely. Restore the key ring from backup, restart, and confirm the pre-existing cookie still authenticates. Record the date the drill was run and by whom; a drill older than twelve months does not satisfy this.

capability_requirements.requirement: Every secret whose loss is unrecoverable MUST have a written recovery procedure that has been executed end-to-end, from the document alone, by a person who did not write it.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: With two engineers there is no bench. An undocumented recovery path held in one person's head is indistinguishable from no recovery path the moment that person is unavailable, and NIST requires archived key material to be protected with strong access control  -  which implies a defined, auditable procedure rather than tacit knowledge.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: NIST SP 800-57 Pt1 Rev5 8.2.2.2 and 8.3.1; system fact of a two-person team with no on-call rotation.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Hand the recovery document for the string-encryption passphrase to the developer who did not write it. Without asking the author a single question, they must retrieve the value and successfully decrypt a known ciphertext produced beforehand. Record the elapsed time and the date. If any clarifying question was needed, the document fails and must be amended.

capability_requirements.requirement: The authorisation server MUST be able to hold more than one token-signing credential simultaneously and select between them deterministically, so that loss or expiry of the primary is a restart rather than an unrecoverable event.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: NIST's stated alternative to backing up a private signature key is to pre-generate a second key pair and distribute its public key. OpenIddict supports this natively with documented ordering. This is both the standards-aligned answer and the cheaper one, and it removes the need to escrow a key whose escrow NIST advises against.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: NIST SP 800-57 Pt1 Rev5 B.3.1.1 and Table 7; OpenIddict encryption-and-signing-credentials documentation (certificates with the furthest expiration date preferred; not-yet-valid certificates unused).
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Register a second signing certificate with a later NotAfter alongside the current one and restart the AuthServer. Fetch the JWKS endpoint and confirm both keys are advertised. Then obtain a token before the restart and confirm it still validates afterwards. Finally remove the primary certificate, restart, and confirm the server starts and issues tokens under the standby.

capability_requirements.requirement: Recovery of the full secret set MUST be possible by at least two people and MUST NOT depend on a single individual, a single device, or a single physical location.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Every option that improves on the status quo introduces a bootstrap key, and encrypting to one recipient recreates exactly the single point of failure the change was meant to remove. On a two-person team the failure of one person is a 50% staffing event, not an edge case.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: NIST SP 800-57 split-knowledge definition and manual-distribution requirements; system fact of a single mode-600 file on one box with no vault and no copies.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Declare the primary holder's laptop unavailable. The second person must, using only what they hold plus documented offline material, decrypt the secret store and bring the full stack up in a clean scratch environment within the time the runbook claims. Confirm at least two of the recovery inputs are stored in physically different locations.

capability_requirements.requirement: Rotating a credential MUST NOT require rebuilding or redeploying an application image.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: If rotation requires a build, it will not happen under time pressure, and the security-relevant response to an exposure (rotate now) collides with the change-management cost of a release. This also forces the design away from build-time injection of runtime values.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: OWASP guidance that manual rotation causes mistakes and should be automated; system fact that deployment is entirely manual over SSH with no CD.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Change the SMTP password in the secret store, then perform whatever the runbook says. No `docker build` may occur. Confirm mail delivery resumes and record the wall-clock time. Repeat for the partner integration token.

capability_requirements.requirement: A per-secret rotation classification MUST exist covering all 35 variables, stating for each: whether it can be rotated with zero downtime, which processes must restart, and what breaks if it is rotated incorrectly.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Several secrets in this system have non-obvious rotation semantics that will otherwise be discovered during an incident: the SQL Server sa password is honoured only at first container initialisation and cannot be changed by editing the variable; MinIO root credentials are entangled with backend config encryption; changing the string-encryption passphrase makes existing encrypted values unreadable. A generic 'rotate quarterly' policy applied to this set produces an outage.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: MSSQL_SA_PASSWORD init-only behaviour (Microsoft docs and mssql-docker issue #471); MinIO root-credential and backend-encryption behaviour; ABP string-encryption semantics; NIST 8.2.2.2 (recovery/rotation decision is per key type and application).
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Pick three entries at random  -  one database credential, the MinIO root secret, and the token-signing PFX passphrase. For each, the document must state the restart set and the blast radius. Then actually execute one of them in a scratch environment and confirm the document's prediction was correct. Any entry marked 'zero downtime' that causes an outage when executed fails the requirement.

capability_requirements.requirement: Every time-bounded secret MUST have its expiry date recorded and monitored with a notice at least 30 days ahead.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: The ABP Commercial licence, the wildcard TLS certificate and the token-signing certificate all fail on a calendar rather than in response to an action, which makes them the only failures in this area that arrive with no triggering change to correlate against. A licence lapse stops the application; a signing-certificate lapse stops token issuance.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: ABP licence runtime check and expiry behaviour; OpenIddict certificate NotAfter selection; system fact that there is no alerting or uptime monitoring of any kind.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Produce a list naming every time-bounded secret with its expiry date. Then, in a scratch environment, set one to expire within the notice window and confirm a notice is actually produced through a channel a human reads. A spreadsheet with no alerting mechanism fails.

capability_requirements.requirement: Secret detection MUST run before code reaches the default branch, and a historical scan of the repository MUST have been performed with its findings triaged and any confirmed exposure rotated.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Values have already been pasted into chat transcripts during setup and are flagged for rotation, which establishes that this team's secrets do leak through human channels. Detection tooling is current and maintained, and while there is no CD, a pre-commit hook satisfies this at zero infrastructure cost.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System fact: 'Several values were pasted into chat transcripts during setup and are flagged for rotation.' OWASP shift-left detection guidance; gitleaks currency (v8.30.1, Mar 2026).
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Create a branch containing a realistic high-entropy credential in a config file and attempt to commit and push it; the commit or the branch protection must block. Separately, produce the output and date of a full-history scan and, for each confirmed finding, evidence that the value was rotated afterwards.

capability_requirements.requirement: Non-secret configuration MUST be separable from secrets so that a non-secret change can be reviewed and diffed in cleartext without decrypting anything.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Roughly half of the 35 variables are not secrets at all  -  base domain, feature flags, schedules, limits. Encrypting them alongside credentials makes ordinary configuration review require the decryption key, which pushes people toward editing values directly on the server and creates the drift that later looks like a mysterious regression.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System fact: 35 variables in one file with no separation; my reasoning about review ergonomics under a two-person budget.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Produce the change history for one non-secret value (for example BASE_DOMAIN) showing the before and after in cleartext, using a command that a person with no decryption key can run. Then confirm the same command reveals nothing about any credential  -  not even its length.

capability_requirements.requirement: The secret store SHOULD record who changed each secret and when, without ever recording the value in cleartext.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: SHOULD rather than MUST because change audit is achievable today at low cost with an encrypted-in-repo approach, and because HIPAA's Required activity-review specification (164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D)) is directed at information system activity rather than specifically at secret edits. It is a strong expectation, not black-letter law.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: 45 CFR 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D) (Required); OWASP secrets-audit expectations.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Change one secret. Produce a record naming the actor, the timestamp and which secret changed. Confirm the record does not contain the old or new value, and confirm the record cannot be silently edited by the person who made the change.

capability_requirements.requirement: The platform SHOULD be able to log and review ACCESS to secrets  -  who read which secret and when  -  as a capability distinct from change audit.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: SHOULD, not MUST, because no secret store here holds ePHI, so 164.312(b) audit controls do not directly compel it, and because the only architectures that provide it are the ones this team should not run yet. But it is the specific capability that encrypted-in-repo structurally cannot provide, so it belongs in the platform requirements: if the eventual platform lacks it, that limitation is being chosen, not discovered.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: OWASP audit expectations (who requested a secret, whether approved, when used and by whom); 45 CFR 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D); the structural limitation of change-log-based approaches.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Read one secret through the sanctioned retrieval path. Then produce a record naming the reading principal, the secret identity and the time, from a source the reader cannot alter. If the only record is a git commit, the requirement is not met  -  that is a change log.

capability_requirements.requirement: An outage of any external secret store MUST NOT take down running application traffic; at most it MUST prevent new process starts.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: This system runs single-instance on one VM with no second application instance and no message broker; adding a network dependency in the request path would create a failure mode with no redundancy behind it. Fetching once at host build and caching in-process bounds the blast radius to restarts, which is acceptable; per-request retrieval is not.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System facts: single VM, single instance of every component, no observability or alerting; my architectural judgement about acceptable coupling.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: With the application serving traffic, make the secret store unreachable (block it at the network layer). Confirm requests continue to be served correctly for at least 30 minutes. Then restart one process and confirm it fails loudly and immediately rather than starting in a degraded state.

anti_requirements: A platform MUST NOT require that secrets be supplied only as environment variables with no file-based alternative. Docker and Microsoft both document environment variables as plaintext, broadly process-readable and prone to appearing in logs and dumps, and this system's own PII-logging-by-default setting makes accidental capture more likely, not less.

A platform MUST NOT print resolved configuration values in build, deploy, or diagnostic output. Any tool whose 'show me the effective config' command emits secrets in cleartext will be run during an incident, into a terminal, into scrollback, and  -  as has already happened here  -  into a chat transcript.

A platform's build service MUST NOT force build-time credentials through build arguments or environment variables with no secret-mount equivalent. Docker documents that build arguments persist in the image and are exposed in mode=max provenance; a build service without an equivalent to RUN --mount=type=secret makes the ABP licence and the per-customer NuGet feed identifier permanently leakable.

No layer of the deploy chain MAY silently substitute an empty value for a missing one. This includes the orchestrator's variable interpolation, any templating step, and the application's own configuration binding. This is the specific behaviour that has broken this stack twice.

A key-storage capability MUST NOT be non-exportable-only for the ABP string-encryption passphrase. ABP consumes it as a plaintext string via AbpStringEncryptionOptions; a hardware or platform key that can never be exported cannot hold it, and adopting one would convert a recoverable secret into an unrecoverable one in a new way. Hardware may protect the key that decrypts the file the passphrase lives in  -  not the passphrase itself.

A platform MUST NOT require Kubernetes in order to deliver file-mounted secrets. Adopting an orchestrator to obtain a secret-delivery mechanism inverts the cost of the decision; the same delivery shape is available in plain Compose today.

The secret store MUST NOT share a failure domain with the database backups. Backups currently land in a bind-mounted directory on the same box and the same disk; putting the secrets that decrypt or restore that data in the same place means one disk loss is simultaneously total data loss and total recovery-material loss.
A rotation mechanism MUST NOT require an image rebuild or a code change. If rotation is a release, it will not be performed promptly after an exposure.

The Data Protection key ring MUST NOT be treated as a rotatable credential or deleted on a schedule. It is auto-rotating state with a 90-day lifetime and a 2-day activation delay, and Microsoft documents key deletion as permanently destroying the data protected by that key with no override.
A managed store MUST NOT be placed in the per-request path such that its unavailability becomes an application outage. This system has no redundancy behind any dependency.
surprises: THE DATA PROTECTION KEY RING IS ALMOST CERTAINLY STORED IN CLEARTEXT IN REDIS  -  BY DOCUMENTED DESIGN, NOT BY BUG. Microsoft states that if you point Data Protection at an explicit key repository, 'the data protection system deregisters the default key encryption at rest mechanism. Consequently, keys are no longer encrypted at rest.' This system persists to Redis under CaseEvaluation-Protection-Keys. So the master keys that protect login state and email-confirmation tokens for BOTH processes sit unencrypted in Redis, in its AOF file on the redisdata volume, and in every copy of that volume. Read access to Redis is functionally the ability to forge authentication payloads for every office. The team believes it has a session-availability problem here ('losing Redis invalidates every session'); it also has a confidentiality problem, and only the availability half is currently on anyone's list. Ten-minute verification: dump the key and look for plaintext <masterKey> base64 versus an encrypted descriptor.

THE TWO 'UNRECOVERABLE' SECRETS ARE IN DIFFERENT NIST KEY CLASSES WITH OPPOSITE GUIDANCE, SO A SINGLE ESCROW POLICY IS WRONG ON ONE OF THEM. NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev 5 Table 7 marks private signature keys as 'No (in general)' for backup, and B.3.1.1 gives the alternative explicitly: 'Instead of backing up the private signature key, a second private signature key and corresponding public key could be generated and the public key distributed... for use if the primary private signature key becomes unavailable.' The same table marks symmetric data-encryption keys as 'OK'. So the standards-aligned move for the OpenIddict signing certificate is a pre-provisioned standby credential  -  which OpenIddict supports natively and prefers by furthest NotAfter  -  while the ABP passphrase is the one that actually wants escrow. The team's instinct will be to put both .pfx and passphrase in a safe; that is half right, and the half that is wrong is also the more expensive half.

BUILD SECRETS DO NOT INVALIDATE THE BUILD CACHE, SO ROTATING THE NUGET FEED KEY WILL NOT CAUSE A REBUILD. Docker: 'The contents of build secrets are not part of the build cache. Changing the value of a secret doesn't result in cache invalidation.' Only the secret's id and mount path participate. This is a security property (the value never enters the cache key) and an operational trap: after rotation the build keeps succeeding off a cached restore layer, and then fails weeks later when an unrelated Dockerfile change busts the cache  -  at a moment nobody connects to the rotation. Docker's own workaround is to pass a throwaway build argument alongside the secret and change it deliberately.

THE ABP COMMERCIAL NUGET FEED URL *IS* THE CREDENTIAL  -  THE PER-CUSTOMER IDENTIFIER IS IN THE PATH. The feed is of the form https://nuget.abp.io/<GUID>/v3/index.json, so NuGet.Config is a secret file wearing a config file's name. The usual mitigation people reach for  -  'it's only COPY'd into a builder stage, the final image is clean'  -  does not address the build cache, and if provenance is ever enabled at mode=max the Dockerfile content is recorded base64-encoded in the attestation. Check `git log -p --all -- '**/NuGet.Config'` before anything else; if it is in history, it is in every clone and every fork.

THE ABP LICENCE IS NOT A BUILD-TIME SECRET  -  IT IS ALSO A RUNTIME SECRET, AND IT IS THE ONLY SECRET IN THE SYSTEM THAT FAILS ON A CALENDAR. AbpLicenseCode is read at runtime from configuration or an environment variable and the licence check runs in the deployed application; an expired licence stops it functioning. So it belongs in BOTH secret sets, and unlike every other secret here it will fail with no triggering change to correlate against  -  which, in a system with no alerting, no metrics and no uptime monitoring, means the first signal is a customer call. The same is true of the wildcard TLS certificate and the token-signing certificate. Nothing currently watches any of these dates.

THE SQL SERVER SA PASSWORD CANNOT BE ROTATED BY CHANGING THE ENVIRONMENT VARIABLE. MSSQL_SA_PASSWORD is honoured only at first container initialisation; on a container reusing the existing sqldata volume the variable is ignored, so the container comes up with the OLD password while every application carries the NEW one. The first credible rotation attempt therefore produces a total outage with an authentication error that looks like a secrets-management bug rather than SQL Server behaviour. Microsoft's own documentation also notes the value stays discoverable inside the container via `echo $MSSQL_SA_PASSWORD` and directs you to ALTER LOGIN via sqlcmd instead. The correct rotation is a two-step: ALTER LOGIN inside the container first, then update the stored value.

THE FIX FOR THE FAILURE THAT HAS BROKEN THIS STACK TWICE IS ONE CHARACTER PER VARIABLE. Docker Compose documents ${VAR:?error} as 'value of VAR if set and non-empty, otherwise exit with error'. Converting every ${VAR} to ${VAR:?...} converts 'stack recreates with no DB password' into 'compose refuses to run and names the variable'. This costs under an hour, requires no new tool, no new dependency and no new expertise, and it is strictly more reliable than a wrapper script that checks the file exists  -  because it validates the variables actually referenced, not the file.

[Required] ALREADY DISTINGUISHES 'MISSING' FROM 'PRESENT BUT BLANK', FOR FREE. RequiredAttribute.AllowEmptyStrings defaults to false, so an empty string fails [Required] validation without any custom validator. Combined with .ValidateOnStart(), that is a complete fail-fast gate for the exact failure this system has  -  and the common instinct to write a custom IValidateOptions with string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace checks is redundant work. What DOES need custom validation is cross-field coherence (for example: if SMTP is enabled then host, port and credentials must all be present)  -  that is where IValidateOptions earns its keep.

COMPOSE SECRETS ARE NOT SWARM SECRETS, AND THE DIFFERENCE MATTERS TO AN ASSESSOR. Docker documents the encrypted-Raft-log storage, mutual-TLS distribution and in-memory-filesystem mount as properties of swarm SERVICES, and states plainly that 'Docker secrets are only available to swarm services, not to standalone containers.' Adopting `secrets:` in plain Compose is genuinely worth doing  -  it removes values from `docker inspect`, `/proc/<pid>/environ`, `docker compose config` and crash dumps  -  but it is a delivery-shape change, not encryption at rest. Describing it as 'we use Docker secrets, they're encrypted' in a security questionnaire would be a misstatement.

ENCRYPTED-IN-REPO GIVES YOU A CHANGE LOG, NOT AN ACCESS LOG  -  AND THOSE ARE DIFFERENT COMPLIANCE ARTEFACTS. OWASP frames secret auditing around who requested a secret, for what role, and when it was used. Git history can only ever answer who edited the ciphertext. If an assessor asks 'who has read the SMTP credentials in the last year', SOPS-in-git has no answer, and neither does a mode-600 file. That single question is the concrete trigger that forces a store  -  it is worth deciding in advance whether you are willing to answer 'we cannot determine that' and document it as an accepted risk, because that answer is defensible today and much harder to give after go-live.

'ADDRESSABLE' IS NOT 'OPTIONAL', AND THE DOCUMENT IS THE ARTEFACT. Encryption of ePHI at rest is Addressable (45 CFR 164.312(a)(2)(iv)), as is password management (164.308(a)(5)(ii)(D)). But 164.306(d)(3) requires assessing whether each addressable specification is reasonable and appropriate and then either implementing it or documenting why not AND implementing an equivalent alternative. A two-person team that has not written that assessment is non-compliant on the paperwork even where the technical posture is defensible. Meanwhile the January 2025 NPRM (90 FR 898, RIN 0945-AA22) proposes deleting the addressable category entirely  -  but it is NOT final, and OMB's agenda now points at July 2027. Designing as if everything were required is a reasonable hedge; citing it as current law is the kind of error that discredits a whole compliance document.

THE ABSENCE OF PHI MAKES ROTATION FREE RIGHT NOW, AND THAT WINDOW IS THE CHEAPEST SECURITY BUDGET THIS PROJECT WILL EVER HAVE. The values pasted into chat transcripts are flagged for rotation; today that rotation costs an outage of a system holding only synthetic records, discoverable by two people at a time of their choosing. After the first real practice takes a real booking, the identical operation needs a maintenance window, a customer notification, and a rollback plan  -  and the MSSQL_SA_PASSWORD and MinIO root-credential traps above mean the first attempt is likely to need one. Rotate everything now, deliberately, as a rehearsal of the runbook, while failure is free.

THE THING MOST LIKELY TO SILENTLY UNDO ALL OF THIS IS THE SECOND ENVIRONMENT. Today there is exactly one environment, so there is exactly one secret set and drift is impossible. The moment a staging environment exists  -  which every other area of this review will recommend  -  the number of secret sets doubles, the deploy script must select between them, and the failure mode 'staging credentials pointed at the production database' becomes reachable for the first time. Design the naming and selection mechanism now, while there is only one set to name, rather than retrofitting it under the pressure of standing up an environment.

not_recommended.pattern: Deploy a self-hosted secret-store daemon (Vault / OpenBao class) as the system of record for all 35 variables.
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It is the only option on the list that provides genuine ACCESS audit  -  who read which secret, when  -  which is exactly the capability encrypted-in-repo structurally cannot give and which a HIPAA assessor may eventually ask for. It gives versioned KV with rollback, per-secret policy, dynamic short-lived database credentials that would eliminate the standing sa password entirely, and a built-in Shamir escrow model (default 5 shares, threshold 3) that solves the two-person-recovery problem in a principled way rather than by photocopying a passphrase. OpenBao is genuinely current (v2.6.2, August 2026), free, and self-hostable. If this team is going to end up needing one, adopting it before there is PHI is the cheapest moment.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It puts a new stateful daemon in front of the application's ability to boot, on the same single VM where every dependency already has no redundancy  -  and the boot chain is already serialised through db-migrator's service_completed_successfully gate. Worse, its characteristic failures are precisely the quiet kind the brief says this team will not catch: a vault sealed after an unplanned host reboot, an expired token, a revoked lease, a policy that returns 403 for one path while the other 34 secrets work. Unsealing after an unexpected reboot is a manual multi-share ceremony performed by two SDE 1s with no on-call rotation at whatever hour the VM restarted. Realistic cost is 30-60h to stand up and 4-8h/month to keep, against a stated budget of roughly one developer-week per month already largely consumed by code-standard remediation. Adopting it would consume the entire secrets budget and deliver a system that fails more subtly than the mode-600 file it replaced.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: When any two of: the team reaches three or more engineers with at least one who has operated one in production; an on-call rotation exists; a customer or assessor asks in writing for secret ACCESS logs; or per-office dynamic database credentials become a contractual requirement. Also immediately if the platform selected in the next exercise provides this as a managed service the team does not operate  -  the objection is to running the daemon, not to the capability.

not_recommended.pattern: Per-office (per-tenant) credential sets  -  a distinct database login, MinIO key and integration token for each of the 11-to-33 offices.
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It is the textbook blast-radius answer for multi-tenant systems and it maps cleanly onto the tenancy model, which is already one database per office. A credential compromised through one office's staff, one office's support incident, or one office's misdirected email would not grant access to another practice's PHI. Given that each office is a separate medical practice and plausibly a separate covered entity, cryptographic separation between them is the kind of thing that reads very well in a security questionnaire, and Microsoft's multi-tenant SaaS guidance generally favours tenant-scoped identities.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It fights the load-bearing design decision the whole system is built on. Office connection strings are DERIVED from one template by swapping the database name, which is precisely what makes relocating every office database a one-key configuration change and makes adding an office a host-UI action rather than a deployment. Per-office credentials would multiply the secret count from 35 to well over 300 at 33 offices, put credential provisioning inside IOfficeDatabaseProvisioner.ProvisionAsync (breaking its idempotency-on-retry property, because a partial failure would now leave a credential half-created), and require the twelve recurring jobs to resolve a different credential per office inside every ICurrentTenant.Change scope  -  in a sweep loop that today has no per-tenant error handling at all. The security gain is also smaller than it looks while every service still connects as sa: per-office logins on top of a shared sa is theatre.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: When offices become separately-contracted covered entities that demand cryptographic separation in writing, or when office databases are relocated to genuinely different SQL instances (which the derived-connection-string design already permits), or immediately after the sa account is eliminated in favour of least-privilege service logins  -  at which point per-office scoping becomes an incremental change rather than a redesign.

not_recommended.pattern: Dynamic, short-lived database credentials issued by a broker at process start or per-connection.
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: OWASP explicitly recommends this: 'Dynamic secrets should be used where possible to reduce the surface area of credential reuse.' It eliminates the standing database password entirely, which is the single highest-value credential in the system; it makes rotation automatic rather than an event; and it neatly sidesteps the MSSQL_SA_PASSWORD init-only trap because the sa password stops being the credential anything uses. It also produces per-process attributable identities, which is the mechanism that makes 45 CFR 164.312(d) achievable at the service layer rather than only at the human-user layer.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: The steady-state connection pattern here is driven by background jobs, not user traffic: three jobs run every 15 minutes and each opens a connection per office database inside an ICurrentTenant.Change scope  -  11 sequential connections per sweep today, 33 at target. Inserting a credential broker into that path adds a lease-expiry failure mode inside a loop that has no per-tenant error handling and produces no report of which offices succeeded. A lease that expires mid-sweep would fail silently for a subset of offices, which is the exact 'split state with no report' failure the migration runner already exhibits and that this team has no observability to detect. It also requires the broker from the rejected option above.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: After two prerequisites, in order: the recurring-job loops gain per-office error handling and a completion report, and the sa account is replaced by named least-privilege logins per service. With those in place, dynamic credentials become a strict improvement rather than a new class of silent partial failure.

not_recommended.pattern: A fixed calendar rotation policy  -  rotate every secret every 90 days.
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It is simple, auditable, requires no judgement, and is what most security questionnaires and many internal policies expect to see. It bounds the exposure window for a credential that leaked without anyone noticing, which is a real risk here given that values have already reached chat transcripts. NIST does define cryptoperiods, and a stated interval is much easier to evidence to an assessor than 'we rotate when something happens'.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: NIST does not actually support the uniform version of this: 8.2.2.2 frames the recovery and change decision as case-by-case, based on key type, application, ownership and role. Applied uniformly to this system the policy is actively dangerous  -  rotating the ABP string-encryption passphrase on a calendar makes previously encrypted values unreadable, rotating the DataProtection key ring manually logs out every user for no benefit against a system that already auto-rotates every 90 days, and rotating MSSQL_SA_PASSWORD by editing the variable produces an outage because it is init-only. OWASP notes that manual rotation 'is a challenging process when implemented manually, and can lead to mistakes'. Two people executing a quarterly manual rotation of 35 heterogeneous secrets will cause more downtime than the policy prevents exposure.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: Once rotation for a given secret class is AUTOMATED and its runbook has been executed successfully at least twice, a calendar for that class becomes safe and worth adopting. The right sequence is: classify -> automate the easy ones (SMTP, partner token, MinIO service accounts) -> then put a calendar on the automated subset only, and keep trigger-based rotation for the rest with a documented cryptoperiod.

not_recommended.pattern: A sealed-secrets style asymmetric controller, or any Kubernetes-native secrets tooling.
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: Sealed-secrets is genuinely current and maintained (v0.39.1, August 2026), and its model is elegant: developers encrypt with a public key and only the in-cluster controller can decrypt, so the ciphertext is safe to commit and no developer ever needs the private key. It is a strictly better trust model than shared-symmetric or multi-recipient-age for teams that already run Kubernetes, and it removes the bootstrap-key custody problem from humans entirely.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: There is no Kubernetes here, and adopting an orchestrator in order to obtain a secrets mechanism inverts the cost of the decision by two orders of magnitude  -  it would add a control plane, an ingress model, a storage class and a networking model to a two-person team that currently runs ten Compose services on one VM. It also directly conflicts with several load-bearing properties of the current design, notably the Host-header-only tenancy resolution, which would have to survive an ingress controller's Host handling. This is the clearest example in the area of a pattern that is standard at larger organisations and wrong here.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: Only if Kubernetes is adopted for reasons that have nothing to do with secrets. If that happens, sealed-secrets or an external-secrets operator becomes the obvious choice and this recommendation should be revisited  -  but the decision must be driven by the platform exercise, not by this one.

not_recommended.pattern: Pass the ABP licence and NuGet feed credentials as build ARGs, on the grounds that the registry is private and the image never leaves it.
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It is the simplest thing that works, it needs no BuildKit syntax directive, it is what most ABP Docker examples on the internet actually show, and the threat model is not obviously wrong: if the registry is private and only two people can pull, who exactly reads the layer? Rewriting the Dockerfile costs hours that could go to features.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: Docker states it without hedging: 'Build arguments and environment variables are inappropriate for passing secrets to your build, because they persist in the final image.' The values are recoverable from `docker history` by anyone who obtains the image  -  including anyone who obtains a backup of the registry, a laptop with a cached pull, or the image after any future decision to publish it. And provenance makes it worse in a way that is easy to miss: 'mode=max exposes the values of build arguments', so enabling attestations later retroactively widens the exposure of a decision made earlier. The private-registry argument also assumes the registry's access control is stronger than it is likely to be for a team with no access audit anywhere. The alternative costs three to four hours once and Docker documents it fully.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: Never for credentials. Build arguments remain correct for non-secret build inputs  -  version numbers, target framework, feature toggles  -  and using them for that is not a compromise.

not_recommended.pattern: Treat the DataProtection key ring as a secret: put it in the secret store and rotate it on the same schedule as everything else.
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It is unambiguously key material, it protects authentication payloads, and every instinct trained on 'rotate your keys' says a 90-day-old master key protecting session cookies should be replaced. Putting it in the same store as everything else gives one place to look, one backup path, and one access policy  -  which is genuinely valuable to a two-person team that cannot afford to remember exceptions.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It is state, not a credential, and the framework already manages its lifecycle: keys are created with an activation date of now+2 days and an expiry of now+90 days, the system rolls them automatically with no interruption of service, and created/active/expired keys can ALL still unprotect incoming payloads  -  which is the entire point. Manual rotation therefore buys nothing the system is not already doing, and manual deletion is catastrophic: Microsoft warns that 'all data protected by the key is permanently undecipherable, and there's no emergency override... Deleting a key is truly destructive behavior.' Forcing it into a secret store also breaks the mechanism, because both processes must read and WRITE the same ring; a read-only secret store cannot host it. The genuine defect is different and is being masked by this framing: the ring is unencrypted at rest because an explicit persistence location was chosen, and the fix is ProtectKeysWithCertificate plus UnprotectKeysWithAnyCertificate, plus backing the ring up as state.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: The wrapping certificate  -  not the ring  -  should live in the secret store and should be rotated, and UnprotectKeysWithAnyCertificate exists precisely to make that rotation non-destructive. That is the version of this instinct worth acting on.

not_recommended.pattern: Hardware-backed key storage (PIV token, TPM, HSM) as the root of the secret hierarchy, adopted now.
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: Deployment today is entirely manual over SSH, so a human is always present and a touch-to-decrypt requirement costs literally nothing in the current workflow. It removes the highest-value secret in the organisation from any disk, defeats laptop theft and repository compromise simultaneously, and for a two-person team a pair of tokens is a genuinely proportionate control. It is also the only option here that makes the bootstrap key non-exfiltratable rather than merely well-hidden.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It quietly constrains a decision that has not been made yet. Every other area of this review points toward continuous deployment, and an unattended pipeline cannot touch a token  -  so the near-certain outcome is that a second, softer, non-hardware-backed recipient gets added to make CI work, at which point the hardware protects nothing while still imposing its custody burden. There is also a hard technical constraint specific to this system: the ABP string-encryption passphrase must be handed to the framework as a plaintext string, so it can never live as a non-exportable hardware key; hardware can only protect the file it lives in. Adopting it now spends real setup effort and a real lost-token risk on a control whose lifetime is bounded by the CD decision.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: After the CD design exists and explicitly answers how unattended decryption works. If the answer is 'a dedicated deploy identity with its own key, separate from the human ones', then hardware-backing the HUMAN identities is strictly good and costs nothing  -  do it then, with the enrolment of a spare token as a mandatory part of the procedure.

not_recommended.pattern: A centralised dynamic configuration service (Consul/etcd/App Configuration class) for the non-secret half of the 35 variables, with hot reload.
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It gives one authoritative place for configuration, change history, and the ability to flip a value without a restart  -  which matters when restarting the API also restarts the Hangfire processing server and interrupts twelve recurring jobs mid-sweep across every office database. ABP already has a settings system, so the team is conceptually familiar with runtime-changeable configuration.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: Thirty-five variables is small, and roughly half are not even secrets. A config service would be a third configuration plane alongside appsettings files and ABP's own database-backed settings, which makes the question 'where does this value actually come from?' genuinely unanswerable at 3am by two people with no distributed tracing, no log aggregation and no metrics. It is another daemon on a single VM, another bootstrap credential, and another thing that can be up-but-wrong. Hot reload is also the enemy of the fail-fast property this area most needs: a value that can change at runtime is a value that cannot be validated once at startup and then trusted.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: When there are multiple environments AND multiple application instances AND a demonstrated need to change a value without a restart  -  all three, not any one. Until then, a restart is an acceptable configuration-change mechanism and its bluntness is a feature, because it makes configuration changes visible events.

what_would_change_the_answer: WHETHER ANYTHING IS ACTUALLY ENCRYPTED WITH THE ABP STRING-ENCRYPTION PASSPHRASE. The brief classifies it as unrecoverable, but that is only true if persisted data depends on it. In the ABP framework itself only SettingEncryptionService (settings declared with IsEncrypted) and the AWS/Aliyun blob client factories use IStringEncryptionService  -  and ABP does not encrypt tenant connection strings by default, which is doubly irrelevant here because office connection strings are DERIVED rather than stored. TEST: grep src for IStringEncryptionService, for SettingDefinition(...IsEncrypted: true), and for AbpStringEncryptionOptions configuration; and check whether the ABP Commercial modules in use declare encrypted settings. If nothing depends on it, it is not an unrecoverable secret at all  -  set it to a strong value, record it, and delete the whole escrow workstream. If something does, the escrow tier is mandatory. This single check changes several hours of recommended work and should be done first.

WHETHER THE DEFAULT ABP PASSPHRASE IS STILL IN USE. AbpStringEncryptionOptions.DefaultPassPhrase is the published constant 'gsKnGZ041HLL4IM8'. If it was never overridden, then anything encrypted today is encrypted with a value in ABP's public documentation  -  which converts 'unrecoverable secret' into 'no secret at all', and changes the recommendation from escrow to a one-time re-encryption exercise done now, while data is synthetic.

WHETHER REDIS REQUIRES AUTHENTICATION AND IS REACHABLE ONLY ON THE COMPOSE NETWORK. If Redis has no password or is exposed beyond the internal network, the unencrypted DataProtection key ring stops being a latent confidentiality issue and becomes an urgent one, because read access to Redis is the ability to forge authentication payloads across every office. This flips the keyring-encryption work from Tier 3 to immediate.

WHETHER THE FOUR DEFAULT ABP __tenant RESOLVERS ARE ACTUALLY DISABLED. The brief records honestly that this has never been tested. It is not a secrets question directly, but it changes what a leaked credential is worth: if a query-string or header tenant override still functions, an attacker holding any office's credentials may be able to reach other offices' data, which raises the blast radius of every credential in the store and strengthens the case for per-office credentials that I have otherwise rejected.

WHETHER A SECOND ENVIRONMENT IS CREATED. One environment means one secret set and no possibility of cross-wiring. Two means the deploy mechanism must select between sets, and 'staging credentials pointed at the production database' becomes reachable. This is the specific threshold at which manual file management stops scaling and a store starts paying for itself.

WHETHER CONTINUOUS DEPLOYMENT ARRIVES. CD removes the human from the deploy path, which kills the hardware-token option outright and moves the build-time credentials (ABP licence, NuGet feed identifier) onto a machine the developers do not control  -  changing the answer for build secrets from 'a local file plus a BuildKit mount' to 'a CI-managed secret with its own access audit'.

WHETHER AN ASSESSOR OR CUSTOMER ASKS IN WRITING FOR SECRET ACCESS LOGS. Encrypted-in-repo structurally cannot answer 'who read the SMTP password'. That one question is the concrete trigger that forces a store, and the answer 'we cannot determine that, and here is our documented risk acceptance under 164.306(d)(3)' is defensible today and much harder to give after go-live.

WHETHER THE TEAM GROWS PAST TWO, OR GAINS SOMEONE WHO HAS OPERATED A SECRET STORE. The rejection of a self-hosted store rests almost entirely on operational capacity and failure-mode visibility, not on the technology. Three engineers with one who has run one before flips that judgement.

WHETHER THE JANUARY 2025 HIPAA SECURITY RULE NPRM IS FINALISED. It would remove the addressable/required distinction and make encryption and MFA mandatory, eliminating the documented-risk-acceptance escape that several of these recommendations currently rely on. Currently targeted July 2027 on OMB's agenda and non-binding  -  but if it lands, the 'document why not' option disappears and encryption at rest becomes a hard requirement rather than a design choice.

WHETHER THE sa ACCOUNT IS REPLACED BY NAMED LEAST-PRIVILEGE SERVICE LOGINS. Several rejected patterns  -  per-office credentials, dynamic credentials  -  become sensible incremental changes rather than redesigns once each service authenticates as itself. Until then, layering credential sophistication on top of a shared sa is decoration.

WHETHER MINIO'S ROOT-CREDENTIAL ROTATION BEHAVIOUR IS WHAT THE ISSUE THREADS DESCRIBE. I could not reach MinIO's canonical reference page (one URL 404'd, another rate-limited), so the entanglement between root credentials and backend config/IAM encryption is only partially verified. If rotation turns out to be a simple restart with no migration semantics, the MinIO row in the rotation classification gets much easier and the case for moving the application off root credentials onto a scoped service account gets easier still. TEST it on a scratch MinIO instance with a populated IAM store before touching production.

results.claim: [1] Docker: build args/env vars inappropriate for secrets because they persist in the final image; RUN --mount=type=secret mounts at /run/secrets/<id> for one instruction, not written to any layer; target= and env= options exist.
results.evidence_quote: Build arguments and environment variables are inappropriate for passing secrets to your build, because they persist in the final image. ... make it temporarily available inside the build container, for the duration of the build instruction.

results.claim: [2] mode=max exposes build-arg values; Docker directs users to refactor to secret mounts; secret mounts never in provenance attestations; PROVENANCE IS NOT GENERATED BY DEFAULT.
results.evidence_quote: Note that mode=max exposes the values of build arguments. / If you're misusing build arguments to pass credentials, authentication tokens, or other secrets, you should refactor your build to pass the secrets using secret mounts instead. / Secret mounts don't leak outside of the build and are never included in provenance attestations. / [attestations overview] Provenance attestations with the mode=min level are added to images by default.
results.correction: The first three quotes are verbatim correct. The fourth assertion is WRONG and reverses a design-relevant default: Buildx DOES generate provenance by default at mode=min (https://docs.docker.com/build/metadata/attestations/ - 'Provenance attestations with the mode=min level are added to images by default'; opt out with --provenance=false or BUILDX_NO_DEFAULT_ATTESTATIONS). Correct statement: provenance IS emitted by default at mode=min, which does not include build-arg values; only mode=max, which must be requested explicitly, exposes them. A requirement that credentials must not appear 'in build provenance output' therefore has to account for an attestation that is produced whether or not anyone asks for one.

results.claim: [3] Build-secret CONTENTS are not part of the build cache key; changing a secret's value does not invalidate cache; only the secret's id and mount path participate in the cache checksum; workaround is a companion build arg.
results.evidence_quote: The contents of build secrets are not part of the build cache. Changing the value of a secret doesn't result in cache invalidation. / Properties of secrets such as IDs and mount paths participate in the cache checksum, and result in cache invalidation if changed. / you can pass a build argument with an arbitrary value that you also change when changing the secret.
results.correction: Substantively correct. One wording nit: the doc says 'Properties of secrets SUCH AS IDs and mount paths', which is non-exhaustive, so the word 'only' in the claim is slightly stronger than the source.

We recommend that you specify an explicit key encryption mechanism for production deployments. / Windows DPAPI: Only applies to Windows deployments. / Windows DPAPI-NG: This mechanism is available only on Windows 8/Windows Server 2012 or later.

The claim that 'ProtectKeysWithCertificate is available cross-platform' is NOT stated on this page - the page is titled 'Key encryption at rest in Windows and Azure', the X.509 section makes no platform statement, and it adds a restriction the claim omits: 'Due to .NET Framework limitations, only certificates with CAPI private keys are supported.' Either drop the cross-platform assertion or source it elsewhere and carry the CAPI caveat with it, since the design depends on this mechanism working on Linux containers.

results.claim: [11] Key ring auto-rotates (activation now+2d, expiry now+90d, min lifetime 7d, ~24h refresh); created/active/expired keys can all unprotect; deleting a key is destructive with no override; UnprotectKeysWithAnyCertificate allows wrapping-cert rotation; SetApplicationName sets ApplicationDiscriminator and lets two apps sharing a repository read each other's payloads.

The default key lifetime cannot be shorter than 7 days. / The system will automatically check the backing store for changes approximately every 24 hours or when the current default key expires, whichever comes first. / Created, active, and expired keys may all be used to unprotect incoming payloads. / At that point, all data protected by the key is permanently undecipherable, and there's no emergency override like there's with revoked keys. Deleting a key is truly destructive behavior.
results.correction: Every numeric threshold (90 days, 7-day minimum, 2-day activation, ~24h refresh) and both quoted warnings check out verbatim on this page. But two sub-claims are attributed to a page that does not contain them: 'UnprotectKeysWithAnyCertificate' appears nowhere on the key-management page, and neither does SetApplicationName, ApplicationDiscriminator, or the quoted sentence 'By default, the Data Protection system isolates apps from one another based on their content root paths, even if they share the same physical key repository.' That sentence and both APIs live on the Data Protection configuration/overview page. Re-cite those two to the configuration overview - they carry the requirement that the wrapping certificate be rotatable without invalidating old sessions, so a bad citation there is a real audit gap.

results.claim: [12] NIST SP 800-57 Pt1 Rev5 Table 7 marks private signature keys as generally not backed up; B.3.1.1 recommends generating a second signature key pair instead; Table 7 marks symmetric data-encryption keys OK to back up; 8.3.1 archive protections; 8.2.2.2 case-by-case.

When required, any backed up keys shall be stored under the owner's control. / Symmetric data encryption key | OK / Instead of backing up the private signature key, a second private signature key and corresponding public key could be generated and the public key distributed in accordance with Section 8.1.5.1 for use if the primary private signature key becomes unavailable. / The key archive shall continue to provide the appropriate protections for each key ... The archive will require a strong access-control mechanism to limit access to only authorized entities. / The decision as to whether key recovery is required should be made on a case-by-case basis.
results.correction: All five citations verified verbatim against the PDF (Table 7 on pp. 105-106, B.3.1.1 on pp. 136-137, 8.3.1, 8.2.2.2). Worth carrying forward: Table 7's full entry contains an explicit exception the claim truncates - 'However, backup may be warranted in some cases, such as a CA's private signing key' - which materially softens claim [29]'s 'never escrow the signing key' conclusion.

results.claim: [13] NIST defines split knowledge as splitting a key into n shares where any k-1 shares reveal nothing; manual key distribution requires each share be distributed separately to its intended recipient.
results.evidence_quote: Split knowledge: A process by which a cryptographic key is split into n key shares, each of which provides no knowledge of the key. ... If knowledge of k (where k is less than or equal to n) shares is required to construct the key, then knowledge of any k - 1 key shares provides no information about the key other than, possibly, its length. / If split-knowledge procedures are used for key distribution ... each key share shall be distributed separately to its intended recipient.

results.claim: [14] OpenIddict supports multiple signing/encryption credentials, orders X.509 certs by NotBefore/NotAfter, skips not-yet-valid certs, prefers furthest expiration; recommends two RSA certificates in production distinct from the HTTPS cert.

results.claim: [15] AbpStringEncryptionOptions has a published default passphrase gsKnGZ041HLL4IM8, default salt hgt!16kl, IV jkE49230Tf093b42, Keysize 256; ABP recommends changing it; IStringEncryptionService is referenced in the framework only by SettingEncryptionService and the AWS/Aliyun blob client factories.

Verify the runtime-check behaviour empirically by starting the app with AbpLicenseCode unset, as the claim itself advises, before writing it into a requirement.

results.claim: [18] MSSQL_SA_PASSWORD is honoured only at first container initialisation and does not change the password on a reused data volume; Microsoft documents that the value stays discoverable in the container and recommends ALTER LOGIN via sqlcmd.

results.correction: The discoverability quote and the ALTER LOGIN remediation are verbatim correct. The PRIMARY assertion of the claim - that the variable is honoured only at first initialisation and is inert on a container reusing an existing data volume - is NOT in this document at all; the page addresses only post-creation password hygiene. That behaviour is corroborated by microsoft/mssql-docker#471, which is a community issue thread, not vendor documentation. Rotating the sa password must therefore be specified as an in-database ALTER LOGIN operation (with the env var updated to match), and the init-only behaviour should be labelled as issue-thread evidence, not documented behaviour.

results.claim: [19] MinIO root credentials are env-only and are used to encrypt backend config/IAM data, making rotation a server-level migration; mismatched _OLD variables produce an 'invalid AEAD algorithm ID' safe-mode failure.
results.evidence_quote: [issue title] Impossible to rotate root credentials ... ERROR Unable to initialize gateway backend: The access key ID you provided does not exist in our records. [labels: community, working as intended] [repo banner] This repository was archived by the owner on Apr 25, 2026. It is now read-only.
results.correction: Two problems. (1) The cited issue does establish that rotating root credentials via env vars breaks a running server and that maintainers call it 'working as intended', but it does NOT mention MINIO_ROOT_USER_OLD/MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD_OLD, backend config/IAM encryption keyed on the root credentials, or the 'invalid AEAD algorithm ID' error - the error shown is a different one ('The access key ID you provided does not exist in our records'). Those specifics are unsupported by this URL. (2) More seriously, and not flagged anywhere in the research: minio/minio was ARCHIVED by its owner on 25 April 2026 and is read-only, with users directed to AIStor. An archived, no-longer-patched object store is a currency finding that outranks the rotation mechanics and belongs in the design write-up; the claim's currency bar (a release within 12 months) was applied to the five tools in claim [26] but never to this incumbent component.

If the machine or process is compromised, environment variables are accessible to untrusted parties. / Secret Manager doesn't encrypt the stored secrets and shouldn't be treated as a trusted store. It's for development purposes only.

Vault requires a certain threshold of shares to reconstruct the unseal key. [page contains no numeric defaults and no mention of audit devices]
results.correction: The cited page supports the existence of Shamir-based sealing but settles NEITHER stated threshold. It gives no numeric defaults, so '5 shares / threshold 3' is stated from memory here (the 5/3 default is real but belongs to the `vault operator init` CLI/API reference, which defaults key-shares=5 and key-threshold=3 - cite that page instead). The page also does not mention audit devices at all, so the entire audit-device half of the claim - both the 'logs every request and response' capability and the Vault-vs-OpenBao bootstrapping difference - has no support at this URL.
