results.claim: [42] Storage projection: ~91 audit rows and ~168 property-change rows per appointment; ~0.25-0.35 MB per appointment; ~4-5 GB/yr at 11 offices x 5/day; ~17-22 GB/yr at 20/day; 6-year retention ~100-130 GB (11 offices) and ~300-400 GB (33); free disk ~9.7 GB
results.correction: No source given, and the measured inputs (1,450 audit rows / 2,689 property-change rows from 16 appointments, 9.7 GB free disk) are not independently checkable here. The per-appointment coefficients are arithmetically right (1450/16 = 90.6; 2689/16 = 168.1). The stated per-appointment size is right at the low end and the row-size assumptions are the author's own: 91 x 1.5 KB + 168 x 0.3 KB = 187 KB, x1.4 index overhead = 0.26 MB, so the honest band is ~0.26-0.30 MB, not 0.25-0.35. The downstream figures then drift high by roughly 15-25%: 55,000 appointments/yr x 0.26-0.35 MB = 14-19 GB/yr (claimed 17-22); six years at that rate = 86-115 GB for 11 offices (claimed 100-130) and 258-346 GB for 33 (claimed 300-400). The claim's own caveat is the right one and should be binding: measure with sp_spaceused before any capacity decision depends on this. Two further gaps  -  the 250-business-day figure behind 13,750/yr and 55,000/yr is never stated, and the projection assumes a flat rate with no growth. Keep this labelled unverified; it must not be cited as a finding.

material_errors: CLAIM 12 - WRONG/SUPERSEDED VERSION: OpenTelemetry.Instrumentation.AspNetCore is at 1.18.0 published 2026-08-21, not 1.17.0 dated 2026-07-17. Compounding this, the cited URL (opentelemetry.io/status/) publishes no package versions or dates whatsoever - it carries only per-language signal maturity - so the version and date were stated from memory against a page that cannot support them.

CLAIM 14 - BEHAVIOUR ASSERTED THAT THE DOC DOES NOT STATE: the redaction processor README does NOT direct users to the attributes processor with delete actions for logs and metrics. I fetched the raw README from main and grepped it: the string 'attributes processor' does not occur anywhere in the file. The README presents the redaction processor itself as the mechanism for spans, logs and metric datapoints. The stability levels (beta traces / alpha logs, metrics) are correct; the redirection sentence is invented.

CLAIM 15 - SUPERSEDED EXPERIMENTAL MARKING: HmacRedactor is no longer experimental in Microsoft.Extensions.Compliance.Redaction 10.9.0. In the dotnet/extensions main source, neither HmacRedactor.cs nor RedactionExtensions.SetHmacRedactor carries an [Experimental] attribute, so no EXTEXP0002 diagnostic is raised. EXTEXP0002 still exists as the repo's generic 'Compliance' experiment constant but is not applied to these APIs.

CLAIM 25 - UNCONDITIONAL CLAIM THAT IS ACTUALLY CONDITIONAL: ABP does not unconditionally swallow audit-store failures. AuditingStore.SaveAsync only enters the try/catch when AbpAuditingOptions.HideErrors is true; when false it awaits SaveLogAsync bare and the exception propagates. HideErrors defaults to true, so the described behaviour is the default, but it is one config flag away from the opposite - material to any remediation that assumes the catch is unavoidable. Separately, the leak is understated: AuditLogInfo.ToString() also emits each action's serialised Parameters JSON and every entity change as 'PropertyName: OriginalValue -> NewValue', so an audit-write failure can copy request payloads and old/new field values into the ordinary application log, not merely URL, username, user id and IP.

CLAIM 27 - THRESHOLDS AND CONVENTIONS NOT IN THE CITED FILE: Install.sql supports only the schema. The ~5-second server heartbeat, the Key='recurring-jobs' convention (the substring 'recurring' does not appear in the file at all), and Score-as-next-execution-timestamp are all asserted from memory against a file that contains none of them. Two schema details are also wrong: [Set] has an [Id] IDENTITY primary key column, and the current score index is the composite IX_HangFire_Set_Score on ([Key],[Score]).

CLAIM 32 - MAINTENANCE/READINESS OVERSTATED: OpenTelemetry.Instrumentation.EventCounters has never shipped a stable release; its current NuGet version is 1.18.0-alpha.1 (2026-08-21), prerelease-only. The claim presents EventCountersInstrumentation as an available consumption bridge without flagging that. The cited SqlClient page also never mentions OpenTelemetry at all, so that half of the claim is entirely unsourced.

CLAIM 42 - ARITHMETIC DRIFTS HIGH: the stated assumptions yield 0.26 MB per appointment (91 x 1.5 KB + 168 x 0.3 KB = 187 KB, x1.4 = 262 KB), so 55,000 appointments/yr is 14-19 GB/yr rather than the claimed 17-22, and six years at 11 offices is 86-115 GB rather than 100-130 (33 offices: 258-346 GB, not 300-400). The undisclosed 250-business-day assumption behind 13,750 and 55,000 should be stated. The claim is correctly self-labelled unverified and must not be cited as a finding.
vendor_neutrality_violations: No violations found. I read all fifteen capability requirements line by line looking for a named product presented as the answer, and there is not one: no cloud provider, no database engine, no telemetry backend, no logging library, no APM or alerting vendor appears anywhere in the requirements. Every requirement is phrased as a capability plus an observable acceptance test ('MUST leave a durable, externally queryable record', 'MUST be writable by the database host but not modifiable or deletable by it', 'SHOULD emit through a vendor-neutral wire protocol'), which is the correct form. The vendor names that do appear - Microsoft, OpenTelemetry, Serilog, ABP, Hangfire, Google SRE, OWASP, NIST - appear only in the CLAIMS section, and in every instance as documentary evidence of a behaviour class or as a named artifact whose version/maintenance status is the fact being checked. That is explicitly permitted. The entries below are ADVISORY observations, not violations; I list them because they are where neutrality is most likely to be lost at the next drafting step.

ADVISORY (not a naming violation): requirements 5 and 6 - 'detection of after-the-fact modification or deletion of audit rows by a party holding database administrator privileges' plus 'storage for audit-integrity digests that is writable by the database host but not modifiable or deletable by it' - are, taken together, drawn to the exact contour of one product pairing (a cryptographically-verified ledger table feature plus immutable/WORM object storage). The wording is capability-shaped and passes, but the pair is effectively single-solution as written. To keep it genuinely open, state the acceptance test in outcome terms - 'a verification procedure that fails detectably if any historical audit row is altered, using integrity material that the database host cannot retroactively rewrite' - so that append-only application-level hash chaining, external WORM log shipping, or a signed off-host archive can all be evaluated against it. Note also that claim 30's own evidence undercuts an over-narrow reading: whoever can rewrite the digests defeats the scheme regardless of which product produces them, so the digest-custody requirement is the load-bearing one, not the ledger feature.

ADVISORY (not a naming violation): requirement 8's 'at least one real office slug in addition to the reserved host slug' imports one framework's multi-tenancy vocabulary ('host' tenant, tenant 'slug') into a requirement that is otherwise product-neutral. No product is named and no product is recommended, so this is not a violation, but a reader outside that framework cannot evaluate the requirement. Restate as 'at least one real tenant hostname in addition to the default/administrative tenant hostname' and the requirement becomes portable without losing any of its force.

ADVISORY (not a naming violation): requirement 15 already says 'vendor-neutral wire protocol' rather than naming one, which is exactly right and should be preserved verbatim through drafting. The failure mode to watch for is the next document silently collapsing it to a specific protocol or a specific collector distribution. Claims 11 and 13 supply the evidence needed to keep it a capability - a stable, multi-signal protocol exists with defined gRPC and HTTP encodings, and direct export without an intermediary is documented as acceptable at small scale - so the requirement can be satisfied and tested without ever naming a destination.

research.area: Area 10  -  Infrastructure as Code and Reproducibility
research.design_space: In 2026 the viable designs for making a deployed system reproducible sit on a ladder, and the rungs are not "better" and "worse" so much as "buys different things at different operating costs". At the bottom is the documented manual runbook, where reproducibility lives in prose and decays silently as the prose and the machine diverge. Above it is the scripted deploy, which encodes the runbook imperatively in a shell script or Makefile and buys deterministic ordering, a single entry point and an exit code. Above that is declarative container composition with a thin wrapper: the composition file is the declared end state, the runtime does convergence, and the wrapper's only job is to enforce preconditions (required configuration present, config syntactically valid) and post-conditions (health gates) so failures are loud  -  this rung got materially stronger in 2026, because Compose reached v5.x with native `pre_start` init containers, `required` env-file entries, duration-windowed `pull_policy`, and `--wait`/`--wait-timeout` gating, closing much of the gap that used to justify reaching for heavier tools. Next is configuration management (Ansible, Chef, Puppet), which converges a long-lived mutable host toward a declared state and buys host-level reproducibility  -  packages, users, firewall, log rotation  -  that container composition genuinely does not cover. Above that is full declarative IaC with state (Terraform, OpenTofu, Pulumi, Bicep), which buys plan-before-apply and drift detection for resources *below* the host, at the cost of a state file that is itself a new production-critical asset holding secrets in plaintext. Orthogonal to the ladder is the mutable/immutable axis: immutable delivery builds an artifact per change and deploys by replacement, guaranteeing that the thing tested is the thing running, but it is only truly immutable once all persistent state lives outside the replaced unit. At the top is GitOps  -  declarative, versioned, pulled automatically, continuously reconciled  -  whose mature implementations are Kubernetes-shaped and whose value proposition (an agent that converges production without a human) is only safe when bringing the system up is a side-effect-free operation. Cutting across every rung is the secrets question: declarative infrastructure must reference material it must not contain, and every rung has its own documented anti-pattern for where that material leaks (image layers, environment variables visible to every process, state files, inventory files, git history). The honest framing is that each rung upward buys reproducibility of a *larger scope* while adding a component that can itself fail, and the correct rung is the highest one whose failure modes the operating team can actually diagnose.

options.name: Documented manual runbook over SSH (status quo)
options.how_it_works: A human SSHes to the VM, runs docker compose invocations by hand with mandatory flags, and force-recreates the reverse proxy afterwards. Reproducibility is carried entirely by prose and by the two operators' memory. The compose file is declarative, but the *procedure* around it is not captured anywhere executable.
options.operational_cost: Setup: zero, already paid. Ongoing: roughly 2-4 hours per month of actual typing, but the real cost is unbounded and lumpy  -  each of the two documented traps has already cost a stack outage, and the cost of a trap recurrence is a full incident. Assumes only shell familiarity, which the team has.
options.why: It is the cheapest rung and requires no new skills, which is a real argument. But both of its documented failure modes are silent-substitution failures, which is the exact category this team is worst equipped to catch. Docker documents that an unset interpolation variable becomes an empty string rather than an error, so omitting --env-file produces a stack that starts successfully with no database password  -  a working-looking system in a wrong state. And nginx bakes resolved upstream IPs into worker memory at configuration load, so a forgotten proxy force-recreate produces routing that silently points at dead IPs. A runbook cannot fix either, because a runbook is a request for human attention and both traps are attention failures.

options.name: Scripted deploy (Makefile or shell wrapper) around the existing compose file
options.how_it_works: One executable entry point  -  `make deploy`  -  encodes the whole procedure imperatively: source the env file, validate, bring the stack up, gate on health, recreate the proxy. The runbook shrinks to 'run this command'. The compose file is untouched; the script carries the ordering knowledge.
options.operational_cost: Setup: 6-12 hours. Ongoing: 1-2 hours per month keeping the script honest as the stack changes. Assumes shell scripting only. Well within reach of two SDE 1s.
options.why: This is a genuine improvement and DORA's guidance supports it  -  it explicitly recommends keeping deployment scripts simple, and measures maturity by the reduction of manual steps. But it fixes the *symptom* of both traps rather than the mechanism: the script remembers the --env-file flag and the force-recreate, so the traps are still there, merely covered. Anyone who deploys without the script  -  an emergency 3am fix, a new contractor, a future you  -  falls into them again. The script also becomes a second source of truth about ordering that can drift from the compose file. It is the right *shape* but the wrong *layer* for the two specific problems this system has.

options.name: Hardened declarative composition with a thin fail-fast wrapper
options.how_it_works: The traps are deleted at their mechanism rather than scripted around. Every required secret is referenced as ${VAR:?message} so Compose exits with an error instead of substituting an empty string; env-file entries carry required: true; the project name is pinned with a top-level name: so state volumes stop being derived from the directory basename; images carry digests or unique tags; nginx uses upstream{zone; server ... resolve;} with a resolver so the proxy re-resolves backends by itself. A thin wrapper does only preflight validation (compose config -q, nginx -t) and gated bring-up (up -d --wait --wait-timeout), and the app validates its own options with ValidateOnStart. Nothing new is installed on the box.
options.operational_cost: Setup: 25-40 hours, most of it one-time and structural. Ongoing: 3-5 hours per month, mostly reviewing pinned-digest bumps. Assumes only the tools the team already runs  -  Compose, nginx, .NET  -  plus reading three reference pages. No new language, no new daemon, no state store.
options.why: This converts both documented traps from silent to loud using primitives the team already has and does not have to maintain. Compose's ${VAR:?err} form is documented to 'exit with error' when the variable is unset or empty; nginx's `resolve` parameter on upstream servers left the commercial tier in 1.27.3 (Nov 2024) and is in the stable branch from 1.28.0. The decisive property for a two-person team is that these are *structural* fixes: once merged they need no monthly attention, so they survive the infrastructure budget going to zero, which the process-based options do not.

options.name: Configuration management (Ansible or equivalent) converging the host and the app
options.how_it_works: A playbook declares the desired state of the VM  -  Docker engine version, users, firewall, log rotation, directory layout, the compose file's content  -  and is run repeatedly to converge. Host-level reproducibility, which composition genuinely does not cover, becomes code.
options.operational_cost: Setup: 40-80 hours including learning the mental model, idempotency discipline and the inventory/vault story. Ongoing: 4-8 hours per month, and it decays badly if not run often. Assumes a second declarative language and comfort with convergence semantics neither developer has.
options.why: The honest case is strong for the *host*: nothing currently captures 'what does a fresh Ubuntu box need before compose will work', and Microsoft's own Well-Architected guidance names Ansible as the right tool for desired-state configuration on VMs. But applied to the application it re-declares in YAML what the compose file already declares, creating two sources of truth. And mutable convergence is exactly the model that produces Kief Morris's automation fear spiral  -  he describes teams that lack confidence in automation because servers are inconsistent, and servers are inconsistent because the automation is not run frequently, and his prescribed escape is running it unattended at least hourly. With exactly one production environment, running it unattended and hourly is not an option, so the team would enter the spiral by construction. Conditional: worth ~50 lines for host bootstrap only, worth nothing for the app.

options.name: Full declarative IaC with state (Terraform / OpenTofu / Bicep)
options.how_it_works: A state file records what exists; plan shows the diff before apply; drift is detectable. Manages resources below and around the host  -  machines, networks, DNS records, certificates, storage  -  and can be extended to container topology through providers.
options.operational_cost: Setup: 60-120 hours to real competence including state backend, locking and module structure. Ongoing: 6-12 hours per month. Assumes a mental model (declared-vs-actual-vs-recorded, three-way) that is genuinely new, plus incident skills for state loss, state corruption and stuck locks.
options.why: Actively maintained and industry-default  -  OpenTofu shipped 1.12.6 in August 2026  -  and plan-before-apply is a real safety property this system lacks entirely. But today there is almost nothing for it to manage: one VM, no cloud resources in scope, and everything inside the box already declared in compose. What it *would* add immediately is a state file that HashiCorp documents as storing secrets in plaintext, and a locking mechanism whose recovery command carries an explicit 'Be very careful with this command' warning about causing multiple writers. That is a new production-critical asset and a new incident type, handed to two engineers who have never seen either, to manage a single machine. The plan/apply benefit is real; the scope it would apply to is currently near-empty.

options.name: Immutable artifact delivery (build once per commit, deploy by replacement)
options.how_it_works: Every change produces a versioned image identified by digest or git SHA; deploying means replacing containers with the new artifact, never mutating a running one. NIST SP 800-190 describes this as the native container model: containers 'should be operated as stateless entities that are deployed but not changed', with updates 'made upstream in the images themselves, which are then redeployed'.
options.operational_cost: Setup: 15-25 hours to tag by SHA, stop using floating tags, and keep the previous artifact retrievable. Ongoing: 1-2 hours per month. Assumes a registry or a disciplined local retention policy. Modest, because the containerisation is already done.
options.why: The single highest-leverage half of immutability for this team is not 'never touch a running container'  -  it is 'the previous artifact still exists'. Today, with images built on the box, there is no rollback artifact at all: rolling back means rebuilding from an older commit, which on this box is also a fleet-wide migration run. Digest-pinned third-party images plus SHA-tagged built images make rollback exist for the first time, and NIST SP 800-190 4.2.2 explicitly warns against relying on a 'latest' tag as a freshness guarantee. Crucially this is the *cheap* half of immutability, and it is available without externalising state.

options.name: GitOps with a pull-based reconciling agent
options.how_it_works: An agent on the box continuously pulls declared state from git and reconciles the running system toward it, per the four OpenGitOps principles: declarative, versioned and immutable, pulled automatically, continuously reconciled. Drift self-corrects; git becomes the audit trail of intent.
options.operational_cost: Setup: 40-80 hours. Ongoing: 4-10 hours per month, plus the standing cost of a new always-running component. For Kubernetes the tooling is mature; for compose-on-a-VM the available reconcilers are small community projects rather than CNCF-graduated software.
options.why: The audit-trail property is genuinely attractive in a HIPAA context, and 'deployment is entirely manual over SSH' is exactly the problem GitOps was invented for. Two things rule it out here. First, ecosystem shape: the mature reconcilers assume Kubernetes; the compose-flavoured ones are hobby-scale, and adopting unmaintained-scale tooling is the specific failure this team cannot absorb. Second and more important, 'continuously reconciled' against *this* stack means an agent authorised to bring the stack up unattended  -  and on this box bringing the stack up runs DbMigrator, which applies migrations and seed contributors across every office database with no per-tenant error handling. Continuous reconciliation would turn the single riskiest operation in the system into an unsupervised background process.

research.recommendation: Adopt the hardened-declarative-composition option as the core, plus the cheap half of immutable delivery, and stop there deliberately. Concretely, in this order: (1) delete trap (a) at its mechanism by referencing every required secret as `${VAR:?...}` and by removing the need for the `--env-file` flag entirely  -  either name the secrets file `.env` in the project directory, which Compose discovers automatically, or set `COMPOSE_ENV_FILES`  -  so that the flag's omission becomes impossible rather than merely remembered; (2) delete trap (b) at its mechanism by moving all four backends to `upstream { zone ...; server <name> resolve; }` with `resolver 127.0.0.11`, which has been open-source nginx since 1.27.3 and stable since 1.28.0, and remove the force-recreate step from the runbook  -  noting that the variable-`proxy_pass` workaround currently used only for MinIO silently forfeits upstream keepalive pooling, passive health checks and load balancing, so it should be replaced rather than propagated; (3) pin the Compose project name with a top-level `name:` so the stateful volumes stop being derived from the directory basename; (4) pin third-party images by digest and tag built images by git SHA, so a rollback artifact exists; (5) give the deploy exactly one entry point that runs `docker compose config -q` and `nginx -t` first and `up -d --wait --wait-timeout <n>` after, so a bad deploy exits non-zero within a bounded time instead of hanging or appearing to succeed; (6) add `ValidateOnStart()` to the load-bearing option classes so the API and AuthServer refuse to start on bad configuration rather than failing on first use; and (7) separate DbMigrator from the bring-up path and make it report per office, because until that is true every increase in deployment automation is an increase in unsupervised migration risk. Then write the rebuild procedure and *execute it once, timed, on a scratch VM*, with pass/fail defined by restored content rather than by containers being healthy. My reasoning, not sourced fact: the organising principle for a two-person team is to prefer structural fixes over procedural ones, because structural fixes keep working when the infrastructure budget goes to zero and procedural ones do not  -  and this team's budget is an estimate that will be raided by feature work. Every item above except (7) and the rehearsal is a one-time merge with no monthly upkeep. The right amount of automation here is: enough to make the two known silent failures loud, enough to make one command the only supported path, and enough to prove the machine can be rebuilt  -  and no state files, no convergence engines, no reconciling agents, because the marginal reproducibility they buy over a hardened compose file is small while the marginal number of things that can break at 3am is large. Do this now, while every record is synthetic; a rehearsed rebuild is a cheap exercise today and an expensive one the moment real bookings exist.
research.operational_cost_of_recommendation:
Setup: roughly 45-70 developer-hours, phased and independently shippable. Fail-fast configuration across the ~35 variables plus env_file `required` plus `ValidateOnStart` on the handful of load-bearing option classes plus a `config -q`/`nginx -t` preflight: 8-12 h. Eliminating the `--env-file` flag (rename or `COMPOSE_ENV_FILES`, runbook update): 1-2 h. nginx upstream/zone/resolve for all four backends and deleting the force-recreate step: 4-8 h. Pinning the project `name:`, digest-pinning third-party images, SHA-tagging built images: 5-8 h. Single gated deploy entry point: 4-6 h. Separating the migrator from the up path with per-office result reporting: 8-14 h (mostly application code; shared with other areas). Writing and first-executing the timed rebuild with content assertions: 12-18 h.

Ongoing: about 4-6 hours per month in steady state  -  reviewing digest bumps as pull requests, keeping the single entry point honest  -  plus 8-10 hours once per quarter for the rehearsed rebuild, which amortises to 2-3 hours per month. Call it 7-9 hours per month.

Threshold, stated because the one-dev-week-per-month figure is an estimate the brief itself flags as unmeasured: this recommendation is comfortably operable at 8 or more hours per month. Between roughly 4 and 8 hours per month it degrades gracefully in a specific and predictable order  -  the quarterly rebuild slips to semi-annual first, then digest pins go stale, then the deploy entry point accumulates unmaintained branches  -  and it is still strictly safer than today throughout, because the structural changes are not the ones that decay. Below roughly 4 hours per month the rehearsal stops happening entirely and only the structural residue survives: fail-fast interpolation, the nginx resolve fix, the pinned project name, the digest pins. That residue requires zero hours per month and still removes both documented traps and the silent-empty-volume failure. That asymmetry is the whole argument for this rung of the ladder: it is the highest rung whose value does not evaporate when the budget does. Upward threshold: the recommendation stops being sufficient at roughly 20+ offices or the moment a second host exists, because a single compose file on one box can no longer express the topology and the answer changes to declarative provisioning plus a real orchestrator.

evidence.claim: Docker Compose substitutes an empty string for an interpolation variable that is not set, rather than failing  -  this is the exact mechanism by which omitting --env-file silently blanks every secret.
evidence.source_name: Docker Docs  -  Set or change predefined environment variables / Variable interpolation
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Unset variable -> empty string; a WARN line is printed but the command proceeds

evidence.claim: Compose supports mandatory-variable interpolation forms: ${VAR:?error} uses the variable if set and non-empty, 'otherwise exit with error'; ${VAR?error} uses it if set, otherwise exit with error. This is the documented fail-fast fix for the --env-file trap.
evidence.source_name: Docker Docs  -  Interpolation (Compose file reference)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: ${VAR:?err} and ${VAR?err} both exit with error

evidence.claim: Compose precedence for interpolation is: shell environment, then a file set by --env-file, then an .env file in the project directory if --env-file is not set. Passing --env-file overrides the default file path. So naming the secrets file .env in the project directory removes the need for the flag entirely.
evidence.source_name: Docker Docs  -  Variable interpolation
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 3-level precedence; project directory resolved from --project-directory, then the directory of the first -f file, then PWD

evidence.claim: Compose env_file long syntax supports required: true (the default), which makes Compose fail to process the configuration when the file is missing; required: false makes Compose silently ignore the entry. Introduced in Compose 2.20.0.
evidence.source_name: Docker Docs  -  Services top-level element, env_file
evidence.threshold_or_limit: required defaults to true; introduced in Compose v2.20.0

evidence.claim: nginx resolves upstream server addresses at configuration load and the resulting IPs are held in worker memory for the lifetime of that configuration; when a backend IP changes nginx keeps routing to the stale address until reloaded. This is the mechanism behind trap (b).
evidence.source_name: GetPageSpeed  -  NGINX Upstream Resolve: Dynamic DNS for Load Balancing (updated 7 June 2026)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Resolution occurs once at configuration load

evidence.claim: Since nginx 1.27.3 (26 Nov 2024) the 'resolve' parameter of the 'server' directive in an 'upstream' block is available in open-source nginx, along with 'resolver' and 'resolver_timeout' directives inside the upstream block. Before 1.27.3 'resolve' was commercial-subscription only. It requires the server group to reside in shared memory (the 'zone' directive) and a resolver to be configured.
