capability_requirements.requirement: Absent or empty required configuration MUST abort the deployment before any container is created, recreated or started, with an error naming the missing item.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: This is the mechanism of documented trap (a). The platform substitutes an empty string for an unset interpolation variable, so the current failure mode is a stack that starts successfully with a blank database password  -  a wrong-state system that looks healthy. For a team with no observability and no on-call, a silent wrong state is the worst possible failure class.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Docker Compose interpolation semantics (unset -> empty string; ${VAR:?err} -> exit with error); the system fact that --env-file is mandatory on every invocation and its omission blanks all 35 secrets.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: On a clean checkout of the deployment repository, remove or blank exactly one required variable (e.g. the SQL sa password) and run the single documented deploy command. The command must exit with a non-zero status and print a message naming that variable. Immediately afterwards run `docker ps -a` and confirm no container was created, recreated or restarted as a result. Repeat with the entire secrets source absent.

capability_requirements.requirement: The deployment MUST NOT depend on an operator remembering a command-line flag, environment export, or working directory in order to behave correctly.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: A procedure that is correct only when a human remembers something is not automation; it is a runbook with extra steps. The platform's own default-discovery behaviour (an .env file in the project directory, or COMPOSE_ENV_FILES) removes the need for the flag entirely, so this is achievable without new tooling.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System fact: '--env-file secrets/env.prod is mandatory on every compose invocation'. Docker Compose documented precedence: --env-file overrides the default, and the default is an .env file in the project directory.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Hand the runbook to someone who has never seen the system and count every flag, export and cd they must type. Then, from a fresh shell in a fresh clone, run the deploy command with no arguments. It must either deploy correctly or fail loudly per the previous requirement  -  it must never produce a running stack with blank values.

capability_requirements.requirement: The reverse proxy MUST continue routing correctly after a backend container is replaced and receives a new IP address, with no human action, restart, reload or force-recreate.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: This is the mechanism of documented trap (b). Name resolution baked in at configuration load means every backend rebuild silently breaks routing. The capability now exists in open-source proxies of this class (nginx >=1.27.3 mainline / >=1.28.0 stable via upstream zone + server ... resolve + resolver), so a workaround that trades away connection pooling and health checking is no longer necessary.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System fact: 'nginx resolves proxy_pass upstreams ONCE at worker start. Only the minio block has the resolver + variable proxy_pass fix.' nginx upstream module documentation for the resolve parameter and its zone/resolver prerequisites.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: For each backend (api, authserver, angular, minio) in turn: record the container's current IP, run `docker compose up -d --force-recreate <service>` so the container gets a new IP, then within 60 seconds issue an HTTP request through the proxy to that backend. All four must succeed with no proxy restart, reload or recreate. Also confirm upstream keepalive is configured and effective (connection reuse observable in proxy metrics or via `ss` on the proxy container).

capability_requirements.requirement: Persistent state MUST be bound to an explicitly declared stack identity rather than to a filesystem path or directory name.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: When state volumes are namespaced by an implicitly derived identity, a rebuild performed from a differently-named directory attaches to a brand-new empty volume set and comes up healthy but empty. That produces a false pass on the very rehearsal intended to prove reproducibility, and in a recovery scenario it looks like successful restoration of an empty system.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Docker Compose project-name precedence: -p flag, then COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME, then top-level name:, then the base name of the project directory. System fact: named volumes sqldata, redisdata, miniodata carry all durable state.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Clone the deployment repository into a directory with a deliberately different name, run the deploy command, and confirm the stack attaches to the same named volumes as the original  -  `docker volume ls` must show no newly created duplicates, and the application must show pre-existing data. If new empty volumes appear, the requirement is not met.

capability_requirements.requirement: Every image the stack runs MUST be identified by an immutable reference  -  a content digest or a build-unique tag  -  and never by a floating tag.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Without immutable references there is no rollback artifact, no way to prove that the thing tested is the thing running, and no way to reproduce a past deployment. NIST warns explicitly that a 'latest' tag is a label, not a freshness guarantee, and vendor architecture guidance independently directs teams to call a specific known-good version rather than latest.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: NIST SP 800-190 4.2.2; Azure WAF OE:05 ('avoid using the latest flag... Be intentional about calling the latest known good version'). System fact: deployment is entirely manual with no CD, so images are built on the box.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Run `docker compose config` and assert that no `image:` value uses `:latest` or a mutable tag, and that every third-party image carries `@sha256:`. Then, for each running container, compare its image ID against the digest or SHA-tag declared in the composition  -  they must match. Finally, confirm the immediately previous deployment's artifact still exists locally or in a registry and can be started.

capability_requirements.requirement: Schema migration MUST be a separately invocable operation that reports a per-tenant result, and MUST NOT be an unavoidable side effect of starting the stack.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: While bringing the stack up is also a fleet-wide migration event, every increase in deployment automation is an increase in unsupervised migration risk  -  and the migrator loops offices with no per-tenant error handling, so a partial failure leaves the fleet on split schema versions with no report of which succeeded. This single property is what gates every higher rung of automation (CD, continuous reconciliation) from being safe.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System facts: 'DbMigrator ... applies migrations and runs seed contributors on EVERY bring-up'; 'db-migrator loops offices with NO per-tenant error handling. One office failing mid-loop leaves the fleet on split schema versions WITH NO REPORT of which succeeded'; authserver and api gate on service_completed_successfully.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Bring the stack up twice consecutively and confirm the second bring-up performs no migration work (inspect migrator output and the migrations history table row counts). Then invoke the migration operation on its own and confirm its output enumerates every office by name with an explicit success or failure, and that its process exit code is non-zero if any office failed. Simulate one office database being unreachable and confirm the remaining offices are still reported individually.

capability_requirements.requirement: A failed deployment MUST terminate with a non-zero exit status within a bounded, documented time, and MUST NOT hang.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: An automation that hangs is worse than no automation, because the operator cannot tell whether to wait or intervene. Chained completion-gated dependencies of exactly this shape have been reported to leave the orchestrator waiting indefinitely rather than exiting. Bounded failure is the difference between an obvious failure and a subtle one  -  the stated design preference for this team.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System fact: authserver and api both gate on db-migrator's service_completed_successfully, forming a dependency chain. Compose documented --wait / --wait-timeout / --abort-on-container-failure options; docker/compose issue #10728.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Introduce a deliberate fault that makes the migrator exit non-zero (e.g. an unreachable SQL host). Run the single deploy command and time it. It must exit non-zero within the documented timeout. Repeat with a fault that makes a service start but fail its health check. In neither case may the command require Ctrl+C.

capability_requirements.requirement: Configuration MUST be validated for syntactic and referential correctness before any change is applied to the running system.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Applying an invalid proxy configuration or composition to the only production environment converts an editing mistake into an outage. Both validation capabilities already exist in the tools in use and cost nothing per run.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System fact: exactly one environment exists; deployment is manual. Azure WAF OE:05: 'Test routine and non-routine activities.'
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Introduce a deliberate syntax error into the composition file, run the deploy command, and confirm it refuses before touching any container. Repeat with a deliberate syntax error in the reverse-proxy template. Both must be rejected at preflight, not discovered at restart.

capability_requirements.requirement: The application processes MUST refuse to start when their own configuration is invalid, rather than starting and failing on first use of the affected setting.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Deployment-layer validation cannot see semantic configuration errors inside the application. Options validation is lazy by default in this runtime  -  it runs on first access  -  which means a misconfigured setting used only by, say, the outbox drain job surfaces hours later as a background-job failure in an unmonitored log rather than as a failed deploy.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft Learn: 'Options validation runs the first time a TOption instance is created...'; ValidateOnStart() moves validation to startup. System facts: no observability, no alerting, container logs capped and rotating.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Set one load-bearing setting (e.g. the SMTP relay host, the MinIO endpoint, or the tenant DB template key) to an invalid value and start the process. The process must exit with a validation error naming the setting. It must not reach a listening state.

capability_requirements.requirement: The complete stack MUST be rebuildable on a clean machine from version control plus secret material plus backup media, following a written procedure with no undocumented step, within a stated time budget.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: This is the operational definition of 'reproducible' for this system. A regulator-facing restoration target already exists in draft  -  a written procedure to restore relevant systems and data within 72 hours  -  and that is the natural budget to design against. It is also the only test that discovers what the compose file does not capture: host prerequisites, certificate material, DNS, and volume seeding.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: HHS OCR HIPAA Security Rule NPRM: 'Establish written procedures to restore the loss of certain relevant electronic information systems and data within 72 hours.' NIST SP 800-34 Rev.1 3.5.4 functional exercise 'including an element of system recovery from backup media'. System fact: no restore has ever been tested.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Give the written procedure and the necessary credentials to a person who has not built the system. On a fresh VM of the documented specification, have them execute it end to end without asking questions, recording elapsed wall-clock time and every point at which they had to guess. Pass requires zero guesses and completion inside the stated budget.

capability_requirements.requirement: The rebuild test MUST be judged on restored content, not on services reporting healthy.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: A stack of this shape will come up entirely green against empty databases, an empty object store and an empty key store. Health checks assert liveness, not restoration. Without content assertions the rehearsal certifies exactly the half of the system that was never at risk.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System facts: 37 aggregate roots across host (46 DbSets, 90 migrations) and tenant (44 DbSets, 15 migrations) contexts; six logical blob containers with tenants/{tenantId:D}/ keys; Redis holds the DataProtection keyring; HealthChecks UI storage is in-memory.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: The written procedure must contain named, pre-agreed assertions and the rehearsal must fail if any assertion fails even while every container reports healthy. At minimum: a named office database returns an expected non-zero appointment count and its expected migration history; a known object key resolves in the object store to the expected bytes; a user completes a full login round-trip across the auth and api subdomains for a named office; and a recurring job runs once and touches every office.

capability_requirements.requirement: The rebuild MUST be rehearsed on a schedule, and the date and outcome of the most recent rehearsal MUST be producible on request.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: An untested restore procedure is a hypothesis. Recognised contingency-planning guidance for a system of this criticality calls for a functional exercise that includes recovery from backup media, and the sample policy language is annual at minimum; the proposed rule would remove the addressable flexibility that currently makes this optional. Recording the date is what converts intent into evidence.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: 45 CFR 164.308(a)(7)(ii)(D) (currently Addressable); HIPAA Security Rule NPRM proposal to make all implementation specifications required; NIST SP 800-34 Rev.1 3.5.4 and NIST SP 800-53 CP-4.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Ask for the date of the last rehearsal, who performed it, how long it took, and the written result including which assertions failed. A system that cannot produce these four facts has not met the requirement, regardless of how good the procedure document looks.

capability_requirements.requirement: Secret material MUST NOT exist in plaintext in version control at any point in history, and the repository MUST be checked automatically on every push.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Declarative infrastructure pulls configuration toward the repository, which increases the chance secrets follow it. Several values here were already exposed in chat transcripts and are flagged for rotation, so the discipline is not hypothetical. Automated checking is required because one-time audits do not survive the next commit.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet (secrets detection at developer level, pre-commit or IDE); Azure WAF OE:05 ('Scan your IaC repos for keys and secrets that are exposed'); system fact of 35 variables in one file, several already exposed.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Run a secret-scanning tool across the full git history (not just HEAD) of every repository involved in deployment and confirm zero plaintext secrets. Then push a commit containing a deliberately planted fake credential and confirm the check blocks or flags it automatically without anyone remembering to look.

capability_requirements.requirement: Secret values MUST NOT be readable from container metadata or process environment by any principal that can reach the container runtime.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Environment variables are broadly readable  -  the platform's own documentation notes they are 'often available to all processes', that access is hard to track, and that they can be printed in logs during debugging. File-mounted secrets give filesystem-permission granularity instead. This matters more here than usual because logs from a PHI system already cannot leave the machine and debugging output is the likeliest leak path.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Docker Docs on Compose secrets vs environment variables; OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet ('environment variables are generally accessible to all processes and may be included in logs or system dumps'); NIST SP 800-190 4.1.4.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Run `docker inspect` on each application container and grep the output for the database password, the token-signing certificate passphrase, the object-store root credential and the SMTP password. None may appear. Repeat by reading /proc/1/environ inside each container.

capability_requirements.requirement: Rotating a secret MUST result in the running system using the new value, by a documented procedure that does not rely on a restart that preserves the old value.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Environment values are injected at container creation. A 'rotate and restart' procedure leaves the old value in the running process and the mismatch surfaces later at an unrelated moment  -  the archetypal subtle failure. Several secrets are already flagged for rotation, so this procedure will be exercised soon.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System facts: 35 variables in one mode-600 file, no rotation process, several values flagged for rotation after exposure. Container runtime semantics: environment is fixed at container creation; `restart` does not re-read the environment file.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Change one non-destructive secret, follow the documented rotation procedure, then verify from inside the container (or from the observable behaviour of the dependent connection) that the new value is in effect. Separately, confirm the procedure does not instruct the operator to use a plain restart, and confirm that using a plain restart demonstrably fails to pick up the change.

capability_requirements.requirement: The rebuild procedure SHOULD produce a second, disposable environment from the same declarations, differing only in variable values.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: SHOULD rather than MUST because standing up a second environment has cost and other areas of this programme may fund it differently. But it is the single highest-value unlock in this area: it is the prerequisite for escaping the automation fear spiral (whose documented escape is running automation unattended and frequently, which one production environment forbids), and it is the prerequisite for any CD at all. Today every change reaching users has been tested only on the machine that serves them.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Kief Morris, The Automation Fear Spiral; DORA deployment automation ('deploy any version of the artifact to any environment on demand'); Azure WAF OE:05 ('avoid using different Terraform files in production and test environments... All environments should use a single file'). System fact: exactly ONE environment.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Bring the whole stack up on a scratch machine using the same declaration files with only variable values differing. Then diff `docker compose config` output between the two environments  -  every difference must be a value, never a structural difference (no extra services, no different dependency graph, no environment-specific branches).

capability_requirements.requirement: Host-level prerequisites SHOULD be captured as an executable artifact rather than as prose in a runbook.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: SHOULD because a well-written prose list is workable for one host and two people, and adding a configuration-management tool has real cost. But everything a fresh VM needs before the composition will run  -  engine version, users, directory layout, disk layout, log rotation  -  is currently invisible to the declarations and is precisely what a rebuild discovers the hard way.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System fact: one VM, Ubuntu 24.04, Docker Engine + compose, ten compose services, manual SSH deployment. Azure WAF OE:05 on documenting and minimising manual steps.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: On a fresh VM of the documented specification, run the bootstrap artifact once and confirm the machine reaches 'ready to deploy' with no further manual commands. Count the manual commands required; the requirement is met at zero and unmet at any number that requires reading prose.

capability_requirements.requirement: Rolling back to the previously deployed version SHOULD be possible using artifacts that already exist, without rebuilding from source.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: SHOULD because with one environment and no CD the rollback path is exercised rarely. But on this system rebuilding from an older commit is not a neutral operation  -  it also re-runs the fleet migrator  -  so 'rebuild the old commit' is a materially riskier rollback than 'start the old artifact'. Immutable, retained artifacts are what make the safer path exist.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System facts: DbMigrator runs on every bring-up and iterates offices with no per-tenant error handling; no CD; images built on the box. NIST SP 800-190 4.2.2 on immutable image names.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Deploy version N, then N+1, then roll back to N using only artifacts already present locally or in a registry  -  no source checkout, no build. Time it. Confirm the running image digest matches N's.

anti_requirements: The deployment tooling MUST NOT silently substitute a default or empty value for absent configuration. Any platform, wrapper or template engine adopted must be checked for this behaviour specifically, because it is the mechanism of the trap this system already has.

The deployment procedure MUST NOT require an operator to remember a flag, an export or a working directory for correct behaviour. Correctness that depends on human memory is not a property of the system.

Bringing the stack up MUST NOT be a schema-changing operation. Until that is true, no continuous-reconciliation agent, no deploy-on-merge pipeline and no auto-restart policy that recreates the migrator may be introduced, because each converts the riskiest operation in the system into an unsupervised one.

The automation MUST NOT hold long-lived plaintext secret material in a state file, inventory file or lock record. This rules out state-bearing IaC as the carrier of database, signing-certificate or object-store credentials regardless of which tool is later selected.

The stack MUST NOT require an always-available external secret service in order to start, unless a documented and rehearsed break-glass path exists. A team with no on-call cannot absorb a start-time dependency on a service that can be down.

Persistent state MUST NOT be bound to a filesystem path, directory name or implicitly derived project identity. A rebuild in a differently-named directory must not be able to produce a healthy, empty system.

The deployment MUST NOT reference any image by a floating tag. This is both a reproducibility and a rollback requirement, and it constrains any future registry or build service that cannot serve or pin by digest.

No component introduced between the client and the application processes may alter, normalise or drop the HTTP Host header, and the rebuild test must prove this rather than assume it. Tenancy resolves from the leftmost DNS label and nothing else; a reproduced environment whose edge rewrites Host is not a reproduction of this system. This is an explicit constraint on any managed L7 tier a future platform might offer.

The team MUST NOT be required to operate a control plane, state store or reconciliation engine whose failure modes they cannot diagnose without external help. An architecture that is theoretically better but needs expertise this team does not have is worse, not better.
No change may be applied to production automatically, without a human-initiated action, while exactly one environment exists. Automation of an untested change path is amplification, not safety.
The rebuild rehearsal MUST NOT be allowed to pass on liveness signals alone. Any tooling or dashboard that reports success from health checks must not be treated as evidence of restoration.
surprises: Running `docker compose up` on this box is a fleet-wide schema migration, not a restart. DbMigrator applies migrations and seed contributors on every bring-up and loops offices with no per-tenant error handling. That means the most common recovery reflex  -  'just bring the stack back up'  -  is simultaneously the riskiest operation in the system, and every step up the automation ladder increases how often it runs unsupervised. This inverts the usual advice: for this system, more deployment automation is more dangerous until the migrator is separated. Nobody frames adopting IaC as increasing migration risk, but here it does.

The Compose project name defaults to the base name of the project directory, and Compose namespaces containers, networks and named volumes by it. So a rebuild performed from a clone in a differently-named directory silently creates fresh, empty sqldata/redisdata/miniodata volumes and the whole stack comes up green and empty. That is a false pass on the exact rehearsal meant to prove reproducibility, and in a real recovery it looks like success. The fix is one line  -  a top-level `name:` in the compose file  -  and almost nobody sets it.

Tenant identity is not reproducible, and object keys depend on it. MinIO keys are shaped `tenants/{tenantId:D}/...` with a lowercase GUID, and office databases are named `CaseEvaluation_{slug}`. If a rebuild restores object storage but re-provisions offices through IOfficeDatabaseProvisioner instead of restoring the host database first, new tenant GUIDs are minted and every existing object key is orphaned  -  with no error anywhere, because the provisioner is idempotent and will happily succeed. The rebuild therefore has a hard ordering constraint (host database restore strictly before any office provisioning) that appears nowhere in the compose file or in any code path.

Redis is inside the reproducibility scope even though it looks like a cache. It carries the ASP.NET DataProtection keyring under CaseEvaluation-Protection-Keys, shared between AuthServer and API via an identical SetApplicationName. Teams reflexively classify Redis as disposable and exclude it from restore procedures  -  here that decision invalidates every session and breaks in-flight email-confirmation links on every rebuild. It also means exactly one of the eight services is a bad candidate for destroy-and-recreate, which quietly breaks the 'immutable everything' story.

Rotating a secret and restarting does not rotate the secret. Environment values are fixed when a container is created; a plain `restart` reuses the existing container and its old environment. Several secrets here are already flagged for rotation after being pasted into chat transcripts, so this will be exercised soon, and the failure surfaces later as an authentication error at an unrelated moment rather than at rotation time.

The documented fix for the more dangerous of the two traps is a one-line-per-variable change the team already has available. Compose's `${VAR:?message}` form is documented to exit with an error when the variable is unset or empty, and env_file entries carry `required: true` by default. Roughly a 35-line diff converts 'the stack silently comes up with no database password' into 'the deploy refuses to start'. Most teams reach for a wrapper script; the primitive is already in the file format.

The nginx workaround currently applied to the MinIO block is now the inferior fix, and it has costs the team may not have priced. Variable-`proxy_pass` forces per-request resolution but gives up upstream keepalive connection pooling, passive health checking via max_fails, backup-server failover and load balancing, and changes URI handling. Since nginx 1.27.3 (Nov 2024 mainline) and 1.28.0 stable, the proper fix  -  `upstream { zone ...; server <name> resolve; }` with a resolver pointed at Docker's embedded DNS at 127.0.0.11  -  is in open-source nginx. It was a commercial-only feature for over a decade, so a team that checked at any point before late 2024 would reasonably believe it is still unavailable to them. This fix deletes the force-recreate step from the runbook entirely.

Compose can hang rather than fail on the exact dependency shape this stack uses. With chained `depends_on: service_completed_successfully`  -  which is precisely how authserver and api gate on db-migrator  -  a failure in the chain has been reported to leave Compose waiting indefinitely, reporting the failure and then doing nothing. Any scripted deploy that shells out to compose therefore needs `--wait --wait-timeout` or the automation itself becomes the thing that hangs at 3am. This is the 'what happens when the automation breaks' question with a concrete answer.

Compose gained native `pre_start` init containers in v5.3.0 (July 2026), which model a migrator as a subordinate step rather than a peer service  -  and which are skipped on subsequent runs if the step previously succeeded and its definition has not changed. That would change the 'runs on every bring-up' property almost for free, which is attractive. It is also a trap: the skip decision is made on the step's definition hash, not on whether the schema is actually current, so a new image containing new migrations with an unchanged pre_start definition would be skipped. Worth knowing about; worth not adopting without understanding that.

There is currently no rollback artifact at all. With images built on the box, deploying overwrites the tag and the previous image becomes unreferenced and prunable. 'Roll back' therefore means 'rebuild the previous commit', which  -  per the first surprise  -  is also a migration event. Digest-pinned third-party images and SHA-tagged built images are the cheapest change that makes rollback exist as a concept.

The compliance clock is already drawn and it is currently in the team's favour. Testing and revision of contingency plans is only Addressable today under 45 CFR 164.308(a)(7)(ii)(D), which is exactly why no restore has ever been tested. The January 2025 NPRM proposes removing the addressable/required distinction entirely, adds written procedures to restore relevant systems and data within 72 hours, and requires a technology asset inventory and network map refreshed at least every 12 months. As of mid-2026 it is still proposed and the OMB agenda has slipped final action to July 2027  -  so it is not law, but 72 hours is the number to design the rebuild budget against, and rehearsing it is free right now precisely because every record is synthetic.

The published escape from the automation fear spiral is structurally unavailable to this team. Kief Morris's prescription  -  run the automation unattended, frequently, at least hourly, on a small scope, and grow confidence from there  -  presupposes somewhere safe to run it. With exactly one environment, every unattended run is a production run. That reframes 'a second environment' from a nice-to-have into a prerequisite for any automation more ambitious than a fail-fast wrapper, and it explains why adding tooling before adding an environment tends to make things worse rather than better.

not_recommended.pattern: Terraform or OpenTofu with remote state to manage this stack
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It is the industry default and both are vigorously maintained (OpenTofu 1.12.6 shipped 19 August 2026). Plan-before-apply is a genuine safety property this system entirely lacks  -  today every change is applied blind to the only environment that exists. It gives real drift detection, and adopting it now would make the eventual platform migration substantially a matter of swapping providers rather than rewriting the deployment model. For a team about to make a platform selection, learning the tool that platform will expect is a defensible investment.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: There is currently almost nothing for it to manage. One VM, no cloud resources in scope, no DNS automation, and the entire container topology already declared in a compose file. What it would add on day one is a state file  -  which HashiCorp documents as storing secrets in plaintext, including any value marked sensitive  -  and a locking mechanism whose recovery command carries an explicit 'Be very careful with this command' warning about causing multiple writers. That is a new production-critical asset plus a new incident class, handed to two SDE 1s who have seen neither, in exchange for managing a single machine. It also violates the ordering constraint of this programme: adopting a provisioning tool now anchors the platform decision that is deliberately scheduled next.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: The moment the platform decision produces resources outside the box  -  a managed database, external object storage, DNS records, certificates, network configuration, more than one machine. Then adopt it for provisioning those resources only, and keep the container topology in the composition file. Do not use it to manage containers.

not_recommended.pattern: Ansible (or Chef, Puppet, Salt) as the deployment mechanism for the application
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It is mature, actively maintained (ansible-core 2.21 released 31 May 2026, supported to November 2027), needs no agent, and is the right answer for the layer that is genuinely uncaptured today: what a fresh Ubuntu box needs before the composition will run. Microsoft's own architecture guidance names Ansible specifically as the desired-state tool for VMs. A team that ran a playbook on every deploy would never again wonder whether the box drifted.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: Applied to the application it re-declares in YAML what the compose file already declares, producing two sources of truth about the same topology and a new class of disagreement between them. More decisively, mutable convergence only works when it is run constantly, and the documented escape from the fear spiral is running it unattended at least hourly  -  which a single production environment forbids. A convergence tool run monthly by a nervous operator is the fear spiral's textbook precondition, not its cure. The honest version is that this team would end up in exactly the position Morris describes: afraid of the tool because the box is inconsistent, and the box inconsistent because the tool is run rarely.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: For host bootstrap only, and preferably capped at around fifty lines  -  install the container engine, create users and directories, set log rotation and firewall, drop the compose file. Or use cloud-init for the same job if the platform provides it. It becomes right for the application layer only when there is more than one host to converge.

not_recommended.pattern: GitOps with a continuously reconciling pull agent
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: The four OpenGitOps principles  -  declarative, versioned and immutable, pulled automatically, continuously reconciled  -  describe precisely the properties missing here, and the audit trail of intent that git provides is genuinely attractive under HIPAA where 'who changed what, when, and who approved it' is a recurring question. 'Deployment is entirely manual over SSH with no CD' is the canonical problem statement GitOps was created to answer, and pull-based reconciliation removes the need to hold production credentials in a pipeline.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: Two independent reasons. First, ecosystem shape: the mature reconcilers assume Kubernetes; for compose on a VM the available options are small community projects, and adopting hobby-scale tooling as a production dependency is precisely the failure this team cannot absorb  -  when it breaks, there is no vendor, no large community, and no second engineer who knows it. Second and stronger: 'continuously reconciled' against this stack means an agent authorised to run the equivalent of `docker compose up` unattended, which is an unguarded migration run across every office database. Continuous reconciliation is not merely premature here, it is unsafe by construction until the migrator is separated from the up path.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: When both conditions hold: the platform provides a first-party reconciler for the orchestration model in use (rather than a community script), and bringing the system up is a genuinely side-effect-free operation. The second condition is the one to build toward regardless, because it also unblocks CD.

not_recommended.pattern: Kubernetes, adopted in order to get reproducibility and declarative deployment
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It makes the topology declarative and portable, provides real init containers with proper failure semantics, gives health gating and rolling replacement natively, and unlocks the entire mature GitOps ecosystem. Everything is already containerised, so the port is mechanical rather than architectural. And it would remove the whole class of problems this area is about  -  no --env-file flag, no stale proxy IPs, no directory-derived volume identity.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: The system has deliberately none of the properties that make orchestration pay: no server-side rendering and therefore no Node runtime, no SignalR or WebSockets and therefore no sticky-session requirement, no message broker, no second application instance, and single-instance operation throughout. What it would add is a control plane that two SDE 1s must operate, upgrade and debug, on top of a tenancy model (Host-header-only resolution across three subdomain patterns, one database per office, connection strings derived by name substitution) that Kubernetes does not simplify at all  -  the ingress would have to be verified not to touch the Host header, which is a new risk rather than a removed one. Google's own SRE writing on simplicity is the counterargument: accidental complexity should be eliminated, and this would be a large, permanent addition of it.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: When office count and traffic force horizontal scale-out of HttpApi.Host, or when the platform offers a control plane the team consumes but never operates  -  and even then, only after the Host-header preservation property is proven end to end rather than assumed.

not_recommended.pattern: A CI/CD pipeline that deploys to production automatically on merge
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: DORA is unambiguous that deployment automation is a driver of both throughput and stability, that manual steps increase both time and error opportunity, and that the same process should be used for every environment. Manual SSH deployment is the single practice most associated with poor delivery performance. Automating it is the highest-consensus recommendation in the entire field, and a small team benefits from it more than a large one because they have fewer people to absorb mistakes.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: Not the pattern  -  the ordering. With exactly one environment and an untested restore, 'automatic deploy on merge' means automatic, unreviewed, fleet-wide schema migration in production, with no per-tenant error handling, no report of which offices succeeded, and no rehearsed way back. That is the exact shape of Google's 'Automation: Enabling Failure at Scale'  -  their diskerase incident cost two days of reinstalls because automation faithfully executed a bad instruction at machine speed, and the remediation was sanity checks and rate limiting, not more automation. Automating a dangerous operation makes it dangerous more often.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: Immediately once two conditions hold: a second environment exists, and the restore has been rehearsed at least once. Even then, build it in the right order  -  CI first, producing a digest-identified artifact and running tests; automatic deployment to the non-production environment second; and leave the production apply as a single human-initiated command for as long as one environment serves all offices.

not_recommended.pattern: Introducing a secrets vault as the first improvement to secrets handling
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: One mode-600 file holding 35 values with no rotation, no access audit and several entries already exposed in chat transcripts is a real and serious finding. OWASP's guidance points toward managed secret storage with lifecycle and rotation, and a vault would give access audit  -  which is a genuine HIPAA-adjacent benefit, not a theoretical one. It is also the answer a security reviewer will reach for first.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It adds a runtime dependency whose unavailability stops the entire stack from starting, plus a bootstrap and unseal problem, to a single-VM system with no on-call and no monitoring. The failure mode is 'nothing starts and the reason is a service nobody has debugged before'. There is a strictly better-ordered sequence at a fraction of the cost: first make missing secrets fail loudly at deploy time; second move values from `environment:` to file-mounted secrets at /run/secrets/, because the platform documents that environment variables are 'often available to all processes' and 'can also be printed in logs when debugging errors'; third encrypt the secrets file at rest in version control with SOPS and age  -  CNCF Sandbox, v3.13.3 released 23 July 2026  -  so the material is versioned, reviewable and recoverable. That sequence delivers most of the risk reduction with no new runtime dependency.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: When there is more than one environment, more than two people who need access, or an access-audit obligation that a file cannot satisfy. Also immediately if the platform selected later provides a managed secret service the team consumes rather than operates  -  that changes the cost calculation entirely, because the failure mode stops being theirs to debug.

not_recommended.pattern: Immutable hosts  -  rebuilding the VM from a golden image on every change
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: NIST SP 800-190 is explicit that host operating systems 'should be operated in an immutable manner with no data or state stored uniquely and persistently on the host', and that this 'provides a more trustworthy way to identify anomalies and configuration drift'. Microsoft's Well-Architected guidance says business-critical workloads are best served by immutable infrastructure. It is the single most effective cure for configuration drift, and it makes the rebuild rehearsal a continuous property rather than a quarterly event.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: All four stateful assets  -  sqldata, redisdata, miniodata and the backup directory  -  live on the host's single 48 GB disk with roughly 9.7 GB free, and the backup target is a bind mount on that same disk. Immutable hosts without externalised state is not immutability; it is scheduled data loss. The prerequisite (get state off the host) is squarely a platform-selection question, which this exercise is deliberately upstream of. Adopting the pattern before the prerequisite would be the most expensive possible way to lose data.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: Once the database, object storage and backups all live off the host. At that point immutable hosts become both cheap and correct, and the rebuild rehearsal collapses into ordinary operation. Note that the second half of immutability  -  retained, digest-identified artifacts so the previous version still exists  -  is available today at low cost and IS recommended; it is only host replacement that must wait.

not_recommended.pattern: Auto-updating containers (Watchtower-style image refresh on the running host)
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It removes real toil, keeps base images patched without anyone remembering, and directly addresses a legitimate concern: a single-VM stack whose images are rebuilt manually will drift months behind on security updates, which matters in a PHI context. For a team with one dev-week a month, 'patching happens without me' is genuinely appealing.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It is unattended container recreation, which on this box means unattended fleet-wide migration runs  -  the same objection as continuous reconciliation, arriving through a different door and with less visibility. It also fights digest pinning directly: it exists to follow a moving tag, and NIST SP 800-190 4.2.2 warns explicitly that a 'latest' tag 'is only a label attached to the image and not a guarantee of freshness'. A team that cannot notice slow degradation should not run a process that changes production while nobody is looking.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: Never for the API, AuthServer or database in this system. It is defensible for genuinely stateless, non-migrating sidecars, and even then the correct mechanism is not an auto-updating agent but automated dependency pull requests that bump a pinned digest and are reviewed and deployed by a human  -  which gets the patching benefit while keeping the change human-initiated and auditable.

what_would_change_the_answer: A second, disposable environment becoming available. This is the single biggest unlock. It converts the automation fear spiral from unavoidable to escapable, makes CI-to-staging correct immediately, and turns the rebuild rehearsal from an event into a routine. Almost every option currently rejected on ordering grounds becomes reconsiderable.

Real patient bookings arriving. Today the rebuild rehearsal is nearly free because every record is synthetic. The moment real PHI exists, the rehearsal becomes a live-data operation with its own disclosure and handling constraints, the restore stops being a technical exercise, and the cost of everything in this area roughly triples. This is the argument for doing the rehearsal now rather than after the next feature.

DbMigrator gaining per-office error handling, an explicit result report, and separation from the bring-up path. This is the gate on the entire upper half of the automation ladder. Until it lands, more automation means more unsupervised migrations; after it lands, continuous deployment and even continuous reconciliation become discussable on their merits.

The platform decision producing resources outside the VM  -  a managed database, external object storage, DNS records, certificates, a second machine. That is the moment declarative provisioning with state earns its keep, and the moment immutable hosts become achievable rather than reckless.

The team gaining a third engineer, or any dedicated operations time. The recommendation here is calibrated to the specific constraint that all automation must survive its maintainer being fully occupied by feature work. Relax that and tooling requiring periodic attention becomes affordable.

The one-dev-week-per-month figure proving optimistic. If actual infrastructure capacity is closer to four hours a month, drop the quarterly rehearsal cadence to semi-annual and ship only the structural items  -  fail-fast interpolation, the nginx resolve fix, the pinned project name, the digest pins. Those four require zero ongoing hours and still remove both documented traps and the empty-volume failure.

The HIPAA Security Rule NPRM being finalised. That converts contingency-plan testing from Addressable to Required, attaches a 72-hour restoration target and a 12-month asset-inventory refresh, and moves the rehearsal from 'good practice' to 'audited obligation'. The OMB agenda currently shows July 2027, but the date has already slipped once.

Discovering that ABP's four default __tenant resolvers (query string, header, cookie, route) are in fact still registered. The brief flags this as never tested. If they are active, tenancy is not Host-header-only, and reproducing the tenancy behaviour of this system in any new environment becomes a security verification rather than a functional one  -  which changes what the rebuild test must assert.

Office count crossing roughly twenty, or the arrival of a second host. Beyond that, a single compose file on one box stops being able to express the topology, the sequential per-office job iteration becomes a scaling problem in its own right, and the answer moves to declarative provisioning plus a real orchestrator.

The reverse proxy being replaced by a managed L7 tier as part of the platform decision. Every DNS re-resolution and Host-header property established here would need re-verifying from scratch against that component's documented behaviour, because both properties are load-bearing for tenancy and neither can be assumed.

material_errors: [12] The version attribution is wrong. The Compose docs attach 'Introduced in Docker Compose version 2.20.0' to the env_file `required` attribute, NOT to depends_on condition: service_completed_successfully. That condition long predates 2.20.0 (it is part of the Compose Specification and shipped in Compose v2 well before mid-2023). The cited docs page carries no version note for it at all, and carries nothing about the reported hang defect.

[15] The three flags are presented as a combinable set, but the cited page documents --wait as 'Implies detached mode' and --abort-on-container-failure as 'Stops all containers if any container exited with failure. Incompatible with -d'. The researcher silently dropped the 'Incompatible with -d' clause. --wait and --abort-on-container-failure therefore cannot be used together; a recommendation built on combining them will fail at the CLI.

[1] The stated threshold includes 'a WARN line is printed but the command proceeds'. The cited page says only 'If an environment variable is not set, Compose substitutes with an empty string' and says nothing about a warning. The warning is real CLI behaviour but is not documented at the cited URL, so the threshold as stated is not supported by the evidence offered.

[44] Mis-flagged as unverified. https://www.martinfowler.com/ieeeSoftware/failFast.pdf is reachable and the PDF fully confirms the claim (Jim Shore, IEEE Software, 2004, '0740-7459/04/$20.00 (c) 2004 IEEE', column editor Martin Fowler; 'when a problem occurs, it fails immediately and visibly'). The 503 note is stale and should be removed rather than carried into the document as a caveat.

[30] https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/0005109883900468 returns HTTP 403 - not reachable, not even the abstract. The '~1800 citations as of Nov 2016' figure is unverifiable from any fetched source and should be dropped.
vendor_neutrality_violations: No violation found in the CAPABILITY REQUIREMENTS list itself. All 18 requirements are phrased as capabilities ('the reverse proxy MUST', 'persistent state MUST be bound to an explicitly declared stack identity', 'host-level prerequisites SHOULD be captured as an executable artifact') and name no vendor or product. That list passes the audit clean.

[26] CLAIM-LEVEL VIOLATION (would become one if carried into the document): 'SOPS, the standard tool for encrypting secrets in-repo alongside declarative configuration'. This elevates a named product to THE standard rather than describing the capability class ('secret material encrypted at rest in version control with key material held outside the repository'). CNCF Sandbox status is a maturity datum, not a neutrality licence. Rewrite as a capability; cite SOPS only as one existing implementation.

[43] CLAIM-LEVEL VIOLATION: 'Podman Quadlet ... is argued to be the more natural fit for single-server production where system integration matters'. Sourced to a single personal blog (matduggan.com), and phrased as a recommendation of a named product over the incumbent. Permissible form: 'expressing containers as native init-system units is one behaviour class that satisfies the host-prerequisite and restart-supervision requirements; Podman Quadlet is one implementation'.

[42] BORDERLINE - names ComposeFlux, a single small community project, as the compose-specific option, sourced to one personal blog post. Descriptive rather than recommending, so not a hard violation, but the sentence 'the compose-specific options are small community projects such as ComposeFlux' is one edit away from becoming a product recommendation. Keep the finding (mature pull-reconcilers target Kubernetes; single-VM compose reconciliation is thin) and drop the named project, or mark it explicitly as an unendorsed example.

[13] NOT a violation but worth policing on write-up: 'Docker positions this as preferable to the peer-service + depends_on pattern' correctly attributes the preference to the vendor rather than adopting it. Preserve that attribution verbatim; do not let it collapse into 'therefore use pre_start'.

results.claim: [1] Compose substitutes an empty string for an unset interpolation variable rather than failing; a WARN line is printed but the command proceeds
results.evidence_quote: If an environment variable is not set, Compose substitutes with an empty string.
results.correction: The empty-string substitution is confirmed verbatim. The 'WARN line is printed' half is NOT on this page - the page mentions no warning output at all (it illustrates the hazard with an invalid 'postgres:' image reference instead). Compose does emit 'WARN[0000] The "X" variable is not set. Defaulting to a blank string.' in practice, but cite CLI behaviour for that, not this page. State the mechanism as: unset -> empty string -> command proceeds.

results.claim: [2] ${VAR:?error} uses the variable if set and non-empty, otherwise exit with error; ${VAR?error} uses it if set, otherwise exit with error
results.evidence_quote: ${VAR:?error} -> value of VAR if set and non-empty, otherwise exit with error; ${VAR?error} -> value of VAR if set, otherwise exit with error
results.correction: None. Both required-value forms are documented exactly as claimed, alongside the default (:-, -) and alternative (:+, +) forms.

results.claim: [3] Interpolation precedence is shell env, then --env-file file, then .env in the project directory if --env-file is not set; so naming the secrets file .env removes the need for the flag
results.evidence_quote: Variables from your shell environment / Variables from a file set by --env-file / If --env-file is not set, variables from an .env file in the project directory ... --project-directory if set; otherwise, the directory of the first Compose file specified with -f/--file; otherwise, your shell's current directory (PWD)
results.correction: The 3-level precedence and the project-directory resolution order are confirmed verbatim. Two qualifications the claim omits: (a) this governs INTERPOLATION of the Compose file only - it does not populate container environments, which is env_file/environment, so a .env rename does not by itself carry secrets into containers; (b) because the project directory falls back to PWD when no -f is given, an automatic .env still depends on invocation location, which only partially satisfies the 'must not depend on working directory' requirement. Pair the .env rename with -f/--project-directory or with ${VAR:?} guards.

results.claim: [4] env_file long syntax supports required: true (default), failing when the file is missing; required: false silently ignores. Introduced in Compose 2.20.0
results.evidence_quote: The required attribute defaults to true. When required is set to false and the .env file is missing, Compose silently ignores the entry. ... Introduced in Docker Compose version 2.20.0.
results.correction: None. Default true, silent-ignore on false, and the 2.20.0 introduction note are all present on the page.

results.claim: [5] nginx resolves upstream server addresses at configuration load and holds the IPs in worker memory for the life of that configuration, routing to stale addresses until reloaded
results.evidence_quote: upstream server addresses are resolved by the operating system's getaddrinfo() during configuration loading, and the resulting IPs are baked into the worker process memory for the lifetime of that configuration
results.correction: Supported, but note the source is a commercial third-party blog (GetPageSpeed sells nginx modules), not nginx.org. Primary corroboration exists: nginx.org's own 'resolve' parameter text ('monitors changes of the IP addresses ... without the need of restarting nginx') only makes sense against exactly this default. Prefer citing nginx.org for the mechanism and keep this URL as supporting colour.

results.claim: [6] 'resolve' on upstream server is OSS from nginx 1.27.3 (26 Nov 2024), previously commercial-only; requires zone + resolver; resolver/resolver_timeout available in the upstream block; stable from 1.28.0; current nginx 1.31.4 dated 19 Aug 2026
results.evidence_quote: resolve - monitors changes of the IP addresses that correspond to a domain name of the server ... The server group must reside in the shared memory. In order for this parameter to work, the resolver directive must be specified ... Prior to version 1.27.3, this parameter was available only as part of our commercial subscription. [resolver / resolver_timeout, Context: upstream] This directive appeared in version 1.27.3.
results.correction: None on substance. Cross-check on nginx.org confirms mainline nginx-1.31.4 released 2026-08-19; note for accuracy that the current STABLE line is 1.30.4 (2026-07-15), not 1.28.x - 1.28.0 was merely the first stable branch to carry the feature, which is what the claim says.

results.claim: [7] The variable-in-proxy_pass workaround forces per-request resolution but forfeits load balancing, max_fails passive health checks, backup failover and keepalive pooling, and adds DNS overhead; nginx documents that with variables, a URI in the directive 'is passed to the server as is, replacing the original request URI'
results.evidence_quote: Parameter value can contain variables. In this case, if an address is specified as a domain name, the name is searched among the described server groups, and, if not found, is determined using a resolver. ... In this case, if URI is specified in the directive, it is passed to the server as is, replacing the original request URI.
results.correction: The URI-replacement quote is verbatim and correct, and the resolver requirement is documented. The forfeited-capability list (load balancing, max_fails, backup, keepalive, per-request DNS cost) is NOT stated anywhere on this page - it is inference. Note also the page contradicts the flat framing: with a variable, a domain name IS first searched among described server groups, so an upstream block named in a variable proxy_pass is still matched (and then behaves statically). Either drop the unsourced list or label it as reasoning from the upstream-module semantics rather than as documented behaviour.

results.claim: [8] nginx's resolver caches answers using the response TTL by default; valid=<time> overrides it; before 1.1.9 nginx always cached for 5 minutes
results.evidence_quote: By default, nginx caches answers using the TTL value of a response. An optional valid parameter allows overriding it ... Before version 1.1.9, tuning of caching time was not possible, and nginx always cached answers for the duration of 5 minutes.
results.correction: None. All three elements are verbatim.

results.evidence_quote: There is no IPv6 equivalent; the IPv4 address works even in IPv6-only containers.
results.correction: None. 127.0.0.11 and the explicit no-IPv6-equivalent statement are both on the page.

results.claim: [10] Compose project-name precedence: -p flag, COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME, top-level name:, base name of the project directory. Compose uses the project name to isolate environments
results.evidence_quote: 1. The -p command line flag. 2. The COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME environment variable. 3. The top-level name: attribute in your Compose file. 4. The base name of the project directory containing your Compose file. 5. The base name of the current directory if no Compose file is specified. ... Compose uses a project name to isolate environments from each other.
results.correction: The precedence has FIVE levels, not four. The claim drops level 5, 'the base name of the current directory if no Compose file is specified'. That omission matters here precisely because it is a second, distinct directory-name dependency - exactly the failure mode the requirement is meant to close. State it as a 5-level precedence.

results.claim: [11] Compose namespaces containers, networks and named volumes by project name, so a rebuild in a differently-named directory attaches to fresh empty volumes and comes up healthy but empty; pinning top-level name: prevents this

results.correction: The cited page supports environment isolation by project name and supports that the default name is the directory basename, so the 'pin a top-level name:' remedy is sound. It does NOT state that containers, networks and named volumes are namespaced by project name, and it says nothing about the empty-volume false-pass scenario. That is correct Compose behaviour but is unsourced here - cite the volumes/networks top-level reference (which documents the project-prefixed naming and the external: escape hatch) as well, or present the false-pass narrative as reasoned consequence rather than documented behaviour.
