research.area: Capacity model  -  method, drivers, connection math, storage growth, measurement and thresholds (Area 11)
research.design_space: In 2026 the viable capacity-modelling approaches for a small line-of-business SaaS span a narrow, well-understood range, and the choice is mostly about how much measurement you buy rather than which theory you adopt. At one end sits reactive operation: no model, respond to incidents, which is defensible only when the failure cost is low and the blast radius is one customer. Next sits an analytic model built from architecture reasoning plus a small observed sample, projected forward with explicit unknowns  -  cheap, honest if the unknowns are labelled, and dangerous if they are not. Next sits passive instrumentation: attach existing runtime counters and database DMVs, sample on a schedule, and let a real growth slope emerge over weeks; this is the first approach that produces facts rather than opinions, and in .NET it costs no code change at all because dotnet-counters attaches to a live process by PID and SQL Server exposes its performance counters through sys.dm_os_performance_counters. Above that sits targeted micro-experimentation  -  deliberately exercising one transaction type or one scale dimension and measuring the delta  -  which converts specific dominant unknowns to measured values for a few hours of work each. Above that sits synthetic HTTP load testing with a current tool (k6, NBomber, Locust, Gatling, JMeter), which answers latency-and-concurrency questions but only those. At the far end sits continuous performance testing in CI with a full observability platform, which is correct at organisations that have someone whose job it is. The methodological frame that survives across all of these is Brendan Gregg's USE method  -  for every resource, check utilisation, saturation and errors  -  because it forces enumeration of resources rather than instrumentation of whatever happened to be easy. The decisive judgement in 2026 is unchanged from 2016: a capacity model's value comes from correctly identifying the driver variables and labelling which are measured, and a model that asserts a throughput number it never measured is actively worse than an empty page, because it will be quoted.

options.name: A. No model  -  react to incidents
options.how_it_works: Nothing is measured. Capacity questions are answered when something breaks: disk full, connection timeouts, users reporting slowness. This is the current state.
options.operational_cost: Setup 0 hours. Ongoing 0 hours/month until the first incident, then unbounded  -  a disk-full on this box stops SQL Server, Redis AOF and MinIO simultaneously because they share one filesystem, and no restore has ever been tested. Assumes no expertise.
options.why: It genuinely does fail obviously, which is this team's stated preference, and at 2 developers there is an honest argument for spending zero hours on capacity. It fails anyway because the failure it produces is simultaneous across five subsystems on a single VM with one untested backup path, and because the cheapest measurements here cost hours, not weeks. Reactive is a defensible posture only when recovery is cheap; here it is unproven.

options.name: B. Analytic model only  -  extrapolate from the 16-appointment sample
options.how_it_works: Build a spreadsheet from the measured audit ratio and architectural reasoning: rows per appointment, offices, months, bytes per row. Project disk and connections. No new measurement.
options.operational_cost: Setup 4-8 hours once. Ongoing ~0 hours/month. Assumes only arithmetic and the ability to read the code.
options.why: The honest case is strong: it costs almost nothing and it does surface the shape of the problem, which is most of the value. It fails subtly because the sample it rests on is incomplete in a way nobody noticed  -  only two of ABP's four audit tables were counted  -  and because the crucial multiplier, appointments per office per month, has never been stated by anyone. A spreadsheet with those two holes produces a confident number that is wrong by roughly 50% on one axis and unbounded on the other, and spreadsheets get quoted in planning meetings. Conditional: acceptable only if every unknown cell is literally coloured as unknown.

options.name: C. Passive instrumentation baseline  -  counters, DMV snapshots, docker stats, df
options.how_it_works: Four cron jobs and no code change. (1) dotnet-counters collect --format csv against the running API and AuthServer PIDs, providers System.Runtime, Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting, Microsoft-AspNetCore-Server-Kestrel and Microsoft.Data.SqlClient.EventSource. (2) A T-SQL snapshot every 5 minutes against sys.dm_os_performance_counters plus per-database row counts and used pages for the four audit tables, appended to CSV. (3) docker stats --no-stream every minute against the per-container memory caps. (4) df on the docker filesystem daily. Trend, do not alert.
options.operational_cost: Setup 4-8 hours. Ongoing 1-2 hours/month to read four numbers and append them to a trend sheet. Assumes shell, cron, basic T-SQL. No new long-running service, no new container, no application change.
options.why: This is the cheapest thing that turns opinion into fact, and it is the floor below which no capacity claim should be made. It fails obviously because the artefacts are CSV files whose absence is visible. Its limit is that it measures the system as it is  -  2 databases, no real users  -  so it establishes the idle floor and the growth slope but cannot answer what happens at 33 offices or what one appointment costs.

options.name: D. C plus two targeted micro-experiments (RECOMMENDED)
options.how_it_works: Adds the two experiments that convert the dominant unknowns to measured values. (i) The growth probe: snapshot rows and used_pages for the four audit tables, drive one appointment through the full 13-state lifecycle via the API, snapshot again, divide. Repeat ~20 times for a stable mean. (ii) The fleet multiplication test: provision offices up to 33 as empty databases using the existing idempotent host-UI provisioner  -  which the architecture already makes a UI action rather than a deployment  -  then let the twelve recurring jobs run for 48 hours with (C) collecting, and tear them down. No load generator, no synthetic traffic, no application change.
options.operational_cost: Setup 20-28 hours one-off total including (C). Ongoing 2-3 hours/month, plus 4-6 hours to re-run the growth probe after any release that changes the audited entity set. Assumes the ability to script an API call sequence and to use the existing office-provisioning UI.
options.why: The fleet multiplication test is the highest value-per-hour measurement available in this entire area and almost nobody thinks of it: the two questions that actually matter about scaling to 33 offices  -  what the connection fan-out does and whether a 15-minute sweep still finishes in 15 minutes  -  are answerable with zero users and zero load tooling, purely by making the tenant count real. The growth probe converts the dominant storage term from a two-table guess to a four-table measurement in an afternoon. Both produce hard artefacts and both fail loudly (a sweep that overruns, a delta that does not match).

options.name: E. D plus a small HTTP load test
options.how_it_works: A short k6 or NBomber script driving five endpoints (list appointments, create appointment, advance state, upload document, request packet) at stepped concurrency of 10/25/50 virtual users for ~20 minutes, with (C) collecting throughout. Separately, a concurrency ramp against the packet renderer alone to find its service time and queue behaviour.
options.operational_cost: Setup 8-16 hours on top of (D). Ongoing 2-4 hours per re-run, realistically once per quarter or before a significant release. Assumes JavaScript (k6) or C# (NBomber), OIDC token handling, and the discipline described below.
options.why: It is the only way to get p95 latency under concurrency, and the renderer ramp is genuinely load-bearing because that component is the likely fleet-wide throughput ceiling. It is conditional on two things this team will not automatically know. First, tenancy resolves from the Host header and nothing else and a bare IP cannot reach the application, so a generator pointed at the container or host address measures the Tenant-not-found path and reports excellent numbers; every request must carry a correct Host header. Second, there is exactly one environment, so this runs against the machine that will serve patients  -  which is safe only while the data is synthetic. The access token lifetime is 15 minutes, so any run longer than that needs refresh.

options.name: F. Full observability platform plus continuous load testing in CI
options.how_it_works: OpenTelemetry instrumentation in the application, a collector, a metrics backend and dashboards, plus load tests wired into a pipeline with pass/fail thresholds.
options.operational_cost: Setup 80-160 hours. Ongoing 8-16 hours/month to keep collectors, dashboards, storage retention and test scripts working. Assumes someone comfortable operating a metrics stack.
options.why: The honest case is real: it is where a growing platform ends up, .NET 10 has first-class OpenTelemetry support, and the capacity data falls out as a by-product of solving observability properly. It is wrong now on three counts. It consumes more than the entire estimated infrastructure budget for several months; it adds three long-running containers to a box with roughly 9.7 GB free disk and per-container memory caps already summing close to the 16 GB of RAM; and PII logging is enabled by default, so exported telemetry would carry PHI off the machine before anyone has decided that it should. It also fails subtly: a dashboard that is stale or wrong looks exactly like a dashboard that is right.

research.recommendation: Adopt Option D: the passive baseline plus the growth probe and the fleet multiplication test, with Option E's load test run once, deliberately, before the first real booking. The reasoning is that this architecture's resource consumption is not shaped like a web application's, so the standard capacity instrument  -  a load test producing a maximum requests-per-second  -  measures the axis this system is least constrained on. Argued from the architecture: user request volume is bounded by staff headcount across 11 to 33 practices, ABP does not audit-log GET requests by default so reads are nearly free, and the SPA is statically served with no server-side rendering and no Node runtime, so read traffic never touches .NET at all. What actually consumes resources is (1) audit write amplification, measured at over 100 rows per appointment across only two of the four audit tables, growing with write requests rather than with appointments; (2) the recurring-job fan-out, which at 33 offices means roughly 11,300 per-office database touches per day, each of which pays a full physical login because the 15-minute sweep interval exceeds the 4-8 minute pool idle-reap window; (3) the Hangfire dequeue loop, which at roughly five statements per second per worker sets a continuous query floor on the host database that does not scale with office count and is almost certainly the system's largest single source of SQL batch requests at idle; (4) blob growth for documents and packets, which is entirely unmeasured and is plausibly the dominant term in bytes even though audit is the dominant term in rows; and (5) the two-worker packet renderer, which is a shared, non-tenant-isolated throughput ceiling of roughly two divided by mean render seconds for the entire fleet. Of those five, three are measurable today with zero users and zero load tooling, and the fourth needs one afternoon of scripting. That is why the recommendation front-loads measurement over load generation. Two corrections to beliefs embedded in the brief follow from the evidence and change what to watch. First, QueuePollInterval = TimeSpan.Zero is Hangfire.SqlServer's own constructor default and the vendor's documented recommendation when SlidingInvisibilityTimeout is set; the dequeue loop sleeps 200 ms between attempts and releases the connection while waiting, so it is a steady modest floor, not aggressive spinning  -  it should be budgeted for, not fixed. Second, HIPAA does not impose six-year retention on application audit logs: 45 CFR 164.312(b) requires audit controls and states no retention period, while the six-year clock in 45 CFR 164.316(b)(2)(i) attaches to the documentation required by 164.316(b)(1)  -  policies, procedures, and records of required actions, activities and assessments. Because audit retention is the multiplier on the dominant storage term, obtaining a written retention decision is a higher-leverage capacity action than any tuning, and it costs an email to counsel rather than developer hours. Finally, the measurement window is closing: with one environment and no real PHI, this is the only period in which the fleet test and the load test can be run safely. Capture the baseline before the first real booking or it will never be captured.
research.operational_cost_of_recommendation: Setup, one-off: 4-8 hours for the passive baseline (four cron entries, one T-SQL snapshot script, one dotnet-counters invocation per .NET container, one df/du line); 4-6 hours for the growth probe (script the 13-state lifecycle against the API, snapshot the four audit tables before and after, repeat ~20 times); 8-12 hours for the fleet multiplication test (provision offices to 33 through the existing host UI, run 48 hours, collect, tear down, write up). Total 20-28 hours  -  roughly two-thirds of one developer-week, spendable across two months. The optional load test adds 8-16 hours. Ongoing: 2-3 hours per month. Thirty minutes a week to record four headline numbers (free bytes on the docker filesystem, total rows in AbpEntityPropertyChanges summed across office databases, longest recurring-job execution duration in the last 24 hours, and the ratio of SqlClient hard-connects to soft-connects), plus one hour a month to extend the trend sheet and re-check the slope. Add 4-6 hours to re-run the growth probe after any release that changes which entities are audited. Threshold: this is operable at 4 hours a month or more. Between 2 and 4 hours a month it degrades to collection without reading, which is the worst state of all  -  the CSVs exist, so the team believes it has a capacity practice, while nobody notices the slope crossing a line; that is a subtle failure in a team that has explicitly said it will only notice hard errors. Below 2 hours a month it is Option A with extra disk usage. Mitigation for the threshold: make the monthly reading a dated calendar item with one named owner and a four-row template, not a background intention. The stated figure of one developer-week per month is an estimate and a separate code-standard exercise already claims much of it, so if only a few hours exist, do the growth probe alone (4-6 hours)  -  it converts the single dominant term from guess to measurement and is the highest-value hour-for-hour item in this area. If even that is unavailable, do the daily df sample: one cron line, and after two weeks it yields a growth slope and a projected date for the first hard failure, which is the single most decision-relevant number the team can hold.

evidence.claim: Microsoft.Data.SqlClient creates a separate connection pool per unique connection string, matched exactly; keywords supplied in a different order are pooled separately. Connections are pooled per process, per application domain, per connection string.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn  -  SQL Server connection pooling (ADO.NET)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 1 pool per distinct connection string per process/AppDomain

evidence.claim: The default maximum pool size is 100. When the maximum is reached and no usable connection is available the request is queued; the pooler tries to reclaim connections until the timeout is reached, default 15 seconds, then an exception is thrown.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn  -  SQL Server connection pooling (ADO.NET), 'Add connections'
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Max Pool Size default 100; connection timeout default 15 s

evidence.claim: If Connection Lifetime / LoadBalanceTimeout is not set (default 0), the connection pooler removes a connection from the pool after it has been idle for approximately 4-8 minutes, in a random two-pass fashion. If MinPoolSize is zero or unspecified, pooled connections are closed after a period of inactivity.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn  -  SQL Server connection pooling (ADO.NET), 'Remove connections'
evidence.threshold_or_limit: idle reap ~ 4-8 minutes

evidence.claim: After a timeout or login error, subsequent connection attempts fail for the next 5 seconds (the 'blocking period'); each subsequent failure doubles the blocking period up to a maximum of 1 minute.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn  -  SQL Server connection pooling (ADO.NET)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 5 s doubling to max 60 s

evidence.claim: Microsoft documents 'Pool fragmentation due to many databases' as a named problem: connecting to a separate database per user or group produces a separate pool of connections to each database, which increases the number of connections to the server. The documented mitigation is to connect to one database and issue USE to switch  -  which is incompatible with a per-tenant connection-string design such as ABP's.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn  -  SQL Server connection pooling (ADO.NET), 'Pool fragmentation'
evidence.threshold_or_limit: n/a

evidence.claim: The default max worker threads value (setting 0) for a 64-bit machine with 4 or fewer logical CPUs is 512. A worker thread is assigned only to active requests and is released once the request is serviced, even if the connection remains open. When all worker threads are active with long-running queries, SQL Server might appear unresponsive until a worker completes.

evidence.claim: In Hangfire.SqlServer, QueuePollInterval defaults to TimeSpan.Zero in SqlServerStorageOptions' constructor, SlidingInvisibilityTimeout defaults to 5 minutes and CommandBatchMaxTimeout to 5 minutes; the documented recommended configuration is exactly QueuePollInterval = TimeSpan.Zero with SlidingInvisibilityTimeout set, DisableGlobalLocks = true and UseRecommendedIsolationLevel = true. TimeSpan.Zero is therefore the vendor default and recommendation, not an aggressive override.
evidence.source_name: Hangfire documentation  -  Using SQL Server; Hangfire source SqlServerStorageOptions.cs
evidence.threshold_or_limit: QueuePollInterval default TimeSpan.Zero; SlidingInvisibilityTimeout default 5 min

evidence.claim: With SlidingInvisibilityTimeout set and QueuePollInterval = TimeSpan.Zero, Hangfire.SqlServer's dequeue loop uses a client-side sleep of 200 ms between attempts (DefaultPollingDelayMs = 200, clamped between MinPollingDelayMs = 100 and PollingQuantumMs = 1000) via WaitHandle.WaitAny, issuing an 'update top (1) ... output inserted.* from JobQueue with (forceseek, readpast, updlock, rowlock)' per attempt. There is no WAITFOR in the T-SQL and the connection is released before waiting, so a poller does not hold a pooled connection while idle.
evidence.source_name: Hangfire source  -  SqlServerJobQueue.cs (master)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 200 ms polling delay -> ~5 statements/second per worker

evidence.claim: DERIVED, not sourced: the idle Hangfire query floor on the host database is approximately 5 x (worker count) statements per second  -  20/s and about 1.73 million statements per day at 4 workers, 40/s and 3.46 million per day at 8  -  and this floor does not increase with office count.

evidence.threshold_or_limit: 5 x workers per second; worker count is UNKNOWN

capability_requirements.requirement: The platform must permit attaching a runtime diagnostics tool to an already-running application process and collecting a counter time series to a file, without restarting the process, redeploying, or modifying application code.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Every leading indicator in the connection model  -  the ratio of physical to pooled connects, and the count of active connection pools  -  exists only inside the application process and is published by the data-access library. Without in-process attachment the office fan-out is invisible, and the alternative (adding instrumentation code) costs developer-weeks this team does not have.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft.Data.SqlClient publishes 16 event counters on Microsoft.Data.SqlClient.EventSource; dotnet-counters attaches by process id with no code change (Microsoft Learn, dotnet-counters and Event counters in SqlClient).
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: On a running instance, without deploying anything, obtain a CSV containing at least 60 samples of hard-connects and number-of-active-connection-pools for the API process within 10 minutes. If this requires a restart, a rebuild, or a sidecar that cannot be added to a running deployment, the requirement is not met.

capability_requirements.requirement: The platform must expose database-engine performance counters and per-table space usage to an operator on a schedule of at most 5 minutes, using only a database connection  -  no in-database scheduling agent and no vendor-specific monitoring agent installed inside the database host.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: There is no SQL Server Agent in this deployment and scheduling is entirely in-process via Hangfire, so any capacity collection that presumes an in-database scheduler cannot be built. A plain connection plus an external cron is the only mechanism that certainly exists.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: sys.dm_os_performance_counters exposes the SQL Statistics and Buffer Manager objects to T-SQL (Microsoft Learn); the brief records that SQL Server Agent is deliberately absent.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: From outside the database host, run one query returning Batch Requests/sec, User Connections and Page life expectancy, plus row counts and used pages for the four audit tables, and confirm it completes with only a SQL login and no agent, extension or additional service. Schedule it externally and confirm 12 samples land in an hour.

capability_requirements.requirement: Storage used for database backups must be a different capacity and failure domain from storage used for database data and log files, such that exhausting the backup target cannot prevent the database from accepting writes.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Backups currently write to a bind-mounted directory on the same disk as the database volume, so backup growth consumes the same headroom as data growth  -  and each retained full backup consumes approximately the used data size again. The same disk also holds the Redis AOF and the object store, so one exhaustion event stops five subsystems simultaneously. This is the failure this capacity model most expects to occur first.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: The brief records ~9.7 GB free on a 48 GB disk shared by named volumes sqldata, redisdata and miniodata plus a default ./backups bind mount, and that no restore has been tested.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Fill the backup target to 100% of its capacity, then insert a row into an office database and read it back. If the insert fails, or if the object store or cache also stops accepting writes, the requirement is not met.

capability_requirements.requirement: The platform must support at least 34 databases on one database instance while allowing an operator to enumerate, in a single query or command, every database with its size and its current connection count.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: One host database plus 33 offices is the stated headroom. The database engine itself permits far more, so the risk sits in whatever platform hosts it imposing a lower per-instance database ceiling or hiding per-database attribution  -  and without per-database attribution the growth model has no unit of measurement.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: SQL Server documents 32,767 databases per instance and 32,767 user connections (Microsoft Learn, Maximum capacity specifications); the brief states 11 offices at launch with headroom to 33.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Create 34 databases on one instance, then run one query that returns 34 rows, each with a database name, its size in megabytes, and the number of sessions currently connected to it. Confirm all 34 rows are present and the sizes are non-zero.

capability_requirements.requirement: The deployment must make the implied maximum server connection count explicit and testable: (1 + number of offices) x configured maximum pool size x number of application processes. Either the platform must sustain that many concurrent server connections, or the maximum pool size must be configured to a stated value rather than left at the default.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Because pools are created per exact connection string and the office connection strings are derived per tenant, pool count grows linearly with offices and nobody has stated the resulting ceiling. Leaving the default in place at 33 offices across two processes implies up to 6,800 connections that no one has decided to allow.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft documents one pool per distinct connection string per process and a default maximum pool size of 100; Microsoft separately names 'pool fragmentation due to many databases' as a known problem (Microsoft Learn, SQL Server connection pooling).
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Compute the number from the deployment's own configuration, then open that many simultaneous connections from a test harness and hold them for 60 seconds. Confirm no connection is refused and record the database server's memory consumption before and after. If the number cannot be computed because the maximum pool size is unstated, the requirement is not met.

capability_requirements.requirement: An operator must be able to observe, per application process, both the number of active connection pools and the rate of physical connections established versus connections served from the pool.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: These two numbers are the only leading indicators of the two most likely connection failures in this architecture. A physical-connect rate close to the pooled-connect rate proves pooling is delivering no benefit  -  which is the expected steady state, because the 15-minute sweep interval exceeds the 4-8 minute idle-reap window. A pool count above (1 + offices touched) proves connection strings are being constructed non-deterministically and pools are silently multiplying.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: hard-connects, soft-connects and number-of-active-connection-pools are documented SqlClient event counters; the pooler removes idle connections after approximately 4-8 minutes when MinPoolSize is zero (Microsoft Learn).
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Ask a reviewer who has never seen the system to state the current value of both numbers within 10 minutes using only tooling already present on the host. Then confirm the pool count equals one plus the number of distinct offices touched since process start.

capability_requirements.requirement: Any store holding session-critical key material must be free of memory-pressure eviction, or that key material must reside in a store separate from any evictable cache.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: The same Redis instance holds the distributed cache, the distributed lock provider, and the ASP.NET DataProtection keyring shared by the API and the AuthServer. Under any allkeys-* eviction policy, memory pressure would silently discard the keyring, invalidating every session and every in-flight email-confirmation link with no error emitted anywhere. That converts a loud failure into a silent one, inverting the team's stated preference.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Redis maxmemory defaults to 0 (no limit) on 64-bit and allkeys-* policies evict any key regardless of expiry (Redis documentation, Key eviction); the brief records the shared keyring under CaseEvaluation-Protection-Keys with SetApplicationName identical in both processes.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Read back the configured maxmemory and maxmemory-policy. If maxmemory is non-zero and the policy begins with allkeys-, the requirement is not met unless the keyring demonstrably lives elsewhere. Then push the store past its memory ceiling and confirm that an existing authenticated session still works afterwards.

capability_requirements.requirement: A load generator used against this system must be able to set an arbitrary HTTP Host header per request, and the capacity test plan must require it.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Classified SHOULD because it constrains the testing tool rather than the running platform, but it is the difference between a valid measurement and a worthless one. Tenancy resolves from the Host header and nothing else, and a bare address cannot reach the application at all, so a generator pointed at a container or host address measures the tenant-not-found path and reports excellent throughput.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: The brief states tenancy resolves from the Host header via HostAwareDomainTenantResolveContributor and that a bare IP address cannot reach the application; a request whose Host matches no office returns 'Tenant not found'.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: From the load generator, issue one request to the application's address with the Host header set to a valid office slug and confirm an authenticated 200 with a body containing office-scoped data. Then issue the same request without the header and confirm it is rejected. If both return 200, the tool is not setting the header and every result gathered with it is invalid.

capability_requirements.requirement: The recurring-job scheduler must record per-execution duration for every occurrence, and must either prevent or explicitly record concurrent execution of the same recurring job.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: The three 15-minute jobs each iterate every office sequentially. As office count grows, or if one office's database is unreachable, sweep duration grows  -  and the connection-pool blocking period (5 seconds, doubling to 60) means a single broken office adds up to a minute of stall per sweep. If a sweep exceeds 15 minutes, occurrences overlap, doubling connection demand and risking double-processing. Duration is the leading indicator; overlap is the lagging failure.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: The brief records three recurring jobs at 15-minute intervals iterating offices with one connection per office database, and a migration runner with no per-tenant error handling that can leave offices in a broken state; the blocking-period behaviour is documented by Microsoft.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Make one office database unreachable, let the 15-minute sweep run three times, and retrieve the recorded duration of each occurrence. Confirm durations are recorded and that either the next occurrence was suppressed while one was running or an overlap is visible in the record. If durations are not retrievable per occurrence, the requirement is not met.

capability_requirements.requirement: The platform must permit standing up a throwaway instance carrying the full target tenant count with no user traffic, for the purpose of measuring background-job fan-out.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Classified SHOULD because the measurement can, today, be taken in the single existing environment while all data is synthetic. It becomes a MUST the moment real bookings exist, because at that point there is nowhere safe to run it and the fan-out question becomes permanently unanswerable. The architecture already makes this cheap  -  adding an office is an idempotent host-UI action, not a deployment.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: The brief records exactly one environment, IOfficeDatabaseProvisioner.ProvisionAsync as an idempotent host-UI action, and that no real patient data exists yet.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Provision offices to the target count on a disposable instance, run for 48 hours with no user traffic, and produce a record of per-sweep duration and physical connection rate across at least 190 fifteen-minute cycles. Then destroy the instance and confirm no residual databases remain.

capability_requirements.requirement: The object store must report total bytes and object count for a given tenant key prefix without enumerating every object.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Document and packet bytes are plausibly the largest byte-growth term in the system and are currently entirely unmeasured, while audit rows are the largest row-growth term. Without per-prefix accounting the storage model has a hole exactly where its dominant term may sit. Listing-based accounting is specifically unavailable on the partner bucket, whose policy deliberately withholds bucket listing.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: The brief records ABP-shaped keys of the form tenants/{tenantId:D}/... across six logical containers in two physical buckets, and a partner policy granting fetch-by-key while deliberately withholding bucket listing.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Request total bytes and object count for one tenant prefix and confirm a result returns without a full object enumeration. Verify it against a manual sum on a prefix containing fewer than 50 objects; the two figures must match.

capability_requirements.requirement: The concurrency limit and per-operation duration of any synchronous shared rendering or document-assembly component must be observable as a metric, not only as user-perceived delay.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: The packet renderer runs two workers and is shared across every office. Its fleet-wide throughput is two divided by mean render seconds, which makes it the most likely hard ceiling in the system and the one place where one tenant can starve all others in an architecture that is otherwise database-isolated. Neither number has ever been measured, and queueing there is invisible today.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: The brief records a Python/Flask packet renderer with 2 workers, and that the Hangfire worker pool was explicitly pinned because bursts oversubscribe that renderer and the SMTP relay into timeouts  -  evidence that saturation has already happened.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Submit four render requests simultaneously against a two-worker deployment and record the completion time of each. Confirm the queue wait for the third and fourth is retrievable from a metric or log line, and that mean render duration can be stated as a number. If the only evidence of queueing is total latency, the requirement is not met.

capability_requirements.requirement: Audit-log retention must be enforceable per database as a configuration or scheduled operation, without a schema migration.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Audit rows are the dominant row-growth term and nothing prunes them today. Because the host and tenant DbContexts share a base model, any schema-level solution requires paired migrations in both and must then be applied to every office by a migrator with no per-tenant error handling  -  a change that can leave the fleet on split schema versions with no report of which offices succeeded. A retention operation that needs no schema change avoids that entire hazard class.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: The brief records unconfigured audit retention with nothing pruning it, two DbContexts sharing a base and shared model configuration requiring paired migrations, and a db-migrator that loops offices with no per-tenant error handling.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Apply a retention of 30 days to one office database, run the operation, and confirm that rows older than 30 days are gone from all four audit tables, that the number of rows removed is reported, and that no schema migration was applied to any database.

capability_requirements.requirement: An operator must be able to determine, for a single named business transaction, the number of rows and the number of bytes it adds to the audit tables.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: This is the unit of the entire storage model. Every projection in this area is the product of this number and a transaction rate, and today only a partial version of it exists  -  the measured baseline covers two of the four audit tables, so the per-transaction cost the team believes is likely understated by roughly half. Without this measurement, no storage projection is defensible.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: The brief's measured baseline of ~1,450 audit-log rows and ~2,689 entity property-change rows for 16 appointments, against the four-table ABP audit schema (audit logs, audit log actions, entity changes, entity property changes).
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Record rows and used pages for all four audit tables, drive one appointment through the full lifecycle, record again, and report the delta as rows-per-transaction and bytes-per-transaction. Repeat 20 times and report the mean and spread. A reviewer must be able to reproduce the figure from the two snapshots alone.

anti_requirements: The platform must NOT require an eviction policy on the store that holds the DataProtection keyring or any other session-critical key material. Eviction there is a silent, total session loss with no error surface  -  precisely the subtle failure mode this team cannot detect.

The platform must NOT aggregate database or application metrics in a way that loses per-database and per-tenant attribution. A single fleet-wide 'connections' or 'queries per second' figure is actively misleading here, because the Hangfire polling floor on the host database is large, constant, and does not grow with office count  -  it will mask per-office growth entirely.

The platform must NOT place backup storage in the same capacity domain as database data files, cache persistence, and object storage. One filesystem shared by all four means the first capacity failure is simultaneous across four subsystems, and the recovery path has never been exercised.

The platform must NOT require installing an agent inside the database host or inside the application container in order to obtain basic capacity metrics. Every added long-running component is a component two SDE 1s must operate, and the required metrics are already reachable through a SQL connection and a diagnostics attach.

The platform must NOT auto-scale application instances without a mechanism to pin the background-job processing server to exactly one instance. A second instance silently duplicates twelve recurring jobs, doubles the polling floor, and multiplies the per-office connection pools  -  with no error anywhere to reveal it.

The platform must NOT retain capacity metrics for a shorter window than 90 days of daily aggregates. Growth here is measured in a slope over weeks; a 7- or 14-day retention makes the dominant term structurally unobservable no matter how good the collection is.

The platform must NOT make standing up an additional full-fleet environment impractical. With one environment, the only alternative to a disposable instance is testing against the machine that serves patients, and that option expires the moment real bookings begin.

The platform must NOT normalise, strip or rewrite the HTTP Host header on the path between a test client and the application. Doing so does not merely break tenancy  -  it silently redirects every measurement to the tenant-not-found path while still returning fast responses.
surprises: QueuePollInterval = TimeSpan.Zero is Hangfire.SqlServer's own constructor default and the vendor's documented recommendation, not an aggressive setting someone chose. The dequeue loop does not spin: it sleeps 200 ms between attempts and releases the SQL connection while waiting. So the brief's characterisation ('aggressive polling') is wrong in mechanism but right in consequence  -  budget for it, do not 'fix' it.

That polling floor is approximately 5 statements per second per worker, all against the host database. At a plausible 4 workers that is roughly 1.7 million statements per day at complete idle, which is almost certainly the largest single source of SQL batch requests in the entire system. A 'quiet' system will not show a quiet database. Critically, this floor does NOT grow with office count  -  so Batch Requests/sec is a bad proxy for tenant growth and will look reassuringly flat while per-office work climbs underneath it.

Every 15-minute sweep pays a full physical login per office. The sweep interval (15 minutes) exceeds the documented connection-pool idle-reap window (4-8 minutes), so with MinPoolSize at its default of 0 every office pool is empty when the next sweep arrives. The office pools deliver essentially no benefit on the job path. At 33 offices the recurring jobs alone generate roughly 11,300 physical connects per day  -  socket, TLS negotiation and SQL login each time. The host pool, by contrast, is kept permanently warm by Hangfire's own polling. The asymmetry is invisible unless you look at hard-connects versus soft-connects.

Microsoft names this exact architecture as a problem, by name, in its own connection-pooling documentation: 'Pool fragmentation due to many databases.' The documented mitigation  -  connect to one database and issue USE to switch  -  is structurally incompatible with ABP's per-tenant derived connection strings, so the antipattern cannot be escaped without changing the tenancy model. Knowing it is a named, documented condition rather than an unknown risk changes how you argue about it.

Two of the four ABP audit tables were never counted. The measured baseline covers audit logs and entity property changes, but not audit log actions (written per audited controller action and application service call) or entity changes (the parent rows of the property changes). A four-table figure is plausibly around 390 rows per appointment against the 259 the team currently believes  -  roughly 50% higher, on the model's single most load-bearing number.

ABP does not audit GET requests by default (IsEnabledForGetRequests is false) and records no entity changes at all unless explicitly configured. So the audit volume is a chosen configuration, not an inherent cost of the framework. The EntityHistorySelectors scope is a tuning knob that can change the dominant storage term with no schema migration and no data loss for anything the business actually needs  -  which is a far cheaper lever than partitioning, archiving or bigger disks.

HIPAA does not require six-year retention of application audit logs. 45 CFR 164.312(b) mandates audit controls and states no retention period at all; the six-year clock in 45 CFR 164.316(b)(2)(i) attaches to the documentation required by 164.316(b)(1)  -  policies, procedures, and records of required actions, activities and assessments. Since retention is the multiplier on the dominant storage term, a written retention decision from counsel changes the six-year projection by a factor of several and costs no developer time. (Caveat: I could not verify whether the January 2025 Security Rule NPRM has been finalised  -  federalregister.gov and ecfr.gov were both blocked by the outbound proxy  -  and California workers' compensation record rules may impose their own period.)

The two-worker packet renderer is the most likely hard throughput ceiling of the entire platform, and it is the one component that is NOT tenant-isolated. Fleet-wide packet throughput is two divided by mean render seconds, shared across all 33 offices. In an architecture whose whole premise is one database per practice, this is the single channel through which one office can starve every other office. Mean render duration has never been measured. The brief already contains the evidence that saturation has occurred  -  the Hangfire worker pool was pinned precisely because bursts oversubscribed this renderer.

Setting Redis maxmemory with an eviction policy  -  the standard production-hygiene advice, and the first thing anyone will recommend on seeing memory pressure  -  would be actively harmful here. This Redis holds the shared DataProtection keyring, so under any allkeys-* policy memory pressure would silently evict it, invalidating every session and every in-flight email-confirmation link with no error emitted. Today's unset maxmemory (Redis defaults to 0 on 64-bit) means a container OOM-kill instead, with AOF recovery  -  a loud failure, which is the safer one. Do not let a well-meaning hardening pass turn an obvious failure into a silent one.

A load generator pointed at the container IP or the host address will measure nothing. Tenancy resolves from the Host header and nothing else, and a bare IP cannot reach the application at all  -  so the generator will exercise the tenant-not-found path and report excellent latency and throughput. This is a highly likely first-attempt mistake and the resulting numbers look completely plausible.

That same load test can, at zero extra cost, settle a security-relevant question the brief flags as never tested: whether ABP's four default __tenant resolvers (query string, header, cookie, route) are still active. Send a request whose Host resolves to office A carrying ?__tenant=<office B's id>, then check which database received the write. One request answers it definitively.

Query plans are cached per database  -  dbid is a documented plan attribute, and sys.dm_exec_plan_attributes exposes an is_cache_key bit per attribute. If dbid is a cache key on this instance, the same EF Core query compiles and caches once per office, so plan-cache memory and SQL Compilations/sec grow with tenant count even if total data volume does not. Verify empirically with the documented query rather than assuming; either way, the point is that memory pressure in this design has a term that scales with office count independently of data.

Backups to the same filesystem mean total disk consumption is data x (1 + number of retained full backups). The disk is shared with the Redis AOF and the object store, so a single exhaustion event stops five subsystems at once  -  and no restore has ever been tested, meaning the recovery path from the most likely capacity failure is entirely unproven.

The connection-pool blocking period (5 seconds after a login failure, doubling to a maximum of 60) couples a known correctness hazard to a capacity one. The migration runner loops offices with no per-tenant error handling, so a partially-migrated fleet produces repeated login failures; each failure extends the blocking period; the sequential sweep gets progressively longer; and if it crosses 15 minutes, occurrences overlap. A schema-migration accident becomes a job-concurrency incident by way of the connection pool.

Capacity measurement has an expiry date. With exactly one environment and no real PHI, this is the only period in which the fleet-scale test and the load test can be run without risking patient data or live bookings. After the first real appointment there is nowhere safe to run either. The pre-PHI window is not just a data-migration advantage  -  it is the measurement window, and it closes on the same day.

not_recommended.pattern: Run a load test to find the system's maximum requests per second, and use that as the capacity number.
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: This is what 'capacity planning' means to most people and to most stakeholders. It produces a single headline figure that fits in a slide, it is directly comparable across releases, and it is genuinely the right first question for a request-driven public web application. The tooling is mature and cheap, and having any number is psychologically better than having none when someone asks 'can we take on 20 more offices?'.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It measures the axis this architecture is least constrained on. User request volume is bounded by staff headcount across 11 to 33 practices; GET requests are not audit-logged by default so reads are nearly free; and the SPA is statically served with no server-side rendering and no Node runtime, so read traffic never reaches .NET. Meanwhile the three things that actually consume resources  -  the per-office job fan-out, audit write amplification, and a two-worker packet renderer shared across the fleet  -  appear nowhere in a max-RPS figure. Worse, the number would be quoted in growth decisions it cannot inform, producing exactly the false confidence the commissioning brief warns against. A capacity model that asserts throughput it did not measure the constraint for is worse than none.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: If the platform ever exposes a patient-facing or public endpoint, or a partner-driven API with callers the business does not control, then request volume becomes unbounded by headcount and max-RPS becomes the right question.

not_recommended.pattern: Instrument the application with OpenTelemetry, run a collector and a metrics backend, and build dashboards as the capacity foundation.
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: This is where a growing platform legitimately ends up. .NET 10 has first-class OpenTelemetry support, so the instrumentation is largely configuration rather than code. It would give per-endpoint latency, cross-process correlation between the API, AuthServer and renderer, and it would solve the observability gap and the capacity gap with one piece of work rather than two. Building it once is arguably cheaper than maintaining ad-hoc scripts forever, and doing it before real traffic means the baseline is captured from day one.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: Three reasons, in order of severity. First, PII logging is enabled by default, so exported telemetry would carry PHI off the machine before anyone has decided that it should  -  a compliance decision disguised as an instrumentation task. Second, it adds three long-running containers to a box with roughly 9.7 GB free disk and per-container memory caps already summing close to the 16 GB of RAM; the monitoring stack would compete for the very resource it is monitoring. Third, and most decisively for this area, the data it produces is per-request latency, which is not the constrained term  -  it answers none of the four questions that matter (bytes per appointment, connections per sweep, sweep duration at 33 offices, renderer throughput) any better than four cron lines do, while costing an order of magnitude more of the scarce developer-week.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: Once PII redaction in logs is settled, and once either real traffic exists in volume or there is more than one application instance so that cross-instance correlation actually buys something. Also right the moment latency attribution across API, AuthServer and renderer becomes a recurring debugging need.

not_recommended.pattern: Scale out the API horizontally  -  a second instance behind the proxy  -  as the answer to capacity growth.
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It removes the most obvious single point of failure, and this application is unusually well-suited to it: there is no SignalR and no WebSocket use, so no sticky-session requirement; the SPA is static; and the DataProtection keyring is already shared through Redis with an identical application name in both processes, which is precisely the prerequisite for multiple instances to read each other's protected payloads. Most systems need work before they can scale out; this one mostly does not.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: As a capacity response it makes the model worse, not better. Pools are created per process, so a second API instance adds another (1 + offices) pools  -  at 33 offices, another 3,400 potential connections against a 4-vCPU database server. If the Hangfire processing server is not pinned to exactly one instance, twelve recurring jobs begin running twice, doubling both the polling floor and the per-office connect rate, and introducing double-processing in the reconciliation and outbox-drain jobs. That failure is silent: nothing in the current system would report it. Scale-out is a resilience answer to an availability question, and applying it to a capacity question here trades an obvious constraint for a subtle correctness bug.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: When a measured constraint is API CPU or memory  -  which this model predicts it is not  -  or when availability requirements independently force redundancy. Even then, only with the background processing server pinned to exactly one instance and that pinning verified, not assumed.

not_recommended.pattern: Partition or archive the audit tables (sliding-window partitioning, columnstore on historical partitions) to handle unbounded log growth.
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: This is the textbook answer to a large, append-only, time-ordered table, and partitioning has been available outside Enterprise edition since SQL Server 2016 SP1. It keeps query performance flat as the table grows, makes purging a metadata operation rather than a large delete, and it is the solution a DBA would reach for without hesitating.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It is schema work, and schema work in this system is unusually expensive and unusually dangerous. The host and tenant DbContexts share a base and a shared model configuration, so an entity mapped in both needs a paired migration in both sets  -  and forgetting one produces an office database missing a table, surfacing as an invalid-object-name exception at runtime. The migration would then have to be applied across up to 33 databases by a runner that loops offices with no per-tenant error handling and no report of which succeeded. All of that risk buys query performance on tables that nothing queries in the hot path. The actual problem is bytes on a shared disk, and the cheap fix for bytes is a retention decision plus a scheduled delete  -  which needs no schema change at all.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: When a single office's audit tables grow past the point where a bounded delete can complete inside an acceptable window, or when the audit log UI becomes a real query workload with users waiting on it. Both are measurable thresholds, not guesses  -  watch rows per office and delete duration.

not_recommended.pattern: Raise Max Pool Size to head off connection-pool exhaustion.
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It is the first suggestion any search for 'timeout expired prior to obtaining a connection from the pool' returns, it is a one-line configuration change, and when a pool genuinely is too small it is the correct fix. Given the arithmetic here looks alarming  -  34 pools at 33 offices  -  pre-emptively raising the ceiling feels prudent.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It treats a symptom that this architecture is unlikely to produce and makes the real one harder to see. The risk here is not that any single office pool fills; the recurring jobs iterate offices sequentially, so per-pool concurrency is near one. The risk is 34 pools that are each perpetually cold, and a total connection ceiling nobody has decided on. Raising the maximum increases the undecided ceiling  -  at 33 offices across two processes the default already implies up to 6,800 connections  -  and it removes the pool-timeout exception, which is one of the few loud signals this system currently has. If a pool timeout ever does occur here, it is far more likely to indicate a leaked connection or a stalled sweep than an undersized pool, and raising the limit hides both.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: If measurement shows a single office pool genuinely holding more than 100 concurrent connections. That would be evidence of a real concurrency change  -  or of a leak  -  and either way the measurement, not the default, should drive the number. Setting Max Pool Size explicitly to a chosen value (in either direction) is good practice; raising it reflexively is not.

not_recommended.pattern: Build a Prometheus and Grafana stack first, so there is somewhere to put the metrics.
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: Metrics need a home, and CSV files scattered on a VM are not a monitoring practice. Building the collection infrastructure once, properly, avoids a pile of throwaway scripts and gives the team dashboards they can glance at rather than files they must read. It is the conventional order of operations and it is what most engineers would do.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It inverts the sequence. The team does not yet know which numbers matter  -  that is the deliverable of this exercise, not its prerequisite  -  so a dashboard built now would display everything and highlight nothing. It also costs three more long-running containers on a machine with roughly 9.7 GB free disk, consuming the scarce infrastructure hours before a single capacity fact exists. Every question in this model is answerable from a CSV produced by dotnet-counters collect and a T-SQL snapshot script. The right order is: measure, learn which five numbers move, then build a display for those five.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: Immediately after this model is calibrated with real measurements and the team can name the five numbers it watches. Build the dashboard for those five, deliberately, and resist adding the rest.

not_recommended.pattern: Size the platform from a vendor sizing guide or an industry rule of thumb (users per vCPU, GB of RAM per thousand records).
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It is instant and free, it requires no measurement, and for the overwhelming majority of ordinary CRUD web applications it lands within an order of magnitude  -  which is often all a planning conversation needs. It also gives a defensible-sounding basis when someone asks for a number today rather than in six weeks.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: Every such rule is calibrated on request-driven web applications where user traffic is the dominant resource consumer. In this system the dominant consumers are a background-job fan-out that scales with tenant count rather than users, an audit write amplification of over 100 rows per appointment, a continuous polling floor that exists at zero users, and a two-worker synchronous renderer. None of those appear in any sizing guide, and none of them scale with the variable the guide keys on. Applying one would produce a confidently wrong number derived from the wrong independent variable  -  the precise failure the commissioning brief exists to prevent.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: Never for this system as designed. It becomes reasonable only if the architecture changes so that user request volume genuinely dominates  -  for example if the background sweeps were replaced by event-driven work and the renderer were made asynchronous and elastic.

what_would_change_the_answer: A stated figure for appointments per office per month. This is the single most load-bearing unknown in the entire model and nobody has given it. Every storage projection is this number multiplied by a per-transaction cost; without it, projections span an order of magnitude. It is a business input, not an engineering measurement, and it should be obtainable in one conversation.

A measured bytes-per-row for each of the four audit tables from a real office database, replacing the estimate. Snapshot used_pages and rows per table and divide; the whole storage model converts from estimate to measurement in one query.

A written retention decision for the audit tables. Because HIPAA's six-year clock attaches to documentation rather than to raw audit rows, a policy choice of 90 days, one year or six years changes the dominant storage term by a factor of up to 24  -  a bigger lever than any tuning available.

The Hangfire worker count. The brief says the pool is 'explicitly pinned' but not to what, and the idle query floor is 5 statements per second per worker. This number sets the entire system's baseline database load and is one configuration line away.

Whether the three 15-minute sweeps carry [DisableConcurrentExecution] or an equivalent guard. If not, sweep duration crossing 15 minutes silently becomes concurrent execution and double-processing, which changes both the connection math and the correctness risk.

Whether /var/lib/docker, the backup directory, and the named volumes are on the same filesystem. One df command settles it. If they are separate mounts, the shared-failure-domain argument weakens considerably; if not, disk is the first hard limit and it takes five subsystems with it.

Measured mean packet-render duration and the renderer's true concurrency. These two numbers determine the fleet-wide throughput ceiling and whether it is the binding constraint. Currently both are unmeasured, and this is the most likely candidate for the real limit.

Whether EntityHistorySelectors is configured as AddAllEntities() or a targeted list. If it is AddAllEntities(), the dominant storage term is reducible by configuration alone, with no schema change  -  the cheapest available lever, and one that stops existing.

Measured object-store growth per appointment. If document and packet bytes exceed audit bytes  -  which is plausible for a PDF-assembly workload  -  the model's centre of gravity moves from rows to blobs and the priority order in the instrumentation plan should be reversed.

Whether dbid is a plan cache key on this instance (checkable with sys.dm_exec_plan_attributes). If it is, plan cache and compilation pressure scale with office count independently of data volume, adding a memory term that grows on the tenancy axis rather than the data axis.

A change to the office ceiling beyond 33, or the arrival of one office generating an order of magnitude more volume than the others. The sequential job fan-out and the shared renderer both degrade linearly with office count but non-linearly with per-office skew, and the current model assumes rough uniformity.

A move to a SQL Server edition with hard scale limits. Developer edition carries Enterprise's scale limits, so the current constraint is licensing rather than capacity  -  but a move to Express would impose a 10 GB per-database ceiling and a 1,410 MB buffer pool across the whole instance, either of which would become the binding constraint immediately and change every conclusion here.

A second application instance, for any reason. It multiplies the connection pools, and if the background processing server is not pinned it duplicates all twelve recurring jobs  -  invalidating the connection and polling arithmetic entirely.

results.claim: [1] One pool per unique connection string, exact match; different keyword order pools separately; pooled per process, per AppDomain, per connection string
results.evidence_quote: Connections are pooled per process, per application domain, per connection string and when integrated security is used, per Windows identity. Connection strings must also be an exact match; keywords supplied in a different order for the same connection will be pooled separately.
results.correction: Verified verbatim, but the stated threshold '1 pool per distinct connection string per process/AppDomain' is an UNDER-COUNT for capacity purposes. The same page adds three further pool-splitting axes the claim omits: per Windows identity under integrated security; per SqlCredential instance ('Different instances of SqlCredential will use different connection pools, even if the user ID and password are the same'); and by transaction enlistment ('Connections are also pooled based on whether they are enlisted in a transaction'). A capacity model that multiplies pools only by connection string can undercount real pool count.

results.claim: [2] Max Pool Size default 100; on exhaustion request is queued, pooler reclaims until timeout (default 15 s) then throws
results.evidence_quote: Connections are added to the pool as needed, up to the maximum pool size specified (**100 is the default**). ... If the maximum pool size has been reached and no usable connection is available, the request is queued. The pooler then tries to reclaim any connections until the time-out is reached (**the default is 15 seconds**). If the pooler cannot satisfy the request before the connection times out, an exception is thrown.
results.correction: No correction. Both numbers and the queue/reclaim/throw sequence are stated verbatim on the page.

results.claim: [3] With Connection Lifetime/LoadBalanceTimeout unset (default 0), idle connections are removed after approx. 4-8 minutes in a random two-pass fashion; MinPoolSize 0 or unspecified means pooled connections close after inactivity
results.evidence_quote: If LoadBalanceTimeout (or Connection Lifetime) isn't set (default value = 0), the connection pooler removes a connection from the pool after it has been idle for approximately **4-8** minutes (in a random two-pass fashion), or if the pooler detects that the connection with the server has been severed.
results.correction: No correction. Also verified: 'If MinPoolSize is either not specified in the connection string or is specified as zero, the connections in the pool will be closed after a period of inactivity.'

results.claim: [4] After a timeout or login error, subsequent attempts fail for 5 s (blocking period), doubling on each subsequent failure up to a maximum of 1 minute
results.evidence_quote: subsequent connection attempts will fail for the next **5** seconds, the "blocking period". ... Subsequent failures after a blocking period ends will result in a new blocking periods that is twice as long as the previous blocking period, up to a *maximum of **1** minute*.
results.correction: Verified verbatim, but the claim omits an exception stated in the same callout: 'The "blocking period" mechanism doesn't apply to Azure SQL Server by default. This behavior can be changed by modifying the PoolBlockingPeriod property.' If the capacity model ever targets a managed SQL endpoint rather than a self-hosted instance, the 5s/60s backoff does not apply by default.

results.claim: [5] Microsoft documents 'Pool fragmentation due to many databases' as a named problem; mitigation is to connect to one database and issue USE
results.evidence_quote: However, there is a separate pool of connections to each database, which increase the number of connections to the server. ... Instead of connecting to a separate database for each user or group, connect to the same database on the server and then execute the Transact-SQL USE statement to change to the desired database.
results.correction: Named section and mitigation verified verbatim. The trailing clause ('incompatible with a per-tenant connection-string design such as ABP's') is the researcher's inference, not on the page - correctly framed as such, but note it is an inference the page neither states nor contradicts.

results.claim: [6] 32,767 user connections; 32,767 databases per instance; max database size 524,272 TB; default TDS packet size 4 KB
results.evidence_quote: | User connections | 32,767 | ... | Databases per instance of SQL Server | 32,767 | ... | Database size | 524,272 terabytes | ... The default packet size is 4 KB.
results.correction: All four values verified verbatim. Note the page applies to SQL Server 2016 (13.x) and later; it is not a statement about managed/cloud SQL offerings, whose connection ceilings are far lower and tier-dependent.

results.claim: [7] Default max worker threads (setting 0) for 64-bit with <=4 logical CPUs is 512; a worker is assigned only to active requests and released after servicing; all-busy workers make the server appear unresponsive
results.evidence_quote: | <= 4 | 256 | 512 | 512 | ... A worker thread is assigned only to active requests and is released once the request is serviced. This happens even if the user session/connection on which the request was made remains open. ... When all worker threads are active with long running queries, SQL Server might appear unresponsive until a worker thread completes and becomes available.
results.correction: Verified, with one qualification the claim states unconditionally: footnote 2 on the same table reads 'Starting with SQL Server 2017 (14.x), the Default Max Workers value is divided by 2 for machines with less than 2 GB of memory.' On a container or VM provisioned under 2 GB the default is 256, not 512 - relevant here because a capacity model for small tenant hosts may sit below that line.

results.claim: [8] 16 event counters on EventSource 'Microsoft.Data.SqlClient.EventSource' including the eight named; readable out-of-process with dotnet-counters; requires Microsoft.Data.SqlClient 3.0.0+ and .NET Core 3.1+
results.evidence_quote: Currently there are 16 different event counters available for Microsoft.Data.SqlClient ... Event counters are available when targeting **.NET Core 3.1** and higher or **.NET Standard 2.1** and higher. This feature is available starting with Microsoft.Data.SqlClient **version 3.0.0**. ... dotnet-counters monitor --counters Microsoft.Data.SqlClient.EventSource -p <process-id> --refresh-interval 3
results.correction: Count (16), EventSource name, version floors, dotnet-counters usage, and all eight named counters verified exactly. One naming nit for anyone scripting this: the pooled-hit counter is 'soft-connects' (rate) and 'active-soft-connects' (level) - there is no 'active-soft-connections'.

results.claim: [9] dotnet-counters attaches to a running process by pid or name with no code change/restart; 'collect --format csv -o' writes a time series; Linux needs shared TMPDIR and same user or root; container outside the process namespace needs --diagnostic-port or running inside the container
results.evidence_quote: On Linux and macOS, using this option requires the target application and dotnet-counters to share the same TMPDIR environment variable. Otherwise, the command will time out. ... To collect metrics using dotnet-counters, it needs to be run as the same user as the user running target process or as root. ... It's usually only necessary to specify the port explicitly when waiting for a process that will start in the future or communicating to a process that's running inside a container that isn't part of the current process namespace. ... --format <csv|json> ... -o|--output <output>
results.correction: All operational constraints verified. Two additions worth carrying into the requirement: the page also warns of bitness matching ('A 32 bit processes cannot access modules of a 64 bit process'), and states 'Counters can be read from applications running .NET 5 or later' - so the attach capability is not available against a .NET Core 3.1 target with a current tool build even though SqlClient counters themselves date from 3.1.

results.claim: [10] Named EventCounters for System.Runtime, Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting and Microsoft-AspNetCore-Server-Kestrel; and on .NET 9+ System.Runtime is a Meter with names like dotnet.thread_pool.queue.length and dotnet.process.memory.working_set
results.evidence_quote: ThreadPool Queue Length (threadpool-queue-length) ... ThreadPool Thread Count (threadpool-thread-count) ... GC Heap Size (gc-heap-size) ... Working Set (working-set) ... CPU Usage (cpu-usage) ... Current Requests (current-requests) ... Failed Requests (failed-requests) ... Request Rate (requests-per-second) ... Total Requests (total-requests) ... Request Queue Length (request-queue-length) ... Connection Queue Length (connection-queue-length) ... Current Connections (current-connections) ... TLS Handshake Rate (tls-handshakes-per-second)
results.correction: All 13 EventCounter names verified exactly on the cited page. The final sentence is NOT supported by this URL: available-counters.md is the legacy EventCounters reference (ms.date 2020-12-17) and contains no Meter names, no mention of .NET 9, and no 'dotnet.thread_pool.queue.length' or 'dotnet.process.memory.working_set'. It only links out to 'the well-known metrics reference'. The Meter claim is true but must be cited to https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/diagnostics/built-in-metrics-runtime (or to the dotnet-counters page, which notes 'If the app uses .NET version 8 or lower, the System.Runtime Meter doesn't exist in those versions and dotnet-counters will fall back to display the older System.Runtime EventCounters').

results.claim: [11] Hangfire.SqlServer: QueuePollInterval defaults to TimeSpan.Zero in the constructor, SlidingInvisibilityTimeout 5 min, CommandBatchMaxTimeout 5 min; documented recommended config is Zero + sliding timeout + DisableGlobalLocks=true + UseRecommendedIsolationLevel=true; therefore TimeSpan.Zero is the vendor default AND recommendation, not an aggressive override
results.evidence_quote: docs.hangfire.io presents the block as recommended settings 'for new installations', and states: 'These settings will be turned on by default in 2.0, but meanwhile we should preserve backward compatibility.' The page does not state TimeSpan.Zero is the default; it describes it as an option available 'starting from Hangfire 1.7.0' when SlidingInvisibilityTimeout is configured.
results.correction: Three problems. (1) The CITED URL contradicts the 'vendor default' framing - it explicitly calls these recommended-not-default. The claim is nevertheless TRUE for Hangfire 1.8.x, but only per source I checked separately: SqlServerStorageOptions.cs at tags v1.8.14 and v1.8.20 sets QueuePollInterval = TimeSpan.Zero, SlidingInvisibilityTimeout = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5), CommandBatchMaxTimeout = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5), UseRecommendedIsolationLevel = true. At v1.7.34 the same constructor sets QueuePollInterval = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(15) and SlidingInvisibilityTimeout = null. So the answer is version-dependent and the claim must state 'default in 1.8.x, 15 s in 1.7.x'. (2) DisableGlobalLocks = true is NOT a default - the 1.8.x constructor sets DisableGlobalLocks = false. The claim lumps it into the same sentence as the defaults. results.claim: [12] Dequeue loop uses a 200 ms client-side sleep (DefaultPollingDelayMs=200, clamped 100..1000) via WaitHandle.WaitAny, issuing one 'update top (1) ... output inserted.* ... with (forceseek, readpast, updlock, rowlock)' per attempt; no WAITFOR; connection released before waiting
results.evidence_quote: private static readonly int PollingQuantumMs = 1000; private static readonly int DefaultPollingDelayMs = 200; private static readonly int MinPollingDelayMs = 100; ... update top (1) JQ set FetchedAt = GETUTCDATE() output INSERTED.Id, INSERTED.JobId, INSERTED.Queue, INSERTED.FetchedAt from [{schemaName}].JobQueue JQ with (forceseek, readpast, updlock, rowlock) ... WaitHandle.WaitAny(waitArray, pollingDelayMs);
results.correction: The constants, the clamp (Math.Min(Math.Max(200, 100), 1000) = 200 ms), the hints, the absence of WAITFOR, and connection-release-before-wait are all correct: FetchJob() wraps the command in _storage.UseConnection(...) which returns the connection before WaitHandle.WaitAny runs outside it. Two corrections. (1) The OUTPUT clause is not 'inserted.*' - it is an explicit four-column list, OUTPUT INSERTED.Id, INSERTED.JobId, INSERTED.Queue, INSERTED.FetchedAt. (2) MATERIAL OMISSION: the loop is gated by a process-wide SemaphoreSlim(initialCount: 1) keyed on Tuple<SqlServerStorage, queuesString> ('semaphore = Semaphores.GetOrAdd(resource, CreateSemaphoreFunc); semaphore.Wait(cancellationToken);'), active unless DisableFetchSemaphores is set - and DisableFetchSemaphores is NOT set in the SqlServerStorageOptions constructor, so it defaults to false. Only one worker per storage+queue-set is inside the 200 ms polling loop at a time. Omitting this is what makes claim 13 wrong.

results.claim: [13] DERIVED: idle Hangfire query floor is ~5 x (worker count) statements/sec - 20/s and ~1.73M/day at 4 workers, 40/s and 3.46M/day at 8 - independent of office count
results.evidence_quote: if (!_options.DisableFetchSemaphores) { semaphore = Semaphores.GetOrAdd(resource, CreateSemaphoreFunc); semaphore.Wait(cancellationToken); } while (!cancellationToken.IsCancellationRequested) { fetchedJob = FetchJob(queues); if (fetchedJob != null) return fetchedJob; WaitHandle.WaitAny(waitArray, pollingDelayMs); ...
results.correction: WRONG BY A FACTOR OF THE WORKER COUNT. The polling loop in DequeueUsingSlidingInvisibilityTimeout is serialized by a per-(storage, queue-set) SemaphoreSlim with initialCount 1, enabled by default (DisableFetchSemaphores is never set in the constructor, so false). At idle, each worker performs ONE unconditional FetchJob and then blocks on the semaphore; exactly one worker occupies the 200 ms loop. The steady-state idle floor is therefore ~5 statements/second PER STORAGE PER QUEUE-SET - about 432,000 statements/day - not 5 x workers. The claimed 20/s (1.73M/day) at 4 workers and 40/s (3.46M/day) at 8 overstate the floor by 4x and 8x. Two corollaries the claim also misses: the floor scales with the number of DISTINCT QUEUE SETS and the number of SqlServerStorage instances (so a per-tenant storage instance WOULD make it scale with office count, contradicting the claim's closing assertion), and if QueuePollInterval were ever set to >= 1 s the long-polling path is disabled entirely (useLongPolling = configuredPollInterval < LongPollingThreshold, 1 second).

(b) The premise holds only when the office database sees NO other traffic in the interval. During business hours interactive user traffic against the same office connection string keeps pooled connections warm, so the full-physical-connect cost applies mainly to off-hours cycles, not to all 343 touches.
