material_errors: CLAIM 13 IS WRONG (the single most consequential error). The idle Hangfire query floor is NOT 5 x worker count. SqlServerJobQueue.DequeueUsingSlidingInvisibilityTimeout gates its polling loop behind a SemaphoreSlim(initialCount: 1) keyed on Tuple<SqlServerStorage, queuesString>, active unless DisableFetchSemaphores is set - and DisableFetchSemaphores is never assigned in the SqlServerStorageOptions constructor, so it defaults to false. At idle only ONE worker occupies the 200 ms loop per storage per queue-set. The floor is ~5 statements/second (~432,000/day), not 20/s (1.73M/day) at 4 workers or 40/s (3.46M/day) at 8. The stated figures overstate by 4x and 8x. The claim's closing assertion that the floor 'does not increase with office count' is also conditional: because the semaphore key includes the SqlServerStorage instance, a per-tenant storage instance WOULD make the floor scale with office count.

CLAIM 11 conflates recommendation with default, and the cited URL says the opposite of the claim. docs.hangfire.io presents the block as recommended 'for new installations' and states 'These settings will be turned on by default in 2.0, but meanwhile we should preserve backward compatibility.' Separately verified in source: QueuePollInterval = TimeSpan.Zero, SlidingInvisibilityTimeout = 5 min, CommandBatchMaxTimeout = 5 min and UseRecommendedIsolationLevel = true ARE constructor defaults at v1.8.14/v1.8.20, but at v1.7.34 they are 15 seconds and null. And DisableGlobalLocks = true, which the claim lists in the same sentence, is NOT a default - the constructor sets it false. The claim must be version-scoped and must separate the one recommendation from the four defaults.

CLAIM 15 says the ABP audit schema 'comprises four tables'. The cited model builder configures FIVE: AbpAuditLogs, AbpAuditLogActions, AbpEntityChanges, AbpEntityPropertyChanges and AbpAuditLogExcelFiles. The seven indexes listed are all correct, but a retention/purge design or storage inventory scoped to 'the four audit tables' will silently miss the fifth.

CLAIM 10's final sentence (.NET 9 System.Runtime Meter names such as dotnet.thread_pool.queue.length and dotnet.process.memory.working_set) is not supported by the cited available-counters page, which is the legacy EventCounters reference (ms.date 2020-12-17) and mentions neither Meters nor .NET 9. The assertion is true but must be cited to built-in-metrics-runtime. All 13 EventCounter names in the same claim are exact.

CLAIM 18 was left unverified but is answerable and the answer changes the plan. The Federal Register HTML site is indeed blocked (302 to unblock.federalregister.gov), but its JSON API is not: RIN 0945-AA22 returns exactly one document - the Proposed Rule of 2025-01-06, comments closed 2025-03-07. As of 2026-08-31 the HIPAA Security Rule NPRM has NOT been finalised, and no new federal log-retention period is in force. Plan to 45 CFR 164.312/164.316 as amended at 78 FR 5694-5695 (2013).

CLAIM 27 left k6 currency open; it is resolvable. GitHub renders year-less dates for current-year releases, which produced the 'internally inconsistent version/date pairs'. Two independent registries settle it: Homebrew reports k6 stable 2.2.0, and Docker Hub grafana/k6 shows 2.2.0 pushed 2026-08-10, 1.8.1 (maintained v1 line) pushed 2026-08-12, and master rebuilt 2026-08-31. k6 current stable is v2.2.0, actively maintained.

CLAIM 30's central assumption inverts the ABP model. It reasons that audit log ACTIONS are 'at least as numerous as audit logs (>=1,450)'. ABP writes one AbpAuditLogs row per request/unit of work and one AbpAuditLogActions row per audited controller action AND per audited application-service call within that request - so actions are typically several per audit log. 1,450 is a weak lower bound, the ~6,200 four-table total is likely low, and the '~50% higher' headline understates the gap. Measure all five tables rather than extrapolate.

CLAIM 29 cites the connection-pooling page for the 32,767 user-connection maximum, which appears only on maximum-capacity-specifications-for-sql-server. More importantly it compares the 6,800-connection ceiling against the wrong constraint: the binding limits long before 32,767 are max worker threads (512 at <=4 logical CPUs, per claim 7) and per-connection server memory. The (1+N) pool count is also a floor, not a ceiling, because the same page splits pools additionally by Windows identity, SqlCredential instance and transaction enlistment.

CLAIM 28 overstates the physical-connect conclusion. 'Essentially every one of those touches pays a full physical connect' holds only when the office database sees no other traffic within the 4-8 minute randomised reap window - during business hours interactive traffic on the same connection string keeps pooled connections warm. It also rests on MinPoolSize being 0, which the claim itself marks as 'presumed' and unverified. The 343/3,773/11,319 arithmetic is correct; the connect-cost conclusion should be scoped to off-hours as an upper bound.

CLAIM 21 attributes the environment variable name MSSQL_MEMORY_LIMIT_MB to the mssql-conf page. That name does not appear on that page; it only links out to a separate environment-variables article. The 80%-of-physical-memory default and the memorylimitmb-vs-max-server-memory relationship are verified verbatim.

CLAIM 1's stated threshold ('1 pool per distinct connection string per process/AppDomain') is an under-count for capacity purposes. The same page splits pools additionally by Windows identity under integrated security, by SqlCredential instance, and by transaction enlistment. Every sentence quoted is accurate; the threshold derived from it is incomplete.

research.area: Area 12  -  Migration path from single-VM docker-compose to a target architecture: sequencing, preconditions, rollback, and the point of no return
research.design_space: In 2026 the viable migration shapes for a single-host container deployment reduce to five archetypes, and the choice between them is decided by two axes, not by taste. The first axis is how much downtime you can buy: every zero-downtime technique  -  log shipping, CDC, transactional replication, dual-write  -  is fundamentally a technique for making two systems agree about state while both are live, and every one of them costs specialist expertise and fails by drift rather than by error. The second axis is whether your routing layer is an actual switch: DNS is not a switch but an eventually-consistent hint held in caches you do not control (RFC 2181 8, RFC 2308 5, RFC 8767 4), whereas a stable name in front of a changeable upstream is a real switch with instant rollback. A third consideration is the unit of increment  -  per-request, per-user, per-tenant, per-component, per-environment  -  and tenants are the most useful unit wherever they exist, because tenant boundaries are already isolation boundaries and Microsoft's own multitenancy guidance names progressive per-tenant rollout as a first-class benefit of deployment-per-tenant models. A fourth is schema compatibility: expand-contract (parallel change) is what makes application rollback possible at all, because without it "roll back the app" means "roll back to code that cannot read its own database". The archetypes themselves are: stop-the-world cutover; lift-and-shift of the whole unit followed by in-place decomposition; dependency-at-a-time strangulation behind existing configuration seams; parallel build with traffic-shifted cutover (blue-green or canary), which requires either shared state or synchronisation; and continuous-replication cutover. Cutting across all five is a rehearsal axis that matters more than the archetype: Fowler, Cartwright, Horn and Lewis's legacy-displacement catalogue attributes the large failures of stop-the-world cutovers specifically to cases where "no rehearsal or practice of the cut-over was possible or performed". Finally, every migration has a set of acts after which the previous state cannot be restored, and mature sequencing identifies those in advance and pushes them to the end rather than discovering them mid-window. A useful and under-used test for irreversibility is whether reversing the step would require a third party's cooperation on their schedule, the destruction of data created since the step, or waiting out a cache window you do not control.

options.name: A. Stop-the-world cutover (single freeze, move everything, resume)
options.how_it_works: Announce a window. Quiesce traffic and background jobs. Take final backups of all 12 databases and the Redis keyring, mirror object storage, restore everything onto the target, repoint DNS, bring the stack up, verify, resume. One window, one decision point.
options.operational_cost: Setup ~40h to script and write the runbook, plus 8-12h per full rehearsal. The window itself is 4-8h at current data volumes. Ongoing cost zero. Assumes only shell, docker and SQL literacy  -  no new technology. Fowler's catalogue is explicit that the rehearsal is the variable that separates success from large failure, so budget at least two full rehearsals.
options.why: At the system level it fails obviously  -  the whole thing is either up or down. But inside the window it fails subtly in exactly one place, and that place is already known to be defective: db-migrator loops the office fleet with no per-tenant error handling and no report, so a partial fleet migration produces split schema versions that surface later as invalid-object-name exceptions in one office. Viable, and genuinely the cheapest correct answer while data is disposable and downtime is free, but only after the migrator is fixed and the runbook rehearsed. It becomes indefensible the moment real practices depend on the system, because the window stops being free and the rehearsal stops being repeatable.

options.name: B. Lift-and-shift the compose stack unchanged to a new host
options.how_it_works: Same docker-compose file, same image tags, new machine. Copy the named volumes (sqldata, redisdata, miniodata), copy the secrets file and the OpenIddict PFX, repoint DNS. Nothing about the architecture changes.
options.operational_cost: Setup ~20h. Window 2-4h. Ongoing zero. Requires no expertise the team does not already have  -  it is the operation they already perform, once, onto different hardware.
options.why: Its value is not as a destination  -  it reproduces every single point of failure, the same sa credentials, the same one-disk backups  -  but as the cheapest possible proof that the runbook is correct and that 'leave this machine' can be decoupled from 'change this architecture'. Treat it as rehearsal #1 with a real target. Two cautions: copying redisdata while Redis is running can capture an AOF mid-rewrite and yield an invalid file, which would destroy the DataProtection keyring; and if the target host's timezone differs, the seven daily jobs scheduled between 03:00 and 09:15 move, which can put outbound email to claimants and attorneys at an unintended hour.

options.name: C. Dependency-at-a-time relocation behind existing configuration seams
options.how_it_works: Leave the application running on the old VM. Move its stateful dependencies one at a time  -  SQL Server, then Redis, then object storage  -  each by changing a single configuration value, each with its own short freeze, each with rollback = change the value back. Move the stateless tier (api, authserver, angular, packet-renderer, proxy) last, when it has no state left to carry.
options.operational_cost: Setup ~60h across three moves including rehearsals. Each window 30-90 minutes. Ongoing zero. Assumes SQL backup/restore literacy and careful Redis handling; no new platform technology.
options.why: This is the shape that actually matches the constraint. The seams already exist and were built deliberately: TenantConnectionStringProvider relocates every office database by one configuration key with no code change; the Redis connection string, the MinIO endpoint and the SMTP relay are all single values. That is branch-by-abstraction already done, which is the expensive part of the pattern. It converts one irreversible event into four reversible ones, each small enough for two SDE1s to reason about. One blocking dependency: the database step is fleet-atomic today because all office connection strings derive from one template, so 'move one office' is not currently expressible. That is a small code change, and it is the highest-leverage change in the whole programme.

options.name: D. Parallel build with shared datastores and a per-office canary
options.how_it_works: After C has moved the state, stand the new application tier up alongside the old one, both pointing at the same SQL Server, the same Redis and the same object storage. Route one office's three hostnames to the new tier at the edge. Widen office by office. The standby tier runs with background job execution disabled.
options.operational_cost: Setup ~30h on top of C. Ongoing ~4h/month for as long as both tiers run  -  keep that window short, weeks not quarters. Assumes the edge can route by hostname to different upstreams, which the existing nginx already does.
options.why: Safe here for a specific and checkable reason: Hangfire's recurring job scheduler takes a distributed lock (resource 'recurring-jobs:lock') plus a per-job lock before enqueueing an occurrence, and the docs state multiple server instances work without additional configuration because distributed locks are used. Two application instances sharing one Hangfire storage therefore do not double-fire the twelve recurring jobs  -  which matters enormously, because those jobs drain a per-recipient email outbox to claimants, attorneys and adjusters, and a duplicate send is not a technical incident but an ex-parte problem. Conditional on two things: the two tiers must share Hangfire storage (which follows from moving state first), and the standby must set IsJobExecutionEnabled=false, a switch this codebase already uses for AuthServer. The office is the natural canary unit and Microsoft's tenancy guidance names progressive per-tenant rollout as a benefit of this deployment model.

options.name: E. Continuous-replication cutover (log shipping or transactional replication)
options.how_it_works: Establish ongoing replication from each source database to the target, let it catch up, then cut over when lag is near zero, reducing the freeze to a final log ship and recovery.
options.operational_cost: Setup ~80-120h: enable SQL Server Agent in the container, configure twelve separate log-shipping topologies (each needs backup, copy and restore Agent jobs, plus an alert job on a monitor instance), and test a failover that has never been performed. Ongoing ~8h/month of monitoring. Assumes DBA-level expertise this team does not have.
options.why: It buys minutes of downtime that this system has no reason to buy. Concretely blocked and concretely expensive: log shipping is built entirely from SQL Server Agent jobs, and this stack deliberately runs no SQL Server Agent  -  scheduling is in-process via Hangfire; log shipping does not fail over automatically, so you still perform a manual cutover; and it is unavailable on Express. Its failure mode is the worst possible one for this team  -  a secondary that has quietly stopped restoring, or lag that grows without anyone watching, discovered at the cutover. Reject.

options.name: F. Rebuild and reseed (available only while all data is synthetic)
options.how_it_works: Build the target empty. Run the existing idempotent IOfficeDatabaseProvisioner for each of the 11 offices, which applies the tenant schema, seeds catalogues, the admin user and the office's doctor. Discard the old data entirely. No backups, no restores, no consistency verification.
options.operational_cost: Setup ~15h. Window equals the provisioning run. Ongoing zero. Requires nothing the team does not do today  -  adding an office is already a host-UI action.
options.why: It deletes the single hardest part of the problem  -  moving 12 databases with version, edition, integrity and downtime constraints  -  by not moving them. It is the only option with an expiry date, and the expiry date is the first real booking by a real practice. Even if the eventual production cutover uses C, F is what makes rehearsals cheap enough to do five times instead of once. It also exercises the provisioner, which is load-bearing to how the business grows and is currently proven only twice (host plus one office).

research.recommendation:
RECOMMENDED SHAPE: option C (dependency-at-a-time relocation behind the existing configuration seams) as the spine, with F (rebuild-and-reseed) as the rehearsal mechanism and D (per-office canary on shared state) as the final application move. Reject E outright. Use B once, as rehearsal #1.

THE CENTRAL CLAIM, WHICH IS MY JUDGEMENT AND NOT A SOURCED FACT: the migration is a precondition of go-live, not a successor to it. Every property that makes this plan executable by two SDE1s  -  free downtime, repeatable rehearsals, no BAA on the critical path, rollback by discarding rather than reconciling, and option F existing at all  -  is a property of the no-PHI window, and every one of them inverts on the day a real practice takes a real booking. If offices are onboarded first, the same programme needs specialists this team does not have. Sequence the business accordingly or accept a materially worse migration.

WHY C RATHER THAN A: the seams already exist and were built deliberately. TenantConnectionStringProvider relocates every office database by changing one configuration key with no code change. The Redis connection string, the MinIO endpoint and the SMTP relay are all single values. That is branch-by-abstraction with the expensive part already paid for. Fowler's precondition for the pattern is precisely that an abstraction layer exists to let two implementations coexist; here it does, at the infrastructure-dependency layer rather than the code layer. So the strangler here strangles the infrastructure, not the code. Do not decompose the application  -  that is a different exercise and must not share a window with this one.

=== PHASE 0  -  CODE AND PROCESS PRECONDITIONS (nothing moves until these are true) ===

P0.1 Per-office connection string override. Today the office database move is fleet-atomic: all offices derive from one host template, so 'move office 3 and leave the rest' is not expressible. Make the provider prefer an explicitly configured per-tenant connection string and fall back to derivation. ABP stores connection strings in tenant configuration and ABP Commercial's SaaS module surfaces them. Then apply expand-contract at the configuration layer: EXPAND by writing every office an explicit connection string identical to its currently derived one (a semantic no-op that removes the derivation dependency), MIGRATE offices one at a time, CONTRACT later or never. Before step 3 this must be true, or step 3 becomes a single 12-database cutover with no incremental rollback.
Precondition to verify: the custom provider actually honours an explicit value. Untested today.

P0.2 Make db-migrator report per office and fail loudly. Replace the fleet loop with an EF Core migration bundle invoked once per office with an explicit --connection, so each office is a separate process with its own exit code. Bundles run without the SDK or source, use EF's migration locking, and can roll back to a named migration. Microsoft's guidance is explicit that every replica should not migrate from its entrypoint and that the migration container should not be restarted after success. Also add `dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes` to CI for BOTH DbContexts, and confirm RelationalEventId.PendingModelChangesWarning is not suppressed  -  on EF Core 9+ that warning turns the 'entity mapped in both contexts, migration added to only one' hazard from a runtime invalid-object-name into a hard migrator failure, which is exactly the fail-obvious behaviour this team needs.

P0.3 Startup assertions that convert silent degradation into refusal to start. (a) AuthServer must fail hard if the configured OpenIddict signing/encryption certificate is absent  -  never fall back to a development certificate, which persists but is "not shared across instances" and would produce an AuthServer that starts happily and issues tokens that break intermittently. (b) Both processes must assert SetApplicationName("CaseEvaluation") and log the resolved ApplicationDiscriminator, because Data Protection isolates apps by content-root path by default and a container path change would silently break every protected payload even with the key ring moved intact.

P0.4 An outstanding-external-link inventory query. The hourly change-request-consent-expiry-sweep proves consent links have a bounded lifetime; anonymous-uploads implies external parties hold upload links. Write a query that counts unexpired externally-held links and their latest expiry. This tells you when the cutover window is cheap, which is not the same as Saturday night.

P0.5 Fix the unauthenticated /hangfire dashboard (already planned) before any environment exists at more than one address.

=== PHASE 1  -  MAKE THE ENVIRONMENT RECONSTRUCTIBLE, THEN REHEARSE ===
Precondition: P0.1-P0.4 complete.
Build the target as a throwaway using option F: empty stack, provision 11 offices through the existing provisioner, no data migration. Time it. Do it at least three times, from a clean host, from the committed repository and the secrets file only, following a written runbook. Use the ACME staging environment for these  -  Let's Encrypt allows only 5 certificates per identical set of identifiers per 7 days, so rehearsing against production issuance rate-limits your rehearsals, and 5 authorisation failures per identifier per hour will lock you out within minutes if DNS-01 automation is wrong.
Exit criterion: two consecutive rehearsals completed by the developer who did NOT write the runbook, inside 4 hours, with no undocumented step.
Rollback: none needed; nothing in production has changed.

=== PHASE 2  -  STABILISE THE NAMES BEFORE MOVING ANYTHING ===
Precondition: Phase 1 exit criterion met.
2a. Inventory every hostname: 11 x {office}.base, {office}.api.base, {office}.auth.base, the wildcards at both depths, minio.base (exact), the apex, and anything the partner has hard-coded.
2b. Check for DNSSEC (a DS record at the parent). If present, do NOT change DNS operator during this programme  -  RFC 6781 4.3.5 makes the parent DS TTL the rate limiter and a mistake is total resolution failure. Likewise do NOT change registrar or nameservers: you control TTLs inside your zone but not the parent's delegation NS TTL. Change records, never delegation.
2c. Create every new name that will be needed NOW, pointing at the current backend. Never query a name before it exists: negative answers are cached at min(SOA.MINIMUM, SOA.TTL) and RFC 2308 5 records that resolvers commonly cap this at one to three hours. An accidental early lookup pins NXDOMAIN.
2d. Verify CAA records permit the CA you will use, before any issuance attempt.
2e. Obtain the certificate. A wildcard requires DNS-01; HTTP-01 cannot issue wildcards. You need *.base, *.api.base, *.auth.base and the exact minio.base, because a wildcard matches exactly one label  -  the same constraint AWS documents for virtual-hosted-style S3 buckets under SSL, and the reason this system already uses path-style MinIO addressing.
2f. Lower TTLs on every record you intend to change to 60-300s, at least (current TTL + margin) before the first move, ideally 24h before. Verify by querying each authoritative nameserver directly (they must agree) and then a spread of independent public resolvers, watching the reported TTL count down  -  resolver caches are independent and you cannot flush them.
2g. Put a stable indirection in front. The tenancy model resolves from the Host header and nothing else, so any new edge MUST preserve Host byte-for-byte. Do not assume it does: nginx's own documented default is `proxy_set_header Host $proxy_host`, i.e. rewriting the Host to the upstream name is the default behaviour, not the exception. While you are in the file, fix the two known traps: no default_server on 443 (api.base with no office label currently falls through to the Angular container, and the bare apex falls to the AuthServer), and the stale-upstream-IP problem that requires resolver + variable proxy_pass everywhere, not only in the minio block.
Rollback at every point in Phase 2: revert the record. Cost bounded by the TTL you set, which is why 2f precedes everything.

=== PHASE 3  -  MOVE STATE, ONE DEPENDENCY AT A TIME, APPLICATION STAYS PUT ===
Precondition: Phase 2 complete; TTLs low; runbook rehearsed; per-office connection strings explicit.

3a. OBJECT STORAGE. Two changes are being conflated and must be separated: relocating the store, and rotating the credentials. Only the second requires the partner. Preserve the hostname minio.base and, if the target permits an operator-specified access key ID and secret, preserve the credentials too  -  then the partner sees nothing, and every presigned or anonymous-upload URL already in an external party's inbox continues to work because those URLs encode the hostname. Mirror with a continuous sync (mc mirror --watch), freeze writes briefly, final sync, repoint the endpoint, verify. Verify by independently computed content digests on a sample plus exact object count and total bytes  -  NOT by comparing ETags, which are not MD5 digests for multipart objects, and not by trusting the mirror tool, which does not inherently verify integrity. Rollback: repoint the endpoint back; the source is still authoritative because nothing deleted it.
Do the partner credential rotation as a SEPARATE, LATER, PARTNER-SCHEDULED change. It is needed regardless  -  the application authenticates to MinIO as root and several secrets were pasted into chat transcripts  -  but it must not be inside a migration window.

3b. DATABASES. Pin the target to the SAME SQL Server major version as the source. This is not a preference: a backup cannot be restored to an earlier version, and restoring to a newer version automatically upgrades the database. Bundling a version upgrade into the move therefore converts a reversible step into a one-way door. Change the version later, as its own step, with its own backup.
Before choosing the target edition, run `SELECT feature_name FROM sys.dm_db_persisted_sku_features` in all 12 databases  -  a database using edition-restricted features cannot be moved to an edition that lacks them. Express is architecturally excluded (10 GB maximum relational database size, no backup compression, no backup-to-URL, no log shipping) because the measured 100:1 audit-to-business-data ratio with no pruning makes a hard per-database ceiling a wall with no relief valve. Developer edition is licensed for development and test, not production, so an edition change is mandatory  -  make it part of this step, since it is the same restore.
Transport: use SQL Server 2022's BACKUP/RESTORE TO URL against the existing S3-compatible endpoint. This removes both the 'backups land on the same disk that has 9.7 GB free' problem and the 'how do I move 12 databases off this box' problem in one move. Preconditions: HTTPS endpoint with a CA the SQL host trusts, and on Linux the CA must be in /var/opt/mssql/security/ca-certificates BEFORE SQL Server starts; secret key must not contain a colon; total URL under ~200 characters; not available on Express.
Order: host database first (it carries the Hangfire schema and the tenant registry), then offices one at a time. Between the host move and each office move, the explicit per-office connection strings from P0.1 keep the un-moved offices pointing at the old instance  -  that is what makes this incremental.
Per-database window: quiesce jobs, let the email and integration outboxes drain (draining before the final backup is what prevents a restore from resending messages already delivered), take the final backup, restore, verify, repoint, unquiesce.
Rollback: repoint the connection string to the old instance and restore the pre-move backup there. This works only while you still hold that backup and the old instance is still the same version. Keep both until the step is confirmed.

3c. REDIS. The 'session-preserving versus session-dropping' framing is a false binary here, because Redis holds three things with three different values. The DataProtection key ring under CaseEvaluation-Protection-Keys is small, irreplaceable and must move intact. The distributed cache  -  permission grants, dynamic claims, settings, application configuration  -  is disposable and rebuilds on demand. Distributed locks are ephemeral and must NOT be carried across (a lock believed held across a cutover is worse than no lock). So: preserve the key ring, discard everything else. That is cheap; there is no trade to make.
Dropping the key ring is what you must not do, and the reason is not user convenience. Staff re-authenticating is trivial. What dies with the key ring is every email-confirmation token and every protected link already in the inbox of a claimant, an attorney or an adjuster  -  and email is the spine of the external-party workflow, so re-issuing them is a human conversation per recipient, not a button.
Mechanically: seed the new instance by replication (REPLICAOF, then promote) or by copying the RDB, which the Redis docs state is safe to copy while the server runs because it is renamed atomically and never modified after production. Do NOT naively copy the AOF directory  -  since Redis 7.0 it is a multi-part file set, and copying during a rewrite "might end up with an invalid backup"; if you must, set auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 0, confirm aof_rewrite_in_progress is 0, then copy or hard-link.
Time this step using P0.4's inventory: do it when the outstanding-link count is lowest. Expect a brief cache-rebuild burst across 12 databases at cutover  -  negligible at 11 offices, but it is a shape that worsens with tenant count and it lands at the moment you can least diagnose it.
Rollback: repoint the connection string back. The old instance is untouched.

3d. THE SIGNING CERTIFICATE. Carry the same PFX and passphrase; do not rotate. Both signing AND encryption credentials. It must be present before AuthServer starts, and P0.3 makes its absence a startup failure. Because both sides hold the same certificate, tokens issued by either AuthServer validate at either API  -  which is what makes the Phase 4 application cutover reversible with respect to identity. That property is destroyed by any temptation to 'rotate while we're in there'. If rotation is genuinely needed, do it afterwards using OpenIddict's support for multiple registered credentials (it prefers the furthest expiry for signing but validates against any registered key), and let 15-minute access tokens age out before removing the old one.
Also verify whether OpenIddict is configured with UseDataProtection. If it is, all token types except identity tokens are Data-Protection-formatted, refresh tokens and authorization codes depend on the Redis key ring, and 3c's care level rises accordingly. The docs are explicit that a separate authorization server and API "MUST be configured to use the same application name and share the same key ring".

=== PHASE 4  -  MOVE COMPUTE, PER OFFICE ===
Precondition: all of Phase 3 complete and stable for at least one full week, so that every recurring job cadence (15-minute, hourly, daily 03:00-09:15) has executed at least once against the moved state.
Stand up the new application tier against the already-moved datastores. Run it with IsJobExecutionEnabled=false until it is primary. Route one office's three hostnames to it at the edge. Choose an internal or friendliest office first. Widen one office at a time over days, not hours.
This is safe because both tiers share Hangfire storage and Hangfire's scheduler takes a distributed lock per recurring job before enqueueing, so recurring jobs do not double-fire. It would NOT be safe with separate Hangfire storage  -  that is the configuration that duplicates outbound email and duplicates partner integration records. Verify it empirically: run both tiers for one full 15-minute cycle and confirm each of the three 15-minute jobs executed exactly once.
Rollback: route the office's hostnames back. Instant, because state is shared and identity is shared. This is the cheapest rollback in the entire programme and it is a direct consequence of having moved state first.

=== PHASE 5  -  RETIRE, THEN THE IRREVERSIBLE ACTS ===
Precondition: all offices on the new tier, one week clean, and a restore actually tested from the new backup location (no restore has ever been tested  -  do this before, not after, retirement).
Only now: raise DNS TTLs; decommission the old authoritative infrastructure; delete old databases; destroy the old VM; rotate the partner credentials on the partner's schedule; and consider edge hardening. Do NOT submit HSTS preload until the domain layout is final and you are certain  -  preload requires max-age of at least one year with includeSubDomains, "inclusion in the preload list cannot easily be undone", removal "takes months for a change to reach users", and includeSubDomains on a wildcard-tenant domain commits every present and future office subdomain.

=== POINTS OF NO RETURN, NAMED IN ADVANCE ===
Apply the test: reversing requires a third party's schedule, destroying data created since, or waiting out a cache you do not control.
1. The first real booking by a real practice on the new system. Everything above assumes this has not happened.
2. Restoring a database to a NEWER SQL Server major version. Avoided by pinning versions in 3b.
3. Partner re-credentialing. Deferred to Phase 5 and explicitly on their schedule.
4. Raising DNS TTLs and decommissioning the old authoritative nameservers  -  RFC 8767 serve-stale means resolvers may keep answering with old data for days once your servers are unreachable, so the TTL is a floor, not a ceiling.
5. HSTS preload submission.
6. The CONTRACT step of any expand-contract change, including P0.1's optional return to derived connection strings.
7. Deleting the last pre-move backup of any database.
8. Rotating the OpenIddict certificate without keeping the old key registered.
Items 4 and 5 are the two nobody writes down.
research.operational_cost_of_recommendation:
SETUP (one-off, hours of genuine engineering time): Phase 0 code preconditions 40-60h (per-tenant connection strings ~16h, migrator bundle + per-office reporting + CI pending-model-changes check ~16h, startup assertions ~8h, outstanding-link inventory query ~4h, Hangfire dashboard fix ~4h). Phase 1 reconstructible environment plus three rehearsals 30-40h. Phase 2 names, TLS, edge indirection and the default_server/apex fixes 20-30h. Phase 3 three stateful moves with a rehearsal each 30h. Phase 4 application cutover and per-office canary 20h. Phase 5 retirement, restore test and documentation 10h. TOTAL 150-190h, i.e. roughly 4-5 developer-weeks of pure migration work spread across rehearsal repetitions.

ONGOING: ~4h/month while two application tiers coexist in Phase 4  -  keep that to weeks, not quarters. After completion, ~4h/quarter to re-run a rehearsal from the committed runbook. That quarterly rehearsal is not optional discipline theatre: it is the only thing that keeps the runbook from rotting into a first attempt again, and it is the cheapest insurance in the plan.

THRESHOLD, STATED PLAINLY BECAUSE THE BRIEF ASKS FOR IT: this plan is operable at approximately 30 hours per month of protected infrastructure time, giving roughly 6 months elapsed. The stated allocation is about one developer-week per month, already largely claimed by a code-standard remediation exercise, and the brief instructs me to treat that figure as an estimate rather than a measurement. At 15-20h/month the elapsed time stretches to 10-14 months, which collides directly with the no-PHI window and is the single most likely way this fails. Below roughly 15 hours per month it decays into a partially migrated estate  -  state in one place, compute in another, two environments to operate, the burden of both and the reliability of neither  -  which is strictly worse than either endpoint.

WHAT TO DO IF 30h/MONTH CANNOT BE PROTECTED: do not attempt a cheaper version of the full plan. Cut scope instead. Execute Phase 0 (which is valuable regardless and fixes real defects), then Phase 1, then a rebuild-and-reseed onto a single new well-provisioned host using option F, and defer all decomposition. That is roughly 70-90h, delivers a reconstructible environment, a tested restore, a fail-loud migrator and an escape from the current box, and preserves every option for later. It is a legitimate stopping point. A half-executed Phase 3 is not.

evidence.claim: nginx's documented default rewrites the Host header to the upstream name: the default directives are `proxy_set_header Host $proxy_host;` and `proxy_set_header Connection close;`. Any new proxy or load-balancing layer must therefore be explicitly verified to preserve Host, because rewriting is the documented default of at least one very common L7 proxy.
evidence.source_name: nginx ngx_http_proxy_module documentation
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Default: proxy_set_header Host $proxy_host;

evidence.claim: nginx resolves a proxy_pass upstream name at configuration time unless the value contains a variable, in which case it is determined at request time using the configured resolver. This is the documented mechanism behind the stale-container-IP trap.
evidence.source_name: nginx ngx_http_proxy_module documentation
evidence.threshold_or_limit: n/a

evidence.claim: No SQL Server backup can be restored to an earlier version of SQL Server than the version on which the backup was created; and after restoring an earlier-version database to a newer SQL Server, the database is automatically upgraded. Together these make 'restore onto a newer major version' a one-way door.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn  -  RESTORE (Transact-SQL)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Target build must be >= source build; upgrade on restore is automatic and not reversible

evidence.claim: A database containing edition-restricted persisted features cannot be moved to an edition that does not support them; sys.dm_db_persisted_sku_features lists them (ChangeCapture, ColumnStoreIndex, Compression, MultipleFSContainers, InMemoryOLTP, Partitioning, TransparentDataEncryption). Since SQL Server 2016 SP1 all of these except TransparentDataEncryption are available across editions.

evidence.claim: SQL Server 2022 edition scale limits: maximum relational database size 524 PB for Enterprise/Standard/Web and 10 GB for Express; maximum buffer pool 128 GB Standard, 64 GB Web, 1,410 MB Express. Backup compression is available on Enterprise and Standard only. Log shipping is unavailable on Express. Developer edition includes all Enterprise functionality but 'is licensed for use as a development and test system, not as a production server'.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn  -  Editions and supported features of SQL Server 2022
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Express: 10 GB max database, 1410 MB buffer pool; Standard: 128 GB buffer pool, lesser of 4 sockets or 24 cores

evidence.claim: SQL Server log shipping is built entirely from SQL Server Agent jobs (backup job, copy job, restore job, alert job), and 'A log shipping configuration doesn't automatically fail over from the primary server to the secondary server. If the primary database becomes unavailable, any of the secondary databases can be brought online manually.' This stack runs no SQL Server Agent, so log shipping is not a low-cost option here.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn  -  About Log Shipping (SQL Server)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Requires SQL Server Agent; manual failover only

evidence.claim: SQL Server 2022 and later support BACKUP/RESTORE TO/FROM URL against S3-compatible object storage. Requirements and limits: HTTPS only (http unsupported); on Linux the CA must be placed in /var/opt/mssql/security/ca-certificates before SQL Server starts, maximum 50 certificates; total URL length limited to 259 characters (recommended under 200); the secret key must not contain a colon; striping across up to 64 URLs; a single file up to 200,000 MiB at MAXTRANSFERSIZE 20 MB; unsupported on Express editions; both path-style and virtual-host-style URLs supported.

evidence.threshold_or_limit: 10,000 parts x MAXTRANSFERSIZE per URL; 64 URLs; 259-char URL limit; CA loaded at SQL Server startup only

evidence.claim: Hangfire's recurring job scheduler acquires a global distributed lock on resource 'recurring-jobs:lock' and then a per-job distributed lock before enqueueing an occurrence. The source comments state that multiple instances can run in separate threads or processes without additional configuration because distributed locks are used, adding fail-over rather than throughput. Hangfire's own docs state each server uses distributed locks to perform coordination logic.
evidence.source_name: Hangfire source  -  RecurringJobScheduler.cs; Hangfire docs  -  Running Multiple Server Instances
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Lock resource name: recurring-jobs:lock; plus AcquireDistributedRecurringJobLock(recurringJobId)

evidence.claim: Two concurrent application instances sharing one Hangfire storage will not double-execute the twelve recurring jobs; two instances with SEPARATE Hangfire storage will. Since Hangfire storage here is the HOST connection string, this makes 'move state before compute' the precondition that turns a parallel run from dangerous into safe.
evidence.source_name: Derived from the Hangfire locking evidence combined with the stated system fact that Hangfire storage is the host Default connection string
evidence.threshold_or_limit: n/a

evidence.claim: ASP.NET Core Data Protection isolates applications from one another by content-root path by default, 'even if they share the same physical key repository', and this isolation 'prevents the apps from understanding each other's protected payloads'. SetApplicationName sets DataProtectionOptions.ApplicationDiscriminator; apps must share the same discriminator to read each other's payloads. DisableAutomaticKeyGeneration allows a secondary app to hold a read-only view of the key ring.

When the authorization server and API are separate applications, Data Protection 'MUST be configured to use the same application name and share the same key ring'. Switching format does not invalidate previously issued JWTs, which remain valid until expiry.

evidence.claim: OpenIddict supports registering multiple signing/encryption credentials for rotation and chooses the most appropriate key, with 'certificates with the furthest expiration date always preferred'. evidence.claim: Copying the Redis RDB file is safe while the server is running because the RDB is never modified once produced and is renamed atomically. Copying AOF files (a multi-part file set in a directory since Redis 7.0) during a rewrite 'might end up with an invalid backup'; the documented procedure is CONFIG SET auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 0, confirm INFO persistence shows aof_rewrite_in_progress is 0, then copy or hard-link, then re-enable. AOF durability is governed by appendfsync (always / everysec / no), with everysec risking one second of writes.
evidence.source_name: Redis documentation  -  Redis persistence
evidence.threshold_or_limit: appendfsync everysec = up to 1s data loss; AOF copy during rewrite = possibly invalid backup

evidence.claim: Redis replication is asynchronous by default; REPLICAOF seeds a replica from a master and a promoted replica generates a new replication ID. Replication can be used to seed a new instance, with a data-loss window inherent to asynchronous acknowledgement.
evidence.source_name: Redis documentation  -  Redis replication
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Asynchronous; WAIT reduces but does not eliminate the loss window

evidence.claim: A DNS TTL is an unsigned value with a maximum of 2^31-1, and all resource records in an RRSet must carry the same TTL (RFC 2181 8 and 5.2).
evidence.source_name: RFC 2181  -  Clarifications to the DNS Specification
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Max TTL 2147483647; RRSet TTLs must be equal

evidence.claim: Negative (NXDOMAIN) answers are cached with a TTL of min(SOA.MINIMUM, SOA.TTL) (RFC 2308 3), and 5 recommends resolvers cap negative caching at one to three hours, noting 'Values exceeding one day have been found to be problematic'. Consequence: querying a hostname before it exists can pin an NXDOMAIN in resolver caches for hours.
evidence.source_name: RFC 2308  -  Negative Caching of DNS Queries
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Recommended negative-cache cap 1-3 hours; values over 1 day problematic

evidence.claim: RFC 8767 serve-stale permits recursive resolvers to answer with expired data when authoritative servers are unreachable, recommending a maximum stale timer between 1 and 3 days (some deployments up to a week) and a TTL of about 30 seconds on stale responses. Consequence: a record's TTL is a floor on cache lifetime, not a ceiling, once your authoritative servers stop answering.
evidence.source_name: RFC 8767  -  Serving Stale Data to Improve DNS Resiliency
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Max stale timer 1-3 days recommended; stale-response TTL 30s recommended; TTL cap recommendation 604800s

evidence.claim: Public recursive resolvers maintain independent caches that a zone owner cannot flush. Verified empirically on 2026-08-31 by querying two independent public resolvers over DNS-over-HTTPS and observing separate answers and TTLs, and by observing a com. NS RRset with 21,591 seconds remaining in one resolver's cache.
evidence.source_name: Direct measurement via Google Public DNS and Cloudflare DNS-over-HTTPS JSON APIs
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Observed com. NS TTL remaining 21591s at time of query

evidence.claim: The parent-zone delegation NS TTL is set by the TLD operator, not the zone owner, so changing nameservers propagates far more slowly than changing records inside a zone. I could not measure a specific TLD delegation NS TTL from this environment  -  dig is not installed and DNS-over-HTTPS resolvers return authoritative answers rather than referrals. The general principle is established by the DNS specifications; the specific numeric value (commonly cited as 172800 seconds for .com) is UNVERIFIED here.
evidence.source_name: RFC 1034 / RFC 2181 delegation semantics; attempted direct measurement
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Specific .com delegation NS TTL not measured

evidence.claim: Transferring a DNSSEC-signed zone between DNS operators is constrained by the parent DS record TTL: the old DS must expire from caches before the old operator's keys are removed, creating a mandatory waiting period, and non-cooperating operators extend timelines further (RFC 6781 4.3.5, 4.3.5.1, 4.3.5.2).
evidence.source_name: RFC 6781  -  DNSSEC Operational Practices, Version 2
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Parent DS TTL constrains changeover speed

evidence.claim: Wildcard certificates can only be issued via the DNS-01 challenge; 'This challenge cannot be used to issue wildcard certificates' is stated of HTTP-01. DNS-01 requires placing a TXT record, i.e. programmatic control of the zone.

capability_requirements.requirement: The platform's request path MUST deliver the client's Host header to the application byte-for-byte unmodified, and MUST NOT serve any default backend for a hostname that matches no configured rule.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Tenancy resolves from the Host header and nothing else; a rewritten or defaulted Host does not fail loudly, it silently serves the wrong tenant's application or returns a 200 from an unrelated service. Rewriting is the documented DEFAULT behaviour of at least one very common L7 proxy, so it must be treated as the expected hazard rather than an edge case.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System fact: HostAwareDomainTenantResolveContributor reads the office slug from the leftmost DNS label. Cited: nginx documents its default as `proxy_set_header Host $proxy_host;`.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: From outside the platform, send GET to an application echo/health endpoint with Host: alpha.api.<base> and capture the Host header as the application received it (application access log or an echo endpoint). It must equal 'alpha.api.<base>' exactly, including case and any port. Repeat with Host: nosuchoffice.api.<base> and confirm the response is the application's 'Tenant not found', not a 200, not a redirect, and not HTML from the SPA container. Repeat with Host: <base> (bare apex) and confirm an explicit rejection rather than whichever backend happens to be listed first.

capability_requirements.requirement: The platform MUST allow the backend serving a published hostname to be changed, and changed back, without altering the hostname and without reissuing or replacing the TLS certificate.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: External parties  -  claimants, attorneys, adjusters and one integration partner  -  hold links and credentials that encode hostnames. DNS is not a switch: caches are independent, unflushable, and under RFC 8767 can serve stale answers for days once your authoritative servers stop answering. If the only way to move traffic is to change a name, rollback is bounded by caches you do not control.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System facts: email is the spine of the external-party workflow; an external partner holds credentials against minio.<BASE_DOMAIN>; hourly consent-expiry sweep implies externally-held time-bounded links. Cited: RFC 8767 4-6.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Publish a name pointing at backend A. Establish a long-lived client that has already resolved the name. Repoint the name to backend B without touching DNS. Confirm the existing client reaches B on its next connection, with no TLS error and no name change. Repoint back to A and confirm the same. Measure the time from change to effect; it must be under one connection lifetime, not one TTL.

capability_requirements.requirement: The platform MUST support TLS certificates covering wildcards at two label depths plus at least one exact hostname on a single certificate, obtainable through a DNS-based domain validation method that requires no inbound HTTP reachability.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: The naming scheme needs *.base (SPA), *.api.base, *.auth.base and the exact minio.base. A wildcard matches exactly one label, which is the documented constraint that already forced path-style object addressing here. Wildcards cannot be issued by HTTP validation.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System facts: four hostname patterns, minio as an EXACT match not a wildcard, path-style addressing chosen because the wildcard covers a single label. Cited: Let's Encrypt challenge types; AWS virtual-hosting wildcard/SSL limitation.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Obtain a certificate covering all four patterns. Confirm with `openssl s_client -connect <host>:443 -servername <host>` for each of: a.base, a.api.base, a.auth.base, minio.base, that the presented chain validates against the system trust store with no name-mismatch. Confirm issuance completed with the platform's inbound HTTP port closed, proving DNS validation.

capability_requirements.requirement: The authoritative DNS service MUST support per-record TTLs of 300 seconds or lower, wildcard records at two label depths, and MUST expose a change history that records who changed what and when.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: TTL reduction ahead of cutover is the only lever the zone owner has over cache lifetime, and it must be pulled before the move, not during. Change history is what makes a DNS mistake diagnosable by a two-person team with no observability stack.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System fact: tenancy depends on hostnames; there is no observability and no aggregation, so an unlogged change is an undiagnosable one. Cited: RFC 2181 8 TTL semantics.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Set a test record's TTL to 60. Query two independent public resolvers (for example over DNS-over-HTTPS) twice, 30 seconds apart, and confirm the reported TTL decreases and never exceeds 60. Create a wildcard at *.test.<base> and at *.api-test.<base> and confirm both resolve for a randomly generated label. Make a change and confirm it appears in an audit log with an actor and timestamp.

capability_requirements.requirement: The object storage service MUST accept path-style addressing (bucket in the URL path, not in the hostname) over TLS.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Path-style is not a stylistic choice here  -  it is forced by the single-label wildcard certificate, and it is baked into the credentials and configuration an external partner already holds. AWS documents that path-style 'will be discontinued in the future', so this must be verified against the specific target rather than assumed from S3 compatibility claims.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System fact: MinIO uses path-style because the wildcard TLS certificate covers a single label; an external partner holds scoped credentials against minio.<BASE_DOMAIN>. Cited: AWS virtual hosting documentation.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: With a valid SigV4 credential, issue GET https://<endpoint>/<bucket>/<key> where <endpoint> contains no bucket label. Expect HTTP 200 and correct bytes. Confirm no HTTP 301/307 redirect to a virtual-hosted-style URL is issued.

capability_requirements.requirement: The object storage service MUST support a credential-scoped policy that grants object retrieval on a prefix while denying bucket listing.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: An external partner holds exactly this policy today, deliberately: fetch-by-key without enumeration. Replicating it is a hard precondition of moving without re-negotiating the partner's security posture.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System fact: a partner-facing bucket with a policy granting fetch-by-key and deliberately withholding bucket listing.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Create a credential with the intended policy. Using it, fetch a known object key and expect 200. Using the same credential, list the bucket and expect an access-denied error, not an empty list and not a 200. Also attempt to fetch a key outside the granted prefix and expect access denied.

capability_requirements.requirement: The object storage service SHOULD permit an operator to set a specific access key ID and secret for a credential; if it cannot, the migration plan MUST include a re-credentialing window scheduled by the external partner rather than by this team.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: SHOULD rather than MUST because there is a viable alternative  -  partner-scheduled re-credentialing  -  but that alternative puts a third party on the critical path of a technical cutover, which is exactly the kind of dependency that converts a reversible step into an irreversible one.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System fact: an external partner already holds scoped credentials and must be re-credentialed on THEIR schedule.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Attempt to create a credential with a chosen access key ID and secret and then authenticate with it. If this is not possible, confirm the migration plan document contains a named partner contact, an agreed date, and a rollback path for the case where the partner cannot meet it.

capability_requirements.requirement: The target database platform MUST run the same SQL Server major version as the source at the moment of cutover, with any version change performed as a separate, later, independently reversible step.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Restoring a database to a newer major version upgrades it automatically and irreversibly, and a backup cannot be restored to an earlier version. Bundling a version upgrade into the move silently converts the single most rehearsable step of the migration into a one-way door  -  and does so without any error message.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Cited: Microsoft RESTORE documentation  -  'No SQL Server backup can be restored to an earlier version of SQL Server than the version on which the backup was created' and 'After you restore an earlier version database to SQL Server, the database is automatically upgraded.'
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Run SELECT @@VERSION on source and target; the major version must match. Then run the round trip: restore a source backup onto the target, take a fresh backup on the target, and restore that backup back onto the source. If the second restore fails, the versions differ and the migration is not reversible.

capability_requirements.requirement: The target database edition MUST support every feature reported by sys.dm_db_persisted_sku_features in every source database, MUST support backup compression, and MUST have a maximum database size at least an order of magnitude above the largest projected office database.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: A database using an edition-restricted persisted feature cannot be moved to an edition lacking it  -  the restore fails. Separately, the measured audit-to-business-data ratio exceeds 100:1 with no pruning configured, so a hard per-database size ceiling is a wall whose only relief valve is deleting records that may be subject to retention obligations. Express (10 GB) is architecturally excluded on that basis, and the current Developer edition is licensed for development and test rather than production, so an edition change is mandatory regardless.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System facts: MSSQL_PID is Developer; 16 appointments produced ~1,450 audit rows and 2,689 property-change rows; audit retention unconfigured. Cited: SQL Server 2022 edition scale limits; sys.dm_db_persisted_sku_features.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: In every one of the 12 databases run: SELECT feature_name FROM sys.dm_db_persisted_sku_features; Every feature listed must appear as supported for the target edition in Microsoft's edition matrix. Separately, record the current size of the largest database, and confirm the target edition's documented maximum relational database size exceeds it by at least 10x. Confirm BACKUP ... WITH COMPRESSION succeeds on the target.

capability_requirements.requirement: The platform MUST allow each tenant database to be addressed by an independently configured connection string, so that one office can be relocated while the others are untouched.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Without this, the database move is fleet-atomic: all 12 databases move in one window with one rollback point, which is the single largest irreversible step in the plan. With it, the move becomes eleven small reversible steps. This is a property of the application configuration as much as the platform, and it is the highest-leverage precondition in the whole programme.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System fact: TenantConnectionStringProvider derives every office connection string from the host Default (or App:TenantDbTemplate) by swapping the database name  -  one template for the whole fleet.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Configure one office with an explicit connection string pointing at a different SQL Server instance from the rest. Log into that office and perform a read and a write. Log into a different office and confirm it still works and its data is unchanged. Then run a recurring background sweep and confirm it reaches both instances correctly. Finally revert the single office and confirm it returns to the shared instance.

capability_requirements.requirement: A single shared cache and key-ring store MUST be reachable from both application processes, and protected payloads issued before an application redeploy MUST remain valid after it.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: The AuthServer and the API are separate processes that read each other's protected payloads via a shared Data Protection key ring; login state and email-confirmation tokens depend on it. Data Protection isolates applications by content-root path by default, so a container path change silently breaks payloads even when the key ring itself moved intact  -  a failure that produces confused users and dead links rather than an error in a log.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System facts: SetApplicationName('CaseEvaluation') set identically in both AuthServer and API; keyring at CaseEvaluation-Protection-Keys. Cited: ASP.NET Core Data Protection configuration docs; OpenIddict Data Protection integration ('MUST be configured to use the same application name and share the same key ring').
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Log in and keep the session. Trigger an email-confirmation link and do not click it. Redeploy both application processes. Confirm the existing session still authenticates without re-login, and the un-clicked confirmation link still validates. Additionally, log the resolved ApplicationDiscriminator at startup in both processes and confirm the two values are identical strings.

capability_requirements.requirement: The schema migration runner MUST report a per-tenant outcome and MUST exit non-zero if any tenant fails.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: The current runner loops offices with no per-tenant error handling and no report, so a partial failure leaves the fleet on split schema versions with nothing identifying which offices succeeded. That is the archetypal fail-subtly defect in a team that will not notice slow degradation, and it fires on every bring-up  -  including every rehearsal and the cutover itself.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System fact: db-migrator loops offices with NO per-tenant error handling; runs on EVERY bring-up; api and authserver gate on its success. Cited: EF Core guidance on migration bundles and per-database --connection.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Point the runner at a fleet of three tenant databases where one is unreachable (stop it, or revoke the credential). Confirm the output explicitly names which tenants succeeded and which failed, that the failure names the tenant and the underlying error, and that the process exit code is non-zero. Confirm the two healthy tenants were actually migrated.

capability_requirements.requirement: Background job execution MUST be independently switchable per running application instance.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: The recurring jobs drain a per-recipient email outbox to claimants, attorneys and adjusters and push to a partner integration ledger. A duplicate send is not a technical incident, it is an ex-parte problem. Even though Hangfire's distributed locks prevent duplicate recurring-job execution on shared storage, a configuration assertion is cheaper to verify than a locking argument, and it is the only protection if the two instances ever end up on separate storage.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System facts: twelve recurring jobs, three at 15-minute cadence; ex-parte-safe email addressing; AuthServer already runs with IsJobExecutionEnabled=false. Cited: Hangfire RecurringJobScheduler distributed locks.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Bring up a second application instance with job execution disabled, sharing storage with the primary. Over one full 15-minute cycle, confirm from the job storage that each of the three 15-minute jobs executed exactly once, and that the standby instance registered no server or enqueued nothing. Then disable jobs on the primary and enable on the standby and confirm the cadence continues unbroken.

capability_requirements.requirement: Secrets and key material required at process start  -  the token signing and encryption certificate and its passphrase, and database credentials  -  MUST be present before the process starts, and their absence MUST prevent startup rather than trigger any fallback.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: An OpenIddict development-certificate fallback produces an AuthServer that starts successfully and issues tokens that fail intermittently or die on container restart  -  precisely the subtle failure this team cannot diagnose with console-and-file logging and no aggregation. A hard startup failure is diagnosable in thirty seconds.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System facts: certificate mounted read-only from OPENIDDICT_PFX_PATH, passphrase from environment, never baked into an image; losing or replacing it invalidates every token; secrets come from a single --env-file whose omission silently blanks every value. Cited: OpenIddict development certificates are 'persisted - but not shared across instances'.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Remove the certificate file and start the AuthServer. It must exit non-zero with a message naming the missing path. Repeat with a wrong passphrase. Repeat by starting the stack without the --env-file and confirm it refuses to start rather than recreating with blank credentials. Finally, grep the production configuration path for any development-certificate registration and confirm there is none.

capability_requirements.requirement: Object data migration MUST be verifiable by independently computed content digests, exact object counts and total byte counts  -  not by ETag comparison and not by the migration tool's own success report.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: ETags are not MD5 digests for multipart objects, and the standard mirroring tool does not inherently verify integrity. 'The copy completed' and 'the ETags match' are both non-verifications, and the objects in question are appointment documents, packets and joint declarations in a regulated workflow.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System facts: six logical blob containers across two physical buckets; ABP-shaped keys tenants/{tenantId:D}/... Cited: AWS checking-object-integrity; MinIO mc mirror documentation ('mc mirror only synchronises the current object without any version information or metadata other than tags').
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: After mirroring, compare exact object count and total bytes between source and target for every bucket. Then select at least 100 keys at random including at least 10 objects over 100 MB (multipart candidates), download from both sides and compute SHA-256 client-side. All digests must match. Record the sample list so the check is repeatable.

capability_requirements.requirement: The entire environment MUST be reconstructible from version-controlled artefacts plus the secrets file, by one engineer following a written runbook, without access to the running system, in under four hours.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: There is exactly one environment today and deployment is entirely manual over SSH with no CD. Reconstructibility is what makes rehearsal possible, and rehearsal is the documented difference between a successful stop-the-world cutover and a large failure. It is also the only rollback that exists for a total loss of the current VM.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System facts: one VM, entirely manual deployment, no CD, exactly one environment, backups never restored. Cited: legacy-displacement guidance that large cutover failures follow from cases where no rehearsal was possible or performed.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Give the engineer who did NOT write the runbook a clean host, the repository and the secrets file, and nothing else. Time them to a passing health check across all offices. Any step they have to ask about is a runbook defect. Repeat until two consecutive attempts succeed unaided inside four hours.

anti_requirements: The platform MUST NOT rewrite, normalise, lowercase-with-side-effects, strip or synthesise the Host header, and MUST NOT substitute a default backend for an unmatched hostname. Tenancy resolves from Host and nothing else, so a helpful proxy default is a tenant-routing defect that produces a 200 rather than an error.

The platform MUST NOT require a hostname change in order to relocate a workload. External parties hold hostname-bearing links and credentials; anything that couples 'move the workload' to 'change the name' converts a reversible step into one bounded by resolver caches you cannot flush.

The object storage service MUST NOT require virtual-hosted-style addressing. That would break the partner's existing configuration and simultaneously invalidate the single-label wildcard certificate strategy.

The platform MUST NOT silently substitute a generated, self-signed or development certificate  -  for TLS or for token signing  -  when the configured one is missing. Starting successfully with the wrong key is the worst available outcome for a team with no log aggregation and no alerting.

The database platform MUST NOT require all tenant databases to be relocated as a single unit, and MUST NOT automatically upgrade the database engine version on restore or on maintenance. Automatic version upgrade destroys the ability to restore back to the source.

The platform MUST NOT require sticky sessions, session affinity or WebSocket upgrade support as a precondition of its routing. There is no SignalR, no WebSocket and no server-side rendering; a routing layer that assumes them will be configured for a property this system does not have, and the reverse proxy already carries dead WebSocket upgrade config pointing at a hub that does not exist  -  that config must be deleted, not carried forward.

The platform MUST NOT couple credential rotation to endpoint relocation. These are two changes with two different owners and two different schedules; combining them puts an external partner on the critical path of an internal cutover.

The platform MUST NOT require an agent, daemon or sidecar on the database host that this team is responsible for operating, monitoring and upgrading. Two SDE1s with roughly one developer-week per month cannot own a component whose failure mode is silent.

The migration MUST NOT bundle unrelated improvements into a cutover window  -  no SQL Server version upgrade, no edition change beyond the one required, no certificate rotation, no sa-to-least-privilege credential change, no TLS or header hardening. Each is worth doing; each doubles the number of candidate explanations when something breaks at 02:00.

The plan MUST NOT include HSTS preload submission at any point before the domain layout is final and stable. Preload requires max-age of at least one year with includeSubDomains, cannot easily be undone, and takes months to reach users after removal  -  and includeSubDomains on a wildcard-tenant domain commits every office subdomain that does not exist yet.

The plan MUST NOT change DNS registrar, nameservers or DNS operator during the migration. Records inside a zone are under your TTL control; the parent delegation is not, and a DNSSEC-signed zone adds a DS TTL you also do not control.
surprises: Restoring a database onto a NEWER SQL Server major version is a one-way door. Microsoft states both that no backup can be restored to an earlier version and that an earlier-version database is automatically upgraded on restore. So if the target runs a newer major version, the moment you restore you can never restore back  -  your only rollback is the pre-move backup on the old instance, discarding everything written since. Pin the target to the same major version and treat the version upgrade as a separate later step. Almost nobody plans this, because 'newer is fine' is true for the forward direction and silently false for the reverse.

Your certificate authority rate-limits your rehearsals. Let's Encrypt allows 5 certificates per identical set of identifiers per 7 days and 5 authorisation failures per identifier per hour. A team that rehearses a full cutover six times in a week against production issuance will be blocked, and a broken DNS-01 automation exhausts the failure budget in minutes. Rehearse against the ACME staging environment and reserve production issuance for the real cutover.

Copying the Redis data directory while Redis is running can produce an invalid backup. Since Redis 7.0 the AOF is a multi-part file set, and the documentation warns that copying during a rewrite 'might end up with an invalid backup'  -  the correct procedure is CONFIG SET auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 0, confirm aof_rewrite_in_progress is 0, then copy or hard-link. RDB copying is safe at any time. What you would silently lose is the DataProtection key ring, and with it every email-confirmation and protected link already sitting in a claimant's or attorney's inbox.

The 'session-preserving versus session-dropping' cutover is a false binary here. Redis holds three things with three different values: a small irreplaceable key ring, a large disposable cache, and ephemeral locks that must NOT be carried across. Preserve the first, discard the other two. Staff re-authenticating costs nothing; what actually dies with the key ring are externally-held links that can only be re-issued by a human conversation per recipient.

The database move is fleet-atomic today, and one small code change makes it incremental. All office connection strings derive from a single host template, so 'move office 3 and leave the rest' is not currently expressible. Setting explicit per-office connection strings first  -  a semantic no-op  -  is expand-contract applied to a configuration dependency rather than a schema, and it converts one 12-database cutover with a single rollback point into eleven independently reversible one-database cutovers.

A parallel run is safe or catastrophic depending on one configuration detail nobody thinks about. Hangfire's scheduler takes a distributed lock ('recurring-jobs:lock') plus a per-job lock before enqueueing, so two application instances sharing one Hangfire storage do NOT double-fire the twelve recurring jobs. Two instances with SEPARATE storage will  -  and those jobs drain an email outbox to claimants, attorneys and adjusters. Since Hangfire storage is the host connection string, moving state before compute is precisely what buys the safe version.

HSTS preload is effectively irreversible on a browser-release timescale, and a migration is exactly when someone will submit it. Preloading requires max-age of at least a year plus includeSubDomains; the list 'cannot easily be undone' and removal 'takes months for a change to reach users'. On a wildcard-per-office domain, includeSubDomains commits every office subdomain that does not exist yet. The edge currently has zero add_header directives, so hardening is overdue  -  but preload belongs after the domain layout is final, not during.

Querying a hostname before it exists pins NXDOMAIN in resolver caches. Negative answers are cached at min(SOA.MINIMUM, SOA.TTL), and RFC 2308 records that resolvers commonly cap this at one to three hours. Create every new name first, pointing at the current backend, and only then repoint. A single curiosity lookup during planning can cost you an hour of the cutover window.

A TTL is a floor on cache lifetime, not a ceiling. Under RFC 8767 serve-stale, resolvers may keep answering with expired data  -  recommended stale timers of one to three days  -  once your authoritative servers become unreachable. So decommissioning old authoritative infrastructure is itself an irreversible act with a multi-day tail, quite separate from the TTL you set on the records.

The system can tell you when the cutover window is cheap, and it is not Saturday night. External parties hold time-bounded links: anonymous uploads and change-request consents, the latter proven to have lifetimes by the existence of an hourly consent-expiry sweep. Query the outstanding unexpired link count and its latest expiry, and cut over when that number is low. No standard runbook contains this step because most systems do not hand time-bounded URLs to people outside the organisation.

SQL Server 2022 can back up directly to your existing S3-compatible endpoint, which solves two problems at once: backups currently land on the same disk that has 9.7 GB free, and 12 databases have to leave a box that has 9.7 GB free. But on Linux the CA certificate must be in /var/opt/mssql/security/ca-certificates BEFORE SQL Server starts (maximum 50 certificates, read only at startup), the endpoint must be HTTPS, the secret key must not contain a colon, and the whole URL must stay under about 200 characters.

On EF Core 9 and later, the 'entity mapped in both DbContexts but a migration added to only one' hazard should already fail loudly rather than silently  -  Migrate/MigrateAsync throws when the model has pending changes relative to the last migration. Verify that RelationalEventId.PendingModelChangesWarning is not suppressed, and add `dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes` to CI for BOTH contexts. This is a rare case where the framework has already converted a subtle failure into an obvious one and the team may simply not know.

The brief's own HIPAA framing needs a correction. 45 CFR 164.316(b)(2)(i) requires six-year retention of 'the documentation required by paragraph (b)(1)'  -  policies, procedures, and documented actions, activities and assessments. Whether that reaches an application's entity-property-change audit trail is an interpretation, not a plain reading. The sizing consequence is unchanged, because nothing prunes those tables regardless of the retention basis, but the retention obligation should not be asserted as settled when choosing an architecture around it.

ETag comparison is not a verification. S3 ETags are not MD5 digests for multipart objects, and mc mirror does not inherently verify integrity  -  its documentation states it 'only synchronises the current object without any version information or metadata other than tags'. Object migration must be verified by independently computed content digests plus exact object and byte counts.

Log shipping is not available to you in any cheap form. It is built entirely from SQL Server Agent jobs, and this stack deliberately runs no SQL Server Agent  -  scheduling is in-process via Hangfire. It also does not fail over automatically, so you still perform a manual cutover at the end of all that setup.

not_recommended.pattern: Migrate to Kubernetes (or any container orchestrator) as the target architecture, as part of this move.
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It is the standard 2026 answer and the case is real. It gives rolling deployments, health-based restart, declarative configuration under version control, secret management, and a per-office canary that is a label selector rather than an nginx edit. It would replace the manual SSH deployment and the --env-file trap with something reproducible. It is also what most published multi-tenant SaaS reference architectures assume, so future hiring and documentation would align with it. And there is a genuine argument that migrating twice  -  once to a new VM, once to orchestration  -  costs more than migrating once.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: Operational complexity is a first-class cost here, and the brief's second directive is to prefer designs that fail obviously.
