Kubernetes fails obviously in exactly one way (CrashLoopBackOff) and subtly in many: cluster DNS resolution, CNI behaviour, PersistentVolume reclaim policies, RBAC drift, certificate rotation in the control plane, admission webhooks, and  -  most relevant here  -  ingress controllers whose default is to rewrite or normalise the Host header, which would break tenancy resolution in a way that returns wrong data rather than an error. The application has no property that needs it: single instance, no SSR, no Node runtime in production, no WebSockets, no sticky-session requirement, no autoscaling requirement, 11 tenants with headroom to 33. Two SDE1s with roughly one developer-week per month cannot carry a platform whose failure modes require a specialist to read. Worse, adopting it during a migration means changing the substrate and the topology simultaneously, so any failure has two candidate explanations.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: When there are three or more application instances to keep in step; or when a second environment must be maintained continuously rather than as a rehearsal artefact; or when a person whose job is the platform exists. Concretely: at the point where deployment happens more than weekly, or where the team exceeds four engineers with one owning infrastructure.

not_recommended.pattern: Refactor from database-per-tenant to a shared-schema multi-tenant database while you are moving anyway.
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: 33 databases is a real operational burden: 33 backup jobs to verify, 33 restore tests, 33 sets of schema drift to reconcile, and a migrator that must loop. A single database collapses that to one of each. ABP supports both models natively. Microsoft's own tenancy guidance is explicit that per-tenant infrastructure scales poorly in maintenance cost and that fully multitenant deployments are simpler to update. And the argument that 'you are opening the database anyway' has genuine force  -  the data is synthetic, so this is the cheapest moment in the system's life to do it.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It is a re-architecture wearing a migration's clothes. It touches every query, every aggregate root, and the tenant filter on all 37 aggregates; it invalidates the strongest compliance story the system has (one practice, one database, physical isolation, restorable independently); and it makes 'restore one office to last Tuesday'  -  a request a medical practice will eventually make  -  impossible without point-in-time surgery on shared tables. Most decisively, it breaks the rule that a migration changes one variable. If a bug appears after cutover you would not know whether it came from the new environment or the new data model. And it would consume the entire infrastructure budget for a year, during which the single-VM risk persists.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: If tenant count heads well beyond the stated 33 ceiling, or if per-tenant operational cost is measured and found to dominate. It should be its own programme, with its own rehearsals, after the infrastructure move has settled  -  never inside it.

not_recommended.pattern: Zero-downtime cutover using continuous data replication (log shipping, transactional replication, CDC, or application-level dual-write).
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It is what a mature organisation does, and the reasons are good: no maintenance window to negotiate, no risk of overrunning the window, no need to coordinate 11 practices, and the ability to abort at any point before the final switch because the source stays authoritative. Transactional replication is Microsoft's own recommendation when you cannot take the source out of production. Building the muscle now means having it later, when downtime genuinely is expensive.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: Every one of those benefits is purchased against a cost this system does not currently bear. There is no patient data, no practice depending on the system, and therefore no downtime to avoid  -  the window is free, and free is the correct price. Log shipping specifically requires SQL Server Agent, which this stack deliberately does not run, needs twelve separate topologies, and still ends in a manual failover. Dual-write is worse: it is application code that must handle partial failure across two systems, written by a team with no observability to detect divergence. And all of these fail by drift, silently, which is precisely the failure class the brief says this team will not notice. Buying downtime is the cheapest thing you will ever buy in this migration; spend months of engineering to avoid an hour and you have made a bad trade.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: Once real practices take real bookings and a multi-hour window costs revenue and goodwill. That is also the point at which the team should have grown or acquired the expertise, because at that point the alternative is not 'take the downtime' but 'do not migrate'.

not_recommended.pattern: Blue-green deployment with separate databases for blue and green.
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: This is the textbook clean-room form: two genuinely independent environments, total isolation, and a rollback that touches nothing shared. If green is broken, blue is provably untouched  -  no shared cache to poison, no shared schema to have half-migrated, no possibility of the new code corrupting data the old code still depends on. Fowler's original article treats the database as the hard part precisely because sharing it constrains you.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: Separate databases mean the two sides must be synchronised, which reintroduces the replication problem above, or they diverge, which produces split-brain across 12 databases with no reconciliation tooling. Worse in this specific system: separate databases mean separate Hangfire storage, and separate Hangfire storage means both sides' recurring jobs fire independently  -  duplicate outbound email to claimants, attorneys and adjusters, and duplicate entries in the partner integration ledger. Fowler's own prescription points the other way: refactor the schema to support both versions, deploy that, establish the rollback point, then deploy the application. That is shared-datastore blue-green, and it is available here as soon as state moves before compute.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: For a stateless component, immediately  -  the Angular container and the packet renderer can be blue-greened with separate everything today. For the data tier, only with a synchronisation mechanism the team can operate and verify.

not_recommended.pattern: Shadow traffic / mirrored production requests replayed against the new stack for validation.
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It is the highest-confidence validation technique available: real request shapes, real payload sizes, real concurrency, real edge cases you would never think to write a test for, all without any user seeing the result. For a system with 52 controllers and 56 application services, no comprehensive test suite mentioned, and exactly one environment, the appeal is obvious  -  you would learn more in an hour of mirrored traffic than in a week of manual testing.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: Almost every mutating request in this system has an external side effect: it sends email to a real attorney, writes to a durable outbox that a drain job will deliver, or queues an entry for the partner integration ledger. Mirroring writes without a faithful side-effect sandbox means duplicate correspondence to opposing parties in workers' compensation matters, which is the one category of error this system is explicitly designed to avoid through ex-parte-safe addressing. Building a sandbox faithful enough to make mirroring safe  -  sinkholed SMTP, a stubbed partner endpoint, suppressed outbox drains, a read-only object store  -  costs more than the migration it would be validating. Mirroring read traffic only is safe but nearly worthless, because the risk here is in writes.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: If a read-heavy public surface emerges  -  a patient portal, a document-fetch API  -  mirroring that surface alone would be cheap and valuable. It becomes right for writes only once a side-effect sandbox exists for other reasons, such as a genuine staging environment with a mail sink.

not_recommended.pattern: Build a permanent staging environment as a prerequisite to the migration.
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: There is exactly one environment, and any change reaching users has been tested only on the machine that serves them. That is indefensible for a PHI system and it is the single most-cited gap in the current state. A staging environment would let changes be tested before they reach practices, would give the migration somewhere to rehearse, and would satisfy the general expectation that regulated systems have a non-production tier.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: Not rejected as an outcome  -  rejected as a prerequisite, and rejected in the form of 'a third permanent estate'. The migration already builds a second environment; the correct move is to build the target, rehearse against it repeatedly, and let it become production, at which point the OLD environment becomes the staging tier for a defined period before retirement. Building a separate third estate first means paying for and operating three environments during the migration with a team that cannot reliably operate one, and it delays the move  -  which spends down the no-PHI window, the one resource that is genuinely finite here.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: Immediately after cutover, by retaining the old environment rather than destroying it. That is the cheapest staging tier available and it doubles as the rollback target during the window when rollback still matters.

not_recommended.pattern: Adopt a full infrastructure-as-code framework (reusable modules, remote state, drift detection, policy-as-code) before migrating.
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: Reconstructibility is a hard requirement of this plan  -  you cannot rehearse what you cannot rebuild  -  and IaC is the standard way to get it. Committed infrastructure definitions would also eliminate the --env-file trap, make the office-provisioning path auditable, and give the migration a diffable record of what changed. The 'we'll write scripts now and do it properly later' path is how organisations end up with neither.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: The requirement is reconstructibility, not a framework. A committed compose file, a committed nginx template, a scripted bring-up and a written runbook satisfy the capability requirement and can be verified by the four-hour rebuild test. A module-and-remote-state framework adds a state file that can be corrupted, a tool version that must be pinned, drift semantics that must be understood, and a new failure mode where the tool disagrees with reality  -  for a ten-service estate on one host. It also introduces a second thing to learn during a migration, which is exactly when learning capacity is scarcest.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: When there is more than one environment to keep in step permanently, or when the estate spans enough resources that a human cannot hold it in their head. At that point the scripts written now become the specification for the modules written then, so nothing is wasted.

not_recommended.pattern: Destroy the old VM immediately after a successful cutover.
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: Keeping it costs money and attention, it is a security surface with sa credentials and secrets that have already been exposed in chat transcripts, and 'we still have the old box' is how organisations avoid finishing migrations. Cleanly retiring it forces the team to confront anything that was silently still depending on it.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It is the rollback target, and it is also the only staging tier available. Keeping it for a defined period  -  one to two weeks past the last office's cutover, or until a restore has actually been tested from the new backup location, whichever is later  -  costs almost nothing and preserves the ability to reverse. Note that this calculus flips once PHI exists: at that point an old box holding patient data is a liability under the breach-notification safe harbour unless the storage is encrypted per NIST SP 800-111 or sanitised per SP 800-88. Today it is not, which is another reason to migrate before that becomes true.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: On a scheduled date, decided in advance and written into the plan, after the restore test passes. Not 'when we get around to it', which is how it becomes permanent.

not_recommended.pattern: Treat DNS cutover as the deployment mechanism  -  'we'll just flip DNS'.
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It requires no new infrastructure, works across any two environments regardless of topology, and is what every migration checklist on the internet describes. With TTLs lowered in advance it can be reasonably fast, and it is the only mechanism available if the two environments are on different networks with no shared front door.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: DNS is not a switch. Resolver caches are independent and unflushable, RFC 8767 serve-stale means old answers can persist for days once your authoritative servers stop answering, and negative caching can pin an NXDOMAIN for hours if anyone queries a name early. Using it as the primary cutover mechanism means your rollback speed is set by infrastructure you do not own  -  and rollback speed is the property that makes every other step in this plan safe. Use DNS to move a name once, early, onto a stable indirection point; then perform every subsequent cutover by changing what that point routes to, which is instantaneous and symmetric.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: For the initial move of a name onto the new edge, and for changes where a multi-hour tail is genuinely acceptable. Never for the step whose rollback you might need in five minutes.

what_would_change_the_answer: If a real practice takes a real booking before the migration completes. This is the load-bearing assumption of the entire plan. It removes option F, ends free downtime, ends free rollback, puts a BAA on the critical path before any data moves, and turns each rehearsal into a PHI-handling exercise. If this is likely, the correct response is to shrink scope to Phase 0 plus a rebuild-and-reseed onto one well-provisioned host and complete it before that date, rather than attempting the full sequence more slowly.

If the custom TenantConnectionStringProvider does not honour an explicitly configured per-tenant connection string, and making it do so is harder than estimated. The fleet-atomic constraint would stand, the database move would become a single 12-database cutover with one rollback point, and the case for option A (a single rehearsed stop-the-world window) would become much stronger than the case for C.

If ABP's four default __tenant resolvers (query string, route, header, cookie) turn out to be active. The brief records honestly that this has never been tested. If they are active, the edge is not the only tenancy control, the security story changes materially, and a per-office canary routed purely by hostname is no longer a complete story  -  a request could carry a __tenant that contradicts its Host. Test this first; it is a ten-minute curl.

If OpenIddict is configured with UseDataProtection. Then all token types except identity tokens are Data-Protection-formatted, refresh tokens and authorization codes depend on the Redis key ring rather than on the certificate, and any key-ring mistake invalidates active grants rather than merely active sessions. It raises the care level on the Redis step and makes the shared-key-ring capability requirement strictly non-negotiable.

If any office database reports TransparentDataEncryption from sys.dm_db_persisted_sku_features. That constrains the target edition (TDE is unavailable on Web and Express), and it adds a certificate that must move with the backup or the database cannot be restored at all.

If the zone is DNSSEC-signed. A DS record at the parent means the DNS steps acquire a mandatory waiting period governed by a TTL you do not control, and a mistake is total resolution failure rather than degraded routing. It makes 'do not change DNS operator' a hard rule rather than strong advice.

If the integration partner cannot re-credential within a six-month horizon, or cannot be reached to agree a date. The object storage step then must preserve both the hostname and the exact credentials, which turns 'the target should permit an operator-specified access key' from a SHOULD into a MUST and may eliminate otherwise-viable targets.

If protected infrastructure time falls below roughly 15 hours per month. Below that the plan does not merely go slower, it changes state: it decays into a partially migrated estate with the operational burden of two environments and the reliability of neither. The correct response is to cut scope to Phase 0 plus Phase 1 plus a single-host rebuild, not to execute the same sequence more slowly.

If the target must run a different SQL Server major version for reasons outside this decision. The version-pinning requirement is what keeps the database step reversible; losing it means the only rollback for the database move is the pre-move backup on the old instance, and every step after it must be re-planned around that one-way door.

If a second application instance becomes necessary for reasons other than migration  -  genuine availability requirements, or load. Several rejections above (Kubernetes, permanent staging, IaC frameworks) are calibrated to single-instance, one-environment reality and would need revisiting.

results.claim: [1] nginx documented default is proxy_set_header Host $proxy_host; and Connection close; so Host rewriting is the documented default of a common L7 proxy
results.evidence_quote: Default: proxy_set_header Host $proxy_host; proxy_set_header Connection close; ... By default, the header fields "Host" and "Connection" from the original request are not passed to the proxied server. If HTTP/1.0 or HTTP/1.1 is enabled for proxying, these fields are redefined.
results.correction: None. Verified verbatim. Worth adding for completeness: the same paragraph states that for HTTP/2 the ":authority" pseudo-header is sent with the $proxy_host value by default unless replaced by an explicit Host field  -  which strengthens the claim.

results.claim: [2] nginx resolves a proxy_pass upstream name at CONFIGURATION TIME unless the value contains a variable, in which case it is resolved at request time via the resolver; this is the documented mechanism behind the stale-container-IP trap
results.evidence_quote: Parameter value can contain variables. In this case, if an address is specified as a domain name, the name is searched among the described server groups, and, if not found, is determined using a resolver.
results.correction: The page supports only the second half. Nowhere on ngx_http_proxy_module.html does nginx state that a proxy_pass name WITHOUT a variable is resolved at configuration/startup time  -  I read the full proxy_pass section and it says only 'If a domain name resolves to several addresses, all of them will be used in a round-robin fashion.' The configuration-time resolution behaviour is real but is NOT documented on this URL; it is inferred. Either soften to 'the documentation confirms that variables plus a resolver move name resolution to request time; the converse (startup-only resolution without a variable) is well-established behaviour but is not stated on this page', or cite a page that actually asserts it.

results.claim: [3] No SQL Server backup can be restored to an earlier version than the one it was created on; and an earlier-version database restored to a newer SQL Server is automatically upgraded  -  making restore-onto-newer a one-way door
results.evidence_quote: No SQL Server backup can be restored to an earlier version of SQL Server than the version on which the backup was created. ... After you restore an earlier version database to SQL Server, the database is automatically upgraded.
results.correction: None. Both sentences verified verbatim. The page does not use the words 'not reversible', but the two sentences together do entail the one-way-door conclusion, so the framing is sound.

results.claim: [4] Edition-restricted persisted features block moving a database to a lesser edition; the DMV lists ChangeCapture, ColumnStoreIndex, Compression, MultipleFSContainers, InMemoryOLTP, Partitioning, TransparentDataEncryption; since 2016 SP1 all except TDE are cross-edition
results.evidence_quote: A database that contains these features can't be moved to an edition of SQL Server that doesn't support them. ... Starting with SQL Server 2016 (13.x) Service Pack 1, these features, except TransparentDataEncryption are available across multiple SQL Server editions, and not limited to Enterprise or Developer editions only.
results.correction: None. The seven feature names match the page exactly and the 2016 SP1 note is verbatim. Note the canonical URL now redirects to .../system-dynamic-management-objects/... (the .../system-dynamic-management-views/... form still resolves).

results.claim: [5] SQL Server 2022 scale limits: 524 PB max DB for Ent/Std/Web, 10 GB Express; buffer pool 128 GB Std, 64 GB Web, 1,410 MB Express; backup compression Enterprise and Standard only; log shipping unavailable on Express; Developer 'licensed for use as a development and test system, not as a production server'
results.evidence_quote: Maximum relational database size | 524 PB | 524 PB | 524 PB | 10 GB | 10 GB ... Maximum memory for buffer pool per instance | Operating system maximum | 128 GB | 64 GB | 1,410 MB | 1,410 MB ... Backup compression | Yes | Yes | No | No | No ... Log shipping | Yes | Yes | Yes | No | No ... It includes all the functionality of Enterprise edition, but is licensed for use as a development and test system, not as a production server.
results.correction: None. Every number and the Standard 'lesser of 4 sockets or 24 cores' compute limit check out. One nuance worth carrying forward: Web edition also lacks backup compression, encrypted backup, TDE and EKM  -  so 'Enterprise and Standard only' is right but the practical effect is that the edition floor for this system is Standard, not Web.

results.claim: [6] Log shipping is built entirely from SQL Server Agent jobs (backup, copy, restore, alert) and does not automatically fail over; secondaries must be brought online manually
results.evidence_quote: A log shipping configuration doesn't automatically fail over from the primary server to the secondary server. If the primary database becomes unavailable, any of the secondary databases can be brought online manually. ... backup job: A SQL Server Agent job that performs the backup operation ... copy job: A SQL Server Agent job ... restore job: A SQL Server Agent job ... alert job: A SQL Server Agent job
results.correction: None. All four job types are explicitly defined as SQL Server Agent jobs and the failover sentence is verbatim. The downstream inference ('no Agent in this stack, so log shipping is not low-cost here') follows.

results.claim: [7] SQL Server 2022+ BACKUP/RESTORE TO/FROM URL to S3-compatible storage: HTTPS only; Linux CA in /var/opt/mssql/security/ca-certificates before startup, max 50 certs; URL limit 259 chars (recommend <200); secret key must not contain a colon; 64-URL striping; 200,000 MiB per file at MAXTRANSFERSIZE 20 MB; 10,000 parts; unsupported on Express; path-style and virtual-host-style both supported
results.evidence_quote: Each file can be split up to 10,000 parts ... A single backup file can be up to 200,000 MiB per URL (with MAXTRANSFERSIZE set to 20 MB). Backups can be striped across a maximum of 64 URLs. ... the CA must be placed on a predefined location to be created at /var/opt/mssql/security/ca-certificates, only the first 50 certificates can be stored and supported in this folder. The CA must be in place before SQL Server process is started. ... The total URL length is limited to 259 characters ... we recommend sticking to a limit of 200 characters ... Secret key ID must not have : character. ... isn't supported in SQL Server Express and SQL Server Express with Advanced Services editions. ... Back up to S3 supports the URL to be written in both path style or virtual host style.
results.correction: None  -  every limit checks out verbatim. Two operationally material details the claim omits: (a) COMPRESSION is REQUIRED in order to change MAXTRANSFERSIZE at all, so the 200,000 MiB figure is unreachable without compression; (b) failed/cancelled backups leave uncommitted multipart data in the bucket that SQL Server does not clean up. Both belong in a migration runbook.

results.claim: [8] Hangfire's RecurringJobScheduler takes a global distributed lock on 'recurring-jobs:lock' then a per-job lock; source comments say multiple instances add fail-over not throughput; docs say each server uses distributed locks for coordination
results.evidence_quote: Multiple instances of this background process can be used in separate threads/processes without additional configuration (distributed locks are used). However, this only adds support for fail-over, and does not increase the performance.
results.correction: None. Lock resource string 'recurring-jobs:lock' and AcquireDistributedRecurringJobLock(recurringJobId) both present in the source. Caveat for the record: this is a raw fetch of the master branch, i.e. a moving target, not a pinned tag  -  cite a tag or commit SHA if this needs to be reproducible.

results.claim: [9] Two instances sharing one Hangfire storage will not double-execute the twelve recurring jobs; two instances with SEPARATE storage will  -  making 'move state before compute' the precondition for a safe parallel run
results.evidence_quote: It is possible to run multiple server instances inside a process, machine, or on several machines at the same time. Each server use distributed locks to perform the coordination logic. [page is banner-marked 'Obsolete since 1.5']
results.correction: Two problems with this URL as the citation. (1) The page says nothing about separate storages double-executing  -  that is an inference, sound but unsourced here. (2) The page's substantive guidance is explicitly banner-marked 'Obsolete since 1.5' (server identifiers are now GUIDs), so it is a weak citation to hang a cutover precondition on. The load-bearing evidence is actually claim [8]'s source file, where the locks are taken against IStorageConnection  -  locks in storage A cannot exclude a scheduler in storage B. Re-anchor claim [9] to the source, keep the 'partial' rating, and state the mechanism (locks are storage-scoped) rather than the conclusion.

results.claim: [10] ASP.NET Core Data Protection isolates apps by content-root path by default 'even if they share the same physical key repository'; SetApplicationName sets ApplicationDiscriminator; DisableAutomaticKeyGeneration gives a secondary app a read-only key ring
results.evidence_quote: By default, the Data Protection system isolates apps from one another based on their content root paths, even if they share the same physical key repository. This isolation prevents the apps from understanding each other's protected payloads. ... SetApplicationName internally sets DataProtectionOptions.ApplicationDiscriminator ... only the primary app is responsible for key management concerns and secondary apps simply have a read-only view of the key ring.
results.correction: None. All three sub-claims verified verbatim. One trap on this page that a container migration will hit and that the claim does not mention: .NET 6 WebApplicationBuilder normalises the content root to end with a directory separator while other hosts do not, so the same app can silently derive two different discriminators  -  the page recommends trimming the separator and calling SetApplicationName explicitly.

results.claim: [11] OpenIddict can format all token types except identity tokens via Data Protection; separate auth server and API MUST use the same application name and share a key ring; switching format does not invalidate previously issued JWTs
results.evidence_quote: ASP.NET Core Data Protection MUST be configured to use the same application name and share the same key ring to allow the OpenIddict validation handler to read ASP.NET Core Data Protection tokens generated by an authorization server located in another project. ... existing tokens can still be used alongside newly issued ASP.NET Core Data Protection tokens until they expire.
results.correction: None. Verified, including the exclusion of identity tokens ('except identity tokens, that are always JWT tokens').

results.claim: [12] OpenIddict supports multiple credentials for rotation, preferring 'certificates with the furthest expiration date'; development certificates are 'persisted - but not shared across instances' and the docs caution against them in hosted production, recommending self-signed certificates in the X.509 store
results.evidence_quote: certificates with the furthest expiration date are always preferred ... development certificates are persisted - but not shared across instances - and will be reused when the application host is restarted ... To avoid that, consider creating self-signed certificates and storing them in the X.509 certificates store of the host machine(s).
results.correction: None. Verified. Precision note for the write-up: the documented failure mode is specifically that development certificates cannot be used on IIS or Azure App Service (an exception is thrown at runtime unless the app pool loads a user profile)  -  the caution is narrower than a general 'not for production' statement, and the page separately recommends two distinct RSA certificates in production, one for encryption and one for signing.

results.claim: [13] RDB is safe to copy while running (never modified once produced, atomically renamed); copying AOF during a rewrite 'might end up with an invalid backup'; documented procedure is auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 0, confirm aof_rewrite_in_progress is 0, copy or hard-link, re-enable; appendfsync everysec risks one second of writes
results.evidence_quote: the RDB is never modified once produced, and while it gets produced it uses a temporary name and is renamed into its final destination atomically using rename(2) ... if this is done during a rewrite, you might end up with an invalid backup. To work around this you must disable AOF rewrites during the backup: 1. Turn off automatic rewrites with CONFIG SET auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 0 ... 2. ... verifying aof_rewrite_in_progress is 0 ... appendfsync everysec: fsync every second ... you may lose 1 second of data if there is a disaster.
results.correction: None  -  every element verified, including the hard-link variant and the multi-part AOF since 7.0.0. Worth noting the page now documents a newer option that supersedes this whole dance: since Redis 8.10.0 the BACKUP command family (BACKUP START / LIST / SEAL / CLEANUP) 'produces a self-contained, restorable backup without stopping writes or manually managing AOF rewrites'. If the target Redis is 8.10+, the auto-aof-rewrite-percentage procedure is the legacy path.

results.claim: [14] Redis replication is asynchronous by default; REPLICAOF seeds a replica from a master; a promoted replica generates a new replication ID; seeding a new instance carries a loss window inherent to async acknowledgement
results.evidence_quote: Redis uses by default asynchronous replication ... you can call the REPLICAOF command and the master host will start a sync with the replica ... the new replication ID of the promoted replica will be different, since it constitutes a different history of the data set ... WAIT is only able to ensure there are the specified number of acknowledged copies ... acknowledged writes can still be lost during a failover.
results.correction: None. All four elements verified, including the threshold framing that WAIT reduces but does not eliminate the loss window.

results.claim: [15] A DNS TTL is unsigned with a maximum of 2^31-1, and all RRs in an RRSet must carry the same TTL (RFC 2181 8, 5.2)
results.evidence_quote: a TTL value is an unsigned number, with a minimum value of 0, and a maximum value of 2147483647. That is, a maximum of 2^31 - 1. ... the TTLs of all RRs in an RRSet must be the same.
results.correction: None. Both sections verified and the section numbering (8 TTL, 5.2 TTLs of RRs in an RRSet) is correct. 8 additionally directs implementations to treat a TTL received with the most significant bit set as zero, which is a relevant hazard if any tooling writes a signed value.

results.claim: [16] Negative answers are cached at min(SOA.MINIMUM, SOA.TTL) (RFC 2308 3); 5 recommends capping negative caching at one to three hours, noting values over one day are problematic
results.evidence_quote: The TTL of this record is set from the minimum of the MINIMUM field of the SOA record and the TTL of the SOA itself ... Values of one to three hours have been found to work well ... Values exceeding one day have been found to be problematic.
results.correction: None. Verified. The operational consequence drawn (querying a hostname before it exists can pin NXDOMAIN in third-party caches for hours) follows correctly, since the cap is a resolver-side recommendation the zone owner cannot enforce.

results.claim: [17] RFC 8767 serve-stale lets resolvers answer with expired data when authoritative servers are unreachable; max stale timer 1-3 days (some up to a week), stale-response TTL about 30 seconds, TTL cap recommendation 604800s
results.evidence_quote: The suggested value is between 1 and 3 days ... Longer values, as much as a week ... a RECOMMENDED value of 30 seconds ... Values SHOULD be capped on the order of days to weeks, with a recommended cap of 604,800 seconds (7 days).
results.correction: None. All figures verified. The conclusion ('a record's TTL is a floor on cache lifetime, not a ceiling, once your authoritative servers stop answering') is a fair reading and is the operationally important half  -  it means decommissioning old authoritative servers at cutover can extend, not shorten, the stale window.

results.claim: [18] Public recursive resolvers keep independent caches a zone owner cannot flush; verified empirically 2026-08-31 by querying two public resolvers over DoH, observing a com. NS RRset with 21,591 seconds remaining in one resolver's cache
results.evidence_quote: Google DoH (re-run 2026-08-31): {"name":"com.","type":2,"TTL":21582,...}. Cloudflare DoH, same instant: {"name":"com","type":2,"TTL":157574,...}
results.correction: The behaviour class is confirmed and I reproduced it  -  two public resolvers returned wildly different remaining TTLs for the same RRSet at the same moment, which is exactly the point. Three corrections. (1) The URL as cited is not a page: a bare GET to https://dns.google/resolve returns HTTP 400; it only works with query parameters (?name=com&type=NS). Cite the parameterised form. (2) The specific figure 21,591 s is a one-shot observation that cannot be re-verified and should not be stated as a threshold. (3) More importantly, that number is being read wrong: ~21,600 s is 6 hours, which is Google's own cache cap on this RRSet, not the delegation TTL. Cloudflare's 157,574 s at the same instant is consistent with the real 172,800 s parent TTL. Presenting 21,591 as a delegation-TTL observation would understate the true propagation window by 8x.

results.claim: [19] The parent-zone delegation NS TTL is set by the TLD operator, not the zone owner, so nameserver changes propagate far more slowly than in-zone record changes; the specific .com value (commonly cited as 172800s) is UNVERIFIED here because dig is unavailable and DoH resolvers return authoritative answers rather than referrals
results.evidence_quote: RFC 2181 5.4.1 ranks 'Data from the authority section of a non-authoritative answer' below authoritative data, but the RFC contains no statement that the parent delegation NS TTL is set by the TLD operator.
results.correction: Credit for flagging this as unverified rather than asserting it  -  that was the right call. But two things need fixing. (1) RFC 2181 does not establish the stated principle; it ranks the credibility of parent-side data, it does not say who sets its TTL. The citation does not support the sentence it is attached to. (2) The 'cannot measure it from this environment' claim is now false: I measured it via DoH. Cloudflare returned com. NS with 157,574 s remaining, which is only consistent with an original TTL of 172,800 s (48 h)  -  so the commonly cited .com figure is corroborated from inside this environment without dig. Upgrade the finding to 'measured indirectly, consistent with 172800s' and drop RFC 2181 as the citation for the ownership principle.

results.claim: [20] Transferring a DNSSEC-signed zone between operators is constrained by the parent DS TTL: the old DS must expire from caches before old keys are removed, creating a mandatory wait; non-cooperating operators extend timelines (RFC 6781 4.3.5, 4.3.5.1, 4.3.5.2)
results.evidence_quote: 4.3.5. Changing DNS Operators ... 4.3.5.1. Cooperating DNS Operators ... 4.3.5.2. Non-Cooperating DNS Operators ... How easy this move will be depends principally on the DNS operator from which the registrant is moving (the losing operator), as the losing operator has control over the DNS zone and its keys.
results.correction: Section numbering and titles verified against the RFC text. The substance is right  -  a changeover cannot outrun cached DS/DNSKEY data and the non-cooperating case is materially worse. Note this only bites if the zone is actually DNSSEC-signed; if it is not, this constraint does not apply and should not be carried into the timeline as a hard dependency.

results.claim: [21] Wildcard certificates can only be issued via DNS-01; 'This challenge cannot be used to issue wildcard certificates' is stated of HTTP-01; DNS-01 requires a TXT record, i.e. programmatic zone control
results.evidence_quote: [HTTP-01] This challenge cannot be used to issue wildcard certificates. ... [DNS-01] You can use this challenge to issue certificates containing wildcard domain names. ... Your client will create a TXT record derived from that token and your account key, and put that record at _acme-challenge.<YOUR_DOMAIN>.
results.correction: None. Verified verbatim on both sides. Scope caveat: this is one CA's documentation, so the correct generalisation is 'ACME wildcard issuance requires DNS-01' rather than a property of TLS certificates as such  -  which matters because the capability requirement is written vendor-neutrally.

results.claim: [22] Let's Encrypt rate limits: 50 certs per registered domain per 7 days; 5 per exact same set of identifiers per 7 days; 300 new orders per account per 3 hours; 5 authorization failures per identifier per hour; staging has significantly higher limits
results.evidence_quote: Up to 50 certificates can be issued per registered domain (or IPv4 address, or IPv6 /64 range) every 7 days. ... Up to 5 certificates can be issued per exact same set of identifiers every 7 days. ... Up to 300 new orders can be created by a single account every 3 hours. ... Up to 5 authorization failures per identifier can be incurred by one account every hour.
results.correction: None. All four numbers verified verbatim, and the operational consequence (five rehearsals per week of the exact production SAN set; a broken DNS-01 loop burns the failure budget in minutes) follows directly. Practical addition: the duplicate-certificate limit keys on the exact identifier set, so a rehearsal cert with one extra or one fewer SAN draws from a different bucket  -  that is the documented way to rehearse without spending the production allowance, alongside staging.

results.claim: [23] HSTS preload requires max-age >= 31536000, includeSubDomains and preload; 'inclusion in the preload list cannot easily be undone'; removal 'takes months for a change to reach users with a Chrome update'
results.evidence_quote: The max-age must be at least 31536000 seconds (1 year). ... The includeSubDomains directive must be specified. ... The preload directive must be specified. ... Be aware that inclusion in the preload list cannot easily be undone. Domains can be removed, but it takes months for a change to reach users with a Chrome update and we cannot make guarantees about other browsers.
results.correction: None. Verified verbatim including the exact max-age threshold. Relevant to a migration plan and not mentioned in the claim: includeSubDomains is mandatory for preload, so every subdomain  -  including any temporary or internal host under the apex  -  must be HTTPS-capable before submission, and that constraint persists for the months-long removal window.

results.claim: [24] S3 supports both path-style and virtual-hosted-style in all regions but 'path-style URLs will be discontinued in the future' (deprecation delayed as of 23 September 2020); the SSL wildcard certificate matches only buckets without dots
results.evidence_quote: Currently, Amazon S3 supports both virtual-hosted-style and path-style URL access in all AWS Regions. However, path-style URLs will be discontinued in the future. ... Update (September 23, 2020) - To make sure that customers have the time that they need to transition to virtual-hosted-style URLs, we have decided to delay the deprecation of path-style URLs. ... When you're using virtual-hosted-style general purpose buckets with SSL, the SSL wildcard certificate matches only buckets that do not contain dots (.).
results.correction: None. Both quotes verified verbatim and the 'no current date' characterisation is accurate  -  the page announces discontinuation with no replacement date. This is correctly used as evidence of a behaviour class (single-label wildcard matching) rather than as a reason to adopt any particular storage service.

results.claim: [25] S3 integrity should use explicit checksums (CRC64NVME default, plus CRC32, CRC32C, SHA1, SHA256, MD5, SHA512 and others); SDKs do not automatically calculate MD5 and legacy Content-MD5 applies to single-part uploads; consequently ETag comparison is not a valid integrity check for multipart objects
results.evidence_quote: The CRC64NVME checksum algorithm is the default checksum algorithm used for checksum calculations. ... AWS SDKs do not automatically calculate MD5 checksums. ... The legacy Content-MD5 header remains available for single part uploads using SSE-S3 encryption.
results.correction: The algorithm list and the SDK/MD5 sentence are verified. Two things to fix. (1) The Content-MD5 sentence is narrower than quoted: the page qualifies it as 'single part uploads using SSE-S3 encryption', not single-part uploads generally. (2) The ETag conclusion is not supported by this URL  -  the page never mentions ETag at all. The conclusion is correct in substance (a multipart ETag is a digest-of-digests with a part-count suffix and is not the object's MD5), but it needs a citation that actually says so, or it should be presented as reasoning rather than as sourced fact. Since the capability requirement explicitly forbids ETag comparison, this is load-bearing and should not rest on an unsourced inference.

results.claim: [26] mc mirror syncs rsync-style with --watch, --remove, --overwrite and --checksum/--md5, 'only synchronises the current object without any version information or metadata other than tags', does not inherently verify integrity; MinIO docs now sit under MinIO AIStor with client releases as recent as RELEASE.2025-07-05, confirming active maintenance
results.evidence_quote: github.com/minio/mc: "This repository was archived by the owner on Jul 14, 2026. It is now read-only." Latest release: RELEASE.2025-08-13T08-35-41Z (published 7 September 2025).
results.correction: This is the material error in the set  -  the exact failure mode of 'tool claimed maintained that is archived'. The upstream MinIO Client repository (github.com/minio/mc) was ARCHIVED by its owner on 14 July 2026 and is read-only; its final release is RELEASE.2025-08-13T08-35-41Z from September 2025. A vendor documentation page for the commercial AIStor product referencing a July 2025 client build is not evidence of active maintenance in August 2026, and the inference 'confirming active maintenance' is false. Secondary corrections: (a) the flag behaviours and the 'only synchronises the current object without any version information or metadata other than tags' quote are correct and verified; (b) 'does not inherently verify object integrity during synchronisation' is NOT stated on the page  -  the page documents --checksum (MD5, CRC32, CRC32C, SHA1, SHA256) and --md5, so this is an inference, not a citation. Practical consequence: do not write a migration plan whose verification step depends on an archived client. This actually reinforces the capability requirement that object migration be verified by independently computed digests and counts rather than by the migration tool's own success report  -  the tool may be unmaintained by the time the cutover runs.

results.claim: [27] EF Core 9+ acquires a database-wide lock before applying migrations via Migrate/MigrateAsync, bundles and CLI tools; throws on pending model changes (RelationalEventId.PendingModelChangesWarning), detectable via dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes; guidance is bundles for automated deployment, not every replica migrating from its entrypoint, no restart of the migration container after success; bundles roll back to a target migration (0 reverts all) with data-loss warnings
results.evidence_quote: Starting with EF Core 9, MigrateAsync and Migrate automatically acquire a database-wide lock before applying any migrations. ... calling Migrate() or MigrateAsync() will throw an exception when the model has pending changes compared to the last migration (warning event ID RelationalEventId.PendingModelChangesWarning). To detect this condition before deployment, use the dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes command in your CI/CD pipeline. ... don't make every application replica run migrations from its entrypoint. Configure the deployment platform not to restart the migration container after it exits successfully. ... If '0', all migrations will be reverted.
results.correction: None  -  every element verified verbatim, including the lock covering bundles and CLI but explicitly NOT SQL scripts. Two caveats worth carrying into the runbook: the page warns that the locking mechanism is provider-specific and can leave abandoned locks if a process dies, and that wrapping MigrateAsync in an explicit transaction is unsupported. Neither changes the claim; both matter if the migration job is killed mid-cutover.

results.claim: [28] ABP registers tenant resolve contributors in order CurrentUser, QueryString, Route, Header, Cookie with key __tenant; 'This should always be the first contributor for the security'; per-tenant connection strings exist but UI management is a Commercial SaaS module feature
results.evidence_quote: This should always be the first contributor for the security ... managing connection strings of tenants from the UI is not available in open source version. You need to have SaaS module (PRO).
results.correction: None. Resolver order, the __tenant key and the SaaS/PRO restriction all verified. Minor wording: the docs say 'SaaS module (PRO)' rather than 'ABP Commercial SaaS module'; same thing, but quote it as written. The two conclusions drawn  -  that the four __tenant resolvers may still be live, and that per-office connection strings are an available mechanism  -  both hold, and the first is a genuine security consideration since query-string and header resolvers are enabled by default.

results.claim: [29] Strangler fig requires identifying seams and accepts transitional architecture as a deliberate cost; article last updated 22 August 2024
results.evidence_quote: When doing this, people often balk at the necessity of building transitional architecture to allow the new and legacy system to coexist, code that will go away once the modernization is complete. ... identifying seams that we can insert into the system to allow it to be split
results.correction: None. Quote, seams discussion and the 22 August 2024 date all verified on the page.

results.evidence_quote: Use an abstraction layer to allow multiple implementations to co-exist in the software system. ... Sometimes you can't swap-out the supplier for only some clients, you have to do it all at once.
