results.claim: [34] 'Stop the World cutover' is a named legacy-displacement pattern covering pausing business activity, reconfiguring integration points and DNS updates; records large failures without rehearsal, need to plan rollback, and very large peak loads on resumption; Cartwright, Horn and Lewis, 5 March 2024
results.evidence_quote: We've seen some large failures occur following this approach, often when no rehearsal or practice of the cut-over was possible or performed. ... Roll back in the event of a problem or overrun needs to be planned for. This approach can also create some very large peak loads as and when normal activities resume. ... by Ian Cartwright, Rob Horn, and James Lewis. Page metadata: og:article:modified_time = 2021-05-26.
results.correction: All three quotes are verbatim, the authors are correct, and the DNS/integration-point framing is supported ('migration of data, reconfiguration of other systems to point to new integration points, update of DNS to point to new websites'). The date is wrong: this page carries og:article:modified_time 2021-05-26. '05 March 2024' is the date on the parent index page (martinfowler.com/articles/patterns-legacy-displacement/), not on the stop-the-world sub-page. Attribute the date to the parent article or drop it. Also worth capturing, since it directly contradicts a stop-the-world cutover strategy: the authors close the section with 'We prefer more incremental approaches that allow migration of business to happen in smaller less risk increments.'

results.claim: [35] There is no 'Parallel Run' page on martinfowler.com (URL returns 404); the related catalogued patterns are Dark Launching, Canary Release, Event Interception, Divert the Flow and Transitional Architecture; therefore no 'parallel run' pattern is attributed to Fowler
results.evidence_quote: HTTP 404 for /articles/patterns-legacy-displacement/parallel-run.html (confirmed, no redirect). Catalogue on the index page: Critical Aggregator, Divert the Flow, Event Interception, Extract Product Lines, Feature Parity, Legacy Mimic, Revert to Source, Transitional Architecture.
results.correction: The 404 is confirmed and the intellectual honesty here is the right instinct  -  do not attribute a pattern to an author who did not write it. But the enumeration is inaccurate: the patterns catalogued on that index are Critical Aggregator, Divert the Flow, Event Interception, Extract Product Lines, Feature Parity, Legacy Mimic, Revert to Source and Transitional Architecture. Dark Launching and Canary Release are separate bliki entries referenced in the narrative, not entries in this catalogue, and Critical Aggregator, Extract Product Lines, Feature Parity, Legacy Mimic and Revert to Source were omitted. Also note the claim as worded ('no Parallel Run page on martinfowler.com') is broader than what was tested  -  only one URL under one article directory was checked, and I could not run a site-wide search to confirm the general negative. Narrow the wording to the directory actually tested. Separately: 'Parallel Run' is a named pattern in Sam Newman's Monolith to Microservices, which is very likely the source of the half-memory being corrected here  -  worth citing properly rather than treating the concept as unattributed.

results.claim: [36] Microsoft's multitenancy guidance says dedicated per-tenant deployments let updates roll out progressively across tenants reducing likelihood of a system-wide outage, while warning ongoing maintenance can be time consuming and advising automation; this system is a horizontally-partitioned deployment (shared app tier, database per tenant)
results.evidence_quote: [under 'Automated single-tenant deployments'] Updates and changes can be rolled out progressively across tenants, which reduces the likelihood of a system-wide outage. ... ongoing maintenance, like applying new configuration or software updates, can be time consuming. Consider automating your operational processes ... [under 'Horizontally partitioned deployments'] With a horizontally partitioned deployment, you still need to consider the automated deployment and management of your components, especially the components that a single tenant uses.
results.correction: Both quotes are verbatim and are correctly attributed in the claim's own wording to 'dedicated per-tenant deployments'. The problem is the juxtaposition: the claim ends by asserting the system is horizontally partitioned, which invites the reader to apply the progressive-rollout benefit to this system. It does not transfer. Under the page's taxonomy those benefits belong to Automated single-tenant deployments, where the whole stack including compute is per-tenant. In a horizontally partitioned deployment the application tier is SHARED, so an application change lands on every tenant simultaneously and the progressive-rollout property is exactly what this system does NOT have  -  only the per-tenant databases can be staged. The page's own guidance for the horizontally partitioned model is the sentence quoted above. Split these into two statements so the benefit is not silently inherited; this bears directly on the capability requirement that each tenant database be independently addressable, which is the only per-tenant staging lever actually available.

results.claim: [37] 45 CFR 164.316(b)(2)(i) requires retaining documentation for 6 years from creation or last effective date, whichever is later; paragraph (b)(1) concerns policies and procedures in written or electronic form; whether it captures an application's entity-property-change audit trail is an interpretation, not a plain reading
results.evidence_quote: Retain the documentation required by paragraph (b)(1) of this section for 6 years from the date of its creation or the date when it last was in effect, whichever is later. ... Maintain the policies and procedures implemented to comply with this subpart in written (which may be electronic) form
results.correction: None, and the self-correction embedded in this claim is the single best piece of work in the set  -  the regulation governs documentation of policies, procedures, actions, activities and assessments, and it is genuinely a stretch to read it as mandating retention of an ORM's property-level change log. Flagging that as interpretation rather than plain reading is correct and should survive into the final document. The sizing conclusion is unaffected as stated, since nothing prunes those tables regardless of the retention basis.

results.claim: [38] 45 CFR 164.308(a)(7): data backup, disaster recovery and emergency mode operation plans are Required; testing/revision and criticality analysis are Addressable; 164.308(b)(1) conditions business associate involvement on satisfactory assurances, and the BAA obligation is conditioned on ePHI being involved
results.evidence_quote: (A) Data backup plan (Required) ... (B) Disaster recovery plan (Required) ... (C) Emergency mode operation plan (Required) ... (D) Testing and revision procedures (Addressable) ... (E) Applications and data criticality analysis (Addressable) ... A covered entity may permit a business associate to create, receive, maintain, or transmit electronic protected health information on the covered entity's behalf only if the covered entity obtains satisfactory assurances, in accordance with  164.314(a), that the business associate will appropriately safeguard the information.
results.correction: None. Every Required/Addressable designation verified and 164.308(b)(1) quoted verbatim. The inference that the synthetic-data window permits trialling infrastructure before a BAA exists is correct on the face of the text, since the obligation attaches to ePHI. Flag as a project risk rather than a citation error: that permission evaporates the moment real ePHI touches the new infrastructure, so the BAA must be in place before the first production data load, not before go-live.

results.claim: [39] HHS breach-notification guidance: ePHI is 'secured' when encrypted per FIPS 140-2 validated processes, referencing NIST SP 800-111 at rest and SP 800-52/800-77/800-113 in motion; media must be destroyed or cleared consistent with NIST SP 800-88
results.evidence_quote: Valid encryption processes for data at rest are consistent with NIST Special Publication 800-111 ... 800-52 ... 800-77 ... or 800-113 ... or others which are Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) 140-2 validated ... Electronic media have been cleared, purged, or destroyed consistent with NIST Special Publication 800-88
results.correction: None  -  all five NIST references and the FIPS 140-2 (not 140-3) designation verified as written on the page. Note for the record that FIPS 140-2 has been superseded by FIPS 140-3 in NIST's own validation programme, but the HHS guidance still says 140-2, so quoting it as 140-2 is correct citation practice. The derived risk  -  an abandoned rollback copy of a PHI-bearing database on unencrypted storage being a breach candidate  -  follows directly from the safe-harbour framing and is the sharpest operational consequence in this set.

results.claim: [40] The HIPAA Security Rule NPRM was published 27 December 2024 (Federal Register 6 January 2025), comments closed 7 March 2025; proposes expressly requiring ePHI encryption and technology asset inventory/ePHI movement mapping; no final rule located; the 72-hour restoration and removal of addressable/required claims could not be verified
results.evidence_quote: The NPRM was issued on December 27, 2024. ... While the Department is undertaking this rulemaking, the current Security Rule remains in effect.
results.correction: The two load-bearing facts are confirmed on the page: the 27 December 2024 issuance and, decisively, that no final rule has taken effect ('the current Security Rule remains in effect'). Everything else attributed to this URL is not on it  -  the 6 January 2025 Federal Register date, the 7 March 2025 comment close, the express encryption requirement and the asset-inventory/ePHI-mapping proposals all come from the Federal Register notice itself, which the page only links to. Either cite the FR notice directly or attribute those details as 'not verified from the reachable source'. The claim's own 'partial' rating and its explicit refusal to repeat the widely circulated 72-hour restoration and addressable/required-removal claims are correct and should be preserved  -  those are exactly the kind of secondhand figures that propagate unchecked. The conclusion to treat the NPRM as direction of travel rather than current obligation is right, and it means no capability requirement should be justified by the NPRM alone.

results.claim: [41] Microsoft's SQL Server migration guidance frames cutover as verify data is the same on source and target, then cut over, planning with business/application teams; prescribes post-migration source/target comparison queries in an isolated test environment
results.evidence_quote: After you verify that data is same on both the source and the target, you can cut over from the source to the target environment. It's important to plan the cutover process with business / application teams to ensure minimal interruption during cutover doesn't affect business continuity. ... You must create the validation queries to run against both the source and the target databases ... Be sure to isolate the test environment.
results.correction: Quotes verified verbatim. One scoping correction: this page is titled 'SQL Server to Azure SQL Database: Migration Guide' and is specific to one migration target, not general SQL Server migration guidance. The cutover sequencing and validation advice are generic enough to travel, but describe it as what it is, and be aware the surrounding recommendations (log generation rate ceilings, service-tier scaling, ExpressRoute bandwidth) are target-specific and should not be carried across. Citing it as evidence of a practice class is fine; citing it as neutral guidance is not.

material_errors: CLAIM 26  -  a tool is claimed actively maintained when it is archived. The MinIO Client repository (github.com/minio/mc) was archived by its owner on 14 July 2026 and is read-only; the last release is RELEASE.2025-08-13T08-35-41Z (September 2025). The claim's evidence for 'confirming active maintenance' is a commercial AIStor documentation page referencing a July 2025 client build  -  that is not evidence of maintenance in August 2026. Any migration step whose verification depends on mc is depending on an unmaintained tool. This reinforces rather than undermines the capability requirement that object migration be verified by independently computed digests and counts rather than by the migration tool's own success report.

CLAIM 36  -  misapplied attribution with a real engineering consequence. The quoted benefit 'Updates and changes can be rolled out progressively across tenants, which reduces the likelihood of a system-wide outage' appears under 'Automated single-tenant deployments' (dedicated stack per tenant). The claim then asserts this system is horizontally partitioned, where the application tier is SHARED  -  so progressive per-tenant rollout of application changes is precisely the property this architecture does NOT have. Only the per-tenant databases can be staged. Left as written, a reader would plan a staged rollout the architecture cannot deliver.

CLAIM 18/19  -  a cited cache observation is misread by roughly 8x. The 21,591 s figure attributed to a com. NS RRset is a public resolver's own 6-hour cache cap (I reproduced 21,582 s from the same resolver), not the parent delegation TTL. A second public resolver returned 157,574 s at the same instant, consistent with the real 172,800 s .com delegation TTL. Claim 19 additionally states this value could not be measured from this environment; it can be, via DNS-over-HTTPS, and I measured it. Planning a nameserver change against a 6-hour window instead of a 48-hour one would materially understate the propagation risk.

CLAIM 25  -  the conclusion that matters is uncited. 'ETag comparison is not a valid integrity check for multipart objects' is correct in substance but appears nowhere on the cited AWS page, which never mentions ETag. Since a capability requirement explicitly forbids ETag comparison, this prohibition currently rests on an unsourced inference and needs either a supporting citation or to be labelled as reasoning.

CLAIM 2  -  a protocol behaviour is asserted that the cited page does not state. nginx's proxy_pass documentation confirms only that a value containing a variable is resolved at request time via the resolver; it never states that a name without a variable is resolved at configuration/startup time. The behaviour is real, but the stale-container-IP trap is presented as documented when it is inferred.

CLAIM 34  -  wrong date. The stop-the-world page carries og:article:modified_time 2021-05-26; '05 March 2024' is the date on the parent Patterns of Legacy Displacement index, not this sub-page. All three quoted passages are verbatim and correct.

CLAIM 35  -  inaccurate enumeration inside an otherwise sound correction. The 404 is confirmed, but the catalogued patterns are Critical Aggregator, Divert the Flow, Event Interception, Extract Product Lines, Feature Parity, Legacy Mimic, Revert to Source and Transitional Architecture. Dark Launching and Canary Release are separate bliki entries, not catalogue members, and five actual entries were omitted. Note also that 'Parallel Run' IS a named pattern in Sam Newman's Monolith to Microservices  -  likely the true source of the half-memory being corrected.

CLAIM 40  -  most of the detail attributed to the cited URL is not on it. Confirmed on the page: the 27 December 2024 issuance, and that no final rule is in effect. NOT on the page: the 6 January 2025 Federal Register date, the 7 March 2025 comment close, the express encryption requirement, and the asset-inventory/ePHI-mapping proposals. The claim's refusal to repeat the unverified 72-hour restoration and addressable/required-removal figures is correct and should be preserved.

CLAIM 9  -  the citation is banner-marked obsolete and does not support the operative half. The Hangfire page is flagged 'Obsolete since 1.5' and says nothing about separate storages causing double execution. The real evidence is claim 8's source file: the locks are taken against IStorageConnection, so locks held in storage A cannot exclude a scheduler running against storage B. Re-anchor to the source and state the mechanism rather than the conclusion.
vendor_neutrality_violations: Requirement 8 ('The target database platform MUST run the same SQL Server major version as the source at the moment of cutover') names a specific commercial product inside a MUST. The underlying intent  -  freeze the engine version across the move so that relocation and upgrade are independently reversible steps  -  is genuinely vendor-neutral and is well supported by claim 3 (restore to an earlier version is impossible; upgrade on restore is automatic). Neutral phrasing: 'MUST run the same major version of the incumbent database engine as the source at the moment of cutover.' Mitigating note: this is an incumbent-continuity constraint on an existing system rather than a recommendation to adopt a product, which is the weakest form of this violation.

Requirement 9 ('The target database edition MUST support every feature reported by sys.dm_db_persisted_sku_features in every source database, MUST support backup compression, and MUST have a maximum database size at least an order of magnitude above the largest projected office database') is expressed entirely in one vendor's product vocabulary  -  'edition' is a SQL Server licensing construct and sys.dm_db_persisted_sku_features is a SQL Server DMV. More seriously, it functions as a product-TIER recommendation: per claim 5, backup compression is available only on Enterprise and Standard, so this requirement silently mandates the purchase of SQL Server Standard or higher. That is 'therefore use <product edition>' wearing the clothes of a capability. Neutral phrasing: 'The target database tier MUST support every storage-format-affecting feature persisted in any source database, MUST support native backup compression, and MUST have a maximum database size at least an order of magnitude above the largest projected office database'  -  with the DMV named in the verification procedure rather than in the requirement itself.

Borderline, listed for completeness and NOT recommended for rewording: requirements 5, 6 and 7 use S3 vocabulary ('path-style addressing', 'access key ID and secret'). These stay on the correct side of the line because each defines the behaviour inline ('bucket in the URL path, not in the hostname') and describes a capability class implemented by many independent products rather than naming one. Requirement 15's prohibition on ETag comparison is likewise a constraint on a verification method, not a product endorsement.

Assessment of the remaining requirements: 1, 2, 3, 4, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14 and 16 are clean. Notably, several are written exactly as the exercise intends  -  requirement 11 says 'a single shared cache and key-ring store' rather than naming Redis; requirement 13 says 'background job execution MUST be independently switchable per running application instance' rather than naming Hangfire; requirement 3 specifies 'a DNS-based domain validation method' rather than naming a certificate authority. The vendor documentation cited throughout the claims (nginx, Microsoft, AWS, Redis, MinIO, Let's Encrypt) is used as evidence of behaviour classes, which is permitted; no claim concludes 'therefore use this product'. The two genuine violations are both in the database requirements and both stem from the same root cause: the incumbent engine's constraints were transcribed into the requirement text instead of being abstracted into capability language with the product-specific detail moved to the verification steps.

research.design_space: In 2026 the viable designs for containing administrative and diagnostic surfaces fall on a spectrum defined by *where the containment decision is made*: at the compile/deploy step (the surface is not present in the production artifact), inside the application (the surface participates in the app's own authorization), at the process's network binding (the surface answers on a listener the public path cannot reach), at the edge (hostname, port, source address, client certificate, or an authenticating proxy), or on the network (private routing, so no public path exists at all). These are not alternatives so much as layers, and mature designs compose two or three. The decisive property that separates a defensible design from a fragile one is not strength but *durability under change*: whether the containment still holds when a developer adds a new administrative route six months later without remembering the design. Containment expressed as a property of a network position (a listener, a hostname, a route) survives new paths automatically because it never enumerates paths; containment expressed as a rule about paths does not, because every new path is a new exception. A second axis is who the surface's consumers are: a design that assumes shell access to the host is cheap and strong for two engineers, and useless the moment a non-engineer needs the surface, at which point an authenticating proxy that fronts a whole hostname becomes the only thing that scales. A third, frequently missed axis is that the edge and the application are two different parsers of the same request, and any control that depends on them agreeing about what a path or a client address *is* inherits every disagreement between them. Finally, current guidance has converged on requiring both network-position containment and identity: OWASP ASVS 5.0 explicitly rejects network location as a *sole* authorization factor, so "it's only reachable from inside" is a risk reducer, never a control on its own.

options.name: Do not deploy the surface in production (compile-time or configuration exclusion)
options.how_it_works: The dashboard/diagnostic UI is registered only under an environment or build gate, so the production artifact never maps the route at all. The route does not exist to be found.
options.operational_cost: Setup 1-3 hours. Ongoing ~0 hours/month. Assumes only that the team can add an environment check. No new components, no new credentials, no new failure modes.
options.why: Strongest possible containment for the one surface it is applied to, and the cheapest. Conditional rather than yes because this system has NO observability at all - Serilog to console and file, HealthChecks UI with in-memory storage, no metrics, no APM, no alerting - and twelve recurring jobs including three that run every 15 minutes across every office database. The Hangfire dashboard is currently the team's only window into whether those jobs are succeeding. Deleting it in production makes an already-blind system blinder, and this team will not notice a slow degradation. It also does not generalise: it protects this route and teaches nothing that protects the next one.

options.name: Fix the surface's own authorization filter (in-application authorization for that one surface)
options.how_it_works: Replace the `return true` authorization filter with one that requires an authenticated administrator, or restore Hangfire's shipped default (`LocalRequestsOnlyAuthorizationFilter`).
options.operational_cost: Setup 2-8 hours. Ongoing ~0 hours/month. Assumes familiarity with the surface's own extension point, which differs per surface (Hangfire filter, HealthChecks UI, Swagger, ABP endpoints each differ).
options.why: This is the planned code fix and it should land, but as the *design* it is the weakest option and it carries a specific trap. Hangfire's shipped default compares `context.Request.RemoteIpAddress` against loopback. Behind nginx in Docker that address is the nginx container's IP, so the safe default denies everyone, and the natural next step is to enable forwarded headers. Microsoft's own documentation states that setting `ASPNETCORE_FORWARDEDHEADERS_ENABLED=true` "doesn't enable features such as the KnownProxies option to restrict which IPs forwarders are accepted from", and shows that flag clearing `KnownNetworks` and `KnownProxies`. At that point any client sending `X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1` is treated as local and the dashboard reopens - silently. The 'safe default' can therefore be worse than an explicit check. It also protects exactly one route and expires the moment a new one is added.

options.name: Deny-by-default authorization inside the application, plus an enforced anonymous allow-list
options.how_it_works: Set `AuthorizationOptions.FallbackPolicy` to `RequireAuthenticatedUser()` in both HttpApi.Host and AuthServer, so every endpoint with no explicit authorization metadata is denied. Genuinely public endpoints (OIDC discovery and token endpoints, health, anonymous document upload, the partner reconcile endpoint) are explicitly marked `[AllowAnonymous]`. A startup or test-time check enumerates `EndpointDataSource.Endpoints` and fails when an endpoint is neither authenticated nor on a reviewed allow-list.
options.operational_cost: Setup 16-26 hours, most of it discovery: finding every genuinely anonymous endpoint across two processes including ABP and OpenIddict framework routes. Ongoing 1-2 hours/month adding reviewed allow-list entries. Assumes only ASP.NET Core knowledge the team already has; no new infrastructure, no new credentials, no new running component.
options.why: This is the only option that survives a code change adding a NEW admin route, because it never enumerates admin routes - it inverts the default so that *anything* unlabelled is denied. Microsoft states the case directly: "Having authorization required by default is more secure than relying on new controllers and Razor Pages to include the [Authorize] attribute." Crucially for this team it fails in the loud direction: forgetting `[AllowAnonymous]` on a genuinely public endpoint produces a hard 401 that shows up immediately, not a silent exposure that shows up never. One real limitation: `FallbackPolicy` applies to endpoints, and a surface mounted as a middleware branch via `app.Map` (which is how `UseHangfireDashboard` mounts) is not an endpoint - it is covered only if it sits after `UseAuthorization` in the pipeline. Mounting via `MapHangfireDashboard`, which returns an `IEndpointConventionBuilder`, brings it under endpoint routing and therefore under the fallback policy.

options.name: Separate listener/port on the same process, never published to the host
options.how_it_works: Kestrel listens on a second port; administrative and diagnostic endpoints are constrained to it with `RequireHost("*:8081")`. Docker compose does not publish that port and nginx has no server block for it, so the only way in is from inside the container network or an SSH local port-forward from a developer's machine.
options.operational_cost: Setup 3-6 hours. Ongoing ~0.5 hours/month. Assumes SSH access, which is already this team's sole deployment mechanism, so it adds no new access path, no new credential store and no new component.
options.why: Microsoft's own routing documentation uses precisely this pattern as its worked example: `app.MapHealthChecks("/healthz").RequireHost("*:8080")`. It makes the containment a property of the binding rather than of a path, so path casing, percent-encoding and slash-collapsing tricks are all irrelevant - there is no path rule to defeat. It is the single highest value-per-hour item available here, because the team already has SSH and already publishes only ports 80 and 443 from one container. The trap to state loudly: this works only if the port is genuinely not published. Docker's documentation states that published ports bypass ufw because "packets are diverted before it reaches the INPUT and OUTPUT chains that ufw uses", so publishing the admin port and 'protecting' it with the host firewall does nothing at all.

options.name: Separate hostname with a dedicated edge server block and source-address restriction
options.how_it_works: An ops hostname gets its own nginx server block containing the admin routes, with `allow`/`deny` on source addresses; the application hostnames' server blocks never proxy those routes.
options.operational_cost: Setup 4-8 hours plus certificate work. Ongoing 1-3 hours/month, rising whenever a developer's home IP changes. Assumes a stable source address, which two developers on residential broadband generally do not have.
options.why: Aligned with NIST SP 800-53 SC-2, whose guidance names "isolating administrative interfaces on different domains" explicitly. Two system-specific constraints make it sharper than it looks. First, `admin` is already a RESERVED tenant slug meaning host scope, so `admin.<base>` cannot be the ops hostname without colliding with tenancy resolution. Second, RFC 6125 restricts a wildcard to the left-most label, so `ops.<base>` is free under the existing `*.<base>` certificate while `ops.api.<base>` would require another wildcard - a real cost difference driven purely by name choice. Source-IP restriction is where it degrades: a changing residential IP produces lockout (obvious, but during an incident), and the usual response is to widen the range until it means little (subtle).

options.name: Private-network-only access (VPN or overlay network)
options.how_it_works: The admin surface binds only to an interface reachable over a private network; there is no public DNS record and no public route to it.
options.operational_cost: Setup 8-16 hours for a new VPN endpoint plus key distribution. Ongoing 2-4 hours/month. Assumes the team can operate key lifecycle and can debug the VPN itself when it is the thing that is broken.
options.why: Architecturally the strongest network-position answer and the direction regulators are moving. But for this team it adds a component whose failure blocks incident response - if the VPN is down during an outage, they cannot reach the box to fix the outage - and there is no on-call rotation to absorb that. The important observation is that they already have an authenticated private channel to the host: SSH. An SSH local port-forward to an unpublished admin port delivers the same security property with zero new production components and zero new key material. Recommend the capability (an authenticated private channel with per-person revocable credentials); note that the existing one already satisfies it.

options.name: mTLS at the edge for the administrative server block
options.how_it_works: The ops server block sets `ssl_verify_client on` with `ssl_client_certificate` naming a trusted CA; only holders of an issued client certificate complete the handshake.
options.operational_cost: Setup 8-16 hours. Ongoing 2-4 hours/month, and a hard cliff at every certificate expiry. Assumes the team operates a small CA: issuance, renewal, revocation, and distribution to developer machines.
options.why: Cryptographically strong and it does survive new routes on that hostname. But it requires this team to run a certificate authority, and their entire current secret management is one mode-600 file with 35 variables, no vault, no rotation and no access audit, with several values already flagged for rotation after being pasted into chat transcripts. A team that cannot yet rotate a database password should not be handed a CA. The failure mode - expired client certificate, no access - reliably arrives at the worst moment, and there is no second person to let you back in.

options.name: Identity-aware proxy fronting the administrative hostname
options.how_it_works: An authenticating reverse proxy sits in front of the admin surfaces (typically via nginx `auth_request`), performs an OIDC flow against the existing AuthServer, and forwards only authenticated, authorized requests.
options.operational_cost: Setup 16-30 hours. Ongoing 2-5 hours/month, including tracking the proxy's own security releases. Assumes comfort with OIDC client configuration, cookie/session secret management, and one more container on a box with ~9.7 GB free disk.
options.why: This is the answer large organisations reach for, and it has the single best durability property in the list: it protects every surface behind the hostname regardless of what the application does, including routes added later by developers who never read this document. It is genuinely the right long-term answer. It is not right *yet* because it adds a ninth long-running service and a new always-on dependency in the authentication path for operations, on a single VM with no redundancy, for exactly two consumers who already hold SSH keys. It also brings its own vulnerability stream: oauth2-proxy v7.15.2 (April 2026) shipped fixes for "multiple authentication bypasses and session fixation vulnerabilities", which is a component this team would need to track and patch. Becomes correct the moment a third person, or any non-developer, needs admin access.

options.name: Path-based deny rules at the edge
options.how_it_works: nginx server blocks carry `location /hangfire { deny all; }` and similar entries for each known administrative path.
options.operational_cost: Setup 1-2 hours. Ongoing cost is unbounded and invisible: every new admin path silently needs an entry that nobody will remember to add.
options.why: Structurally unsound here, and demonstrably so rather than as a matter of taste. nginx documents that prefix location matching ignores case only "For case-insensitive operating systems such as macOS and Cygwin" - so on this Ubuntu host `location /hangfire` does not match `/Hangfire`. ASP.NET Core matches the other way: `PathString.StartsWithSegments` defaults to `StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase` in the framework source, and the routing documentation states "Text matching is case-insensitive and based on the decoded representation of the URL's path." So `GET /Hangfire` passes the deny rule and is served by the application. The edge and the application are two different parsers and the deny rule lives entirely inside their disagreement. Beyond that it is whack-a-mole by construction: it can only deny paths someone already knew to list.

options.name: Path allow-list at the edge (deny by default at the HTTP layer)
options.how_it_works: nginx serves only explicitly enumerated path prefixes and returns 404 for everything else, so an unlisted admin route is unreachable even if nobody knew it existed.
options.operational_cost: Setup 12-24 hours to enumerate the current surface. Ongoing 2-6 hours/month, and it couples every new controller to an nginx change.
options.why: The principle is right - NIST SC-7(5) requires denying traffic by default and allowing by exception - and unlike the deny-list this one fails closed, which suits this team's need for loud failures. It is rejected on maintenance coupling, not on principle. The surface is 52 HTTP controllers plus ABP framework endpoints plus OpenIddict's discovery, token and identity UI routes plus 45 Angular routed paths, and deployment is manual over SSH with a documented trap where nginx must be force-recreated after any backend rebuild or routing silently breaks on stale container IPs. An allow-list maintained by hand in that environment will either block new features constantly or be widened to a wildcard within two months. The correct move is to keep the principle and relocate it to the layer that actually knows what a route is: the application.

research.recommendation:
Compose three layers, and put the allow-list in the application rather than at the edge. That is the direct answer to the key design question: the correct answer is an allow-list, but not at the edge - the edge should do containment by hostname and port so that path questions never arise, and the allow-list belongs in the application, which is the only layer that knows what a route is.

The reasoning is that the edge and the application are different parsers of the same request. Any edge rule about paths lives inside their disagreements, and I verified a disagreement that defeats the deny-list outright: nginx prefix matching is case-sensitive on Linux, while ASP.NET Core path matching is `OrdinalIgnoreCase`, so `location /hangfire { deny all; }` does not stop `GET /Hangfire`. An edge allow-list does not have that defect and is the right principle (NIST SC-7(5)), but it couples every new controller to a manual nginx change in a deployment process that already has a known nginx-staleness trap, so it will rot. Move the deny-by-default to where routes are defined.

Layer 1, placement (3-6 hours): bind administrative and diagnostic surfaces to a second Kestrel port constrained with `RequireHost("*:<adminport>")`, do not publish that port in compose, and give it no nginx server block. Microsoft's routing documentation uses this exact pattern for a health endpoint. Access is by SSH local port-forward, which costs nothing new because SSH is already the only deployment channel. This is what NIST SP 800-53 SC-2 asks for - "Separate user functionality, including user interface services, from system management functionality" - and its guidance names separation "by using different computers, instances of operating systems, central processing units, or network addresses". It is durable because it is a property of a binding, not of a path.

Layer 2, deny-by-default in the application (16-26 hours): set `AuthorizationOptions.FallbackPolicy` to `RequireAuthenticatedUser()` in *both* HttpApi.Host and AuthServer, and mark genuinely public endpoints `[AllowAnonymous]`. Both processes matter: sign-in is served by AuthServer, whose Razor pages call application services in-process, so anything applied only to the API misses it. This is the layer that survives a new admin route added by someone who never read this document, because it never enumerates admin routes. It also fails in the loud direction this team needs: a forgotten `[AllowAnonymous]` is an immediate 401, not a silent exposure.

Layer 3, an enforced inventory (4-6 hours): a test that walks `EndpointDataSource.Endpoints` and fails when any endpoint is neither authenticated nor on a reviewed anonymous allow-list. This converts "did we remember?" from a discipline question into a build failure, which is the only form of vigilance a two-person team can sustain.

Two corrections to the obvious fixes. First, do not restore Hangfire's shipped `LocalRequestsOnlyAuthorizationFilter` as the answer. Behind nginx in Docker the remote address is the proxy's container IP, so it denies everyone, and the natural remedy - enabling forwarded headers - is documented by Microsoft to clear `KnownProxies` and `KnownNetworks` when driven by `ASPNETCORE_FORWARDEDHEADERS_ENABLED`, at which point `X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1` reopens the dashboard silently. Second, mount via `MapHangfireDashboard` (which returns an `IEndpointConventionBuilder`, so it accepts `RequireHost` and `RequireAuthorization` and participates in endpoint routing and therefore in the fallback policy) rather than `UseHangfireDashboard`, which mounts a middleware branch outside endpoint routing.

Also close the ingress default: add a `default_server` block on 443 that denies, because nginx documents that "If none of the directives have the default_server parameter then the first server with the address:port pair will be the default server" - which is why the bare apex currently lands on AuthServer.

On object storage: the application authenticating to MinIO as root is a separate and independently fixable defect, and the fix does not touch the partner. ASVS 5.0 requires backend authentication using "individual service accounts, short-term tokens, or certificate-based authentication and not unchanging credentials such as passwords, API keys, or shared accounts with privileged access" (13.2.1) with least privilege (13.2.2) and not default credentials (13.2.3). Root can administer identity, so a compromise of the application does not merely read the partner bucket - it can mint a scoped credential that survives rotating the root password. Issue the application a scoped access key limited to the application bucket, keep the root credential offline for break-glass, and leave the partner's credential untouched so re-credentialing stays on the partner's schedule. Treat the partner credential as a migration constraint on any future storage move rather than something to change now.
research.operational_cost_of_recommendation:
Setup: roughly 25-38 developer-hours total. Layer 1 (second listener, RequireHost on admin surfaces, unpublish the port, nginx default_server deny block, remove the dead WebSocket upgrade config) 6-11 hours. Layer 2 (FallbackPolicy in both processes plus discovering and marking every genuinely anonymous endpoint across ABP, OpenIddict, health, anonymous upload and the partner reconcile path) 16-26 hours - the discovery, not the code, is the cost. Layer 3 (endpoint inventory test) 4-6 hours. The MinIO scoped-credential change is a further 4-8 hours and is independent. A runbook for the SSH port-forward is 2 hours.

That is essentially one full developer-week, which is the team's entire stated monthly infrastructure budget. It must therefore be scheduled as THE infrastructure item for one month, not fitted around feature work and not run concurrently with the code-standard remediation exercise that already claims a large share of that budget. Attempting it in parallel is the most likely way for it to half-land, and a half-landed FallbackPolicy (fallback set, allow-list incomplete) breaks production sign-in.

Ongoing: 1-2 hours per month - adding reviewed allow-list entries for new anonymous endpoints and occasionally fixing the inventory test.

Thresholds, stated explicitly because the one-developer-week-per-month figure is an estimate and not a measurement. The design is operable at 4 or more infrastructure hours per month. Between 2 and 4 hours per month it still holds but the inventory test's allow-list starts accumulating unexplained entries. Below roughly 2 hours per month it decays to Option B: the inventory test becomes the thing that gets silenced to make CI green, entries are added with `[AllowAnonymous]` to unblock a release, and within two quarters the fallback policy is nominal. The observable early-warning signal is allow-list entries added without a comment justifying why the endpoint is public - require that comment in review, and treat its absence as the decay indicator rather than waiting for an incident.

The design stops being the right one, rather than merely under-resourced, when more than about three people need administrative access or when any non-developer does. SSH port-forwarding does not scale past people who already hold host credentials, and at that point the identity-aware proxy stops being over-engineering and becomes the correct answer.
