capability_requirements.requirement: The platform MUST allow an application process to serve administrative and diagnostic endpoints on a network listener that is not reachable from the public ingress path, without requiring a separate deployment artifact.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: This is the containment-by-position control that survives the addition of new administrative routes. NIST SC-2 names separate network addresses as an accepted realisation of separating management from user functionality. Without it, every containment control degrades to a rule about paths.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 SC-2 guidance ('different ... network addresses'); the system fact that only the reverse proxy publishes host ports (80, 443).
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: From a host outside the deployment, attempt a TCP connection to the administrative listener's port on the public address. The connection must fail (refused or timed out), not return an HTTP response. Then, from inside the deployment (or via an authenticated forward), request the same endpoint and confirm it responds. Both results are required: one proves containment, the other proves the surface still exists.

capability_requirements.requirement: Protection of administrative surfaces MUST NOT depend on the edge and the application agreeing on the textual form of a request path.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Verified parser disagreement: nginx prefix locations are case-sensitive on Linux while ASP.NET Core path matching is OrdinalIgnoreCase. Any control living in that gap is bypassable by changing letter case, and the bypass leaves no distinguishing signal in logs.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: nginx location directive documentation; ASP.NET Core PathString.StartsWithSegments source (StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase) and routing documentation ('Text matching is case-insensitive').
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Request the administrative path in at least four forms from an external client: exact lowercase, mixed case (/Hangfire), percent-encoded first character (/%68angfire), and with a doubled leading slash (//hangfire). All four must produce the identical denial. If any form returns different content or a different status than the others, the design has failed this requirement.

capability_requirements.requirement: The application MUST deny any HTTP endpoint that carries no explicit authorization decision, in every process that serves HTTP.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: This is the only mechanism in the list that automatically covers a route added in the future by a developer who is unaware of the containment design. Microsoft recommends it for exactly this reason. 'Every process' is a MUST because this system serves sign-in from a second process whose Razor pages call application services in-process, so a policy applied only to the API silently misses it.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft Learn AuthorizationOptions.FallbackPolicy guidance; the system fact of two HTTP-serving processes (HttpApi.Host and AuthServer).
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Add a new controller action with no authorization attributes to each HTTP-serving process, deploy, and request it with no credentials. Both must return 401 or 403, never 200. Repeat with a minimal API endpoint and with a middleware-branch mount to confirm coverage is not limited to controllers.

capability_requirements.requirement: There MUST be an automated, build- or startup-time check that enumerates every registered HTTP endpoint and fails when an endpoint is neither authenticated nor present on an explicit, reviewed anonymous allow-list.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Deny-by-default protects against the forgotten route; this protects against the deliberate but unconsidered exception. For a two-person team with no QA and no security review, converting vigilance into a failing build is the only form that survives. It also makes the anonymous surface an explicit, reviewable inventory rather than an emergent property.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: EndpointDataSource.Endpoints ('Returns a read-only collection of Endpoint instances'); OWASP ASVS 5.0 13.4.5 (monitoring and documentation endpoints not exposed unless explicitly intended).
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Add an endpoint marked [AllowAnonymous] that is not on the allow-list and run the check; it must fail and name the offending route. Then add it to the allow-list and confirm the check passes. Then remove an existing allow-list entry for an endpoint that is genuinely anonymous and confirm the check fails again. A check that passes in all three cases is not enforcing anything.

capability_requirements.requirement: If the application derives client IP or scheme from forwarded headers, the platform MUST allow restricting which peer addresses are trusted to set them, and that restriction MUST be active.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: An unrestricted forwarded-headers configuration converts any IP-based control into a client-supplied assertion. Microsoft documents that the common enabling flag clears the trusted-proxy lists entirely, so this is a live trap rather than a theoretical one, and it is the specific way a well-intentioned fix to the current defect can reintroduce it.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft Learn proxy-load-balancer documentation: ASPNETCORE_FORWARDEDHEADERS_ENABLED 'doesn't enable features such as the KnownProxies option'; defaults KnownNetworks 127.0.0.0/8, KnownProxies IPv6 loopback, ForwardLimit 1.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: From an external client, send a request carrying 'X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1' to any endpoint that logs or echoes the observed client address. The observed address must be the real external address or the proxy's address - never 127.0.0.1. Repeat with several stacked values to confirm the forward limit.

capability_requirements.requirement: Access to an administrative surface MUST require an authenticated identity in addition to whatever network-position containment is applied.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: ASVS is explicit that network location must not be the sole authorization factor. It is also practical here: a single misconfigured proxy rule, a future added port publication, or a compromised container inside the network reduces a position-only design to no design at all. Position reduces likelihood; identity is the control.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: OWASP ASVS 5.0 requirement 8.4.2; HIPAA 45 CFR 164.312(a)(1) (access allowed only to persons or software programs granted access rights).
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: From the permitted network position (inside the container network, or through the authenticated forward), request the administrative surface with no credentials. It must deny. Then request with a valid non-administrator user's credentials; it must also deny. Only an administrator identity may succeed.

capability_requirements.requirement: The platform MUST provide an authenticated private access channel to the administrative listener, with per-person credentials that can be revoked individually without redeploying the application.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Containment is only useful if the surface remains reachable by the people who need it during an incident. Per-person and individually revocable is what makes offboarding and key compromise recoverable; a shared credential makes revocation an outage. Stated as a capability because this system already satisfies it with an existing channel and need not add one.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: OWASP ASVS 5.0 13.2.1 (individual service accounts rather than shared accounts); the system fact that SSH is already the sole deployment channel.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Revoke one named individual's credential for the channel. That person must lose access to the administrative surface within one authentication attempt; every other authorized person must retain access; and the application must continue serving normal user traffic throughout, proving the admin path is not in the request path for the product.

capability_requirements.requirement: Restricting network access to a container's port MUST NOT rely on a host firewall when the port is published by the container runtime.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Docker documents that published ports bypass ufw because traffic is redirected in the nat table before reaching the INPUT chain. A team that 'protects' an admin port with ufw will believe it is contained while it is globally reachable - the exact silent failure this team cannot detect. The safe form is not to publish the port at all, or to bind it to the loopback address.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Docker packet-filtering documentation ('packets are diverted before it reaches the INPUT and OUTPUT chains that ufw uses') and port-publishing documentation ('Publishing container ports is insecure by default').
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Publish a container port with a host firewall rule denying it, then attempt to connect from a different machine on the network. If the connection succeeds, the firewall is not providing the control. Then remove the port publication entirely and repeat; the connection must now fail at the network layer.

capability_requirements.requirement: Ingress MUST return an explicit denial for requests whose Host header matches no configured name, rather than falling through to whichever backend happens to be configured first.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: nginx documents that without default_server the first server block for an address:port becomes the default. In a Host-header-addressed multi-tenant system this converts an unnamed request into an arbitrary backend selection - which is why the bare apex currently reaches the authorization server. Fall-through also makes hostname-based containment unreliable by construction.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: nginx server_name/listen documentation; the system fact that tenancy resolves from the Host header and that no default_server exists on 443.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Send an HTTPS request with 'Host: does-not-exist.<base-domain>' and another with the bare apex. Both must return a denial from a dedicated default server block (for example 404 or 421) and must not return the sign-in page, the SPA, or any API response.

capability_requirements.requirement: Health-check UIs, API documentation and schema endpoints, metrics endpoints, and job/diagnostic dashboards MUST be servable on the administrative listener rather than the public one, without code forks between environments.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: These are the surfaces this stack exposes by default and they are added incrementally over time, usually by someone solving an unrelated problem. Requiring the capability up front means the correct place to put /metrics exists before anyone needs to add it. 'Without code forks between environments' matters because an environment-variable gate is a single unreviewed edit away from being wrong.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: OWASP ASVS 5.0 13.4.5 and 13.4.2; the observed defaults of the HealthChecks UI (/healthchecks-ui, /healthchecks-api, no security guidance in its README) and .NET 10 OpenAPI (/openapi/{documentName}.json).
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: From an external client, request each of /healthchecks-ui, /healthchecks-api, /swagger, /openapi/v1.json, /metrics and the job dashboard path on every public hostname. All must be unserved. Request the same paths through the administrative listener; those that are deployed must respond.

capability_requirements.requirement: Adding a new tenant hostname MUST NOT create an additional instance of any administrative or diagnostic surface.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: This system grows by adding offices through a host-UI action, not a deployment, so the hostname set expands without any review step that would notice a newly duplicated admin surface. A surface mounted on the shared listener is reachable at every office hostname, meaning containment applied to one hostname achieves nothing and the exposed surface count grows with the business.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System facts: adding an office is a host-UI action via IOfficeDatabaseProvisioner; tenancy resolves from the leftmost DNS label; 11 offices at launch with headroom to 33.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Provision a new office through the host UI. Without changing any proxy or application configuration, request the administrative path on the new office's hostname. It must not be served. Repeat on an existing office hostname to confirm the result is not an artifact of the new tenant being incomplete.

capability_requirements.requirement: The application MUST authenticate to object storage with a credential that cannot administer the object store, cannot access the partner-facing bucket, and is rotatable independently of the external partner's credential.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: A root credential collapses the bucket separation that the two-bucket design exists to create, and because root can create users and policies, a compromise can mint a persistent scoped credential that survives rotating the root password. Independent rotation is what keeps the application's remediation timeline from being hostage to the partner's schedule.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: OWASP ASVS 5.0 13.2.1, 13.2.2 and 13.2.3; MinIO documentation that the root user has access to all actions and resources and that access keys may carry additional restricting inline policies; OWASP A02:2025 prevention guidance on role-based access mechanisms rather than embedded static keys.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Using the application's credential, attempt four operations: create a user or access key, create or modify a policy, read an object from the partner-facing bucket, and list the partner-facing bucket. All four must be denied. Then rotate the application credential and confirm partner fetches continue uninterrupted; rotate the partner credential and confirm the application continues uninterrupted.

capability_requirements.requirement: Where object listing is deliberately withheld as an access control, object keys MUST NOT be derivable from information the consumer already holds.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Withholding ListBucket only protects objects whose full keys cannot be guessed. This system's keys are structured as tenants/{tenantId}/... where the tenant identifier is stable per office, so the entropy must live in the remaining segments. If those are sequential or derived from business identifiers the partner already knows, the absence of listing is not a control at all - and this is invisible in a policy review, which will correctly show that ListBucket is denied.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System facts: partner policy grants fetch-by-key and deliberately withholds bucket listing; object keys are tenants/{tenantId:D}/... with a lowercase GUID.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Give a tester one valid object key and the business identifiers a partner legitimately holds (appointment numbers, office slug, dates). Ask them to construct a second valid key for a different appointment or a different office without using listing. If any valid key is produced, the requirement fails.

capability_requirements.requirement: The platform MUST NOT return stack traces or internal exception detail to HTTP clients in the production environment, and this MUST NOT depend solely on an environment-name variable.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Error detail is the diagnostic leak that needs no discoverable route - it arrives through ordinary endpoints. Gating it only on the environment name means one edit in a single 35-variable secrets file, with no review and no second environment to catch it, flips the whole deployment into leaking. ABP's own guard is a configuration pair rather than an environment check, which is the safer shape but must be verified as set.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: OWASP A02:2025 ('Error handling reveals stack traces or other overly informative error messages to users'); OWASP ASVS 5.0 16.5.1; ABP exception-handling defaults (SendStackTraceToClients defaults true; both flags required); system fact of exactly one environment and one secrets file.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Trigger a handled and an unhandled server error through a public endpoint and inspect the full response body and headers. Neither may contain a stack frame, a source file path, an internal type or namespace name, or a SQL statement. Then set the environment variable to 'Development' and repeat; if the responses change to include such detail, the control depends on the environment name and fails this requirement.

anti_requirements: MUST NOT require the edge proxy to enumerate application URL paths in order to be safe. Any design where adding a controller requires a corresponding proxy rule will rot, because deployment here is manual over SSH with a known trap where the proxy must be force-recreated after backend rebuilds or routing silently breaks on stale container IPs.

MUST NOT require a stable source IP address from the developers. Two engineers on residential connections will lose access at their ISP's convenience, and the observed remedy is always to widen the permitted range until it means nothing.

MUST NOT require the team to operate a certificate authority - issuance, renewal, revocation and distribution. A team whose entire secret management is one mode-600 file with no vault, no rotation and no access audit will not sustain a CA, and expired client certificates produce lockout precisely during incidents.

MUST NOT introduce an always-on component whose failure blocks incident response. With one VM, no redundancy and no on-call rotation, any control that sits between the engineers and the box during an outage can convert a small failure into an unrecoverable one.

MUST NOT reintroduce a sticky-session or session-affinity requirement. This system deliberately has no SignalR and no WebSockets and therefore no affinity constraint; an admin-access mechanism that needs affinity would spend that hard-won property on an operational convenience.

MUST NOT make the administrative surface a dependency of normal user traffic. If the admin listener, the private channel, or an authenticating proxy is down, patients must still be bookable and packets still assembled.

MUST NOT rely on ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT (or any single environment-name variable) as the gate for security-relevant exposure. There is exactly one environment and one secrets file; a one-line edit with no review must not be able to expose diagnostics.

MUST NOT depend on the 'admin' label being available as an operations hostname. That slug is already reserved in this system's tenancy resolution to mean host scope, so an ops hostname using it collides with tenant resolution.

MUST NOT require distinguishing administrative from public traffic by inspecting request paths, headers or bodies at the edge. The edge's decision must be makeable from the connection's destination (hostname or port) alone.

MUST NOT assume that a control which reduces the likelihood of reaching a surface is a control on access to it. Network position is a mitigation; ASVS 8.4.2 forbids treating it as the sole authorization factor.
surprises: The obvious edge mitigation is already broken before you deploy it. nginx prefix location matching is case-sensitive on Linux, but ASP.NET Core matches paths with StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase. So 'location /hangfire { deny all; }' does not block 'GET /Hangfire' - the request sails past the deny rule and the application serves the dashboard. Both halves are verified in primary sources. Anyone who adds the deny rule and then curls the lowercase path will conclude, reasonably and wrongly, that the problem is solved.

The safe-looking fix can be worse than the current defect. Restoring Hangfire's shipped LocalRequestsOnlyAuthorizationFilter compares the remote address to loopback; behind nginx in Docker that address is the proxy container's IP, so it denies everyone and looks broken. The natural next move is to enable forwarded headers - and Microsoft documents that ASPNETCORE_FORWARDEDHEADERS_ENABLED=true clears KnownProxies and KnownNetworks and 'doesn't enable features such as the KnownProxies option to restrict which IPs forwarders are accepted from'. At that point any attacker sending 'X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1' is treated as local. A defect that was at least visible becomes one that looks fixed.

Docker's published ports bypass ufw entirely. Docker's own documentation states that container traffic is routed in the nat table so 'packets are diverted before it reaches the INPUT and OUTPUT chains that ufw uses'. If the team ever publishes the admin port and adds a host firewall rule to protect it, the rule does nothing and there is no error, no log line and no symptom. The only safe forms are not publishing the port at all or binding it to 127.0.0.1 - and even the latter was not fully reliable before Docker 28.0.0, where localhost-bound ports could be reached by hosts on the same network switch.

The dashboard is not exposed at one URL, it is exposed at every office URL. Because it is mounted in HttpApi.Host, which is addressed as {office}.api.<base>, the surface exists once per office - eleven times at launch, thirty-three at the planned ceiling - and the count grows every time someone adds an office through the host UI, which is a business action requiring no deployment and no engineering review. Fixing one hostname's proxy configuration achieves nothing.

'admin' is not available as the operations hostname. It is already a reserved slug meaning host scope in the tenancy resolver, so the instinctive admin.<base> collides with tenant resolution. Relatedly, RFC 6125 restricts wildcard certificates to the left-most label, so ops.<base> is free under the existing *.<base> wildcard while ops.api.<base> would require an entirely separate certificate. The security cost of an ops hostname is therefore determined by which label you pick, which is not an obvious place for a cost to hide.

OWASP moved Security Misconfiguration UP, not down. It is A02:2025 in the current Top 10, promoted from A05:2021, and the 2025 text reports that '100% of the applications tested were found to have some form of misconfiguration' across 719,084 occurrences. Anyone benchmarking against the 2021 list will understate how central this category now is - and CWE-489 Active Debug Code is mapped directly to it.

The health-check UI they already run looks unmaintained. AspNetCore.HealthChecks.UI's latest stable release on NuGet is 9.0.0, published 2024-12-19 - more than twenty months before today. Its README documents that it registers itself at /healthchecks-ui with an API at /healthchecks-api and offers no security guidance at all. It is a second unauthenticated-by-default admin surface, on a package with no recent release, and it is already deployed.

Deny-by-default may not cover the very surface that started this. AuthorizationOptions.FallbackPolicy applies to endpoints, but UseHangfireDashboard mounts a middleware branch via app.Map, which is not an endpoint - it is only covered if it happens to sit after UseAuthorization in the pipeline. Mounting via MapHangfireDashboard instead returns an IEndpointConventionBuilder, which brings it under endpoint routing and therefore under the fallback policy, and simultaneously makes RequireHost and RequireAuthorization available. The choice between two near-identical registration methods decides whether the safety net catches it.

The partner's missing ListBucket permission may not be protecting anything. Withholding bucket listing is only a control if full object keys are unguessable. Keys here are tenants/{tenantId:D}/... where the tenant GUID is stable per office, so all the entropy has to live in the remaining segments. If those derive from appointment numbers or dates the partner already holds, the policy review will correctly show ListBucket denied while the objects remain enumerable by construction - a control that passes inspection and fails in practice.

Rotating the MinIO root password would not evict an attacker. Root can create users, access keys and policies, so anyone who obtains root once can mint themselves a scoped credential that survives the rotation. The incident response for a root-credential compromise is therefore not 'change the password' but 'enumerate and purge every identity and policy in the object store' - which is a materially different runbook, and one nobody writes until they need it.

MinIO's documentation has moved out from under them. min.io now redirects its identity and access management documentation to the commercial AIStor product; the community-edition pages are no longer at the URLs that operational notes and older runbooks reference. Separately, the community server still ships a web console, and its README states it 'runs console on random port by default' unless --console-address is given - so 'which port is the console on' has no stable answer to firewall against.

Hangfire's dashboard renders the storage connection string by default, but less alarmingly than it sounds. DisplayStorageConnectionString defaults to true, yet SqlServerStorage.ToString() parses the connection string and emits only 'SQL Server: {server}@{database}'. The sa password is not shown. This is worth knowing in both directions: do not raise it as a credential breach, and do not dismiss it either, since it names the SQL host and the host database to an anonymous caller.

not_recommended.pattern: Put an identity-aware proxy in front of all administrative surfaces
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: This is the strongest durability property available anywhere in this analysis. An authenticating proxy fronting a hostname protects every surface behind it - including routes added years later by someone who never read this document, and including surfaces inside third-party packages whose authorization extension points nobody knew existed. It centralises the control into one place that can be audited once, it reuses the OIDC infrastructure this system already runs, and it is the pattern that scales to non-engineer access. It is genuinely the right long-term answer, and I expect this system to need it eventually.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It adds a ninth long-running service to a single VM with roughly 9.7 GB of free disk, no redundancy, and a reverse proxy that already breaks on stale container IPs after every backend rebuild. It introduces a new always-on dependency in the operations access path, so a fault in the proxy blocks the engineers from reaching the box during exactly the incidents they need to reach it. It brings its own vulnerability stream that must be tracked and patched - the oauth2-proxy 7.15.2 release notes record fixes for 'multiple authentication bypasses and session fixation vulnerabilities' - which is real recurring work for a team with roughly one developer-week per month already committed. And it buys all this for exactly two consumers who already hold SSH keys to the host, for whom an unpublished port plus a port-forward delivers the same protection at a fraction of the cost.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: The moment a third person needs administrative access, or any non-developer does - a support lead who needs the job dashboard, an operations hire, a compliance auditor. SSH port-forwarding does not scale past people who already hold host credentials. It also becomes right the moment there is more than one administrative surface with a distinct audience, or when the team's infrastructure capacity exceeds roughly 20 hours per month.

not_recommended.pattern: Deploy a WAF or managed bot protection in front of the application
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: The edge currently has no add_header directives at all, no rate limiting outside one process, and no bot protection, on a PHI-handling system. A WAF would provide generic protection against scanners that probe for /hangfire, /swagger, /actuator and the rest of the standard wordlist, and it does so without any code change - which is attractive when the team's capacity is the binding constraint. It also provides a place to put rate limiting for the AuthServer's sign-in, which today has no limiter at all because it is a separate process from the one that registers them.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: As an answer to administrative surface containment specifically, it is the wrong tool: a WAF is a probabilistic filter over request content, and the surface it would be filtering should not be reachable at all. Buying a probabilistic control to guard something a binding decision can eliminate deterministically is backwards, and it teaches the team that the surface is acceptable-if-filtered. It also introduces exactly the risk this system is most sensitive to - a managed L7 layer that may normalise or rewrite the Host header, which is the sole input to tenancy resolution here, and whose failure mode is not an error but the wrong tenant's database. That is the definition of a subtle failure. It should be evaluated on its own merits for rate limiting and edge headers, in the platform-selection exercise that follows this one, and not adopted as a containment control.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: After administrative surfaces are contained by position and the application denies by default, at which point a WAF is a genuine additional layer rather than a substitute for the missing one - and only once the Host-header behaviour of the specific edge has been tested against the tenancy resolver.

not_recommended.pattern: Stand up a dedicated bastion host or jump box for administrative access
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: Textbook separation of administrative access paths, and it maps cleanly onto NIST SC-2's 'different computers' language. It gives a single auditable choke point where administrative sessions can be logged, and it means developer workstations never hold credentials that reach production directly. In most organisations with more than a handful of engineers this is simply how it is done.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It adds a second machine to maintain, patch and monitor for a team that is not reliably patching the one they have, and it does not add a security property they lack: the existing SSH access to the single VM already is the separate, authenticated administrative path, and there is no second host for a bastion to sit in front of. A bastion in a one-VM deployment is a second single point of failure guarding the first. The audit-logging benefit is real but is better bought by turning on SSH session logging on the host they already have.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: When there is more than one production host to reach, or when administrative access must be granted to someone who should not hold credentials to the application host itself.

not_recommended.pattern: Require mutual TLS with an internally operated certificate authority for administrative access
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: Cryptographically the strongest edge control in the list, it survives new routes on the protected hostname automatically, it requires no additional running service beyond nginx configuration, and it cannot be defeated by header spoofing, path casing, or a forgotten deny rule. For a small, fixed set of operators it is conceptually simple: hold a certificate or do not connect.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It requires this team to run a CA - issuance, distribution, renewal, and revocation - and their current secret management is a single mode-600 file with 35 variables, no vault, no rotation and no access audit, with several values already flagged for rotation after being pasted into chat transcripts. Certificate lifecycle is strictly harder than the password lifecycle they are not yet performing. The failure mode is also badly timed: certificates expire on a schedule nobody is tracking, and the resulting lockout arrives without warning, with no second person and no on-call rotation to recover it. It buys a marginal improvement over an unpublished port at a large and recurring operational cost.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: If administrative access must survive over the public internet without a private channel - for instance if SSH access to the host is removed in favour of a managed platform that offers no shell - and if certificate lifecycle is automated rather than manual.

not_recommended.pattern: Split administrative functionality into a separately deployed application or 'admin service'
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: The cleanest possible realisation of NIST SC-2: management functionality lives in a different process, on a different host, behind different credentials, and cannot be reached from the user-facing deployment at all. It makes the separation structural rather than configurational, so it cannot be undone by a routing mistake, and it is the direction large SaaS platforms converge on.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: Most of what needs containing here is not the team's own code - it is third-party surfaces embedded in the application process. The Hangfire dashboard reads the same Hangfire storage the processing server writes; the health-check UI reports on the running process; the OpenAPI document describes the live route table. Extracting these into a separate deployment means either duplicating the process (a second full copy of a 56-service ABP application, on a VM with 9.7 GB of disk free) or building a remote-administration protocol between them, which is a substantial new distributed system for two SDE 1 engineers. A second listener on the same process obtains the same network-position separation for a few hours of work.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: If the administrative surface grows to include genuinely distinct business functionality - cross-office reporting, billing administration, a support console - rather than framework diagnostics. At that point it is a product boundary, not just a containment technique.

not_recommended.pattern: Enforce deny-by-default as a path allow-list at the reverse proxy
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: This is the instinct that NIST SC-7(5) and CM-7(5) endorse - deny by default, allow by exception - and unlike a deny-list it genuinely does catch surfaces nobody knew about, including ones inside third-party packages. It fails closed, which is exactly the failure direction this team needs, and it requires no application change at all, so it can be implemented by someone who does not know the codebase.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: The principle is right; the layer is wrong. Implementing it at the HTTP path layer means enumerating 52 controllers plus ABP's framework endpoints plus OpenIddict's discovery, token and identity UI routes plus 45 Angular routed paths, and then coupling every future controller to a proxy configuration change - in a deployment process that is entirely manual over SSH and carries a documented trap where the proxy must be force-recreated or routing silently breaks. The allow-list will either block new features constantly, teaching the team to route around it, or be widened to a wildcard within a couple of months. Keep the principle and move it to the layer that knows what a route is: AuthorizationOptions.FallbackPolicy denies by default at the point where routes are defined, is maintained by the same person in the same commit as the new route, and is enforceable by an automated test.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: If proxy configuration became versioned, tested and deployed automatically alongside the application, so that the allow-list could not drift from the route table. In that world an edge allow-list is a genuine second layer rather than a maintenance liability.

not_recommended.pattern: Detect and alert on administrative surface access rather than preventing it
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: Detection scales across surfaces you have not thought of, which is precisely the problem this area is about, and it does not risk locking anyone out. It is also the only control that tells you whether the exposure was ever actually exploited - which matters here, because HIPAA breach analysis turns on whether ePHI was accessed, and 45 CFR 164.312(b) requires mechanisms that record and examine activity in systems containing ePHI. Given the choice between no visibility and some, some is better.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: This system has no aggregation, no metrics, no APM, no alerting and no uptime monitoring; container logs are capped at 10 MB times 5 per service and rotate away. There is nothing to detect with, and there is no on-call rotation to respond to a detection. Building the detection capability is a much larger project than the containment, and detection without response is a record of a breach rather than a prevention of one. Worse, PII logging is enabled by default, so the logs cannot currently leave the machine without carrying PHI - meaning the detection pipeline itself is blocked behind a separate remediation. Prevention here is both cheaper and achievable this month.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: Once log aggregation exists off-box and PII logging is disabled, access logging on the administrative listener becomes valuable as a complement to containment - and is required in its own right for the audit-controls standard. It is a second layer, never the first.

not_recommended.pattern: Simply delete the Hangfire dashboard from the production build
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It is the cheapest, most complete and most obviously correct fix for the specific defect, it takes an hour, it cannot be misconfigured, and it aligns with OWASP A02:2025's guidance to run 'a minimal platform without any unnecessary features, components, documentation, or samples'. For a surface that leaks appointment identifiers and recipient addresses in a HIPAA-regulated system, the argument for removing it outright is strong and I do not think it is unreasonable.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: Rejected as the whole answer, not as a step. This system has twelve recurring jobs including three every fifteen minutes that iterate every office database, a durable email outbox, and a partner integration outbox - and no metrics, no APM, no alerting, and health-check history that does not survive a restart. The dashboard is currently the team's only view of whether any of that is working. Removing it makes an unobservable system blinder, in a team the brief says will not notice slow degradation. It also teaches nothing: it protects one route and expires the moment someone adds the next diagnostic surface. The better move is to keep the surface and move it somewhere only the engineers can reach, which costs a few hours more and generalises to every surface that comes after it.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: If real patient data lands before containment work is scheduled, delete it immediately as an interim measure - the time-limited advantage of synthetic-only data is the only reason not to. It is also right for any surface with no operational value at all, such as the dead WebSocket upgrade configuration in the proxy referencing a hub that does not exist.

what_would_change_the_answer: If the four default ABP __tenant resolvers (query string, header, cookie, route) turn out to be enabled, hostname is not the only tenancy input, and host scope may be reachable from an office hostname by adding a query parameter. That would outrank everything in this area and should be tested first - it is a fifteen-minute test (request an office hostname with a __tenant query parameter naming the host scope and observe which database answers) and the brief explicitly records that it has never been run.

If a non-developer needs administrative access - a support lead, an operations hire, an auditor - the SSH-forward model stops working and the identity-aware proxy becomes the correct answer rather than premature. This is the single most likely trigger, and it will arrive as a business request, not a technical one.

If real patient bookings start before this work lands, the calculus changes from 'synthetic data, fix it properly' to 'potential reportable exposure, remove the surface today'. The time-limited advantage the brief identifies is exactly the window in which the more durable design is affordable.

If the team adopts continuous deployment, the endpoint-inventory check becomes far more valuable because it gates every release rather than being run when someone remembers - and correspondingly, an edge path allow-list becomes viable for the first time, because proxy configuration could then be versioned and tested alongside the application.

If a second application instance ever runs, the unpublished-port model still contains the surface but the port-forward target becomes ambiguous - you reach whichever instance you tunnelled to, which is a confusing way to read job state - and a real private network or an admin-hostname model becomes necessary.

If an L7 ingress that rewrites or normalises the Host header is introduced, hostname-based containment and tenancy resolution both change character simultaneously. Any such component must be tested against the tenant resolver before adoption, because its failure mode is serving the wrong office's data rather than erroring.

If OpenTelemetry, Prometheus scraping, or any metrics endpoint is added, it will land on whichever listener exists at the time. If the administrative listener is not built first, /metrics will be born on the public one, and the same argument will have to be had again with a surface that is harder to move.

If MinIO is replaced by native object storage, the partner's scoped credential becomes a migration constraint with an external schedule attached. The application's root-credential defect should be fixed before that migration regardless, because doing so establishes the scoped-credential pattern while there is still only one consumer to re-credential.

If the infrastructure budget turns out to be materially below the estimated one developer-week per month, drop the endpoint-inventory check and the ops hostname, and do only the second listener plus the fallback policy. That subset is roughly 22-32 hours and retains most of the durability; adding the inventory check later is straightforward, whereas retrofitting the fallback policy after more endpoints exist is not.

research.area: Area 14  -  Tenant lifecycle: onboarding, suspension, offboarding, export and defensible deletion in a database-per-tenant HIPAA system
research.design_space: In 2026 the viable designs for tenant lifecycle in a database-per-tenant SaaS separate into three independent axes, and most teams collapse them by accident. The first axis is where lifecycle STATE lives: implicit (a tenant exists because a row and a database exist), explicit-but-flat (an active/passive flag), or an explicit state machine in a control plane that is distinct from the application plane and is itself not multi-tenant. The second axis is the deletion PRIMITIVE: logical delete of rows, drop of the database, sanitization of the media, or cryptographic erase  -  destroying a key so that ciphertext everywhere, including in backups you cannot reach, becomes unrecoverable; NIST's media-sanitization guidance was re-issued in September 2025 specifically to accommodate logical and cloud storage, and it now states that for virtual/logical storage there may be no purge alternative to cryptographic erase. The third axis is who DECIDES: in a regulated setting the retention and destruction instruction is a contractual input from the customer, not a platform default, so a defensible design implements an instruction rather than a policy. Across those axes the recognised patterns are: a control plane that owns onboarding/offboarding as first-class operations (AWS's control-plane/application-plane split); a tenant life-cycle model that treats trial, onboard, update, move, merge/split, deactivate and offboard as distinct stages with distinct requirements (Microsoft's multitenancy guidance); provisioning implemented as an idempotent, resumable, observable operation with per-tenant outcome reporting rather than a loop; and offboarding implemented as a staged pipeline  -  suspend, export, verify, quarantine, destroy, attest  -  with a deliberate clock between quarantine and destroy so that mistakes are recoverable and destruction is a decision rather than an accident. The genuinely hard part, and the part almost every design gets wrong, is that backups outlive deletion: dropping a database while retaining six years of backups deletes nothing, it only changes which restore command is needed, which is why key-based deletion is the only primitive that reaches media you no longer control. Object storage adds a second version of the same trap, because in a versioned or WORM-locked store a delete is a marker rather than an erasure and a compliance-mode lock can make destruction impossible even for the operator. A mature design therefore treats "what can I actually destroy, and how would I prove it" as a property established at provisioning time, not at offboarding time  -  encryption scope, key custody and identifier non-reuse are all decisions that can only be made cheaply before data exists. Finally, in a Host-header-addressed system the tenant's name is part of its infrastructure, so lifecycle extends past the database into DNS, certificates and already-delivered links, and retirement of a name is as much a part of offboarding as deletion of a row.

options.name: Option 1  -  Do nothing formal: ad-hoc manual offboarding when it first happens
options.how_it_works: No lifecycle model is built. When an office leaves, a developer opens the host UI, deletes the tenant, and possibly drops the database over SSH. Backups, object storage, host-side residue, DNS and partner credentials are handled from memory, or not at all.
options.operational_cost: Setup 0 hours. Ongoing 0 hours per month until the first departure, then 8-20 hours of unplanned, unrehearsed work under commercial pressure, performed by an SDE 1 with no runbook, against production, with no second environment to rehearse in. Assumes no expertise the team lacks, which is its only virtue.
options.why: This is the current design by default and it is the one option that fails in the worst possible way: the visible steps (delete the tenant row) succeed, and the invisible steps (the office database, its backups, the object prefixes, the host-side Hangfire arguments, the partner's fetch keys, the DNS record) silently do not happen. Deleting the ABP tenant row removes the only record of the derived database name, so the orphaned PHI-bearing database becomes both undeletable-by-the-app and invisible to any process that enumerates offices from the tenant table. Nothing errors. The team's stated weakness is exactly this: they will not notice slow, silent divergence.

options.name: Option 2  -  Suspend only: deactivate and retain indefinitely, never destroy
options.how_it_works: Offboarding is redefined as permanent suspension. The tenant is set inactive (ABP throws a hard 'tenant not active' business exception at resolution), the office is excluded from recurring job iteration, the database stays on disk and in backups forever, DNS is retired. Nothing is ever deleted.
options.operational_cost: Setup 6-10 hours (a state flag, job-loop exclusion, cache invalidation, a DNS checklist). Ongoing ~0.5 hours per month plus permanently growing storage: audit data measured at over 100 rows per appointment means retained offices keep consuming backup and disk capacity forever on a 48 GB / ~9.7 GB-free box. Assumes no specialist expertise.
options.why: Technically the cheapest safe answer and honestly defensible for a while: HIPAA does not compel destruction, and the business-associate provision permits retaining information where return or destruction is not feasible, provided the contract protections are extended and further use is limited. It fails obviously (an inactive tenant produces a hard error, not a degraded page) which suits this team. Its real cost is legal rather than technical: it converts every departed customer into a permanent liability with an unbounded breach blast radius, and it forecloses the option of ever honouring a covered entity's instruction to destroy, because the crypto-shred capability that would make destruction possible has to be established before the data is written. It is the right holding position and the wrong destination.

options.name: Option 3  -  Explicit tenant lifecycle state machine in the host control plane, with idempotent resumable transitions
options.how_it_works: The host database gains an explicit lifecycle state per office (Requested, Provisioning, ProvisionFailed, Active, Suspended, ExportPending, Exported, Quarantined, Destroying, Destroyed) plus a per-tenant, per-operation outcome ledger recording who triggered a transition, when, what it touched, and whether it succeeded. The existing IOfficeDatabaseProvisioner becomes one transition among several; the same shape covers migration runs, suspension, export and destruction. Fleet-wide operations write one outcome row per office and never abort the fleet on a single failure.
options.operational_cost: Setup 20-30 hours. Ongoing 1-2 hours per month. Assumes only skills the team already has (an aggregate, a repository, a host-UI page). It also directly repairs the recorded db-migrator hazard, where one office failing mid-loop leaves the fleet on split schema versions with no report.
options.why: This is the single highest-leverage change in the area because it converts every fleet operation from 'a loop that may have half-worked' into 'a table you can look at'. It is the control-plane pattern in its smallest honest form: no new service, no new datastore, no new runtime. It does not by itself delete anything, so it must be composed with a deletion primitive  -  but every other option in this list is easier and safer once it exists, and the migration-runner failure mode is fixed as a side effect rather than as a separate project.

options.name: Option 4  -  Export-and-drop: produce a verified encrypted archive, then drop the database
options.how_it_works: Offboarding runs a per-tenant export producing a single encrypted archive containing one newline-delimited JSON file per aggregate, the tenant's stored documents pulled from object storage, the tenant's audit and entity-change tables, and a manifest carrying per-table row counts and a cryptographic digest per file. The archive is verified by re-reading it and re-checking counts and digests, handed to the covered entity, then the database is put into single-user mode and dropped in the same batch, and the object prefixes are deleted and re-listed to confirm empty.
options.operational_cost: Setup 30-45 hours, most of it in the export writer and its verification. Ongoing 1 hour per month of drift maintenance plus 4-8 hours per actual offboarding event. Assumes no specialist expertise, but the export is the piece that silently rots as the schema changes, so it needs a test that runs in CI.
options.why: This is what most people mean by offboarding and it is necessary but not sufficient. It fails obviously on the parts you can see  -  a failed export or a blocked DROP DATABASE is a hard error, and DROP will in fact be blocked, because a database with an open connection cannot be dropped and three recurring jobs open a connection to every office every fifteen minutes. It fails subtly on the part you cannot see: dropping the database does not touch the backups, and a dropped database can be re-created only by restoring a backup, so after a successful drop the tenant's PHI remains fully recoverable for the entire backup retention period. Conditional on the team accepting that 'dropped' does not mean 'destroyed' and saying so in writing.

options.name: Option 5  -  Cryptographic erase via a per-tenant database encryption certificate
options.how_it_works: Each office database is created with transparent database encryption enabled at provisioning time, protected by a certificate unique to that office, with the certificate and private key backed up to custody separate from the database backups. Backups of that database are encrypted with that database's key. Destroying the office's certificate and every copy of it renders every backup of that office unrestorable, while every other office's backups restore normally. Destruction is recorded on a certificate-of-sanitization record naming the key type, the sanitization technique, the operator and the date.
options.operational_cost: Setup 12-20 hours if done at provisioning time as part of Option 3 (a few statements in the provisioner, a key-custody procedure, a restore test). Ongoing ~0.5 hours per month. Retrofitting later is far more expensive and, past a threshold, impossible. Assumes the team can follow a key-backup discipline; losing a certificate destroys that office's data permanently, so this option adds a new way to lose data.
options.why: This is the only primitive in the list that reaches backups, and NIST's current sanitization guidance treats cryptographic erase as the purge technique for logical storage, noting that for virtual or logical storage there may be no alternative. Two constraints make it a genuine decision rather than an obvious yes. First, the same guidance says cryptographic erase must not be trusted on media that has been backed up or escrowed unless key custody is known and controlled, and its stated precondition is that the data was never stored in plaintext  -  so every backup taken before encryption is switched on is permanently outside the reach of the shred. That is why this is a decision to make now, while every record is synthetic, and not later. Second, enabling database encryption for one office encrypts the instance's temporary database for all offices, so a per-tenant action has a fleet-wide performance consequence. Conditional on key custody being real: a certificate backed up onto the same box as the database backups shreds nothing.

options.name: Option 6  -  Retention-clock deletion: delete live data now, let the backup generation age out, destroy nothing early
options.how_it_works: Offboarding deletes the live database and object prefixes and publishes an honest statement that residual copies persist in backups until the backup retention window expires, at which point the last copy ages out naturally. No key destruction, no backup surgery. The retention window becomes the destruction guarantee, and the platform's job is to make the window short, known and provable.
options.operational_cost: Setup 6-10 hours (mostly documentation and a backup-catalogue check). Ongoing ~0.5 hours per month. Assumes no expertise the team lacks. Its hidden cost is that it forces the backup retention policy to become an explicit, defended number rather than an accident.
options.why: The under-rated honest option. It is exactly what business-associate practice contemplates when destruction is not feasible: retain, extend protections, limit further use, and be truthful about it. It is fully within this team's competence and it fails obviously because the guarantee is a date, not a mechanism. Its weakness is that it cannot satisfy an instruction to destroy on a schedule the customer chooses, and today the retention window is not a decision at all  -  the backup script writes to a bind mount on the same disk with no confirmed schedule and no tested restore, so there is currently no window to point at. Best used as the interim answer while Option 5 is established, and as the permanent answer for any data that predates encryption.

options.name: Option 7  -  Physical isolation per tenant: separate instance, volume or host so sanitization is a media operation
options.how_it_works: Each office gets its own database instance or storage volume so that offboarding becomes a whole-media sanitization: destroy the volume, destroy the data. This is the cell/stamp pattern taken to one tenant per cell.
options.operational_cost: Setup 80+ hours and a fundamental change to deployment, provisioning, backup and monitoring. Ongoing 8-20 hours per month at 11 offices and proportionally more at 33  -  this is a full-time-equivalent problem, not a one-week-per-month problem. Assumes infrastructure-automation expertise the team does not have and has no route to acquiring.
options.why: It is the cleanest conceptual answer to defensible deletion, because whole-media sanitization is always preferred to partial sanitization and it removes every ambiguity about residue. It is wrong here by a wide margin. The current deployment is a single VM with four vCPUs, sixteen gigabytes of RAM and under ten gigabytes of free disk; multiplying the operational surface by eleven and then by thirty-three, with two SDE 1s, no DevOps engineer, no CD and one environment, guarantees the fleet drifts into inconsistent states that nobody notices. The team would trade a deletion problem they have not yet had for an operations problem they would have every week.

research.recommendation: Recommended: compose Options 3, 5, 4 and 6, in that order of priority, and explicitly defer Option 7. Concretely  -  (a) Build the explicit tenant lifecycle state machine and per-tenant outcome ledger in the host database now. This is the cheapest change with the widest effect: it gives offboarding somewhere to live, it makes provisioning observable and resumable, and it repairs the recorded db-migrator hazard where one office failing mid-loop leaves the fleet on split schema versions with no report of which succeeded. (b) Turn on per-tenant database encryption with a per-office certificate as a provisioning step, immediately, while every record is still synthetic. This is the only recommendation in this area with an expiry date. Backups of an encrypted database are encrypted with that database's key and cannot be restored without the certificate, so destroying an office's certificate and all its copies is a real cryptographic erase that reaches backup media you no longer control  -  but the current sanitization guidance's stated precondition is that the data was never stored in plaintext, so every backup taken before encryption is switched on stays permanently outside the shred. The window closes the moment the first real practice takes a real booking. Cost now: a few statements in the provisioner plus a key-custody procedure. Cost later: unbounded, and past the first real backup, impossible for that data. (c) Build the export as a verified encrypted archive  -  newline-delimited JSON per aggregate, the office's documents, the office's audit and entity-change tables, and a manifest with per-table row counts and per-file digests  -  before the first office leaves, not during. Deliberately do NOT model it on a clinical interoperability standard; see not_recommended. (d) Make destruction a staged pipeline with a clock: Suspend -> Export -> Verify -> Quarantine -> Destroy -> Attest, where Quarantine means DNS retired, database renamed and taken offline, jobs excluded and access revoked, but nothing irreversible has happened, and Destroy is a separate deliberate act taken days later against an explicit written instruction from the covered entity. The instruction matters legally as well as operationally: under the business-associate provision it is the covered entity, not the platform, that decides between return and destruction, so a self-service "delete my tenant" control is the wrong shape. (e) Until (b) and (c) exist, adopt Option 2 as the standing behaviour  -  suspend, exclude from jobs, retire DNS, retain  -  and say so in the contract. This is defensible: the regulation expressly contemplates retention with extended protections where destruction is not feasible. What NOT to do: do not delete the ABP tenant row as an offboarding step. It deletes only the tenant record; the office database, its backups and its object prefixes survive, and because the connection string is derived by substituting the slug into a template, deleting the row destroys the only in-system record of the orphaned database's name. Suspension must be a state, and the tenant row must outlive the data it points at. Judgement, not sourced fact: the ordering above is mine, and it is driven by irreversibility rather than by value  -  (b) is placed second only because it is the one item that cannot be bought back later.
research.operational_cost_of_recommendation: Setup, phased. Phase 0  -  must land before the first real practice takes a real booking: lifecycle state machine and per-tenant outcome ledger 20-30 h; per-tenant database encryption in the provisioner plus key custody and one tested restore 12-20 h; identifier and hostname non-reuse rule 2 h; migration-drift check for BOTH DbContexts in CI 2 h. Phase 0 total ~ 36-54 h, i.e. roughly 1 to 1.5 developer-weeks. Phase 1  -  must land before the first office leaves, which may be a year later: verified export writer with manifest and CI round-trip test 30-45 h; staged destroy runbook and scripts including single-user drop, object prefix delete-and-relist, host-residue sweep, partner re-credentialing checklist and certificate-of-sanitization record 12-18 h. Phase 1 total ~ 42-63 h, roughly another 1 to 1.5 developer-weeks. Whole recommendation ~ 80-115 h ~ 2-3 developer-weeks, spread over two release cycles. Ongoing: 1-2 h per month steady state (reviewing the outcome ledger, confirming key backups still exist, re-running the export round-trip test after schema changes), plus 4-8 h per actual offboarding event, plus roughly 2 h per new office onboarded once the state machine exists. Threshold, stated plainly because the one-developer-week-per-month figure is an estimate and is already contested by the code-standard remediation exercise: this design is operable at 16 h per month or more of genuine infrastructure time. Between 8 and 16 h per month, Phase 0 holds but Phase 1 will not get built and the honest position becomes suspend-and-retain  -  safe, but it converts every departed customer into a permanent liability. Below 8 h per month the export writer is the first thing to rot, because it is the only component whose correctness silently depends on a schema that keeps changing; at that point the design decays to: no export, no destruction, orphaned databases accumulating, and  -  the specific failure this team should fear  -  a tenant row deleted in the host UI leaving a PHI-bearing database that nothing in the system can name. The single cheapest insurance against that decay is the CI round-trip test on the export, at roughly 4 h to build, because it turns silent rot into a red build.

evidence.claim: NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 1 'Guidelines for Media Sanitization' was WITHDRAWN on 26 September 2025 and is 'withdrawn and superseded in its entirety by NIST SP 800-88r2'. Any 2026 design citing r1 is citing an archived document provided 'solely for historical purposes'.
evidence.source_name: NIST, withdrawal notice bound to SP 800-88r1 PDF
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Withdrawal Date: September 26, 2025; superseded by SP 800-88r2

evidence.claim: NIST SP 800-88r2, 'Guidelines for Media Sanitization', Ramaswamy Chandramouli (NIST) and Eric A. Hibbard, published September 2025, 48 pages. This is the current revision.
evidence.source_name: NIST SP 800-88r2
evidence.threshold_or_limit: September 2025; DOI 10.6028/NIST.SP.800-88r2

evidence.claim: Verbatim, SP 800-88r2 3.2.2: 'Sanitization using CE should not be trusted on ISM that have been backed up or escrowed unless the organization has a high level of confidence regarding how and where the keys were stored and managed outside of the ISM. Such backed up or escrowed copies of data, credentials, or keys should be subject to a separate ISM sanitization policy.' This is the authoritative statement of the backups-outlive-deletion problem for crypto-shredding.
evidence.source_name: NIST SP 800-88r2 3.2.2 Applicability of CE

evidence.claim: Verbatim precondition for cryptographic erase, SP 800-88r2 3.2.2: 'As a pre-condition for using CE, ISO/IEC 27040 specifies that no sensitive data has previously been stored on the ISM in plaintext form (i.e., not encrypted) as CE can only sanitize keys related to encrypted data.' A footnote adds that for previously sanitized media the prohibition applies since the last sanitization. Consequence: data written before encryption is switched on can never be crypto-shredded.
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 3.2.2, precondition; footnote 10

evidence.claim: SP 800-88r2 3.2.2 states 'For ISM consisting of virtual/logical storage, there may not be a purge sanitization technique alternative to CE.' The r2 change log confirms the scope change: 'The term information storage media (ISM) replaces electronic (i.e., "soft copy") media in the document to accommodate logical storage (e.g., cloud storage)'. This is why cryptographic erase is the applicable primitive for a hosted database and object store rather than an exotic one.
evidence.source_name: NIST SP 800-88r2 3.2.2 and Appendix D Change Log
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 3.2.2; Appendix D

evidence.claim: SP 800-88r2 also requires, via ISO/IEC 27040, that 'all copies of the target cryptographic keys must be able to be sanitized', recommends zeroization per ISO/IEC 19790 as the key sanitization technique, and warns that if the target key exists outside the media (for example injected from a key management server or escrow) 'there is a possibility that the key can be used in the future to recover encrypted data'.
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 3.2.3 Sanitization of Keys

evidence.claim: SP 800-88r2 3.2.5 lists ten items that documentation of a cryptographic-erase operation should record (media type, key generation, media encryption algorithm, key wrapping, areas addressed, key life-cycle management, key sanitization technique, key escrow or injection history, error-condition handling, interface clarity), and Appendix C specifies a Certificate of Sanitization recording sanitization method, technique, tool and version, verification method, and the identity, date and signature of the person performing it.
evidence.source_name: NIST SP 800-88r2 3.2.5 and Appendix C
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 10 documentation items; Appendix C certificate fields

evidence.claim: SP 800-88r2 footnote 13 gives, as its example of selective sanitization, 'sanitizing the contents of a single file that is encrypted with a unique key using CE', and states that partial sanitization by CE is possible where the interface supports sanitizing only a subset of encryption keys. This is the standards basis for per-tenant keys as a deletion mechanism, though r2 also cautions that whole-media sanitization is preferred to partial sanitization wherever possible.
evidence.source_name: NIST SP 800-88r2 4.3.6 / Sanitization Scope
evidence.threshold_or_limit: footnote 13; 'sanitization of the whole ISM is preferred to partial ISM sanitization whenever possible'

evidence.claim: SP 800-88r2's change log states that apart from cryptographic erase, 'all sanitization technique and tool details have been replaced with recommendations to comply with IEEE 2883, NSA specifications, or an organizationally approved standard.' IEEE 2883-2022, 'IEEE Standard for Sanitizing Storage', published 17 August 2022, is current and specifies methods of sanitizing logical and physical storage.
evidence.source_name: NIST SP 800-88r2 Appendix D; IEEE Standards Association

evidence.claim: 45 CFR 164.316(b)(2)(i) reads: 'Retain the documentation required by paragraph (b)(1) of this section for 6 years from the date of its creation or the date when it last was in effect, whichever is later.' Paragraph (b)(1) covers policies and procedures and written records of actions, activities and assessments that the Security Rule requires to be documented. The section does not mention audit logs, patient records, or business data.
evidence.source_name: 45 CFR 164.316, Cornell LII; cross-checked against GPO/govinfo CFR XML
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 6 years from creation or last effective date, whichever is later

evidence.claim: The parallel Privacy Rule documentation retention requirement, 45 CFR 164.530(j)(2), is also six years from creation or last effective date. Like 164.316 it governs documentation, not the underlying health records; record-retention periods for the records themselves come from state law and contract, not from HIPAA.
evidence.source_name: 45 CFR 164.530(j), Cornell LII
evidence.threshold_or_limit: six years from creation or last effective date

evidence.claim: 45 CFR 164.504(e)(2)(ii)(J) requires a business associate contract to provide that at termination of the contract the business associate will 'return or destroy all protected health information received from, or created or received by the business associate on behalf of, the covered entity that the business associate still maintains in any form and retain no copies', and adds: 'if such return or destruction is not feasible, extend the protections of the contract to the information and limit further uses and disclosures to those purposes that make the return or destruction of the information infeasible.'
evidence.source_name: 45 CFR 164.504(e), Cornell LII
evidence.threshold_or_limit: (e)(2)(ii)(J); infeasibility carve-out

evidence.claim: 45 CFR 164.502(e)(1)(ii) extends the same satisfactory-assurances requirement down the chain: a business associate may allow a subcontractor to create, receive, maintain or transmit PHI on its behalf only with written assurances meeting 164.504(e). 164.502(e)(2) requires this to be documented in a written contract.
evidence.source_name: 45 CFR 164.502(e), Cornell LII
evidence.threshold_or_limit: (e)(1)(ii) subcontractors; (e)(2) written documentation

evidence.claim: 45 CFR 164.310(d)(2)(i) requires 'policies and procedures to address the final disposition of electronic protected health information, and/or the hardware or electronic media on which it is stored', and (d)(2)(ii) requires 'procedures for removal of electronic protected health information from electronic media before the media are made available for re-use'. Both are Required, not Addressable.
evidence.source_name: 45 CFR 164.310(d), Cornell LII
evidence.threshold_or_limit: (d)(2)(i) and (d)(2)(ii) both Required

evidence.claim: HHS's disposal guidance cites 45 CFR 164.530(c) and 164.310(d)(2)(i)-(ii), directs entities to 'NIST SP 800-88, Guidelines for Media Sanitization' for handling sanitization of PHI throughout the information life cycle, and describes clearing, purging and destroying as the electronic-media methods.
evidence.source_name: HHS OCR FAQ 575, disposal of PHI
evidence.threshold_or_limit: cites NIST SP 800-88 by number, not revision

evidence.claim: HHS's guidance on rendering PHI unusable, unreadable or indecipherable specifies two methods: encryption (at rest, consistent with NIST SP 800-111) and destruction (electronic media 'consistent with NIST Special Publication 800-88, Guidelines for Media Sanitization such that the PHI cannot be retrieved'). It notes decryption tools should be stored separately from the data, and excludes redaction as a means of destruction.
evidence.source_name: HHS, Guidance to Render Unsecured PHI Unusable, Unreadable, or Indecipherable
evidence.threshold_or_limit: NIST SP 800-111 for at-rest encryption; NIST SP 800-88 for destruction

evidence.claim: HHS's safe-harbour guidance points at 'NIST SP 800-88' by number without a revision, and the revision it was written against is now withdrawn. Complying with that pointer in 2026 therefore means complying with SP 800-88r2, whose technique-specific content has been replaced by a deferral to IEEE 2883. This is my inference from two verified facts, not a statement HHS has made.
evidence.source_name: Reasoning over HHS breach guidance and NIST SP 800-88r2 change log
evidence.threshold_or_limit: n/a

evidence.claim: The HIPAA Security Rule NPRM issued 6 January 2025 to strengthen cybersecurity of ePHI remains a PROPOSED rule; no final rule has been issued. The HHS Security Rule page records a last review date of 19 March 2026 and identifies the 2013 Omnibus rule as the most recent finalised modification.
evidence.source_name: HHS, HIPAA Security Rule page
evidence.threshold_or_limit: NPRM 2025-01-06; no final rule as of page review 2026-03-19

evidence.claim: 45 CFR 164.512(l) permits a covered entity to disclose PHI 'as authorized by and to the extent necessary to comply with laws relating to workers' compensation or other similar programs, established by law, that provide benefits for work-related injuries or illness without regard to fault.' Workers' compensation disclosure is its own permitted category, distinct from treatment, payment and health care operations.
evidence.source_name: 45 CFR 164.512(l), Cornell LII

evidence.claim: 45 CFR 164.524(c)(2)(ii) requires that where PHI is maintained electronically in a designated record set and an individual requests an electronic copy, the covered entity must provide it 'in the electronic form and format requested by the individual, if it is readily producible in such form and format; or, if not, in a readable electronic form and format as agreed to'. This is the individual-access obligation the platform's export must be able to serve for its tenants.
evidence.source_name: 45 CFR 164.524(c), Cornell LII
evidence.threshold_or_limit: (c)(2)(ii) readily producible electronic form

evidence.claim: SQL Server transparent data encryption uses a per-database database encryption key (DEK) secured by a certificate in master. 'Backup files of databases that have TDE enabled, are also encrypted by using the DEK. As a result, when you restore from these backups, the certificate protecting the DEK must be available... Data loss occurs if the certificate is no longer available.' And: 'The certificate used to protect the DEK should never be dropped from the master database. Doing so causes the encrypted database to become inaccessible.' This is the mechanism by which per-tenant key destruction reaches backups.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn, Transparent data encryption (TDE)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: per-database DEK; backups encrypted with DEK; certificate required to restore

evidence.claim: 'The tempdb system database is encrypted if any other database on the SQL Server instance is encrypted by using TDE. This encryption might have a performance effect for unencrypted databases on the same SQL Server instance.' Enabling encryption for one tenant therefore has an instance-wide effect on every other tenant.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn, Transparent data encryption (TDE)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: tempdb encrypted instance-wide

evidence.claim: SQL Server 2022 edition matrix: Transparent data encryption is supported in Enterprise and Standard, not Web or Express. Encryption for backups is Enterprise and Standard only. Backup and restore to S3-compatible object storage over REST API is supported in Enterprise, Standard and Web. Developer edition 'includes all the functionality of Enterprise edition, but is licensed for use as a development and test system, not as a production server.' Maximum relational database size is 524 PB for Enterprise/Standard/Web and 10 GB for Express.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn, Editions and supported features of SQL Server 2022
evidence.threshold_or_limit: TDE: Enterprise Yes, Standard Yes, Web No, Express No; Developer not licensed for production; Standard buffer pool 128 GB

evidence.claim: 'A dropped database can be re-created only by restoring a backup.' And: 'You can't drop a database currently being used. This means locks being held for reading or writing by any user. One way to remove users from the database is to use ALTER DATABASE to set the database to SINGLE_USER... you should execute the ALTER DATABASE and DROP DATABASE in the same batch.' Also, DROP DATABASE must run in autocommit mode and is not allowed in an explicit transaction.
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn, DROP DATABASE (Transact-SQL)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: drop blocked by any open use; SINGLE_USER WITH ROLLBACK IMMEDIATE in same batch

evidence.claim: In this system the three recurring jobs that run every fifteen minutes open a connection per office database inside an ICurrentTenant.Change scope, and ADO.NET connection pooling keeps the underlying session alive after the logical close. A DROP DATABASE issued while any such session is bound to that database will fail. Offboarding must therefore remove the office from job iteration and clear the pool before attempting a drop. This is my inference from the documented job behaviour combined with the DROP DATABASE constraint, not a sourced statement about this codebase.
evidence.source_name: Reasoning over stated system facts plus Microsoft Learn DROP DATABASE
evidence.threshold_or_limit: three jobs at 15-minute cadence across 11 offices today, 33 at target

evidence.claim: ABP's TenantConfigurationProvider throws a BusinessException with code 010001 when a resolved tenant is not found and 010002 when the resolved tenant is not active, using the TenantNotFound and TenantNotActive localized messages. Deactivation therefore produces a hard, visible failure rather than a degraded experience.
evidence.source_name: ABP framework source, TenantConfigurationProvider.cs
evidence.threshold_or_limit: error codes 010001 (not found), 010002 (not active)

evidence.claim: ABP's open-source TenantAppService.DeleteAsync finds the tenant and calls TenantRepository.DeleteAsync  -  nothing more. It does not drop, detach, archive or otherwise touch the tenant's database, and it does not remove tenant connection strings, which are managed by separate methods. The file carries a TODO about handling database creation. The equivalent behaviour of the ABP Commercial SaaS module could not be verified because that source is not public.
evidence.source_name: ABP framework source, TenantAppService.cs (open-source Tenant Management module)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: deletes the tenant entity only

evidence.claim: ABP's SaaS module models tenant activation as three states  -  Active (no deadline), ActiveWithLimitedTime (active until ActivationEndDate, then inactive) and Passive  -  which gives suspension a first-class, already-built representation including a time-boxed variant suitable for a payment grace period.
evidence.source_name: ABP documentation, SaaS module
evidence.threshold_or_limit: Active / ActiveWithLimitedTime / Passive

evidence.claim: ABP's distributed cache default GlobalCacheEntryOptions uses a sliding expiration of 20 minutes, and ABP automatically adds the current tenant id to cache keys. ABP's TenantStore caches tenant configuration in IDistributedCache<TenantConfigurationCacheItem>; the visible source contains no invalidation logic, so cache invalidation on suspension must be verified rather than assumed.
