evidence.source_name: ABP documentation, Caching; ABP source TenantStore.cs
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 20-minute default sliding expiration

evidence.claim: ABP's blob storing abstraction implements multi-tenancy at the PROVIDER level, not through a standardised key naming convention: 'All the providers implement multi-tenancy as a standard feature. They isolate BLOBs of different tenants from each other', and the same BLOB name may be reused across tenants. Multi-tenancy can also be disabled for a specific container so its blobs are available to all tenants. Consequently, 'delete the tenants/{id}/ prefix' is a provider-specific assumption that must be verified per container rather than taken as guaranteed.
evidence.source_name: ABP documentation, BLOB Storing
evidence.threshold_or_limit: per-container multi-tenancy can be disabled

evidence.claim: In a versioned bucket a delete does not remove data: 'Performing a DELETE operation on a versioned object creates a 0-byte DeleteMarker as the latest version of that object... The delete marker hides the object. Nothing is actually removed.' Permanent removal requires deleting by version id, or mc rm --versions. The same semantics are specified by the S3 API this store implements.
evidence.source_name: MinIO documentation, Object Versioning; AWS S3 DeleteObjects API reference
evidence.threshold_or_limit: delete without version id = delete marker, data retained

evidence.claim: The S3 multi-object delete request 'can contain a list of up to 1,000 keys that you want to delete', and returns a per-key success or failure result. A prefix deletion over more than 1,000 objects is therefore inherently multi-request and partially-failable, and per-key errors are reported individually rather than failing the request.
evidence.source_name: AWS S3 API Reference, DeleteObjects
evidence.threshold_or_limit: maximum 1,000 keys per DeleteObjects request

evidence.claim: Object locking in COMPLIANCE mode means 'no MinIO AIStor user can modify the object or its settings, including the MinIO AIStor root user', and legal hold protects objects indefinitely until a privileged user lifts it. Versioning is a prerequisite for object locking. A WORM lock adopted to satisfy retention can therefore make a contractual destruction obligation impossible to perform.
evidence.source_name: MinIO documentation, Object Retention / Object Locking
evidence.threshold_or_limit: COMPLIANCE mode: not modifiable even by root until retention expires

evidence.claim: MinIO lifecycle rules support prefix scoping, expiry of noncurrent versions (--noncurrent-expire-days) and expiry of delete markers (--expire-delete-marker), but the scanner is a low-priority background process, so 'the scanner may therefore not detect an object as eligible for a configured transition or expiration lifecycle rule until after the lifecycle rule period has passed.' Lifecycle expiry is therefore eventual and unsuitable as a deletion guarantee with a deadline.
evidence.source_name: MinIO documentation, Object Lifecycle Management
evidence.threshold_or_limit: expiry timing not guaranteed at the rule boundary

evidence.claim: Microsoft's multitenancy guidance treats offboarding as a distinct lifecycle stage with three named considerations  -  retention period ('Determine how long to maintain the customer data. Identify any legal requirements that mandate data destruction after a specific period'), reonboarding ('Decide whether to support reonboarding. Clarify whether the tenant's data remains available during the retention period') and rebalancing  -  and separates it from deactivation, which 'differs from offboarding because it's intended to be a temporary state.'
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Azure Architecture Center, Tenant life cycle considerations in multitenant solutions
evidence.threshold_or_limit: article date 2025-06-13, page updated 2025-10-31

evidence.claim: The recognised SaaS structural pattern separates a control plane  -  'all the functionality and services that are used to onboard, authenticate, manage, operate, and analyze a multi-tenant environment'  -  from the application plane, and notes 'the control plane and its services are not actually multi-tenant... These services are global to all tenants.' The same source explicitly flags provisioning as contested: it places provisioning in the application plane while acknowledging 'Some could argue that this belongs in the control plane.' Note this AWS whitepaper is banner-marked 'for historical reference only'.
evidence.source_name: AWS Whitepaper, SaaS Architecture Fundamentals  -  Control plane vs. application plane
evidence.threshold_or_limit: marked historical reference only

evidence.claim: Starting with EF Core 9, Migrate and MigrateAsync automatically acquire a database-wide lock before applying migrations, and calling them throws when the model has pending changes compared to the last migration (RelationalEventId.PendingModelChangesWarning), with 'dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes' available to detect the condition in CI. EF guidance also says to run migrations as a one-shot deployment job and not to 'make every application replica run migrations from its entrypoint.'
evidence.source_name: Microsoft Learn, Applying Migrations (EF Core)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: EF Core 9+; database-wide migration lock; has-pending-model-changes command

evidence.claim: MITRE ATT&CK T1584.001 documents dangling-DNS subdomain takeover: 'Subdomain hijacking can occur when organizations have DNS entries that point to non-existent or deprovisioned resources. In such cases, an adversary may take control of a subdomain to conduct operations with the benefit of the trust associated with that domain.' The only listed mitigation is pre-compromise, and detection is noted as difficult because the activity occurs outside the target's visibility.
evidence.source_name: MITRE ATT&CK T1584.001, Compromise Infrastructure: Domains
evidence.threshold_or_limit: no effective post-hoc mitigation listed

evidence.claim: Certificate Transparency logs are public and append-only: a log is 'a single, append-only Merkle Tree of submitted certificate and precertificate entries', the system exists so that 'anyone' can audit CA activity, and log operators 'SHOULD NOT impose any conditions on retrieving or sharing data from the log'. A certificate naming a customer's subdomain is therefore permanently and publicly disclosed and cannot be withdrawn at offboarding.
evidence.source_name: RFC 9162, Certificate Transparency Version 2.0
evidence.threshold_or_limit: append-only; entries cannot be removed

evidence.claim: California Civil Code 56.06 deems, among others, 'any business that offers software or hardware to consumers, including a mobile application or other related device that is designed to maintain medical information' and businesses 'organized for the purpose of maintaining medical information' to be providers of health care subject to the Confidentiality of Medical Information Act. This is a California-specific overlay independent of HIPAA. Whether a business-to-business IME scheduling platform falls within it is a legal question requiring counsel, not an engineering determination.
evidence.source_name: California Civil Code 56.06 (Confidentiality of Medical Information Act)
evidence.threshold_or_limit: deemed 'provider of health care' subject to this part only

evidence.claim: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 37(e) applies where electronically stored information 'should have been preserved in the anticipation or conduct of litigation' and is lost because a party failed to take reasonable steps to preserve it; on a finding of prejudice a court may order measures no greater than necessary to cure it, and only on a finding of 'intent to deprive another party of the information's use in the litigation' may it presume the information unfavourable, so instruct a jury, or dismiss or enter default judgment. A scheduled deletion that runs over data under a preservation duty is the failure mode this rule addresses.
evidence.source_name: Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, Rule 37(e), Cornell LII
evidence.threshold_or_limit: 37(e)(2) requires intent for the severest sanctions

evidence.claim: The information-blocking regulations apply to 'actors', defined at 45 CFR 171.102 as a health care provider, a health IT developer of certified health IT, or a health information network / health information exchange  -  the last being an entity that determines, controls or has discretion to administer any requirement, policy or agreement enabling electronic health information exchange among multiple unaffiliated parties for treatment, payment or health care operations. Whether this platform is an actor is a legal question; on its face it is not certified health IT, and workers' compensation disclosure is a separate permitted category from treatment, payment and operations.
evidence.source_name: 45 CFR 171.102, Cornell LII
evidence.threshold_or_limit: three actor categories

evidence.claim: The certified-health-IT EHI export criterion at 45 CFR 170.315(b)(10) requires a user to be able to create an export file with all of a single patient's electronic health information, and a population-level export of all EHI in the system, in an electronic and computable format, executable by identified users or administrators without developer assistance and at a time of the user's choosing, with publicly accessible up-to-date documentation of the export format's structure and syntax. This is a useful template for a defensible export even where the criterion does not legally bind.
evidence.source_name: ASTP/ONC HealthIT.gov, Electronic Health Information Export test method
evidence.threshold_or_limit: single-patient and population export; computable format; published documentation

evidence.claim: The recognised bulk health-data export pattern, FHIR Bulk Data Access (Flat FHIR) v3.0.0 STU 3 on FHIR R4, mandates newline-delimited JSON  -  'The server SHALL support Newline Delimited JSON, but MAY choose to support additional output formats'  -  and an asynchronous kick-off/poll pattern returning 202 Accepted with a Content-Location polling URL, then a completion manifest of file URLs. The file format and the async manifest pattern are worth borrowing even where the FHIR resource model is not.
evidence.source_name: HL7 FHIR Bulk Data Access Implementation Guide
evidence.threshold_or_limit: v3.0.0 STU 3; NDJSON SHALL; 202 + Content-Location + manifest

evidence.claim: In this system the audit data lives inside the tenant database  -  16 appointments produced roughly 1,450 audit-log rows and 2,689 entity property-change rows in one office database  -  so the record of who accessed a departed office's PHI is physically inside the object that offboarding destroys. Any export or destruction design must treat the audit tables as first-class export content, not as system noise. This is my inference from the stated measurement, not an external source.
evidence.source_name: Reasoning over stated system measurements
evidence.threshold_or_limit: ~100:1 audit rows to business rows measured

capability_requirements.requirement: The platform MUST hold an explicit, queryable lifecycle state for every tenant, drawn from a closed set that distinguishes at minimum: being provisioned, provision failed, active, suspended, exported, quarantined, and destroyed. Tenant existence MUST NOT be inferred from the existence of a database or a hostname.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Without an explicit state there is nowhere for offboarding to live, no way to tell a half-provisioned tenant from a healthy one, and no way to distinguish 'suspended' from 'gone'. Every other requirement in this list depends on it.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft multitenancy tenant life-cycle guidance names onboard, deactivate/reactivate and offboard as distinct stages; system fact that adding an office is a host-UI action with no lifecycle model beyond it.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: As an administrator with no prior knowledge of the system, open the host administration UI and list all tenants. Every tenant must show a lifecycle state. Then interrupt a provisioning run (kill the process mid-provision) and re-list: the affected tenant must show a distinct failed or in-progress state, not 'active' and not absent.

capability_requirements.requirement: Every fleet-wide operation that iterates tenants MUST record a per-tenant outcome (tenant identifier, operation, start time, end time, success or failure, error detail) and MUST continue past a failing tenant rather than aborting the remaining tenants.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: The recorded migration-runner behaviour  -  a loop with no per-tenant error handling that leaves the fleet on split schema versions with no report of which succeeded  -  is a silent-divergence failure mode, and silent divergence is precisely what a two-person team will not notice.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System fact: db-migrator loops offices with no per-tenant error handling and produces no report. EF Core guidance to run migrations as a discrete one-shot deployment job.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Deliberately break one non-first tenant (revoke the login used for its database, or rename its database). Run the fleet-wide migration. Assert three things: the process reports a non-zero failure result; the tenants after the broken one in the iteration order were still processed; and a per-tenant outcome record exists for every tenant naming exactly which one failed and why.

capability_requirements.requirement: Tenant provisioning MUST be idempotent and resumable, and MUST perform pre-flight validation before making any change  -  at minimum confirming the slug is well-formed, is not a reserved word, is not in use by any tenant in any lifecycle state including destroyed, that the target database name is free or belongs to this tenant, and that the required schema migrations exist for both database contexts.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Provisioning already claims idempotency; pre-flight is what converts a half-failed provision from a mystery into a refusal. Validating before acting is the difference between an obvious failure and a subtle one.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System fact: ProvisionAsync is idempotent, so retry after partial failure completes; 'admin' is a reserved slug; two DbContexts share a base model so an entity mapped in both needs a migration in both.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Attempt to provision a tenant using the reserved slug, then using the slug of an already-destroyed tenant, then using a slug whose target database already exists and belongs to a different tenant. Each attempt must be refused before any write occurs, with a distinct message. Then run a successful provision twice in a row and confirm the second run makes no changes and reports success.

capability_requirements.requirement: The build pipeline MUST fail when the entity model has changes not represented by a migration, checked independently for BOTH the host and tenant database contexts.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: The stated hazard  -  an entity mapped in both contexts but migrated in only one, surfacing later as an invalid-object-name exception in a newly provisioned office  -  is a provisioning-time failure that a CI check turns into a build-time failure. This is the cheapest conversion of a subtle failure into an obvious one in the whole area.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft EF Core documentation: EF Core 9+ throws on pending model changes and provides 'dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes'; system fact that host and tenant contexts share a model configuration.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Add a property to an entity that is mapped in both contexts, generate a migration for the host context only, and push. The build must fail, and the failure message must name the tenant context. Reverting the model change or adding the missing migration must make the build pass.

capability_requirements.requirement: The platform MUST support suspending a tenant as a reversible state distinct from deletion, and a suspended tenant MUST fail closed with a hard error rather than degrading, partially serving, or falling back to any other tenant's or the host's data.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Suspension is the common case (non-payment, a pause, a dispute) and is far more frequent than deletion. Failing closed and loudly matches the team's stated ability to notice hard errors and inability to notice slow degradation. The fallback clause matters because the system already has a recorded ambient-tenant fallback to the host database.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft guidance that deactivation is a temporary state distinct from offboarding; ABP already models Active / ActiveWithLimitedTime / Passive and raises a tenant-not-active business exception.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Suspend a tenant. From a browser, request that tenant's application hostname, API hostname and auth hostname. Each must return a definite error identifying the tenant as inactive. Confirm no request returns host-scoped or another tenant's data. Then reactivate and confirm normal service resumes with no data loss.

capability_requirements.requirement: Suspension MUST take effect within a stated, tested bound, and the platform MUST document that bound. Any cached tenant configuration, permission or connection-string state MUST be invalidated as part of the suspension transition rather than relied on to expire.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: A suspension that quietly does not apply for twenty minutes is a suspension that failed. The framework's default distributed-cache sliding expiration is twenty minutes and the visible tenant-store source contains no invalidation, so this must be verified for this system rather than assumed.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: ABP caching documentation: default GlobalCacheEntryOptions sliding expiration of 20 minutes; ABP TenantStore caches tenant configuration with no invalidation visible in source.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Make an authenticated request to a tenant to warm the cache. Suspend the tenant. Immediately, and then every ten seconds, repeat the request. Record the elapsed time until the tenant-inactive error first appears. It must be within the documented bound. Repeat with the cache service restarted mid-test to confirm behaviour does not depend on cache contents surviving.

capability_requirements.requirement: A suspended or offboarding tenant MUST be excluded from all recurring background-job iteration, and that exclusion MUST be driven by the same lifecycle state, not by a second list that can drift.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Twelve recurring jobs iterate offices, three of them every fifteen minutes. A suspended tenant that is still swept continues to open database connections, send outbound integration and email traffic on behalf of a customer who is suspended, and blocks any later attempt to drop the database.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System facts: 12 recurring jobs iterate offices, three at 15-minute cadence; a database cannot be dropped while in use (Microsoft DROP DATABASE documentation).
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Suspend a tenant. Wait for at least two full cycles of the fifteen-minute jobs (35 minutes). Then inspect the database server's active sessions and confirm no session is bound to the suspended tenant's database, and inspect the outbound email and integration outboxes and confirm no new rows were created for that tenant.

capability_requirements.requirement: The platform MUST be able to produce, without developer assistance and without writing code at the time of the request, a single self-describing export of one tenant containing all of that tenant's business data, its stored documents, and its audit and entity-change records.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Export is the precondition for both of the outcomes the business-associate provision contemplates. Requiring it to be executable without developer assistance is what stops it decaying into an ad-hoc script that only one person can run and that nobody has run this year. Audit records are named explicitly because in a database-per-tenant design they are inside the thing being deleted.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: 45 CFR 164.504(e)(2)(ii)(J) return-or-destroy obligation; the certified-health-IT EHI export criterion's requirement that users execute exports 'without subsequent developer assistance to operate'; system measurement placing audit rows in the office database.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Give an administrator who has never seen the codebase the documentation and a test tenant. They must produce a complete export unaided. Then verify the export contains at least one file per aggregate root, the tenant's document objects, and the audit and entity-change tables, by cross-checking row counts against direct queries of the tenant database.

capability_requirements.requirement: The export MUST include a manifest recording, for each included file, its name, the table or aggregate it came from, its row or object count, and a cryptographic digest of its contents; and the export process MUST verify the manifest by re-reading the produced archive before the export is marked complete.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: An unverified export is a promise, not a deliverable, and the failure mode  -  a truncated or partially written export accepted as valid, followed by destruction of the source  -  is unrecoverable. Verification converts it into an obvious failure.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: NIST SP 800-88r2's sanitization-assurance model, which separates verification (did the operation do what it claimed) from validation (do we accept it); the EHI export criterion's requirement to publish format documentation.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Produce an export, then corrupt one byte of one file inside the archive and re-run the verification step. It must fail and name the affected file. Then produce an export of a tenant with zero records and confirm the manifest still exists and reports zero counts rather than erroring or producing an empty archive with no manifest.

capability_requirements.requirement: The export MUST be encrypted at rest, and the decryption key MUST NOT be stored alongside the archive or with the credentials needed to retrieve it.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: An export is a complete, portable, de-contextualised copy of one customer's entire PHI holdings  -  the highest-value single artefact the system will ever produce. HHS's guidance conditions the encryption safe harbour on the decryption tools being held separately from the data.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: HHS guidance on rendering PHI unusable, citing NIST SP 800-111 for data at rest and stating decryption tools should be stored separately from the data they decrypt.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Obtain a produced export archive by every route an operator or attacker could reach it (the object store, the host filesystem, the backup target). Attempt to read any PHI from it using only credentials available at that location. This must fail. Then confirm the key material is retrievable only from a distinct store with distinct credentials.

capability_requirements.requirement: Destruction MUST be a staged sequence with an enforced, configurable delay between a reversible quarantine state and any irreversible action, and the irreversible action MUST require an explicit, separately recorded human confirmation naming the tenant.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Deletion is the only operation in the system with no undo. A clock plus a second deliberate act is the standard control for irreversible operations and costs almost nothing to build. It also creates the window in which a mistaken offboarding is recoverable, which for a two-person team with one environment is the difference between an incident and a catastrophe.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft multitenancy guidance on retention period and reonboarding during that period; 45 CFR 164.504(e)(2)(ii)(J), under which the covered entity, not the platform, decides between return and destruction.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Move a test tenant to quarantine. Attempt the destroy action immediately: it must be refused, naming the remaining delay. Confirm that during quarantine the tenant can be restored to suspended state with all data intact. Advance past the delay and attempt destroy without the confirmation input: it must be refused. Supply the confirmation and confirm the action proceeds and is recorded with the operator identity and timestamp.

capability_requirements.requirement: The platform MUST maintain an enumerable map of every store that can hold tenant-scoped data, and the destruction procedure MUST address each entry in that map explicitly with a recorded per-store outcome. At minimum the map must cover: the tenant database, its backups, each object-storage bucket including any partner-facing bucket, host-database residue including background-job payloads, the distributed cache, secrets, DNS records, and any third-party credential scoped to the tenant.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Incomplete deletion is the default outcome of deletion attempted from memory, and every store missed is retained PHI that nobody knows exists. Enumerating the stores in advance is the only way a stranger can check completeness. The partner bucket is called out because an external party holds fetch-by-key credentials with bucket listing deliberately withheld, so its contents cannot be enumerated from the partner side.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System facts: two physical buckets one of which is partner-facing with listing withheld; Hangfire storage on the host connection string with job arguments carrying appointment identifiers and recipient addresses; tenant-prefixed cache keys; a single secrets file.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Ask an engineer who has never seen the system to read the data map and then, for a test tenant, independently search each named store for that tenant's identifier or slug after destruction completes. Every store in the map must return nothing. Any store they find holding tenant data that is not in the map is a defect in the map.

capability_requirements.requirement: The platform MUST provide a means of rendering a departed tenant's data unrecoverable from backup media without rendering any other tenant's backups unrecoverable, and that means MUST be established at provisioning time rather than at deletion time.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: This is the single capability that separates real deletion from the appearance of deletion. Dropping a database while retaining backups changes nothing about recoverability  -  a dropped database can be re-created by restoring a backup. Stated as a capability rather than a mechanism because more than one mechanism can satisfy it, but every one of them has to exist before the data is written, not after.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Microsoft DROP DATABASE documentation: 'A dropped database can be re-created only by restoring a backup'; NIST SP 800-88r2 3.2.2 on cryptographic erase, backups and escrow, and its precondition that data was never stored in plaintext.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Take a full backup of a test tenant's database. Perform the destruction procedure including the key-destruction step. Then attempt to restore that backup onto a clean server using every key, certificate and credential the organisation still possesses. The restore must fail. In the same session, restore a different tenant's backup taken at the same time and confirm it succeeds.

capability_requirements.requirement: Encryption at rest MUST be enabled for a tenant's data store as part of provisioning, before that tenant's first record is written, and the key custody procedure MUST be documented and tested before the platform accepts real patient data.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: This is the only requirement in this document with a deadline that the platform cannot extend. The applicable sanitization guidance's stated precondition for cryptographic erase is that the data was never stored in plaintext, so every backup taken before encryption is switched on is permanently outside the reach of any later key destruction. The system currently holds only synthetic data, which makes this cheap today and impossible for the affected data tomorrow.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: NIST SP 800-88r2 3.2.2 precondition; system fact that there is no real patient data yet and every record is synthetic; SQL Server edition matrix confirming database-level encryption is available outside the top edition.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Provision a brand-new tenant through the normal administrative flow with no extra steps. Immediately query the database server for that database's encryption state: it must report encrypted. Then attempt to restore that tenant's first backup onto a clean server without the tenant's certificate: it must fail. Separately, confirm a documented key-custody procedure exists and that a restore using the escrowed key has been performed at least once.

capability_requirements.requirement: Deletion of tenant objects from object storage MUST be verified by re-listing the affected prefixes after deletion, in every bucket in the data map, and the verification result MUST be recorded. The procedure MUST also account for object versions and delete markers rather than assuming a delete removes data.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: In the S3 object model a delete without a version identifier creates a delete marker and removes nothing, multi-object delete is capped at 1,000 keys per request and reports failures per key rather than failing the request, and lifecycle expiry is applied by a background scanner with no timing guarantee. Every one of those is a way for a deletion to report success while leaving data behind.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: MinIO object versioning documentation ('The delete marker hides the object. Nothing is actually removed'); AWS S3 DeleteObjects API reference (1,000-key limit, per-key results); MinIO lifecycle documentation on scanner timing.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Create a test tenant with more than 1,000 objects across all logical containers. Run the destruction procedure. Then, using credentials that can list all versions in every bucket, list the tenant's prefix including non-current versions and delete markers. The result must be empty, and the recorded verification outcome must match. Repeat with versioning enabled on the bucket to confirm the procedure still empties it.

capability_requirements.requirement: Retention and destruction behaviour MUST be driven by a per-tenant recorded instruction rather than by a global platform default, and the platform MUST record who gave that instruction and when.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Under the business-associate provision the choice between return and destruction, and the retention period, belong to the covered entity. A platform that destroys on its own default has taken a decision it does not own; a platform that retains on its own default has done the same in the other direction. Recording the instruction is what makes either action defensible afterwards.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: 45 CFR 164.504(e)(2)(ii)(J) return-or-destroy with an infeasibility fallback; 45 CFR 164.502(e)(2) requiring assurances to be documented in a written agreement.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Inspect two tenants configured with different instructions (one destroy-on-termination, one retain-with-extended-protections). Run the offboarding flow for each and confirm the resulting actions differ accordingly. Confirm that a tenant with no recorded instruction cannot reach the destroy step at all, and that the recorded instruction, its author and its date are retrievable after the tenant is destroyed.

capability_requirements.requirement: A preservation hold MUST be settable per tenant and MUST block every irreversible destruction step while set, including any scheduled or automated expiry, and MUST be removable only by an explicit recorded action.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Litigation is routine in workers' compensation, and the sanction regime for losing electronically stored information that should have been preserved is severe where a court finds intent to deprive. As a flag that gates one step, this costs a few hours; as a retrofit after a hold has been violated, it costs a case. Classified MUST rather than SHOULD because the implementation is trivially small relative to the exposure.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 37(e), including 37(e)(2) measures available on a finding of intent to deprive.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Set a hold on a quarantined tenant, then attempt every destruction path including the scheduled or automated one. Each must refuse and cite the hold. Confirm the hold cannot be cleared as a side effect of any other operation, and that clearing it records the operator and timestamp.

capability_requirements.requirement: Tenant identifiers and tenant hostnames MUST NOT be reused after a tenant is offboarded, and the platform MUST enforce this by refusing to allocate a previously used slug even when no active tenant holds it.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: Tenancy resolves from the Host header and nothing else, and object keys, cache keys and email links all embed the tenant identity. Reusing a slug silently redirects every stale bookmark, every already-delivered email link and every cached artefact to a different customer's data. This is a cross-tenant disclosure with no error message.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System facts: tenancy resolves from the leftmost DNS label only; object keys are tenants/{tenantId}/...; cache keys are prefixed with the tenant id; email is the spine of the external-party workflow so links persist in third-party mailboxes.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Offboard a tenant with slug 'x'. Attempt to create a new tenant with slug 'x' through the administrative UI. It must be refused with a message identifying the prior use. Separately, confirm the destroyed tenant's record is retained in the host database in a destroyed state so the refusal survives a restart.

capability_requirements.requirement: Retirement of a tenant's hostname MUST be part of the offboarding procedure and MUST NOT leave a DNS record pointing at infrastructure that no longer serves that tenant.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: A dangling record pointing at deprovisioned or reassignable infrastructure is a documented takeover vector for which the only listed mitigation is pre-compromise  -  there is no effective control after the fact, and detection is explicitly noted as difficult because the activity is outside the target's visibility. Because tenancy is Host-derived, the hostname is functionally part of the tenant's identity.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: MITRE ATT&CK T1584.001 subdomain hijacking; system fact that a request whose Host matches no office returns 'Tenant not found' and that a bare IP address cannot reach the application at all.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Offboard a test tenant. Query DNS for its application, API and auth hostnames from an external resolver. Either no record must exist, or the record must resolve to infrastructure the organisation still controls and which returns a definite refusal. Record which of the two was chosen and why.

capability_requirements.requirement: Completion of a destruction MUST produce a durable record naming the tenant, the stores addressed, the method and technique used for each, the tool and version, the verification performed, and the identity and date of the person who performed and approved it. That record MUST survive the destruction of the tenant's data.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: After destruction, this record is the only evidence the destruction happened correctly, and it is what a covered entity, an auditor or a regulator will ask for. The field list is not invented: it is the certificate-of-sanitization content specified by the current sanitization standard, adapted from physical media to logical stores.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: NIST SP 800-88r2 Appendix C certificate-of-sanitization fields and 3.2.5 additional documentation items for cryptographic erase; 45 CFR 164.316(b) documentation retention.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Destroy a test tenant, then retrieve the destruction record from a system that no longer holds any of that tenant's data. Check every listed field is populated. Confirm the record is retained under the documentation retention period and is not stored inside anything that gets destroyed with the tenant.

capability_requirements.requirement: An exported archive SHOULD be proven restorable by an independent process that reconstructs a readable dataset from it, and that proof SHOULD be repeated whenever the schema changes materially.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: An export nobody has ever consumed is an untested backup by another name, and the same team has never tested a database restore. Classified SHOULD rather than MUST because a manifest-verified, digest-checked archive already provides meaningful assurance and a full restore harness is a genuine additional cost that may not fit the available hours; if it is skipped, that must be a stated decision rather than an omission.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System fact that no restore has ever been tested; NIST SP 800-88r2's distinction between verification and validation.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: Take an export produced by the normal flow and, on a machine with no access to the source system, load it and produce a human-readable listing of a named appointment with its documents and its audit trail. Record the elapsed time and the number of manual steps required.

capability_requirements.requirement: Third-party credentials scoped to tenant data SHOULD be revocable and re-scopeable per tenant, and offboarding SHOULD record the date on which each external party's access to the departed tenant's objects was actually withdrawn, separately from the date the platform's own deletion completed.
capability_requirements.why_that_classification: An external partner already holds scoped credentials against the partner bucket with fetch-by-key granted and bucket listing deliberately withheld, so the platform cannot determine what that party can still retrieve. Re-credentialing happens on the partner's schedule, not the platform's, which means the two dates genuinely differ and pretending otherwise makes the destruction record false. SHOULD because the platform cannot unilaterally guarantee a third party's timeline.
capability_requirements.traceable_to: System fact of a partner-facing bucket with scoped credentials and no listing; 45 CFR 164.502(e)(1)(ii) and 164.504(e) on subcontractor assurances.
capability_requirements.how_to_test_it: For an offboarded tenant, take a known object key from the partner bucket and attempt to fetch it using the partner's credentials. It must fail. Then confirm the destruction record carries two distinct dates  -  platform deletion complete, and partner access withdrawn  -  and that they are separately sourced.

anti_requirements: The platform MUST NOT treat deletion of the tenant record as offboarding. Deleting the tenant row removes the only in-system record of the derived database name  -  the connection string is produced by substituting the slug into a template  -  leaving a live, PHI-bearing, fully backed-up database that no code path can name, no job enumerates, and no operator will find. The tenant record must outlive the data it points at.

The platform MUST NOT allow a self-service, single-action, immediate 'delete this office and all its data' control in the administrative UI. The choice between return and destruction belongs to the covered entity under the business-associate contract, and an irreversible action with no clock and no second confirmation is the wrong shape for the one operation in the system that has no undo.

The platform MUST NOT reuse a tenant slug, hostname or tenant identifier after offboarding. Because tenancy resolves from the Host header and nothing else, and because object keys, cache keys and already-delivered email links all embed tenant identity, reuse silently maps a departed customer's stale links to a different customer's data with no error anywhere.

The platform MUST NOT report a destruction as complete on the basis of a delete call returning success. Multi-object delete in the S3 model reports failures per key rather than failing the request, is capped at 1,000 keys, and in a versioned bucket removes nothing at all. Completion must be established by re-listing, not by the absence of an exception.

The platform MUST NOT apply write-once or compliance-mode retention locks to stores that hold tenant PHI unless the retention period has been reconciled against the destruction obligations in the business-associate contracts. In compliance mode no user including the root user can remove an object before expiry, so a control adopted to satisfy retention can make a contractual destruction obligation impossible to perform.

The platform MUST NOT rely on background lifecycle expiry as a deletion guarantee with a deadline. Object-store lifecycle rules are evaluated by a low-priority scanner that may not detect an object as eligible until after the configured period has passed, so 'expires after N days' is a floor, not a commitment.

The platform MUST NOT destroy a tenant's audit and entity-change records as a side effect of destroying its business data. Those records are the evidence of who accessed that patient information, they are the class of record most likely to be demanded after the relationship ends, and in a database-per-tenant design they are physically inside the object being dropped.

The platform MUST NOT allow any scheduled, automated or unattended process to perform an irreversible destruction step. Automated expiry is exactly the mechanism that runs over data under a preservation duty, and the sanctions available for losing electronically stored information that should have been preserved are severe.

The platform MUST NOT store an export archive's decryption key in the same store, backup set, secrets file or credential scope as the archive itself. The encryption safe harbour is conditioned on the decryption tools being held separately from the data they decrypt, and an export is the most concentrated PHI artefact the system produces.

The platform MUST NOT depend on cache entries expiring for a suspension or revocation to take effect. Expiry-driven revocation means the window is defined by a framework default rather than by a decision, and it silently changes whenever that default or the cache contents change.
surprises: The standard the brief asked us to research has been withdrawn. NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 1 was withdrawn on 26 September 2025 and superseded in its entirety by SP 800-88r2. Anything written against r1  -  including most vendor 'NIST 800-88 compliant' claims and most internal destruction policies  -  is now written against an archived document. Worse for this team: HHS's breach-notification safe-harbour guidance still points at 'NIST Special Publication 800-88' by number with no revision, and r2 deleted almost all technique-specific content in favour of a deferral to IEEE 2883-2022. So satisfying the HHS pointer in 2026 routes you to a different standards body than it did in 2024.

The window in which crypto-shredding is possible is closing, and nobody would think to look for a deadline on an architectural choice. SP 800-88r2's stated precondition for cryptographic erase is that no sensitive data was ever stored on the media in plaintext form. Every backup taken before encryption is switched on is therefore permanently outside the reach of any later key destruction. The brief identifies the absence of real patient data as a time-limited advantage for migration; it is also, and more urgently, a time-limited advantage for deletability. Turning on per-tenant encryption costs a few hours today and cannot be bought back for the affected data after the first real backup.

Crypto-shredding here does not require building envelope encryption. Most teams assume per-tenant crypto-shredding means an application-layer key hierarchy and a key management service  -  a large project this team cannot afford. But SQL Server's database-level encryption already gives each database its own key, and backups of an encrypted database are encrypted with that key and cannot be restored without the certificate: Microsoft's own warning is that dropping the certificate 'causes the encrypted database to become inaccessible.' The property everyone tries to build with application code is a side effect of a feature already present in the edition tier being used. The catch is that it turns a documented data-loss hazard into a deliberate mechanism, so key custody has to be real.

Enabling encryption for one tenant changes performance for all of them. 'The tempdb system database is encrypted if any other database on the SQL Server instance is encrypted by using TDE. This encryption might have a performance effect for unencrypted databases on the same SQL Server instance.' A per-tenant action has an instance-wide consequence  -  which is an argument for enabling it for every office at once rather than as an opt-in, and an argument for doing it while the fleet is small and the data is synthetic.

The audit trail you must keep longest lives inside the thing you are deleting. The measurement in the brief  -  16 appointments producing roughly 1,450 audit rows and 2,689 property-change rows in one office database  -  establishes that the record of who touched that office's patient data is physically inside that office's database. In a shared-database design deleting a tenant's business rows leaves the audit trail behind; in database-per-tenant, deleting the tenant destroys the evidence. Offboarding must extract audit before it destroys anything, and the destruction record itself must live somewhere that survives.

DROP DATABASE will fail, and it will fail for a reason that has nothing to do with deletion. A database cannot be dropped while any session holds it, and three recurring jobs open a connection to every office database every fifteen minutes, with connection pooling keeping those sessions alive between runs. The team will discover this at the worst possible moment, mid-offboarding, and the obvious workaround  -  retrying until it succeeds  -  races the job scheduler. The correct sequence is to remove the office from job iteration first, clear the connection pool, then set single-user mode and drop in the same batch as Microsoft's own example does.

The framework's tenant delete does far less than its name implies, and the residue is unnameable. ABP's tenant delete removes the tenant entity and nothing else  -  no database, no connection strings. Combined with this system's derived connection strings, where the database name is produced by substituting the slug into a template, deleting the tenant row destroys the only place the orphaned database's name is recorded. The database is then live, holding PHI, still being backed up if the backup script enumerates databases, or silently no longer backed up if it enumerates tenants  -  and invisible either way. Recovering its name would mean reading DNS records or backup filenames.

Host-side residue is PHI-adjacent and is in a database you are explicitly not deleting. The Hangfire schema lives in the host database on the host connection string, and the brief records that job arguments carry appointment identifiers and recipient email addresses  -  that is why the unauthenticated dashboard is a disclosure risk. Those arguments survive tenant deletion entirely, and Hangfire's retention is time-based, not tenant-based, so a departed office's identifiers persist in the host database on a schedule nobody chose with a tenant in mind.

Object-storage deletion by prefix is incomplete by construction in this specific system. Keys are tenant-prefixed, so a prefix delete looks total  -  but the brief also records a correctness hazard where a background job without a tenant argument falls back to a null ambient tenant that resolves to host scope. Anything written under that condition lands outside the tenant prefix and survives the prefix delete. The container named 'anonymous-uploads' is, by its name, the most likely candidate for objects written with no tenant context. The framework documentation compounds this: blob multi-tenancy is implemented per-provider rather than by a guaranteed naming convention, and a container can be configured to be shared across all tenants.

You cannot enumerate what the partner can still fetch. The partner-facing bucket is accessed by an external party with fetch-by-key granted and bucket listing deliberately withheld. That policy is good security and it makes offboarding verification impossible from the partner's side: the platform cannot ask 'what can you still retrieve' and get an answer. Offboarding therefore has a step that is not in the platform's control at all  -  re-credentialing a third party on that third party's schedule  -  and the honest destruction record has to carry two different dates.

Turning on the retention control can make the destruction obligation impossible. Object Lock in compliance mode means no user, explicitly including the root user, can modify or remove an object before its retention expires; legal hold is indefinite until lifted. A team that adds WORM locking to satisfy a six-year retention expectation, which sounds unambiguously prudent, can find itself contractually obliged to destroy data it has made itself technically incapable of destroying. The two obligations must be reconciled before either control is enabled, not after.

If they ever move from a wildcard certificate to per-office certificates, every client practice's name becomes permanently public. Certificate Transparency logs are append-only and entries cannot be removed, and log operators are directed not to restrict who retrieves the data. The current wildcard-plus-path-style design, adopted for an unrelated reason (the certificate covers a single label, which is why object storage uses path-style addressing), is accidentally protecting the confidentiality of the customer list. Offboarding cannot un-publish a certificate that names a departed office.

Because tenancy resolves from the Host header and nothing else, offboarding has a DNS half that is genuinely part of the data-protection design. Leaving a record pointing at deprovisioned infrastructure is a documented takeover technique whose only listed mitigation is pre-compromise  -  there is no post-hoc control and detection is explicitly noted as difficult. And email is described as the spine of the external-party workflow, so office-specific URLs are sitting in insurers' and attorneys' mailboxes for years after the office leaves. What those links do after offboarding is a design decision that nobody has made.

The six-year figure everyone quotes is about the wrong thing. 45 CFR 164.316(b)(2)(i) requires six-year retention of the documentation the Security Rule requires  -  policies, procedures, and records of required actions and assessments. It says nothing about patient records and nothing about audit logs; the Security Rule sets no explicit audit-log retention period at all. The retention period for the actual content is set by the business-associate contract, by state law and by the covered entity. A design that hard-codes 'six years' as the retention for appointment and audit data is implementing a requirement that does not exist while possibly missing the one that does.

The platform does not get to decide whether to destroy. The business-associate provision requires return or destruction at termination and the covered entity chooses; where neither is feasible the fallback is to extend the contract's protections and limit further use. Building a destruction capability is necessary, but building it as a platform default  -  in either direction  -  takes a decision the platform does not own. This reframes the whole area: the right deliverable is a configurable, evidenced execution of an instruction, not a policy.

There is a California overlay independent of HIPAA that a HIPAA-only analysis will never surface. Civil Code 56.06 deems businesses organised to maintain medical information, and businesses offering software designed to maintain medical information, to be providers of health care subject to the Confidentiality of Medical Information Act. Whether a business-to-business IME scheduling platform falls inside it is a question for counsel and not for engineers, but it is the kind of state-law hook that changes retention, disclosure and remedy exposure, and this is a California workers' compensation system.

A build-time check already exists for the two-DbContext hazard and nobody is using it. EF Core 9 and later throw when the model has changes not represented by a migration, and ship 'dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes' precisely so CI can catch it. Run against both contexts, that converts the stated failure mode  -  an entity mapped in both, migrated in one, surfacing as an invalid-object-name exception in a freshly provisioned office  -  from a production incident during onboarding into a red build. It is roughly two hours of work and it is the highest ratio of risk removed to effort spent anywhere in this area.

Suspension in this stack already fails the right way, which is a rare piece of good news worth not breaking. The framework raises a distinct business exception for an inactive tenant, separate from the not-found exception, so a suspended office produces a hard, specific error rather than a blank page or a partially-served application. That matches the team's stated ability to notice hard failures. The thing that can quietly undermine it is caching: the framework's default distributed-cache sliding expiration is twenty minutes and the visible tenant-store source shows no invalidation, so suspension may not bite immediately. That is a five-minute test that nobody has run.

not_recommended.pattern: Application-layer envelope encryption with a per-tenant data key held in a dedicated key management service or HSM, so that individual columns and objects can be crypto-shredded independently.
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: This is the textbook crypto-shredding architecture and it is genuinely more capable than database-level encryption. It survives a change of database engine or hosting model, it lets you shred at finer granularity than a whole tenant (a single patient, a single document), it protects against a database administrator with file access, and it produces exactly the key custody documentation the current sanitization guidance asks for  -  key type, wrapping, escrow history, sanitization technique. If the platform ever needs to honour a single-individual erasure request rather than a whole-tenant one, this is the only design that can do it. Larger healthcare SaaS organisations build it for precisely these reasons.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: The cost is not the encryption, it is everything downstream of it. Encrypted columns break query predicates, sorting and joins, which means touching a large share of 56 application services and 32 domain managers  -  against a team of two SDE 1s who already have a code-standard remediation exercise consuming their infrastructure time. It adds a key-management service to a stack that currently has no vault at all and whose 35 secrets live in one mode-600 file, so the new dependency is also a new single point of failure and a new way to lose all data irrecoverably. And it delivers a capability the platform has no requirement for: the unit of deletion here is the office, and database-level encryption already shreds at exactly that granularity, including in backups, with no application changes. Building the more capable mechanism would consume the entire infrastructure budget for two quarters to reach the same practical outcome for the actual use case.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: When the platform must honour erasure at an individual level rather than a tenant level  -  a state privacy statute reaching this data, a contractual right-to-delete for individual claimants, or an expansion outside workers' compensation into a jurisdiction with a general erasure right. Also when tenant databases move to a managed platform where the operator holds the encryption keys and per-tenant key custody can no longer be demonstrated.

not_recommended.pattern: Fully automated self-service offboarding: a 'close this account and delete my data' control in the customer-facing UI that runs the whole deprovisioning pipeline unattended.
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: Self-service deprovisioning is the natural counterpart to self-service onboarding, and the same argument that makes automated onboarding good  -  repeatable, fast, no human in the critical path, no forgotten steps  -  applies literally to offboarding. It is the pattern most SaaS control planes converge on. It also removes the failure mode where a departure is handled inconsistently because a different person handled it, and it means the deletion actually happens rather than sitting on somebody's list for a year.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: Onboarding and offboarding are not symmetric operations and the automation argument does not transfer. Onboarding is idempotent and its failure mode is retry; offboarding is irreversible and its failure mode is unrecoverable. More decisively, the destruction decision is not the tenant's to make unilaterally: under the business-associate provision the covered entity decides between return and destruction, and there may be a preservation duty, an unpaid invoice, or an unresolved dispute that the button knows nothing about. Automating it also removes the one control that costs nothing and catches everything  -  a human reading the state of the tenant before the irreversible step. With one environment, no CD, and no staging, an automated destruction path is also a path that has never been exercised anywhere except production.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: When there is a second environment in which the full pipeline is exercised on every release, a preservation-hold mechanism that provably gates it, a recorded per-tenant destruction instruction the automation can read, and enough offboarding volume that manual handling is genuinely the larger risk. At 11 to 33 offices, offboarding is a rare event and rare events should be deliberate.

not_recommended.pattern: Producing the tenant export as a clinical interoperability payload  -  FHIR resources, US Core profiles, NDJSON bulk export with an asynchronous kick-off and manifest, or a CDA document set.
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: This is the recognised answer to health data portability and it has real advantages. It is a published, versioned, vendor-neutral format that a receiving system can consume without bespoke work; the bulk access specification mandates newline-delimited JSON and an asynchronous kick-off-and-poll pattern with a completion manifest, which is a well-designed shape for large exports; the certified-health-IT export criterion sets a defensible bar  -  single-patient and population export, computable format, executable without developer assistance, with published format documentation. Choosing a standard also means the format is not a thing the team has to defend or maintain a specification for. If a departing office asks 'can you give this to my new vendor', a standards-conformant file is a much better answer than a bespoke archive.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: The data is the wrong shape for the standard. This system's aggregates are appointments, document packets, joint declarations, consent and change requests, integration outbox entries and a 13-state scheduling lifecycle  -  administrative and workflow data for an independent examination, not a clinical record. Mapping it into clinical resources would be lossy in the direction that matters, because the thing the departing office actually needs back is the workflow state and the documents, and the standard has no faithful representation of a 13-state IME lifecycle. It would also be a genuine research-and-modelling project for two SDE 1s with no informatics background, competing directly against the export existing at all. And the legal driver is weaker than it looks: the platform is not certified health IT, so the export criterion does not bind it, and the information-blocking actor definitions do not obviously reach a workers' compensation scheduling platform. Borrow the shape  -  newline-delimited JSON, one file per entity type, an asynchronous job producing a manifest with counts and digests  -  and skip the resource model. That captures most of the benefit for a fraction of the cost.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: If the platform starts holding clinical content that a treating provider would import  -  if the IME report itself becomes structured clinical data rather than a document, or if the business seeks certified health IT status or is determined to be an information-blocking actor. Also if a receiving vendor on the other side of an offboarding specifically requires a conformant payload, at which point building it for one real consumer beats building it speculatively for none.

not_recommended.pattern: A durable workflow or saga orchestration engine to run the offboarding pipeline  -  a dedicated workflow runtime with compensating transactions, retries and visual state inspection.
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: Offboarding is genuinely a long-running, multi-step, partially-failable distributed process touching a database, two object-storage buckets, DNS, a third party and a key store  -  the exact problem statement durable workflow engines were built for. Compensation semantics would let a half-completed offboarding roll back cleanly instead of leaving the tenant in an undefined state, and the visual inspection these tools provide is precisely the observability this team lacks everywhere else. It would also generalise: the same engine would improve the provisioning path and the migration fleet run.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It adds a distributed-systems runtime, and with it a new datastore, a new failure mode, a new upgrade path and a new body of expertise, to a single-VM deployment with no message broker by design, no second application instance, no observability, no CD and two SDE 1s. The brief is explicit that an architecture needing expertise this team does not have is worse, not better. And the problem does not need it: offboarding runs a handful of times a year, its steps are naturally ordered, and its 'compensation' is not a rollback but a deliberate human decision to stop. The lifecycle state machine plus a per-step outcome ledger  -  one aggregate and one table in a database that already exists  -  delivers the resumability and the inspectability, in tens of hours instead of hundreds, with nothing new to operate. The engine would be a correct solution to a problem this system does not have at this scale.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: When tenant count reaches the low hundreds, or when offboarding becomes frequent enough to be routine rather than exceptional, or when the platform already runs such an engine for another reason  -  at which point the marginal cost of using it here is near zero rather than being the whole cost.

not_recommended.pattern: Cell-based or deployment-stamp isolation: a separate database instance, storage volume or virtual machine per tenant, so that deletion becomes whole-media sanitization.
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It is the strongest possible answer to the question this area asks. Whole-media sanitization is explicitly preferred over partial sanitization by the current guidance, because partial sanitization carries the risk that data spilled outside the region being sanitized. Per-tenant infrastructure also gives real blast-radius isolation, per-tenant restore without touching other tenants, per-tenant performance isolation against the noisy-neighbour problem, and per-tenant data residency if that is ever required. It removes every residue argument in this document in one move, and it is the direction large multi-tenant platforms move as tenants get bigger and more regulated.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: It multiplies the one thing this team has least of. The current deployment is a single VM with four vCPUs, sixteen gigabytes of RAM and under ten gigabytes free, deployed entirely by hand over SSH with two documented traps that have each broken the stack in practice  -  a mandatory environment-file flag and a reverse proxy that resolves upstreams once at worker start. Multiplying that surface by 11 and then by 33, with no CD, no configuration management, no monitoring and no on-call, produces a fleet that drifts into inconsistent states silently, which is the specific failure mode the team is least equipped to detect. It would also cost more ongoing hours per month than the entire stated infrastructure budget, permanently, in exchange for solving a problem that occurs a few times a year and that per-tenant encryption already solves adequately.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: When a single tenant's regulatory or contractual requirements genuinely cannot be met on shared infrastructure  -  a customer-specific data residency obligation, a contractual demand for physical separation  -  or after the platform has continuous deployment, configuration management and monitoring, at which point the marginal operational cost per cell drops by an order of magnitude. It is a destination, not a starting point.

not_recommended.pattern: A separate control-plane service with its own database and its own deployment, cleanly split from the application plane.
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: The control-plane/application-plane split is the foundational structural idea in SaaS architecture, and the reference material is explicit that the control plane's services 'are not actually multi-tenant' and are global to all tenants  -  which is exactly true of tenant lifecycle management. Separating it would keep administrative capability out of the tenant-serving process, give it its own security boundary and its own rate limits, and make it possible to reason about administrative surfaces independently. Given that this system currently mounts an unauthenticated administrative dashboard inside the production API process, the argument for physical separation of administrative surfaces is not abstract here.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: The valuable part of the pattern is the conceptual boundary, and that can be had without a fourth runtime process. This deployment already runs three processes with a gating dependency between them and a manual deployment procedure; a fourth adds another service to the compose file, another certificate and hostname, another set of secrets, and another thing to forget to restart after a rebuild  -  against a reverse proxy that is documented to silently break routing on stale container IPs after any backend rebuild. Note too that the reference material itself declines to place provisioning in the control plane, acknowledging the boundary is contested. The right move here is to make the control plane a clearly bounded module inside the host scope, with its own authorization and its own audit, rather than its own process. Containment of administrative surfaces is a real requirement; a separate deployable is one implementation of it and, at this scale, the expensive one.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: When there is a second application instance or a real deployment pipeline, so that adding a process is close to free; or when an administrative surface must be reachable on a network path the tenant-facing application is not, which is a genuinely strong argument and may arrive sooner than the others.

not_recommended.pattern: Scheduled automatic purge: a background job that deletes suspended or offboarded tenant data once a retention timer expires.
not_recommended.honest_case_for_it: It is the standard way retention policies are enforced, it guarantees the deletion actually happens rather than depending on somebody remembering, it produces a consistent, auditable retention posture, and it directly limits the accumulation of departed-customer liability. The system already has twelve recurring jobs, so the mechanism is free. Manual retention is famously the retention that never runs.
not_recommended.why_rejected_here: An automated irreversible action in a system with no observability, no alerting, one environment, in-memory health-check history that does not survive a restart, and container logs that rotate away at 10 MB is an action whose failures nobody will see and whose successes nobody will review. If it deletes the wrong tenant, the first signal is a customer phone call. Worse, an automated purge is precisely the mechanism that runs over data subject to a preservation duty, and the sanctions available where information that should have been preserved is lost are severe  -  including, on a finding of intent to deprive, dismissal or default judgment. A scheduler that cannot read a litigation hold cannot be trusted with an irreversible act. The right shape is an automated process that identifies and proposes tenants due for destruction and files them for review, with the destruction itself remaining a deliberate human act.
not_recommended.when_it_would_become_right: When a preservation-hold flag provably gates the job, the destruction path has been exercised in a non-production environment, and there is alerting that a human actually receives  -  that is, once the observability gap in this system is closed, not before.

what_would_change_the_answer: Whether real patient data has been loaded. This is the single largest variable. Every recommendation about per-tenant encryption assumes the current state  -  every record synthetic, no PHI-bearing backup taken. Once the first real backup exists in plaintext, that data is permanently outside the reach of cryptographic erase, the recommendation changes from 'enable encryption now' to 'enable encryption now AND separately account for the plaintext generation', and the honest destruction guarantee for pre-encryption data becomes retention expiry rather than key destruction.

What the business-associate agreements actually say. The entire retention-versus-destruction question is settled by contract, not by architecture. If the agreements already specify return, or destruction, or a retention period, the design implements that; if they are silent or use the standard return-or-destroy language with the infeasibility fallback, the platform needs the configurable per-tenant instruction described above. These documents have not been read as part of this analysis and reading them should precede building anything.

Whether the tenants are covered entities and what this platform is to them. The analysis assumes the platform is a business associate of the practices. IME physicians performing examinations for insurers are not always covered entities in the way treating providers are, and workers' compensation disclosure sits in its own permitted category separate from treatment, payment and operations. If the chain of relationships is different from the assumption, the party who owes the retention and destruction duties changes, and so does who the export is delivered to.

Whether backups will ever leave the current box. Today the backup script writes to a bind mount on the same disk with no confirmed schedule and no tested restore, so there is effectively no independent backup generation to reason about. If backups become properly independent  -  offsite, versioned, longer-retained  -  the backups-outlive-deletion problem gets much larger and the case for per-tenant encryption gets correspondingly stronger. If backups are also made immutable, the destruction obligation and the retention control collide and must be reconciled before either is enabled.

Whether object versioning or object locking is enabled on either bucket. The prefix-deletion analysis assumes unversioned buckets. If versioning is on, every deletion becomes a two-phase operation over versions and delete markers; if compliance-mode locking is on, deletion may be impossible for the lock duration regardless of contractual obligation. This is a five-minute check that materially changes the deletion design.

The actual number of hours available per month. The recommendation is phased specifically because the one-developer-week-per-month figure is an estimate and is already being consumed elsewhere. At 16 or more hours per month the whole design is operable; between 8 and 16, Phase 0 holds and Phase 1 does not get built; below 8, the export writer rots first and the honest position becomes suspend-and-retain permanently. If the real figure is at the bottom of that range, the right answer is to build Phase 0 only and say so explicitly rather than to start Phase 1 and leave it half-finished.

Whether the four default framework tenant resolvers are actually disabled. The brief records honestly that this has never been tested. If a query-string, header, cookie or route parameter can still select a tenant, then Host-header-based offboarding is incomplete by construction  -  retiring a hostname would not prevent access to a suspended or offboarded tenant  -  and several requirements in this document would need a second enforcement point at the application layer rather than relying on hostname retirement.

Whether the partner integration can be re-credentialed on demand. The two-dates requirement for the destruction record exists because the partner's access withdrawal is on the partner's schedule. If it turns out the partner's credentials can be rotated or re-scoped unilaterally and immediately, the offboarding sequence simplifies considerably and the partner bucket stops being a permanently unverifiable residue.

Whether growth stays within the stated envelope. All of this is sized for 11 offices growing to 33 with rare departures. If the business model shifts to many small, short-lived tenants  -  trials, per-case tenants, high churn  -  then offboarding becomes routine rather than exceptional, and several patterns rejected here (automated deprovisioning, a workflow engine, scheduled purge) start to earn their cost.

Whether the platform is determined to be an information-blocking actor, or whether the California Confidentiality of Medical Information Act is determined to reach it. Both are legal determinations, not engineering ones, and both would add obligations  -  around export capability and around state-law remedies respectively  -  that would raise the priority of the export work and possibly change its required format.
