'Back up to S3-compatible object storage isn't supported in SQL Server Express and SQL Server Express with Advanced Services editions.' 'Backups can be striped across a maximum of 64 URLs.' 'URLs can be specified either in virtual host or path style format.'

evidence.finding: Sizing inputs for the audit tables (MY CALCULATION from ABP's declared column limits, not a sourced measurement): a single EntityPropertyChange row can reach ~3.4 KB (NewValue 512 + OriginalValue 512 + PropertyName 128 + PropertyTypeFullName 512 chars, nvarchar at 2 bytes/char), and a single AuditLogAction row can reach ~4 KB of serialised method parameters. Those parameters are the same PHI-bearing arguments the brief flags as exposed by the unauthenticated Hangfire dashboard  -  meaning the audit database is unambiguously a PHI store and must keep full HIPAA controls after separation.
evidence.quote: EntityPropertyChangeConsts: MaxNewValueLength = 512, MaxOriginalValueLength = 512, MaxPropertyNameLength = 128, MaxPropertyTypeFullNameLength = 512. AuditLogActionConsts: MaxParametersLength = 2000. AuditLogConsts: MaxBrowserInfoLength = 512, MaxUrlLength = 256.

questions.question: Can this application run more than one API instance today? Work through each blocker (Hangfire, DataProtection keyring, the distributed lock, the migration runner, and anything else) with cited evidence, give a definitive yes or no, name precisely what blocks it and the smallest change that unblocks it. Second: is horizontal scale even the right goal for 11-33 offices with a two-person team, given that a second instance is an availability mechanism and not only a capacity one?
questions.answer:
NO  -  not today, not safely.

Four things block it. Only one of them is the one the team would guess.

=== METHOD NOTE: THE RANGE OF VIABLE DESIGNS FIRST ===
For a workload of this shape (11-33 tenants, business-hours booking desk, database-per-tenant, 12 office-iterating sweeps) the viable topologies are: (A) single instance, no failover  -  today; (B) single instance + tested rebuild-and-restore (cold standby); (C) single active + warm standby VM with replicated state; (D) N active API instances + exactly ONE elected job runner; (E) N active instances all running jobs, with work partitioned by durable row-claim. (E) is what a larger org would build and is wrong here. The interesting finding is that (D)'s prerequisites are all worth doing at ONE instance, and that (B) addresses a materially larger risk than any of them.

=== (a) HANGFIRE ===
Multiple servers against one storage IS supported. Hangfire: "It is possible to run multiple server instances inside a process, machine, or on several machines at the same time... Each server use distributed locks to perform the coordination logic."

Recurring jobs will NOT normally fire twice. Verified in Hangfire source: RecurringJobScheduler wraps its batch in AcquireDistributedLock("recurring-jobs:lock", LockTimeout = 1 min) and each job in AcquireDistributedRecurringJobLock(recurringJobId, 1 min). Its own comment on lock timeout: "DistributedLockTimeoutException here doesn't mean that recurring jobs weren't scheduled. It just means another Hangfire server did this work." Its XML doc: "Multiple instances of this background process can be used in separate threads/processes without additional configuration (distributed locks are used). However, this only adds support for fail-over, and does not increase the performance." Scheduler polls once a minute. Separately, ABP's HangfireBackgroundWorkerManager registers via RecurringJob.AddOrUpdate(recurringJobId, ...) with a deterministic id, so N instances produce ONE definition, not N.

But ENQUEUE-once is not EXECUTE-once. Hangfire's throttling doc: "As there are no reliable automatic failure detectors in distributed systems, it is possible that the same job is being processed on different workers in some corner cases." With SlidingInvisibilityTimeout = 5 min and sweeps that open a connection per office (11 today, 33 later), a slow sweep can exceed the invisibility window and be re-fetched by the second server while the first still runs. THAT is the blocker  -  not Hangfire, but what these particular jobs do: two durable outbox drains that send patient/attorney email (ex-parte-safe addressing, one primary + CC) and post to Case Tracker. A duplicate send is real-world harm.

DisableGlobalLocks = true  -  what it actually changes (source-verified, and the opposite of the intuition): it affects ONLY SqlServerWriteOnlyTransaction.AcquireLock, which with it false takes one coarse sp_getapplock per data-structure type ({schema}:List:Lock, :Set:Lock, :Hash:Lock) and with it true takes none. It does NOT touch SqlServerConnection.AcquireDistributedLock, which always calls sp_getapplock @LockMode='Exclusive', @LockOwner='Session'. So recurring-job dedup is unaffected by it. Directionally it makes N servers behave BETTER by removing a serialization point, and it is Hangfire's own recommendation for 1.7+ (auto-detected as schema >= 6).

QueuePollInterval = TimeSpan.Zero with N servers  -  exact numbers from SqlServerJobQueue.cs: LongPollingThreshold 1s, PollingQuantumMs 1000, DefaultPollingDelayMs 200, MinPollingDelayMs 100. Zero < 1s means long polling; the delay is clamp(200, [100,1000]) = 200 ms. A static in-process SemaphoreSlim(1) per (storage, queue-set) means only ONE thread per PROCESS polls at a time  -  so the idle floor is ~5 FetchJob statements/sec per process, NOT workers x 5. That semaphore is in-process, so it does not coordinate across processes: N instances = N x ~5 statements/sec against the host database forever. Two instances ~10/s. That is a real but small permanent floor; it is NOT the reason to say no. (Also NewItemInQueueEvents is an in-process AutoResetEvent, so a second instance only learns of new work on its 200 ms poll  -  harmless.)

SMALLEST CHANGE: bind AbpBackgroundJobOptions.IsJobExecutionEnabled to configuration in the API module and set it false on every instance but one. Verified in ABP source  -  AbpBackgroundJobsHangfireModule.OnPreApplicationInitialization sets hangfireOptions.BackgroundJobServerFactory = _ => null when it is false, while still resolving JobStorage so enqueue keeps working. It is the same switch the AuthServer already uses. One line. It fails OBVIOUSLY: no runner means jobs visibly stop, rather than subtly double-running.
REJECT the alternative of running Hangfire everywhere and trusting its locks. It is supported, and it converts every latent non-idempotency in 12 office-iterating jobs into an incident you discover in a patient's inbox.

=== (b) DATAPROTECTION KEYRING  -  NOT A BLOCKER, ALREADY CORRECT ===
Microsoft's web-farm doc: "Under the default configuration, a unique key ring is stored on each node of the web farm... The default configuration isn't generally appropriate for hosting apps in a web farm." The two requirements are stated exactly: "To share protected payloads among apps: Configure SetApplicationName in each app with the same value. Use the same version of the Data Protection API stack across the apps." And: "SetApplicationName internally sets DataProtectionOptions.ApplicationDiscriminator... For the apps to be able to read each other's cryptographic payloads, they must have the same application discriminator."

Both are already satisfied: shared Redis keyring at CaseEvaluation-Protection-Keys, SetApplicationName("CaseEvaluation") identical in both processes, one image so an identical DP stack version. Redis persistence also satisfies MS's constraint: "Only Redis versions supporting Redis Data Persistence should be used to store keys"  -  AOF with a named volume qualifies. Nothing is required here to run two instances.

What IS still missing (already true at one instance, more load-bearing at N): key encryption at rest. MS: "If you change the key persistence location, the system no longer automatically encrypts keys at rest, since it doesn't know whether DPAPI is an appropriate encryption mechanism." Persisting to Redis is a changed location, so the keys are almost certainly plaintext in a Redis that also holds every permission grant  -  INFERENCE, not verified in your code. Anyone who can read that Redis can read and mint every protected payload. MS is blunt that this is a read-access mitigation only: "You can choose to encrypt keys at rest, but this doesn't prevent cyberattackers from creating new keys." Optional hardening: ProtectKeysWithCertificate using the same read-only-PFX-mount pattern OpenIddict already uses.
CAPABILITY REQUIREMENT (no product named): the platform must provide a shared, durable, access-controlled key repository plus a key-encrypting key held OUTSIDE that repository.

=== (c) THE DISTRIBUTED LOCK  -  NOT A BLOCKER; IT IS WHAT MAKES OTHER THINGS SAFE, AND IT IS A SPOF ===
ABP: "ABP's current distributed locking implementation is based on the DistributedLock library" (Medallion). A source search of abpframework/abp for IAbpDistributedLock returns the framework's own use sites: StaticPermissionSaver, StaticSettingSaver, StaticFeatureSaver, DynamicPermission/Setting/FeatureDefinitionStore, OutboxSender, InboxProcessor, BackgroundJobWorker, BackgroundJobCleanupWorker, EfCoreRuntimeDatabaseMigratorBase, EfCoreDatabaseMigrationEventHandlerBase, AbpIdentityUserValidator, and OpenIddict's TokenCleanupBackgroundWorker.

The decisive one at N instances is StaticPermissionSaver.SaveAsync, which does DistributedLock.TryAcquireAsync(GetApplicationDistributedLockKey()) and on null returns with the literal comment "/* Another application instance is already doing it */", then takes a 5-minute common lock and throws AbpException("Could not acquire distributed lock for saving static permissions!") if it cannot. So: yes, it matters at N instances  -  N instances would otherwise race to rewrite permission/setting/feature definitions at every startup  -  and it is ALREADY handled, but only because Redis is up.

Consequence you should internalise: at N instances Redis moves from "losing it invalidates sessions" to "losing it blocks startup". The distributed lock, the DataProtection keyring and every permission grant sit in ONE 512 MB single-instance Redis with no replica. Horizontal scale concentrates that risk rather than diluting it.
Honest correctness caveat: RedisDistributedLock implements RedLock, and the library's own doc says robustness comes from "a set of databases instead of just a single database. The lock is only considered aquired if it is successfully acquired on more than half of the databases." With one Redis you have a lease-based mutex, not a RedLock guarantee. Adequate for startup definition-saving. NOT adequate for anything that must never double-execute  -  use a database row claim for the outbox drains.
Maintenance: DistributedLock.Redis 1.1.1 published 2025-10-26; Volo.Abp.DistributedLocking 10.6.0 current. Both maintained.
SMALLEST CHANGE: none required. Optional: a startup health gate that fails hard if the resolved provider is NullAbpDistributedLock.

=== (d) THE MIGRATION RUNNER  -  THE HARD BLOCKER, AND THE ONLY ONE THAT CAN CORRUPT DATA ===
Two distinct problems.

(1) Topology. EF Core's guidance is explicit: "don't make every application replica run migrations from its entrypoint" and "Configure the deployment platform not to restart the migration container after it exits successfully." You already follow the first half  -  db-migrator is a separate one-shot service and both processes gate on service_completed_successfully, which is a dependency not a mutex but is the right shape. You violate the second: db-migrator runs on EVERY bring-up and its seed contributors run every time. Scaling the API to N replicas does not by itself re-run it N times, so this is a hygiene problem, not the blocker.

(2) The real one: IOfficeDatabaseProvisioner.ProvisionAsync calls Database.MigrateAsync() AT RUNTIME, FROM THE API PROCESS, on a host-UI action. Good news, verified: "Starting with EF Core 9, MigrateAsync and Migrate automatically acquire a database-wide lock before applying any migrations. This protects against database corruption that could result from multiple application instances running migrations concurrently... The lock is held for the duration of the migration execution, including any seeding code." .NET 10 means EF Core 10, so the SCHEMA is protected.

But the lock covers seeding configured via UseSeeding. ABP seed contributors run through IDataSeeder AFTER MigrateAsync returns and the lock is released. So catalogue seeding, the admin user and the office's doctor are UNPROTECTED against a concurrent second call. The recorded idempotency of ProvisionAsync is idempotency-on-retry (sequential)  -  a different property from concurrency-safety. Two admins, or one admin plus a retry, landing on two instances gives you duplicate catalogue rows or a duplicate-key exception that leaves an office half-provisioned. This is the thing that breaks at N instances and it fails SUBTLY.

Bonus, and it is good news: "calling Migrate() or MigrateAsync() will throw an exception when the model has pending changes compared to the last migration (warning event ID RelationalEventId.PendingModelChangesWarning)." Given your two-DbContext hazard (an entity mapped in both needs a migration in BOTH), this now throws at provisioning time instead of surfacing as invalid-object-name at runtime. Do NOT suppress that warning. Add "dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes" to CI  -  the doc names it explicitly for this.

SMALLEST CHANGE: wrap the WHOLE of ProvisionAsync (migrate plus all seeding) in IAbpDistributedLock.TryAcquireAsync("OfficeProvision_" + slug), returning a clear "provisioning already in progress" to the second caller. Copy ABP's own pattern verbatim  -  EfCoreRuntimeDatabaseMigratorBase does DistributedLock.TryAcquireAsync("DatabaseMigration_" + DatabaseName) and on null logs "Distributed lock could not be acquired for database migration: {DatabaseName}. Operation cancelled." and returns. ~15 lines. This is the single highest-value change in this whole answer, because it is worth doing at ONE instance too: it stops a double-clicked provision button.
Also: EF Core says "Use a separate identity for deployment that has permission to change the schema. The identity used by the application at run time should normally have only the permissions the application needs to read and write data." That directly contradicts every service connecting as sa.

=== (e) EVERYTHING ELSE ===
HARD BLOCKERS:
1. NGINX. One proxy; it resolves proxy_pass upstreams ONCE at worker start; only the minio block has the resolver + variable fix. A second API container gets an IP nginx never learns, so it would receive ZERO traffic and you would not notice, because instance one keeps serving. Worst possible failure mode for this team. It also means a second API behind a single nginx improves nothing if nginx or the VM is what fails.
2. Job-runner election  -  see (a).
3. Provisioning seed concurrency  -  see (d).

SUBTLE RISKS (the category this team must avoid):
4. THE IN-PROCESS EVENT BUS. Verified in ABP source: LocalDistributedEventBus is [ExposeServices(typeof(IDistributedEventBus))]  -  it is what you get when no broker provider is registered, and the brief confirms NO message broker. So today IDistributedEventBus.PublishAsync is a lie by omission: at one instance it works; at two, an event published on instance A is never seen by instance B, with NO ERROR. Any cache invalidation, cross-aggregate reaction, or "recompute the packet when a document lands" handler silently stops working half the time. This is the subtlest multi-instance hazard in any ABP app and it will not throw. Counter-note for fairness: ABP's own tenant-config invalidation survives, because TenantStore and TenantConfigurationCacheItemInvalidator both use IDistributedCache<TenantConfigurationCacheItem>  -  Redis-backed, so deleting the key on one node deletes it for all (verified in ABP source). Invalidation THROUGH Redis is safe; behaviour triggered BY an event handler is not.
5. HEALTHCHECKS UI. In-memory storage means N disagreeing dashboards, N independent pollers hitting the endpoints, and history wiped on restart. Maintenance flag: AspNetCore.HealthChecks.UI latest stable on NuGet is 9.0.0, published 2024-12-19  -  no 10.x for .NET 10, and the GitHub releases page shows nothing since Feb 2024. This dependency is drifting behind your runtime. CAPABILITY REQUIREMENT: health history must live outside the process.
6. RATE LIMITING BECOMES PER-INSTANCE. ASP.NET Core's limiter is in-process; N instances multiply every configured limit by N. Your one AddRateLimiter covering password reset and public upload silently becomes 2x more permissive  -  and still does not cover sign-in, which is a different process.
7. THE 2-WORKER PACKET RENDERER AND SMTP RELAY. The worker pool was pinned precisely because bursts oversubscribe them. Two instances = two independently-pinned pools against the same 2 workers; the pinning stops meaning what it means. Another argument for one elected runner.
8. CONNECTION POOLS. Microsoft: "Connections are pooled per process, per application domain, per connection string"; default Max Pool Size is 100; on exhaustion "the request is queued... the default is 15 seconds. If the pooler cannot satisfy the request before the connection times out, an exception is thrown." And directly on your architecture: "Pool fragmentation due to many databases... there is a separate pool of connections to each database, which increase the number of connections to the server." Your TenantConnectionStringProvider derives a DISTINCT connection string per office. MY ARITHMETIC (reasoning, not source): 33 offices + host = 34 pools x 100 = 3,400 pooled connections per process; two instances 6,800. SQL Server's ceiling is 32,767 user connections, so the ceiling is not the constraint  -  the 10 GB SQL container's memory and worker threads are. Cap Max Pool Size explicitly in the derived connection string BEFORE adding any instance; the derived-string design makes that a one-line change.
9. LOCAL DISK. Serilog writes per-container files; N instances = N unaggregated log files on a disk with 9.7 GB free. Not a correctness blocker, but it makes absent observability worse. MinIO is shared, so blobs are fine.
10. OPENIDDICT. Signing cert mounted from a path with the passphrase from env, identical in every replica of one image, so validation is consistent. Not a blocker. I did not verify OpenIddict's own in-process caching at N instances  -  UNVERIFIED.

=== VERDICT AND THE SMALLEST CHANGE ===
NO. What blocks it, precisely: (1) nginx cannot route to a second instance and fails silently; (2) two Hangfire servers would run 12 office-iterating jobs including two outbox drains that send patient/attorney email and post to Case Tracker, whose idempotency under CONCURRENT execution is unverified; (3) ProvisionAsync seeds outside EF Core's migration lock; (4) IDistributedEventBus is in-process, so any behaviour depending on event delivery silently halves.

Smallest unblocking change, in order (~1 to 1.5 developer-weeks, i.e. roughly one whole month's infra budget):
1. nginx upstream block with the resolver + variable proxy_pass fix on the api/auth blocks, the way minio already has it. Do this regardless  -  it also fixes the stale-IP trap that has already broken the stack twice.
2. Bind IsJobExecutionEnabled to configuration; true on exactly one instance.
3. Wrap ProvisionAsync in IAbpDistributedLock.TryAcquireAsync("OfficeProvision_" + slug), mirroring EfCoreRuntimeDatabaseMigratorBase.
4. Set explicit Max Pool Size in the derived tenant connection string.
5. Audit IDistributedEventBus / ILocalEventBus handlers; anything whose correctness depends on delivery moves to the outbox that already exists.
Note that 2 through 5 are all worth doing at ONE instance. That is the tell.

=== IS HORIZONTAL SCALE THE RIGHT GOAL? BOTH CASES, HONESTLY ===
FOR HORIZONTAL SCALE: it is the only mechanism that removes the API process from the SPOF list, and it is the standard answer. Microsoft's web-farm doc names four real benefits  -  reliability, capacity, scalability, maintainability. The genuinely strong version of the argument is workload separation: at 33 offices the three 15-minute jobs alone open 33 sequential connections per sweep, and there is a real case for keeping that off the process serving users. Zero-downtime deploys matter: today every deploy is a full outage for a California booking desk in business hours, forever. And doing the work NOW is cheapest, because there is no real PHI yet and that advantage expires the moment a practice takes a real booking.

FOR SINGLE INSTANCE + FAST RELIABLE FAILOVER: the API is not the thing that fails. Every item on the SPOF list  -  one VM, one SQL container, one Redis, one MinIO, one nginx  -  is stateful or edge, and a second API instance makes none of them redundant. Two API containers on the same VM protect against exactly one failure mode that a container restart policy already largely covers. Two APIs on two VMs requires making SQL, Redis, MinIO and nginx redundant first, which is a different order of complexity  -  plus a load balancer that must PRESERVE THE HOST HEADER, because tenancy resolves from Host and nothing else; any L7 hop that rewrites Host returns "Tenant not found" for a whole office. That is a capability requirement to verify per product, never to assume. Meanwhile the measured availability risk is not capacity, it is recovery: backups to a bind mount on the same disk, no confirmed cron, and NO RESTORE EVER TESTED. HIPAA is unambiguous about which of these is mandatory  -  45 CFR 164.308(a)(7)(ii): (A) Data backup plan REQUIRED, (B) Disaster recovery plan REQUIRED, (C) Emergency mode operation plan REQUIRED, (D) Testing and revision procedures ADDRESSABLE, (E) criticality analysis ADDRESSABLE. Nothing in the Security Rule requires redundancy or high availability. It requires that you can restore. You cannot currently demonstrate that. A second API instance does not move that needle at all. And every multi-instance failure mode above  -  silent blackholing, doubled rate limits, halved event delivery, N unaggregated logs  -  is SILENT, in a system with no metrics, no aggregation and no alerting.

MY RECOMMENDATION (judgement  -  argue with it): do NOT pursue horizontal scale as a goal. Pursue three things in order.
1. A TESTED RESTORE. Backups off the box; a documented, timed, actually-executed restore drill of the host database plus one office database. Required under 164.308(a)(7)(ii)(A)-(C), largest real risk, costs days not weeks. Nothing else goes first.
2. SPLIT THE JOB RUNNER OUT OF THE API into its own process  -  same image, IsJobExecutionEnabled true there and false in the API. This is the workload separation that actually addresses the sweep load, it makes the API stateless in practice, and it is the prerequisite for any future second instance. Crucially it FAILS OBVIOUSLY: worker down means jobs stop and the outbox backlog grows visibly. Cost: the same one-line config change plus one compose service.
3. MAKE A SECOND INSTANCE POSSIBLE BUT DO NOT RUN ONE. Land the nginx fix, the provisioning lock, the pool cap, the event-bus audit. You then hold the option, proven by briefly running two during one deploy, without owning the ongoing complexity.

ON AVAILABILITY, DIRECTLY: yes, a second instance is an availability mechanism and I am not dismissing that. But its availability value is capped by the least-redundant thing in the request path, and here that is nginx on a single VM sharing a disk with the backups. A second API behind a single nginx on a single VM buys protection against one failure mode at the cost of four new SILENT ones. That trade is bad. The best availability ratio for 4 vCPU / 16 GB / 9.7 GB free and two SDE-1s is: tested restore, then a rehearsed rebuild-from-image-and-restore procedure with a stated RTO, then  -  only if that RTO is unacceptable to the business  -  a warm standby VM. Zero-downtime deploys are the ONE benefit a standby does not give you; if that is the actual pain, name it and buy it deliberately with steps 2 and 3, rather than buying "horizontal scalability".

VIABILITY THRESHOLD (as required): this plan is operable at roughly 20-24 hours a month  -  a quarterly restore drill (~4 h), the worker split, routine patching. BELOW ABOUT 12 HOURS A MONTH IT DECAYS TO: the restore drill silently stops happening, worker failures go unnoticed because there is no alerting, and the outbox backlog is discovered by a customer. At that level do item 1 ONLY and explicitly defer the rest  -  a tested restore without a worker split is strictly better than a worker split without a tested restore. HORIZONTAL SCALE IS NOT VIABLE BELOW ROUGHLY 40 HOURS A MONTH at any point, because it requires standing observability to be safe and this team has none.

WHAT NOT TO BUILD (standard at larger orgs, wrong here):
- A MESSAGE BROKER to fix the in-process event bus. Two durable database outboxes already exist and work. A broker adds a stateful clustered dependency, a new failure mode and a new skill, to solve a problem better solved by not depending on cross-instance events.
- KUBERNETES / an orchestrator. Nothing here needs scheduling. It swaps one trap they know (--env-file) for a dozen they do not.
- REDIS CLUSTER OR A REDLOCK QUORUM. The lock's only current job is startup definition-saving; a single-node mutex suffices. Chasing RedLock's majority property buys a guarantee nothing depends on.
- STICKY SESSIONS. No SignalR, no WebSocket, no server-side session  -  the brief confirms no sticky requirement. Do not let an LB config introduce one, and DELETE the dead WebSocket upgrade block in the proxy config so nobody later concludes it is needed.
- AUTOSCALING. Load is bounded, predictable and business-hours. It would add nondeterminism to a system whose job-runner election depends on knowing exactly how many instances exist.
- A SECOND INSTANCE AS THE ANSWER TO THE HANGFIRE DASHBOARD EXPOSURE. That is a containment problem (network-level restriction of the admin path), not a topology problem.
questions.reasoning: I established the range of viable topologies first (single/cold-standby/warm-standby/N-active-with-elected-runner/N-active-partitioned) before comparing against the current design, so the findings are not limited to what the current architecture already hints at. I then verified each named blocker against first-party sources rather than memory: Hangfire's own docs plus its actual source on GitHub, Microsoft Learn for Data Protection, web farm, EF Core migrations and SqlClient pooling, the ABP framework source via GitHub code search, the NuGet registration API for maintenance currency, and the eCFR versioner API for the statute. The most valuable results were the ones that contradicted the intuitive reading: DisableGlobalLocks=true makes multi-server operation better rather than worse because it only removes coarse sp_getapplock calls in SqlServerWriteOnlyTransaction and never touches AcquireDistributedLock; QueuePollInterval=Zero is not a spin loop but a clamped 200 ms long-poll gated by an in-process semaphore, so the idle floor is ~5 statements/sec per process rather than per worker; and Data Protection is already configured correctly for a web farm, so the item the team would most expect to block them does not. The genuine blockers turned out to be elsewhere. EF Core 9+ migration locking protects the schema during ProvisionAsync but explicitly covers only UseSeeding delegates, and ABP's seed contributors run through IDataSeeder after the lock releases  -  that gap is the one that can corrupt an office database, and idempotency-on-retry is not the same property as concurrency-safety. LocalDistributedEventBus being the default IDistributedEventBus registration when no broker exists means cross-instance events silently vanish at N=2, which is precisely the fail-subtly class this team cannot detect. And nginx's once-at-worker-start upstream resolution means a second instance would receive zero traffic while the first keeps serving, so the deployment would look successful. On the second question I deliberately separated what HIPAA actually requires  -  backup, disaster recovery and emergency mode operation are Required; testing is only Addressable; redundancy is not mentioned at all  -  from what engineering instinct suggests, because the untested restore is a larger and cheaper-to-fix risk than the missing second instance. My core judgement, which is mine and not sourced, is that a second API instance's availability value is capped by the least-redundant element in the request path (a single nginx on a single VM sharing a disk with the backups), so it buys protection against one failure mode at the cost of four silent ones. I have labelled the connection-pool arithmetic, the plaintext-keys-at-rest inference and the viability thresholds as my reasoning rather than sourced fact.
questions.the_binding_constraint: The binding constraint is nginx's single once-at-worker-start upstream resolution, and it binds before the others because it is the only blocker that makes the whole experiment invisible. Add a second API container today and nginx never learns its IP, so the new instance receives zero traffic while the first keeps serving normally  -  the deploy looks successful, no error appears anywhere, and every downstream conclusion the team draws about whether multi-instance works is drawn from a system that is still running one instance. Hangfire double-execution, the unguarded provisioning seed and the vanishing distributed events are all more dangerous, but none of them can even manifest until traffic actually reaches instance two, and none can be diagnosed while the routing layer is silently discarding the evidence. It also binds independently of instance count: it is the same defect that has already broken the stack after backend rebuilds, so fixing it is owed regardless of the multi-instance decision. Second in line is the job-runner election, because it is the only blocker whose failure reaches a patient's inbox rather than a log file.
questions.smallest_change_that_unblocks: Five changes, roughly 1 to 1.5 developer-weeks, in this order. (1) Give the api and auth nginx blocks the resolver plus variable proxy_pass treatment the minio block already has, so upstreams re-resolve; this is owed regardless of the multi-instance decision because it is the same defect that already breaks routing after every backend rebuild. (2) Bind AbpBackgroundJobOptions.IsJobExecutionEnabled to configuration in the API module and set it true on exactly one instance  -  verified in ABP source, AbpBackgroundJobsHangfireModule sets BackgroundJobServerFactory to null when false while still resolving JobStorage so enqueue keeps working; this is the same switch AuthServer already uses, and it fails obviously rather than subtly. (3) Wrap the whole of IOfficeDatabaseProvisioner.ProvisionAsync  -  migration and all seeding  -  in IAbpDistributedLock.TryAcquireAsync("OfficeProvision_" + slug), copying ABP's own EfCoreRuntimeDatabaseMigratorBase pattern which acquires "DatabaseMigration_" + DatabaseName and returns with a clear log on null; about 15 lines, and worth doing at one instance because it also stops a double-clicked provision button. (4) Set an explicit Max Pool Size in the derived tenant connection string in TenantConnectionStringProvider, since the database-per-tenant design creates a separate 100-connection pool per office per process. (5) Audit every IDistributedEventBus and ILocalEventBus handler and move anything whose correctness depends on delivery onto the durable outbox that already exists. Changes 2 through 5 are all worth doing at a single instance, which is the strongest evidence that they are the right changes.
questions.what_i_could_not_determine: I had no access to this codebase  -  the working directory is a personal profile repo, not the application  -  so every claim about THIS application is taken from the brief, while everything about framework and library behaviour is source- or doc-verified. Specifically unverified: (1) whether the AppNotificationOutboxItems and AppIntegrationOutboxItems drain jobs are idempotent under CONCURRENT execution rather than merely on sequential retry  -  this is the single decisive fact for (a), and if they claim rows with a durable UPDATE-then-SELECT the Hangfire risk drops from severe to tolerable; (2) whether IDistributedEventBus is actually used anywhere in src and for what, which determines how severe the in-process-event-bus finding is; (3) whether DataProtection keys are currently unencrypted at rest  -  inferred from Microsoft's statement that changing the persistence location disables automatic encryption, plus no ProtectKeysWith* appearing in the brief; (4) whether ABP 10.x's IDistributedCache<T> adds an in-process L1 layer that would need cross-instance invalidation; (5) OpenIddict's own in-memory caching behaviour at N instances; (6) whether the four default ABP __tenant resolvers are disabled, which the brief already flags as never tested and which becomes more consequential behind a load balancer. Method limitation: the WebSearch budget for this session was already exhausted (200/200) before I began, so I could not do broad discovery. I compensated by going directly to first-party sources  -  docs.hangfire.io plus raw Hangfire source on GitHub, Microsoft Learn, abpframework/abp via GitHub code search, the NuGet registration and search APIs, and the eCFR versioner API when the eCFR HTML page redirected to an unblock URL. I could not cross-reference the Hangfire recurring-scheduler locking claim against a second independent source; I cross-referenced the documentation against the implementation source instead, which I consider stronger.

evidence.finding: Hangfire explicitly supports multiple server instances against one storage, coordinated by distributed locks.
evidence.quote: It is possible to run multiple server instances inside a process, machine, or on several machines at the same time. Each server use distributed locks to perform the coordination logic.

evidence.finding: RecurringJobScheduler acquires a storage-wide distributed lock named 'recurring-jobs:lock' with a 1-minute timeout, plus a per-job lock, and treats a lock timeout as evidence another server already did the work  -  so a recurring job does not normally fire twice across N servers. Its XML doc states multi-instance adds fail-over only, not throughput.
evidence.quote: private static readonly TimeSpan LockTimeout = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1); ... var resource = "recurring-jobs:lock"; ... using (connection.AcquireDistributedLock(resource, LockTimeout)) ... // DistributedLockTimeoutException here doesn't mean that recurring jobs weren't scheduled. // It just means another Hangfire server did this work. ... using (connection.AcquireDistributedRecurringJobLock(recurringJobId, LockTimeout))

evidence.finding: Hangfire's recurring scheduler polls on a minute-based interval and requires an always-on server.
evidence.quote: A special component in Hangfire Server checks the recurring jobs on a minute-based interval and then enqueues them as fire-and-forget jobs. ... Your Hangfire Server instance should be always on to perform scheduling and processing logic.

evidence.finding: Hangfire concedes that the same job can be processed on different workers in corner cases  -  execution is at-least-once, not exactly-once. This is the decisive risk for the office-iterating outbox drains.
evidence.quote: Mutex doesn't prevent simultaneous execution of the same background job. As there are no reliable automatic failure detectors in distributed systems, it is possible that the same job is being processed on different workers in some corner cases.

evidence.finding: QueuePollInterval=TimeSpan.Zero is only legal when SlidingInvisibilityTimeout is set, and DisableGlobalLocks=true is Hangfire's own recommendation for 1.7+ installations, requiring schema 7.
evidence.quote: Starting from Hangfire 1.7.0 it's possible to use TimeSpan.Zero as a polling interval, when SlidingInvisibilityTimeout option is set. ... [DisableGlobalLocks] Migration to Schema 7 is required.

evidence.finding: With QueuePollInterval=Zero the actual idle poll delay is a clamped 200 ms, and a STATIC IN-PROCESS SemaphoreSlim(1) per (storage, queue-set) means only one thread per process polls at a time. The semaphore does not cross process boundaries, so N API instances produce N times the idle query floor against the host database (~5 fetch statements/sec each).

TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(Math.Min(Math.Max(configuredPollInterval == TimeSpan.Zero ? DefaultPollingDelayMs : (int)configuredPollInterval.TotalMilliseconds, MinPollingDelayMs), PollingQuantumMs)) : configuredPollInterval; ... if (!_options.DisableFetchSemaphores) { semaphore = Semaphores.GetOrAdd(resource, CreateSemaphoreFunc); semaphore.Wait(cancellationToken); }

evidence.finding: DisableGlobalLocks only removes coarse sp_getapplock calls on the List/Set/Hash resources inside the write transaction  -  it makes N-server contention LOWER, not higher, and does not affect recurring-job dedup.
evidence.quote: private void AcquireListLock(string key) { AcquireLock(_storage.Options.DisableGlobalLocks ? $"List:{key}" : "List"); } ... private void AcquireLock(string resource) { if (!_storage.Options.DisableGlobalLocks || _storage.Options.UseFineGrainedLocks) { _lockedResources.Add($"{_storage.SchemaName}:{resource}:Lock"); } }

evidence.quote: public override IDisposable AcquireDistributedLock([NotNull] string resource, TimeSpan timeout) { ... return AcquireLock($"{_storage.SchemaName}:{resource}", timeout); }  // and in SqlServerDistributedLock.cs: private const string LockMode = "Exclusive"; private const string LockOwner = "Session"; ... .Create("sp_getapplock", CommandType.StoredProcedure, ...)

evidence.finding: THE SMALLEST FIX FOR (a), verified in ABP source: setting IsJobExecutionEnabled=false nulls the Hangfire BackgroundJobServerFactory so no processing server starts, while JobStorage is still resolved so enqueueing continues. Default is true. This is the same switch AuthServer already uses.
evidence.quote: public override void OnPreApplicationInitialization(ApplicationInitializationContext context) { var options = context.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<IOptions<AbpBackgroundJobOptions>>().Value; if (!options.IsJobExecutionEnabled) { var hangfireOptions = context.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<IOptions<AbpHangfireOptions>>().Value; context.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<JobStorage>(); hangfireOptions.BackgroundJobServerFactory = _ => null; } }

evidence.finding: ABP registers recurring jobs by deterministic id via RecurringJob.AddOrUpdate, so N instances produce ONE recurring job definition rather than N.
evidence.quote: RecurringJob.AddOrUpdate(recurringJobId, queueName, methodCall, cronExpression ?? GetCron(period!.Value), new RecurringJobOptions { TimeZone = workerAdapter.TimeZone });

evidence.finding: Data Protection default config is per-node and unsuitable for a web farm; the required fix is a shared key ring plus the same SetApplicationName. Both are already satisfied here, so (b) is NOT a blocker.
evidence.quote: Under the default configuration, a unique key ring is stored on each node of the web farm. Consequently, each web farm node can't decrypt data that's encrypted by an app on any other node. The default configuration isn't generally appropriate for hosting apps in a web farm.

evidence.finding: The two documented requirements for sharing protected payloads: identical SetApplicationName (which sets ApplicationDiscriminator) and the same Data Protection stack version.
evidence.quote: To share protected payloads among apps: Configure SetApplicationName in each app with the same value. Use the same version of the Data Protection API stack across the apps. ... SetApplicationName internally sets DataProtectionOptions.ApplicationDiscriminator. ... For the apps to be able to read each other's cryptographic payloads, they must have the same application discriminator, which can be set by calling SetApplicationName.

evidence.finding: Changing the key persistence location (to Redis) disables automatic key encryption at rest  -  the basis for my inference that the keyring is plaintext in Redis today. Microsoft also warns encryption at rest does not stop an attacker with write access from minting keys. Redis must support persistence, which AOF satisfies.
evidence.quote: If you change the key persistence location, the system no longer automatically encrypts keys at rest, since it doesn't know whether DPAPI is an appropriate encryption mechanism. ... You can choose to encrypt keys at rest, but this doesn't prevent cyberattackers from creating new keys. ... Only Redis versions supporting Redis Data Persistence should be used to store keys.

evidence.finding: ABP's distributed lock wraps the Medallion DistributedLock library.
evidence.quote: ABP's current distributed locking implementation is based on the DistributedLock library.

evidence.finding: Enumeration of ABP's OWN internal IAbpDistributedLock use sites  -  answering (c) directly. The list includes StaticPermissionSaver, StaticSettingSaver, StaticFeatureSaver, the three Dynamic*DefinitionStores, OutboxSender, InboxProcessor, BackgroundJobWorker, BackgroundJobCleanupWorker, EfCoreRuntimeDatabaseMigratorBase, EfCoreDatabaseMigrationEventHandlerBase, AbpIdentityUserValidator, and OpenIddict's TokenCleanupBackgroundWorker.
