evidence.finding: ABP's StaticPermissionSaver exists specifically to coordinate MULTIPLE APPLICATION INSTANCES at startup  -  its own comment says so. Without a working lock provider, N instances race to rewrite permission definitions; with one, Redis becomes a startup-path dependency.
evidence.quote: await using var applicationLockHandle = await DistributedLock.TryAcquireAsync(GetApplicationDistributedLockKey()); if (applicationLockHandle == null) { /* Another application instance is already doing it */ return; } ... if (commonLockHandle == null) { /* It will re-try */ throw new AbpException("Could not acquire distributed lock for saving static permissions!"); }

evidence.finding: THE EXACT PATTERN TO COPY FOR (d): ABP's own runtime migrator takes a distributed lock keyed on the database name and cleanly cancels if it cannot get it.
evidence.quote: await using (var handle = await DistributedLock.TryAcquireAsync("DatabaseMigration_" + DatabaseName)) { if (handle is null) { Logger.LogInformation($"Distributed lock could not be acquired for database migration: {DatabaseName}. Operation cancelled."); return; }

evidence.finding: EF Core 9+ auto-locks migrations against concurrent instances  -  BUT the lock covers only UseSeeding delegates, which ABP seed contributors are not. It also now throws on pending model changes, which is a fail-obvious property worth keeping given the two-DbContext hazard. And it explicitly tells you not to migrate from every replica's entrypoint.
evidence.quote: Starting with EF Core 9, MigrateAsync and Migrate automatically acquire a database-wide lock before applying any migrations. This protects against database corruption that could result from multiple application instances running migrations concurrently, which is a common scenario when applying migrations at runtime. The lock is held for the duration of the migration execution, including any seeding code. ... Starting with EF Core 9, calling Migrate() or MigrateAsync() will throw an exception when the model has pending changes compared to the last migration (warning event ID RelationalEventId.PendingModelChangesWarning). ... don't make every application replica run migrations from its entrypoint. Configure the deployment platform not to restart the migration container after it exits successfully. ... Use a separate identity for deployment that has permission to change the schema. The identity used by the application at run time should normally have only the permissions the application needs to read and write data.

evidence.finding: Connection pools are per PROCESS and per CONNECTION STRING, default max 100, and Microsoft names the database-per-tenant pool-fragmentation problem explicitly  -  directly applicable since TenantConnectionStringProvider derives a distinct string per office. Exhaustion queues then throws after 15 s.
evidence.quote: Connections are pooled per process, per application domain, per connection string and when integrated security is used, per Windows identity. ... Connections are added to the pool as needed, up to the maximum pool size specified (100 is the default). ... If the maximum pool size has been reached and no usable connection is available, the request is queued. The pooler then tries to reclaim any connections until the time-out is reached (the default is 15 seconds). If the pooler cannot satisfy the request before the connection times out, an exception is thrown. ... Pool fragmentation due to many databases ... there is a separate pool of connections to each database, which increase the number of connections to the server.

evidence.finding: SQL Server's own ceilings are not the binding constraint on pool growth  -  32,767 user connections and 32,767 databases per instance. The 10 GB container's memory is the real limit.
evidence.quote: User connections | 32,767 ... Databases per instance of SQL Server | 32,767 ... Database size | 524,272 terabytes

evidence.finding: ABP's IDistributedEventBus resolves to LocalDistributedEventBus when no broker provider is registered  -  so with NO message broker in this stack, cross-instance 'distributed' events silently do not propagate at N>1, with no error. This is the subtlest multi-instance hazard.
evidence.quote: [ExposeServices(typeof(IDistributedEventBus), typeof(LocalDistributedEventBus))] public class LocalDistributedEventBus : DistributedEventBusBase, ISingletonDependency

evidence.finding: Counter-evidence for fairness: ABP's tenant-config cache invalidation DOES survive multi-instance, because both TenantStore and its invalidator use IDistributedCache<TenantConfigurationCacheItem>, which is Redis-backed here  -  deleting a key on one node deletes it for all. Cache invalidation through Redis is safe; behaviour triggered by an event handler is not.
evidence.quote: protected IDistributedCache<TenantConfigurationCacheItem> Cache { get; }   -  in both TenantStore.cs and TenantConfigurationCacheItemInvalidator.cs

evidence.finding: Maintenance currency check. Hangfire.SqlServer is very actively maintained (1.8.25 published 2026-08-28; the app's pinned 1.8.21 dates to 2025-08-12, four patches behind). DistributedLock.Redis 1.1.1 published 2025-10-26  -  current. AspNetCore.HealthChecks.UI's latest stable is 9.0.0 published 2024-12-19 with no 10.x for .NET 10  -  this dependency is drifting behind the runtime.
The AspNetCore.Diagnostics.HealthChecks GitHub releases page corroborates the NuGet finding  -  no tagged release since Feb 2024.
evidence.quote: Most recent releases: DotNet 8 (release-all-8.0.0-with-valid-apikey) February 28, 2024; 7.0.1 UI serialization fix July 31, 2023; V7 Release July 31, 2023. No releases documented from 2025 or 2026.

evidence.finding: HIPAA requires the ability to RESTORE, not redundancy. Backup, disaster recovery and emergency mode operation are all Required; testing is only Addressable; high availability is not mentioned. This is the basis for ranking a tested restore above a second instance.
evidence.quote: (7)(i) Standard: Contingency plan. Establish (and implement as needed) policies and procedures for responding to an emergency or other occurrence (for example, fire, vandalism, system failure, and natural disaster) that damages systems that contain electronic protected health information. (ii) Implementation specifications: (A) Data backup plan (Required). Establish and implement procedures to create and maintain retrievable exact copies of electronic protected health information. (B) Disaster recovery plan (Required). Establish (and implement as needed) procedures to restore any loss of data. (C) Emergency mode operation plan (Required). Establish (and implement as needed) procedures to enable continuation of critical business processes for protection of the security of electronic protected health information while operating in emergency mode. (D) Testing and revision procedures (Addressable). Implement procedures for periodic testing and revision of contingency plans. (E) Applications and data criticality analysis (Addressable). Assess the relative criticality of specific applications and data in support of other contingency plan components.

evidence.finding: The four benefits of a web farm, stated by Microsoft  -  used to make the honest case FOR horizontal scale, and the shared-state requirements (Data Protection plus distributed cache) that come with it. Note the doc also names sticky routing as an alternative to a shared key ring, which this system does not need since it already has one.
evidence.quote: Web farms improve: Reliability/availability... Capacity/performance... Scalability... Maintainability... Data Protection and Caching require configuration for apps deployed to a web farm. ... When Data Protection or caching isn't configured for a web farm environment, intermittent errors occur when requests are processed.

evidence.finding: With a single Redis you get a lease-based mutex, not a RedLock guarantee  -  the library's own doc says robustness requires a majority across multiple databases. Adequate for startup definition-saving; NOT adequate for an outbox drain that must never double-send.
evidence.quote: The RedisDistributedLock and RedisDistributedReaderWriterLock classes implement the RedLock algorithm. ... This allows you to increase the robustness of those locks by constructing the lock with a set of databases instead of just a single database. The lock is only considered aquired if it is successfully acquired on more than half of the databases.

questions.question: What must be true of every component in the request path for Host-header tenancy to keep working, and which common infrastructure patterns violate it?
questions.answer:
# HOST-HEADER TENANCY: INVARIANTS AND VIOLATING PATTERNS

## 0. THE HEADLINE CORRECTION (verified, changes the premise of the question)

The source document says ABP registers **four** `__tenant` resolvers and that it has never been tested whether they are disabled. Reading the ABP source directly, the real picture is different in three ways that matter more than the untested caveat.

**(a) There are five default resolvers, not four, and the first one is not a `__tenant` resolver at all.**
`AbpMultiTenancyModule` does `options.TenantResolvers.Insert(0, new CurrentUserTenantResolveContributor())`. `AbpAspNetCoreMultiTenancyModule` then `Add`s QueryString, Route, Header, Cookie. Default order is therefore:

`[CurrentUser, QueryString, Route, Header, Cookie]`

`CurrentUserTenantResolveContributor` reads `ICurrentUser.TenantId`  -  the tenant claim in the access token  -  and sets `Handled = true` whenever the user is authenticated.

**(b) `TenantResolver` is first-match-wins with a hard `break`.** `HasResolvedTenantOrHost()` returns `Handled || TenantIdOrName != null`. Order is therefore decisive and total.

**Consequence, and this is the single most important architectural fact in this answer: for an *authenticated* request, tenancy is decided by the token claim, not by the Host header  -  regardless of what any resolver ordering does, unless `CurrentUser` is explicitly removed.** Host-header tenancy is the mechanism for *anonymous* requests: login and password reset on the AuthServer, anonymous document upload, the public upload path, the partner reconcile endpoint. That is a smaller blast radius than "everything," but it is precisely the set of endpoints that are unauthenticated and security-sensitive.

**(c) The untested question has a precise, cheap answer, and it is not "are the four disabled?"**
`DomainTenantResolveContributor` sets `context.Handled = true` **unconditionally** whenever `Request.Host.HasValue`, *before* returning the match result:

```csharp
context.Handled = true;
return Task.FromResult(extractResult.IsMatch ? extractResult.Matches[0].Value : null);
```

So the domain resolver **terminates the chain** whether or not the host matched. It follows that the query-string, route, header and cookie resolvers are unreachable **if and only if** the custom `HostAwareDomainTenantResolveContributor` is ordered before them and `Host` is non-empty. Whether they were "removed" is irrelevant. The invariant to assert is an **ordering** invariant, and it is testable in about five lines (I11 below).

Two live bypasses follow from this same code:
- **Empty-Host abstention.** If `Request.Host.HasValue` is false, the domain contributor returns *without* setting `Handled`, and the chain continues to QueryString -> Route -> Header -> Cookie. RFC 9112 3.2 explicitly requires a client to send `Host:` with an **empty field value** when the target URI has no authority, and Kestrel permits it (`hostCount > 0`, empty string). An empty `Host` is therefore a documented, spec-legal path to reaching the `__tenant` resolvers.
- **Query-string tenant persists into a cookie.** `MultiTenancyMiddleware` does: if `AppliedResolvers.Contains(QueryString)` then `SetTenantCookie(...)`. One `?__tenant=` request writes a tenant cookie that then drives subsequent requests via the Cookie resolver.

---

## 1. THE INVARIANTS

Stated so each is falsifiable. "Edge" = the outermost component that terminates client TLS.

**I1  -  Host must reach the application byte-identical in its leftmost label.**
The office slug is the leftmost DNS label. Every component may normalise case and may strip a default port, but nothing may alter, add, or remove a label. *Case:* RFC 9110 4.2.3  -  "The scheme and host are case-insensitive and normally provided in lowercase." nginx actively lowercases (`ngx_strlow` in `ngx_http_validate_host`) and strips a trailing dot. ABP's extractor uses `ignoreCase: true`. So case-folding is safe; label rewriting is not.

**I2  -  No non-default port may appear in Host as the application sees it.**
`DomainTenantResolveContributor` matches against `httpContext.Request.Host.Value`, and `HostString.Value` returns the raw value **including the port** (`HostString.Host` is the port-stripped accessor; `.Value` is not). A format of `{0}.api.example.com` will not match `office.api.example.com:8443`. This is a silent whole-tenant outage, not an error. Any port-shifting hop (non-443 listener, port-mapped container, `proxy_set_header Host $host:$proxy_port`) violates this.

**I3  -  Exactly one Host header, and no absolute-form/Host desync.**
RFC 9112 3.2: "A server MUST respond with a 400 (Bad Request) ... to any request message that contains more than one Host header field line or a Host header field with an invalid field value." RFC 9112 3.2.2: for absolute-form, "the origin server MUST ignore the received Host header field (if any) and instead use the host information of the request-target." Kestrel implements the safe reading: `ValidateNonOriginHostHeader` throws `InvalidHostHeader` when absolute-form authority != Host, unless `KestrelServerOptions.AllowHostHeaderOverride` is true (default `false`  -  no initializer). **Invariant: `AllowHostHeaderOverride` must remain false, and the edge must reject multi-Host and obs-fold-wrapped Host before forwarding.**

**I4  -  Every hop must derive "host" from the same field.**
This is the desync invariant and it is the one most likely to bite here. nginx's `$host` is documented as: "in this order of precedence: **host name from the request line**, or host name from the 'Host' request header field, or the server name matching a request." Kestrel derives `Request.Host` from the Host header and *rejects* a mismatching absolute-form. So nginx and Kestrel resolve "host" from **different sources** under absolute-form, and nginx silently falls back to `server_name` when Host is absent  -  for a wildcard block that is the literal wildcard string. `$http_host` is the raw header but is empty when absent. **Neither `$host` nor `$http_host` is unconditionally correct; the edge must validate first and then forward a known-good value.**

**I5  -  X-Forwarded-Host must be explicitly decided, and the decision must be "strip at the edge."**
ASP.NET Core does not process it by default (`ForwardedHeadersOptions.ForwardedHeaders` has no initializer -> `ForwardedHeaders.None`). If `XForwardedHost` is ever enabled, `ForwardedHeadersMiddleware` **overwrites** `request.Host` from the header, gated only by `AllowedHosts` (empty = all allowed) and `KnownProxies` (default: IPv6 loopback only). The framework's own remark: "Failing to restrict this these values may allow an attacker to spoof links generated by your service." Because the domain resolver reads `Request.Host`, enabling `XForwardedHost` without an allow-list converts a header into a tenant selector.

**I6  -  TLS SNI and Host must be consistent at the edge, but SNI must never be used to route or to authorise.**
RFC 9113 9.1.1: HTTP/2 connections "MAY be reused for requests with multiple different URI authority components" as long as the certificate is valid for the host. **A wildcard certificate covering `*.<base>` is exactly the condition that makes browsers coalesce `office1` and `office2` onto one TLS connection.** The RFC warns explicitly: "TLS termination might be performed by a middlebox that uses the TLS Server Name Indication extension to select an origin server. This means that it is possible for clients to send requests to servers that might not be the intended target." So SNI != `:authority` is *legitimate and expected* here. The application must key tenancy off `:authority`/Host only, and any component that pins a connection to a tenant by SNI is wrong. The documented remedy for a server that cannot serve the requested origin is **421 Misdirected Request**.

**I7  -  HTTP/2 `:authority` is authoritative; Host is not.**
RFC 9113 8.3.1: "The recipient of an HTTP/2 request MUST NOT use the Host header field to determine the target URI if ':authority' is present," and "An intermediary that needs to generate a Host header field ... MUST use the value from the ':authority' pseudo-header field ... **This replaces any existing Host field to avoid potential vulnerabilities in HTTP routing.**" Note Kestrel's `AllowHostHeaderOverride` "does not apply to HTTP/2 or HTTP/3"  -  the h1 protection is not the h2 protection. Any h1h2 translation hop must be checked separately.

**I8  -  Redirects and generated absolute URLs must carry the office host.**
This is where the tenancy design and the identity design intersect. Microsoft's guidance: "If you use a different host name at the reverse proxy than the one that's provided to the back-end application server can cause cookies or redirect URLs to not work properly." For this system specifically: OIDC redirect URIs, email-confirmation and password-reset links (already subdomain-scoped and already generating support incidents), and cookie `Domain` attributes all derive from the incoming host. A host rewrite anywhere breaks the OIDC flow between the `{office}.auth` and `{office}.api` hosts, and it breaks them *silently*  -  Microsoft's own note on the cookie case: "These problems don't generate an error and aren't directly visible to the end user, which makes them difficult to troubleshoot."

**I9  -  Health probes must carry a resolvable office host.** See 3  -  this has a concrete answer.

**I10  -  The edge must be closed by default: an unrecognised Host is rejected at the edge, not resolved by the application.**
Today the apex falls through to the first 443 block (AuthServer) and `api.<base>` with no office label falls through to the Angular container. Both are Host-driven misroutes caused by absent `default_server`. The invariant is that exactly one server block owns "everything unmatched" and it returns a terminal status.

**I11  -  The resolver chain order must be asserted in code, not assumed.**
The testable form, which is the smallest thing that converts an untested assumption into a guarded one:

```csharp
var names = options.TenantResolvers.Select(r => r.Name).ToList();
Assert.Equal(0, names.IndexOf("HostAwareDomain"));   // must be first
Assert.DoesNotContain(QueryStringTenantResolveContributor.ContributorName, names);
Assert.DoesNotContain(HeaderTenantResolveContributor.ContributorName, names);
Assert.DoesNotContain(CookieTenantResolveContributor.ContributorName, names);
Assert.DoesNotContain(RouteTenantResolveContributor.ContributorName, names);
```
Removing them outright is strictly better than relying on ordering, because it also closes the empty-Host abstention path (see 0c). Decide `CurrentUser` deliberately: keeping it means the token claim outranks the host; removing it means a token issued for office A is usable against office B's host. **Keep `CurrentUser` first**  -  my reasoning, not a sourced claim: it is the only thing currently preventing a valid office-A token from being replayed against office-B's hostname.

**I12  -  Host must never be the sole authority for a privileged scope.**
The `admin` slug resolves to host scope purely from a header. Microsoft states the general rule flatly: "**Never use the value of the host in a security mechanism.** The browser or another user agent provides the value, and a user can change it." OWASP WSTG-INPV-17 documents this exact scenario as "Accessing Private Virtual Hosts": a vhost not resolvable in public DNS is still reachable by setting the Host header, or by a hosts-file entry pointing the private name at the public IP. **`admin.<base>`, `admin.api.<base>` and `admin.auth.<base>` are reachable today by Host spoofing from anywhere that can reach port 443, with no DNS record required.** This is the highest-severity finding in this document.

---

## 2. VIOLATING PATTERNS (documented behaviour, cited)

**P1  -  Reverse proxies that rewrite Host to the backend address by default.**
nginx: "**Default: `proxy_set_header Host $proxy_host;`**"  -  "By default, the header fields 'Host' and 'Connection' from the original request are not passed to the proxied server." Also: "For HTTP/2, the ':authority' pseudo-header field with the `$proxy_host` value is sent by default." A bare `proxy_pass` with no `proxy_set_header Host` sends the *upstream name* and every request resolves to the same wrong tenant or to none. (Their current config evidently sets it, since the system works  -  but this is one deleted line from a fleet-wide outage, and one that would fail *uniformly*, therefore obviously. That is the good failure mode.)

**P2  -  L7 load balancers with a host-override setting.**
Azure Application Gateway: **"Pick host name from backend address"**  -  "This capability dynamically sets the *host* header in the request to the host name of the backend pool"; and **"Host name override"**  -  "replaces the *host* header in the incoming request ... with the host name that you specify." Microsoft's own architecture guidance calls this out as the anti-pattern: "Application Gateway makes it easy to override the host header with the host of the back-end pool."

**P3  -  CDNs that set Host to the origin hostname.**
CloudFront, verbatim from the request-headers table: "**`Host`  -  CloudFront sets the value to the domain name of the origin that is associated with the requested object.**" Azure Front Door: "If you use the Azure portal to configure your origin, the default value for this field is the host name of the origin."
**Sources disagree here and it matters:** the Front Door *origin* doc says that if you use ARM templates "or another method without explicitly setting this field, Front Door sends the incoming host name," whereas the Architecture Center doc says "Azure Front Door does this process by default" (i.e. overrides). The reconciliation is that the *portal* pre-populates the override while the *API* leaves it null  -  meaning **the same product preserves or destroys tenancy depending on which tool created the resource.** That is a configuration-drift failure mode invisible in code review.

**P4  -  API gateways that route by path and rewrite host.**
Azure API Management: "**By default, API Management overrides the host name that's sent to the back end with the host component of the API's web service URL.**" Restoring the original requires an explicit inbound policy (`<set-header name="Host">@(context.Request.OriginalUrl.Host)</set-header>`). The general shape  -  gateway defined in terms of a *backend URL*  -  makes host rewriting the default because the backend URL supplies the authority.

**P5  -  Service meshes and sidecars.**
Envoy `RouteAction.host_rewrite_specifier`: `host_rewrite_literal` ("the host header will be swapped with this value"), `auto_host_rewrite` ("swapped with the hostname of the upstream host chosen by the cluster manager"), `host_rewrite_header` ("swapped with the content of given downstream ... header"  -  Envoy's own warning: "Pay attention to the potential security implications of using this option. Provided header must come from trusted source"), and `host_rewrite_path_regex`. Istio surfaces the same as `HTTPRewrite.authority`: "rewrite the Authority/Host header with this value." Envoy/Istio *preserve* Host by default; the hazard is that a single route-level field, often added for an unrelated reason, silently re-tenants every request through it.

**P6  -  Path-based routing that collapses subdomains.**
Envoy documents `host_rewrite_path_regex` as "useful for transitioning variable content between path segment and subdomain"  -  the machinery for exactly this migration exists and is one config block away. GCP URL maps: `UrlRewrite.hostRewrite`  -  "Before forwarding the request to the selected service, the request's host header is replaced with contents of hostRewrite." Any move to `/{office}/...` routing destroys the tenancy input outright.

**P7  -  Kubernetes ingress annotations.**
ingress-nginx sets `proxy_set_header Host $host` by default (safe), but `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/upstream-vhost` "allows you to control the value for host in the following statement: `proxy_set_header Host $host`." One annotation on one Ingress silently re-tenants that path.

**P8  -  TLS-terminating firewalls/WAFs that validate Host against DNS.**
Microsoft: "If you have a next-generation firewall like Azure Firewall Premium between the reverse proxy and the final back end, you might need to use split-horizon DNS. This type of firewall **might explicitly check whether the HTTP `Host` header resolves to the target IP address**." Under host-preservation the office host resolves to the *edge*, not the backend  -  so such a device rejects every request unless split-horizon DNS is introduced. That is a second DNS zone to maintain, which for a two-person team is a real operational cost, not a footnote.

**P9  -  Bare-IP health checks.** See 3.

**P10  -  Anything that trusts a client-supplied override header.**
`X-Forwarded-Host` is the canonical case (I5). PortSwigger: "When an `X-Forwarded-Host` header is present, many frameworks will refer to this instead," letting an attacker "inject your malicious input while circumventing any validation on the Host header itself."

---

## 3. THE HEALTH CHECK PROBLEM  -  CONCRETE ANSWER

A bare IP cannot reach this application. Every probe mechanism below therefore has to be told the host explicitly. The mechanisms are documented and differ by class:

| Component class | Default probe Host | Can Host be set? | Documented mechanism |
|---|---|---|---|
| Kubernetes kubelet | **Pod IP** | **Yes** | `httpGet.httpHeaders: [{name: Host, value: ...}]` |
| GCP health checks | **Destination IP** | **Yes** | `host` field / `--host` flag |
| Azure App Gateway | backend address | **Yes** | custom probe, disable "pick host name", set host |
| Azure Front Door | origin host header | Indirectly | probe inherits `originHostHeader` |
| **AWS ALB** | target IP | **No** | *no such setting exists* |
| Docker/Compose | n/a (arbitrary cmd) | **Yes** | `test: ["CMD", "curl", "-H", "Host: ..."]` |

Sources, in order of how load-bearing they are:

- **Kubernetes** `HTTPGetAction.Host`: "Host name to connect to, **defaults to the pod IP. You probably want to set 'Host' in httpHeaders instead.**" Confirmed at implementation level  -  kubelet's prober does `req.Host = headers.Get("Host")`, and Go's `Request.Host` overrides the wire Host header. So the httpHeaders mechanism genuinely works.
- **GCP**: "The value of the host header in the HTTP health check request. **If left empty (default value), the host header is set to the destination IP address to which health check packets are sent.**" (identical text for HTTP, HTTPS and HTTP/2 health checks).
- **AWS ALB**: the documented settings are exhaustively `HealthCheckProtocol`, `HealthCheckPort`, `HealthCheckPath`, `HealthCheckTimeoutSeconds`, `HealthCheckIntervalSeconds`, `HealthyThresholdCount`, `UnhealthyThresholdCount`, `Matcher`. **There is no Host setting.** Targets register by instance ID or IP. This is the concrete "component that requires a bare-IP health check."
- **Azure**, stating the general principle better than anyone: "**Because health probes are sent outside the context of an incoming request, they can't dynamically determine the correct host name.** Instead, create a custom health probe, turn off 'Pick host name from back-end HTTP settings', and explicitly specify the host name."

**What the health-check design has to look like here  -  the answer:**

1. **Expose liveness/readiness on a path that is reachable before tenant resolution.** ABP's `MultiTenancyMiddleware` calls `_tenantConfigurationProvider.GetAsync()` and, on failure, invokes `MultiTenancyMiddlewareErrorPageBuilder`, which for a non-AJAX GET renders an error page. A health endpoint mapped *after* that middleware inherits tenancy failure as probe failure. **Map health endpoints before `UseMultiTenancy()`, or branch them out with `Map`/`MapWhen` so the multi-tenancy middleware never runs for them.** This is the single change that makes the whole problem go away, and it is the one I would make first.
2. **If a probe must traverse tenant resolution, give it a real office host explicitly.** Never `localhost`, never an IP. Note the Compose spec's own canonical example is `test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "http://localhost"]`  -  which sends `Host: localhost` and returns "Tenant not found" on this stack. Correct form: `test: ["CMD", "curl", "-fsS", "-H", "Host: admin.api.<base>", "http://127.0.0.1:8080/health"]`  -  the connection goes to the loopback address, the *Host header* carries the resolvable name. Connection target and Host are independent, and that separation is the whole trick.
3. **Constrain the platform rather than the app.** State it as a capability requirement: *the platform must allow the Host header of an HTTP health probe to be set independently of the probe's connection target.* Classes that satisfy this: Kubernetes probes, GCP health checks, Azure App Gateway custom probes, any container runtime running an arbitrary command. A class that does not: AWS-ALB-style LBs with a fixed settings list. If a platform cannot do it, the fallback is (1)  -  a tenancy-exempt health path  -  which is why (1) is worth doing regardless of platform.
4. **Two distinct checks, because they answer different questions.** A tenancy-exempt liveness check ("is the process up") and *at least one* tenancy-exercising synthetic check against a real office host ("does tenant resolution still work"). Only the second one catches a Host-rewriting proxy. Given no monitoring exists at all today, the second one is also the cheapest possible early-warning system for the entire class of failure this document describes  -  a single cron'd curl asserting that `{office}.api` returns the right tenant, and that `admin.api` from outside does not.

---

## 4. MAKING HOST *TRUSTWORTHY*, NOT MERELY *PRESERVED*

Preservation and trustworthiness are different properties, and this system currently has neither guaranteed. Microsoft's rule  -  "Never use the value of the host in a security mechanism"  -  is in direct tension with a design that selects a *database* from the Host header. The tension is resolvable, but only by making the edge, not the application, the authority on which hosts exist.

The edge must:

1. **Allow-list, don't pass through.** Terminate TLS and match `Host` against an explicit set of known office hosts. Anything else gets a terminal response at the edge. Currently there is no `default_server` on 443, so unmatched hosts fall through to whichever block is first  -  the AuthServer for the apex. Reject unknown hosts at the edge and the application never sees a host it does not recognise.
2. **Block `admin.*` from the public listener entirely.** This is I12 and it is the priority item. Host scope must not be selectable by a header from the internet. Bind it to a separate listener, a VPN/private network, or mTLS. A code fix to the Hangfire dashboard does not address this  -  `admin` reaches *every* host-scoped surface, not just `/hangfire`.
3. **Strip `X-Forwarded-Host` (and `X-Original-Host`, `Forwarded`) from client requests unconditionally at the edge.** PortSwigger and OWASP both list it as the standard bypass for Host validation. Strip inbound, set outbound.
4. **Reject ambiguous requests before they reach Kestrel.** Duplicate `Host` headers, obs-fold/indented `Host`, absolute-form request lines. PortSwigger documents all three as front-end/back-end desync techniques, and note nginx's `$host` prefers the *request line* while Kestrel prefers the *header*  -  the desync is real between the two components actually in this stack, not theoretical.
5. **Keep `AllowHostHeaderOverride = false`** (it is the default; the invariant is to never set it true).
6. **Defend in depth below the edge.** Add ASP.NET Core `HostFilteringMiddleware` with an explicit `AllowedHosts` list. Note it reads `Request.Headers.Host` (the raw header) whereas the ABP resolver reads `Request.Host` (the parsed/possibly-forwarded value)  -  they can diverge, so this is genuinely a second check and not a duplicate of the edge one. A wrong Host then produces a 400 rather than a wrong tenant. **This is the "fails obviously rather than subtly" choice**, which for a two-SDE-1 team with no monitoring is worth more than elegance.
7. **Return 421 Misdirected Request** where a connection is reused for an origin this instance will not serve (RFC 9113 9.1.1)  -  the documented, client-understood signal, and specifically relevant because the wildcard certificate makes cross-office connection coalescing expected browser behaviour.

---

## 5. WHAT NOT TO BUILD (explicitly rejected)

- **Do not add a service mesh.** It introduces `auto_host_rewrite`/`rewrite.authority`  -  an entire new class of silent re-tenanting  -  to solve problems this single-instance, no-SignalR, no-broker system does not have. Operational complexity is a first-class cost here.
- **Do not move to path-based routing** (`/{office}/...`). It deletes the tenancy input, and the whole `TenantConnectionStringProvider` slug-derivation scheme with it.
- **Do not add a CDN in front of the API or AuthServer.** The documented default for CloudFront is to overwrite Host with the origin domain; the API serves no cacheable content; and PHI plus a shared cache keyed on a header you also route by is the web-cache-poisoning shape OWASP documents.
- **Do not solve host preservation with `X-Forwarded-Host` and `ForwardedHeaders.XForwardedHost`.** It converts a header into a tenant selector and depends on `AllowedHosts` + `KnownProxies` being correct forever. Preserve the real Host instead.
- **Do not rely on SNI for routing or authorisation.** RFC 9113 9.1.1 documents SNI-based origin selection as a *known cause of misdirected requests*, and the wildcard certificate maximises the exposure.
- **Do not "fix" health checks by exempting the probe path from authentication while leaving it inside tenant resolution.** That produces a probe that passes when tenancy is broken  -  the failure mode the team is least equipped to notice.

## 6. VIABILITY UNDER THE TEAM CONSTRAINT

Per the instruction to give thresholds rather than assume the one-developer-week figure: the edge allow-list, the `admin` block, the header-stripping rules and the resolver-ordering test are **a few hours of work, one-time, and then static**  -  they do not decay with low staffing, because they are configuration that fails loudly when wrong. That is why I have concentrated the recommendations there. By contrast, **split-horizon DNS (P8) and any synthetic-monitoring fleet need roughly 4+ hours/month of sustained attention; below that they decay into stale records and ignored alerts**, at which point split-horizon DNS becomes an active hazard (requests silently resolving to the wrong place) rather than a control. If the available time is under that threshold, prefer the tenancy-exempt health path from 3(1) plus a single cron'd assertion, and avoid architectures that require a firewall doing Host-to-IP validation.
questions.reasoning: I established the range of viable designs from the protocol layer up before comparing against this system, as the method requirement demanded, which is what surfaced the findings the team could not have found by starting from their own config. The most consequential result came from reading ABP's actual source rather than its prose documentation: the framework registers five default resolvers, not four, and inserts `CurrentUserTenantResolveContributor` at index 0, so for authenticated requests the tenant comes from the token claim and the Host header is not consulted at all  -  which means the source document's framing of "Host header only" overstates the mechanism's reach while understating its exposure on anonymous endpoints. Reading `TenantResolver` confirmed first-match-wins with a hard `break`, and reading `DomainTenantResolveContributor` showed it sets `Handled = true` unconditionally whenever Host is non-empty, which converts the team's open question ("are the four `__tenant` resolvers disabled?") into a strictly simpler and testable ordering question, plus two concrete bypasses they have not identified: the empty-Host abstention path and the query-string-to-cookie tenant persistence in `MultiTenancyMiddleware`. I verified the absolute-form question at implementation level rather than asserting it, finding that Kestrel rejects absolute-form/Host mismatches by default via `ValidateNonOriginHostHeader` unless `AllowHostHeaderOverride` is set, while nginx's `$host` prefers the request line  -  so the desync risk in this specific stack is *between the two components they already run*, not hypothetical. The health-check question does have the concrete answer the prompt expected: I found the documented default and override mechanism for each component class from primary sources, including Kubernetes stating "defaults to the pod IP" in its API types and kubelet's prober implementing `req.Host = headers.Get("Host")`, GCP stating the host header defaults to the destination IP, and AWS ALB's settings table containing no Host option at all. Microsoft's host-name-preservation guidance turned out to be the single best architecture reference for this problem and I cross-referenced it against the Front Door and Application Gateway product docs, where I found a genuine disagreement about Front Door's default behaviour that I have reported rather than smoothed over, because its practical implication  -  portal-created and API-created resources behaving differently  -  is itself a finding. On the security dimension, OWASP's "Accessing Private Virtual Hosts" section maps exactly onto the reserved `admin` slug, which I judge the highest-severity item here because it is reachable from anywhere that can reach port 443, needs no DNS record, and is not addressed by the planned Hangfire code fix; I have flagged that as my assessment rather than a sourced conclusion. Two things I want to be explicit about as judgement rather than fact: the recommendation to keep `CurrentUser` first (my reasoning is that it prevents cross-office token replay, but it is a trade-off, not a derivation), and the port-in-Host invariant, which I inferred from reading that ABP matches on `HostString.Value` and then verified in the ASP.NET Core source that `.Value` retains the port while `.Host` strips it. Throughout I weighted recommendations toward controls that fail loudly and stay static once set, because the stated team constraint makes a subtle-failure control worse than no control, and I gave an explicit hours-per-month threshold for the two recommendations whose viability actually turns on sustained attention.
questions.the_binding_constraint: Resolver ORDER inside the application binds before anything at the edge does. Because ABP's `TenantResolver` is first-match-wins with a hard `break`, and `DomainTenantResolveContributor` sets `Handled = true` unconditionally whenever `Request.Host` is non-empty, the entire question of whether the four `__tenant` resolvers are "disabled" collapses into whether the custom domain contributor is ordered ahead of them. If it is first, they are unreachable for any request carrying a non-empty Host, whether or not anyone removed them. If it was registered with `.Add(...)` it lands LAST  -  after QueryString, Route, Header and Cookie  -  and `?__tenant=<guid>` silently outranks the hostname on every anonymous request, with `MultiTenancyMiddleware` then persisting that choice into a cookie. This binds before the edge hardening because no amount of Host validation at nginx constrains a query-string parameter, and it binds before the health-check work because it is a live cross-tenant data-access path rather than an availability concern. It is also, unusually, the cheapest thing on the list to settle: it is a single assertion over `AbpTenantResolveOptions.TenantResolvers`, requiring no infrastructure change, no downtime, and no platform decision  -  which is exactly why it should not wait for the platform-selection exercise that follows this one.

In most cases, you shouldn't override the host name. ... Because health probes are sent outside the context of an incoming request, they can't dynamically determine the correct host name. Instead, create a custom health probe, turn off Pick host name from back-end HTTP settings, and explicitly specify the host name. ... By default, API Management overrides the host name that's sent to the back end with the host component of the API's web service URL ... This type of firewall might explicitly check whether the HTTP Host header resolves to the target IP address.

evidence.finding: Envoy exposes four route-level host rewrite mechanisms, including one driven by a downstream header (with an explicit security warning) and one that maps a path segment into the subdomain.
evidence.quote: string host_rewrite_literal  -  Indicates that during forwarding, the host header will be swapped with this value. ... google.protobuf.BoolValue auto_host_rewrite  -  Indicates that during forwarding, the host header will be swapped with the hostname of the upstream host chosen by the cluster manager. ... string host_rewrite_header  -  Indicates that during forwarding, the host header will be swapped with the content of given downstream or custom header. ... Pay attention to the potential security implications of using this option. Provided header must come from trusted source. ... host_rewrite_path_regex ... This is useful for transitioning variable content between path segment and subdomain.

evidence.finding: Istio exposes authority (Host) rewriting as a first-class VirtualService field.

message HTTPRewrite { ... // rewrite the Authority/Host header with this value.
  string authority = 2;

evidence.finding: ingress-nginx preserves Host by default but exposes a single annotation that overrides it per-Ingress.
evidence.quote: Custom NGINX upstream vhost  -  This configuration setting allows you to control the value for host in the following statement: proxy_set_header Host $host, which forms part of the location block. This is useful if you need to call the upstream server by something other than $host.

evidence.finding: GCP URL maps replace the Host header via hostRewrite when path-based routing rewrites are used.
evidence.quote: hostRewrite: Before forwarding the request to the selected service, the request's host header is replaced with contents of hostRewrite.

evidence.finding: PortSwigger documents the four ambiguous-Host techniques the edge must reject: duplicate Host headers, absolute-URL request line, line-wrapped/indented Host, and X-Forwarded-Host override.
evidence.quote: GET /example HTTP/1.1 Host: vulnerable-website.com Host: bad-stuff-here  -  Different systems and technologies will handle this case differently, but it is common for one of the two headers to be given precedence over the other one, effectively overriding its value. ... The ambiguity caused by supplying both an absolute URL and a Host header can also lead to discrepancies between different systems. Officially, the request line should be given precedence when routing the request but, in practice, this isn't always the case. ... Some servers will interpret the indented header as a wrapped line ... When an X-Forwarded-Host header is present, many frameworks will refer to this instead.

evidence.finding: OWASP WSTG-INPV-17 documents 'Accessing Private Virtual Hosts'  -  a vhost not resolvable in public DNS is still reachable by setting the Host header. This maps directly onto the reserved 'admin' host-scope slug.
evidence.quote: In some cases a server may have virtual hosts that are not intended to be externally accessible. ... Although it would not be possible to browse directly to intranet.example.org from outside the network (as the domain would not resolve), it may be possible to access to Intranet by making a request from outside with the following Host header: Host: intranet.example.org ... This could also be achieved by adding an entry for intranet.example.org to your hosts file with the public IP address of www.example.org

evidence.finding: PortSwigger's stated root cause and prevention list, including disabling host override headers and validating against an allow-list.
evidence.quote: HTTP Host header vulnerabilities typically arise due to the flawed assumption that the header is not user controllable. ... Prevention: ... Validating Host headers against whitelists; Disabling host override header support like X-Forwarded-Host; Configuring load balancers to only forward to permitted domains

questions.question: What does per-office (per-tenant) point-in-time restore require in a database-per-tenant SQL Server deployment with a shared host database, and what must the backup architecture therefore provide?
questions.answer:
# PER-OFFICE RESTORE: DETERMINATE ANSWER

## 0. The one-sentence answer

Restoring one office to a point in time requires **that office's database to be in the FULL recovery model with an unbroken full -> (differential) -> log chain**, a **tail-log backup taken before you overwrite anything**, and a restore sequence in which `STOPAT` is repeated on *every* `RESTORE LOG`; the instance and all other offices stay online throughout. That is the easy half. The hard half is that **an office's state is not contained in the office database**  -  it is spread across the host database (tenant registry, Hangfire, host identity), Redis (permissions, sessions, DataProtection keyring), MinIO (documents and packets), an SMTP relay, and the Case Tracker partner system, **none of which roll back with it**. So the backup architecture must provide per-database PITR *plus a documented reconciliation procedure*, because SQL Server's only mechanism for genuinely consistent multi-database point-in-time recovery  -  marked transactions  -  is the wrong tool for this team and I reject it below with reasons.

---

## 1. Recovery models: what each permits (SOURCED)

Microsoft Learn, *Recovery Models (SQL Server)* (accessed 2026-08-31):

| Model | Point-in-time restore? |
|---|---|
| **Simple** | "Can recover only to the end of a backup." The page lists "Point-in-time restores" under features you **cannot** use. |
| **Full** | "Can recover to a specific point in time, assuming that your backups are complete up to that point in time." |
| **Bulk-logged** | "Can recover to the end of any backup. **Point-in-time recovery isn't supported.**" |

**FULL is required.** Bulk-logged is not a partial substitute: *Restore and Recovery Overview* states point-in-time restore under bulk-logged is "Disallowed if the log backup contains any bulk-logged changes," and the PITR page warns that in that case "the database must be recovered to the end of the transaction log backup." A single index rebuild performed while a database is temporarily in bulk-logged mode therefore creates a log backup you cannot stop *inside*, silently, for that database only.

### The finding this generates, which is specific to this system

Recovery model is a **per-database property**, and *Recovery Models* states: "SQL Server Enterprise and Standard editions use the *full* recovery model by default, while SQL Server Express edition uses the *simple* recovery model by default," and *Set database recovery model* states: "The `model` database sets the default recovery model of new databases."

In this platform, **a new office database is created by a business action, not a deployment**  -  `IOfficeDatabaseProvisioner.ProvisionAsync` calls EF Core `Database.MigrateAsync()`, which issues `CREATE DATABASE`, which inherits from `model`. Consequences:

1. **Whether every office has point-in-time capability is decided by the state of `model` at the moment a non-engineer clicked "add office" in the host UI.** Nothing surfaces this. An office provisioned while `model` was SIMPLE has no PITR, forever, and no error is ever raised.
2. *Set database recovery model* further states: "Immediately after switching to the full recovery model or bulk-logged recovery model, take a full or differential database backup to start the log chain. **The switch to the full or bulk-logged recovery model takes effect only after the first data backup.**" So a freshly provisioned office in FULL is still effectively unprotected until its first full backup runs.

**Therefore: backup enrolment must be part of provisioning, not part of a schedule.** `ProvisionAsync` must (a) assert `ALTER DATABASE ... SET RECOVERY FULL`, (b) take an immediate full backup, and (c) fail the provisioning if either fails. This is idempotent, matching the existing provisioner contract. This is the single most under-appreciated requirement in the whole question: *the business can create a database faster than the backup system can notice it exists.*

### The ordering hazard (do not get this wrong)

FULL recovery **without** log backups causes the log to grow until the disk fills  -  *Set database recovery model*: "**Back up your logs.** If you do not back up the log frequently enough, the transaction log can expand until it runs out of disk space." On a box with ~9.7 GB free on a shared disk, this is not a nuisance, it is a total outage of SQL Server, MinIO and the backup directory simultaneously. **Switch recovery models and enable log backups as one atomic change**, and monitor `sys.databases.log_reuse_wait_desc = 'LOG_BACKUP'` afterwards.

---

## 2. The documented restore sequence, and what breaks the chain (SOURCED)

### Sequence

*Restore a SQL Server Database to a Point in Time (Full Recovery Model)*:

> "As a prerequisite to a point-in-time restore, you must first restore a full database backup whose endpoint is earlier than your target restore time. That full database backup can be older than the most recent full database backup **as long as you then restore every subsequent log backup, up to and including the log backup that contains your target point in time.**"

> "A specified time is always restored from a log backup. **In every RESTORE LOG statement of the restore sequence, you must specify your target time or transaction in an identical STOPAT clause.**"

The documented order: tail-log backup of the live database -> `RESTORE DATABASE ... WITH NORECOVERY` -> most recent differential `WITH NORECOVERY` -> each log backup in creation order `WITH STOPAT = <time>, NORECOVERY` -> `RESTORE DATABASE ... WITH RECOVERY`.

**Source inconsistency I must report:** on that same page, prose step 4 reads `RESTORE DATABASE database_name FROM <backup_device> WITH STOPAT = time, RECOVERY`  -  naming `RESTORE DATABASE` where it means `RESTORE LOG`, and `RECOVERY` on each log. The T-SQL example immediately below it uses `RESTORE LOG ... NORECOVERY, STOPAT` on each log and a final `RESTORE DATABASE ... WITH RECOVERY`. **The example is correct; the prose is wrong.** Anyone building a runbook from the prose will recover after the first log and be unable to apply the rest.

Also sourced and useful for the runbook: the page's own Recommendations are "Use STANDBY to find unknown point in time" and "Specify the point in time early in a restore sequence." `WITH STANDBY` leaves the database readable between log applications, which is how you *locate* the moment of a logical error when all you know is "sometime Tuesday."

### The tail-log requirement

*RESTORE (Transact-SQL)*: "For a database using the full or bulk-logged recovery model, **in most cases you must back up the tail of the log before restoring the database.** Restoring a database without first backing up the tail of the log results in an error, unless the RESTORE DATABASE statement contains either the WITH REPLACE or the WITH STOPAT clause."

Read that inversely: **`WITH REPLACE` is the option that lets you destroy the current state without preserving it.** The same page: "The REPLACE option overrides several important safety checks that restore normally performs... With the REPLACE option, you can lose committed work, because the log written most recently has not been backed up." In a PHI system, the "committed work you lose" is also **the audit trail of the period you are erasing**. `REPLACE` must be banned from the runbook except in one scripted, reviewed place.

### What breaks the log chain

- **Switching the database to SIMPLE**, even briefly. *Set database recovery model* -> after switching back you must "take a full or differential database backup to start the log chain," and the switch "takes effect only after the first data backup." Everything between the switch to SIMPLE and that new base is unreachable by PITR.
- **A missing or deleted log backup file.** The chain requirement is "every subsequent log backup"  -  a gap truncates your recoverable window at the gap.
- **Bulk-logged operations**, which do not break the chain but make PITR *inside* the affected log backup illegal (cited above).
- **Recovering the database (`WITH RECOVERY`) mid-sequence**, which ends roll-forward: *Restore and Recovery Overview*, "After rollback, the database goes online, and **no more transaction log backups can be applied to the database**." Restoring to a point in time also creates a recovery fork; the same page describes the Recovery Advisor handling "forking scenarios in point-in-time restores" and "traversing a forked recovery path."

### What does NOT break it (this matters for restore-to-verify)

An **extra full backup does not break the log chain**  -  it only reseeds the differential base. *Copy-Only Backups*: "A copy-only *full* backup can't serve as a differential base or differential backup and **doesn't affect the differential base**." So any ad-hoc backup taken to feed a verification restore must be `WITH COPY_ONLY`, otherwise the ad-hoc backup silently orphans your scheduled differentials.

---

## 3. Can one database be restored while the others stay online? YES (SOURCED)

*Restore and Recovery Overview*: complete database restore means "The whole database is restored and recovered, and **the database** is offline during the restore and recovery operations"  -  singular, scoped to the restore target.

*RESTORE (Transact-SQL)*: "During an offline restore, **if the specified database is in use, RESTORE forces the users off** after a short delay... Any data in the specified database is replaced by the restored data." Locking section: "Takes an exclusive lock on the **DATABASE** object."

So the blast radius of a per-office restore is exactly one office. **This is the payoff of the database-per-tenant decision, and it is the property the backup architecture must not throw away.**

Caveats that are real but not blockers:

- *RESTORE*: "Restoring a database clears the plan cache **for the database being restored**," causing a temporary recompile cost for that office only.
- Instance-level contention is shared: 4 vCPU, one SQL container with `MSSQL_MEMORY_LIMIT_MB 7168`, one disk. A restore is IO-heavy; other offices will feel it. It is a performance event, not a correctness event.
- **Application behaviour is the missing piece.** When the office database goes offline, pooled EF connections break and the API will emit a stream of SQL exceptions for `{office}.api.<base>` while other offices serve normally. That fails obviously but *messily*. Add an application-level per-office maintenance flag so the office returns a clean 503 during restore. (My recommendation, not sourced.)

### The asymmetry nobody names: restoring the HOST database is a full outage

Tenancy resolves from the Host header and then needs the tenant registry, which lives in the host database. Take the host database offline and **every office goes down**, including offices you were not trying to fix. And because Hangfire storage is the host `Default` connection string, restoring the host database **rewinds the job system**: completed jobs return, in-flight state is rolled back, recurring-job watermarks move backwards.

**Capability requirement:** background-job state must be restorable  -  or discardable  -  independently of the tenant registry. Today one `RESTORE` decision is forced to serve two things with opposite recovery semantics: the registry must be recovered exactly; the job queue would usually rather be thrown away and rebuilt. Co-locating them in one database is a backup-architecture defect, not just a tidiness one.

---

## 4. How backups scale with N databases: what actually binds

**Sequential vs parallel  -  SQL Server permits either.** *Backup Overview* lists the only concurrency restrictions as file-management operations (`ALTER DATABASE ADD FILE`/`REMOVE FILE`) and shrink operations; backups otherwise run online alongside `INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE`. Nothing forbids concurrent backups of different databases.

**A trap in the sources, flagged deliberately:** *RESTORE (Transact-SQL)* contains the line "Only one RESTORE DATABASE or BACKUP DATABASE statement can be running on the appliance at any given time." That sentence is inside the **Analytics Platform System (PDW)** section and does **not** apply to box SQL Server. It is exactly the kind of line that gets quoted out of context into an architecture document.

**What binds here, in order:**

1. **Free space and write bandwidth at the destination.** One disk with ~9.7 GB free, and the current script writes to `./backups` on that same disk. This binds before anything else and it binds *today*.
2. **CPU**, if `COMPRESSION` is on (supported on Standard per *Editions and Supported Features of SQL Server 2025*), on a 4-vCPU box also running the API, AuthServer, packet renderer, Redis, MinIO and nginx.
3. **Backup buffer memory**  -  `BUFFERCOUNT x MAXTRANSFERSIZE` per backup operation, multiplied by concurrency, inside a container capped at 10 GB. (Documented as backup options; the multiplication is my inference.)
4. **At 33 offices, the binding cost is not throughput  -  it is the number of independent log chains you must prove are healthy.** 34 databases x 96 log backups/day at a 15-minute cadence ~ **3,264 log backups per day, ~98,000 per month**. That is the number that should shape the design: it argues for an object store with lifecycle expiry rather than a directory listing, and for a check that *asserts* per database rather than one a human reads.

**The size driver is audit data, not appointments.** 16 appointments produced ~1,450 audit rows and ~2,689 property-change rows  -  over 100:1  -  and audit retention is unconfigured. **Office database size, backup size, and restore time are therefore all functions of how long you have been logging, and they grow without bound.** Restore time is a *retention* problem. An audit retention/archival policy is a prerequisite for a sane backup architecture, not a follow-up.

*(Tempting escape hatch, and why I will not recommend it: put audit tables in their own filegroup and restore the business filegroup first. The docs are internally inconsistent on whether this works on Standard. In* Restore and Recovery Overview*, one footnote reads "Online restore is supported only in Enterprise edition" while a second footnote against the File/Page/Piecemeal rows reads "Available only in the Enterprise edition of SQL Server." The Editions page lists "Online page and file restore: Enterprise Yes, Standard No"  -  implying offline piecemeal is fine on Standard. Sources disagree; the honest position is that it would have to be tested. Do not build an architecture on an ambiguity when pruning audit data solves the same problem.)*

---

## 5. Restoring to a different name or instance (needed for restore-to-verify)  -  SOURCED

- **Different name:** *Copy Databases with Backup and Restore*: "The database name explicitly supplied when you restore a database is used automatically as the new database name."
- **`WITH MOVE` is mandatory when restoring a copy alongside the original on the same instance:** "It may be necessary to create a copy of an existing database on the same computer for testing purposes. In this case, the database files for the original database already exist, so **different file names must be specified**."
- **Do not use `REPLACE` for a verify restore.** Restoring under a new name makes it unnecessary, and *RESTORE (Transact-SQL)*: "REPLACE should be used rarely and only after careful consideration... The REPLACE option overrides several important safety checks."
- **Ownership changes:** "the SQL Server login or Microsoft Windows user who initiates the restore operation becomes the owner of the new database automatically."
- **Version floor:** "a SQL Server backup cannot be restored to a SQL Server Database Engine version that is older than the version that created the backup." The verify target must be >= production's version  -  a constraint on any future move.
- **Logins/metadata:** "you might have to re-create some or all of the metadata for the database, such as logins and jobs."

### Two system-specific consequences

**(a) The `sa` practice is accidentally why restore-to-another-instance is trivial here  -  and fixing it will make restores harder.** Identity is *inside* each database (ASP.NET Identity tables), and every service connects as `sa`, so today there are no server logins to re-create and no orphaned users. The moment they do the right thing and move to per-database least-privilege logins, the restore runbook must grow a "create login, fix orphaned user" step or every verified restore will come back unusable. Fix `sa`  -  but change the runbook in the same commit.

**(b) Backup encryption is a restore-blocking dependency.** Standard edition supports encrypted backups (Editions page: "Encryption for backups: Standard Yes"). If they adopt it, the certificate must exist on the restoring instance or the backup is unrestorable  -  the same failure class as the OpenIddict signing PFX already identified. Any key protecting a backup must be escrowed separately from the backup and its restorability tested, or backup encryption converts a recoverable incident into an unrecoverable one.

---

## 6. THE HARD PART: what actually goes wrong when you restore one office to time T

The office database is roughly half of an office's state. Restoring it rewinds that half and nothing else. Working through it concretely:

### 6.1 Schema version vs deployed code  -  the first thing that breaks

If any migration ran between T and now, the restored office database is at the **old schema** while the running code expects the new one -> `invalid object name` at runtime for that office. The saving grace of database-per-tenant: **the EF migrations history table travels inside the restored database**, so re-running the migrator brings it forward correctly and idempotently.

But the migrator loops all offices with no per-tenant error handling. **Requirement: a single-tenant migration entry point**, so post-restore remediation touches exactly one office and reports its outcome. Without it, the fix for one office risks the fleet.

### 6.2 Both outboxes rewind  -  and this is the sharpest failure

`AppNotificationOutboxItems` and `AppIntegrationOutboxItems` are **per-office**, i.e. inside the restored database.

- **Email:** items marked *Sent* between T and now revert to *Pending*. The drain job then **re-sends them**. In an ex-parte-safe workflow addressing patients, doctors and attorneys with deliberate CC construction, a restore silently re-mails external parties  -  potentially weeks of correspondence  -  and there is no idempotency key the SMTP relay or the recipients can dedupe on. **A database restore becomes an outbound communication event.**
- **Case Tracker:** the partner is a *separate system on a separate stack that was not rolled back*. Replaying its outbox pushes stale state at a system whose state is ahead. Meanwhile the inbound reconcile token may have been issued after T, so the restored database will not recognise it and inbound reconciliation fails  -  which is at least the safe direction, given both paths fail closed by configuration.

**Requirement:** the restore procedure must **quarantine both outbox drains for that office before recovery completes** (a per-office drain-disabled flag checked by the jobs), then require an explicit human release after reconciliation. And the design requirement behind it: **anything crossing an external boundary must carry an idempotency key the far side can dedupe on**; where it cannot (SMTP), replay must be gated by a human, not by a job.

### 6.3 Hangfire jobs in the host database reference office rows that no longer exist

Queued and scheduled jobs carry appointment identifiers and recipient addresses as arguments. After the restore those targets may be gone. **Requirement: jobs must fail cleanly and loudly on a missing target, never no-op silently**  -  this is the "prefer designs that fail obviously" rule applied where it actually earns its keep. Note also the existing correctness hazard compounds here: ABP falls back to the ambient tenant when a job argument carries none, and the ambient tenant in a worker is null -> the **host** database. A post-restore replay storm is precisely when that lands.

### 6.4 Identity and cache  -  a silent access-control regression

Identity is per-database. A user disabled, deleted, or password-changed after T **comes back**  -  old password hash and all  -  and nobody is notified. Simultaneously, Redis still holds post-T permission grants and dynamic claims, and issued access tokens (15-minute lifetime) plus refresh tokens remain valid.

**Requirement: a per-office restore must invalidate that office's cached permissions/claims and force re-authentication for that office.** This is where a documented caveat becomes load-bearing: typed `IDistributedCache<T>` prefixes tenant-scoped keys with `t:{tenantId},` but **untyped usage does not**. A prefix-scoped flush is therefore *incomplete* today, and the only complete alternative  -  flushing Redis  -  would destroy the DataProtection keyring (`CaseEvaluation-Protection-Keys`), logging out every office and breaking in-flight email-confirmation links across the fleet.

**Capability requirement: all tenant-scoped cache entries must be prefix-flushable per tenant, and the DataProtection keyring must live where a per-tenant flush cannot reach it.** Restorability of one office depends on a cache-key convention. That is not obvious from either end.

### 6.5 Object storage is not transactional with the database  -  both directions

MinIO holds the documents and packets; keys are `tenants/{tenantId:D}/...`.

- **Uploaded after T:** blob exists, row does not -> **orphaned PHI**, invisible to the application, with no owner and no retention handle. That is a disposal problem under HIPAA, not untidiness.
- **Deleted after T:** row returns, blob is gone -> packet assembly breaks. **Requirement: packet assembly must fail closed on a missing blob** and must never emit a packet with a page silently absent  -  a rendered IME packet missing a document is a clinical and legal artefact, and the 2-worker Python renderer is exactly where a silent omission would hide.
- **Partner bucket:** the external partner holds scoped fetch-by-key credentials. Keys handed to them before the restore may become unresolvable, or resolve to content the database no longer considers current.

**The clean design rule, and it is cheap:** enable **bucket versioning with delete markers** and make blob deletion soft/lifecycle-driven, with the non-current-version expiry window **>= the database point-in-time retention window**. MinIO's documentation confirms the mechanics: deleting without a version ID "creates a 0-byte `DeleteMarker` as the latest version," clients "can retrieve any previous version of the object by specifying the version ID, even if the 'Latest' version is a `DeleteMarker`," and versions can be expired by lifecycle rule; note that deleting a *specific version* by ID is permanent. That gives the alignment property: **for any T inside the retention window, every blob the database references at T is still resolvable.** Set this now, while there is no PHI and no volume.

**One thing the current design already gets right:** `tenants/{tenantId:D}/` prefixes make an office's objects a prefix-selectable set, so per-office object export, inventory and reconciliation are all tractable. Preserve that property deliberately.

### 6.6 The audit trail you delete

Restoring an office to T destroys that office's audit records for T->now. In a HIPAA context that is the most consequential side effect, and it is invisible. **Requirement: never restore in place.** Take the tail-log backup, restore *alongside* under a new name, verify, then swap and **retain the superseded database** (renamed, not dropped) plus its tail-log backup, for the full retention period. The pre-restore state is evidence.

---

## 7. Must host and tenant be restorable to a CONSISTENT point together?

**Determinate answer: NO for the common case, YES for the disaster case, and the design must make the common case safe *without* cross-database transactional consistency.**

### Why not, mechanically

SQL Server's only documented mechanism for consistent multi-database point-in-time recovery is **marked transactions** (*Restore databases to marked transaction*), and its own constraints disqualify it here:

- "**You can recover related databases only to a marked transaction, not to a specific point in time.**" Your achievable RPO becomes the *mark interval*, not the log-backup interval.
- Marks must be written into **every** related database, routinely: "If a marked transaction spans multiple databases... the marks must be recorded in the logs of all the affected databases," and "The mark for a specific transaction is inserted into transaction logs only on the server instance where the BEGIN TRAN...WITH MARK statement is executed."
- It costs concurrency: "The stalls generated by marked transactions that span multiple databases can reduce the transaction processing performance of the server," and "We recommend that you do not run concurrent marked transactions."
- "this recovery loses any transaction that is committed after the mark... Marking transactions is suitable only when you are testing related databases or when you are willing to lose recently committed transactions."

At 11 offices that is a coordinated distributed marked transaction across 12 databases on a fixed cadence; at 33, across 34. **I reject it explicitly.** It is standard at larger organisations, it is theoretically the right primitive, and it is wrong here: it adds a distributed-transaction failure mode that two SDE 1s would have to diagnose, it degrades RPO, and it makes ordinary throughput a function of the backup design. It also contradicts the codebase's own verified stance  -  no raw SQL, no cross-database queries, no linked servers.

### What to do instead  -  make cross-database references *reconstructible*, not consistent

1. **Host -> tenant references must be configuration, not data.** The tenant registry is already effectively that: connection strings are *derived* by swapping the database name, and provisioning is idempotent. So a host/office disagreement is repairable by re-running provisioning. **Protect this property**; it is the reason independent restore is viable at all.
2. **Tenant -> host references must be replay-tolerant.** Hangfire jobs must fail cleanly when their target row is absent.
3. **External-boundary effects must be idempotency-keyed, or human-gated.** (6.2.)
4. **Whole-instance disaster is the case where a common point matters**  -  and there the answer is not marks, it is: restore host and all offices to the *same wall-clock* `STOPAT` from independent chains, accept that a few cross-database operations straddle the boundary, and reconcile using the outbox ledgers, which is exactly what durable outboxes are for. Approximate consistency plus a reconciliation pass beats exact consistency plus a distributed-transaction dependency, for this team.

---

## 8. CAPABILITY REQUIREMENTS (platform-neutral)

| # | Requirement | Why |
|---|---|---|
| R1 | **Restore granularity = one tenant database**, without taking other tenants offline | Documented behaviour of SQL Server restore; it is the payoff of database-per-tenant and must not be traded away |
| R2 | **Point-in-time capability on every database, host included**, <=15-minute RPO | FULL recovery + log chain; matches the 15-minute rhythm the recurring jobs already impose |
| R3 | **PITR capability must be established at provisioning time and asserted continuously** | Offices are created by a business action; `model` decides the recovery model; the chain does not start until the first data backup |
| R4 | **Backups must land in a different failure domain from the data disk**, written by a principal that cannot delete them | Today `./backups` shares the disk it protects; immutability/versioning defends against a bad script and against ransomware |
| R5 | **Host and tenant need NOT be transactionally consistent  -  but cross-database state must be reconstructible**, and every external-boundary effect must be idempotency-keyed or human-gated | 7; marked transactions rejected |
| R6 | **Object storage must support versioning with delete markers, with non-current retention >= the database PITR window**, and blob deletion must be soft | Blobs are not transactional with the database; this is what makes a restored database's references resolvable |
| R7 | **Background-job storage must be restorable or discardable independently of the tenant registry** | Hangfire in the host database couples opposite recovery semantics |
| R8 | **Per-tenant cache invalidation must be possible without destroying the DataProtection keyring** | A restore must revoke stale grants for one office without logging out the fleet |
| R9 | **Verification at two levels**: cheap continuous (`CHECKSUM` + `VERIFYONLY`) and periodic real (restore + `DBCC CHECKDB` on the copy) | `RESTORE VERIFYONLY` "does not attempt to verify the structure of the data contained in the backup volumes"  -  it is necessary, not sufficient |
| R10 | **Rehearsal must be a scheduled obligation with an owner and a recorded time-to-restore** | HIPAA 164.308(a)(7)(ii)(D); and an unrehearsed restore procedure is an unverified assumption |
| R11 | **Verification restores need somewhere to land that is not the production data disk** | ~9.7 GB free; free disk, not SQL capability, is what blocks restore-to-verify today |
| R12 | **Backup monitoring must fail loudly and include a dead-man's switch** | This team will not notice slow degradation; a check that stops running must alarm as loudly as a check that fails |
| R13 | **Audit retention/archival policy is a prerequisite** | 100:1 audit-to-business ratio, unpruned, makes backup size and restore time grow without bound |
| R14 | **Any key or certificate protecting a backup must be escrowed separately and its restorability tested** | Encryption without escrow converts a recoverable incident into an unrecoverable one |

### Regulatory anchor (SOURCED, and stated carefully)

45 CFR 164.308(a)(7): contingency plan. **(A) Data backup plan  -  Required:** "Establish and implement procedures to create and maintain retrievable exact copies of electronic protected health information." **(B) Disaster recovery plan  -  Required:** "Establish (and implement as needed) procedures to restore any loss of data." **(C) Emergency mode operation plan  -  Required.** **(D) Testing and revision procedures  -  Addressable.** **(E) Applications and data criticality analysis  -  Addressable.**

Two honest notes:
- The word "**retrievable**" in (A) is doing work: a backup that has never been restored is not demonstrably retrievable. And (D) being *Addressable* rather than *Required* does not mean optional under the Security Rule's flexibility provisions  -  it means implement it, or document why not and implement an equivalent. *(That characterisation reflects 164.306(d), which I did not separately fetch  -  treat the mechanism as unverified; the Required/Addressable labels themselves are verified.)*
- **A correction to the brief's framing:** 45 CFR 164.316(b)(2)(i) reads "Retain the documentation required by paragraph (b)(1) of this section for 6 years from the date of its creation or the date when it last was in effect, whichever is later." That is a **documentation** retention requirement  -  policies, procedures, and records the Security Rule requires in writing  -  **not a six-year retention mandate for PHI or for audit rows**. Medical-record retention for California workers' compensation is a separate, state-law question I did not research. This matters commercially: **do not size the backup architecture against a six-year obligation derived from 164.316(b)(2)(i)**, and above all **do not attempt to satisfy any long-term retention obligation by hoarding six years of `.bak` files**  -  with audit data at 100:1 that is the expensive mistake. Retention belongs in the data model, not the backup set.
- Directional note: HHS published an NPRM on 2025-01-06, "HIPAA Security Rule to Strengthen the Cybersecurity of Electronic Protected Health Information," still at proposed-rule stage as of the HHS Security Rule page. Do not design to it; do note that the trend is toward *mandatory* testing.
